body_md: Have the client write the specific prediction and a confidence rating before the event, then the actual outcome afterward, without editing the earlier entry. Tally the week's accuracy rate together rather than letting a single lucky guess stand for the pattern. Most clients are startled by how the total lands; let the total speak instead of pointing it out.

fields.label: Situation I am worried about
My predicted outcome
My confidence in that prediction, zero to ten
What actually happened
How accurate my prediction turned out to be

title: Worry Backpack Unpacking Practice
summary: A metaphor exercise for noticing how much a client is carrying versus how much is actually happening now.
goal: Use it to build a physical sense of setting worry down rather than carrying it everywhere.
body_md: Ask the client to literally hold a heavy bag while describing their week, then set it down and describe the same week again. The exercise makes the weight of anticipatory worry tangible rather than abstract. Practice a short, repeatable gesture, like setting a hand down flat, that the client can use outside session to signal setting the backpack down for now.

fields.label: What is in my worry backpack this week
How the week sounded while holding the bag
How the week sounded after setting it down
My gesture for setting the backpack down

title: Anxiety Interrupt and Redirect Card
summary: A short DBT skills card pairing a quick interrupt action with a redirect toward something values-driven.
goal: Use it to give a client a two-step move for the moment anxiety spikes mid-task.
body_md: Pick one fast interrupt, cold water, a hard exhale, standing up, and pair it with one specific redirect back to the task at hand rather than a full escape. Practice the pairing in session until it feels automatic rather than something to remember under pressure. Track over the week whether the pair actually gets used and adjust either half if it does not.

fields.label: My interrupt action
My redirect action
A moment this week I tried the pair
How it went

title: Worry Monster Feeding Chart
summary: A child decides which worries to feed with attention and which to let their Worry Monster go hungry on.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful, concrete way to choose which worries get their attention.
body_md: The parent helps the child draw or name their Worry Monster and sort recent worries into feed now, in the worry box, or throw away. Keep the sorting language playful and let the child make the final call on each worry rather than the parent deciding for them. Revisit the chart weekly and notice which worries the child stops feeding on their own.

fields.label: A worry I am feeding right now
A worry going in my worry box for later
A worry I am throwing away
What my Worry Monster looks like

title: Anxiety Facts Relay Game
summary: Teams race to sort true statements about how anxiety works from common myths, then discuss the misses.
goal: Use it to correct unhelpful beliefs about anxiety through a low-stakes group format.
body_md: Prepare a set of true and myth cards about how anxiety behaves in the body and mind, and have teams sort them quickly before checking answers together. The misses are the most useful part; slow down there rather than moving on fast. Close by asking what surprised the group most and how that changes how they think about their own anxiety.

fields.label: A myth I believed before this game
A fact that surprised me
How this changes what I do when anxiety shows up

title: Micro-Momentum Activity Log
summary: Logs the smallest possible version of an activity a client can complete on a low-energy day.
goal: Use it to keep behavioral activation going on the days full activities feel impossible.
body_md: Scale each planned activity down to a version so small it feels almost silly, one page instead of a chapter, one dish instead of the whole kitchen. Log mood before and after even the tiny version. The point is proving to the client's own nervous system that action is still possible, not producing an impressive amount of output.

fields.label: The activity I scaled down
The tiny version I actually did
Mood before, zero to ten
Mood after, zero to ten
What I noticed

title: Values Anchor for Low-Energy Days
summary: Picks one small values-aligned action a client can do even on the hardest, lowest-energy days.
goal: Use it to keep one thread of meaning intact when most of the day's plans fall away.
body_md: Ask what matters to the client even when energy is at its lowest, then find one action so small it survives a bad day, texting one person, watering one plant, stepping outside for a minute. Hold this separate from the client's full activity plan as a floor, not a replacement. Review which low-energy actions actually got used and keep only those.

fields.label: What still matters to me even on a hard day
The smallest action that honors it
A day this week I used my low-energy action
How it felt to do even that much

title: Withdrawal Warning Signs Worksheet
summary: Catalogs a client's early signs of pulling away from people and routines before a full withdrawal sets in.
goal: Use it to catch withdrawal early, while a small nudge back still works.
body_md: Ask the client to think back to the start of a past low period and name what changed first, canceled plans, unanswered texts, skipped meals, rather than what changed last. Agree together on one early sign to watch for and one small counter-action tied to it. Revisit the list after any low stretch and add whatever the client notices in hindsight.

title: Opposite Action for Withdrawal Card
summary: A DBT skills card for acting opposite to the urge to withdraw, in small, planned amounts.
goal: Use it to practice moving toward contact even when everything points toward pulling away.
body_md: Name the urge honestly, cancel the plan, do not answer, stay in bed, and pick one small opposite action that still fits inside what the client can manage today. Full opposite action is not the goal on a first try; a five-minute version counts. Log which opposite actions actually got tried and how mood moved afterward.

title: Supporting Low Mood Without Fixing Script
summary: A short script for a partner to offer presence during a low-mood stretch without trying to fix it.
goal: Use it to give both partners a shared plan for the hard weeks, not just the good ones.
body_md: Ask the client with low mood what actually helps, being asked how they are, being left alone, having a task taken off their plate, and have the partner practice offering exactly that instead of guessing. Name together what unhelpful support tends to look like for this couple specifically. Revisit the script after a real low-mood week and adjust it based on what worked.

fields.label: What actually helps me on a low-mood day

title: Energy Mapping by Hour Worksheet

goal: Use it to schedule demanding tasks into the hours where focus is actually available.
body_md: Have the client rate focus and energy every couple of hours for several days, without trying to fix the pattern while logging it. title: External Memory System Audit
summary: Reviews where a client currently tries to hold information in their head versus writing it down.
goal: Use it to shift reliance from working memory onto a system the client trusts.

A system only works if the client will actually open it, so favor the boring, low-friction option over the elegant one. Agree on a single place for one category of information and test it for a week before adding more.

title: Body Double Buddy Craft
summary: A child makes a small figure or drawing of a body double buddy who sits with them during homework.
goal: Use it to give a child a comforting visual cue for working alongside someone, even in imagination.

Place the buddy at the workspace during homework or chores as a visual anchor. Pair it with real body doubling from a parent or sibling when possible, since the craft supports the habit rather than replacing another person.

title: Beat the Clutter Timer Game

goal: Use it to make a tedious task feel like a game with a clear, short endpoint.
body_md: Set a short timer, five or ten minutes, for one specific small area rather than an entire room, and celebrate what got done when time is up rather than what did not. Some clients do best racing against their own last time; others do better with a partner. Repeat in short bursts with breaks rather than one long push.

title: Present-Task Return Practice
summary: Practices noticing when attention has drifted and gently returning to the task at hand, without self-blame.
goal: Use it to build the skill of returning to task as a repeated practice, not a one-time fix.
body_md: Have the client work on a real task while noting each time attention wanders and simply marking a tally rather than judging the drift. The tally is not a score to minimize; a high count just means more practice returning. Emphasize the return itself as the skill being built, since attention will keep wandering no matter how this goes.

goal: Use it to build evidence that urges pass in minutes rather than the hours they can feel like.
body_md: Have the client rate the urge every five minutes during an episode rather than only at the start and end, since the shape of the curve is the useful part. Most urges peak and fall within fifteen to twenty minutes if nothing feeds them. Compare the client's prediction of how long it would last against the actual tracked curve.

title: Values Beyond the Next Use Practice
summary: Connects a client's reasons for changing their substance use to concrete values rather than rules alone.
goal: Use it to anchor change work in what the client actually wants their life to hold.
body_md: Ask what substance use has cost the client in terms of what actually matters to them, not just in problems it has caused. Build a short values statement the client can return to when willpower alone is not enough. This sits alongside a change plan rather than replacing the practical steps a client also needs.

title: Riding the Urge Skills Card
summary: A short DBT card for tolerating an urge to use without acting on it or fighting it away.
goal: Use it to practice staying present with an urge long enough for it to pass on its own.
body_md: Teach the client to notice the urge without immediately either giving in or white-knuckling against it, describing it out loud instead: where it is, what it feels like, how it changes. Pair it with one grounding action the client can do while riding the urge out. Practice with a mild version of the urge in session before relying on it during a real high-risk moment.

summary: Explores who a client wants to be day to day, separate from a substance-focused daily rhythm.
goal: Use it to build a picture of a life worth having, not just a list of things to avoid.
body_md: Ask what a typical day looks like now around substance use, and then ask the client to describe a typical day in the life they are building instead, in as much concrete detail as they can manage. Avoid making this a punishment list of what to give up; keep it forward-looking. Return to the description regularly as a north star rather than a one-time exercise.

title: Support Versus Enabling Map
summary: Helps a couple map the line between supporting recovery and covering for continued substance use.
goal: Use it to give both partners a shared, specific picture of what support looks like here.
body_md: Have each partner list, separately at first, what they consider supportive versus what crosses into covering up or managing the other's substance use, then compare lists together. Disagreement here is common and worth slowing down on rather than resolving quickly. Agree on two or three concrete lines the non-using partner will hold, and revisit the map as recovery progresses.

title: Anger Escalation Ladder Worksheet
summary: Maps a client's own anger from a one to a ten, naming what each rung actually looks and feels like.
goal: Use it to build a personal early-warning system before anger reaches the top of the ladder.
body_md: Ask for the client's own words at each rung rather than generic descriptions, since annoyed and furious feel different in every body. Mark the rung where a cooling skill still works versus the rung past which it usually does not. Use the ladder together to plan an exit or pause before the client reaches their point of no return.

fields.label: What a level 2 looks like for me

title: Fair Fight Rules Reality Check
summary: Compares a client's actual conflict behavior against a short set of self-chosen ground rules for arguing fair.
goal: Use it to catch the gap between the rules a client believes in and what happens under pressure.
body_md: Have the client write their own rules for fighting fair before reviewing a recent conflict against them, so the standard is theirs, not imposed. Be specific about which rule broke first and what was happening in the client's body right before it did. Use the pattern to plan one rule to protect first next time, rather than trying to fix all of them at once.

fields.label: My rules for fighting fair, in my own words

title: Slow Burn Cooling Card
summary: A skills card for anger that builds slowly over a day rather than spiking suddenly.
goal: Use it to catch and cool a slow-building irritation before it reaches a flashpoint.
body_md: Ask the client to notice the small irritations that stack across a day rather than waiting for the final trigger that gets blamed. List one cooling action for the middle of the day and one for the end, since a slow burn needs interruption earlier than a sudden spike does. Track which point in the day the stacking usually starts.

fields.label: What tends to stack up across my day

title: Anger Weather Forecast Craft
summary: A child makes a weather forecast board that shows their anger as sunny, cloudy, stormy or clear again.
goal: Use it to give a child and parent a shared, simple language for talking about building anger.
body_md: The parent helps build the forecast board and agrees with the child on what each weather symbol means for their own anger, sunny for calm, stormy for a meltdown. Practice checking the day's forecast together at a few set times rather than only during a blow-up. The goal is a shared word the family can use in the moment, not a permanent record.

fields.label: What sunny anger looks like for me

title: Cool Head Trivia Relay
summary: Teams answer quick trivia questions about what happens in the body during anger, racing for points.
goal: Use it to teach the biology of anger in a format a group actually wants to play.
body_md: Prepare short trivia questions about what heart rate, breathing and muscles do during anger, and let teams race to answer before a timer runs out. Correct wrong answers with the real explanation rather than just the right choice, since the explanation is what sticks. Close by asking how knowing the biology changes what the group tries the next time anger builds.

fields.label: A fact about anger and the body I learned today

title: Certainty Demand Audit
summary: Lists the specific certainties a client's mind keeps demanding before it will let a worry rest.
goal: Use it to make the impossible standard behind compulsions visible and questionable.
body_md: Ask the client what percentage of certainty would actually be enough to stop checking or seeking reassurance, and notice when the honest answer is one hundred. Point out, without arguing, that no one operates at that standard anywhere else in life. Use the gap to open a conversation about tolerating a lower, ordinary level of certainty.

title: Sitting With the Itch Practice
summary: Practices noticing the urge to complete a compulsion as a passing sensation rather than an instruction.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for the urge itself, separate from acting on it.
body_md: Ask the client to describe the urge to complete a compulsion the way they would describe an itch, where it is, how strong, whether it changes if they do not scratch it. Track how the urge moves over a few minutes without engaging the compulsion. This builds a felt sense that the urge itself is bearable, not just an intellectual fact.

fields.label: The urge and what it wants me to do

title: Response Delay Ladder Card
summary: A skills card for building delay time between an obsessive thought and a compulsive response, in small steps.
goal: Use it to grow the gap between urge and response gradually rather than all at once.
body_md: Start from whatever delay is currently realistic, even thirty seconds, and add time only once the current step feels manageable. Pair the delay with a specific skill to use during the wait, breathing, describing the urge, rather than leaving the client to just wait it out unaided. Celebrate the delay itself, whether or not the compulsion eventually happens.

fields.label: The compulsion I am working on delaying

summary: A child decides which what-ifs to feed with checking and which to let their Uncertainty Monster go hungry on.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful way to notice and resist feeding compulsive checking.
body_md: The parent helps the child name and draw their Uncertainty Monster and sort recent what-if worries into feed or starve, with the child making the final call each time. Praise not feeding the monster as the brave choice, even when checking would have felt easier. If a child discloses anything during this activity that raises safety concerns, stop the activity and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: A what-if I am not feeding today

title: Mental Ritual Spotting Worksheet
summary: Helps a client identify rituals that happen entirely in their head, which are easy to miss on a checklist.
goal: Use it to bring invisible mental compulsions into view alongside the visible ones.
body_md: Ask directly about counting, silent praying, mental reviewing or replaying, and repeating phrases internally, since these rarely get reported unless asked about by name. List what each mental ritual is meant to prevent or undo. Once spotted, mental rituals can be worked with the same delay and response-prevention approach as visible ones.

goal: Use it to separate the sensation itself from the alarming meaning attached to it.
body_md: List each sensation, racing heart, tight chest, dizziness, specifically, then write the alarming interpretation next to it and a more accurate, harmless explanation beside that. Bring in a medical clearance already on file rather than reopening that question here. Use the finished inventory as a reference the client can reread when a sensation starts to spiral.

goal: Use it to reclaim activity and place from the fear of where an attack might strike.

Choose one low-avoidance item to reintroduce this week with a concrete plan for support if an attack occurs. The goal is a life that is not shaped around avoiding panic, not the elimination of panic itself.

goal: Use it to replace guessing with a calm, practiced response in the moment.
body_md: Ask the client having panic attacks what actually helps versus what makes things worse, being talked through breathing, being left quiet, being reminded this will pass, and have the partner rehearse exactly those words. Agree on what the partner should avoid, such as rushing to call for help unless there is a real medical concern. Revisit the script after it has been used for real and refine it.

goal: Use it to teach a calming skill a scared or panicky child can use anywhere.

Count breaths together on the chart rather than asking the child to count alone at first. Practice when calm so the skill is familiar before it is needed during a scared moment.

goal: Use it to build the habit of connecting with a child before correcting their behavior.
body_md: The parent adds a sticker each time they pause to connect, a moment of eye contact, a calm tone, a named feeling, before giving a correction or consequence. The chart tracks the parent's practice, not the child's behavior, which keeps the focus where change is actually needed first. Review the week together and notice whether corrections landed differently on the days connection came first.

goal: Use it to build small pockets of presence inside an otherwise overwhelming stretch.

title: Would You Rather: Small Talk Edition

goal: Use it to practice speaking in a group on questions with no wrong answer.
body_md: Use questions with genuinely no wrong answer, since the low stakes are the point, and let players pass to a neutral corner of the room if they cannot decide. Keep the pace quick so no one has time to overthink their turn. Debrief briefly on what it felt like to speak up in front of the group, since that is the actual skill being practiced.

fields.label: A question I answered
My answer
How it felt to speak up in front of the group
What got easier as the game went on

title: Friend-Making Script Cards
summary: A child practices short, specific scripts for starting play with another child, using illustrated cue cards.
goal: Use it to give a socially anxious child rehearsed, concrete words for approaching another kid.
body_md: The parent and child practice each script out loud, taking turns playing both roles, before the child tries it for real. Keep the scripts short and simple, one clear sentence a child can actually remember under nerves. Celebrate the attempt itself in the debrief afterward, whatever the other child's response turned out to be.

fields.label: My script for asking to join a game
My script for asking someone's name
How my practice attempt went this week
What I want to try next time

title: What I Still Do Because of You List
summary: Lists the habits, phrases and choices a client carries forward that came from the person who died.
goal: Use it to make an ongoing bond visible rather than treating grief as something to move past entirely.
body_md: List habits and phrases that clearly trace back to the person, a recipe, a saying, a way of greeting people, and let the client notice how much of that person is still present in daily life. This supports a continuing bond rather than a clean break, which fits how most people actually experience loss over time. Revisit the list as new entries occur to the client between sessions.

fields.label: A habit I carry that came from them
A phrase or saying of theirs I still use
A choice I make differently because of them
One more I want to add later

title: Carrying It Forward Values Practice
summary: Identifies a value the person who died embodied, and one way the client can carry that value forward.
goal: Use it to give grief a forward-facing thread alongside the pain of the loss.
body_md: Ask what the person valued or stood for, in the client's own words, and explore one small, concrete way to live that value out this week. This is not about replacing the person or rushing past grief, only about finding one place grief and living forward can coexist. Return to it periodically rather than treating it as a single exercise.

fields.label: A value this person embodied
How I want to carry that value forward
One small way I can live it out this week
How it feels to think about carrying this forward

title: Remembering Together Craft
summary: A child makes a small craft, a drawing or collage, showing a favorite memory of someone who died.
goal: Use it to give a grieving child a concrete way to hold and share a memory.
body_md: The parent sits with the child while they choose and create the memory, asking open questions rather than steering toward a particular emotion. Some children will want to talk while making it, others will work quietly, and both are fine. Keep the finished piece somewhere the child can revisit it, and let them decide whether to share it with others.

fields.label: The memory I chose
What I made to show it
How I feel when I think about this memory
Who I want to show it to, if anyone

title: Grieving on Different Timelines Conversation
summary: Helps a couple name and accept that each partner may be grieving the same loss on a different timeline.
goal: Use it to reduce conflict that comes from expecting a partner's grief to match one's own.
body_md: Have each partner describe where they currently are in their own grief, without comparing it to the other's pace, since grief timelines rarely match even within the same loss. Ask what each partner needs from the other right now, which may be very different needs. Agree on one way to check in with each other going forward without either partner having to perform grief on a schedule.

fields.label: Where I am in my grief right now
Where I sense my partner is in theirs
What I need from my partner right now
How we will check in with each other going forward

title: Unmet Need Behind the Complaint Sheet
summary: Traces a recurring complaint back to the specific, unmet need underneath it, for both partners.
goal: Use it to move a couple from surface complaints to the needs actually driving them.
body_md: Ask each partner to state a recurring complaint, then keep asking what need is not being met underneath it until something concrete emerges, being seen, feeling like a priority, having space. Complaints stated as needs are far easier for a partner to actually respond to than complaints stated as criticism. Practice restating one complaint as a need out loud before the session ends.

fields.label: My recurring complaint
The need underneath it
My partner's recurring complaint
The need underneath theirs
How I will restate my complaint as a need

title: Letting Go of Being Right Practice
summary: Practices noticing the urge to win an argument and choosing connection instead, as a values-based act.
goal: Use it to build willingness to prioritize the relationship over being proven correct.
body_md: Ask the client to recall a recent argument and rate how much energy went into being right versus staying connected. Explore what being right actually costs when it comes at connection's expense, and what the client values more in the relationship overall. This is not about giving up valid points, only about noticing the choice being made in the moment.

fields.label: A recent argument where being right mattered a lot to me
What being right cost me in that moment
What I value more than winning that argument
What choosing connection would have looked like instead

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Priority Check
summary: Weighs whether a relationship goal, an objective, the relationship or self-respect, matters most in a given conflict.
goal: Use it to choose a communication strategy that matches what actually matters most right now.
body_md: Walk through the situation and ask which priority matters most this time, getting the specific outcome, protecting the relationship, or keeping self-respect intact, since the right approach shifts depending on the answer. A client who always defaults to one priority regardless of the situation is worth naming that pattern to. Use the answer to choose which skills to lean on for this particular conversation.

fields.label: The situation
My objective, if I have one
What matters most this time: outcome, relationship, or self-respect
What approach fits that priority

title: Mind-Reading Interrupt Sheet
summary: Catches a client's assumptions about a partner's thoughts or motives and checks them against what was actually said.
goal: Use it to replace assumed motives with information actually gathered from the partner.
body_md: Write down the assumption about the partner's thinking exactly as it occurred, then write what the partner actually said or did, separate from the interpretation layered on top. Most assumptions turn out to be untested guesses dressed up as facts. Practice one question the client could ask instead of assuming, and use it before the next conversation.

fields.label: What I assumed my partner was thinking
What my partner actually said or did
The gap between the two
A question I could ask instead of assuming

title: Relationship Non-Negotiables Worksheet
summary: Separates a client's true non-negotiables in a relationship from preferences they can flex on.
goal: Use it to clarify what actually needs to hold firm versus what is open to compromise.
body_md: List everything currently causing friction, then sort each item into a true non-negotiable or a preference that could flex, and push back gently on anything labeled non-negotiable without a clear reason why. A list where everything is non-negotiable usually needs more sorting, not validation. Use the finished list to decide where energy for negotiation is actually worth spending.

fields.label: Something currently causing friction
Is it a true non-negotiable or a flexible preference?
Why it belongs in that category
One item I am willing to negotiate on

title: Body Ownership Affirmation Sheet
summary: Builds a short list of present-day statements affirming a client's ownership and authority over their own body.
goal: Use it to reinforce bodily autonomy in the present, without revisiting what happened.
body_md: Write the statements in the client's own words and voice, keeping them about today and going forward rather than about the past. Practice reading them aloud in session, since saying them out loud often lands differently than reading silently. This is a present-focused affirmation tool, not an invitation to describe any past event.

fields.label: A statement about my right to say no
A statement about who gets to touch my body
A statement about trusting my own signals
Where I will keep these statements

title: Self-Blame Interrupt Sheet
summary: Interrupts a self-blaming thought by comparing it against what a survivor is actually responsible for.
goal: Use it to redirect responsibility for what happened away from the client and toward the person who harmed them.
body_md: Write the self-blaming thought exactly as it occurs, then list, plainly, who holds responsibility for causing harm versus who does not. Keep this grounded in the present, working with the belief itself rather than asking the client to recount events. A thought that shifts even slightly toward accurate responsibility is real progress, not a fixed outcome to reach in one sitting.

fields.label: The self-blaming thought
Who actually holds responsibility for causing harm
What I am not responsible for
A more accurate thought I am willing to try on

title: Choosing Safety Now Practice
summary: Practices making one small, values-based choice about safety and boundaries in the client's life today.
goal: Use it to build a felt sense of agency and choice in the present.
body_md: Ask about a current, everyday situation where the client can exercise choice around safety or boundaries, and rehearse making that choice in session. This stays entirely about the present and future; it is not a space for describing what happened before. Repeat with new, small choices over time to build the practiced experience of agency.

fields.label: A present-day situation where I can choose safety
The choice I am making
How it feels to make this choice on purpose
Another small choice I want to practice next

title: Grounding Menu for Hard Moments
summary: Builds a personalized menu of grounding skills a client can turn to when flooded or dissociating.
goal: Use it to have a ready set of grounding options rather than searching for one under stress.
body_md: Build the menu with a range of options, quick and slow, so the client has something for a two-minute break and something for a longer reset. Test each one in session while regulated, since a skill practiced calm works better under real stress. Keep the tool focused on present-moment grounding rather than processing content.

fields.label: A quick grounding option, under two minutes
A longer grounding option
A grounding option I can use around other people
Which one I want to try first this week

title: Partner Pace and Consent Check-In Script
summary: A short, repeatable script for a couple to check pace and consent around physical closeness.
goal: Use it to give both partners a low-pressure, ongoing way to check in about pace.
body_md: Build a plain, specific check-in phrase either partner can use at any point, and agree in advance that using it is always honored without question or negotiation in the moment. Practice saying the phrase out loud together so it feels familiar rather than awkward when it is actually needed. Revisit the script periodically as comfort and pace shift over time.

fields.label: Our check-in phrase
What happens when either of us uses it
How we will practice this before we need it
One thing we agree never happens without a clear yes

title: Five-Minute Reset Menu Card
summary: A quick-reference card of coping options a client can complete in five minutes or less.
goal: Use it to have a low-barrier option ready for moments with little time or energy.
body_md: Fill the card with options that genuinely take five minutes or less and require no special equipment, since a coping plan that needs too much setup will not get used in a rushed moment. Test each one for real before finalizing the card. Keep the card somewhere it will actually be seen, a phone lock screen or a wallet, rather than filed away.

fields.label: A reset I can do in under a minute
A reset I can do in two to five minutes
Where I will keep this card
One I tested this week and how it went

title: Coping Versus Avoiding Sort
summary: Sorts a client's go-to strategies into ones that help them face life and ones that mainly help them dodge it.
goal: Use it to tell the difference between a coping skill and an avoidance strategy wearing its clothes.
body_md: List current go-to strategies honestly, including the ones the client is not proud of, and sort each by whether it moves them toward their life or mainly away from a feeling. Some strategies belong in both columns depending on how they are used, which is itself worth discussing. The goal is not to eliminate every avoidance strategy, only to see clearly which is which.

fields.label: A strategy I use often
Does it move me toward my life or away from a feeling?
Another strategy
Does it move me toward my life or away from a feeling?
One strategy I want to use more of

title: Coping Skills Pictionary Round
summary: Players draw a coping skill without words or numbers while the group guesses what it is.
goal: Use it to build familiarity with a wide range of coping skills through active recall.
body_md: Prepare a deck of specific coping skills and let players draw quietly while the group calls out guesses. A skill that is hard to draw is often a good prompt for discussion about how it actually works, not just what it looks like. Close by asking which drawn skill the group wants to try together before the session ends.

fields.label: A coping skill I drew or guessed
How I would actually use this skill
One skill from the game I want to try this week

title: Coping Tree Craft
summary: A child builds a paper tree where each leaf names one thing that helps them feel better.
goal: Use it to give a child a growing, visible collection of their own coping skills.
duration: 20 minutes to start, ongoing to grow
body_md: The parent helps the child add a new leaf whenever they discover something that helps, so the tree grows over weeks rather than being finished in one sitting. Keep leaves specific, a song, a hug, a certain blanket, rather than vague. Hang the tree somewhere the child can point to a leaf when they need an idea in the moment.

fields.label: A leaf for something that calms me down
A leaf for something that makes me feel brave
A leaf for someone who helps me feel better
The next leaf I want to add

title: Coping Skill Access Cost Worksheet
summary: Rates each of a client's coping skills by how easy it actually is to access in the moment it is needed.
goal: Use it to favor coping skills that are realistically available over ones that only work in theory.
body_md: List current coping skills and rate each on how much setup, privacy or equipment it actually requires, since a skill that needs all three is unlikely to get used during a rough morning at work. Sort the list by access cost from lowest to highest. Build a short list of the lowest-cost options to lean on when time and privacy are limited.

fields.label: A coping skill I use
What it requires to access (time, privacy, equipment)
How realistic that is on a hard day
My three lowest-cost, most realistic options

title: Feared Outcome Reality Check Log
summary: Logs a client's predicted feared outcome against the far more mundane thing that usually actually happens.
goal: Use it to build evidence, over time, that the feared object rarely delivers the predicted catastrophe.
body_md: Before each exposure or encounter, write the specific feared outcome and a confidence rating, then log the actual outcome immediately after. Resist smoothing over a close call; log it exactly as it happened. Tally the pattern together at the end of the week rather than letting any single dramatic entry dominate the conversation.

fields.label: The feared object or situation
My predicted outcome
My confidence in that prediction, zero to ten
What actually happened
How accurate my prediction turned out to be

title: Approach With Willingness Practice
summary: Practices approaching a feared object or situation while making room for fear rather than waiting for it to go away first.
goal: Use it to decouple taking an approach step from needing fear to be absent first.
body_md: Rate willingness to approach separately from fear level before and after a step, and point out when willingness rose even though fear did not fall, since that gap is the actual skill being built. Choose an approach step collaboratively rather than assigning one, so the client has genuine ownership of the pace. Avoid promising the fear will disappear; promise only that it does not have to be gone to take the step.

fields.label: The step I am willing to try
My fear level before, zero to ten
My willingness level before, zero to ten
My fear level after
My willingness level after

title: Fear Sensation Tolerance Card
summary: A skills card for tolerating the physical sensations of fear during an approach step without escaping early.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for fear's physical sensations long enough to stay in the situation.
body_md: Name the specific body sensations that show up, racing heart, sweating, shaking, and pick one grounding action to pair with staying rather than leaving. Practice describing the sensations out loud during a mild version of the fear before relying on the skill for a bigger step. Track how long the sensations actually lasted against how long the client expected them to.

fields.label: The sensations I notice
My grounding action for staying
How long the sensations actually lasted
How that compares to what I expected

title: Brave Steps Sticker Trail Craft
summary: A child builds a paper trail of stickers, each one marking a small brave step toward a feared thing.
goal: Use it to make a step-by-step approach to a fear visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to build, ongoing to fill
body_md: The parent and child plan the steps together first, from easiest to hardest, before adding any stickers, so the trail matches a real, workable plan rather than being decorated after the fact. Celebrate each step as it happens rather than only the final one. Let the child set the pace for how many stickers get added in a week.

fields.label: My first small step
My next step
My biggest step, saved for later
How I felt after my last sticker

title: Fear Ladder Board Race
summary: Players move a token up a shared game board by naming and normalizing common fears along the way.
goal: Use it to normalize having fears through a light, shared group format.
body_md: Players land on spaces naming common fears and share, briefly, whether they relate, with passing always allowed. The game works because it makes having a fear ordinary rather than something to hide, especially in a group setting. Close by asking whether hearing other people's fears changed how big anyone's own fear felt.

fields.label: A fear I shared during the game
A fear someone else shared that I related to
Whether the game changed how big my fear feels

title: Appearance-Focused Time Audit
summary: Logs how much time in a day goes toward appearance-checking behaviors, compared to what the client would choose.
goal: Use it to make the time cost of appearance-checking visible and open to change.
body_md: Have the client log each appearance-checking moment, mirrors, reflections, photos, without judgment attached to the entry itself. Total the week's time and compare it to how the client would rather have spent those minutes. The goal is informed choice, not shame about the current pattern, so keep the tone factual throughout.

fields.label: An appearance-checking moment today
Roughly how long it took
What I would rather have been doing
This week's rough total

title: Body as Home, Not Ornament Practice
summary: Shifts attention from how the body looks to what it lets the client do, feel and experience each day.
goal: Use it to build a functional, lived relationship with the body alongside the appearance-focused one.
body_md: Ask what the body allowed the client to do today, carry something, laugh, hug someone, walk somewhere, separate entirely from how it looked while doing it. Some clients find this hard at first; a single functional moment is enough to start. Practice noticing function throughout an ordinary day, not only during the exercise itself.

fields.label: Something my body let me do today
Something my body let me feel today
A moment my body carried me through something hard
What I want to notice more of this week

title: Media Message Awareness Worksheet
summary: Tracks the appearance messages a client absorbs from media in a day and how each one lands afterward.
goal: Use it to build awareness of appearance messaging the client is exposed to and its actual effect.
body_md: Log a few examples of appearance-related media encountered in a day, an ad, a post, a show, and rate mood immediately after seeing each one. Patterns often emerge quickly between certain kinds of content and a mood dip. Use the pattern to make one deliberate choice about media use this week, rather than a blanket rule.

fields.label: A piece of media I encountered
The appearance message it sent
How I felt right after seeing it
One choice I want to make about my media use this week

title: Supporting Without Commenting Script
summary: Helps a partner learn to support a client through body image struggles without commenting on appearance at all.
goal: Use it to give a partner a way to be supportive that does not rely on appearance-based reassurance.
body_md: Ask the client what kind of support actually helps, being asked how they are feeling, a distraction, a hand held, rather than comments about how they look, which can backfire even when meant kindly. Have the partner practice offering exactly that instead. Agree on a signal the client can use when appearance comments, even well-meant ones, are not landing well.

fields.label: What actually helps me on a hard body image day
What does not help, even if well-meant
What my partner will say or do instead
A signal I can use if a comment does not land well

title: Nonjudgmental Body Noticing Card
summary: Practices describing body sensations and appearance thoughts factually, without the usual judgment attached.
goal: Use it to build the skill of observing the body without the automatic evaluative commentary.
body_md: Practice describing what is noticed in purely factual terms, this is my hand, it is resting on the table, rather than good or bad, and catch judgmental words as they show up, swapping them for neutral ones. This is a skill built through repeated short practice, not a single insight. Use it especially in moments an appearance thought would normally take over.

fields.label: A judgmental thought I caught about my body
A neutral, factual way to describe the same thing
A moment I want to practice this skill next

title: Structured Problem-Solving Worksheet
summary: Walks a client through defining a problem, generating options, and picking one to try.
goal: Use it to replace circular worrying about a problem with a concrete, testable next step.
body_md: This works best on a problem the client has been turning over without acting on, not a crisis needing an immediate decision. The brainstorming step should stay judgment-free — write down every option including bad ones — since clients who edit as they go tend to land back on the option they already rejected. Set a date to review what happened with the option they picked.

fields.label: The problem, stated in one specific sentence
Every option I can think of, including bad ones
Pros and cons of my top two options
The option I will try
My first concrete step
Date I will review how it went

title: Habit Reversal Planner
summary: Pairs an unwanted habit with an early warning sign and a competing response to use instead.
goal: Use it to interrupt an automatic habit at the moment it usually starts, not after.
body_md: Start with awareness before change: have the client track the habit for a few days first so the early warning sign is specific rather than guessed at. The competing response should be something physically incompatible with the habit and easy to do without planning, since anything that requires setup will get skipped in the moment it's actually needed.

fields.label: The habit I want to change
What usually happens right before it (place, feeling, time)
My earliest warning sign that it's about to happen
A competing response I can do instead
Who I've told about this plan
How this week went

title: Procrastination Value Timeline
summary: Compares how good delay feels right now against the cost the client expects later.
goal: Use it to make the short-term relief of putting something off visible against its real cost.
body_md: Clients rarely lack the reasoning to see that delay has a cost — the problem is that the reasoning arrives too late, after the relief of avoiding the task has already been felt. Filling this out ahead of a task the client is likely to delay again gives them something concrete to reread at the moment they reach for the delay instead.

fields.label: The task I keep delaying
How doing it now would feel in the next ten minutes
How delaying it will feel in the next ten minutes
What delaying it will cost me by this time next week
The smallest first step I could take right now

title: Should Statement Rewrite Sheet
summary: Catches a client's rigid should statements and rewrites them as a preference instead.
goal: Use it to loosen the guilt and pressure that rigid should statements tend to create.
body_md: Collect a handful of the client's own should statements before the session rather than inventing examples, since the rewrite lands better on language they actually use. Walk through why the rigid version generates guilt or resentment even when the underlying goal is reasonable, then rewrite it as something the client wants rather than something they're required to do.

fields.label: A should statement I say to myself often
Where I think this rule came from
What it costs me to hold it this rigidly
A rewrite as a preference instead of a rule
How it felt to say the rewrite out loud

title: Silly Voice Defusion Practice
summary: Has a client say a sticky thought aloud in a silly voice to loosen its grip.
goal: Use it to shift a client's relationship to a thought without arguing over whether it's true.
body_md: Pick a thought the client already knows isn't fully accurate but that still pulls at them, then have them say it in a cartoon voice, a slow-motion voice, and their own voice back to back. Some clients laugh, some feel silly and resist — both are useful to discuss. The point isn't to make the thought funny forever, just to prove in the room that its grip can loosen without the content changing at all.

fields.label: The thought that keeps pulling at me
How it felt to hear it in a silly voice
How much it felt like 'the truth' before, out of ten
How much it felt like 'the truth' just after, out of ten
When I could try this again this week

title: Ten-Year Values Letter
summary: Has a client write a letter from ten years ahead describing a life built on their values.
goal: Use it to clarify what actually matters to a client beneath their current worries.
body_md: Ask the client to write as their future self, ten years on, describing an ordinary week lived in line with what matters most to them — not a fantasy of achievement, just the texture of the days. Clients who struggle often default to describing outcomes, a job title, a relationship status, rather than qualities of how they show up; gently redirect toward the latter, since that's what committed action can actually be built from.

fields.label: An ordinary day, ten years from now, if I'm living by what matters to me
What kind of person am I being in that day
What's one thing from that day I could bring into this week
What gets in the way of that right now

title: Sky Mind Observing Practice
summary: Uses the sky and passing weather as a metaphor for the self that notices thoughts and feelings.
goal: Use it to build a client's sense of a stable self that is not the same as their passing thoughts.
body_md: Guide the client to picture themselves as the sky, with each thought, mood, or urge as weather passing through — sometimes calm, sometimes a storm, but the sky itself unchanged underneath. This tends to click for clients who feel defined by whatever mood is loudest that day. Bring it back to a recent difficult moment and ask what stayed constant while the weather in it was rough.

fields.label: A recent difficult moment and what the 'weather' was
What stayed the same underneath that weather
A thought I've been treating as permanent that might just be passing
What I notice trying this practice

title: Willingness Ladder
summary: Ranks situations by how willing a client is to feel discomfort while still moving toward what matters.
goal: Use it to build willingness gradually rather than asking for it all at once.
body_md: Unlike a hierarchy built around reducing distress, this ladder is ranked by willingness — how much discomfort the client is prepared to carry while still taking a values-aligned step. Start low enough that the first rung feels genuinely doable this week, and debrief every attempt by asking what the client did while feeling the discomfort, not whether the discomfort went away.

fields.label: The value this ladder is in service of
A step I'm willing to take even with some discomfort (lowest rung)
A step further up the ladder
The top rung, whether or not I'm ready for it yet
What I noticed after trying the lowest rung

title: Committed Action Contract
summary: A short written agreement a client makes with themselves to take one values-aligned action.
goal: Use it to turn a values discussion into a specific, dated commitment the client can keep or revisit.
body_md: Keep the action small enough to actually happen this week and tie it explicitly back to a value named earlier in the session, not to an outcome the client can't control. When a client doesn't follow through, treat the contract as information about the size of the step rather than a failure, and rewrite it smaller together before ending the session.

fields.label: The value behind this action
The specific action I'm committing to
By when
What might get in the way
How I'll handle that if it happens
My signature and today's date

title: What Skills Practice Card
summary: Walks a client through observing, describing, then participating in a moment as it happens.
goal: Use it to practice the DBT 'what' skills as a sequence, not just as ideas.
body_md: Have the client pause during an ordinary moment — a meal, a walk, a conversation — and move through the three skills in order: notice what's here without words, then put words to it, then step fully into doing it. Most clients skip straight to participating out of habit, so the card works best used in short, deliberate bursts rather than as a running commentary on the whole day.

fields.label: The moment I practiced with
What I observed, before I put words to it
How I described it
What it was like to then just participate

title: Mastery Moment Planner
summary: Schedules one activity a client can do well as a planned confidence and mood boost.
goal: Use it to build a client's sense of competence on purpose, ahead of a hard stretch.
body_md: The activity needs to be slightly challenging but realistically achievable this week — too easy and it does nothing for confidence, too hard and a client already running low on mood will avoid it. Schedule it like an appointment rather than leaving it to motivation, and check afterward what doing it well actually felt like in the body, not just whether it got done.

fields.label: An activity I can reliably do well, even if small
When this week I'll do it
What might get in the way
How it felt afterward

title: Turning Toward Acceptance Log
summary: Logs the repeated choice to turn toward acceptance of something a client cannot change.
goal: Use it to show a client that acceptance is a decision made again and again, not one event.
body_md: Turning the mind is not the same as being at peace with something — it's the moment of choosing, again, to stop fighting a fact that won't change right now. Clients often expect one big turn to be enough and get discouraged when the resistance comes back an hour later; this log makes the repetition visible and normal instead of a sign the skill isn't working.

fields.label: The fact I keep resisting
A moment today I turned my mind toward accepting it
What pulled me back toward fighting it
How many times I noticed myself turning today

title: Mindfulness of Current Emotion Practice
summary: Has a client observe a strong emotion moving through them without pushing it away or feeding it.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for a feeling's rise and fall without acting on it right away.
body_md: Ask the client to notice where the emotion sits in the body, name it, and watch it rise and change without trying to fix, judge, or extend it — much like watching a wave rather than surfing or fighting it. This is best introduced with a moderate emotion first, not the client's most intense one, so they can build the skill before testing it under real pressure.

fields.label: The emotion I practiced with
Where I felt it in my body
What I noticed as it changed
Whether I acted on it or just watched it

title: Partner Boundary Negotiation Sheet
summary: Has each partner name a boundary they need and negotiate one both can actually keep.
goal: Use it to turn a vague complaint about overstepping into a specific, agreed boundary.
body_md: Have each partner fill out their side alone first, since boundaries proposed in the moment tend to be reactions to the last conflict rather than what's actually needed. In session, look for the version each partner can actually sustain, not the most generous-sounding one — a boundary that gets broken in a week does more damage than a smaller one that holds.

fields.label: Partner A: a boundary I need right now
Partner A: why this one, specifically
Partner B: a boundary I need right now
Partner B: why this one, specifically
What we agreed to try
How we'll check back in on it

title: Partner Decision Matrix
summary: Lays out both partners' ratings of shared options side by side before a joint decision.
goal: Use it to make a couple's disagreement about a decision specific instead of circular.
body_md: Works best for a decision with a real deadline — a move, a schedule change, a purchase — rather than an open-ended values debate. Each partner rates every option alone first so the ratings aren't shaped by the other's reaction in the room, then compare where they land closest together and where the real gap is, which is usually smaller than the argument made it feel.

fields.label: The decision we're facing
Options we're actually considering
Partner A: rating and reasoning for each option
Partner B: rating and reasoning for each option
Where we already agree
The real gap, stated plainly

title: Shared Life Transition Map
summary: Maps what each partner expects to gain and lose as a couple moves through a shared change.
goal: Use it to surface mismatched expectations about a transition before they turn into conflict.
body_md: Any major shared change — a move, a career switch, an aging parent moving in, an empty nest — carries a private list of hopes and losses each partner may not have said out loud. Have both fill this in separately, then read each other's answers before discussing; the gap between what one partner assumed the other felt and what they actually wrote is usually where the real conversation starts.

fields.label: The transition we're facing
Partner A: what I'm hoping for in this
Partner A: what I'm afraid of losing
Partner B: what I'm hoping for in this
Partner B: what I'm afraid of losing
One thing we can do to support each other through it

title: Partner Confidence Mirror
summary: Has each partner name something they're proud of and hear it reflected back by the other.
goal: Use it to build a couple's habit of noticing and reinforcing each other's strengths.
body_md: This is a short, structured exchange, not a general compliment session — each partner names one specific thing they did recently that they're quietly proud of, and the other partner reflects it back in their own words before adding anything of their own. Couples under strain often stop noticing each other's wins at all, and this rebuilds that muscle in a low-stakes, repeatable way.

fields.label: Partner A: something I did recently that I'm proud of
Partner B: reflecting that back in your own words
Partner B: something I did recently that I'm proud of
Partner A: reflecting that back in your own words
What it was like to hear this from each other

title: Habit Change Support Agreement
summary: Sets out exactly how a partner can support a habit change without nagging or policing it.
goal: Use it to replace well-meant nagging with support the changing partner actually asked for.
body_md: The partner making the change should write the first two fields alone, since support that hasn't been requested tends to land as pressure no matter how well intended. Be specific about what to say and when — 'remind me' and 'don't remind me' both need exact wording, or the couple will fall back into the same pattern within a week.

fields.label: The habit I'm working on changing
Support I'm actually asking for
Support I do NOT want, even if well meant
Partner: what I heard being asked for
How we'll check in on whether this is working

title: Friendship Recipe Craft
summary: A child writes and decorates a recipe card for being a good friend.
goal: Use it to make abstract friendship skills concrete and easy for a child to picture and reuse.
body_md: Give the child a blank recipe card and ask what 'ingredients' go into being a good friend — sharing, listening, saying sorry — and let them decorate it however they like. Younger children often name actions rather than qualities, which is fine and actually more usable. Send the card home and ask the caregiver to reference it by name when they catch the child using one of its ingredients that week.

fields.label: Ingredients for being a good friend
How much of each one (a little or a lot)
A time I already used one of these ingredients
One I want to practice more

title: Confidence Cape Craft
summary: A child decorates a paper cape listing things that make them feel strong and capable.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete object to picture when a hard moment calls for confidence.
body_md: Cut a simple cape shape from paper and have the child decorate it with drawings or words for things they've done that took courage or skill, however small. Keep the caregiver in the room to help remember real moments the child might not think to name themselves. Hang the cape somewhere visible at home and have the caregiver mention it by name before something the child is nervous about.

fields.label: Things I've done that took courage or skill
What my cape looks like
When I might wear my cape (for real or in my head)
Caregiver: a moment I saw that I'll add to the list

title: Habit Tracker Caterpillar
summary: A child colors in one segment of a paper caterpillar for each day they complete a target habit.
goal: Use it to make daily habit follow-through visible and rewarding for a child.
body_md: Draw or print a caterpillar with as many segments as days in the plan, and pick one specific, observable habit to track — brushing teeth, packing a bag, a chore — rather than several at once. The caregiver colors in a segment with the child each day it happens, out loud and without lecturing on the days it doesn't, since the visible chain is doing the motivating work here.

fields.label: The one habit we're tracking
What the caterpillar looks like so far
A day it was hard to do the habit, and what happened
Caregiver: how I'll celebrate a full caterpillar

title: Decision Wheel Spinner Craft
summary: A child builds a spinnable paper wheel of calming choices to use when they feel stuck.
goal: Use it to give a child a fun, physical way to pick a coping choice instead of freezing or arguing.
body_md: Have the child draw and decorate several choices around a paper circle — a drink of water, ten jumping jacks, squeezing a pillow, asking for a hug — then attach a spinnable arrow with a brass fastener. The caregiver keeps the wheel somewhere accessible and offers a spin as a first step at the very start of a hard moment, before things escalate, rather than as a punishment afterward.

fields.label: Choices I put on my wheel
Which one I decorated the most
A time I used my wheel
Caregiver: when I'll offer the wheel next time

title: Family Meeting Talking Stick Craft
summary: A child decorates a talking stick the family passes around during a weekly family meeting.
goal: Use it to teach a child turn-taking and listening through a hands-on family routine.
body_md: Any sturdy stick, spoon, or tube works as the base — the decorating is what makes it the child's. Explain the one rule: whoever holds it talks, everyone else listens, then it passes on. Coach the caregiver to run a short weekly family meeting where each person gets a turn with the stick to share one good thing and one thing they'd like to change, keeping it brief enough that younger children stay engaged.

fields.label: What I decorated my talking stick with
One good thing I said at our meeting
One thing I asked to change
Caregiver: when our next family meeting will be

title: Values Charades
summary: Players act out a value word without speaking while the group guesses which one it is.
goal: Use it to make abstract values concrete and get a group talking about why each one matters.
body_md: Write values like honesty, courage, or connection on separate cards and have players draw one at a time to act out silently while the group guesses. Once a value is guessed, spend a minute asking who in the group already lives that value in some way and how. The guessing is just the warm-up; the debrief about real examples is where the game earns its place in session.

fields.label: Values we used
The hardest one to act out
A value I guessed that surprised me
A value from the game I want more of in my own life

title: Assertive Comeback Relay
summary: Teams race to respond assertively to scripted pushy lines, scoring points for tone as well as words.
goal: Use it to rehearse assertive responses under mild pressure before they're needed for real.
body_md: Prepare a stack of pushy or guilt-tripping lines a player might hear from a friend, boss, or family member. One player reads a line, the next in line has ten seconds to respond assertively — not aggressively, not passively — before the group scores it and the relay moves on. The time pressure is deliberate: real pushback rarely comes with time to plan the perfect line.

fields.label: Lines we used
A response the group scored highest
A response that tipped into aggressive or passive, and why
A line I want to practice more on my own

title: Habit Tracker Race Game
summary: Players move a token forward on a shared board for each day they kept a target habit.
goal: Use it to make weekly habit follow-through visible and a little competitive within a group.
duration: 10 minutes at the start of each session
body_md: Draw a simple path board with a few bonus and setback spaces scattered along it. Each player names one habit at the start of the week and moves their token forward one space per day it happened, landing on bonus or setback spaces at random. The debrief matters more than the race: ask what helped on the days a player moved forward and what happened on the days they didn't.

fields.label: The habit I'm tracking this week
Where my token landed by the end
A bonus or setback space that fit something real that happened
What helped me move forward this week

title: The Decision Dice Game
summary: A die with six decision-making steps that players roll before working through a real choice.
goal: Use it to give a group a repeatable structure for talking through a decision out loud.
body_md: Label the six sides of a blank die with steps such as pros, cons, values check, gut check, ask someone, sleep on it. A player names a real decision they're facing, then rolls the die and works through whatever step comes up before rolling again. Rolling the steps out of the usual order tends to surface angles a straight list would have skipped.

fields.label: The decision I brought to the game
The steps I rolled, in order
The step that gave me the most new information
Where I landed after playing

title: Friendship Skills Scavenger Hunt
summary: Players complete a list of small friendship actions during the week and report back at the next meeting.
goal: Use it to turn friendship skills into small, trackable actions instead of vague advice.
body_md: Give each player the same short list of friendship actions to look for chances to do that week — compliment someone, invite someone to join in, check in with someone having a hard day. At the next session, go around and have each player report which ones they managed and how it went, treating a missed item as information about what's hard rather than a failure to note.

fields.label: Actions on my list
Which ones I managed this week
What happened when I tried one
One I want to try again

title: Five-Minute Start Rule Tracker
summary: Tracks whether committing to just five minutes on a delayed task actually got it started.
goal: Use it to test whether lowering the bar to start is enough to break a pattern of delay.
body_md: The rule is simple: commit to five minutes only, with full permission to stop after that. Most of the value here is in the data, not the rule itself — some clients find they keep going past five minutes almost every time, others find they genuinely stop, and that's useful too, since it means the task itself needs breaking down further, not just an easier entry point.

fields.label: The task I'm applying this to
Day 1: did I start? What happened after five minutes?
Day 2: did I start? What happened after five minutes?
Day 3: did I start? What happened after five minutes?
What this tells me about this particular task

title: Weekly Balance Check-In Worksheet
summary: Has a client rate how much time and energy went to work, rest, people, and health this week.
goal: Use it to make an overloaded week visible before it turns into burnout.
body_md: Have the client rate the past week, not an ideal week, across a handful of life domains, then circle the one that got the least attention and wasn't supposed to. This works well as a recurring check-in rather than a one-time exercise, since the pattern across several weeks usually says more than any single week does on its own.

fields.label: Work or responsibilities: how much time and energy this week
Rest and downtime: how much time and energy this week
People who matter to me: how much time and energy this week
My own health: how much time and energy this week
The one that got less than it needed
One small change for next week

title: Compassionate Pause Card
summary: A short three-step script a client can use in the moment when they're being hard on themselves.
goal: Use it to give a client a fast, repeatable alternative to self-criticism in a difficult moment.
body_md: The three steps are short on purpose so a client can actually use them mid-moment rather than only later in reflection: naming that this is a hard moment, remembering that struggling is something everyone goes through, and offering themselves a kind phrase they choose ahead of time. Have the client write their own phrase in session, since a phrase supplied by someone else rarely feels believable when it's needed.

fields.label: A hard moment I could use this for
Step 1: naming it ('this is a hard moment')
Step 2: remembering I'm not the only one ('struggling is part of being human')
Step 3: my own kind phrase to offer myself

title: Gratitude Letter Worksheet
summary: Guides a client through writing a specific letter of thanks to someone who mattered to them.
goal: Use it to build gratitude through one detailed act rather than a running list.
body_md: Unlike a running gratitude list, this asks for one specific person and one specific reason, written as an actual letter. Encourage detail over generality — what they did, when, and how it affected the client specifically — since vague thanks tends to feel flat to write and to read. Whether the client ever sends it is optional; the writing itself is where most of the benefit shows up.

fields.label: Who this letter is to
What they did that mattered
How it affected me at the time
How it still affects me now
The letter, in my own words
Whether I plan to send it

title: Decision Fatigue Reset Plan
summary: Identifies small daily decisions a client can automate or eliminate to save energy for bigger ones.
goal: Use it to free up a client's decision-making energy for the choices that actually matter to them.
body_md: Have the client list the small decisions that repeat every day — what to wear, what to eat, when to check messages — and sort them into ones worth automating (same choice every time) versus ones worth eliminating outright. This tends to land well with clients who describe feeling drained by the end of an ordinary day with no single obvious cause; the fatigue is often the sum of many small, unnecessary decisions rather than one big one.

fields.label: Small decisions that repeat every day for me
Ones I could automate with a standing default
Ones I could eliminate outright
What I'll do with the energy this frees up

title: Hyperarousal Interpretation Record
summary: A thought record that reframes a racing heart or jumpiness as an old alarm, not present danger.
goal: Use it to help clients separate a body's alarm response from an actual present-moment threat.
body_md: Run this once grounding skills are already in place, since it asks a client to look closely at body sensations that can themselves feel activating. The work is reinterpretation, not exposure: a sensation gets relabeled as a leftover signal from the body's protective system rather than evidence of current danger. Keep the focus on right now, never on what happened, and pause if a client's arousal climbs instead of settling.

fields.label: A body sensation I noticed (racing heart, tight chest, jumpiness)
What my mind says this sensation means about right now
Evidence this is my body's alarm system rather than a present threat
One fact about my current surroundings that tells me I am safe enough right now
A calmer, more accurate way to describe this sensation to myself

title: Anchor and Choose Practice
summary: A brief practice pairing a grounding anchor with one small, values-based action after a spike.
goal: Use it to help clients move from a flooded moment back into one small, values-aligned step.
body_md: Use this right after a spike in distress has already started to ease, not during the worst of it. The two moves matter in order: ground first, then choose, since asking a flooded client to act on values before they are anchored usually fails. Coach clients toward genuinely small actions, since an ambitious choice can undo the settling that grounding just produced.

fields.label: What I noticed in my body that told me my alarm had switched on
The grounding step I used to come back into the room
Something that matters to me that I can act on right now, even in a small way
The one small action I will take
How steady I feel now, 0 to 10

title: Flashback Recovery Roles Plan
summary: A plan both partners complete for what helps right after a flashback or dissociative moment.
goal: Use it to give partners a rehearsed, agreed script instead of improvising in a hard moment.
body_md: Complete this together while both partners are calm and settled, then revisit it after any real moment to fine-tune it. Keep every prompt about present-moment needs and helpful responses, never about what happened to bring on the flashback, since that detail is not required for either partner's part of this plan. The code word in the last prompt is often what partners use most, since it removes the pressure to explain anything in the moment itself.

fields.label: Partner A: what it can look like when I'm having a flashback or feel unsafe in the moment
Partner A: what I need Partner B to do right when that happens
Partner A: what Partner B should not do, even if well-meaning
Partner B: what helps me know whether you need support or space right now
Both: a code word or signal we'll use so words aren't needed in the moment
Both: what we'll do together once the moment has passed

title: Calm Places Passport Craft
summary: A decorated passport-style booklet of places and objects that help a child's body feel calm now.
goal: Use it to build a ready list of present-moment safe places instead of talking through what happened.
body_md: This stays entirely present-focused: a child draws or decorates calm places and comforting objects, never the event itself, so redirect gently back to the here-and-now if a child starts to narrate details. The caregiver's page turns the passport into a shared plan for actually revisiting these places together during the week. As with any safety-related work with a child, if a child discloses abuse or harm at any point, follow your mandated reporting duties right away.

fields.label: Decorate the cover of my Calm Places Passport
A place at home where my body feels calm — draw it or tell about it
A place away from home where I feel calm
Something I can hold, look at, or listen to that helps me feel calm
A grown-up's page: how we'll practice visiting a calm place together this week

title: Body Alarm and Grounding Match
summary: A card-matching game pairing body alarm signals with a grounding skill that answers each one.
goal: Use it to rehearse fast recognition of alarm signals and the grounding response that fits them.
body_md: Shuffle two piles, one of body-alarm cards and one of grounding-skill cards. Each turn, a player draws one card from each pile and argues whether it's a good match, and the group votes on whether the pairing works. Deliberate mismatches often generate the best discussion, so let a player defend an odd pairing before moving on. Debrief on which grounding skill each player would actually reach for first outside of the room.

fields.label: Body alarm cards we used
Grounding skill cards we used
Our best match this round, and why
A pairing that surprised us
The grounding skill I'd reach for first outside of here

title: Nighttime Anxiety Wind-Down Log
summary: A nightly log that pairs an anxious bedtime thought with one short wind-down step.
goal: Use it to separate lying-awake worry from the body's need to wind down before sleep.
duration: Five minutes nightly for two weeks
body_md: This is narrower than a full sleep hygiene review: it targets the specific moment anxiety shows up at bedtime and gives the client one alternative to problem-solving under the covers. Watch for clients using the log itself to keep planning or ruminating rather than noticing a pattern, and steer them back to the single wind-down step. Review the pattern line together after a week or two rather than each night.

fields.label: Tonight's worry, in a few words
Where I notice it in my body right now
One wind-down step I'll do instead of scrolling or planning in bed
What time I think I actually fell asleep
One pattern I'm noticing after a few nights

title: Anxious Moment Choice Point
summary: A choice-point map for an anxious moment, sorting hooked, avoidant moves from values-based ones.
goal: Use it to help clients notice the pull toward avoidance and pick one toward move instead.
body_md: Draw the choice point live with the client the first time, since sketching the fork between away moves and toward moves usually lands better than reading it off a sheet. Anxiety-specific away moves tend to be subtle, such as checking, seeking reassurance, or over-preparing, so help clients name the version they actually do rather than a generic one. The toward move at the end should be genuinely small enough to attempt this week.

fields.label: The anxious moment: what happened right before anxiety showed up
The hooked or away moves I'm pulled toward (avoid, escape, check, control)
What matters to me in this situation
One unhooking or grounding move I can use right here
One small toward move I can take next

title: DEAR MAN for Anxious Requests
summary: A DEAR MAN script for making a request or saying no despite anxiety about the reaction.
goal: Use it to help clients state a need clearly instead of avoiding the ask altogether.
body_md: This applies the standard DEAR MAN sequence to a specific kind of moment: an ask the client keeps avoiding because anxiety predicts a bad reaction. Have the client script the words out loud in session before trying it for real, since anxious clients tend to soften the Assert line until it no longer functions as a request. The last prompt keeps the anxious prediction visible instead of pretending the ask will feel comfortable.

fields.label: The anxious situation where I need to make a request or say no
Describe: the facts of the situation, without judgment
Express: how I feel and why this matters to me
Assert: the specific request or 'no' I want to state
Reinforce: what's in it for the other person if they agree
The anxious prediction I expect, and my plan to make the ask anyway

title: Worry-Calming Recipe Card Craft
summary: A decorated recipe card listing a child's own ingredients for calming their worry.
goal: Use it to turn a child's coping steps into a memorable, personalized recipe they can reuse.
body_md: Have the child decorate the card like a real recipe, with a title, a short ingredients list, and simple steps, so the format feels playful rather than clinical. Keep ingredients concrete and physical, such as breathing, a hug, or a specific phrase, rather than abstract advice a child can't picture using. The caregiver's line turns this into something usable at home: a cue for catching early worry signs and prompting the recipe before worry builds.

fields.label: Decorate the title of my worry-calming recipe
Ingredient 1: something I do with my body
Ingredient 2: something I say to myself
Ingredient 3: someone I can ask for help
