Partner B: how does your grief usually show up?
Partner B: what do you need from your partner right now?
One assumption about each other’s grief you are ready to drop

title: Feelings About Goodbye Storybook Craft
summary: A child makes a simple illustrated booklet about their loss, in their own words and pictures, with a parent nearby.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete, contained way to tell their own story about the loss, at their own pace.
body_md: Children often process loss in pieces rather than one conversation, and a small illustrated booklet gives them somewhere to put those pieces over time rather than needing to say everything at once. The parent stays nearby to help with words but lets the child lead the pictures and the pace, adding pages over days or weeks rather than finishing in one sitting.

fields.label: What happened, in your own words or pictures
What you miss most
A happy memory to include
Who helps you when you feel sad about it

title: Relationship Pattern History Sheet
summary: Has a client trace a recurring relationship pattern across several relationships, not just the current one.
goal: Use it to show a client a pattern is theirs to work on, not just a feature of one difficult partner.
body_md: A pattern that shows up across several relationships, always the one who chases, always drawn to someone unavailable, always the one who goes quiet first, is more useful to examine than one blamed entirely on the current partner. The client lists past and current relationships and marks where the pattern shows up in each, then considers what role they tend to play in keeping it going.

fields.label: The pattern you keep noticing
Where did it show up in past relationships?
Where does it show up now?
What is your part in keeping the pattern going?

title: Mind-Reading Check for Relationships
summary: Tests an assumption about a partner’s thoughts or intentions against what they actually said when asked.
goal: Use it to interrupt the habit of assuming a partner’s intent instead of checking it directly.
body_md: ‘They didn’t text back because they’re losing interest’ is a guess dressed up as a fact, and relationships absorb a lot of friction from guesses like it going unchecked. The client writes the assumption, rates how certain they feel, then actually asks the partner and logs the real answer. Comparing the guess to the answer over a few entries usually reveals how often the guess was simply wrong.

fields.label: The assumption about your partner’s thoughts or intent
How certain did you feel, 0 to 100 percent?
What did they actually say when you asked?
How far off was the assumption?

title: Committed Relationship Values Check
summary: Practices willingness to sit with discomfort, an awkward conversation, being vulnerable, in service of the relationship.
goal: Use it when avoiding discomfort is quietly costing a client the relationship closeness they say they want.
body_md: Avoiding an awkward conversation or staying guarded to sidestep discomfort often costs more closeness than the discomfort itself would have. The client names a relationship value, honesty, closeness, repair, and one uncomfortable action that would actually serve it, then practices willingness to feel the discomfort rather than waiting for it to go away first.

fields.label: A relationship value that matters to you
What uncomfortable action would actually serve it?
What discomfort shows up when you imagine doing it?
Are you willing to feel that, in service of the value?

title: Relationship Check the Facts Sheet
summary: Applies DBT’s check the facts skill to a relationship conflict interpretation before reacting to it.
goal: Use it to test whether a reaction to a partner’s words actually fits the facts of what was said.
body_md: An emotional reaction to a partner’s comment sometimes fits the facts and sometimes runs ahead of them, shaped by past hurts more than the present moment. The client writes exactly what was said, their interpretation of it, and the emotion that followed, then checks whether the interpretation is the only one that fits the actual words. Where it does not, a different response usually becomes available.

fields.label: What was actually said, word for word if possible
Your interpretation of it
The emotion that followed, and its intensity
Is your interpretation the only one that fits the facts?

title: Repeated Argument Autopsy
summary: Has a couple analyze the structure of a recurring argument, how it starts, escalates and ends, rather than its content.
goal: Use it to interrupt a recurring argument’s pattern once both partners can see its shape.
body_md: The same argument often repeats not because the topic keeps changing but because the structure never does, a familiar opening line, a predictable escalation, the same ending. Each partner separately describes the pattern’s stages, then the two compare notes and name the exact moment where a different move could change the outcome. Working on the structure tends to help more than re-litigating the last instance.

fields.label: Partner A: how does this argument usually start?
Partner B: how does this argument usually start?
How does it usually escalate, and how does it usually end?
Where is the one moment a different move could change it?

title: Safety Signal Card
summary: A card naming a client’s own signals of safety in the present, built for quick reference during distress.
goal: Use it to give a client something concrete pointing to present safety, ready before it is needed.
body_md: Built on a calm day, the card lists specific, personal signals that the present is safe — a locked door, a trusted person’s number, a phrase that has worked before. It does not ask for any account of what happened; it works entirely in the present tense. If distress escalates toward a crisis, 988 (call or text) and the client’s own safety plan come next, not this card alone.

fields.label: A place that feels safe to you right now
A person you can reach out to
A phrase or reminder that has helped before
Where will you keep this card?

title: Self-Blame Versus Responsibility Sheet
summary: Separates a client’s self-blame from where responsibility actually sits, without needing the details of what happened.
goal: Use it to loosen self-blame that has settled somewhere it does not belong.
body_md: Self-blame after sexual abuse often attaches to choices the client made, what they wore, where they were, what they said, as though those choices caused the abuse. The client can name the self-blaming thought and test it against a simple question: who chose to cause harm? The exercise works without any account of the abuse itself; it stays with the thought, not the story.

fields.label: A self-blaming thought you carry
What choice does it blame you for?
Who actually chose to cause harm?
What would you say to someone else carrying this same blame?

title: Reclaiming Choice Practice
summary: Practices noticing small present-day choices a client has, to rebuild a sense of agency at their own pace.
goal: Use it to rebuild a felt sense of choice in the present, without needing to revisit the past.
body_md: Abuse involves choice being taken away, and rebuilding a felt sense of agency can matter as much as any other part of healing, entirely apart from processing what happened. The practice has the client notice small, real choices available right now, what to eat, when to rest, who to see, and name each one as evidence that choice is theirs again. No account of the abuse itself is needed for this to work.

fields.label: A small choice you made today
How did it feel to notice it as your choice?
What is one more choice available to you this week?
What does having choice again mean to you?

title: Body Safety Grounding Card
summary: A grounding sequence for the body-based distress that can follow sexual abuse, without revisiting any details.
goal: Use it to bring the body back to a felt sense of safety when distress spikes.
body_md: Distress after sexual abuse can show up first in the body, tension, disconnection, a racing heart, before any thought is even named. The card walks through a short, body-based grounding sequence: feet on the floor, hands on a solid surface, a slow count of the breath. It works without any narrative content and can be practiced calm, in session, before it is needed elsewhere.

fields.label: Where do you notice the distress in your body first?
Feet on the floor — what do you notice?
Hands on a solid surface — what do you notice?
Rate the distress before and after this sequence

title: Trusted Grown-Ups Map
summary: A child maps the trusted grown-ups they could go to if something felt wrong or unsafe.
goal: Use it to build a child’s concrete list of safe adults to turn to, before it is ever needed.
body_md: The child draws or names a small circle of trusted grown-ups, at home, at school, in the family, they could go to if something ever felt wrong or unsafe, without needing to describe any specific worry to complete the map. Clinician note: if a child discloses anything during this or any session, follow your setting’s mandated reporting duties promptly, before continuing any other work.

fields.label: Draw or name your trusted grown-ups
How could you find each one if you needed to?
What could you say to a grown-up if something felt wrong?
Parent or caregiver: is this map somewhere the child can remember it?

title: Coping Skills Audit by Situation
summary: Sorts a client’s coping skills by which situations they actually work best in, rather than one skill for all.
goal: Use it to match a coping skill to the situation instead of reaching for the same one every time.
body_md: A skill that works well for a racing mind at 2am may do nothing for a tense conversation at work, and clients often keep reaching for the same familiar skill regardless of fit. The client sorts their current coping skills by situation type, physical activation, racing thoughts, interpersonal conflict, low energy, building a reference to pull from instead of one default.

fields.label: Skills that help with physical activation (racing heart, tension)
Skills that help with racing or looping thoughts
Skills that help in interpersonal conflict
Skills that help on low-energy days
Which situation type do you have the fewest skills for?

title: Workable Coping Sort
summary: Sorts coping behaviors into those that move a client toward their values and those that only move away from pain.
goal: Use it to notice which coping strategies build a life a client wants, not just relieve a moment.
body_md: Two coping behaviors can both bring short-term relief while pointing in opposite directions, one toward a life the client actually wants, the other only away from discomfort with nothing gained. The client sorts a list of their current coping behaviors into these two columns and looks at which column they reach for most, then considers where one ‘away from’ behavior could shift toward a ‘toward’ one.

fields.label: Coping behaviors that move you toward something you value
Coping behaviors that only move you away from discomfort
Which column do you reach for most?
One ‘away from’ behavior you could shift toward a value

title: Skills Chain Backup Plan
summary: Plans a second and third coping skill in advance, in case the first choice does not work in the moment.
goal: Use it so a client has a next move ready instead of stalling when the first skill falls short.
body_md: A single coping plan can leave a client stuck if the first skill they reach for does not work in the moment, which can feel like the whole plan failing rather than one option not fitting. The client plans a short chain, first skill, then a backup, then a third, ahead of time, so there is always a next move ready rather than starting from scratch mid-distress.

fields.label: Your first-choice skill for this kind of moment
Backup skill if the first one does not work
Third option if neither works
Which one did you actually end up using, and how far down the chain?

title: Calm-Down Card Deck Craft
summary: A child illustrates a small deck of cards, one coping skill per card, to shuffle through when upset.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on deck of options they made themselves and can physically shuffle through.
body_md: The child draws one coping skill per card, blowing bubbles, squeezing a pillow, counting to ten, asking for a hug, building a small deck over several sessions. When upset, the child (or parent, at first) shuffles through the deck to pick one to try, which turns ‘use a coping skill’ into a concrete, game-like action instead of an abstract instruction to remember.

fields.label: What coping skill is on today’s new card?
Draw a picture for it
Which card did you pick the last time you were upset?
Did it help? Parent: what did you notice?

title: Skill or Bluff
summary: A guessing game where players describe a coping skill, real or invented, and the group votes on which it is.
goal: Use it to review real coping skills while keeping the format playful and a little competitive.
body_md: Each player describes a coping skill with a straight face, some real, some invented on the spot, and the group votes on whether it is genuine or a bluff, earning a point for a correct guess either way. The debrief sorts out which described skills were real and worth remembering, folding review into a game that plays more like a party game than a therapy exercise.

fields.label: The skill you described — real or a bluff?
Did the group guess correctly?
Which real skills came up that you want to remember?
Which bluff skill was the funniest?

title: Safe Zone Shrinking Map
summary: Maps how a client’s everyday ‘safe zone’ of places and activities has shrunk as a specific fear grew.
goal: Use it to show a client how much territory avoidance has quietly claimed, and pick one edge to push back.
body_md: A specific phobia tends to expand its no-go zone gradually enough that a client stops noticing how much has been given up, avoiding driving on highways can end up limiting a job search; avoiding dogs can end up limiting which friends’ homes get visited. The client draws their current safe zone against what it used to include, then picks one edge of the shrunken territory to reclaim first.

fields.label: What does your safe zone include today?
What did it used to include before the fear grew?
Which edge of the shrunken zone matters most to reclaim?
What would the first small step back into it look like?

title: Feared Outcome Likelihood Sheet
summary: Has a client estimate the real-world odds of their feared outcome, then compares it to base rates.
goal: Use it to put a number on a feared outcome instead of letting it stay an unexamined certainty.
body_md: A specific phobia often runs on an outcome that feels certain but is, in fact, rare, the plane will crash, the dog will bite, the elevator will get stuck. The client estimates their own odds, then the two of you look together at what is actually known about the base rate for that outcome. The gap between the felt certainty and the real odds becomes something concrete to work with.

fields.label: The feared outcome
Your estimate of the odds it happens, in percent
What is actually known about the real odds?
How does that gap change how certain the fear feels?

title: Fear Passenger Exposure Log
summary: Logs approach steps toward a feared object or situation with fear allowed to come along, not required to leave first.
goal: Use it to decouple doing the approach step from feeling calm enough to do it first.
body_md: Waiting to feel calm before approaching a feared situation usually means waiting indefinitely, since the calm tends to arrive after repeated approach, not before it. The client logs each approach step alongside how much fear was present and whether they did the step anyway, treating the fear as an unwelcome passenger rather than a stop sign.

fields.label: Today’s approach step
Fear level going in, 0 to 10
Did you do the step with the fear present?
What did the fear do during and after the step?

title: Fear Ladder Sticker Chart
summary: A sticker chart tracking a child’s steps up their own fear ladder, one small approach step at a time.
goal: Use it to make gradual progress up a fear ladder visible and rewarding for a child.
body_md: Built together with the parent, the ladder breaks a specific fear into small graded steps, and each completed step earns a sticker on the chart. Progress up a fear ladder can feel invisible day to day, and the chart gives the child something to look back at and see how far they have actually climbed. Celebrate effort at each step, not only reaching the top.

fields.label: Your fear ladder, from easiest to hardest step
Which step did you try today?
How scared were you before, and after?
Parent: sticker earned — yes or no?

title: Fear Facts Quiz Show
summary: A quiz game that corrects common myths about feared objects and situations, in a playful group format.
goal: Use it to chip away at threat overestimation with real information, delivered as a game rather than a lecture.
body_md: Questions test common beliefs about feared things, how likely a dog is to bite, how safe air travel actually is, how elevators are inspected, and players guess true or false before hearing the real answer. Presenting accurate information as a game rather than a lecture tends to land better with a group that already feels defensive about being told their fear is irrational.

fields.label: Which question surprised you the most?
What did you believe before, and what is actually true?
Does this change how big the fear feels?
What is one question you would add to the quiz?

title: Body Talk Audit
summary: Tracks how often a client’s day includes appearance-focused talk or comparison, in conversation or media.
goal: Use it to make an often-invisible daily habit of appearance talk visible and open to change.
body_md: Appearance-focused comments, from others, in media, or self-directed, can run through a day almost unnoticed until they are tracked on purpose. The client logs each instance along with how it affected their mood, then looks for patterns: certain people, certain apps, certain times of day. The goal is awareness first; specific changes come once the pattern is visible.

fields.label: The appearance-focused moment (conversation, media, self-talk)
Where did it come from?
How did it affect your mood?
What pattern are you noticing across entries?

title: Body as Vehicle Practice
summary: Shifts attention from how the body looks to what it allows a client to do in service of their values.
goal: Use it to widen a client’s relationship with their body beyond appearance alone.
body_md: The body carries a person toward the things they value, a walk with a friend, picking up a child, standing at a job that matters, regardless of how it looks doing it. The client names a recent moment the body made a valued activity possible and practices noticing that function, not appearance, as what the moment was actually about. Repetition matters more than any single entry here.

fields.label: A recent moment your body made something you value possible
What did your body let you do in that moment?
What would you have missed without it?
What does thanking your body for function, not appearance, feel like?

title: Body Image Opposite Action Card
summary: Applies the DBT opposite action skill to the urge to avoid or hide that body image distress often brings.
goal: Use it to interrupt avoidance driven by body image distress before it narrows a client’s life further.
body_md: Body image distress often comes with an urge to avoid, skip the event, cancel the photo, stay home, that can quietly shrink a client’s life over time if it goes unexamined. The client names the urge, checks whether acting on it fits the actual situation, and practices the opposite action fully when it does not, going to the event rather than only partly showing up.

fields.label: The situation and the urge to avoid or hide
Does the urge fit the actual situation?
The opposite action, described fully
What happened when you did the opposite action?

title: Body Image Support Conversation Guide
summary: Helps a partner learn to support body image struggles without appearance-focused comments that can backfire.
goal: Use it to replace well-meaning appearance comments with support that actually helps.
body_md: A partner’s well-meant reassurance about appearance can land badly for someone struggling with body image, since it keeps the conversation centered on looks either way. The guide has the struggling partner describe what kind of support actually helps, distraction, a hug, a change of subject, and the other partner practices offering that instead of a compliment about appearance.

fields.label: Struggling partner: what kind of support actually helps you?
Struggling partner: what comments, even kind ones, make it worse?
Supporting partner: what will you try saying or doing instead?
How did it go the last time you tried this?

title: Weekly Energy Budget Planner
summary: Maps where a client's energy goes across a typical week against where they want it to go.
goal: Make energy, not just time, a visible resource the client can budget on purpose.
body_md: Have the client list the week's regular commitments and rate each one as energy-giving or energy-costing, then compare the total against how the week actually felt. Most clients are surprised by how lopsided the ledger is. Use it to find one costly commitment worth trimming and one giving one worth protecting.

fields.label: Commitments in a typical week
Which ones give energy, which cost it
Where the week felt most drained
One costly commitment I could trim
One energy-giving thing I want to protect
What a better-balanced week would look like

title: Decision Fork Worksheet
summary: Lays out a stuck decision as a fork with the real costs and pulls of each path.
goal: Turn circular worry about a decision into a side-by-side comparison the client can act on.
body_md: Useful when a client has been turning the same decision over for weeks without moving. Naming both paths concretely, including what staying the same actually costs, often breaks the freeze better than more pros-and-cons debate. Ask what information, if any, is still missing versus what is just discomfort with choosing.

fields.label: The decision I keep circling
Path A, plainly stated
Path B, plainly stated
What each path costs me
What each path gives me
What I actually still need to know before choosing

title: Self-Talk Audit
summary: Catalogs the client's habitual inner commentary across a few situations to see its tone.
goal: Make an automatic internal voice something the client can hear and evaluate.
body_md: Ask the client to jot the exact words their mind used in a handful of recent moments, not a summary of the gist. Reading them back aloud in session is often the most useful part, since clients rarely notice the tone until they hear it said to someone else. Compare the voice to how the client would actually talk to a friend in the same spot.

fields.label: A recent moment and what my mind said, word for word
Another moment, same instructions
A third moment
The tone across all three, in one word
What I would say to a friend in the same spot
One phrase I want to try instead

title: Identity Roles Inventory
summary: Lists the roles a client currently carries and how much weight each one holds.
goal: Locate which roles are overloaded and which parts of identity have gone quiet.
body_md: Have the client list every role currently in play, worker, parent, partner, sibling, friend, and rate how much of the week each one takes versus how much it feels chosen. Roles that took over without being chosen are worth a closer look, as are ones the client used to hold and has let go of. This works well alongside a values conversation.

fields.label: Every role I currently carry
How much of my week each takes
Which ones feel chosen versus just happening
A role that has quietly disappeared
A role I would add if I could
One small shift I could make this month

title: New Habit Trial Sheet
summary: Structures a two-week trial of one small habit with a plain way to track it.
goal: Test a habit change on a short timeline before the client commits to it long term.
body_md: Pick one small, specific habit and a daily yes-or-no mark rather than a graded rating, since graded scales invite second-guessing. Review at the two-week mark and treat missed days as data about the plan, not about the client's willpower. A habit that needed constant force to keep up usually needs redesigning, not more discipline.

fields.label: The habit I am trialing
Why this one, right now
Day-by-day yes or no tally
What made it easier on the good days
What got in the way on the missed days
Keep it, change it, or drop it

title: Prediction vs Outcome Log
summary: Tracks what a client predicts will happen against what actually happens across a week.
goal: Build a running record that challenges an overconfident worry pattern with the client's own data.
body_md: Before a feared situation, have the client write the specific prediction and how certain they feel, then fill in the actual outcome afterward without editing the earlier entry. The gap between predicted and actual certainty across several entries is usually more persuasive than any single conversation. Keep the log going past the point it seems to be working.

fields.label: Situation coming up
My exact prediction
How certain I am (0 to 100)
What actually happened
How the outcome compared
What I notice across this week's entries

title: Core Belief Origins Timeline
summary: Traces a core belief back through the client's history to where it first took hold.
goal: Give a rigid belief a beginning, middle and present so it reads as learned rather than as fact.
body_md: Start from the belief itself, then work backward through the client's life for the earliest memory it fits, the moments it got reinforced, and any evidence along the way that never got counted. Clients often locate the belief's origin in a much younger version of themselves than they expected. Close by asking what that younger self needed to hear instead.

fields.label: The belief, in the client's own words
Earliest memory it connects to
Moments over the years that reinforced it
Evidence that contradicted it but got overlooked
What the younger self needed to hear
A more accurate belief to test out

title: Hot Thought Bullseye
summary: Narrows a tangle of thoughts in a distressing moment down to the single hottest one.
goal: Find the one thought driving most of the distress so the rest of the work can target it.
body_md: When a client brings a messy, multi-thought moment, list every thought that showed up and have them rate each for how much distress it carries on its own. The bullseye center is whichever thought scores highest; that is the one worth a full thought record, not the others. This keeps sessions from spreading thin across low-value thoughts.

fields.label: The situation
Every thought that showed up
Distress rating for each thought
The hottest thought
What makes that one the hottest
The angle to work on first

title: Rule for Living Rewrite
summary: Surfaces an unspoken personal rule and drafts a more workable version of it.
goal: Turn a rigid if-then rule the client lives by into something flexible enough to actually follow.
body_md: Many clients operate on an unstated rule, such as needing to be useful to deserve rest, that drives behavior more than any belief they would state out loud. Help the client word the rule plainly, list what it costs to keep it, and draft a looser version that still respects what the original rule was trying to protect. Test the new rule for a week before treating it as settled.

fields.label: The rule, put into words
Where it likely came from
What it costs to follow it
What it was trying to protect
A more workable version of the rule
How I will test the new version this week

title: Alternative Explanations Wheel
summary: Generates several possible explanations for an ambiguous situation before settling on one.
goal: Loosen a client's default explanation by putting real alternatives next to it.
body_md: Ambiguous situations, an unanswered text, a flat tone from a coworker, tend to get filled in with the client's most familiar and usually harshest explanation by default. Have the client generate at least four different explanations before rating how likely each one actually is. The point is not to force optimism but to break the habit of stopping at the first, worst guess.

fields.label: The ambiguous situation
My first, automatic explanation
Three other possible explanations
How likely each one actually is
What evidence would tell them apart
What I will do while I do not know

title: Tug-of-War With the Monster Metaphor
summary: Walks through the classic tug-of-war image to loosen a client's grip on an ongoing struggle.
goal: Let go of unproductive effort by noticing the rope, not the monster, is the thing to drop.
body_md: Describe the scene together: a monster on one end of a rope, the client straining on the other, the harder they pull the harder it pulls back. Ask what happens to the client's life while both hands are on the rope. The move is not winning the tug-of-war but noticing the rope can simply be set down, which is a strange and sometimes uncomfortable idea worth sitting with.

fields.label: The struggle this fits for me
What pulling harder has actually gotten me
What I have missed while both hands were on the rope
What it would mean to set the rope down
What I am afraid would happen if I did

title: Silly Voice Thought Replay
summary: Has the client repeat a sticky thought aloud in a series of silly voices.
goal: Loosen the grip of a literal, believable thought through simple, repeated defusion practice.
body_md: Pick one recurring thought and have the client say it in their normal voice, then a cartoon voice, then singing it, then very slowly. Most clients start laughing partway through, which is the point: the words have not changed but the relationship to them has loosened. Note how differently the thought lands by the end compared to the first read.

fields.label: The sticky thought, written plainly
How it felt to say it normally
How it felt in a silly voice
How it felt sung or slowed down
How much I believe it now, compared to before

title: Values in Ten Years Letter
summary: Has the client write from ten years ahead, describing a life shaped by their values.
goal: Use distance in time to clarify which values matter enough to build a life around.
body_md: Ask the client to write as their future self looking back, describing what mattered enough to keep showing up for even on hard days. Steer away from achievements and toward the qualities the client wants to have brought to their days, since that framing tracks values rather than outcomes. Bring the letter back into the present by asking what one line points to doing this month.

fields.label: Opening: where I am, ten years from now
What I kept showing up for
How I want to have treated people along the way
A hard stretch I got through and how
One line from this letter I want to act on this month

title: Acceptance Ladder for Difficult Feelings
summary: Ranks a set of hard feelings from most to least willing to make room for, and works up the rungs.
goal: Build willingness gradually rather than asking for full acceptance all at once.
body_md: List several feelings the client tends to fight rather than allow, from mildly uncomfortable to the ones that trigger the most avoidance, and order them into a ladder. Start practice on the lowest rung: naming the feeling, making room for it in the body, and continuing with the activity at hand anyway. Move up only once a rung feels workable, not once it feels comfortable.

fields.label: Feelings I tend to fight, listed low to high
The lowest rung I will start on
What making room for it looks like in my body
What I can still do while feeling it
Signs I am ready to move up a rung

title: Sky and Weather Self-Metaphor
summary: Uses the image of sky and weather to separate a client's sense of self from passing moods.
goal: Give the client language for being the container for a feeling rather than the feeling itself.
body_md: Introduce the image simply: the client is the sky, thoughts and feelings are the weather passing through it, and no storm, however severe, changes what the sky fundamentally is. Ask the client to describe today's weather without describing the sky as changed by it. This exercise pairs well with a values or committed action conversation once the distinction has landed.

fields.label: Today's weather, in my own words
How intense this weather feels, out of ten
What stays the same about the sky underneath it
A past storm that has already passed through
What the sky can still do while the weather happens

title: Emotion Vulnerability Factors Log
summary: Tracks the physical and situational factors that make emotions harder to manage on a given day.
goal: Spot the vulnerability factors, not just the trigger, behind an emotional spike.
body_md: Each evening, have the client rate sleep, eating, physical illness and substance use for the day alongside the day's emotional intensity. Patterns usually surface within a week: a short night or a skipped meal often explains a reaction better than the event that seemed to trigger it. Use the log to plan which vulnerability factor to shore up first.

fields.label: Sleep last night
Meals today
Physical illness or pain today
Substance use today, if any
Most intense emotion today and its cause
The vulnerability factor most worth addressing

title: Middle Path Both/And Worksheet
summary: Practices holding two seemingly opposite truths about a situation at the same time.
goal: Replace either-or thinking with a both-and statement that fits the situation better.
body_md: Give the client an either-or statement they have been stuck on, such as being a good parent or needing space, and have them draft a both-and version that holds both truths without canceling either one. This is dialectical thinking in practice: two things that feel contradictory can both be true. Practice on a few different situations until the both-and move starts to feel available in the moment, not just on paper.

fields.label: The either-or statement I keep landing on
What is true about the first side
What is true about the second side
A both-and version that holds both
A situation this week where I could try the both-and version

title: Nonjudgmental Stance Practice
summary: Practices describing a recent moment in purely factual terms, with the judgments removed.
goal: Build the mindfulness skill of separating what happened from the verdict placed on it.
body_md: Have the client describe a recent moment twice: once exactly as they first told it, judgments included, and once again with every good, bad, should and shouldn't stripped out, leaving only what a camera would have recorded. Most clients are surprised how much shorter and calmer the second version reads. This skill takes repeated practice before it shows up automatically under stress.

fields.label: The moment, told as I first would
Judging words I used (good, bad, should, terrible, etc.)
The same moment with those words removed
What is left when only the facts remain
How the two versions felt different to say

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Priorities Sheet
summary: Ranks objectives, the relationship and self-respect before a hard conversation to decide what to prioritize.
goal: Choose in advance what matters most in a conversation so the DEAR MAN script actually fits the goal.
body_md: Before a difficult conversation, have the client rank getting the objective met, keeping the relationship intact and keeping self-respect intact, since a script that tries to maximize all three at once often backfires. Naming the real priority in advance changes tone, timing and how firmly to push. Revisit after the conversation to see whether the priority held.

fields.label: The conversation coming up
How much the objective matters, out of ten
How much the relationship matters, out of ten
How much self-respect matters, out of ten
My actual priority for this one
How that priority should change my approach

title: Building Mastery Weekly Plan
summary: Schedules one activity a day the client is likely to do well, to build a sense of competence.
goal: Counter a low mood or low confidence spiral with small, engineered wins.
body_md: Have the client plan one activity each day that is slightly challenging but achievable, not a chore and not a stretch goal, and note afterward how it actually went. The aim is a felt sense of competence accumulating across the week, which tends to lift mood more reliably than rest alone. Keep the bar low enough on hard days that the plan does not become one more thing to fail at.

fields.label: Monday's planned activity and how it went
Tuesday's
Wednesday's
Thursday's
Friday's
What I noticed about my confidence across the week

title: Money Talk Agenda for Couples
summary: Structures a recurring money conversation so it stays practical instead of turning into a fight.
goal: Get both partners talking about money on a schedule instead of only in the middle of a crisis.
body_md: Money conversations that only happen during a crisis tend to go badly, so this sets a standing time and a fixed order: numbers first, feelings second, decisions last. Each partner gets uninterrupted time on the feelings section before any decision gets discussed. Keep the first few sessions short and low-stakes to build the habit before tackling a bigger decision.

fields.label: Partner A: the numbers as I see them
Partner B: the numbers as I see them
Partner A: how money feels to talk about
Partner B: how money feels to talk about
One decision we need to make
What we agreed

title: Stonewalling Time-Out Plan
summary: Builds an agreed way to pause a conversation before either partner shuts down, with a return plan.
goal: Replace an unplanned shutdown with a structured pause that both partners trust will lead back to the conversation.
body_md: Shutting down mid-conflict often feels necessary to the partner doing it and abandoning to the other, so the fix is agreeing on the pause in advance rather than in the moment. Set a physical signal, a minimum and maximum break length, and what each partner will do to calm down during it. The plan only works if the return to the conversation is guaranteed, not optional.

fields.label: Partner A: what shutting down looks like for me
Partner B: what it looks like for me
The signal we will use to call a pause
What each of us will do during the break
How long the break will be
How we will restart the conversation

title: Partner Appreciation Interview
summary: Has each partner interview the other about a specific quality they admire, in detail.
goal: Slow down a vague compliment into a specific, well-observed appreciation.
body_md: Rather than trading general compliments, have each partner pick one quality in the other and ask follow-up questions until the appreciation gets specific: a moment it showed up, why it matters, what it makes possible. Being interviewed about a strength lands differently than being told about it in passing. Switch roles so both partners get to ask and be asked.

fields.label: Partner A: the quality I admire in you
Partner A: a specific moment it showed up
Partner B: the quality I admire in you
Partner B: a specific moment it showed up
What it was like to be interviewed this way

title: In-Law and Extended Family Boundaries Sheet
summary: Maps where extended family involvement feels welcome versus intrusive for each partner.
goal: Get a couple's boundaries with extended family stated out loud instead of assumed.
body_md: Extended family friction is often less about the family and more about the couple never having agreed on the line together, leaving one partner to defend a boundary the other never signed onto. Have each partner list where involvement feels welcome and where it does not, then draft one shared position to present as a united front. Revisit before a holiday or major event.

fields.label: Partner A: where family involvement feels welcome
Partner A: where it feels intrusive
Partner B: where family involvement feels welcome
Partner B: where it feels intrusive
A shared position we can both stand behind
How we will handle it if one side pushes back

title: Couple Check-In Ritual Card
summary: Sets a short, repeatable weekly check-in with the same four questions every time.
goal: Build a low-effort ritual that catches small friction before it becomes a bigger conflict.
body_md: The value of this ritual is its repetition, so keep it to the same four questions every week rather than letting it expand into a full conversation. Sit facing each other, no phones, and take turns answering before either partner responds. Most couples find the habit itself, not any single answer, is what changes things over a few months.

fields.label: Partner A: best part of my week
Partner A: hardest part of my week
Partner B: best part of my week
Partner B: hardest part of my week
Something I need from you this coming week

title: Worry Jar Craft
summary: A child decorates a jar to hold written worries so they have somewhere to go besides the child's head.
goal: Give a child a concrete place to put a worry down instead of carrying it all day.
body_md: The parent helps the child decorate a small jar, then the two of them write worries on slips of paper together and drop them in whenever one comes up during the day. Set a regular time, after dinner works well, to open the jar together and sort which worries still need attention and which have already passed. The physical act of putting the worry in the jar is often more calming than solving it.

fields.label: A worry I want to put in the jar
How big the worry feels (small, medium, big)
Does this worry need a grown-up's help?
What I want to do with this worry now

title: Breathing Pinwheel Craft
summary: A child builds a paper pinwheel and practices slow breaths by making it spin gently.
goal: Turn a breathing skill into something a child can see working, not just feel.
body_md: The parent helps the child assemble a simple paper pinwheel, then practices blowing on it together: fast breaths spin it wildly, slow steady breaths spin it smoothly. Once the child can make it spin slowly on purpose, they have a body skill they can use without the pinwheel later, since the breath pattern is what actually matters. Keep the pinwheel somewhere visible as a reminder.

fields.label: How my breath made the pinwheel spin fast
How my breath made it spin slow and smooth
A time I could use slow breathing today
Where I will keep my pinwheel

title: My Safe People Drawing
summary: A child draws and labels the people they can go to when something feels wrong or scary.
goal: Give a child a concrete, visual map of who is safe to tell.
body_md: The parent sits with the child while they draw and name each safe person, at home, at school and elsewhere, and what each one could help with. This works well as a general safety-building activity and also as a gentle check on whether the child can name enough safe adults across enough settings. If a child discloses anything concerning while drawing, the clinician follows their reporting duties before the session ends.

fields.label: A safe person at home
A safe person at school
Another safe person somewhere else
What each person could help me with
How I would find them if I needed to

title: Feelings Weather Mobile Craft
summary: A child builds a hanging mobile with a symbol for each feeling-as-weather they experience.
goal: Give a young child a playful, ongoing way to name and display shifting feelings.
body_md: The parent helps the child cut out and hang shapes for sun, rain, storm clouds and rainbows, each one paired with a feeling word, then the child can flip a marker to whichever shape matches their current mood. Revisiting the mobile daily builds feeling vocabulary without asking the child to sit still and talk about it. Keep it somewhere the child passes often, like a bedroom door.

fields.label: The feeling that matches sun for me
The feeling that matches rain
The feeling that matches a storm cloud
The feeling that matches a rainbow
Which shape matches today

title: Brave Cape Craft
summary: A child decorates a cape and names the brave moments that earn it a new patch or symbol.
goal: Give a child a wearable, visible marker of moments they did something hard.
body_md: The parent helps the child make a simple cape from felt or fabric, then adds a new symbol each time the child names a brave moment from the week, trying something new, sitting with a big feeling, speaking up. The cape becomes a record the child can point to on harder days. Let the child choose what counts as brave rather than setting the bar for them.

fields.label: A brave thing I did this week
How my body felt right before I did it
What I told myself to help
The symbol I want to add for this one
A brave thing I want to try next

title: Coping Skills Bingo
summary: A bingo card of coping strategies the client marks off as they actually try them over a set stretch.
goal: Turn practicing a range of coping skills into a game instead of a chore.
body_md: Give the client a bingo card with a different coping skill in each square and have them mark a square only once they have actually tried it, not just read it. A full row or a blackout can be a small, agreed reward. This works well in a group format too, comparing which skills different members marked off and why.

fields.label: Skills I marked off this week
The one that surprised me most
The one I avoided and why
A square I want to try next
What a full row or blackout would mean to me

title: Thought Trap Trivia
summary: A quiz-style game where players spot the thinking trap in short example statements.
goal: Build quick recognition of common thinking traps through repetition and a bit of competition.
body_md: Read out short example statements, one at a time, and have players call out which thinking trap it shows: mind-reading, catastrophizing, all-or-nothing and so on, before revealing the answer. Keep score if the group likes competition, or just track it for fun. Close by asking each player for one real example from their own week that fits a trap from the game.

fields.label: A trap I spotted quickly
One that tricked me
My own recent example of a thinking trap
Which trap shows up most for me
What I could say instead next time

title: Pass the Prompt Circle Game
summary: A group passes a card with a reflection prompt around the circle, each person answering in turn.
goal: Get a group talking with low pressure by giving everyone the same starting prompt.
body_md: Shuffle a set of open prompt cards, one clinician-approved question per card, and pass them around the circle so each member draws and answers one before passing the deck on. Members can pass on any card without explanation, which keeps the game safe for a quieter group. Debrief by asking which prompt was hardest to answer honestly.

fields.label: A prompt I answered easily
A prompt I passed on or found hard
Something I heard from someone else that stuck with me
A prompt I would add to the deck

title: Priority Ladder Card Game
summary: Players rank a mixed set of value cards into a ladder and defend their top choices to the group.
goal: Make values clarification social and a little competitive instead of a solo worksheet.
body_md: Give each player the same deck of value cards and have them build a five-rung ladder from most to least important, then take turns defending why their top rung landed where it did. Other players can ask questions but not argue the ranking. This surfaces how differently people weigh the same set of values and often sparks better discussion than a private worksheet would.

fields.label: My top value and why it is first
A value I ranked lower than I expected
A value a group member ranked that surprised me
Whether my ladder would look different next month

title: Roll and Reflect Dice Game
summary: Rolling a die sends the client to a matching reflection prompt to answer before the next turn.
goal: Add a low-stakes element of chance to a reflection exercise so it feels lighter.
body_md: Number six prompts one through six, have the client or group roll a die, and answer whichever prompt comes up before rolling again for the next round. Repeats are fine and often land differently the second time. This is a light way to fill extra session time productively or to warm a quiet group up before a harder conversation.

fields.label: Prompt one: what I rolled and how I answered
Prompt two
Prompt three
Which prompt I would want to roll again
Which prompt I would skip if I could

title: Grounding Object Kit Sheet
summary: Helps a client choose and plan how to use a small set of grounding objects when memories intrude.
goal: Give the client something physical to reach for that pulls attention back to the present.
body_md: Have the client pick three or four small objects, a stone, a scented item, something textured, that reliably pull attention into the present, and write exactly how they will use each one. Keep this to planning and rehearsal in session rather than asking the client to relive a memory to test it. Review which objects actually got used between sessions and swap out ones that did not help.

fields.label: Object one and how I will use it
Object two and how I will use it
Object three and how I will use it
Where I will keep them
A moment this week I could have used one

title: Safety Cue Recognition Sheet
summary: Lists the present-day cues a client's body reads as danger and the safety facts that counter them.
goal: Help the client's body catch up to the fact that a past danger is not today's danger.
body_md: List a handful of everyday cues, a loud noise, a certain tone of voice, that trigger a body response left over from the past, and next to each one write the concrete facts of the present moment that are actually true right now. This stays a grounding and orienting exercise, not a request to describe what happened in detail. Keep the pace slow and check in on distress throughout.

fields.label: A cue that triggers a strong body response
What my body does in that moment
The facts that are true about right now
Something in the room I can point to that proves it

title: Present-Moment Safety Scan
summary: A brief guided scan of the five senses to anchor the client in the current, safe environment.
goal: Bring a client's attention fully into the present room when the past starts to feel close.
body_md: Walk the client through naming what they can currently see, hear, feel underfoot, smell and touch, slowly and without rushing to the next sense. This is a stabilizing, present-focused practice and is meant to be run in session first before the client tries it alone. Pair it with a brief word for the client to use as a private cue to start the scan on their own later.

fields.label: What I can see right now
What I can hear right now
What I feel under my feet or in my hands
What I can smell or taste
A word I will use to remind myself to do this

title: Window of Tolerance Check-In Card
summary: A quick, repeatable check on whether a client is inside, above or below their window of tolerance.
goal: Give the client a fast read on their own state so they can choose a matching skill.
body_md: Teach the client to notice whether they feel keyed up, shut down or steady, and to name it against their own window rather than judging it. Each state points toward a different skill: calming for keyed up, gentle activation for shut down, nothing needed when steady. If the check-in ever points toward thoughts of self-harm, that is worked through in session and 988 (call or text) is available right away, not left for later.

fields.label: How keyed up, shut down or steady I feel
What in my body tells me that

If thoughts of harming myself show up, what I will do (988, call or text)
How I feel after using the matching skill

title: Partner Support Signals Sheet
summary: Helps a couple agree on quiet signals for when one partner needs space or closeness after a hard moment.
goal: Give partners a shared, low-pressure way to ask for and offer support around trauma responses.
body_md: Trauma responses do not always come with words attached, so this gives the couple two or three simple signals, a hand on the shoulder, a specific phrase, for asking for space and for asking for closeness. Practice using the signals outside of a hard moment first so they feel familiar under stress. Review after a few weeks and adjust anything that was not landing the way it was meant to.

fields.label: Partner A: my signal for needing space
Partner A: my signal for needing closeness
Partner B: my signal for needing space
Partner B: my signal for needing closeness

title: Worry Volume Dial Craft
summary: A child builds a paper dial to show how loud a worry feels and practices turning it down.
goal: Give a young child a hands-on way to rate and lower a worry's intensity.
body_md: The parent helps the child make a simple paper dial with a spinning arrow from quiet to loud, then the child points to how loud a current worry feels. Practice a calming skill together, slow breathing works well, and have the child move the dial down afterward to see the change. Keep the dial handy so the child can use it independently once the routine feels familiar.

fields.label: A worry I have right now
Where the dial points before I calm down
The calming skill I tried
Where the dial points after

title: Worry or Wonder Sorting Game
summary: Players sort a stack of statement cards into worries versus simple wonderings, then discuss the split.
goal: Practice telling anxious prediction apart from ordinary curiosity in a light, repeatable format.
body_md: Prepare a deck of short cards, some phrased as anxious predictions and some as neutral curiosity, and have players sort each one into a worry pile or a wonder pile before discussing any they disagreed on. The discussion is usually where the learning happens, since the line between the two is not always obvious. Close by having each player add one real card from their own week.

title: Worst Case Best Case Likely Case Sheet
summary: Lays out three versions of an anxious prediction side by side to widen a narrowed focus.
goal: Pull a client's attention off the worst case alone and onto the full range of outcomes.
body_md: Anxious thinking tends to fixate on the worst case as if it were the only possible outcome, so this asks the client to write the worst, best and most likely case for the same situation side by side. Ask which case the client has actually been planning their day around. Most clients notice the likely case gets the least airtime despite being the most probable.

title: Uncertainty Tolerance Ladder
summary: Ranks situations by how much uncertainty they carry and schedules practice sitting with each rung.
goal: Build a client's capacity to tolerate not knowing, one deliberately chosen situation at a time.
body_md: List several everyday situations that involve some uncertainty, from mild to significant, and rank them into a ladder. Starting on a low rung, have the client deliberately sit with the not-knowing rather than seeking reassurance or certainty, and log how the discomfort moved over time without any action taken. Move up a rung only once the lower one feels manageable.

title: Anxious Mind as Passenger Practice
summary: Uses the bus-driver metaphor to practice acting on values while an anxious voice keeps talking.
goal: Let the client keep moving toward what matters while anxious thoughts run in the background.
body_md: Introduce the image of the client as the driver and the anxious mind as a loud passenger who does not get to grab the wheel. Ask what direction the client wants to drive regardless of what the passenger says, then plan one small action this week that moves that direction even with the passenger talking. The goal is not a quieter passenger but a driver who keeps driving.

title: Opposite Action for Low Mood Planner
summary: Plans a small opposite action to take when the urge to withdraw sets in.
goal: Give the client a concrete counter-move for the pull to isolate and stay still.
body_md: When low mood pulls toward withdrawing, staying in bed, canceling plans, this plans a small, opposite action in advance for a handful of likely moments in the coming week. Pick actions genuinely doable at a low-energy baseline rather than ambitious ones, since an unreachable plan just becomes another failure. If low mood ever comes with thoughts of ending things, that gets addressed in session directly and 988 (call or text) stays visible as an option, not something saved for later.

title: Partner Support Without Fixing Sheet
summary: Helps the non-depressed partner practice offering support that does not slide into trying to fix the mood.
goal: Give a supporting partner language that helps without adding pressure to feel better.
body_md: The partner supporting someone through low mood often defaults to solutions, which can land as pressure rather than help. This has both partners name what support actually helps, sitting nearby, a specific task taken off the plate, versus what tends to backfire, being told to think positive. Revisit after a hard week to see what held up.

fields.label: Partner with low mood: what support actually helps
Partner with low mood: what tends to backfire

title: Small Joys Treasure Hunt
summary: A child hunts around the house or yard for small things that gave a spark of good feeling that day.
goal: Help a child with low mood notice small good moments instead of only the heavy ones.
body_md: The parent walks with the child on a short hunt for anything, a toy, a color, a sound, that gave even a small spark of good feeling that day, collecting them in a basket or on a list. This is not about forcing cheerfulness but about practicing noticing, since low mood tends to filter small good moments out entirely. Keep the hunt short and let the child lead which items count.

title: Would You Rather: Low-Energy Edition
summary: A would-you-rather game built around small, low-effort choices to practice deciding when motivation is low.
goal: Keep decision-making muscles active with playful, genuinely low-stakes choices.
body_md: Low mood often makes even small decisions feel heavy, so this uses playful would-you-rather questions built around low-effort choices, a walk or a shower, tea or water, to keep the decision muscle moving without real stakes attached. Keep the tone light and let any answer be fine. Close by picking one real low-effort choice to actually follow through on today.

title: Minimum Viable Day Planner
summary: Sets a bare-minimum version of the day's tasks for when energy and motivation are at their lowest.
goal: Lower the bar enough on the hardest days that the client can still meet it.
body_md: On a hard-energy day, have the client write the smallest possible version of each task that still counts as done, one dish instead of the whole sink, five minutes instead of a full workout. The point is a day the client can actually complete, which protects momentum better than an ambitious plan abandoned by noon. Revisit the ordinary version of the plan once energy returns.

title: Task Friction Point Log
summary: Identifies the exact moment a task gets abandoned to target the real sticking point.
goal: Find where a task actually breaks down instead of treating all stalled tasks the same way.
body_md: Rather than asking why a task did not get finished in general, have the client log the exact moment it stalled, at the start, midway, or right before finishing, across several tasks. Different friction points call for different fixes: a starting problem needs a smaller first step, a midpoint stall needs a check-in cue. Use the pattern across entries to pick one fix to try next.

goal: Use values, not willpower alone, to get the client back to a task that keeps losing their attention.
body_md: Attention often drifts fastest from tasks that feel disconnected from anything that matters, so this asks the client to name a genuine, personal value the task connects to, even a boring one like filing paperwork. Write the connection down somewhere visible before starting the task. This will not fix attention on its own but gives the client something to return to when it wanders.

summary: Logs a client's prediction of how much others noticed a perceived social mistake against the likely reality.
goal: Challenge the sense that others are watching and judging as closely as it feels.
body_md: After a social situation the client felt went badly, have them write their prediction of how much others noticed and judged it, then estimate honestly how much attention the client themselves pays to other people's small stumbles. The comparison usually reveals a large gap between the felt spotlight and the likely reality. Repeat across several situations to build the pattern.

fields.label: The situation
What I think others noticed
How much attention I actually pay to other people's small mistakes
The likely gap between my prediction and reality
What I want to remember next time

title: Safety Behavior Drop Experiment
summary: Tests dropping one small safety behavior in a social situation to see what actually happens.
goal: Show the client that a safety behavior was not the thing preventing disaster.
body_md: Have the client identify one small safety behavior, rehearsing lines in advance, avoiding eye contact, and plan to drop it in one specific, low-stakes social situation this week. Predict the outcome beforehand, then compare it to what actually happened. Dropping even one safety behavior and surviving it tends to do more than any amount of discussion about why it is unnecessary.

fields.label: The safety behavior I will drop
The situation I will drop it in
My prediction beforehand
What actually happened
What this tells me about the safety behavior

title: Values-Guided Social Approach Ladder
summary: Builds a graded ladder of social situations to approach, anchored to what the client actually wants from connection.
goal: Use values as the reason to approach social situations, not the absence of anxiety.
body_md: Before building the exposure ladder itself, ask what the client actually wants from social connection, closer friendships, being known at work, and use that as the anchor for choosing which rungs matter most. Anxiety will likely be present at every rung, and that is treated as expected, not as a sign to stop. Track willingness to approach alongside anxiety level at each rung.

fields.label: What I actually want from social connection
Rung one on my ladder
Rung two
Rung three
Anxiety level versus willingness at the last rung I tried

title: Pre-Event Skills Prep Card
summary: A short pre-event routine of skills to use before a dreaded social event.
goal: Give the client a rehearsed routine to lower the spike right before a social event.
body_md: List two or three skills the client will use in the minutes before a social event, a paced breath, a grounding phrase, a reminder of one value-based reason for going, so there is a rehearsed routine instead of a scramble in the moment. Practice the routine ahead of an actual event so it feels familiar. Log how the event went compared to the pre-event dread.

fields.label: The event coming up
Skill one I will use beforehand
Skill two
My dread level before the event (0 to 10)

title: Grieving Together Differently Sheet
summary: Helps a couple name their different grieving styles so neither reads the other's pace as not caring.
goal: Prevent a couple's different grieving styles from being misread as indifference or excess.
body_md: Partners often grieve on different timelines and in different visible ways, one talking often, one going quiet, and without naming this explicitly, it can be misread as not caring or as being stuck. Have each partner describe their own style and what they need from the other during it. Revisit around anniversaries or other hard dates, when styles can shift again.

fields.label: Partner A: how I tend to grieve
Partner A: what I need from you during it
Partner B: how I tend to grieve
Partner B: what I need from you during it
A moment this month our styles clashed

title: Memory Keepsake Box Craft
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with small items and drawings connected to someone or something lost.
goal: Give a child a concrete, ongoing place to keep memories of a loss.
body_md: The parent and child decorate a small box together and add items over time, a photo, a drawing, a small object, connected to the person or pet who died. Opening the box together on hard days gives the child a way to stay connected to the memory rather than feeling like they have to avoid it. There is no wrong way to fill the box, and the child leads what goes in.

fields.label: Something I put in my box today
Why I chose it
A memory it brings up
How I feel when I open the box

title: Grief Wave Weather Report Game
summary: Players give a short weather-style report on their grief that day, then compare reports over a few sessions.
goal: Normalize grief's unpredictable rise and fall through a repeatable, playful check-in.
body_md: Each player gives a short weather report for their grief that day, stormy, partly cloudy, calm, and can add a brief reason if they want to. Repeating this over several sessions shows the group that grief moves in waves rather than a steady decline, which is often a relief to hear from peers rather than just from a clinician. Keep it brief and optional to elaborate.

fields.label: My grief weather report today
What is behind today's report, if I want to share
How my reports have changed over recent sessions
Something that helped on a stormy day

title: Unfinished Conversations Letter
summary: Has the client write what they wish they had said to someone who died.
goal: Give the client a place to say what was left unsaid.
body_md: Have the client write directly to the person who died, saying whatever was left unsaid, an apology, a thank you, an update on life since. There is no right content and no expectation of sending or reading it aloud unless the client wants to. Some clients want to write more than one over time, and that is fine.

fields.label: What I wish I had said
What I want them to know now
A memory I keep coming back to
What I want to do with this letter

title: Grief and Guilt Untangling Sheet
summary: Separates genuine responsibility from guilt that has attached itself to a loss without real basis.
goal: Sort what the client is actually responsible for from guilt that grief has generated on its own.
body_md: Grief often pulls guilt along with it, including guilt about things the client had no real control over. Have the client list each guilty thought separately, then sort it into genuine responsibility versus grief-generated guilt, using the same evidence-weighing questions used for any other belief. This is slow, sensitive work and should not be rushed toward a tidy conclusion.

fields.label: A guilty thought connected to the loss
The evidence I actually had control
The evidence I did not have control
Which category this thought falls into
What I want to do with this thought now

title: Values for This Relationship Sheet
summary: Clarifies what the client wants a specific relationship to stand for, separate from current conflict.
goal: Reconnect a strained relationship to what the client actually wants it to be about.
body_md: Ask the client to describe what they want this particular relationship to stand for, honesty, humor, reliability, independent of any current conflict, then compare that to how the relationship has actually been running lately. The gap is not evidence of failure but a direction to work toward. Pick one small action this week that moves toward the stated values.

fields.label: What I want this relationship to stand for
How it has actually been running lately
The gap between the two
One small action toward the values this week
How that action went

title: Relationship Distress Tolerance Plan
summary: Plans skills to use during an especially painful relationship moment without making it worse.
goal: Give the client a way to get through an acute relationship low point without a reaction that compounds it.
body_md: Painful relationship moments, a breakup conversation, a betrayal discovered, call for surviving the moment more than solving anything, so this plans specific skills, calling a support person, physical movement, a distraction that actually works, to use right then. Decide these in advance rather than in the moment itself. Revisit which skills actually helped afterward.

fields.label: The kind of moment this plan is for
Skill one I will use
Skill two
A support person I can call
Which skills actually helped last time

title: Attachment Needs Disclosure Sheet
summary: Has each partner name an underlying attachment need behind a recurring complaint.
goal: Get past the surface complaint to the attachment need actually driving it.
body_md: A recurring complaint, always working late, never initiating plans, often sits on top of a deeper need for reassurance, closeness or respect that never gets named directly. Have each partner trace one recurring complaint back to the need underneath it, then share the need rather than the complaint. This shift in language often changes the entire tone of the conversation that follows.

fields.label: Partner A: a recurring complaint
Partner A: the need underneath it
Partner B: a recurring complaint
Partner B: the need underneath it
How naming the need changed the conversation

title: Family Feelings Weather Check Craft
summary: A child and parent each place a marker on a shared weather chart to show how the family feels that day.
goal: Give a family a simple, visual way to check in about tension at home.
body_md: Each family member places a small marker on a shared sun-to-storm chart once a day, giving the family a quick, low-pressure way to notice tension building before it becomes a bigger issue. The child gets equal say in the chart, which itself communicates that their read on the household matters. Talk briefly about any storm markers, but do not force a full conversation if no one is ready.

fields.label: Where I placed my marker today
What is behind my marker, if I want to share
Where other family members placed theirs
Something that could move the weather toward sun

title: Repair Attempt Recognition Game
summary: Partners practice spotting and rewarding each other's small repair attempts during a mock disagreement.
goal: Build a couple's ability to notice and accept a repair attempt in real time.
body_md: Have the couple act out a mild, scripted disagreement and practice inserting small repair attempts, a joke, a softer tone, reaching for a hand, then pause and name out loud when a repair attempt happened and whether it landed. Missed repair attempts are common and worth discussing without blame. Repeat with a slightly different scenario to build the recognition habit.

fields.label: A repair attempt I made
Whether my partner caught it
A repair attempt my partner made

title: Body Safety and Choice Reclaiming Sheet
summary: Lists small, everyday choices the client can make about their own body and space to rebuild a sense of control.
goal: Rebuild a felt sense of choice and control over the client's own body, in small everyday ways.
body_md: List small, ordinary choices the client already has about their own body and personal space, what to wear, whether to hug someone hello, how close to sit to another person, and note which ones currently feel accessible versus which still feel hard to claim. This stays focused on present-day choice and control, never on recounting what happened. Build from the choices that already feel available.

fields.label: A choice about my body that feels accessible right now
A choice that still feels hard to claim
What would help make it more accessible
