title: Appearance Comparison Interrupt Sheet
summary: Interrupts an in-the-moment appearance comparison with a short, practiced redirect.
goal: Give the client a fast response to reach for the moment a comparison starts rather than after it spirals.
body_md: Ask the client to notice the exact moment an appearance comparison starts, then practice a short redirect, such as naming one function-based thing about their own body or shifting attention to the present task. The goal is interrupting early, before the comparison has a chance to spiral into a longer, harsher thought chain. Rehearse the redirect a few times in session before expecting it to hold up in the moment.

fields.label: A recent moment a comparison started

title: Emotion Regulation Skills Menu
summary: A personalized menu of emotion regulation skills sorted by which emotion each one targets.
goal: Give the client a ready reference instead of trying to recall a skill mid-emotion.
body_md: Work through the client's usual difficult emotions one at a time and list which skill actually helps with each: opposite action for one, a self-soothe option for another, a cognitive skill for a third. A skill that works for anger will not always work for sadness, and building the menu in advance saves the client from improvising while already dysregulated. Keep the finished menu somewhere quick to reach.

fields.label: An emotion I regularly struggle to manage

title: Low-Mood Day Check-In Script
summary: A short script partners use on a low-mood day to check in without either one needing to fix anything.
goal: Give partners words to reach for on a hard day instead of silence or over-managing.
body_md: On a day the depressed partner is struggling, have the other partner ask a short, fixed set of questions: how the day has been, what would help right now, and whether they want company or space. The depressed partner answers as honestly as they can, even I don't know. Using the same script each time takes the guesswork out of a hard moment for both partners.

fields.label: Partner A: how the day has been
Partner A: what would help right now
Partner A: company or space right now

title: Small Talk Bingo
summary: A bingo card of small talk topics group members practice bringing up with each other during the session.
goal: Turn practicing small talk into a low-pressure, structured game instead of an open-ended ordeal.
body_md: Give each member a bingo card of common small talk topics and have them mingle, marking a square each time they successfully bring one up with another member. Because the topic is assigned by the card, no one has to come up with what to say on the spot, which is usually the hardest part. Debrief on which squares felt easiest and which took the most nerve.

fields.label: A square that felt easy

title: Forgiveness Ledger
summary: Separates what a client is ready to let go of from what still needs time, one grievance at a time.
goal: Give the client language for partial forgiveness instead of an all-or-nothing verdict.
body_md: Have the client list a grievance, what happened, and what forgiving it would and would not mean, since it does not mean approval or renewed contact. Some entries will sort into ready, others into not yet, and both are fine outcomes. Revisit the ledger every few weeks rather than pushing for resolution in one sitting.

What forgiving this would NOT mean for me
Where this sits right now: ready, partway, or not yet

title: Overcommitment Pattern Map
summary: Traces the pattern behind a client's yeses to find where overcommitment keeps starting.
goal: Help the client spot the moment they say yes before they have decided to.
body_md: Walk through three recent times the client agreed to something they later regretted, noting who asked, what they felt in the moment, and what they said instead of pausing. A pattern usually shows up fast: a person, a feeling, or a phrase that predicts the yes. Use the map to rehearse a delay line for next time rather than an outright no.

fields.label: A recent time I said yes and regretted it

title: Weekend Reset Planner
summary: Plans a weekend around what actually restores a client instead of what fills the time.
goal: Turn a client's weekend from another to-do list into deliberate recovery.
body_md: Have the client separate weekend hours into obligations that cannot move and open hours that can, then choose two or three restorative activities for the open hours before the week's chores creep in. Ask what usually eats the open hours by default, since naming the default is often more useful than the plan itself. Review Monday morning what actually happened against the plan.

fields.label: Obligations that cannot move this weekend

title: Motivation Dip Troubleshooter
summary: Sorts a motivation slump into fatigue, unclear goals, or a mismatch with the client's values.
goal: Help the client sort out what kind of motivation dip this is instead of just pushing through it.
body_md: Motivation dips have different causes and different fixes, so before troubleshooting, ask whether this looks more like fatigue, a goal that has gone fuzzy, or a task that stopped connecting to anything the client cares about. Each answer points to a different next step: rest, clarifying the goal, or reconnecting to a value. Avoid the client's instinct to treat every dip as a discipline problem.

title: Mental Filter Spotlight
summary: Has the client find the one negative detail their mind kept while the rest of the day disappeared.
goal: Show the client how a mental filter edits out everything that does not fit the low mood.
body_md: Ask the client to describe a day, then ask what stuck with them by evening. Usually one flawed moment survives the edit while several fine or good ones do not, and naming that gap in front of the client is often the useful part. Practice rebuilding the fuller day from memory, moment by moment, to weaken the filter's grip.

title: Should Statements Rewrite
summary: Rewrites a client's should and must statements into flexible preferences they can actually live with.
goal: Loosen the grip of a rigid rule before it turns into guilt or resentment.
body_md: Collect a handful of the client's should and must statements, then rewrite each one as a preference: what they would like, and why the original rule sets an unreachable standard. Notice which shoulds are aimed at the client and which are aimed at other people, since both tend to cause trouble. Keep the rewritten versions somewhere the client can find them when the old rule resurfaces.

title: Evidence For and Against Card
summary: A quick two-column card for weighing the evidence on both sides of a stuck thought.
goal: Give the client a faster tool than a full thought record for a thought that will not settle.
body_md: This is the pocket version of a thought record for a client who will not sit down and do the full six columns: name the thought, list what supports it, list what does not, then write a fairer statement that accounts for both columns. Keep the card somewhere accessible so it gets used in the moment rather than saved for session. A few uses usually loosen the thought's grip.

title: Thought Record Shortcut Card
summary: A three-line version of a thought record built for use between sessions, not instead of one.
goal: Keep the thought-record habit alive on a week the client will not do the full worksheet.
body_md: Some weeks the full thought record is too much, so this asks for only three things: the situation, the automatic thought, and one alternative thought that also fits the facts. It is meant to keep the skill warm, not replace the longer version entirely. Bring the shortcut cards into session and expand the interesting ones together.

title: Unwanted Guest Metaphor
summary: Uses the image of an unwanted houseguest to explore making room for a difficult feeling.
goal: Practice hosting a difficult feeling without giving it control of the house.
body_md: Ask the client to imagine the feeling as a guest who showed up uninvited and refuses to leave; fighting the guest at the door takes all day, while going about the house anyway, guest included, leaves room for a life. Notice what the client's usual strategy with the guest looks like: arguing, hiding, or appeasing. Practice imagining a day where the guest is present but not in charge.

title: Values vs Goals Sort
summary: Sorts a client's list of goals into the underlying values that give each one its pull.
goal: Show the client the difference between a goal they can finish and a value they keep living by.
body_md: Have the client list several goals, then ask what each one is in service of; a goal is a checkbox, a value is a direction that stays useful even after the box is checked. Some goals will turn out to serve no clear value, which is worth noticing too. Use the sorted list to choose which goal to prioritize based on the value behind it, not just urgency.

title: Willingness Thermometer
summary: Rates a client's willingness to feel a specific emotion, situation by situation, across a week.
goal: Track willingness as its own skill instead of waiting for a feeling to become comfortable.
body_md: Before a situation that usually triggers avoidance, have the client rate their willingness to feel whatever shows up, from fighting it off to making full room for it. Willingness is not the same as wanting the feeling or feeling calm about it, and the rating can move independently of both. Compare ratings across the week to see whether willingness is growing with practice.

title: Two Mountains Metaphor
summary: Compares the mountain a client is climbing to reach comfort against the one worth climbing for its own view.
goal: Redirect effort from chasing comfort toward a climb the client actually values.
body_md: Describe two mountains: one climbed only to feel better, which never quite has a summit, and one climbed because the view itself matters, discomfort included. Ask which mountain the client has been climbing lately and what it would mean to choose the other one on purpose. This is not about ignoring pain, only about choosing what the effort is for.

title: Mind as Radio Station Practice
summary: Practices noticing the mind's running commentary the way a person notices background radio.
goal: Build distance from automatic self-talk without arguing with it.
body_md: Ask the client to imagine their thoughts as a radio station playing in the background, always broadcasting something, whether or not anyone is tuned in. The goal is not to turn the station off but to notice when it has taken over the foreground and gently turn the volume back down. Practice narrating a stretch of the day as the station is now saying, to build the habit of noticing.

goal: Track skills use across the week instead of relying on memory in session.
body_md: Each day, have the client note one moment a skill was needed, which one they used, and how it went, even a partial or failed attempt. The point is not a perfect record but a running sense of which skills are actually getting used and which stay theoretical. Bring the diary into session to decide what to practice next.

title: Personal Crisis Survival Kit Card

goal: Cut the decision time between crisis and skill down to almost nothing.
duration: 20 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Rather than teach one crisis skill, build a short, personal list of the two or three that have actually worked for this client before, in the order they are willing to try them. Test the card at a lower distress level first so using it under real pressure is a rehearsal, not a first attempt. Include 988, call or text, as the last line on the card.

title: Effectiveness Over Being Right Practice
summary: Practices choosing the response that works over the response that proves a point.
goal: Shift the client's goal in a hard moment from winning to getting what actually matters.
body_md: Walk through a recent conflict and ask two separate questions: what would have proven the client right, and what would have actually gotten them what they wanted. The two answers are often different, and dialectical thinking means the client can be right and still choose effectiveness. Practice picking the effective option even when the urge to be right is strong.

title: Skills Chain Substitution Plan
summary: Takes a chain analysis one step further by planning a skill to swap in at the weakest link.
goal: Turn an already-completed chain analysis into a concrete plan for next time.
body_md: Starting from a chain the client has already mapped, find the single link where a different choice would have changed the outcome most, then attach a specific skill to that exact link rather than a vague intention to do better. Rehearse the substitution out loud before the client leaves session. Revisit after the next similar chain to see whether the substitution held.

title: Difficult Topic Pre-Talk Agreement
summary: Sets ground rules together before a hard conversation instead of discovering them mid-fight.
goal: Give both partners a shared structure to fall back on when a topic gets heated.
body_md: Before raising the actual topic, have both partners agree on how long the conversation will run, a signal either can use to pause, and what happens if it gets too heated to continue. Doing this while calm means neither partner is negotiating ground rules in the middle of a spike. Revisit the agreement afterward and adjust anything that did not hold.

title: Solo Time and We Time Balance Sheet
summary: Maps how much time each partner gets alone against time spent together, and where the balance feels off.
goal: Make an unspoken imbalance between independence and togetherness visible and negotiable.
body_md: Have each partner estimate their current solo time and couple time in an average week, then rate whether each feels like enough, too much, or too little. Mismatches here are common and rarely about wanting less of the other person; often one partner recharges alone and the other recharges together. Use the sheet to negotiate a small, concrete adjustment rather than a full overhaul.

summary: Builds a graded ladder of situations, ranked by how much willingness to feel panic sensations each one takes.
goal: Practice willingness in graded steps instead of an all-or-nothing leap.
body_md: List situations that bring on panic sensations, from mildly uncomfortable to most avoided, and rank them by how much willingness each one would take right now. Start practicing willingness at the bottom of the ladder rather than the top, since a small, winnable step builds more confidence than a large one that fails. Move up the ladder only as willingness genuinely grows.

title: Panic Descent Tracker
summary: Tracks how long a panic episode actually takes to fade once it peaks, building a record over time.
goal: Give the client their own evidence for how long panic actually lasts, not how long it feels like it lasts.
duration: Ongoing, a few minutes per episode
body_md: After a panic episode, have the client note the peak intensity and roughly how long it took to noticeably fade, without needing to catch every detail in the moment. Panic almost always peaks and starts descending within minutes, but it rarely feels that way while it is happening. A growing log of real descent times becomes more convincing than being told the timeline in the abstract.

title: Panic Trigger Environment Map
summary: Maps the places, times and situations where panic episodes have actually occurred.
goal: Separate real situational patterns from the sense that panic could strike absolutely anywhere.
body_md: Have the client list recent panic episodes along with the place, time of day and what was happening just before each one. Panic often feels completely random, but a map across several episodes frequently reveals a pattern the client had not noticed. Use the map to decide where extra preparation or support might help most, without turning it into a reason to avoid those places.

title: Parent Assumed Intent Check
summary: Tests a parent's assumption about why their child misbehaved against other explanations that fit just as well.
goal: Slow down a parent's story about a child's motive before it drives a harsher response than needed.
body_md: Ask the parent what they believe their child's misbehavior meant, defiance, disrespect, manipulation, then list other explanations that fit the same facts, such as tiredness, a skill the child has not built yet, or a need not being met. Parents often respond to the story about the behavior more than the behavior itself. Practice picking the most generous explanation that still fits the facts before responding next time.

title: Values-Based Discipline Pause
summary: Chooses a discipline response that fits the parent's values, not just the urge of the moment.
goal: Give a parent a values check to run through before reacting in a heated discipline moment.
body_md: Ask what kind of parent the client wants to be in a hard moment, then compare that to how a recent discipline moment actually went. The gap is not a verdict on the parent, just information about where the urge of the moment took over. Practice naming the value out loud, even silently, in the pause before responding next time.

title: Parent Wise Mind Pause
summary: Gives a parent a short pause practice to find wise mind before responding to a child's behavior.
goal: Interrupt an emotional-mind reaction with a brief, practiced pause before responding to a child.
duration: 10 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Teach the parent a short pause, a breath and a single grounding question, what does this moment actually need, to use in the gap between a child's behavior and the parent's response. This is not about suppressing the emotion, only about not acting straight from it. Practice the pause in a calm role-play before expecting it to hold up during an actual flashpoint.

title: Discipline Alignment Conversation
summary: Gets both parents on the same page about consequences before the next discipline moment, not during it.
goal: Prevent a child from playing mismatched parents against each other by aligning ahead of time.
body_md: Ask each parent to describe how they typically respond to a common misbehavior, then find where the approaches match and where they genuinely differ. Disagreeing in front of the child usually costs more than picking an imperfect but shared approach. Agree on one consistent response for one common situation and revisit after trying it for a week.

title: Would You Say That to a Friend? Parent Game
summary: A parent group rewrites a harsh line they have said to their child into one they would say to a friend's kid.
goal: Use a quick reframing game to build a gentler, still-clear discipline voice.
body_md: Each parent shares a line they have said in frustration, then the group rewrites it as something they would say to a friend's child in the same situation, keeping the same limit but changing the tone. Notice out loud how the rewritten version still sets the limit without the harshness. Take the rewritten lines home to try during the next real moment.

title: Big Sibling Helper Craft
summary: An older sibling decorates a helper badge and picks small ways to help with a new baby.
goal: Give an older sibling a positive role during a family transition instead of feeling displaced.
body_md: The parent and older child decorate a simple badge together, then pick a short list of small, real jobs the child can do to help with the new baby, such as choosing an outfit or singing a song during a diaper change. Praise the helping specifically rather than just being good. Check in regularly about how the child is feeling about all the change, not just the helping.

title: New Parent Worry Sorting Sheet
summary: Sorts a new parent's worries into ones worth a plan and ones that just need to be noticed and set down.
goal: Reduce the load of constant worry by separating what needs action from what does not.
body_md: Have the new parent list current worries, then sort each into one that has a concrete next step and one that is really just uncertainty running on a loop. The first group gets a short plan; the second group gets practice noticing and setting down, since planning has nothing left to grab onto there. Revisit the sorted list weekly as new worries replace old ones.

goal: Give a new parent soothing options that actually fit a newborn's schedule, not a full self-care routine.
body_md: Build the self-soothe menu around what is actually available in a two-minute window with a baby nearby: a scent kept by the changing table, a song, a warm mug within reach. Skip anything that requires leaving the room or a long stretch of time, since that version of self-care usually goes unused right now. Revisit the menu as the baby's schedule changes.

title: Birth Recovery Expectations Reset
summary: Compares what a client expected postpartum recovery to feel like against how it has actually gone.
goal: Close the gap between an unrealistic recovery expectation and what is actually normal and survivable.
body_md: Have the client write down what they expected recovery to look like by this point and what it has actually looked like, in plain terms. The gap is often the source of a lot of quiet shame, and naming it plainly tends to loosen that. Ask what a more realistic expectation for the next stretch would sound like.

summary: A group game where new parents trade one true surprise and one common myth about early parenthood.
goal: Normalize the surprises of new parenthood through shared, low-stakes group disclosure.
body_md: Going around the group, each parent shares one thing about early parenthood that genuinely surprised them and one myth they had believed beforehand, and the group guesses which is which before finding out. The game format lowers the pressure of admitting something feels harder than expected. Debrief on what it was like to hear how common the surprises are.

title: Self-Worth Beyond Achievement Practice
summary: Separates a client's sense of worth from their most recent achievement or failure.
goal: Loosen the tie between self-worth and performance so a bad day does not define the client.
body_md: Ask the client to notice how much their sense of worth moved after a recent win and after a recent setback, then ask what stayed the same underneath both. Worth tied entirely to achievement means it is never stable for long. Practice naming something true about the client that does not depend on the outcome of anything.

title: Nonjudgmental Self-Talk Practice
summary: Catches a judging word aimed at the self and rewrites it as a plain, descriptive statement.
goal: Practice describing behavior instead of judging the self for it.
body_md: Have the client notice a recent moment of harsh self-talk, identify the judging word, such as stupid, lazy, or failure, and rewrite the statement using only what actually happened, without the label. This is a specific application of a nonjudgmental stance turned toward the self rather than outward. Practice catching the judging word earlier each time it shows up.

title: Reflected Worth Check-In
summary: Checks in on how each partner's recent comments have landed on the other's sense of worth.
goal: Catch an unintentional pattern of comments that chip at a partner's self-esteem before it settles in.
body_md: Ask each partner to name a recent comment, even a joking one, that landed harder than intended, and a recent comment that genuinely helped their sense of worth. Most partners are unaware of the specific comments that stick. Agree on one thing each partner will say more of and one they will watch for going forward.

title: Strength Swap Circle
summary: Each group member shares a strength someone else named in them that they had not noticed themselves.
goal: Build a fuller, more accurate self-view using strengths the group actually observed.
body_md: Before the game, collect one strength each member has shown in group from the facilitator's own notes or quick peer input, then reveal them one at a time without saying who it is about until the member guesses. Being handed a strength observed by someone else often lands differently than naming one for yourself. Close by asking each member to say the strength out loud in their own words.

title: Self-Esteem Weather Log
summary: Tracks how much a client's sense of self-worth swings from day to day and what tends to drive the swings.
goal: Show the client that self-esteem naturally fluctuates rather than being a fixed, failing trait.
body_md: Each day, have the client rate their overall sense of self-worth and note anything that seemed to move it up or down. Most clients discover their self-esteem moves with events and comparisons rather than staying low consistently, which is itself useful information. Use the week's pattern to spot the specific triggers worth working on directly.

title: Social Event Support Plan for Partners
summary: Plans in advance how a partner can help before, during and after a social event that brings on anxiety.
goal: Give both partners a concrete plan instead of improvising support in the middle of an event.
body_md: Before an upcoming event, ask the anxious partner what kind of support actually helps at each stage, before leaving, once there, and on the way home, and ask the other partner what they can realistically offer at each point. Agree on a subtle signal for when the anxious partner needs a break. Debrief afterward on what worked so the plan improves for next time.

title: Social Anxiety Cost of Avoidance Sheet
summary: Tallies what avoiding a social situation actually cost against the short-term relief it gave.
goal: Make the long-term cost of social avoidance as visible as the short-term relief that drives it.
body_md: Have the client list a few recent situations they avoided because of social anxiety, note the relief avoidance gave right away, and separately note what it cost over the following days or weeks: a missed connection, an opportunity, a growing sense of isolation. The relief column usually wins in the moment while the cost column wins over time. Use the comparison to choose one situation worth approaching differently next time.

title: Post-Social Self-Validation Card
summary: Has the client validate their own effort after a social event instead of only reviewing what went wrong.
goal: Balance the post-event replay with credit for the effort it took to show up at all.
body_md: Right after a social event, before the rumination has a chance to take over, have the client write down what it took to show up and one thing that went fine, alongside anything that felt awkward. This is not about ignoring what went wrong, only about not letting it stand alone. Use the card as a fixed first step before any longer post-event review.

title: Social Anxiety Attention Trap Log
summary: Logs the moments during a social situation when attention turned inward instead of outward.
goal: Show the client how often self-focused attention, not the situation itself, drives the discomfort.
body_md: After a social situation, have the client note moments they noticed their attention turn toward monitoring themselves, how they looked, sounded, or were being judged, versus moments they were tuned into the actual conversation. Self-focused attention tends to amplify anxiety and cost the client information about how the interaction is really going. Use the log to plan where to practice redirecting attention outward.

title: Grief Wave Distress Tolerance Card
summary: A card of distress tolerance skills sized for the sudden waves of grief that can hit without warning.
goal: Give the client fast options for the moment a wave of grief arrives, not just the planned ones.
duration: 15 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Grief waves often arrive without warning, in a store, a meeting, a quiet moment, so build a short card of skills that work fast and do not require leaving wherever the client is. Distinguish these from longer coping strategies that need privacy or time, since a wave rarely gives that much notice. Test the card during a smaller wave first.

title: Carrying Grief and Living Forward Practice
summary: Practices holding grief and a moving-forward life at the same time, rather than treating them as opposites.
goal: Loosen the idea that moving forward means leaving the person or loss behind.
body_md: Ask the client what moving forward seems to require giving up, then explore whether grief and a forward-moving life can actually sit side by side rather than trading off. Most clients carry an unspoken rule that healing means forgetting, which this gently questions. Practice naming one value-based step forward the client can take while still carrying the grief, not after it is gone.

title: Grief Support Circle Map
summary: Maps who in a client's life can hold which part of their grief, since no one person can hold all of it.
goal: Spread the weight of grief across a wider circle instead of resting it all on one relationship.
body_md: Have the client list people in their life and what each one is actually good for around this loss: practical help, sitting in silence, talking about the person who died, distraction. Expecting one person to be everything often strains that relationship and leaves other kinds of support unused. Use the map to reach out more deliberately for what is actually needed.

title: Remembering Ritual Craft
summary: A child and parent create a small, repeatable ritual for remembering someone who died.
goal: Give a child a concrete, repeatable way to stay connected to a memory instead of one that only happens once.
body_md: The parent and child choose something simple that can be repeated, like watering a plant chosen in the person's memory or looking at a photo together on a set day, and agree on when they will do it. A repeatable ritual gives grief a regular, predictable place to go instead of showing up unexpectedly. Let the child decide how long they want to keep the ritual going.

title: Grief Thought Sorting Sheet
summary: Sorts a client's grief-related thoughts into ones worth sitting with and ones worth gently questioning.
goal: Help the client tell painful-but-true grief thoughts apart from distorted ones adding extra suffering.
body_md: Have the client list thoughts that have come up since the loss, then sort each into one that is simply a true, painful part of grieving and one that adds extra suffering through distortion, such as an all-or-nothing judgment about how they are grieving. The first group gets space and time; the second gets gently questioned. Revisit the sort as new thoughts come up.

title: Relationship Expectations Inventory
summary: Lists what a client expects from a relationship and where those expectations were formed.
goal: Trace an unspoken expectation back to its source before deciding whether it still fits.
body_md: Have the client list expectations they hold for a close relationship, then ask where each one came from: a family pattern, a past relationship, a cultural message. An expectation that made sense in its original context does not always fit the current relationship, and naming the source often loosens its grip. Sort the list into expectations worth keeping and ones worth revisiting.

title: Assumed Intent Log

goal: Slow down a confident story about someone's intent before it drives a reaction.
body_md: Have the client write down what they assumed someone meant by a recent action, then, when possible, check that assumption against what the person actually says they meant. The gap between assumed and actual intent is often wide enough to be worth noticing on its own, even without checking. Use the log to build the habit of holding an assumption loosely until it is confirmed.

goal: Give a child a rehearsed script for repairing a friendship instead of avoiding the friend afterward.

Rehearsing the words in a low-stakes moment makes them easier to reach for during a real one. Check in after the child tries a real repair to see how it went.

goal: Help group members clarify what they actually value in a relationship, out loud and together.

Differences in ranking are a useful discussion point, not a disagreement to resolve. Ask what it would look like to bring more of a top-ranked quality into a current relationship.

goal: Separate the interpretation of a conflict from the facts of what actually happened.

goal: Give the client repeated, everyday evidence of safety and choice in the present.

goal: Replace judgment about coping strategies with acknowledgment that they served a real purpose.
