title: Good Enough Parent Values Practice
summary: Helps a new parent define what good enough actually means to them, apart from an impossible standard.
goal: Help a new parent replace an impossible standard with a workable, values-based one.
body_md: New parents often measure themselves against an impossible standard of doing everything right, and this practice has them instead define what good enough parenting means in their own words, rooted in values like presence or warmth rather than flawless execution. Revisit the definition on hard days, since the impossible standard tends to creep back in during exhaustion.

fields.label: The impossible standard I have been holding myself to

title: New Parent Intimacy Timeline Sheet
summary: Has both partners talk openly about how physical and emotional intimacy has shifted since the baby arrived.
goal: Give a couple language for discussing how intimacy has changed since becoming parents.
body_md: Physical and emotional intimacy often shift substantially after a baby arrives, exhaustion, recovery and a changed sense of self all playing a part, and unspoken assumptions about when or whether things will go back to how they were can create distance. This sheet has both partners describe how intimacy currently feels and what they each need right now, without a deadline attached to any particular change.

fields.label: Partner A: how intimacy currently feels to me
Partner A: what I need right now
Partner B: how intimacy currently feels to me

title: New Parent PLEASE Skills Check
summary: Rates sleep, food and physical care against the PLEASE skills to flag what is slipping in early parenthood.
goal: Help a new parent notice which basic physical needs are slipping during a demanding stretch.
body_md: Early parenthood can make even the most basic physical needs, sleep, food, treating illness, hard to keep up with, and those slips make emotional regulation much harder on top of an already demanding stretch. This check has a client rate each PLEASE area quickly, then pick just one to focus on improving this week rather than trying to fix everything at once.

fields.label: My sleep this week, rated 0 to 10

title: Inner Critic Volume Dial Sheet
summary: Has a client rate how loud their inner critic gets across different situations to find a pattern.
goal: Help a client map when their inner critic gets loudest instead of treating it as constant.
body_md: A client's inner critic is rarely equally loud all the time; certain situations, a mistake at work, a comparison with a peer, tend to turn the volume up further than others. This sheet has a client rate the critic's volume across a handful of situations from the week and look for what those loudest moments have in common. Spotting the pattern gives a specific place to practice a quieter response.

fields.label: A situation from this week and the critic's volume, 0 to 10

title: Evidence for the Whole Self Log
summary: Logs moments that reflect strengths, effort and values, not just outcomes, to widen self-evaluation.
goal: Help a client build evidence for a fuller self-picture beyond performance and outcomes alone.
body_md: A client's self-evaluation can narrow down to outcomes only, a grade, a sale, a compliment, while effort, kindness and values-consistent action go unrecorded entirely. This log has a client note one entry each day that reflects something about who they are beyond an outcome, an act of patience, a value they lived by, a moment of honesty. Read the week's entries back together in session.

title: Worthiness Without Conditions Practice
summary: Practices naming a sense of worth that does not depend on achievement, appearance or approval.
goal: Help a client explore a sense of worth that holds regardless of external conditions.
body_md: A client's sense of worth is often quietly conditional, tied to achievement, appearance or others' approval, without that condition ever being named out loud. This practice has a client name the conditions they have been running on, then explore what an unconditional sense of worth might mean instead, not earned, simply present. This is exploratory work and rarely resolves in a single session.

fields.label: A condition I have been placing on my own worth

title: Self-Kindness in the Mirror Practice
summary: Pairs a brief mirror moment with a self-validating statement instead of self-criticism.
goal: Give a client a brief daily practice of pairing a mirror moment with self-validation instead of critique.
body_md: A mirror moment often triggers an automatic critique, so this practice has a client pause during one ordinary mirror check each day and pair it with a short self-validating statement instead, something true and kind rather than flattering. Keep the statement simple and specific rather than a big general compliment, since specific statements tend to feel more believable and land better.

title: Strength Spotting Bingo
summary: A group fills a bingo card by spotting different strengths in themselves and others during the session.
goal: Use a bingo format to help a group notice strengths in themselves and each other.
body_md: Each player gets a bingo card with different strengths listed, patience, creativity, honesty, and marks a square whenever they notice that strength in themselves or a fellow player during the session's activities. The format turns strength-spotting into something active rather than a static list. Debrief on which strengths were easiest and hardest to notice in oneself.

fields.label: A strength I marked in myself

title: Post-Event Replay Interrupt Sheet
summary: Has a client catch a post-event mental replay and redirect to a planned activity instead.
goal: Help a client interrupt a mental replay of a social event before it spirals.
body_md: After a social event, a client's mind can loop back over every moment searching for what went wrong, a process that tends to feed anxiety rather than resolve it. This sheet has a client notice when a replay starts, note it briefly, and redirect to a planned activity instead, kept ready in advance. Reviewing how often replays got interrupted across a week helps build the habit further.

fields.label: The event my mind kept replaying

title: Safety Behavior Reduction Plan
summary: Lists small safety behaviors used in social situations and plans to gradually drop them one at a time.
goal: Help a client gradually reduce the small safety behaviors that quietly maintain social anxiety.
body_md: Small safety behaviors, avoiding eye contact, rehearsing every sentence, holding a drink for something to do with your hands, can quietly keep social anxiety in place by preventing a client from learning that the feared outcome would not happen anyway. This plan has a client list their own safety behaviors and choose one to drop in a low-stakes situation first, tracking what actually happens without it.

fields.label: A safety behavior I use in social situations

title: Post-Social Skills Debrief Card
summary: A short structured debrief for after a social event, balancing what went well with what felt hard.
goal: Give a client a balanced way to review a social event instead of only cataloguing what went wrong.
body_md: Without structure, a debrief after a social event tends to become a one-sided list of everything that went wrong, so this card asks for both sides deliberately: one thing that went fine or well, and one thing that felt hard, kept to a fixed short format. Doing this consistently after events helps counter the pull toward an entirely negative recap.

fields.label: The event I am debriefing

title: Brave Hello Practice Chart
summary: A child tracks small brave social moments, like a hello or a question, on a simple chart.
goal: Give a socially anxious child a way to notice and build on small brave social moments.
body_md: For a child who finds social moments hard, even a small hello to a classmate can take real courage, and this chart gives them a way to notice and track those small brave moments rather than only measuring themselves against bigger goals like making a new friend. The parent's role is celebrating the small moment itself, not pushing for a bigger one right away.

fields.label: A brave social moment I had today

title: Would They Even Notice Game
summary: A group compares predicted versus actual audience attention to a small social slip using a quick game format.
goal: Use a light group game to test whether others notice a small social slip as much as it feels like they would.
body_md: Socially anxious clients often overestimate how much other people notice or remember a small slip, a stumble over words, a quiet moment, and this game has players predict how much a group would notice a minor scripted slip, then compares that prediction with what group members actually report noticing afterward. The gap between predicted and actual attention is usually the point that lands.

title: Grief Comes in Waves Log
summary: Logs the timing and intensity of grief waves across a week to show they rise and pass rather than build steadily.
goal: Help a client see that grief arrives in waves rather than as one steadily building weight.
body_md: Grief can feel like a single, ever-growing weight, which makes each new wave feel like a setback rather than a normal part of the pattern, so this log has a client note when a wave of grief arrives, how intense it is, and how long it lasts across a week. Looking at the pattern together often shows waves rising and passing rather than one continuous climb, which can be a relief on its own.

fields.label: When a wave of grief arrived today

title: Grieving on Different Timelines Sheet
summary: Helps a couple name how each partner's grief looks different and what support each actually needs.
goal: Give a couple language for the fact that partners often grieve differently and on different timelines.
body_md: Partners grieving the same loss often move through it differently, one wanting to talk, the other wanting quiet, one ready to laugh again sooner than the other, and without a shared understanding this difference can feel like a lack of care rather than simply a difference. This sheet has each partner describe their own grief and what support actually helps, so neither has to guess or feel judged for grieving differently.

fields.label: Partner A: what my grief tends to look like
Partner A: what actually helps me right now

title: Remembering Together Drawing
summary: A child and parent draw a memory of the person or pet who died to make space for remembering.
goal: Give a child a gentle, concrete way to hold onto a memory of someone or something they lost.
body_md: A young child may not have words ready for a loss, and this activity gives them a concrete way in instead: drawing a favorite memory together with the parent, talking about it as they draw. Let the child lead how much or little they want to say. Keep the drawing somewhere the child can return to when they want to remember again.

title: Grief Question Jar Game
summary: A group draws gentle open-ended questions about loss from a jar to spark conversation at their own pace.
goal: Give a grief group a low-pressure way to open conversation about loss at each person's own pace.
body_md: Talking directly about a loss can feel too exposed for some group members, so this game has players draw a gentle open-ended question from a jar, such as what they miss most or a tradition connected to the person, and answer only as much as feels comfortable. Passing is always allowed. The structure gives quieter members an entry point without forcing anyone to share more than they choose.

title: Bids for Connection Tracking Sheet
summary: Has both partners notice and log small bids for attention and how often each is turned toward.
goal: Help a couple notice how often small bids for connection are turned toward versus missed.
body_md: A bid for connection can be as small as a comment about the weather or a glance across the room, and whether it gets turned toward, turned away from, or missed entirely tends to add up over time far more than any single big gesture. This sheet has both partners log a few bids they made or noticed each day and whether they were turned toward. Reviewing the week together usually surfaces small, fixable patterns.

fields.label: Partner A: a bid I made and what happened
Partner A: a bid I noticed from my partner and how I responded

title: Unspoken Rules of the Relationship Sheet
summary: Surfaces the unstated rules each partner has been operating on to check whether both actually agree to them.
goal: Help a couple name the unspoken rules quietly running their relationship and decide together whether to keep them.
body_md: Every relationship accumulates unspoken rules over time, who initiates plans, who apologizes first, what topics are off-limits, and partners often follow them without ever agreeing to them out loud. This sheet has each partner name a few rules they have noticed themselves following, then discuss together which ones both actually want to keep. Some surprise both partners once said out loud.

title: Relationship Thought Trap Spotter
summary: Has a client catch a thinking trap specifically about their relationship, like mind reading a partner's intent.
goal: Help a client notice thinking traps that specifically distort how they read their partner's behavior.
body_md: Thinking traps show up in relationships just as they do elsewhere, assuming a partner's silence means anger, or that one late reply means the relationship is failing, and these traps can drive a reaction before the client ever checks the facts. This sheet has a client catch a relationship-specific trap, name it, and consider a more balanced reading of the same behavior. Bring a few examples back to session.

title: Relationship Willingness Practice
summary: Helps a client identify one values-based action toward a partner they can take despite current hurt or resentment.
goal: Help a client act on relationship values even while hurt or resentment is still present.
body_md: Waiting for hurt or resentment to fully clear before acting warmly toward a partner can mean waiting a long time, so this practice has a client identify one small values-based action, patience, warmth, honesty, they are willing to take even while the difficult feeling is still present. This is not about suppressing the feeling, only about not letting it be the only thing that decides the next action.

title: Relationship Distress Tolerance Menu
summary: A menu of skills a client can use to tolerate a hard relationship moment without acting impulsively.
goal: Give a client a menu of skills to reach for during a hard relationship moment instead of an impulsive reaction.
body_md: A hard moment in a relationship, a hurtful comment, a broken plan, can trigger an impulsive reaction that makes things worse before the client has had a chance to think, so this menu offers a few distress tolerance options to reach for first: a short walk, paced breathing, or naming the urge out loud before acting on it. The goal is buying time, not suppressing the feeling.

goal: Help a client build a concrete, present-day map of safety rather than dwelling in the past.
body_md: A client working through the aftermath of sexual abuse benefits from a strong, concrete sense of who and where feels safe right now, separate from anything about what happened. This sheet has them map current safe people, places and objects, building a resource they can return to whenever grounding is needed. It is intentionally forward-facing and does not ask for any account of the past.

goal: Help a client build present-day evidence of choice and ownership over their own body.
body_md: Reclaiming a felt sense of ownership over one's own body can be a slow, present-focused process, and this sheet supports it by having a client name small choices they currently hold, what to wear, who to be touched by, how to move through their day, and notice each one as an exercise of that ownership. This stays entirely in the present and does not ask about the past.

title: Compassion Toward the Body Practice

goal: Support a client in extending compassion toward their body rather than treating it as separate or at fault.
body_md: Sexual abuse can leave a client relating to their own body with distance or blame, as though it were separate from them or somehow responsible, and this practice offers a slow, gentle way to extend compassion toward the body instead, a hand placed gently, a few kind words directed inward. Go at whatever pace feels tolerable and stop if it becomes too activating; this is stabilizing work, not exposure work.

goal: Give a client control over the pace of their own grounding practice.
body_md: Being rushed through anything, including a coping skill, can itself feel unsafe for a client recovering from abuse, so this card is built around pacing: a menu of grounding options with permission to move as slowly as needed and to stop at any point. Complete this in session first, and let the client set the pace and choose which options to keep. 988 can be called or texted anytime support is needed between sessions.

goal: Give a couple a shared, explicit agreement about pacing physical closeness during healing.
body_md: A partner supporting someone healing from sexual abuse often wants to help but is unsure what is welcome, and guessing wrong can cause real hurt on both sides, so this sheet has both partners talk openly about pacing: what kinds of touch feel safe right now, what does not, and how to check in without it feeling like a test. Revisit the agreement as things shift, since pacing that works today may change.

goal: Help a client match the right coping skill to the right kind of situation instead of using one skill for everything.
body_md: Clients often default to one familiar coping skill regardless of the situation, even when it is not the best fit, a calming skill used when what is actually needed is problem-solving, or vice versa. This sort has a client write out their coping skills on cards and sort them by situation type: needs calming, needs distraction, needs a decision. Use the sorted set to plan ahead for likely upcoming situations.

My sorted list by situation type

title: Coping Skill Barrier Troubleshoot Sheet
summary: Identifies what specifically gets in the way of using a known coping skill in the moment it is needed.
goal: Help a client troubleshoot why a known coping skill does not get used when it is actually needed.
body_md: A client often knows a coping skill well in theory but still does not reach for it in the moment it is needed, and this sheet digs into why: too complicated to remember, feels silly, not physically available, forgotten in the moment. Naming the specific barrier makes it possible to solve, whether that means simplifying the skill or building a reminder into the environment.

fields.label: The coping skill I know but do not use enough
What specifically gets in the way of using it
A way to make it simpler or more available
A reminder I could build into my day
What I want to try this week

title: Coping Skills as Acts of Care Practice
summary: Reframes coping skills as an expression of self-care values rather than a fix for a problem.
goal: Help a client experience coping skills as an act of care toward themselves rather than a chore.
body_md: Coping skills can start to feel like homework, one more task on a list, which paradoxically makes them harder to reach for, so this practice reframes each skill as an act of care a client is choosing to offer themselves, the same way they might offer it to someone they love. Pick one skill and practice it deliberately from that frame rather than from obligation, and notice whether it feels different.

fields.label: The coping skill I practiced from a place of care
What it felt like to frame it that way
How this compared with doing it out of obligation
A value this act of care connects to
What I want to bring this frame to next

title: Coping Recipe Steps Craft
summary: A child writes their own coping skill as a step-by-step recipe card to make it easy to follow.
goal: Give a child an easy-to-follow, personalized recipe for calming down.
body_md: Framing a coping skill as a recipe, with clear steps and a picture of the finished result, a calmer feeling, gives a young child something familiar and concrete to follow instead of an abstract instruction to calm down. The parent and child write the steps together and decorate the card like an actual recipe. Keep it somewhere the child can grab it when needed.

fields.label: Step one of my calm-down recipe
Step two of my calm-down recipe
What the finished result feels like
A time I used my recipe
What I want to change about the recipe

title: Coping Skill Charades Game
summary: Players act out a coping skill without speaking for the group to guess, followed by a real-life discussion.
goal: Use charades to make learning and remembering coping skills active and fun for a group.
body_md: A player draws a coping skill card and acts it out silently, deep breathing, counting, a favorite stretch, while the group guesses which skill it is, then the group briefly discusses when that skill might actually be useful for them. Acting the skill out physically tends to help it stick better than simply reading a list. Keep the pace playful and celebrate creative acting attempts.

fields.label: The skill I acted out
A skill I guessed correctly
A skill that was fun or funny to act out
When I might actually use one of the skills from the game
A skill I want to remember most

title: Feared Object Fact File Sheet
summary: Has a client research and record plain facts about a feared object or situation to sit alongside the fear.
goal: Give a client a factual counterweight to sit alongside an exaggerated feared image.
body_md: A phobia often runs on an exaggerated mental image of the feared object or situation, and this sheet has a client build a simple fact file, plain, verifiable information, to sit alongside that image rather than replace it outright. The point is not to argue the fear away but to give the client a second, factual reference point available when the exaggerated image takes over.

fields.label: The feared object or situation
A fact I found about it
Another fact I found
How the exaggerated image compares with the facts
What I want to remember when the fear spikes

title: Micro-Exposure Ladder Builder
summary: Builds an exposure ladder with steps small enough that the first one feels almost too easy.
goal: Help a client build a graded exposure ladder starting from a step that feels genuinely manageable.
body_md: A ladder with its first rung set too high often stalls before it starts, so this builder deliberately aims for a first step small enough to feel almost too easy, then works upward from there. A client lists the full range of situations connected to the fear, rates each for difficulty, and orders them into a ladder. Move up only once a rung feels manageable, not simply tolerable.

fields.label: The fear this ladder is built around
My first, easiest step
The next few steps in order of difficulty
The hardest step at the top
Which step I am ready to try next

title: Distress Tolerance for Exposure Card
summary: A pocket card of skills to use during an exposure step to stay with the discomfort rather than escape it.
goal: Give a client skills to stay present through an exposure step rather than leaving early.
body_md: Leaving an exposure step early because the discomfort feels unbearable can reinforce the fear rather than reduce it, so this card offers a short menu of distress tolerance skills, paced breathing, brief grounding, a coping statement, to help a client stay in the step a bit longer. The goal is staying with discomfort long enough for it to shift, not eliminating it.

fields.label: The exposure step I am working on
The skill I used to stay with it
Distress level at the start, 0 to 10
Distress level after staying with it
Whether I stayed as long as planned

title: Partner Cheerleader Not Rescuer Sheet
summary: Helps a supporting partner learn to encourage an exposure step rather than step in to rescue from it.
goal: Help a supporting partner learn to encourage rather than rescue during a phobia exposure step.
body_md: A supporting partner's instinct to protect can accidentally undercut an exposure step, stepping in to handle the feared thing before the client gets the chance to face it themselves. This sheet has both partners agree on what genuine encouragement looks like versus rescuing, and what signal the client can give if they truly do need the partner to step in. Practice the signal in advance.

fields.label: Partner facing the fear: what encouragement, not rescue, looks like to me
Partner facing the fear: my signal for if I truly need help
Supporting partner: what I will say instead of stepping in
Supporting partner: what makes it hard not to rescue
One agreement we are making about the next exposure step

title: Fear Ladder Board Game
summary: Players move a token up a drawn ladder board as they answer prompts about facing small fears.
goal: Use a simple board game to make talking about facing fears feel playful rather than heavy.
body_md: Players move a token up a drawn ladder by answering a prompt each turn, naming a fear, a step that would face it, or a time they were brave, with each correct or honest answer moving the token up one rung. Keep it light and let players choose how much detail to share. Whoever's token reaches the top first can cheer the rest of the group up the ladder too.

fields.label: A prompt I answered during the game
A fear I named
A step that would help face it
A time I was brave that I remembered during the game
How far my token climbed

title: Appearance Talk Awareness Sheet
summary: Logs how often a client talks about appearance, their own or others', to see how much airtime it takes up.
goal: Help a client see how much daily conversation and thought is going toward appearance.
body_md: Comments about appearance, one's own or someone else's, can become so routine they go unnoticed, quietly reinforcing how much attention the body's look receives relative to everything else. This sheet has a client log each appearance comment they make or hear across a week, then reflect on what that adds up to. The goal is awareness, not guilt about any single comment.

fields.label: An appearance comment I made or heard today
Whether it was about my own appearance or someone else's
How I felt saying or hearing it
A non-appearance comment I could offer instead next time
What I notice about the week's total

title: Function Over Appearance Practice
summary: Practices describing the body by what it does across a day rather than how it looks.
goal: Help a client build the habit of noticing their body by function rather than appearance.
body_md: Body image work often benefits from practicing an entirely different lens on the body, one built around function rather than appearance, and this practice has a client narrate their body's actions across an ordinary day, carrying groceries, laughing, climbing stairs, without any reference to how it looked doing so. Repetition matters more than any single entry; the lens takes practice to hold.

fields.label: Something my body did for me today
Another thing my body did for me today
How it felt to describe my body this way
A moment I noticed myself slipping back to appearance language
What I want to notice more of tomorrow

title: Nonjudgmental Body Scan Practice
summary: A brief mindfulness body scan practiced with nonjudgmental, descriptive language only.
goal: Give a client practice noticing the body with neutral, descriptive attention instead of evaluation.
body_md: A body scan practiced with strictly descriptive language, noticing warmth, tension or ease without labeling any of it good or bad, gives a client a different way of relating to their own body than the evaluative lens they usually bring. Guide the scan slowly through a few body areas, redirecting gently back to description any time a judgment slips in. This is a mindfulness skill, not a body-checking exercise.

fields.label: What I noticed in my body during the scan, described neutrally
A moment a judgment slipped in
How I redirected back to description
How this scan compared with how I usually relate to my body
What I want to practice noticing next time

title: My Body's Superpowers Drawing
summary: A child draws their body as having superpowers based on what it can do, not how it looks.
goal: Help a child build an early function-focused, playful relationship with their own body.
body_md: Framing the body's abilities as superpowers, running fast, hugging tight, climbing high, gives a young child a playful, function-focused way to think about their own body well before appearance-focused messages take hold more strongly. The parent and child draw the child as a superhero with powers based on real things the body can do. Keep the conversation led by what the child brings up.

fields.label: A superpower my body has
Another superpower my body has
How I drew myself using my superpowers
How my body helped me today
My favorite thing my body lets me do

title: Media Message Spot the Trick Game
summary: A group spots editing and marketing tricks in sample images to build media literacy around appearance.
goal: Use a group activity to build critical media literacy around appearance-focused images.
body_md: Players look at a set of sample images and try to spot the tricks used to shape how bodies appear, lighting, angles, editing, posing, earning a point for each trick correctly identified. The game builds a habit of critical viewing that can carry over to everyday media, gently loosening the pull of comparison. Debrief on how it felt to look at the images differently once the tricks were visible.

fields.label: A trick I spotted in one of the images
How the image looked different once I saw the trick
A trick I want to look for in media on my own now
How many points I earned
What I want to remember next time I compare myself to an image

title: Weekly Boundaries Review Sheet
summary: A weekly page for noticing where a client held, bent or dropped a limit they set.
goal: Use it to help a client see which limits held and what got in the way of the rest.
body_md: Have the client fill it in before the session and read one entry aloud. Look for the situation that made a limit hard, not for a grade on the week. Ask what they would want to say differently next time. It works best when the limits were chosen by the client rather than suggested by others.

fields.label: A limit I set this week
Where it held
Where it slipped, and what was happening
One sentence I could say next time

title: Decision Values Filter Sheet
summary: A sheet that runs one stuck decision through what the client says matters to them.
goal: Use it to help a client weigh a choice against their own stated values.
body_md: Ask the client to name a decision they keep circling, then to list three values in their own words. Each option is then read against each value. Expect some values to conflict; that is useful material for the session. The sheet does not pick the answer, the client does.

fields.label: The decision I am stuck on
Three things that matter most to me here
How option one fits each one
How option two fits each one
The step I could take this week

title: Session Takeaway Card
summary: A short card a client fills in at the end of a session so the main point goes home with them.
goal: Use it to help a client leave with one idea and one action in their own words.
body_md: Hand it over in the last few minutes and let the client write before you summarize, so you hear what actually landed. Compare their version with yours and be curious about the gap. Keep the card in the file or photograph it for the next session opener.

fields.label: The main thing I want to remember
Something that surprised me today
One small thing I will try before we meet again
A question I still have

title: Energy Leaks and Refills Inventory
summary: Two lists a client builds: what drains their day and what gives something back.
goal: Use it to give a client a plain picture of where their energy goes during a week.
body_md: Have the client fill both columns from a recent ordinary week, not an ideal one. Then look at timing: which leaks cluster before which refills. Avoid turning it into a should list; the aim is a map the client can adjust one small piece at a time.

fields.label: Things that drained me this week
Things that gave something back
A leak I could shrink a little
A refill I could add or protect
Who or what could help with that

title: Difficult Conversation Preparation Sheet
summary: A planning page for a conversation a client is dreading, from goal to first sentence.
goal: Use it to help a client plan what they want from a hard conversation before they have it.
body_md: Work through it in session and rehearse the opening line aloud. Help the client separate what they want to say from what they hope the other person will do, since only the first is in their hands. Save the page so you can debrief afterward.

fields.label: Who I need to talk to and about what
What I hope comes out of it
Facts I want to state without blame
How I feel, in a sentence
What I will do if it goes badly

title: Thought Record With Balanced Alternative
summary: A seven-column style thought record ending in a balanced alternative thought.
goal: Use it to walk a client from a hot thought to a more balanced one, step by step.
body_md: Teach it in session with a recent, moderate situation before sending it home. Ask the client to rate belief in the thought before and after so they can see the shift, even a small one. Watch for a rewritten thought the client does not believe; go back to the evidence column.

fields.label: The situation
What I felt, and how strong (0 to 100)
The automatic thought
Evidence that supports the thought
Evidence that does not fit the thought
A more balanced thought, and how much I believe it

title: Cognitive Distortion Detective Sheet
summary: A sheet for spotting common thinking traps in a client's own thoughts.
goal: Use it to help a client name the thinking trap behind a thought and question it.
body_md: Give the client a short list of traps in plain words and ask them to find one in each of three recent thoughts. Naming a trap is a way to step back from a thought, not proof that it is wrong. Invite them to write a question that would loosen the trap.

fields.label: A thought that bothered me this week
Which thinking trap it sounds like
A question I could ask to test it
What I would tell a friend who had this thought

title: Activity and Mood Diary
summary: An hourly or blocked diary linking what a client does with how they feel.
goal: Use it to give a client and clinician real data on how activities and moods line up.
duration: Ten minutes daily for a week
body_md: Start with a few blocks a day rather than every hour so it stays doable. Ask for a mood number and a quick note of what they were doing. In session, look for the activities that sit near better and worse moments and let the client draw the conclusion first.

fields.label: What I was doing this morning, and my mood (0 to 10)
What I was doing this afternoon, and my mood (0 to 10)
What I was doing this evening, and my mood (0 to 10)
The activity that felt best or most meaningful
The activity I would change

title: Worry Time Scheduling Sheet
summary: A sheet for setting a daily worry period and parking worries until then.
goal: Use it to help a client set aside a short daily worry period and postpone worries to it.
duration: Ten minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Agree on a time and place that is not near bedtime. During the day the client jots worries on the page and returns to what they were doing. At the worry period, ask which worries still feel live. Many clients find the list shorter than expected; some do not, and that is worth discussing.

fields.label: The time and place I chose for worry time
A worry I noticed and postponed
What I did instead in the moment
At worry time: is it still a worry, and can I act on it?
One action I can take or let go of

title: Values Compass Check-In
summary: A simple weekly check on how closely a client's actions pointed toward what matters to them.
goal: Use it to help a client compare a week of actions with the directions they say they value.
body_md: Ask the client to choose two or three life areas and name a value in each. Then they rate how closely the week matched and name one small action that would move it. Keep the tone curious. A low number is information, and it is not a verdict.

fields.label: A life area and a value I chose
One thing I did this week that fit it
One thing that pulled me away
A small action for next week

title: Leaves on a Stream Practice Notes
summary: A guided defusion practice using leaves on a stream, with a notes page for afterward.
goal: Use it to give a client a way to watch thoughts pass without following each one.
body_md: Read the exercise slowly in session, then ask what it was like rather than whether it worked. Some clients find the image hard; invite a substitute such as clouds or a conveyor belt. Send home a short version and a place to note what they noticed.

fields.label: The thoughts that floated by
What it was like to watch them go
A moment I got pulled onto a leaf
What I noticed when I stepped back

title: Willingness Dial Exercise
summary: A dial from unwilling to fully willing for clients to place on a hard but valued step.
goal: Use it to help a client find how willing they are to feel discomfort for something that matters.
body_md: Name a specific step the client cares about and ask where the dial sits today. Then ask what would move it one notch, not to the top. The number is not something to push. Talk through what discomfort they would be making room for and how they could carry it.

fields.label: The step that matters to me
Where the dial sits today (0 to 10)
What would move it up one notch
The discomfort I would be making room for

title: Hands as Thoughts Metaphor Sheet
summary: A brief metaphor in which held-up hands stand in for how thoughts crowd the view.
goal: Use it to show a client the difference between holding thoughts and holding them at a distance.
body_md: Have the client hold their hands over their eyes, then lower them to the lap. Ask what they could do and see in each position. The point is that the thoughts do not have to go anywhere; they can sit where the client can still act. Follow with the prompts.

fields.label: What I could see with my hands over my face
What changed when I lowered them
A thought I tend to hold up close
One thing I could do with that thought resting in my lap

title: Chessboard and Pieces Self Practice
summary: A chessboard metaphor separating the observing self from thoughts and feelings.
goal: Use it to help a client take an observer position toward their own thoughts and feelings.
body_md: Draw or lay out a board with two teams of pieces standing for thoughts and feelings, and the board as the client. Ask which team they have been trying to beat. Point out that the board holds every piece and takes no side. Let them describe it in their own words.

fields.label: The pieces I have been fighting
What has that fight cost me
What the board holds without taking sides
How I could act from the board today

title: TIPP Skills Practice Card
summary: A card for practicing the TIPP skills to bring intense arousal down fast.
goal: Use it to help a client practice a set of quick body-based skills before they need them.
body_md: Practice each skill in session when the client is calm, such as cool water on the face or paced breathing, and check any health limits first. Then ask which one they would reach for and where they will keep the card. Note that the skills lower arousal; solving the problem comes after.

fields.label: A time I felt very worked up
Which TIPP skill I want to try first
Where I will keep what I need for it
How my body felt before and after

title: Wise Mind Check-In Sheet
summary: A brief practice for checking what emotion mind, reasonable mind and wise mind say.
goal: Use it to help a client find the place where feeling and reason both have a voice.
body_md: Walk the client through a decision, asking what emotion mind says, what reasonable mind says, and what settles in the middle. Some clients need a breath or a minute of quiet before the third answer arrives. Do not supply it for them.

fields.label: The situation
What emotion mind says
What reasonable mind says
What wise mind says

title: DEAR MAN Request Rehearsal Sheet
summary: A fill-in script for making a request or saying no using the DEAR MAN steps.
goal: Use it to help a client draft and rehearse an assertive request or refusal.
body_md: Build the script in session and role-play it, taking the other person's part with a few realistic pushbacks. Ask the client to keep the ask to one clear sentence. Remind them to plan for the other person saying no, since asking well does not guarantee the answer.

fields.label: Describe the situation in facts
Express how I feel about it
Assert: what I am asking for or declining
Reinforce: what is in it for the other person
What I will do if they say no

title: Pros and Cons of Acting on Urges Sheet
summary: A four-box sheet weighing acting on an urge against tolerating it, short and long term.
goal: Use it to help a client see the short and long term of acting on or riding out an urge.
body_md: Fill in all four boxes in session, including the real short-term payoffs of acting, since skipping them loses credibility. Encourage the client to keep the sheet where the urge tends to show up. If the urge involves risk to safety, follow your own plan; this sheet does not replace it.

fields.label: The urge I am looking at
Pros of acting on it
Cons of acting on it
Pros of riding it out
Cons of riding it out

title: Self-Validation Statements Sheet
summary: A sheet for writing validating statements a client can offer themselves.
goal: Use it to help a client practice acknowledging their own feelings without judging them.
body_md: Explain that validating does not mean approving of a behavior or agreeing with a thought; it means saying that the feeling makes sense given what happened. Draft three statements together and try them aloud. Clients who find this odd often warm to it with practice.

fields.label: A feeling I had this week
What happened that made it make sense
A validating sentence I could say to myself
How it felt to say it

title: Turning Toward Bids Tracker
summary: A weekly tracker where both partners note small bids for attention and how they were met.
goal: Use it to help partners notice small bids and how each of them responds.
body_md: Each partner keeps a tally of bids they made and bids they noticed from the other. Bring both sheets to session and read one example from each. Expect partners to have missed some. The aim is to notice, not to keep score against each other.

fields.label: Partner A: a bid I made and how it was met
Partner A: a bid I noticed and how I responded
Partner B: a bid I made and how it was met
Partner B: a bid I noticed and how I responded
One thing we will each try next week

title: Shared Goals Vision Sheet
summary: A page where both partners write what they each want for the next year and merge a shared list.
goal: Use it to help partners name what they want for the next year and find where they overlap.
body_md: Partners first write separately, then share, then build a joint list. Point out the overlaps before the differences. Where goals conflict, note them for a later session rather than settling them on the spot.

fields.label: Partner A: what I hope for us in a year
Partner B: what I hope for us in a year
Where our hopes overlap
One shared goal we will start on this month
What each of us will do first

title: Softened Start-Up Practice Cards
summary: Cards for turning a complaint into a gentle start with a feeling and a request.
goal: Use it to help partners practice raising an issue without blame at the start.
body_md: Take a mild complaint from each partner and rewrite it in the form of "I feel, about, and I need". Partners read them aloud, and the listener says what they heard. Slow the pace if either partner tenses. Use small issues first.

fields.label: Partner A: my complaint, rewritten as I feel, about, I need
Partner B: how I heard it
Partner B: my complaint, rewritten as I feel, about, I need
Partner A: how I heard it

title: Outside Stress Daily Talk Guide
summary: A guide for a daily short talk where each partner listens to the other's outside stress.
goal: Use it to help partners give each other a place to talk about stress outside the relationship.
body_md: Partners take turns for about ten minutes each on stress from work, family or other outside sources. The listener does not fix or advise unless asked, and shows interest and understanding. Debrief what helped and what did not.

fields.label: Partner A: a stress I want to talk about
Partner B: what I heard and how I showed I was on their side
Partner B: a stress I want to talk about
Partner A: what I heard and how I showed I was on their side

title: Rituals of Connection Planner
summary: A planner where partners choose small daily and weekly rituals to keep connected.
goal: Use it to help partners choose a few small rituals that keep them connected.
body_md: Ask each partner to name a moment in their week that feels like closeness and then choose two rituals that fit a real schedule. Start small. Revisit them in a couple of weeks and drop any that feel like chores.

fields.label: Partner A: a moment that feels close to me
Partner B: a moment that feels close to me
Our daily ritual
Our weekly ritual
How we will remember to do them

title: Feelings Face Paper Plates Craft
summary: Children decorate paper plates with faces for the feelings they know.
goal: Use it to help a child put shapes and words on a handful of feelings through making them.
body_md: Let the child make a plate face for each feeling they pick, such as happy, mad, scared or calm. Ask when they last had that feeling. The parent joins in by making one of their own and naming when they felt it. If a child mentions being hurt or unsafe, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: A feeling I made a face for
When I felt that feeling
What my body did when I felt it
Something that helps me when I feel it

title: Calm-Down Bottle Craft
summary: Children make a glitter bottle to watch settle while they breathe.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on cue for slowing down and breathing.
body_md: Help the child fill a clear bottle with water, glue and glitter, seal it well, and shake it. The child watches the glitter settle while breathing slowly. The parent learns to offer it as an invitation rather than a punishment. Keep it in a place the child can reach.

fields.label: What color glitter I picked
What my mind looks like when the glitter is swirling
What I noticed as the glitter settled
When I could use my bottle at home

title: Helping Hands Support Drawing
summary: A child traces their hand and writes a helper on each finger.
goal: Use it to help a child name people who help them and what those people do.
body_md: The child traces one hand and puts a helper on each finger, with a picture or a name. The parent adds one helper of their own and says what they do for the child. Notice children who list few helpers. If a child hints that someone is not safe, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: A helper I put on my thumb
What that person does to help
A helper for another finger
Who I would go to first if I felt upset

title: Stop and Think Traffic Light Craft
summary: Children make a traffic light to remember stop, think, then go.
goal: Use it to give a child a simple picture for pausing before acting.
body_md: The child colors a red, yellow and green light and writes or draws what they do at each. Red means stop, yellow means think of choices, and green means try one. The parent practices it with a pretend problem and then points it out at home in calm moments.

fields.label: What I do at red
A choice I can think of at yellow
What I try at green
A time I could use my light

title: Kindness Coupons Making Activity
summary: Children design coupons to give others as small acts of kindness.
goal: Use it to help a child practice noticing and giving small acts of kindness.
body_md: The child designs three coupons, such as a hug, a drawing or help with a chore, and decides who receives each. The parent takes part by receiving one and saying how it felt. It works well for children who are more used to hearing correction than praise.

fields.label: A coupon I made
Who it is for
How I think they will feel
Another kind thing I could do

title: Feelings Charades Game
summary: A group game in which players act out feelings and others guess.
goal: Use it to help a group practice reading and naming feelings through movement.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a feeling card and acting it without words. The rest guess and say what in the body or face gave it away. Rotate so quiet players are not put on the spot. Debrief which feelings were easy to spot and which were similar.

fields.label: A feeling that was easy to act out
A feeling that was hard to tell apart
Where I feel one of these in my body
What I learned about reading others

title: Values Auction Game
summary: Players get play money to bid on values, finding out what they would give up for what.
goal: Use it to help players find which values they will spend on when they cannot have everything.
body_md: Give each player the same amount of play money and a list of values to bid on. There are more values than anyone can buy. Afterward ask what they chose, what they let go and how it felt. There are no right buys. Keep the mood light.

fields.label: A value I bid the most on
A value I let go and how that felt
Something that surprised me about my bids
One way I could act on my top value this week

title: Strengths Bingo Game
summary: A bingo card of strengths that players mark when they see them in others.
goal: Use it to help a group notice and name strengths in each other.
body_md: Each card lists strengths in the squares. During a group activity, players mark a square when they notice a strength in someone else and say who. Debrief by reading squares aloud. Make sure everyone receives at least one mark.

fields.label: A strength someone noticed in me
A strength I noticed in someone else
A strength I did not expect to be noticed
How it felt to hear it

title: Five Senses Grounding Menu
summary: A menu of sensory grounding options a client picks from and rates.
goal: Use it to help a client find grounding options that suit them before they are needed.
body_md: Try each sense in session at a low level of distress and ask the client to rate how much each one helps. Keep the client's top three on a card. Nothing here asks for details of what happened; the work is about staying present and pacing.

fields.label: Something I can see that helps me feel here
Something I can touch or hold
A sound or smell that steadies me
My top three, in order
Where I will keep this list

title: Helpful and Unhelpful Coping After Trauma Sort
summary: A sort of coping habits into those that help now and those that cost more later.
goal: Use it to help a client look at how their coping habits work for them over time.
body_md: Ask the client to list what they do when reminders show up, without describing the event. Sort the list together by short-term relief and longer-term cost. Avoid judgment; every habit was doing a job. Choose one to build on and one to try shrinking.

fields.label: Things I do when a reminder shows up
What each one gives me right away
What each one costs me later
One I want to build on
One I want to try changing slowly

title: Distress Tolerance Crisis Kit Planner
