summary: Partners each hold half of a puzzle and earn pieces by sharing their own parts of a conflict.
goal: Help couples practice speaking and listening in turns, each partner with a role.
body_md: Each partner holds half of a simple puzzle. Partner A shares a feeling and a need using I statements; Partner B reflects it back, then earns a piece. Swap. The puzzle only completes when both have had both roles. Stop and reset the game if either partner escalates. Debrief on how it felt to listen without defending.

fields.label: Partner A: a feeling and a need I shared
Partner B: what I reflected back
Partner B: a feeling and a need I shared
Partner A: what I reflected back
One thing we will try at home this week

title: Coping Menu Restaurant Role-Play
summary: Players order from a coping menu as customers while a server suggests sides.
goal: Help clients build a personal menu of coping skills they would use.
body_md: Write a menu with starters for quick skills, mains for longer ones and desserts for treats that feel good. One player serves, one orders for a stressful moment, and the server suggests a pairing. Swap roles. Debrief on what clients would order first in real life. Encourage clients to take a photo of the menu and keep it handy.

fields.label: Starters I would order in a hard moment
A main I would want when stress is high
A dessert that feels good to me
Who I would share my menu with

title: Fear Ladder Floor Game
summary: Players climb a taped floor ladder of small steps toward a feared thing, with a cheer at each rung.
goal: Make gradual steps toward a feared thing playful and paced by the client.
body_md: Tape a ladder on the floor with five rungs, each holding a card with a small step the client helps write. The client moves up only when ready, rating the fear at each rung and stopping whenever they choose. A parent cheers, and helps plan practice between sessions. If a child discloses anything worrying, follow your reporting duties. Debrief on the bravest moment.

fields.label: The feared thing at the top of my ladder
My rungs from easiest to hardest
My fear rating at each rung
The bravest moment today
How my parent can cheer me on

title: Rest Types Inventory
summary: Sorts rest into physical, mental, social, sensory and creative kinds so a client can see which kind is missing.
goal: Match the kind of rest a client needs to the kind of tiredness they have.
body_md: Many clients equate rest with sleep or screens and stay tired anyway. Ask the client to rate last week kind by kind before filling in the plan, and notice whether the missing kind surprises them. Keep the plan small, one change this week, and review how it went at the next session.

fields.label: Last week, when did you feel truly rested, and what kind of rest was it?
Which of these kinds of rest did you get a little of: physical, mental, social, sensory, creative?
Which kind is most missing right now?
What usually gets in the way of that kind of rest?
One small way to add that kind of rest this week
When and where it will happen
How you will know it helped

title: Emotion Vocabulary Ladder
summary: Moves a client from broad words like bad or fine to more precise feeling words, one rung at a time.
goal: Build a more precise feeling vocabulary so emotions are easier to name and respond to.
body_md: Start with a recent moment the client called bad, stressed or fine, and climb one rung at a time rather than offering a long word list. Let the client reject words that do not fit; the point is a closer match, not a correct answer. Revisit the ladder when a new strong feeling comes up.

fields.label: A recent moment you described as bad, fine or stressed
The broad word you used for it
Where you felt it in your body
A more specific word that fits a little better
An even closer word, or two words that fit together
What this feeling might be telling you it wants or needs
One small thing that would respond to it

title: Asking for Help Ledger
summary: Tracks small requests for help, what the client predicted and what actually happened.
goal: Test the client's predictions about asking for help with small, real requests.
body_md: Useful for clients who carry things alone or expect to be a burden. Agree on two or three small, low-stakes requests in session and have the client write the prediction before each one. Review the gap between predicted and actual responses together, and honor any request that did not go well without rushing to reassure.

fields.label: A small request you could make this week
Who you would ask
What you predict will happen, and how sure you are
What you actually asked, and when
What happened, including how the other person responded
How it felt afterward
What this tells you about asking next time

title: Life Transition Preparation Sheet
summary: Maps what is ending, what is starting and what stays steady during a move, job change, breakup or other transition.
goal: Help a client prepare for a life change by naming losses, hopes and anchors.
body_md: Transitions bring mixed feelings, and clients often feel they should only be excited or only be sad. Make space for both columns before moving to planning. The anchors question is often the most useful, since routines and people who stay constant can steady the first weeks. Revisit it after the change begins.

fields.label: The change you are going through or approaching
What is ending or being left behind
What is starting or might be gained
Feelings you notice about it, including mixed ones
Routines, people and places that will stay steady
One thing you want to prepare before the change
Who you want to tell about how it is going
What you will do in the first two weeks to look after yourself

title: Friend Standard Flip Sheet
summary: A side-by-side page comparing what a client says to themselves with what they would say to a friend.
goal: Expose a harsher inner standard and practice a fairer, more balanced voice.
body_md: Pick a situation where your client is clearly hard on themselves. Have them fill in the friend column first, since it usually comes easily, then read both aloud. Watch for 'but that's different'; gently ask what makes it different, and let them draft one sentence they could believe.

fields.label: The situation, in one or two sentences
What I say to myself about it
If a close friend were in the same spot, what I would say to them
What is different between those two voices
Which voice feels kinder, and which feels more accurate
One sentence from the friend voice I could try this week

title: Graded Task Assignment Ladder
summary: A ladder that breaks a task a client has been avoiding into small, doable rungs with predictions and outcomes.
goal: Rebuild momentum on a stalled task by starting small and checking predictions against results.
body_md: Choose a task that feels too big, such as a pile of mail or a phone call. Help your client cut it into rungs they would rate as very doable, and have them predict difficulty before each one. Review mismatches next session; finishing a rung counts even if it is small.

fields.label: The task I have been putting off
Why it feels too big right now
Rung 1: the smallest first step
Rung 2: a slightly bigger step
Rung 3: a bigger step still
Rung 4 and beyond: the rest of the task
How hard I predicted each rung would be (0-10)
How hard each rung actually was (0-10)
What I noticed when I finished a rung

title: Problem-Solving Six Steps Sheet
summary: A step-by-step page for naming a problem, brainstorming options, weighing them, and trying one.
goal: Move a client from feeling stuck to choosing and testing one concrete solution.
body_md: Use a problem that has a real action available, not a worry about something out of reach. Encourage wild options in the brainstorm step and hold judgment until the weighing step. If your client skips the review step, bring it back in session so a partial result still teaches something.

fields.label: The problem, stated in one specific sentence
What I want to be different
Every option I can think of, even silly ones
Pros and cons of my top three options
The option I will try
Exactly what I will do, when, and with whom
What happened when I tried it
What I would keep, change, or try next

title: Emotional Reasoning Check
summary: A worksheet for separating a strong feeling from the facts about the situation that set it off.
goal: Help a client notice when a feeling is being treated as proof, and look at the facts too.
body_md: Start with a moment when your client said something like 'I feel stupid, so I must be.' Make clear that feelings are real and worth respecting; the question is whether the feeling tells us everything about the situation. Revisit the facts column together before assigning it for the week.

fields.label: The situation
The feeling and how strong it was (0-100)
The 'I feel ___, so it must be ___' thought
Facts that fit that thought
Facts that do not fit that thought
How a neutral observer would describe what happened
How strong the feeling is after looking at the facts (0-100)

title: Sleep Thoughts and Night Log
summary: A bedtime and morning log of racing thoughts, sleep beliefs, and how the night actually went.
goal: Show how thoughts about sleep and the night's real pattern relate, using a week of data.
body_md: Ask your client to fill in the evening section before bed and the morning section within an hour of waking, without checking the clock during the night. Look for beliefs like 'I cannot function without eight hours' and compare them with the next day's notes. Medical questions about sleep belong with your client's physician.

fields.label: Time I got into bed and what I did in the hour before
Thoughts that showed up as I tried to sleep
How much I believed each thought (0-100)
What I did when I could not sleep
My best guess of how long it took to fall asleep
How I felt the next morning (0-10)
How the day actually went compared to what I feared
A more balanced thought about sleep for tonight

title: Hexaflex Snapshot
summary: A one-page check of six flexibility processes, each rated and paired with one small next move.
goal: Show the client and clinician where flexibility is strong and where to focus next.
body_md: Walk the six processes in plain language rather than jargon, and let the client rate each one from their own experience instead of offering your view. The ratings are a conversation starter, not a score. Pick one low-rated area together and keep the next move small. Revisit every few weeks to see what has shifted.

fields.label: Present moment: how much am I here, and how much am I elsewhere?
Acceptance: how willing am I to let hard feelings be there?
Defusion: how tightly do my thoughts grab me?
Self as context: can I notice my thoughts and feelings from a step back?
Values: how clear am I about what matters to me?
Committed action: how often do my actions follow my values?
Which one area do I want to work on first?
One small move I will try this week

title: Values and Goals Two-Column Sort
summary: Sorts a client's wants into ongoing directions (values) and finishable targets (goals).
goal: Help the client tell a direction worth living by from a target that can be checked off.
body_md: Use the compass and destination image: a value is the direction you keep traveling, a goal is a place you can arrive. Clients often list goals when asked about values, so expect to sort together. Once sorted, link each goal back to the value it serves, and notice any goal that serves no value at all. Keep your own preferences out of the sorting.

fields.label: Things I want in my life right now (list freely)
Which of these can be finished or checked off? (goals)
Which are ongoing ways I want to act or be? (values)
For one goal, the value it serves
A goal I have that does not seem to serve any value
One value I can act on today, whether or not any goal moves
How does it feel to act on a value without needing a finish line?

title: Naming the Old Story
summary: Gives a recurring life story a title so the client can notice it appearing and choose a response.
goal: Help the client see a repeating story as a story, and respond with values rather than habit.
body_md: Invite the client to name the story the way they might title a book, such as the I Always Fail story, and keep the title short and a little playful. The point is not to argue that the story is false but to notice when it shows up and what it pulls them toward. Do not rush a client who finds the story painful. Stay curious about what it protects.

fields.label: The story my mind tells again and again
A short title for it, like a book or film
When it tends to show up
What it tells me to do, or not do
What I usually do when it appears
What that costs me or my values
What I could say to my mind when I notice it: Ah, the old story again
One thing I could do this week with the story present

title: Control Strategies Inventory
summary: Lists what the client has tried to control or avoid a feeling, and what each try gave and cost.
goal: Let the client see for themselves how well control strategies have worked over time.
body_md: Draw out the full list without judgment, including strategies that look healthy. For each, ask what it did in the short run and over months. Let the client reach the conclusion about workability rather than telling them. Expect some sadness when the costs add up, so leave time to close with values and what they would like to do instead. If hopeless thoughts about life arise, stay with the client in session and follow your own risk steps.

fields.label: The feeling or thought I have been trying to get rid of
Things I have tried to make it go away
What each one did for me in the short run
What each one has cost me over weeks and months
Has the feeling actually gone away for good?
What would I be doing if I did not have to win this fight?
If 988 (call or text) is ever needed, the one person I would tell first: complete this in session

title: IMPROVE Skills Pocket Card
summary: A card for picking one IMPROVE skill to get through a painful moment without making it worse.
goal: Practice choosing a fitting IMPROVE skill before the hard moment arrives.
body_md: Have your client pick the moment first, then browse imagery, meaning, prayer, relaxation, one thing in the moment, vacation and encouragement. Clients often choose the same skill every time, so ask which one they would try that they never have. Rehearse one choice in session and note what it felt like in the body.

fields.label: A painful moment I expect this week
Imagery: a safe or calming scene I could picture
Meaning: something I can find worthwhile in this situation
Relaxation: one way I can loosen my body
One thing in the moment: what I will focus on fully
A brief vacation: a short, healthy break I can take
Encouragement: what I will say to myself
The skill I will try first, and when

title: Current Emotion Noticing Log
summary: A short log for noticing an emotion as a wave, naming it, and letting it pass without acting on it.
goal: Build the habit of observing an emotion without pushing it away or feeding it.
duration: Five minutes, several times a week
body_md: Introduce this after your client can name basic emotions. The aim is to watch the emotion rise and fall, not to change it. Watch for clients who describe the story instead of the sensations; gently bring them back to the body. Review two or three entries together and ask what changed once they stopped fighting the feeling.

fields.label: The emotion I noticed and what set it off
Where I felt it in my body
How strong it was at its peak, 0 to 10
What the urge was
What I did instead of acting on it
How I reminded myself that emotions come and go
How strong it was five minutes later, 0 to 10
What I noticed about watching it

title: Turning the Mind Commitment Card
summary: A card for noticing when the mind has turned away from acceptance and choosing to turn it back.
goal: Recognize the moment of refusing reality and practice turning toward acceptance.
body_md: Clients often describe turning the mind as a single decision, but it is usually a choice they must make again and again. Ask for a specific situation where they are stuck in refusal or sulking. Help them find the early signs, and keep the commitment small enough to repeat today.

fields.label: A situation I am fighting right now
How I know I have turned away from accepting it
What my body does when I refuse it
What I tell myself in those moments
What turning my mind back would look like
One small action that shows I have turned
A reminder I can put where I will see it
What might get in the way, and how I will start again

title: Emotion Problem-Solving Steps
summary: A step-by-step page for deciding whether to change a situation or change how the feeling is handled.
goal: Sort a stuck problem into what can be solved and what must be tolerated.
body_md: Use this when a client keeps replaying one problem. The first step is deciding together whether the situation is solvable now; if it is not, point toward acceptance or soothing skills. Ask your client to brainstorm freely before judging options, since clients often cross off ideas too early.

fields.label: The problem, described in observable facts
What I want to be different
Is this solvable right now? Why or why not
Three or more possible solutions, even odd ones
The pros and cons of my top two choices
The option I will try first
The first step and when I will take it
How I will tell whether it helped

title: One-Mindfully Practice Sheet
summary: A weekly sheet for doing one ordinary activity with full attention and noting when attention drifts.
goal: Strengthen the skill of doing one thing at a time and returning when attention wanders.
body_md: Clients commonly multitask and then judge themselves harshly when focus slips. Choose a plain activity such as washing dishes or walking, and coach them to count each return of attention as success. Review what pulled them away and any urges that came with it.

fields.label: The one activity I chose this week
Where I did it and for how long
What I noticed through my senses
What pulled my attention away
How I brought it back, without judging myself
What I noticed in my body or mood afterward
Where else I could try doing one thing at a time
What I want to bring to next session

title: Roommate Drift Inventory
summary: Lists where the couple's days run in parallel and where they still touch.
goal: Show the couple where connection has thinned so they can choose one place to rebuild.
body_md: Useful when a couple says nothing is wrong but nothing is close either. Each partner fills in their own column first, then they compare. Keep the tone curious, not accusing. Let them pick one small place to rebuild, since a long list of fixes tends to feel like another chore.

fields.label: Parts of our day we spend in the same room
Parts of our day we spend apart without choosing to
Something we used to do together that faded
What I do that may keep us in separate lanes
What I miss most about how we used to be
One small place I would like us to touch each day
What I am willing to do this week toward that
What would tell us it is working

title: Yes, No, and Maybe Request Sheet
summary: Each partner sorts the other's requests into yes, no and maybe, with a reason for each.
goal: Practice making and answering requests without it turning into a verdict on the relationship.
body_md: Have each partner bring three requests. The listener answers yes, no or maybe, and a maybe must name what would make it a yes. Watch for a no that is heard as rejection of the person; slow down and have the speaker reflect what was said. Partners often discover that maybe is the most useful answer.

fields.label: A request I am making of my partner
Why this matters to me
How I answered my partner's request (yes, no or maybe)
What I need to hear to say yes to a maybe
How it felt to hear a no from my partner
How it felt to say a no to my partner
A request we both said yes to
What I will do differently when I make the next request

title: Speaker-Listener Floor Practice
summary: A turn-taking script where one partner holds the floor and the other reflects before replying.
goal: Slow a hot topic down so each partner is heard before anyone responds.
body_md: Use a small object as the floor. The speaker shares a few sentences, the listener paraphrases and asks if they got it right, and only then do roles switch. Begin with a low-stakes topic, then move to a real one. Partners often rush the paraphrase or sneak in a rebuttal; gently stop that and coach it in the moment.

fields.label: The topic I will speak about
My point in one or two short sentences
What I heard my partner say, in my own words
What my partner said I missed or got wrong
What I most needed my partner to understand
What I felt in my body as I waited my turn
What helped me stay in the listener role
What we want to try again next time

title: Social Energy Negotiation Sheet
summary: Maps each partner's need for company and quiet and plans a week that fits both.
goal: Help the couple talk about differing social energy without treating either need as a flaw.
body_md: Partners often read a difference in social energy as a statement about the relationship. Name the difference as a preference that each of them has, then work through the week together. Look for trades that are specific, such as one night out and one night in, rather than broad promises.

fields.label: What kinds of company give me energy
What kinds of company drain me
How much time alone I need in a typical week
How I usually tell my partner when I need space
How I usually tell my partner when I want company
Plans this month that I am looking forward to or dreading
A trade I could offer my partner this week
How we will check in when the plan is not working

title: Reassurance Request Card
summary: Helps one partner ask for reassurance in a clear way and the other decide what they can offer.
goal: Move from hints and tests to direct requests for reassurance that both partners can carry out.
body_md: Suited to couples where one partner seeks closeness through checking or hinting and the other pulls back. Have both complete the card, and let the reassuring partner say what is realistic to offer. Be alert to reassurance that has become endless; agree on a few specific gestures rather than unlimited answers.

fields.label: A moment lately when I wanted reassurance
What I did or said at the time
What I actually wanted to hear or feel
A clear way I could ask for it next time
What my partner can realistically offer
What my partner cannot offer, and what I can do for myself then
A signal we will use when I need a moment of reassurance
How we will tell whether this is helping

title: Calm-Down Glitter Jar Craft
summary: The child builds a sealed jar of water and glitter to shake, watch settle and name as their mind calming.
goal: Give a child a visual, hands-on picture of big feelings settling when they pause.
body_md: Let the child pour, stir and seal the jar, then shake it together and narrate the swirl as a busy mind. Ask the parent to keep a copy at home and to sit beside the child while it settles rather than telling them to calm down. If a child discloses something worrying while you build, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What color glitter did I pick for my big feeling?
What does the swirl look like to me?
What happens to the glitter when I sit still?
What do I notice in my body as it settles?
When could I use my jar at home?
How will my grown-up help me use it?

title: Hello and Goodbye Ritual Card
summary: The child and parent draw a short goodbye and reunion routine on a card the child can keep.
goal: Make drop-offs predictable with a drawn, practiced routine the child helps design.
body_md: Have the child draw each step of a quick goodbye: a hug, a special wave, a phrase, then the parent leaving. The parent practices it in the room, keeping it short and warm and following through on the plan. Note what the parent does when the child protests. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw our goodbye hug or wave.
What special words do we say?
Draw what I can do after my grown-up leaves.
Where does my grown-up go, and what will they do?
Draw our hello when we are back together.
What small thing can I hold to feel close?

title: Friendship Ingredients Recipe Card
summary: The child draws a recipe card listing the ingredients of being a good friend and how to mix them.
goal: Help a child picture concrete friendship moves they can try at school or play.
body_md: Frame it as a pretend cooking show, with ingredients such as sharing, asking, and listening. Let the child draw each one and act out a mini scene with you. Ask the parent to try one ingredient at home that week and name it when they see it. If a child discloses mistreatment by peers or adults, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The name of my friendship recipe
Ingredient one: something I can say or do
Ingredient two: something I can share or ask
Ingredient three: how I can listen
What happens if the recipe gets a little burnt?
Who will I try my recipe with this week?

title: Repair Comic Strip
summary: The child draws a four-panel comic of a conflict, a pause, a repair and what happens next.
goal: Teach a child that arguments can be repaired and practice what to say afterward.
body_md: Choose a small, recent squabble and let the child pick the characters. Draw what happened, the moment of pause, how each character feels, and a repair that fits the child's own words. Invite the parent or sibling to act the repair out. If a child discloses harm at home, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Panel one: draw what happened.
Panel two: draw how each character felt.
Panel three: draw a pause and a calm choice.
Panel four: draw a way to make it right.
What words could the characters use to repair?
What will I try next time this happens?

title: Traffic Light Pause Craft
summary: The child builds a red, yellow and green paper traffic light that maps stop, think and go.
goal: Give a child a handmade cue for pausing before acting on a strong urge.
body_md: Build the light from paper circles and a card strip, then practice with low-stakes pretend scenes before real ones. Red is stop and breathe, yellow is think of choices, green is pick one. The parent uses the same colors at home, calmly and out loud. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What does my body do at red?
What can I do to stop and breathe?
What are two choices I could think of at yellow?
What happens after each choice?
What is my green go choice?
Where will I hang my light at home?

title: Five Senses Treasure Hunt
summary: A timed hunt for objects in the room that match a sense, followed by a quick debrief.
goal: Practice anchoring attention in the present by noticing the room through each sense.
body_md: Call out a sense and give each player a minute to find something in the room that fits, then take turns naming it. Keep the prompts neutral and about the room only. Let anyone pass or sit out a round, and end by asking which sense settled them most so they can reuse it outside the office.

fields.label: Something I found for sight
Something I found for sound
Something I found for touch
The sense that helped me feel most settled
A place outside this room where I could play this quietly

title: Kindness Coupon Trade
summary: Players write small self-kindness coupons, trade them, and redeem one during the week.
goal: Build a habit of offering ourselves the same small kindnesses we offer others.
body_md: Each player writes three coupons for realistic acts of self-kindness, such as a ten minute walk or an early night. Shuffle, deal, and let players trade once if a coupon feels out of reach. Watch for coupons that are really chores or self-criticism in disguise, and ask the group to rewrite them gently.

fields.label: Three coupons I wrote
The coupon I received
Whether I traded it and why
When I will redeem it this week
What got in the way of writing for myself

title: One Word Story Relay
summary: Players build a story one word at a time, then talk about listening, letting go and surprise.
goal: Practice flexibility and shared attention by building on what another person says.
body_md: Sit in a circle and build a story one word per turn, with a gentle rule that you may not steer it back to your own idea. Run two rounds, the second with a calm story goal. In the debrief, ask what it felt like when the story went somewhere unexpected and how each player handled it.

fields.label: My favorite moment in the story
A time I wanted to steer the story
How I felt when it went somewhere unexpected
What helped me keep listening
Where else I could try going with it

title: Red Light Green Light Feelings
summary: A stop and go game where each color is paired with a body signal and a calming move.
goal: Help children notice early body signals and practice pausing before reacting.
body_md: Play classic red light, green light, then add a card for each stop naming a feeling and a body signal, such as hot face or tight fists. Children pick a calming move before the next go. Invite the parent to learn the signal words and use the same stop cue at home. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The feeling I stopped on most
Where I felt it in my body
The calming move I picked
What my grown-up can say to cue me
When I could use stop at home

title: Support Circle Yarn Web
summary: Players toss a ball of yarn to name a support person, building a web they can see.
goal: Make a client's sources of support visible and name how each one helps.
body_md: Hold the yarn, name one person or place you can lean on and what they offer, then toss it on while keeping hold of your strand. When the web is done, gently tug and ask what happens when one strand is loose. Let anyone with few supports name a pet, a routine or a hotline, and note gaps for later.

fields.label: A support I named and what they offer
A support I forgot until I saw the web
Who is missing that I would like to add
One small step to reach out this week
What it was like to see the web

title: Safe People and Places Inventory
summary: Lists the people, places and activities that currently feel steady, rated by how safe they feel.
goal: Build a shared, concrete picture of present-day sources of safety and support.
body_md: Useful early, when a client needs stabilizing resources more than anything else. Keep it entirely in the present: the sheet asks what feels safe now and never what happened. If a client cannot name many, that is information about where to build support, so note it gently and start with one small entry.

fields.label: A person who feels safe to be around, and what they do that helps
A place where my body can relax a little
An activity that steadies me
Rate each of these from 0 to 10 for how safe it feels today
Something that makes a safe place feel less safe
One safe person or place I could add this month
How I can reach one of these when I need it this week

title: Then and Now Thought Check
summary: Sorts thoughts about danger into what feels true in the body and what is true in the present moment.
goal: Help a client separate a past-linked alarm from what is happening right now.
body_md: Have the client pick a recent moment when they felt on alert and record only the thought and the setting today, not the original events. The aim is to notice the difference between a body that is sounding an alarm and a present that may be safe enough. Go slowly, and stop to ground if the exercise raises distress.

fields.label: Where I was and what was happening around me just now
The thought that said I was in danger
How strong the alarm felt in my body, 0 to 10
What I can see, hear and touch right now that tells me about today
Facts that fit with this moment being safe enough
A kinder, more balanced thought for next time
How strong the alarm feels now, 0 to 10

title: Values Compass for Returning to Life
summary: Maps what a client has stepped back from, what they care about, and one small step toward each.
goal: Reconnect a client with valued living at a pace their body can manage.
body_md: Pair this with grounding already in the client's toolkit. Invite them to name areas of life that have shrunk, then pick one value and one very small step, sized so it can be done even on a hard day. Willingness here means making room for whatever shows up, never pushing into reminders; adjust the pace to the client.

fields.label: Areas of life I have stepped back from
What I care about in one of those areas
What kind of person I want to be there
One very small step I could take this week
Feelings or sensations that may show up when I try it
What I can do to make room for them and ground myself
Who could support me with this step

title: TIPP Body Reset Plan
summary: Plans which TIPP skill (temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation) fits which surge.
goal: Give a client a body-first reset to try when distress climbs fast.
body_md: Walk through each TIPP skill in session and let the client try the ones that feel tolerable. Ask about health or medical limits before suggesting temperature change or intense exercise, and skip any step that feels unsafe or too activating. Aim for a short written plan the client can keep on a phone or card.

fields.label: How my body feels when distress is rising fast
Temperature: what cool option I could use, and how it felt
Intense exercise: a short movement I could do, if my body allows
Paced breathing: how long I breathe in and out, and how it felt
Paired muscle relaxation: where I tense and release
Which of these helped most, and which I will skip
My distress before and after, 0 to 10
Where I will keep this plan so I can find it quickly

title: Partner Pacing Agreement
summary: Sets how a couple will pause, pace and return to hard topics without either partner being pushed.
goal: Help both partners agree on signals and limits that keep closeness steady around trauma reminders.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own part. The partner with the trauma history names what helps, what a pause looks like and how much they want to share; the other partner names what they can offer, what they need for themselves and how they will check in. Nothing here requires details of past events, and either partner can say stop.

fields.label: Partner A: topics I am not ready to go into yet
Partner A: the signal I will use to ask for a pause
Partner A: what helps me come back to the present
Partner B: how I will respond when I see the pause signal
Partner B: what I need so I do not feel shut out
Partner B: a way I take care of myself during a pause
Together: how long a pause lasts and who restarts the talk
Together: one thing we will do afterward to reconnect

title: Anxiety Weather Report Drawing
summary: A child draws the weather inside their body, from sunny to stormy, and plans what helps each kind.
goal: Give a child a playful way to name how big a worry feels and what helps.
body_md: Hand over paper and colors and let the child draw a weather scene for today, then a sunny, cloudy and stormy version. Ask the parent to join for the last few minutes so they can learn the words the child uses and what the parent does when it turns stormy. If a child discloses harm or abuse, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw the weather inside you today
Draw what a sunny feeling looks like
Draw what a stormy feeling looks like
What happens in my body when a storm comes
Something that helps a storm pass, drawn or written
What a grown-up can do to help when it is stormy

title: Prediction Check Game
summary: Players predict how a feared situation will go, try it, and score the gap between guess and outcome.
goal: Let a client see how often predictions about anxious situations are off, through play.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a small, safe challenge card, such as saying hello to a stranger or ordering something new. Each writes a prediction, tries it in or after session, then scores the match. Keep the cards mild and chosen by the client. In the debrief, look for what surprised them and what that suggests about next steps.

fields.label: Rules: take turns, write a guess first, then try the challenge
The challenge I drew
My prediction, and how sure I am, 0 to 100
What actually happened
How close my guess was, and my score
Anything that surprised me
One thing I learned from the debrief
The challenge I will try next

title: Before During After Event Plan
summary: Lays out a plan for an upcoming anxious event in three stages: the lead-up, the moment and the aftermath.
goal: Help a client prepare for a worrying event and avoid replaying it afterward.
body_md: Pick one real event in the next week or two. Many clients plan only the event and are caught out by the lead-up and the replay afterward, so give those two stages equal attention. Revisit the sheet at the next session and look at what the plan got right and what to adjust.

fields.label: The event I am preparing for and when it is
What I tend to worry about in the days before
What I will do in the lead-up to stay steady
What I will do during the event if anxiety rises
What I want to do instead of replaying it afterward
A kind thing I will do for myself once it is over
Who I could tell about my plan

title: Probability Pie Chart
summary: Splits a feared outcome into a pie of all the other things that could happen, then adds how the client could cope.
goal: Loosen the pull of a single feared outcome by looking at the full range of possibilities.
body_md: Ask the client to write the feared outcome, then brainstorm every other outcome before assigning slices; work the biggest slices first so the feared one is not sized by feeling alone. Close with coping: even if it happens, what would they do? Expect some clients to resist, and keep the numbers approximate.

fields.label: The outcome I am afraid of
My gut sense of how likely it is, 0 to 100
Other things that could happen, even unlikely ones
How big each slice should be, once I list them all
Evidence for and against my first guess
If the feared outcome did happen, how I would cope
How likely it seems now, 0 to 100

title: Anxiety Choice Point
summary: Maps a hooked moment: what showed up, what moves away from values and what moves toward them.
goal: Help a client notice an anxious moment as a choice about where to put their energy.
body_md: Choice Point is a familiar ACT tool; draw the fork with the client and fill it in from a recent moment. Be even-handed about away moves, because they often work in the short term, and ask what they cost over time. Keep the focus on the next small toward move, not on getting rid of the feeling.

fields.label: A recent moment when anxiety showed up
Thoughts, feelings and sensations that showed up
What I did that moved me away from what matters
What that gave me in the short term, and what it cost
What matters to me in this situation
What I could do that moves me toward it
What I could say to myself to make room for the anxiety

title: Check the Facts for Low Mood
summary: Walks a client through the DBT Check the Facts steps when a low mood is shaping how an event looks.
goal: Help a client notice whether an emotion fits the facts of a situation and act accordingly.
body_md: Use a recent event where the client's mood felt larger than the facts. Work through the steps in order: name the emotion, describe what happened as a camera would, list interpretations, and ask whether the emotion and its intensity fit. Some feelings fit the facts, and that is useful to learn too.

fields.label: The emotion I noticed and how strong it was, 0 to 100
What happened, described only with facts
The story or interpretation I added
Other ways to see the situation
Does the emotion fit the facts? Does its strength fit?
What I want to do next, and whether it fits my goals
If it fits, what a skillful response could be

title: Low-Energy Connection Plan
summary: Helps partners agree on small, doable ways to stay connected when one partner's energy is low.
goal: Keep a couple connected through low-mood weeks without pressure on either partner.
body_md: Each partner has their own section so that neither feels blamed. The partner with low energy names what they can offer and what feels like too much; the other partner names what they can offer and how they will look after themselves. Keep the plan small and revisit it weekly, because energy changes.

fields.label: Partner A: what I can do on a low-energy day
Partner A: what feels like too much right now
Partner A: how I will let my partner know how I am
Partner B: how I can show care without taking over
Partner B: how I will take care of myself
Partner B: what I need to hear from my partner
Together: a small daily moment of connection
Together: when we will check how the plan is going

title: Mood Color Garden Drawing
summary: A child draws a garden where each flower color is a feeling, then adds sunshine and watering for the gloomy patches.
goal: Give a child a way to show low or flat feelings and plan small things that help them grow.
body_md: Let the child choose colors for sad, tired, mad and happy and fill the garden however they like. Then talk about what each flower needs. Invite the parent in at the end to hear which watering ideas the child picked and to choose one thing the parent will do this week. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw a garden and pick a color for each feeling
Which flowers are growing the most lately
Draw what the gloomy flowers need
One thing that is like sunshine for me
One thing that is like watering for me
What a grown-up can do to help my garden this week

title: Energy Budget Game
summary: Players spend a limited pile of energy tokens on daily tasks and trade off what to do, delay or drop.
goal: Help a client plan low-energy days by choosing what matters most with limited energy.
body_md: Each player starts with the same number of tokens and draws task cards, such as showering, answering a message or a walk. Players take turns spending tokens, and special cards shift the budget up or down. In the debrief, ask what they would drop first, what they would protect and what rest is worth.

fields.label: Rules: each turn, spend tokens on one task or rest
How many tokens I started with
The tasks I chose and why
What I delayed or dropped
What I protected even when tokens were low
How this looks like my real days
One real task I could drop or shrink this week
One real thing that gives me energy back

title: Daily Basics Anchor Sheet
summary: Tracks a few daily anchors, such as sleep, light, movement, a meal and one contact, to build a steady floor.
goal: Give a client a short, doable list of daily basics that support mood on hard days.
body_md: Choose three or four anchors with the client and keep each one small, like opening the curtains or sending one message. The point is a floor, not a performance, so score completion simply and discuss what got in the way without judgment. Coordinate with their physician on any health-related anchor.

fields.label: The anchors I chose for this week
What time I woke and went to bed
How much daylight or outside time I got
Movement I did, even a little
A meal or drink I had
One person I had contact with
What got in the way on hard days
Which anchor I want to keep next week

title: Deadline Panic Thought Record
summary: A thought record for the last-minute surge of dread before something is due.
goal: Separate the thoughts that fuel last-minute panic from the steps that are still possible.
body_md: Use it with a recent deadline your client met in a rush or missed. Many clients list only the feelings, so ask for the exact sentence in their head at the moment they froze. The balanced-thought box works best when it names one small step that is still available, not a pep talk. Your judgment decides how far to push the evidence column.

fields.label: The deadline and when you first noticed it
What I felt in my body when it got close
The thought that hit hardest, in my own words
Evidence the thought is true
Evidence that is missing or leaves it out
A more balanced thought
One small step still open to me right now
How strong the dread feels now, 0 to 10

title: Distraction Defusion Cards
summary: Cards for noticing a pull toward something else and labeling it without obeying it.
goal: Practice noticing the pull of a distraction and returning to a chosen task.
duration: 20 minutes, then daily for a week
body_md: Clients often try to force the pull away, which tends to make it louder. Have them write the pulls as phrases, such as I should check my phone, and practice prefacing them with I am having the thought that. Keep the aim on returning to the task, not on silencing the thoughts. Review the cards together at the next session.

fields.label: Three pulls that show up when I try to focus
Write each one starting with I am having the thought that
What I was working on when the pull came
Where I felt the pull in my body
What I did next, and what I would choose to do instead
One value this task connects to
A sentence I can say when a pull arrives

title: STOP Skill Impulse Card
summary: A pocket card that walks a client through Stop, Take a step back, Observe, Proceed mindfully.
goal: Build a short pause between an impulse and the action that follows it.
body_md: Rehearse with a low-stakes impulse first, such as interrupting or an unplanned purchase, before the client tries it when emotions run high. Clients often skip the observe step, so have them name one thing they notice in the body and one in the room. The card is a prompt for practice between sessions, and you decide how to pace it.

fields.label: An impulse I often act on too fast
What stopping would look like for me
What I notice in my body when I step back
What I notice in my thoughts and the room
What I want in this situation
My mindful next move
Where I will keep this card

title: Weekly Household Meeting Agenda
summary: A shared agenda for a short weekly meeting about chores, calendars and appreciation.
goal: Give both partners a predictable time to coordinate the week without nagging.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own boxes before the meeting, then you walk through them in session first. The partner who tends to hold the calendar practices handing over one item, and the other partner practices owning it, with a reminder they set themselves. Keep it short and end on appreciation. Adjust the order to fit how the pair actually talks.

fields.label: Partner A: what is on my calendar this week
Partner B: what is on my calendar this week
Partner A: one task I will own and how I will remember it
Partner B: one task I will own and how I will remember it
Something I appreciated about my partner last week
Something that did not work, said without blame
What we will try differently this week

title: Morning Routine Picture Track
summary: A child draws each morning step on a strip and builds a track the parent helps them follow.
goal: Help a child see their morning steps in order and take ownership of them.
body_md: Have the child draw four to six morning steps on cards and lay them along a paper track with a start and a finish flag. The parent's role is to point to the card, not to repeat instructions, and to cheer at the finish. Send the track home and ask the parent to report back on which step needs a redesign. If a child discloses harm while you draw together, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Steps I drew on my track, in order
The step that is hardest for me
What my parent does to help, like pointing to a card
What I do when I get stuck on a step
How I celebrate at the finish flag
What my parent noticed and wants to change

title: Refusal Skills Role-Play Cards
summary: A turn-taking card game for practicing how to decline substance use offers.
goal: Rehearse short, firm ways of declining when substance use is offered.
body_md: Players draw a situation card, such as a coworker offering a drink or an old friend stopping by, and the other player reads the offer while the first responds. Rotate roles every turn. Keep the responses short and practice saying them out loud. Debrief on which replies felt natural and which felt scripted, and let the client choose two to keep.

fields.label: Situations I most want to practice
My shortest way of saying no
A reply that gives a reason, and one that gives none
A person I would text for help after an offer
What I noticed in my body while declining
The two replies I will keep, and when I will use them

title: Weekly Rhythm Rebuild Planner
summary: A seven-day planner for filling the times that used to involve substance use.
goal: Plan meaningful activities for the hours that used to be built around substance use.
body_md: Ask the client to mark the hours when substance use used to happen and plan something concrete in each one, with a person attached where possible. Many clients plan too much at once, so help them choose a few anchors and leave space. Check in on what actually happened the following session and treat gaps as information, not failure.

fields.label: Times of day and days of the week that used to involve substance use
What I will do in each of those times
Who I will do it with or tell about it
What I need to have ready ahead of time
One thing I enjoy that I have not made time for
What got in the way last week
One change I will make to next week's plan

title: Permission Thoughts Record
summary: A record for catching I deserve this and one will not hurt thoughts before substance use.
goal: Spot permission-giving thoughts and weigh them against what the client values.
body_md: Permission-giving thoughts often sound reasonable in the moment, so ask for the exact words and the situation around them. Work through one recent example in session before assigning it. The alternative thought should be one the client believes, not a slogan. You decide whether to keep going into the beliefs underneath.

fields.label: The situation and what I was feeling
The permission thought, word for word
How believable it felt, 0 to 100
What it let me do or told me I could skip
What happened afterward
A response I could say to that thought
What I would want to have done instead

title: Urge Passengers on the Bus
summary: An ACT bus metaphor worksheet for carrying urges along without letting them drive.
goal: Practice carrying urges as passengers while the client keeps driving toward their values.
body_md: Walk through the bus metaphor aloud, then let the client draw their own bus with the urges as passengers. Clients often want to throw the passengers off the bus, so notice that effort and ask what it costs them. Keep returning to the direction they chose. Read the last prompt aloud together.

fields.label: Where I want my bus to go, in a few words
The urges that ride along, and what they say
What I have done to try to get them off the bus
What that cost me or what happened
What I could do if they stay on while I keep driving
One small step in my chosen direction this week

title: Pros and Cons Decision Card
summary: A DBT pros and cons grid comparing acting on an urge with tolerating it.
goal: Compare short-term and long-term outcomes of acting on an urge versus tolerating it.
body_md: Fill in all four quadrants, and be sure the client includes the real pros of using, which builds trust and keeps the exercise honest. Complete it when the client is calm, then carry the card for use when an urge arrives. Look at what the long-term cons of tolerating are, and ask whether any are workable.

fields.label: Pros of acting on the urge, now and later
Cons of acting on the urge, now and later
Pros of tolerating the urge, now and later
Cons of tolerating the urge, now and later
What stands out when I look at all four
One thing I will do to ride out an urge this week

title: Calm-Down Jar Craft
summary: A child fills a jar with water and glitter and watches it settle while breathing.
goal: Give a child a hands-on picture of big feelings settling when they pause and breathe.
body_md: Make the jar together and let the child shake it as the big feeling, then breathe until the glitter settles. The parent's role is to keep a jar at home, offer it without commands, and stay close while the child uses it, never as a punishment. Ask the child to draw what the jar looks like when they are calm. If a child discloses harm while you draw together, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What my big feeling looks like when I shake the jar
A drawing of my jar when it is calm
What I did while I watched the glitter settle
When I could use my jar at home
What my parent does when I use my jar
What I notice in my body when it settles

title: Trigger Tag Team Cards
summary: A group card game where players trade trigger situations and brainstorm calmer moves.
goal: Practice naming triggers and generating a calmer choice for each in a safe, playful setting.
body_md: Each player writes a trigger on a card, such as being interrupted or ignored, and the deck is shuffled. On a turn, a player draws a card and names a first body sign, then tags a teammate for a calmer move. Keep it light and watch that no one is put on the spot. Debrief on which moves players would actually try.

fields.label: A trigger I put in the deck
The first body sign I notice with it
A calmer move a teammate suggested
A move I would try this week
How it felt to hear that others share triggers
One thing I will do differently

title: Anger Cost and Payoff Ledger
summary: A two-column ledger of what anger gets a client and what it costs them.
goal: Help a client weigh honestly what anger gives them against what it takes away.
body_md: Start with the payoffs, since anger tends to work in the short run and clients stop trusting a list that skips this. Then fill the cost column across relationships, health and work. Avoid arguing with any entry. Ask the client what they see when they read both columns and what need the payoff points to.

fields.label: What anger gets me in the moment
What need sits under each payoff
What anger has cost me with people
What it has cost me in my body and health
What it has cost me at work or in daily life
What I see when I read both columns
One cost I would most like to change

title: Other Reasons Spoke Sheet
summary: A spoke diagram for generating other explanations for a behavior that sparked anger.
goal: Loosen the first hostile explanation by generating other possible reasons for what happened.
body_md: Pick one recent event where the client assumed the other person meant harm. Have the client write the first explanation in the center and fill the outer spokes with at least four others, including ones they find unlikely. The aim is flexibility, not deciding the person meant well. Ask what they would need to know to tell which fits.

fields.label: What happened and what the person did
My first explanation of why they did it
How angry I felt, 0 to 10
Four other explanations, even unlikely ones
What I would need to know to tell which one fits
How angry I feel now, 0 to 10
What I could do or say next

title: Compulsion Choice Point Sheet
summary: A choice point map of the pull toward a ritual, the away move, and the toward move.
goal: Help the client notice the moment of choice between a ritual and a values-based action.
body_md: Work from a recent example where the urge to do a ritual showed up. Clients often find the hooks (what the thought says, how the body feels) easy to name and the toward move harder, so spend time on what they would be doing if the urge were not in charge. Keep it a map of choices, not a test of willpower.

fields.label: The situation where the urge showed up.
The thoughts and feelings that hooked me.
What I did to get relief (my away move).
What that move cost me over the next hour.
Someone or something that matters to me in this moment.
One toward move I could try next time, even a small one.
What I will say to the urge while I do it.

title: Radical Acceptance of Intrusive Thoughts Card
summary: A pocket card that walks through radical acceptance when an unwanted thought arrives.
goal: Practice letting an unwanted thought be there without fighting it or performing a ritual.
body_md: Introduce radical acceptance as agreeing that the thought is present right now, not agreeing that it is true or wanted. Rehearse it once in session with a mild thought before the client uses it alone. Watch for acceptance turning into a covert ritual, such as repeating the phrase until the anxiety drops, and name that gently.

fields.label: An unwanted thought that shows up for me.
What I usually do to push it away.
How it feels to fight it.
What it would mean to let it be here, like weather passing.
The accepting statement I will say (for example, this thought is here right now).
What I will do next, with the thought still present.
How it went when I tried it.

title: Kind No Agreement for Reassurance
summary: A written plan for how one partner asks for reassurance and the other responds with warmth instead of answers.
goal: Give both partners a shared, caring way to handle reassurance requests together.
body_md: Have the partner who struggles with doubt write their part first, then the supporting partner writes theirs, so neither one feels managed. Both partners should agree on a warm response that does not answer the question, and on what the asking partner does with the feeling afterward. Expect to revisit the wording after the first week.

fields.label: Partner A: how I will notice I am about to ask for reassurance.
Partner A: what I will do instead of asking, or after I ask.
Partner B: how I will recognize a reassurance request.
Partner B: the kind words I will use that do not answer the question.
Both: what we will do together when it is hard for both of us.
Both: how we will thank each other afterward.
Both: when we will review this plan.

title: Brave Choice Comic Strip
summary: The child draws a four-panel comic of a bossy worry, the urge, a brave choice and what happens next.
goal: Help a child see the choice between obeying the worry and trying a brave move.
body_md: Draw the panels with the child, letting them design the worry character and decide how the hero responds. The parent joins for the last panel and learns one cheer-on phrase that does not give reassurance or help with the ritual. If a child discloses something worrying about their safety, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Panel 1: Draw the bossy worry and what it says.
Panel 2: Draw the urge in my body.
Panel 3: Draw the brave choice the hero makes.
Panel 4: Draw what happens when the hero waits.
What my parent will say to cheer me on.
What my parent will not do, so the worry does not win.

title: Maybe Roulette Game
summary: Players spin or roll for an uncertain statement and answer it with a calm maybe.
goal: Practice sitting with not knowing in a playful group setting.
body_md: Write cards such as maybe the door is unlocked or maybe I said something wrong, and keep the early ones mild. Each player draws, reads the card aloud and replies with a maybe statement and one small thing they would do anyway. Nobody may check, ask for reassurance or fix the card. Use the debrief to compare how hard each card felt.

fields.label: Cards we wrote for our deck.
The card that felt easiest.
The card that felt hardest.
What I said back to the maybe.
What I noticed in my body while I waited.
Something I would try with an uncertain thought this week.

title: Panic Trigger Place Map
summary: A map of places and situations the client has started to avoid or enter with dread.
goal: Show how a pattern of avoidance has grown around panic and where it has shrunk life.
body_md: Ask the client to draw home at the center and mark places by how much dread they carry, from easy to hard. Look together at what has dropped off the map and which places matter most. This is raw material for planning practice, so avoid pushing toward the hardest spot while the map is still being drawn.

fields.label: Places I go easily.
Places I enter with dread.
Places I have stopped going to.
What I do to make it through the hard ones.
Who or what I carry with me for safety.
What I miss most on the places I avoid.
The place I would most like to get back.

title: Panic Safety Behavior Test
summary: A behavioral experiment that compares a feared situation with and without a safety behavior.
goal: Test whether the feared outcome happens when a safety behavior is dropped.
body_md: Pick one safety behavior, such as carrying water, sitting near the exit or checking a pulse, and plan the experiment in session. Have the client predict the outcome with a rating, run it once with and once without the behavior, and then compare. Go slowly and agree on the size of the step, since a step too big can reinforce the fear.

fields.label: The safety behavior I rely on.
What I fear will happen if I drop it.
How much I believe that, from 0 to 100.
How I will run the experiment, and where.
What actually happened.
What I learned about the prediction.
How much I believe it now, from 0 to 100.

title: Passengers on the Bus: Panic Edition
summary: A bus metaphor where panic sensations and thoughts ride along while the client keeps driving toward a value.
goal: Help the client keep moving toward what matters while panic rides along.
body_md: Draw the bus with the client, with panic sensations and frightening thoughts as loud passengers. The point is not to throw them off but to keep driving. Ask what direction the client wants to take, and expect them to say at first that the passengers have to be quiet. Stay with what they would do if the passengers could stay.

fields.label: Where I want my bus to go (a value or a place that matters).
The loud passengers: sensations I notice.
The loud passengers: thoughts they shout.
What they tell me to do.
What happens when I do what they say.
What I could do while they ride along.
One small drive I will take this week.

title: TIPP Cool-Down Plan for Panic
summary: A plan built around temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing and paired muscle relaxation.
goal: Let the client choose and rehearse TIPP skills ahead of a surge of panic.
body_md: Walk through each TIPP skill and let the client choose which two to rehearse in session. Check for any health concerns, such as a heart condition, before cold water or intense exercise, and confirm with the client's own provider where that applies. Clients often find paced breathing with a longer out-breath helps most; encourage practice while calm.

fields.label: The signs that panic is rising for me.
T: How I will use cold, like a cold pack or cold water.
I: A short burst of exercise I can do where I am.
P: How I will breathe, with a longer out-breath.
P: How I will tense and release my muscles.
The two skills I will rehearse this week.
How I felt after practicing them.

title: After the Panic Debrief Conversation
summary: A short guide for both partners to talk through a panic episode once it has passed.
goal: Help both partners reflect on what helped and what to change next time.
body_md: Teach this as a calm conversation held hours after panic, never during it. The partner who had the panic leads with what helped, and the other partner shares what they noticed and felt. Watch for the supporting partner slipping into fixing or lecturing, and for the other partner feeling like a burden. Keep it brief and kind.

fields.label: Partner A: what I experienced, in my own words.
Partner A: what my partner did that helped.
Partner B: what I noticed and how I felt.
Partner B: what I wasn't sure how to do.
Both: one thing to keep doing.
Both: one thing to change next time.
Both: how we will care for ourselves after.

title: Calm-Down Corner Builder
summary: The child designs and builds a cozy corner at home with things that help big feelings settle.
goal: Give a child a familiar place and tools for settling, set up together with a parent.
body_md: Build a mock corner on paper or from pillows, letting the child pick the items, colors and a name for the space. The parent's role is to offer the corner as a calm place, never as a punishment, and to sit nearby when asked. If a child discloses something about their safety while drawing, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw or list what goes in my corner.
What I will call my corner.
Something soft to hold or sit on.
Something to look at or listen to.
How my parent will help when I go there.
How I will know I am ready to come back out.

title: Rewind and Redo Family Game
summary: Family members act out a tough moment, then rewind and play it again with a calmer response.
goal: Give a family a playful way to practice a different response to a hard moment.
body_md: Set the rules first: each person chooses a real but mild scene, one parent and one child swap roles, and anyone can call rewind with a hand signal. Play the scene as it went, then redo it with one new move. Keep it silly enough to laugh and stay in charge of the pace. Close with a debrief and cheer the effort, not the performance.

fields.label: A scene we picked to act out.
What happened the first time.
The rewind move we tried.
What changed in the second round.
What it was like to play each other's part.
One redo we will try at home this week.

title: Weekly Family Meeting Agenda
summary: A fifteen-minute agenda for a weekly family check-in with thanks, planning and one problem to solve.
goal: Create a predictable weekly time for a family to appreciate, plan and solve together.
body_md: Help the parent set a fixed time and keep the meeting short and mostly positive. Each person gets a turn to share thanks, and only one problem is picked per meeting. Parents often try to use it for lectures; coach them to listen first, let children suggest solutions and let the family choose together.

fields.label: Day and time of our meeting.
Who will run it this week.
One thing each person appreciates about someone else.
What is coming up this week.
The one problem we will solve today.
Ideas everyone offered.
The idea we chose and how we will check it.

title: Child Behavior Meaning Check
summary: A parent thought record for the story they tell about a child's behavior in a hard moment.
goal: Help a parent notice and test the meaning they give to a child's behavior.
body_md: Choose a recent moment when the parent's reaction felt bigger than the event. Look for mind-reading and permanent labels, such as he is doing this on purpose or she never listens, and have the parent consider other explanations, including what the child might need. Keep the tone curious; parents often carry shame about their reactions.

fields.label: What my child did, as a camera would record it.
The story I told myself about why.
How I felt and what I did.
How much I believed the story, from 0 to 100.
Other explanations that might also be true.
What my child may have needed in that moment.
A response that fits what I now think.

title: Hooked and Unhooked Parent Moments
summary: A sheet for spotting the hooks that pull a parent off course and what unhooking looks like.
goal: Help a parent notice when thoughts and feelings pull them away from the parent they want to be.
body_md: Ask for one recent hooked moment and one unhooked one so the client sees that the skill already exists. Name the hooks together, such as the thought that others will think I am failing, and let the client pick a way to unhook in the moment. Expect self-judgment, and invite compassion for how hard the moments are.

fields.label: A moment when I got hooked with my child.
The thoughts that hooked me.
The feelings that hooked me.
What I did, and what it cost.
The kind of parent I want to be in that moment.
How I could unhook, for example by naming the hook or pausing.
A moment this week when I did unhook.

title: Sleep-Deprived Wise Mind Card
summary: A wise mind check-in card for the foggy, emotional hours of newborn care.
goal: Help a new parent find a steadier choice when exhaustion is driving.
body_md: Walk your client through the card once in session using a recent rough night. Exhaustion tends to push people toward emotion mind, so keep the steps short enough to use half awake. Help them pick one cue, such as a feed or a diaper change, to prompt the card, and invite them to adapt the wording until it sounds like them.

fields.label: A recent moment when exhaustion made everything feel bigger
What emotion mind was telling me
What reasonable mind would point out
What I already know deep down that I need right now
One small wise action I can take in the next hour
The cue that will remind me to pause (a feed, a diaper change, a sound)
Who I can text if the card is not enough

title: Handover Words for New Parents
summary: Partners script the words they use when handing the baby over and asking for a break.
goal: Make asking for and giving a break feel cooperative instead of critical.
body_md: Ask both partners to fill in their own side before sharing. The partner at home with the baby often holds back requests for fear of sounding ungrateful, while the other partner may be guessing at what helps. Have each partner say their script aloud and let the other respond, then adjust wording together. Keep the focus on the handover moment, not on who does more overall.

fields.label: Partner A: a handover moment that goes badly for me now
Partner B: a handover moment that goes badly for me now
Partner A: words I will use to ask for a break
Partner B: words I will use to ask for a break
Partner A: how I want to be thanked or acknowledged
Partner B: how I want to be thanked or acknowledged
What we will say when either of us has nothing left to give
The one handover habit we will try this week

title: Big Sibling Feelings House
summary: A child draws a house with a room for each feeling about the new baby.
goal: Give an older child a safe way to show mixed feelings about a new sibling.
body_md: Have the child draw a house and fill each room with a feeling about the baby, using any colors they like. Jealousy and pride often sit in rooms side by side, and both are fine. Show the parent how to answer with listening instead of fixing, and set up one short one-on-one time at home. If a child discloses harm or neglect, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw a house with a room for each feeling about the baby, then name the rooms
Which room is the biggest right now?
What does the baby do that makes the angry room bigger?
What does the baby do that makes the happy room bigger?
Something I would like to do with just my parent
What my parent will do when I show them a room (parent fills in)
One thing I can do when a feeling room gets too full

title: Night Shift Bingo
summary: A bingo game where new parents mark off the shared and surprising parts of the first months.
goal: Normalize common new-parent experiences and open up honest conversation.
body_md: Make cards of 16 squares with experiences such as crying in a parking lot, loving and resenting the baby in the same hour, and not recognizing yourself. Players take turns calling a square from their own life and marking it; others mark it only if it is true for them. After a line, the caller shares what helped. Debrief on what felt surprising. Allow passes so no one has to disclose more than they choose.

fields.label: Squares I would add to our bingo card
The square I marked that surprised me
A square nobody else marked
Something I heard that made me feel less alone
One thing someone said that I might try
How I felt when I said a square out loud
What I would tell a friend who marked the same squares

title: Good-Enough Day Planner
summary: A one-page plan that sets a minimum, a middle and a bonus version of the day.
goal: Replace an all-or-nothing day with a flexible version a tired parent can meet.
body_md: Fill it out together using a typical tough day. Many new parents grade themselves against an imagined perfect day, so help your client name a true minimum that still counts, such as one meal, one shower or one outside moment. Review the page next session and adjust the tiers, since needs change quickly with a baby.

fields.label: The things that must happen on a hard day, the true minimum
A realistic middle version of a day
Bonus items that are nice but never required
What I tell myself when I only manage the minimum
What I will say to myself instead
One thing I will let go of for now
Who can cover one item if I need it

title: Worth Without Doing More Record
summary: A thought record for moments when self-worth drops after a perceived mistake.
goal: Test the thought that worth depends on performance and find a more balanced view.
body_md: Choose a recent moment where your client felt small after a mistake or criticism. The key step is separating the event from the verdict they drew about themselves. Ask them to look at what they would say to a friend and what they actually did well in the same moment. Revisit the balanced thought over a week to see whether the feeling shifts.

fields.label: What happened
The verdict I gave myself
How strongly I believed it (0 to 100)
Facts that support the verdict
Facts that do not fit the verdict
What I would say to a friend in this spot
A more balanced thought
How strongly I believe the original verdict now (0 to 100)

title: Willing to Be Imperfect Practice
summary: A short ACT practice for making room for self-doubt while acting on what matters.
goal: Help clients take a valued step without waiting for self-doubt to fade.
body_md: Ask your client to pick one small valued action they have delayed because they do not feel good enough. Build willingness by naming the doubt, thanking the mind for it, and taking the step with the doubt present. Keep the step small and specific, and review it next session by asking what the doubt did and what they did.

fields.label: A valued action I have been holding back on
The doubt that comes with it
How I will name it (I am noticing the thought that...)
What the doubt wants me to do
What I would do if the doubt could come along
The smallest version of the step
When and where I will do it
What I noticed afterward

title: Kind Voice Skills Card
summary: A DBT-style card pairing self-validation with a plan for harsh self-talk.
goal: Practice speaking to yourself in a steadier, kinder voice when you feel not enough.
body_md: Introduce validation as saying what makes sense about a feeling without agreeing it is a fact. Rehearse the card in session with a real moment of harsh self-talk and let your client hear how it lands. Some will find kindness hard at first, so keep wording plain and credible rather than glowing. Invite them to test one line at home.

fields.label: A moment this week I was hard on myself
The feeling underneath
What makes sense about feeling that way
A sentence a caring friend might say
A skill I can use when I notice the harsh voice
My own words for validating myself
How I felt after saying them

title: Seeing the Good in Each Other
summary: Partners notice and name what they value in each other, and how it affects self-view.
goal: Build self-esteem through appreciation shared between partners.
body_md: Each partner writes appreciations privately, then reads them aloud while the other listens without deflecting. Many people brush off praise, so coach the listener to simply say thank you and notice how it feels. Afterward each partner names one thing they need to hear more often. Watch for backhanded compliments and redirect them gently.

fields.label: Partner A: three things I value in my partner
Partner B: three things I value in my partner
Partner A: a time my partner helped me feel capable
Partner B: a time my partner helped me feel capable
Partner A: a compliment I find hard to accept
Partner B: a compliment I find hard to accept
What each of us would like to hear more often
One way we will notice the good this week

title: My Proud Poster
summary: A child decorates a poster of things they are good at, kind about and proud of.
goal: Help a child collect and keep real evidence of their own strengths.
body_md: Give the child paper, markers and stickers to make a poster in their own style. Aim for specific, true things, not general praise, and let others add to it only if the child agrees. Ask the parent to hang it where the child sees it and to add one new thing weekly. If a child discloses harm or neglect, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Things I am good at
Times I was kind
Something hard I did anyway
What my friends or family like about me
A picture of me doing something I love
What my parent will add to my poster (parent fills in)
What I will do when I feel not good enough

title: One Small Hello Game
summary: A card game of tiny social steps, played in turns with a debrief.
goal: Make small social approaches feel doable and a little playful.
body_md: Write small social actions on cards, such as making eye contact, saying hello, or asking a question. Players draw in turns, rate their nerves from 0 to 10, and try the action with the group or clinician. Use a pass card once per player. Debrief on what happened versus what was predicted, and encourage repeating the same card until the nerves ease.

fields.label: Cards I added to the deck
The card I drew first and my nerves (0 to 10)
What I predicted would happen
What actually happened
Nerves after trying it (0 to 10)
The card I would like to repeat
What I noticed about other players

title: After the Event Reality Check
summary: A page for reviewing a social event with facts instead of replaying every flaw.
goal: Replace post-event replay with a fair, balanced summary of what happened.
body_md: Use it within a day of a social event. Clients tend to recall every awkward moment and few neutral ones, so ask them to separate what was observable from what they inferred about others' thoughts. The aim is a short, fair summary, not a positive spin. Review the pattern over several events.

fields.label: The event and who was there
What I remember going wrong
What I actually know happened, facts only
What I assumed others thought
Evidence that others noticed or did not notice
Things that went fine or neutral
A fair summary in two sentences
What I will do with the replay when it starts

title: Worst Case Scenario Ladder
summary: A ladder that unpacks the feared social outcome and checks what would really follow.
goal: Examine feared social outcomes and how likely and how survivable they are.
body_md: Walk your client down the ladder with a specific upcoming situation. Ask what would happen, then what would that mean, and so on, until the core fear is visible. Then work back up, asking how likely each step is and how they would cope. This works best when the fear is concrete, so keep pressing for details.

fields.label: The situation I am dreading
The worst thing I think could happen
If that happened, what would it mean about me
What I fear would follow after that
How likely each step is (0 to 100)
How I would cope if it did happen
What I can try to test the prediction

title: Social Values Compass
summary: A values exercise connecting social effort to what the client wants for their relationships.
goal: Link social discomfort to what matters so effort has a purpose.
body_md: Ask your client what kind of friend, partner or colleague they want to be, then link it to small social actions.
