fields.label: Something I care about, even if it feels far away
A goal that fits that value
The smallest step toward it I could take this week
What could get in the way of that step
What I will do if the barrier shows up
How I will notice and mark the effort, not just the result
If the hopeless feelings get heavy, I can call or text 988 and tell my therapist

title: Burning Bridges and Building New Ones
summary: Maps what keeps substance use close and plans how to cut those ties while building supportive connections.
goal: Help the client commit to stepping away from substance use by changing who and what is within reach.
body_md: This is drawn from the DBT idea of burning bridges and building new ones. Ask the client to list what makes substance use easy to return to, such as contacts, saved numbers and places, and pick what they are willing to cut. Then work on what to build in its place. Expect ambivalence, name it without pressure, and let the client set the pace.

fields.label: People, places or things that keep substance use close
The bridges I am ready to cut, and how
The bridges I am not ready to cut yet
What I will do when an urge pulls me back toward them
New bridges I could build, such as people or activities
One step I will take this week toward a new bridge
Who I will tell about this plan

title: Uncertainty Radical Acceptance Card
summary: Practices accepting not knowing for sure when intrusive thoughts push a client toward rituals.
goal: Help the client practice sitting with uncertainty and choosing wise mind over a ritual.
body_md: Radical acceptance here is about not getting certainty, rather than agreeing with the thought. Ask the client to name the intrusive thought and the urge to ritualize or seek reassurance, then rehearse a short acceptance statement and a body cue. Start with lower-stakes moments, and discuss with the client how much they want to take on before the next session.

fields.label: The intrusive thought or what-if that showed up
The urge it brought, such as checking or seeking reassurance
What I would like to know for certain
An acceptance statement in my own words
A body cue that helps me accept (open hands, slow breath)
What I will do with my attention instead
How it went and what I noticed

title: Observe and Describe Sensations Log
summary: Has the client watch and describe physical sensations in neutral words during or after a surge of panic.
goal: Replace fear of sensations with curious, nonjudgmental observing and describing.
body_md: This borrows the observe and describe mindfulness skills for the body. The client uses plain words for sensations, such as tight, warm or buzzing, and leaves out predictions and judgments. Practice in session with a mild sensation first, then assign it for after an episode. Expect clients to slip into catastrophic descriptions, so gently ask for just the facts.

fields.label: Where I noticed a sensation
Describing it in plain words, like tight, warm or buzzing
A thought that tried to interpret it
Rewriting that thought as just a description
What I noticed as the sensation changed over time
What I did while I watched it
What I noticed about how it ended

title: Asking for Help DEAR MAN for New Parents
summary: Drafts a DEAR MAN request for practical help or rest from a partner, relative or friend after a baby arrives.
goal: Turn an unspoken need for rest or help into one clear request the client can make.
body_md: New parents often feel guilty asking, so start with what they need and what they believe about asking. Work through the letters on one specific request, such as a protected stretch of sleep, and rehearse it aloud in session. Keep requests small and concrete, and encourage the client to say thanks afterward, which helps the next ask go smoothly.

fields.label: What I need help with, in one specific request
Describe: the facts of the situation
Express: how I feel about it
Assert: the exact ask, with a time
Reinforce: what is good for both of us if they say yes
Mindful: how I will stay on my point
Appear confident: how I will sound and stand
Negotiate: what I could offer if they cannot do all of it

title: Shame Opposite Action Plan
summary: Uses opposite action to shame, helping a client act against urges to hide when the shame does not fit the facts.
goal: Help the client check whether shame fits the facts and take steps that loosen its hold.
body_md: Opposite action for shame applies when the client has done nothing against their values, so first help them check the facts. If the shame does fit, repair is the focus. If it does not, support them in doing the opposite of hiding, such as sharing something with a safe person, and doing it all the way. Stay warm, and notice the client's own pace.

fields.label: The situation that brought up shame
The thought behind it
Does the shame fit the facts? What I know for certain
What shame is urging me to do (hide, shrink, stay silent)
The opposite action I could take
A safe person I could share or connect with
How I will do it all the way, including posture and tone
What I noticed afterward

title: Participate Fully Conversation Practice
summary: Shifts a client's attention outward in conversation using the participate skill instead of monitoring themselves.
goal: Practice engaging fully with others and noticing when attention turns to self-monitoring.
body_md: Social worry often pulls attention to how the client appears. This skill gives them somewhere else to put it: the other person, the words and the moment. Choose small conversations first, such as a cashier or a coworker, and have the client note where attention went. Review together and increase the challenge only as they feel ready.

fields.label: A conversation I plan to practice in
What I will pay attention to outside myself
When I noticed my attention turn to myself
How I brought it back
Something I learned about the other person
What I did with the urge to leave early or stay quiet
What went better than I expected
What I will try next

title: Time-Out and Return GIVE Plan
summary: Plans a pause from a heated conflict and a return conversation that uses GIVE skills.
goal: Help the client step away from conflict effectively and come back ready to be heard.
body_md: A time-out only helps if the other person knows it is coming back. Help the client plan the sentence they will say when stepping away, the skills they will use while apart, and the time they will return. When they come back, GIVE keeps the tone gentle. Rehearse both parts in session, and where a partner is present, decide the plan together.

fields.label: What I notice in my body when a conflict is heating up
The sentence I will say to pause, including when I will return
What I will do while I cool down (STOP, breathing, self-soothe)
What I want to say when we come back
Gentle: how I will keep my tone kind
Interested: what I will ask about their side
Validate: what I can honestly validate
Easy manner: how I will keep it light and open

title: Imagery and Safety Card
summary: Builds a calming place the client can picture, plus supports and skills for staying steady when things feel unsafe.
goal: Give the client a stabilizing image and a short safety list they can use between sessions.
body_md: This is purely stabilizing. It draws on the imagery part of IMPROVE the Moment and never asks for details of anything that happened. Build the calming image together in session, adjust anything that feels off, and let the client stop or change it. The safety prompts, including 988, are best completed in session, so you can talk through each one.

fields.label: A place, real or imagined, that feels calm and safe
What I see, hear and smell there
A word or phrase that brings me back to it
People I trust that I can reach out to
One skill I can use if I feel overwhelmed
If I ever feel in danger of hurting myself, I can call or text 988 right away
What I will do if the image stops feeling safe

title: Fear Approach Opposite Action Steps
summary: Plans small approach steps to a feared thing using opposite action, after checking whether the fear fits the facts.
goal: Break approach into small steps the client can choose, and keep it from being all-or-nothing.
body_md: Opposite action for fear means approaching rather than avoiding, done all the way and in small steps. Start by checking the facts on the actual danger, then build a short ladder with the client choosing each rung. Practice rung one in session if you can. Keep pace in the client's hands, and treat any attempt as useful information.

fields.label: The thing I fear and what I usually do to avoid it
Does the fear fit the facts? What I know about the actual risk
What fear is urging me to do
A first approach step that feels doable
A second step a little harder
A third step I am working toward
A skill to use while I approach, such as breath or wise mind
What I noticed after I tried a step

title: Appearance Thoughts Check the Facts
summary: Applies check the facts to a harsh thought about appearance by separating what happened, the thought and the feeling.
goal: Help the client separate a harsh appearance thought from observable facts and notice how it shapes feelings.
body_md: Keep the focus on the thought and feeling rather than how the client looks, and avoid debating the body itself. Ask for the situation in neutral words, then the interpretation, then other readings of the event. Notice whether the emotion fits the facts. Clients often swap one harsh thought for another, so aim for a balanced, kinder one.

fields.label: The situation, described like a camera would see it
The thought I had about my appearance
The emotion that came with it and how strong it was
Other ways to read what happened
Facts that support or do not support the thought
Does my emotion fit the facts?
A more balanced, kinder thought
What I could do next that fits what I value

title: Two-Calendar Week Planner
summary: A side-by-side look at each partner's week that makes shared time and solo time visible.
goal: Use it to turn vague frustration about time into a concrete plan for the coming week.
body_md: Have each partner fill in their own prompts before comparing, then read them aloud to each other. Couples often discover that one partner counts solo time differently than the other. Keep the focus on the next seven days rather than a full scheduling overhaul, and watch for who tends to give up their time first.

fields.label: Partner A: the three commitments in my week that cannot move.
Partner B: the three commitments in my week that cannot move.
One stretch of time I most want to spend together this week.
One stretch of time I need for myself, and what it gives me.
Where our two calendars collide, and one way we could ease it.
What I will do to protect our shared time this week.

title: Family Rules Exchange
summary: A paired reflection on the unspoken rules about conflict, affection and money each partner grew up around.
goal: Use it to help partners see where their reactions come from before they judge them.
body_md: Invite each partner to answer for their own family first, with curiosity and no ranking of whose family did it better. Partners are often surprised by how different the unwritten rules were. Slow the pace if a memory is heavy, and leave room for the listener to reflect back what they heard before responding.

fields.label: In the home I grew up in, what happened when someone was angry?
In my family, how did people show affection, or how did they not?
A rule about money or work I absorbed without anyone saying it.
A family rule I want to keep in our home.
A family rule I would like us to do differently.
One thing I understand about my partner's reactions after hearing their answers.
What I would like my partner to know about how I respond to conflict.

title: Reunion Ritual Planner
summary: A planning sheet for the first twenty minutes when partners reconnect at the end of a day apart.
goal: Use it to help partners replace a rushed or tense reunion with a small, repeatable one.
body_md: Ask each partner to describe the reunion they would want, then look for one overlap to try. Many couples arrive carrying the day's stress and meet each other's mood by accident. Keep the ritual small enough to repeat on a hard day, and check in at the next session about what got in the way.

fields.label: What the first twenty minutes at home are usually like for me.
What I tend to need first when I walk in the door.
What my partner might notice that tells them what I need.
One small reunion ritual I would like us to try.
What each of us does to make a reunion easier.
What we will do on days when the ritual does not fit.

title: Reassurance Menu
summary: A menu where each partner lists the specific words and actions that help them feel secure.
goal: Use it to replace guessing about reassurance with requests each partner can actually meet.
body_md: Have each partner build their own menu, then trade and talk through it. Mind-reading is common here, so ask for concrete, doable items rather than general ones like more love. Notice whether a partner struggles to ask, and help the other hear requests as invitations rather than criticism.

fields.label: Words from my partner that help me feel secure.
Actions from my partner that help me feel close.
Times of day or situations when I most need reassurance.
What I do when I do not get reassurance, and how it looks to my partner.
One item on my partner's menu I can offer this week.
One item on my own menu I will ask for out loud.

title: Decision Styles Working Together Sheet
summary: A comparison sheet of how each partner makes decisions, with room to plan how the two styles can work together.
goal: Use it to help partners stop reading each other's decision style as stubbornness or neglect.
body_md: Walk through a recent real decision together and have each partner describe how they approached it. Differences in pace and information needs are often mistaken for lack of care. Keep the tone light, and note which decisions each partner is happy to hand over and which they want a voice in.

fields.label: Partner A: when a decision comes up, I usually start by.
Partner B: when a decision comes up, I usually start by.
A recent decision we handled well, and what helped.
A recent decision that went badly between us, and what happened.
Decisions I am glad to hand to my partner.
Decisions where I want an equal voice.
One agreement we will try for our next big decision.

title: Shared Grounding and Pacing Plan
summary: A plan where partners agree on grounding steps, a pause signal and how fast to go with heavy topics.
goal: Use it to give partners shared steps for steadying the room when a reminder of past trauma shows up.
body_md: Build this at a calm moment in session, and keep it about steadiness and pacing. Never ask either partner to write out what happened. Agree on a pause signal the partner can honor without asking questions. Complete the 988 prompt together in session, not as homework, and revisit the plan as it changes.

fields.label: Partner A: things that help me feel steady and present when I am stirred up.
Partner B: things that help me feel steady and present when I am stirred up.
A pause signal we both agree to honor, and what happens right after.
What I would like my partner to do, and not do, when a reminder shows up.
Topics we will save for session or a calmer day.
Support people we can reach, such as a friend, family member or my therapist.
If either of us feels unsafe or in crisis, we will call or text 988 or call 911. Who will make the call?

title: Conversation Focus Agreement
summary: An agreement for how partners signal and recover when attention drifts during an important talk.
goal: Use it to help partners handle drifting attention and interruptions without hurt feelings or blame.
body_md: Describe the pattern as a mismatch of timing, not a flaw in either partner. Let the partner whose attention drifts name what helps, such as one topic at a time or movement. Let the other name what the drift feels like to them. Try the agreement on a low-stakes topic before a hard one.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me stay with a conversation.
Partner B: what helps me stay with a conversation.
What it feels like to me when my partner's attention drifts.
What it feels like to me when I realize I have drifted.
A signal we both agree to use, and what comes right after it.
Best times and places for our important conversations.
One topic we will try the agreement on this week.

title: Rising Heat Signal Chart
summary: A chart where each partner names their early signs of rising anger and what the other can do about it.
goal: Use it to help partners notice heat earlier and agree on a way to step back and return.
body_md: Work through each partner's signs in the body, thoughts and behavior, and keep the talk about patterns rather than blame. Early signs are easy to miss in the moment, so ask for specific cues. Agree on what a return conversation looks like. If anyone feels unsafe, handle that in session before using a chart like this.

fields.label: Partner A: the earliest signs in my body that I am heating up.
Partner B: the earliest signs in my body that I am heating up.
What my voice or behavior looks like when I am past the point of talking well.
What I would like my partner to say or do when they see my signs.
What I will say to pause, in my own words.
How we will return to the topic once we both feel calmer.
What each of us needs from the other after a heated moment.

title: Partner Uncertainty Phrases Card
summary: A card of supportive phrases a partner can use in place of answering repeated requests for reassurance.
goal: Use it to help partners respond to intrusive thoughts with warmth and without feeding the urge to check.
body_md: Draft the phrases with the client who has intrusive thoughts, so the card sounds like something they would accept. Partners often answer the question out of love and it grows. Let the client choose which questions the card covers. Expect awkwardness at first, and check in on how both partners felt using it.

fields.label: The questions I tend to ask my partner when a worry hits.
How I feel right after my partner answers, and an hour later.
Partner B: how I feel when I am asked, and what I usually say.
Phrases that feel warm and honest and do not answer the question.
What I would like my partner to do if I ask anyway.
What I can do on my own for a few minutes after the phrase.
How we will talk about the card afterward, without blame.

title: Panic Wave Aftermath Check-In
summary: A short conversation guide for partners to use after a panic wave has passed.
goal: Use it to help partners debrief once the body has settled so the next wave goes more smoothly.
body_md: This is a calm-after conversation, not a rehearsal for the moment itself. Have the partner who felt the panic describe what helped, and the other what was hard to watch. Partners often leave out their own reactions, so make room for them. Suggest checking in with a clinician or doctor if something feels physically different.

fields.label: Partner A: what I noticed in my body and thoughts, as best I remember.
What my partner did that helped, even a little.
What my partner did that did not help, said kindly.
Partner B: what it was like for me to be there.
What we would both like to try differently next time.
How I would like us to return to the rest of our day.
Something kind we can do for each other tonight.

title: Small Moments Reconnection Plan
summary: A plan for new parents to protect small moments of connection when sleep and time are scarce.
goal: Use it to help partners stay close as a couple while their days revolve around a baby.
body_md: Keep expectations modest. Many new parents grieve the closeness they had and fear saying it. Invite each partner to name small, realistic moments such as a text or five minutes after bedtime. Ask who can help with practical tasks, and check how each partner is coping with the shift in roles.

fields.label: A moment with my partner I have missed since the baby came.
What I am feeling about our time as a couple right now.
Five-minute connection ideas that fit our days.
Where each of us feels unseen in the work of parenting.
People we can ask for practical help, and what to ask for.
One small connection we will try this week, and when.
What I would like my partner to know about how I am doing.

title: Inner Critic Partner Exchange
summary: An exchange where one partner names their inner critic and the other practices answering it with honesty and care.
goal: Use it to help partners support each other's self-worth without arguing with the critic or ignoring it.
body_md: Have the speaker write what their inner critic says in its own words, then let the partner try replies that are warm and true instead of flattering. Partners often rush to contradict. Notice if the speaker deflects kindness and practice receiving a statement slowly. Switch roles if time allows.

fields.label: Partner A: the harsh things my inner critic tells me, in its own words.
Partner B: how I feel when I hear my partner's critic.
A reply from my partner that feels honest, not just nice.
How I tend to deflect kindness, and what I could try instead.
Partner B: now share your own inner critic, if you wish.
A moment this week my partner saw something good in me.
One signal I can give when my critic is loud.

title: Hard Dates Planner for Grieving Partners
summary: A planner for anniversaries, birthdays and holidays that are hard because of a loss.
goal: Use it to help partners plan ahead for difficult dates and say what each needs, even when needs differ.
body_md: Have partners list the coming dates together and talk about what each would like. One may want company and the other quiet, and both are fine. Remind the couple that plans can change on the day. Review afterward in session and let them adjust it for next time.

fields.label: Dates in the next few months that may be hard for us.
Partner A: what I think I will want on a hard date.
Partner B: what I think I will want on a hard date.
Ways to honor the person or loss that we can both live with.
What we will say if one of us needs space or company suddenly.
Who else we could invite to be part of the day.
What we will do for each other the day after.

title: Stuck Point Experiment Card
summary: A card where each partner picks one small change to try for a week on a recurring sticking point.
goal: Use it to move partners from talking about the problem to testing a small change.
body_md: Pick one recurring sticking point, and have each partner choose a small behavior they can change on their own, not one they ask the other to change. Keep it small and specific. Review it the next session, including what got in the way, and avoid scoring who tried harder.

fields.label: The recurring sticking point we chose, in neutral words.
Partner A: the small change I will try on my side.
Partner B: the small change I will try on my side.
When and where each of us will try it.
How we will notice if it makes any difference.
What we will say to each other if it goes badly.
What we noticed at the end of the week.

title: Touch Pacing and Pause Signal Agreement
summary: An agreement on pacing, pause signals and choice around touch and closeness for partners where one has survived abuse.
goal: Use it to give both partners predictable, consent-based steps that keep closeness safe and paced.
body_md: Build this together in session, going at the pace of the partner who is more cautious. Do not ask either partner to write what happened, and tell them they never need to. Make pausing or declining always welcome, with no explanation required. Complete the 988 prompt in session, not as homework.

fields.label: Partner A: kinds of closeness that feel okay for me right now.
Partner B: kinds of closeness that feel okay for me right now.
A pause word or signal, and how we respond when one of us uses it.
What I need to hear from my partner when I say no or not now.
Grounding steps we can use together if one of us feels overwhelmed.
Support people and my therapist I can lean on between sessions.
If either of us feels unsafe or in crisis, we will call or text 988 or call 911. What is our plan?

title: Feared Situation Trip Planning Sheet
summary: A planning sheet for trips and events where one partner's fear shapes the plans.
goal: Use it to help partners plan outings together, with fear in view and without either partner giving up the plan.
body_md: Pick a real upcoming trip or event and plan it with both partners at the table. Ask what the fearful partner wants to try and what the other fears losing. Avoid either partner quietly arranging everything around the fear. Decide on one stretch step and one back-up, and review how it went.

fields.label: The trip or event we are planning, and what each of us hopes for.
Partner A: the parts that feel scary to me.
Partner B: how I have adjusted plans, and how that has felt.
One step I am willing to try, with my partner nearby.
One back-up plan if the step is too much that day.
How my partner can encourage me without pushing.
What we will do afterward to celebrate or recover.

title: Comfort and Being Seen Conversation Guide
summary: A guide for partners to talk about comfort with being seen and how that shapes closeness.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about self-consciousness and affection with kindness and without pressure.
body_md: Keep the focus on comfort and feelings, not on looks or comparisons. Let each partner say what helps them feel at ease and what does not. Partners often guess wrong about each other's reasons. Stop if the talk turns critical, and invite each partner to name one thing they appreciate about being together.

fields.label: Partner A: situations when I feel self-conscious around my partner.
Partner B: situations when I feel self-conscious around my partner.
What helps me feel at ease and close, such as setting or pace.
Words from my partner that land well, and words that do not.
What I would like my partner to know about my comfort that I rarely say.
One thing I appreciate about how my partner treats me.
One small step toward more ease that we both agree on.

title: Feelings Hide-and-Seek Game
summary: Feeling cards are hidden around the room and the child finds them, names each feeling, and acts it out.
goal: Build a shared feelings vocabulary through movement and play.
body_md: Draw or write six to eight feeling faces on index cards and hide them before the child comes in. The parent hunts alongside the child, then takes a turn acting out a card for the child to guess. Keep it silly; the parent's job is to name feelings out loud and show that all of them are welcome. Notice which cards the child skips or lingers on.

fields.label: Which feeling card was the easiest to find?
Which feeling did I act out?
Which feeling was hard to act out?
When did I last feel this one at home?
What does my face do when I feel it?
What can a grown-up say when they see that feeling on me?

title: Pause Button Craft
summary: The child builds a big paper pause button and practices pressing it before reacting, with the parent modeling it first.
goal: Give a child a concrete cue to stop, breathe, and choose.
body_md: Cut a circle from cardboard and let the child decorate it. Practice together by having the parent narrate pressing the button during a mildly frustrating moment, such as a tower that falls. Then play a quick game where the child presses it whenever a silly trigger is called out. Send the button home so the parent can point to it gently rather than demand calm.

fields.label: I made my pause button look like...
When I press pause, my body does this...
One thing I can do during a pause is...
A time I might want to press pause is...
Who can remind me to press it?
How did it feel when my grown-up pressed theirs?

title: Story Stones Set
summary: The child paints pictures on smooth stones, then draws stones from a bag to tell a story with the parent.
goal: Open up storytelling that lets a child express ideas through characters.
body_md: Have the child paint or draw simple pictures on stones: a house, a heart, a storm, an animal, a door. Afterward the parent and child take turns pulling a stone from a bag and adding a sentence to a shared story. Stories often carry themes the child cannot say directly; follow the story with curiosity and leave interpretation to your clinical judgment.

fields.label: The pictures I put on my stones are...
My favorite stone is...
In our story, the main character is...
What did the character want?
What helped the character in our story?
How would I end our story?

title: Helping Hands Tracing
summary: The child traces both hands and fills each finger with a way they help, and a way others help them.
goal: Highlight a child's helpful actions and the people who support them.
body_md: Trace the child's hands on paper, then trace the parent's. In each finger the child writes or draws one thing they do to help and one way a grown-up helps them. The parent adds fingers of their own. Hang the hands where the family sees them. Ask the parent to notice helping moments during the week and mention them out loud.

fields.label: A way I help at home is...
A way I help a friend is...
A way I help myself feel better is...
A person who helps me is...
How do they help me?
One more helping thing I want to try is...

title: Worry Shrinking Comic Strip
summary: The child draws a three-panel comic where a worry starts big and gets smaller as the character tries something brave.
goal: Show a child that worries can change size when they try small brave actions.
body_md: Fold a page into three panels. In the first the worry is huge, in the second the character tries one small brave thing, and in the third the worry has shrunk. Let the child pick the character. The parent draws a comic of their own about a grown-up worry, which models that everyone has them. Notice if the child includes help-seeking in the story.

fields.label: My character is...
The worry in panel one is...
How big does the worry look in panel one?
The brave thing my character tries in panel two is...
What does the worry look like in panel three?
What would my character tell a friend with the same worry?

title: Energy Battery Drawing
summary: The child draws a battery and fills it with what charges them up and what drains them, then picks one charging activity with a parent.
goal: Help a child notice low energy and plan one small thing that helps.
body_md: Draw a large battery and divide it into sections. Let the child color how full it feels today. Then list things that charge it, like outdoor play or a hug, and things that drain it. The parent commits to one charging activity during the week and joins in. Complete this together in session. If the child says anything about hurting themselves or being hurt, follow your reporting duties and safety judgment.

fields.label: My battery today looks like...
Things that charge my battery are...
Things that drain my battery are...
One charging thing I want to try this week is...
Who can do it with me?
If feelings ever get too big or scary, a grown-up can call or text 988. Who is my grown-up?

title: Body Break Spinner Game
summary: The child decorates a spinner with movement breaks and plays it with a parent between tasks.
goal: Build short movement breaks that help a child reset during homework or chores.
body_md: Draw a circle split into six sections and add a paper arrow. The child picks one movement for each section: wall push, animal walk, jumping jacks, and so on. Parent and child spin for a break during a short task, then return to it. Keep breaks about a minute. Ask the parent to let the child spin before frustration builds rather than as a reward or a punishment.

fields.label: The six movements on my spinner are...
My favorite movement is...
What helps my body when it feels wiggly?
What is hard to keep doing for a long time?
When could I spin the spinner at home?
How can my grown-up help me remember?

title: Safe Outlet Board Game
summary: The child makes a simple path board where each space asks for a safe way to let anger out, like stomping or squeezing a pillow.
goal: Practice safe anger outlets through play before a hard moment arrives.
body_md: Draw a winding path with spaces for safe outlets and feeling prompts. The child and parent take turns moving a game piece and doing what each space says. Add a few spaces for words a child can say to a grown-up. Listen for what the child says about home; if they disclose harm or fear, follow your reporting duties. The parent's role is to join in and show calm responses.

fields.label: A safe way I let anger out is...
Something that makes my body feel hot is...
What can I say when I am mad?
What helps me feel calm after?
A place I can go to cool down is...
Who can I tell when I feel mad or unsafe?

title: Doubt Doodle Comic: Maybe Is Okay
summary: The child draws a comic where a character hears a what-if voice and answers with a calm maybe-maybe-not.
goal: Practice sitting with uncertainty instead of seeking another answer.
body_md: Have the child draw the what-if voice as a character and write what it says. Then draw the main character replying, 'Maybe, maybe not,' and doing something fun. The parent practices the same reply without giving extra reassurance or answers to repeated questions. Walk through the parent's part carefully, since pulling back reassurance is often the harder half. Keep the tone light.

fields.label: The what-if voice in my comic looks like...
What does the voice say?
How does my character reply?
What fun thing does my character do next?
What does my body feel when I do not get an answer?
What can my grown-up say to cheer me on?

title: Calm Parent Signal Card
summary: Parent and child design a signal card together that either can hold up when a moment is getting heated.
goal: Create a shared, blame-free signal for taking a breather together.
body_md: Both parent and child decorate a card with a symbol they choose together, such as a stop sign or a paper leaf. Agree on what holding it means: a short break, a deep breath, then coming back to talk. The parent practices holding the card first, so the child sees the grown-up use it. Rehearse it during a low-stakes pretend disagreement.

fields.label: Our signal card looks like...
What does it mean when someone holds it up?
What do we do for our break?
Where can we keep it at home?
What will my grown-up do when I hold it up?
What will I do when my grown-up holds it up?

title: Big Sibling Photo Book
summary: The child makes a small book with drawings of life before and after a new baby, and what only a big kid can do.
goal: Give a child room for mixed feelings about a new baby and family changes.
body_md: Staple a few pages together and let the child draw or paste photos: our family before, the baby coming, and my big-kid jobs. Include a page for hard feelings. The parent reads along and answers with warmth, not fixes. It can also open a gentle talk about a parent who is tired or needs rest, using the child's words and your clinical judgment.

fields.label: Our family before the baby looked like...
The baby is...
A big kid job I like is...
A feeling I have about the baby is...
Something I miss is...
Something special just for me and my grown-up is...

title: Proud Moments Trophy Shelf
summary: The child builds small trophies from cups and foil, each marking a proud moment, then displays them on a shelf at home.
goal: Help a child notice and keep real moments of pride.
body_md: Provide paper cups, foil, and stickers. The child makes a trophy for each moment they are proud of, including small ones like trying again. The parent makes one too and says what they noticed. Ask the parent to add one new trophy a week for effort, kindness, or courage rather than only for winning, and to display them in plain sight.

fields.label: A moment I am proud of is...
What did I do?
How did my body feel?
A time I tried again was...
A kind thing I did was...
The next trophy I want to earn is...

title: Memory Garden Drawing
summary: The child draws a garden where each flower stands for a memory of someone who died, and the parent adds a flower too.
goal: Give a child a gentle way to remember someone and share it with family.
body_md: Provide paper and colored pencils and ask the child to draw a garden. Each flower can hold a memory, a favorite thing, or a feeling about the person. The parent draws a flower and shares a memory. Let the child set the pace, and expect play or silence. If a child discloses fear, harm, or a safety concern, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The person I am remembering is...
A flower for a happy memory is...
A flower for something I miss is...
A flower for something I wish I could say is...
What do I like to do to remember them?
Who can I share my garden with?

title: Sorry and Fix-It Plan Cards
summary: The child decorates cards listing ways to repair after a fight with a sibling or friend, and practices one with a parent.
goal: Teach a child that repair is a skill, beyond just saying sorry.
body_md: Make a small set of cards with repair choices: say sorry, share, ask what would help, draw a card, or take a break and return. The child decorates each one. Parent and child role-play a small squabble and use a card. The parent's job is to model repair too, naming their own mistakes. Use the child's choices to see what feels doable.

fields.label: A time I had a fight with someone was...
How did my body feel?
One fix-it card I like is...
Another way to make it better is...
What would help me feel ready to try?
How can my grown-up help me?

title: Calm Choice Spinner Build
summary: The child builds a paper-plate spinner with coping choices and uses it with a parent when feelings get big.
goal: Make coping choices visible and playful so a child can pick one in the moment.
body_md: Divide a paper plate into sections and let the child draw a coping choice in each, such as breathing, drawing, hugging a stuffed animal, or asking for help. Spin with the parent and try the chosen skill together. The parent needs to offer the spinner as an invitation, not a demand. Revisit which choices the child actually used at the next visit.

fields.label: The choices on my spinner are...
My favorite one is...
One I want to try this week is...
How does it help my body?
Where will I keep my spinner?
How can my grown-up help me use it?

title: Silly Makeover for a Big Fear
summary: The child draws a feared thing, then gives it a silly makeover with funny hats and sounds, while the parent joins in.
goal: Shift a child's relationship with a feared thing toward play and curiosity.
body_md: The child draws what scares them in a size they choose, then adds silly details such as a clown nose or a tutu. The parent draws one too and the two share their makeovers. This is a warm-up for gradual practice, not a replacement for it. Let the child decide how close to get. Stop if distress rises, and use your own judgment on pacing.

fields.label: The thing that scares me is...
How big is my scared feeling from 1 to 5?
My silly makeover for it is...
What does it sound like now?
What did my body feel while I drew it?
What is one small brave step I could try next?

title: Fun I Love Doing Collage
summary: The child cuts and pastes pictures of activities they love doing with friends and family, with the parent adding a few too.
goal: Shift attention toward what a body gets to do and enjoy.
body_md: Give magazines, scissors, glue, and paper. The child collects pictures of things they love doing, such as dancing, swimming, or hugging a pet, and the parent adds their own. Keep talk on play, enjoyment, and what bodies do for us. Steer away from looks. Ask the parent to be mindful of how they speak about their own appearance and about other bodies at home.

fields.label: The fun things I put on my collage are...
My favorite thing to do with friends is...
What do I love doing at home?
Which activity makes me feel strong or silly?
Who do I do it with?
What is one new fun thing I want to try?

title: Choice Point Board Game
summary: A board game where each turn sends a piece toward what matters or away from it, then names the move.
goal: Use it to help a client notice moves toward and away from what matters.
body_md: Draw a path on paper with a start and a goal square for a value the client names. Players take turns rolling a die and drawing a situation card you wrote. They say what they might do, then decide whether the move goes toward the goal or away from it, and move one space either way. Allow passes. Debrief by asking which away moves felt the most tempting and what the toward moves cost.

fields.label: The value on my goal square is...
A toward move I made in the game was...
An away move that tempted me was...
What the toward move would cost me in real life is...
One toward move I could try this week is...

title: Defusion Word Race
summary: A fast group race where players say a sticky thought in silly ways until it loosens its grip.
goal: Use it to let clients feel a thought as words rather than as a fact.
body_md: Each player writes one mildly sticky thought, not their heaviest, on a card. Take turns drawing a style card such as singing it, slow motion, a cartoon voice or a news anchor, and say the thought that way while others time it. Points go for committing, not for being funny. Keep the thoughts light at first and let clients opt out. Debrief on what changed when the thought was spoken that way and what stayed the same.

fields.label: The thought I put on my card was...
The style that changed it the most was...
Before the game the thought felt like...
After the game the thought felt like...
A time this week I could say it in a silly voice is...

title: Oops Pass Game
summary: A group game where players make a planned small mistake, pass it on, and respond kindly to the next one.
goal: Use it to practice meeting mistakes with a steadier, kinder response.
body_md: Set up a simple task like drawing a house, stacking cups or reading a sentence aloud. On each turn a player makes a deliberate small error, says Oops, and names one kind thing they could say to a friend who did the same. The next player repeats it as a response to themselves. Model first and keep errors low stakes. Debrief on what the voice in their head said and how the kind line felt to say aloud.

fields.label: The mistake I made on purpose was...
What my inner voice said right then was...
The kind line I used was...
How the kind line felt to say was...
A small mistake I could meet kindly this week is...

title: Silent Story Build
summary: A group game where players build a story one picture at a time without speaking, then compare what each meant.
goal: Use it to show how easily intentions get misread without checking in.
body_md: Pass one sheet of paper around the circle. Each player adds one drawing to a shared story, with no talking and no erasing. After a full round, every player writes what they think the story is about, then reads it aloud. Notice how different the versions are. Debrief on what it felt like to guess at someone else's meaning and what each person could have said to check it.

fields.label: The story I thought we were telling was...
The drawing I added was meant to show...
What surprised me about the other versions was...
A time I guessed at what someone meant was...
A question I could ask next time to check is...

title: Body Signal Hide and Seek
summary: A playful hunt where children find hidden body-signal cards and show how each feels in their own body.
goal: Use it to help children link body signals to feelings in a playful way.
body_md: Hide cards around the room that name body signals such as tight tummy, hot cheeks, heavy arms or fast heart. The child finds one, reads it with you and shows where it lives on a body outline, then chooses a feeling it might go with. Take turns, hiding a card for the child to find. Keep it light and let the child pass. Debrief on which signals they notice most and what a helper could do when one shows up.

fields.label: The body signal I found was...
I feel it in my...
A feeling it might go with is...
A time I noticed it was...
Something that helps when I feel it is...

title: Prediction Check Board Game
summary: A board game where players predict what will happen, try a small experiment, and score how close the prediction was.
goal: Use it to compare a worried prediction with what really happens.
body_md: Build a simple path board and a deck of small experiment cards you choose with the client, such as asking a question or waiting five minutes before checking a message. On each turn the player draws a card, writes a prediction and a worry rating, does the experiment, then moves forward by how different the outcome was. Keep experiments small and agreed in advance. Debrief on where predictions and outcomes differed and what that suggests about next steps.

fields.label: My prediction for this card was...
How worried I felt before, from 0 to 10, was...
What actually happened was...
How different it was from my prediction was...
The next experiment I want to try is...

title: Energy Token Budget Game
summary: A tabletop game where players spend a limited set of energy tokens on activities and notice what refills them.
goal: Use it to plan activity around low energy and spot what gives some back.
body_md: Give the client ten tokens for a pretend day and a set of cards listing tasks and activities, each with a token cost and some that give a token back. They pick cards in turn, spend and earn tokens, and see how the day ends. Let the client set the costs to match their real days. Debrief on which choices felt worth it, which refilled energy, and one small change to try this week.

fields.label: On my pretend day the cards I spent tokens on were...
The card that gave me tokens back was...
The choice that felt most worth it was...
The one that cost more than I expected was...
One small change I could try this week is...

title: Trigger Plan Matching Game
summary: A card-matching game that pairs situations tied to substance use urges with plans the client chooses.
goal: Use it to build a menu of ready responses to common urge situations.
body_md: Write situation cards such as payday, a stressful call, a familiar place or time alone, and leave a stack of blank plan cards. Take turns drawing a situation, naming how an urge might show up, and writing a plan card to match, such as calling a support person or leaving the place. Others can offer ideas but the player decides. Debrief on which pairings feel realistic and which need backup. Review the final cards at a later visit.

fields.label: A situation that raises urges for me is...
The way an urge shows up in me is...
The plan I wrote to match it is...
Who I could contact in that moment is...
A backup plan if the first one is hard is...

title: Pause Point Card Game
summary: A card game where players spot early anger cues in a scenario and choose a pause move before it builds.
goal: Use it to practice catching early cues and picking a pause before anger builds.
body_md: Write scenario cards that describe building frustration. On each turn the player reads one, names the earliest body cue they would notice, then draws or picks a pause card such as stepping away, slow breaths or a count. They place it where it fits on a line from calm to boiling. Others may suggest but not decide. Debrief on which cues come earliest for them and which pauses they would actually use.

fields.label: The earliest cue I notice when I get angry is...
The pause move I picked in the game was...
Where it sits between calm and boiling is...
A pause I would really use is...
A situation this week where I could try it is...

title: Doubt Dare Cards
summary: A dare-card game where a client picks small uncertainty challenges to try with the clinician beside them.
goal: Use it to rehearse tolerating uncertainty in small steps agreed with the client.
body_md: Write dare cards together that invite a small uncertainty, such as touching a doorknob once or leaving a sentence unfinished, matched to the client's own pace. Take turns drawing a card, and the client may pick, swap or pass, while you model one yourself. They rate the urge to do a ritual before and after, and wait before responding. The client sets the pace. Debrief on what the urge did while they waited and which cards to repeat.

fields.label: The dare card I picked was...
The urge I felt, from 0 to 10, was...
What I did while I waited was...
What the urge did after a few minutes was...
A dare I want to repeat is...

title: Parent Reset Role-Play Game
summary: A role-play game where parents draw a tense moment, pause, and replay it with a reset line.
goal: Use it to help parents rehearse a pause and a calmer reply before real moments.
body_md: Write cards describing everyday tense moments such as a bedtime stall or a morning rush. A parent draws one, plays the scene with you as the child, then calls a pause and says a reset line aloud before replaying it. Swap roles so they feel the child's side. Keep it playful and let parents skip a card. Debrief on what they noticed in their body, which reset line fit best, and when they might use it.

fields.label: The tense moment I drew was...
What I noticed in my body at the pause was...
The reset line I used was...
How the replay felt different was...
A moment this week I could try a reset is...

title: Night Shift Swap Game
summary: A card game where new parents trade care tasks and rest blocks and practice asking for help out loud.
goal: Use it to help new parents plan shared care and practice asking for help.
body_md: Make cards for care tasks, household tasks and rest blocks, and give each player a hand. On each turn a player may trade a card and must ask for the swap out loud with a clear request. The other can agree, offer a counter, or say not today kindly. Include a support person such as a friend or relative when possible. Debrief on what it felt like to ask, what was hard to hand over, and one swap to try this week.

fields.label: A task I would most like to hand off is...
How I asked for the swap was...
What was hard about asking was...
Who else could take a card from my hand is...
A swap I will try this week is...

title: Spotlight Estimate Game
summary: A group game where players guess how much others noticed something, then ask them what they actually saw.
goal: Use it to compare how much a client thinks others notice with what others report.
body_md: Each player does a small thing in front of the group, such as a quiet pause, a stumble over a word or a mismatched sock, and writes a guess of how many noticed and what they thought. Then the group reveals what they saw. Keep the tasks very small and let people choose their own. Debrief on gaps between the guess and the reality, and what that suggests for situations the client avoids.

fields.label: The small thing I did was...
How many people I guessed noticed was...
What I thought they would think was...
What they actually noticed was...
A situation where I could check this again is...

title: Memory Jar Draw Game
summary: A gentle group game where players draw memory prompts from a jar and share only as much as they wish.
goal: Use it to make room for remembering someone at a pace each person chooses.
body_md: Fill a jar with prompt slips such as a favorite meal, a sound, a saying or a place. Players draw in turn and may share, pass, or write the memory for themselves. Set a pause card anyone can lay down at any time. Keep a calm tone, expect mixed feelings including laughter, and watch for anyone who needs to stop. Debrief on which memories felt warm, which felt heavy, and what the client wants to carry forward.

fields.label: The prompt I drew was...
The memory it brought up was...
What I felt as I shared or wrote it was...
A memory I want to keep close is...
Someone I could share a memory with this week is...

title: Soft Start-Up Rewrite Game
summary: A couples game where partners take turns rewriting harsh openers into softer ones and score each other's tries.
goal: Use it to help couples practice raising a concern without blame.
body_md: Write sample harsh openers on cards, such as You never help. Each partner draws one and rewrites it with a feeling, a situation and a small request, then reads it aloud. The other partner scores it on how easy it would be to hear and offers one tweak. Play with sample cards first and move to real issues only if both agree. Debrief on what made a rewrite land and what each partner will try this week.

fields.label: The opener I drew was...
My softer version was...
What made my partner's version easy to hear was...
What I would tweak in mine is...
A concern I could raise softly this week is...

title: Intensity Match Dominoes
summary: A domino game that pairs each feeling intensity with a skill sized to fit it.
goal: Use it to match the size of a coping skill to the size of the feeling.
body_md: Make dominoes with an intensity from 1 to 10 on one half and a skill on the other. Players take turns laying a domino so that a skill sits next to a matching intensity, and must explain why the fit works. Allow the client to rewrite any domino to fit their own life. Debrief on which skills fit low, middle and high intensities, and which cards they would carry with them this week.

fields.label: The skill I matched to a low intensity was...
The skill I matched to a high intensity was...
A match I disagreed with was...
A skill I rewrote to fit my life was...
The skills I want to carry this week are...

title: Brave Step Dice Game
summary: A dice game where each roll picks a small, agreed step toward a feared thing and a way to cheer it on.
goal: Use it to make approaching a feared thing small, chosen and playful.
body_md: Before play, build a short list of steps with the client, from very small to bigger, and number them. On each turn the client rolls, can choose that step or an easier one, and tries it with you beside them while naming a rating before and after. Add a cheer card for each try. The client sets the pace and can stop at any point. Debrief on what the rating did, what helped, and which step to repeat.

fields.label: The step I rolled was...
How scared I felt before, from 0 to 10, was...
How scared I felt after was...
What helped me try it was...
The step I want to repeat is...

title: Willing to Be Seen Practice
summary: Builds willingness to be noticed in small social moments while carrying nervous feelings along.
goal: Choose social actions by what matters rather than by how nervous the body feels.
body_md: Link one social action to a value such as friendship or learning, then rehearse making it while nervousness stays present. Ask the client to name what they are willing to feel instead of aiming for calm. Plan a small real-world action before the next session and review what showed up.

fields.label: A person or place I would like to connect with, and why it matters
The nervous feelings and thoughts that show up around it
What I do to avoid being seen
What those escapes have cost me
What I am willing to feel to take one step
The step I will take, with a day and time

title: Double Standard Technique Sheet
summary: A two-column sheet comparing what a client tells themselves with what they would tell a friend in the same spot.
goal: Use it to help a client notice a harsher inner rule and try a fairer one.
body_md: Pick a recent moment where your client was hard on themselves. Have them fill the friend column first, since kind words come more easily there, then the self column. Watch for answers like 'but I'm different'; ask what makes the rule apply to one person and not the other. The aim is a fairer sentence they can try, not forced self-praise.

fields.label: The situation and what I told myself about it.
What I would say to a friend who was in exactly the same situation.
Words and tone I used with myself versus with the friend.
Reasons I give for why the rule is different for me.
Does each reason hold up when I look at it closely?
A fairer sentence I could try saying to myself this week.

title: Hyperfocus Exit Plan
summary: A thought-and-behavior plan for noticing deep absorption and stepping out of it on purpose when something else matters.
goal: Give a client a way to leave absorbing activity at a chosen time without feeling jolted or resentful.
body_md: Use this with a client who loses hours to an engaging task and then misses meals, appointments or people. Work out the thoughts that keep them in (just five more minutes) and the cost afterward, then design an exit cue and a landing activity. Choose the cue together; one that feels punishing will not last.

fields.label: An activity that absorbs me completely
What it costs me when I stay too long
Thoughts that keep me going (just five more minutes)
A cue that will reach me, such as an alarm or a person
A small landing activity for after I stop
How the exit went this week

title: Graded Task Ladder
summary: A ladder that breaks a task a client keeps avoiding into small rungs, each with a predicted difficulty and an actual one.
goal: Use it to turn an overwhelming task into steps a client can start this week.
body_md: Choose one task your client has been putting off and agree on the top rung together. Work backward until the bottom rung feels doable in a few minutes. Ask for a difficulty guess before each rung and a rating afterward; the gap is often useful. Stay on a rung until it feels manageable rather than hurrying upward, and make sure rungs are about doing, not about how it feels.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off.
Why it feels too big, in my own words.
My top rung: the task as I would like to finish it.
The bottom rung: something I could do in under five minutes.
Rungs in between, from easiest to hardest.
Predicted difficulty (0 to 10) before each rung.
Actual difficulty after trying it.
What I noticed about the gap between the two.

title: Difficult Conversation Prep Sheet
summary: Guides a client through preparing for one hard conversation, from goal to opening line.
goal: Prepare for a hard talk so the client says what matters instead of freezing or exploding.
body_md: Use this when a client is putting off a conversation or fears it will go badly. They clarify what they actually want from it, the main point in one sentence, an opening line, and a plan for what to do if the other person reacts strongly. Rehearse the opening aloud in session. The client decides whether and when the conversation happens, and the sheet works just as well for deciding not to have it.

fields.label: Who the conversation is with and what it is about
What I hope will be different afterward
The one sentence I most want them to hear
How I could open the conversation
What the other person might say, and how I might respond
What I can do to steady myself beforehand and afterward
When and where I would choose to have it, or whether I will

title: Weekly Reset Review
summary: Gives a client a brief end-of-week look back and a plan for the week ahead.
goal: Close one week and set up the next with a short, steady habit of review.
body_md: A short weekly look back helps clients see what is working before the next week fills up. Have the client note what went well, what drained them, and one thing they learned, then choose one or two realistic priorities. Bring the sheet to session as a ready-made agenda. Keep entries brief and non-judging; a week with little to report is still useful information.

fields.label: One thing from this week that I am glad about
One thing that drained me more than I expected
Something this week taught me about what I need
What I want to carry into next week
One or two realistic priorities for next week
One thing I can let go of or lower the bar on
Who or what could support me with next week

title: Work-to-Home Transition Ritual Planner
summary: Helps a client design a short ritual that marks the shift from work mode to home mode.
goal: Build a small, repeatable transition so the workday stops spilling into the evening.
body_md: Some clients carry the day's tension through the door and find the evening is gone before they notice. Use this to name what they are still carrying at the end of work, pick one small cue that marks a stopping point, and plan how it fits the actual commute or routine. Keep it small enough to repeat on a tired day, and review in session how it went.

fields.label: What I usually carry home from work in my mind or body
What the first hour at home looks like right now
One small action that could mark the end of my workday
Where and when I would do it, even on a busy day
What I want to be able to give the evening
How I will notice if the ritual helps, and what I will adjust

title: Hands as Thoughts Exercise
summary: A hands-on defusion demonstration where thoughts are held up close, then held out at a distance.
goal: Let the client feel the difference between being fused with a thought and holding it.
body_md: Ask the client to cup their hands over their face and describe how the room looks, then lower them to the lap and describe it again. Let them pick a sticky thought to hold in their hands. The point is not to make the thought vanish but to notice what changes in how much it steers behavior. Go slowly, and check in about what they noticed in the body.

fields.label: The thought I chose to hold in my hands
What I could see and do with my hands over my face
What shifted when I held my hands out or lowered them
What the thought still said, and how much it ran things
One moment this week I could try holding a thought this way

title: Soft Start-Up Rewrite Sheet
summary: Each partner turns a harsh complaint into a soft start-up and names their own part and what they need.
goal: Help both partners raise a concern gently, own their side and ask clearly for what they need.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B each pick a recent complaint and rewrite it as a soft start-up: how I feel, about what, and what I would like. Each also names their own part in the pattern. Read the rewrites aloud in turn while the listener only reflects back what they heard. Step in if either partner slips into blame, and keep the tone curious rather than corrective.

fields.label: Partner A: the complaint as I would usually say it
Partner A: my feeling, the situation and what I would like
Partner A: my part in how this tends to go
Partner B: the complaint as I would usually say it
Partner B: my feeling, the situation and what I would like
Partner B: my part in how this tends to go
What we each heard the other say

title: Hooked and Unhooked Tracker
summary: A short daily log of moments when a thought or feeling pulled the client off course, and what helped them step back.
goal: Help the client spot hooks sooner and name what unhooking looks like for them.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Introduce being hooked as an ordinary experience rather than a fault, and have the client log two or three moments a day. Look through the log together for patterns in hooks, such as people, places or times of day. Notice which small unhooking moves worked and build on those instead of asking for a perfect week.

fields.label: The moment I got hooked
What my mind said or what I felt in my body
What I did while hooked
What I noticed when I started to unhook
What I did next that moved me toward something I care about
What I want to remember for next time

title: Values Versus Goals Sort
summary: A card or list sort that separates directions the client values from goals that can be checked off.
goal: Clarify the difference between a direction to live by and an outcome to reach.
body_md: Have the client list several things they are working toward, then sort each into a goal, which can be finished, or a value, which is a way of moving that never ends. Many clients discover a goal sitting on top of a value they had not named. Ask what the goal is in service of, and let them find the words themselves rather than supplying yours.

fields.label: A goal I am working toward right now
Why it matters to me, and what it is in service of
The value underneath it, in my own words
A goal I have already reached that still left me wanting something
One small way to live this value today whether or not the goal happens
What gets in the way of that, and what I would be willing to carry along

title: Five Senses Landing Practice
summary: A brief present-moment exercise that moves attention through sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.
goal: Give the client a portable way to come back to the present when thoughts pull them away.
body_md: Walk the client through noticing something with each sense, naming each aloud, and then ask what they notice about where their mind went. Keep it light and optional, and let them skip any sense that feels unpleasant. Frame it as contacting the present rather than clearing the mind, and invite them to practice it in an ordinary moment before they need it in a hard one.

fields.label: Something I can see right now
Something I can hear
Something I can feel touching my body
Something I can smell or taste
Where my mind went while I was noticing
A time this week I could try landing like this

title: Obstacle Rehearsal Sheet
summary: A planning page that names the thoughts and feelings likely to show up and pairs each with a willing response.
goal: Prepare the client for inner obstacles before they meet them on the way to a chosen action.
body_md: Choose one small committed action with the client and ask what their mind will predict will go wrong. Write the likely thoughts, feelings and urges, then plan a willing response to each. Rehearse aloud in session if time allows. Keep the action small enough that the client can succeed, and read any miss as information about the plan rather than a failure.

fields.label: The action I plan to take and when
The thoughts my mind is likely to offer
The feelings or body sensations I expect
The urge I may feel to put it off or stop
What I am willing to carry with me while I do it
How I will know I took the step, however small

title: Beliefs About Worry Sheet
summary: A sheet that explores what a client believes worrying does for them and what it costs, separate from what they worry about.
goal: Use it to open up a client's beliefs about worry itself before changing how they respond.
body_md: Many clients defend worry as protective ('if I stop, something will slip'). Rather than argue, get curious about the belief and ask them to list what worry seems to do and what it costs. Notice any belief that worry is uncontrollable or harmful in itself. A small experiment on one belief can follow, chosen by the client. Keep it exploratory.

fields.label: A recent worry and how long it stayed with me.
What I believe worrying does for me.
What I believe would happen if I worried less.
What worrying has cost me in time, energy or relationships.
Times I did not worry and things still went fine.
A small experiment I could try on one of these beliefs.

title: Perfectionism Standards Experiment
summary: A planned test where a client does one task to a deliberately looser standard and compares the real outcome with the prediction.
goal: Use it to test whether a rigid standard is needed to get acceptable results.
body_md: Choose a low-stakes task where your client over-checks or over-polishes. Name the current standard, then set a looser one with a clear time limit. Record predictions about other people's reactions and about how they will feel, then compare. Expect discomfort; that is part of the data. Revisit what the extra effort actually bought, and let the client decide which standards stay.

fields.label: The task and the standard I usually hold myself to.
What I do to meet that standard, and how much time it takes.
The looser standard I will try, with a time limit.
What I predict will happen, and how upset I expect to feel.
What actually happened, including how others reacted.
What the extra effort was buying me, if anything.
The standard I want to keep, and one I want to loosen.

title: Step-by-Step Problem Solving Sheet
summary: A structured sheet that moves a client from naming a problem to brainstorming options, weighing them and trying one.
goal: Use it to give a client a repeatable way to approach a problem that feels stuck.
body_md: Start with a problem that is real and solvable, not a worry about something outside their control. Guide your client to state it in one concrete sentence, then brainstorm without judging. Judge options only after the list is long. Many clients skip the review step, so schedule a check-in on how the chosen plan went and what to adjust.

fields.label: The problem, in one concrete sentence.
What I would like to be different, specifically.
All the options I can think of, even silly ones.
Pros and cons of my top three options.
The option I will try, and exactly when.
What might get in the way, and my plan for that.
How it went and what I will change next time.

title: Decision Compromise Circles
summary: Maps each partner's non-negotiables and flexible areas on a decision so a couple can find overlap.
goal: Help partners stuck on a decision find where they can bend and what each truly needs.
body_md: Have each partner fill in the inner circle (what I cannot give up, and why it matters) and the outer circle (what I can flex on) before sharing. Read inner circles first, aloud, with the listener only reflecting back. Many couples find the inner circles are smaller and more compatible than they feared. Watch for a partner listing everything as essential, and ask what is underneath it.

fields.label: Partner A inner circle: what I cannot give up on this decision
Partner A: the feeling or value behind it
Partner A outer circle: what I can flex on
Partner B inner circle: what I cannot give up on this decision
Partner B: the feeling or value behind it
Partner B outer circle: what I can flex on
One option that honors both inner circles

title: Jealousy Reassurance Request Sheet
summary: Lets a partner name a jealous or insecure moment and ask for a specific kind of reassurance.
goal: Turn jealous moments into clear requests instead of accusations or silent withdrawal.
body_md: Partners often show jealousy as accusation or retreat, so this slows it down into a feeling, a story, and one concrete ask. The partner who feels jealous completes their side first; the other writes what they can offer and what they cannot promise. Keep the focus on reassurance and trust, not on proving anything, and check that the requests are realistic for both people.

fields.label: What happened just before the jealous feeling showed up
The feeling in my body and the story I told myself
What I am afraid this means about us
One specific thing I would like to hear or see
Partner: what I can offer that is true for me
Partner: what I cannot promise, and what I can do instead
How we will check in about this again

title: Phone-Free Connection Agreement
summary: Has a couple agree on when devices go away so shared time gets full attention.
goal: Build a realistic, shared agreement about devices that protects time together.
body_md: Device use is a common source of quiet resentment, and it goes better as a shared agreement than as one partner's complaint. Have each partner describe how it feels when attention drifts, then choose one or two small windows to start, such as meals or the first ten minutes after reunion. Keep it specific and revisit it in a week. Notice whether either partner hears the request as blame.

fields.label: How I feel when my partner is on a device during our time
What my own device use gives me, honestly
Times and places we will put devices away
What counts as an exception, such as work or family calls
What we will say when one of us slips
When we will review how this is going

title: Daily Reunion Ritual Planner
summary: Designs a short, repeatable way for partners to greet each other after time apart.
goal: Create a small daily reunion routine that sets the tone for the evening.
body_md: The first few minutes after partners reunite often set the mood for the whole evening, yet most couples leave them to chance. Each partner names what they usually need on arrival, such as quiet, a hug, or a quick download, and the pair designs a short ritual that fits both. Start small, try it for a week, and adjust. Watch for one partner's needs being quietly dropped.

fields.label: What the first ten minutes at home usually look like for us
What I need when I arrive or when my partner arrives
What I would like my partner to do or not do
Our reunion ritual in one or two sentences
What gets in the way, and our backup plan
How it felt after a week of trying it

title: Five-Year Shared Picture
summary: Walks partners through describing a shared future one area at a time and noticing where they match.
goal: Help partners talk about the future together and find shared direction.
body_md: Couples drifting along day to day sometimes have never described the future out loud. Each partner pictures a good ordinary day five years from now, covering home, work, family, friends, and rest, then they compare. Treat differences as information to explore, not a verdict. Note any area with strong feeling and revisit it with a dreams-within-conflict style conversation if needed.

fields.label: Partner A: a good ordinary day five years from now
Partner B: a good ordinary day five years from now
Where our pictures match
Where our pictures differ or leave something out
One thing I am excited to build with you
One step we can take in the next three months

title: Pushing Away Container Practice
summary: Builds an imagined container where a client can set a painful topic aside on purpose, for now.
goal: Give a client a way to set a topic down until a better time to face it.
body_md: Frame this as a short break from a topic, never as denial. Have the client picture the container in detail, then practice placing one small worry in it during session before trying anything heavier. Agree on when the topic will be picked up again, so the client trusts the pause is temporary.

fields.label: What is the topic I want to set down for now?
What does my container look like (material, size, lid, lock)?
Where does it sit, and what do I do to place the topic inside?
What will I do with my hands and attention right after I close it?
When and with whom will I come back to the topic?
What did I notice when I practiced with a small worry first?

title: Mindfulness of Current Emotions Log
summary: Guides a client to observe an emotion as it rises, peaks and fades, without pushing it or feeding it.
goal: Practice noticing an emotion as a passing wave rather than a verdict on the day.
duration: Ten minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Pick a mild emotion for early practice. Clients often turn observing into judging, so listen for words like should and shouldn't in the log and gently return them to description. Ask where the feeling lives in the body and how its intensity moved. Review one or two entries together each week.

fields.label: What emotion did I notice, and what was happening just before?
Where did I feel it in my body?
How strong was it at the start, from 0 to 100?
What did I do to simply watch it, without fighting or feeding it?
How strong was it a few minutes later?
What judgments showed up, and how did I let them go?
What do I want to remember about this wave?

title: One-Mindfully Practice Log
summary: Tracks everyday moments where a client does one thing at a time with full attention.
goal: Strengthen attention by doing one activity at a time and returning when the mind wanders.
body_md: Start with a low-stakes activity like washing a mug or walking to the car. Expect clients to report that their mind wandered and count it as failure; the return is the practice. Ask what helped them come back, and which routine task could become a daily anchor.

fields.label: Which one activity did I choose to do one-mindfully today?
What was I tempted to do at the same time?
What did my mind wander to?
How did I bring my attention back?
What did I notice that I usually miss?
What activity will I try tomorrow?

title: Make and Keep Friends Planner
summary: Lays out steps for finding people, reaching out, and keeping a friendship warm over time.
goal: Plan small, repeatable steps toward connection and maintaining the ones that matter.
body_md: Useful when a client wants closeness but stalls at the first step. Keep the first action very small, such as one message or one invitation, and rehearse it aloud. Link the GIVE skills from earlier work to the keep-it-going section, and check back on what actually happened next session.

fields.label: Who are two or three people I already know a little and could reach out to?
Where could I meet people who share an interest of mine?
What is one small first step I will take this week?
What will I say or write, word for word?
What worries come up, and how will I respond to them?
How will I show interest in the other person (GIVE)?
What will I do to keep this connection alive over the next month?

title: Solve or Accept Decision Sheet
summary: Helps a client sort a painful situation into four options: solve it, change feelings, tolerate it, or stay stuck.
goal: Choose deliberately between changing a problem and accepting it, rather than drifting.
body_md: Walk through one real situation and let the client name all four options before choosing; staying miserable is included on purpose so the choice is visible. Notice whether the client defaults to fixing everything or accepting everything. Revisit the chosen option after a week and see what shifted.

fields.label: What is the situation that is bothering me?
Could I solve it? What would that look like?
Could I change how I feel about it? How?
Could I accept and tolerate it as it is? What would help me do that?
What would staying miserable look like, and what does it cost me?
Which option am I choosing for now, and why?
What is my first step, and when will I take it?

title: Body Clue Detective Game
summary: Players draw situation cards and name the body clues that might show up, then trade guesses.
goal: Build body awareness by linking everyday moments to physical sensations.
body_md: Write ten to fifteen everyday situation cards together, some pleasant and some tense. Each player draws one and names the body clues that might show up, then others add guesses. Stress that there are no wrong sensations. Watch for a client who goes quiet on the tense cards, and let them pass without comment.

fields.label: Situation cards we wrote
A body clue I named for myself
A clue someone else named that surprised me
A sensation that shows up in more than one situation
Which clue tells me first that something is shifting
One clue I will watch for this week

title: Pause Button Pass-Along Game
summary: A circle game where a prop passes only after the holder names a pause move before reacting.
goal: Rehearse a short pause between a trigger and a reaction in a playful setting.
body_md: Pass a soft prop around while you read quick trigger cards such as a cut line or a surprise change of plan. The holder names one pause move before the prop moves on. Keep the pace brisk, then slow down for the debrief. Invite the group to notice which pause moves came easily and which felt silly, and let clients keep their own favorites.

fields.label: Trigger cards we used
The pause move I picked most often
