A pause move I heard from someone else that I want to try
What got in the way of pausing in the game
A real moment this week where a pause could help
What I will do first when that moment comes

title: Perspective Swap Role Cards
summary: Two players act out a short scene, then swap roles and replay it from the other seat.
goal: Practice seeing a shared moment from another person's point of view.
body_md: Write short everyday scenes on cards, such as a late text or a borrowed item. Pairs act out the scene, swap seats, and replay it. Keep the scenes low-stakes at first and choose them together. Ask what each person felt and wanted in each seat. This builds understanding, not agreement, so avoid steering anyone toward deciding who was right.

fields.label: The scene we played
What I felt and wanted in my first seat
What I felt and wanted after swapping
Something I noticed about the other seat
A situation in my life where I could try this swap
What I want to ask or say next time

title: Plan B Pitch Game
summary: Teams pitch backup plans for a stuck problem card, then vote on which one they would try first.
goal: Widen the list of options when one plan has stopped working.
body_md: Give each team a stuck-problem card or let a client write their own. Teams get five minutes to pitch up to three backup plans, silly ones allowed, then everyone votes on one to try. The playful rules take pressure off and help rigid thinking loosen. Ask the client to pick one small step from the winning pitch, and leave the final choice to them.

fields.label: The stuck problem on my card
Plans pitched by my team
The silliest plan, and anything useful hiding in it
The plan I would try first
The smallest first step for that plan
Who or what could support me with it

title: Energy Battery Cards Game
summary: Players sort activity cards into drains and chargers, then build a balanced day with limited battery.
goal: Notice what spends and restores energy, and plan a day that fits it.
body_md: Make activity cards together, everyday items such as a phone call, a walk, or cleaning. Players sort them into drains, chargers, or both, then plan a day within ten battery points. Expect disagreement, because the same card can be a drain for one person and a charger for another. Use that to talk about pacing, and let the client set the point values.

fields.label: Cards I sorted as drains
Cards I sorted as chargers
A card that was both, and why
My day plan within ten points
What I would trade out if the day ran long
One charger I will add this week

title: Mood Soundtrack Drawing
summary: The child draws what each feeling would sound like, using wavy, spiky or soft lines and colors.
goal: Give a child a playful, wordless way to describe feelings they cannot yet name.
body_md: Offer paper, crayons and markers, and let the child draw sound waves instead of faces. Some children can show a feeling long before they can say it. Ask about the loudest and quietest drawings, and invite the parent to guess first, then hear the child's answer.

fields.label: Draw what a happy feeling sounds like. How loud is it?
Draw what a mad feeling sounds like.
Draw what a worried feeling sounds like.
Draw what a calm feeling sounds like.
Which sound drawing is the loudest, and why?
What sound would I like to hear more of this week?

title: Five Finger Helpers Hand
summary: The child traces a hand and names a helper, grown-up or friend, on each finger to build a circle of support.
goal: Help a child see the people they can turn to when a feeling gets big.
body_md: Trace the child's hand and let them decorate it. Each finger holds one person or helper, and the palm holds the child's own best calming move. Younger children may need help finding more than two names, so include pets, teachers and neighbors. Send the hand home for the parent to post on the fridge.

fields.label: Thumb: someone at home I can go to
Pointer finger: someone at school who helps me
Middle finger: a friend who is kind to me
Ring finger: another grown-up I trust
Pinky: a helper that is not a person, like a pet or a toy
Palm: the thing I can do by myself to feel calmer

title: Feelings Matching Card Game
summary: The child and clinician make a deck of paired feeling cards, then play a memory match and share a story for each pair.
goal: Practice naming feelings and the moments that bring them through a turn-taking game.
body_md: Make about eight pairs of index cards together, one card with a drawn face and one with a color or symbol for the same feeling. Play memory match, and each time a pair is found the player tells a moment they felt that way. Parents can join as a player and share their own stories, which shows that grown-ups have feelings too.

fields.label: Which feelings did we put in our deck?
Which pair was easiest to draw?
Which pair was hardest to draw?
Tell about a time I felt this feeling.
Which feeling would I like to play again at home?
Who will I play this game with at home?

title: Stoplight Solutions Poster
summary: The child builds a red, yellow and green poster for stopping, thinking of choices and trying one.
goal: Teach a child a simple pause-and-choose routine for everyday problems.
body_md: Have the child color three circles on a poster, red to stop and breathe, yellow to think of two or three ideas, green to try one. Practice with a small pretend problem such as a toy someone else is using. The parent learns the colors too and can say the color word as a gentle cue at home rather than giving the answer.

fields.label: Red light: what I do to stop my body
Yellow light: my first idea for solving a problem
Yellow light: my second idea
Green light: the idea I want to try
What happened when I tried it?
What color word can my grown-up say to remind me?

title: Cozy Corner Blueprint
summary: The child draws and then builds a small calm space at home from pillows, blankets and favorite things.
goal: Give a child a chosen, predictable place to settle when feelings get big.
body_md: Start by letting the child draw a blueprint, then plan the real corner with the parent. The child chooses what goes in it, and the parent agrees it is never used as a punishment or a place to be sent. Review what worked and what to change after the first week.

fields.label: Draw my cozy corner and label what is in it.
Where in our home will it go?
Three things I want in my corner
What helps my body feel calm there?
How will I know when I want to go there?
What will my grown-up do when I am in my corner?

title: Savoring Moments Log
summary: Has a client capture small pleasant moments and notice what made each one register.
goal: Train attention toward ordinary good moments so they are noticed and remembered.
duration: 10 minutes a day for a week
body_md: Clients with a heavy week often say nothing good happened, because the small moments went by unnoticed. Ask for one brief entry a day: what the moment was, what the senses picked up, and how long the client stayed with it. In session, look for patterns in what supports these moments and plan to make room for more of them. Go at the client's pace and never push positivity.

fields.label: The moment I noticed today
What I could see, hear, smell, taste or feel in it
How long I stayed with it before moving on
What made it possible, such as a person, a place or a pace
One thing I could do to give myself another moment like it

title: Automatic Yes Audit
summary: Looks at recent times a client said yes without thinking, and what it cost them.
goal: Slow down automatic agreement so the client can choose what to take on.
body_md: Clients who agree on reflex often feel stretched thin and resentful without seeing the pattern. Work through three recent yeses: what was asked, what the client felt in the moment, and what saying yes cost them afterward. Then draft a pause phrase they can use to buy time. Explore in session what makes a no feel risky, and keep the choice about whether to decline with the client.

fields.label: A recent time I said yes right away
What I felt in my body when I was asked
What I was afraid would happen if I said no
What saying yes cost me afterward
A pause phrase I could use to buy myself time
One request I could revisit or renegotiate this week

title: Five Senses Orienting Round
summary: A client names what they notice in the room through each sense to anchor attention in the present.
goal: Help a client orient to the here and now using what the room offers right now.
body_md: Use this at the start or end of a session, or when your client seems pulled away from the room. Go at your client's pace and let them skip any sense. It stays in the present on purpose: nothing here asks about what happened, and you decide when it fits. Invite them to keep a copy for use between sessions.

fields.label: Something I can see that is calm or neutral
Something I can hear right now
Something I can feel touching my body, like the chair or my feet
A smell or taste I notice, or one I would choose
Where I am, what day it is, and one thing that tells me I am safe now

title: Wave Riding Skills Card
summary: A pocket card that lists distress tolerance steps a client picks from when a reminder of the past surges.
goal: Build a short, personal list of skills a client can reach for when a surge of distress arrives.
body_md: Work through the card together so it fits your client's body and daily life, using distress tolerance skills such as paced breathing, temperature change, and self-soothing with the senses. Rehearse one in session when your client is calm. If thoughts of self-harm come up, complete 988 (call or text) with them in session and keep your own safety steps in place.

fields.label: A sign in my body that a surge is starting
A skill using temperature or movement that helps me
A skill using my senses that settles me
A slow breathing pattern I can do for one minute
A kind sentence I can say to myself while it passes
A person I can text, and 988 (call or text) if I feel unsafe

title: Safe Helper Circle Drawing
summary: A child draws a circle of safe people and places, while a parent helps name who is on the team.
goal: Help a child see the trusted people and safe places around them.
body_md: The child draws themselves in the middle of a page with safe people and places around them, and the parent sits alongside, adds names the child asks for, and listens without questioning. The drawing is only about safety and support, so do not ask for details of any scary event. Remind the parent that you and they have reporting duties if a child discloses harm, and tell them how you will handle it.

fields.label: The people I draw in my circle
The places where I feel safe
Who I can tell when I feel scared
One thing that helps my body feel calm
What my grown-up can do when I feel scared

title: Trigger Plan for Two
summary: Partners each name what helps and what does not when a reminder hits, then agree on a shared plan.
goal: Help partners agree on how to support each other when one is hit by a reminder.
body_md: Partner A, who lives with the reminders, names signals, helpful responses, and unhelpful ones in their own words and chooses how much to share. Partner B names what they feel and need while supporting, and what they can offer. Keep it to the present plan and pacing; no one needs to describe the past. Stop and slow down if either partner floods.

fields.label: Partner A: early signs that a reminder has hit
Partner A: what helps when that happens
Partner A: what does not help right now
Partner B: what I feel when I see this happen
Partner B: what I can offer and what I need for myself
What we both agree to do, and a word for taking a pause

title: Safe Landing Spots Game
summary: Players take turns naming places, objects, or people that bring a feeling of safety, building a shared board.
goal: Help a group or family build a bank of safe landing spots through simple turn-taking play.
body_md: Each player draws a card with a prompt, such as a place that feels calm or a smell that is comforting, and answers or passes. Players earn a token for each answer and for each kind comment, and anyone may pass without comment. Debrief by asking which spots they could use this week. Keep every prompt in the present and stop any share that heads toward details of past events.

fields.label: The safe place or thing I named
What I notice in my body when I picture it
A spot someone else named that I would like to try
One landing spot I will use this week
What helped me take part today

title: Worry Postponement Planner
summary: A client schedules a daily worry window and jots worries down to return to later.
goal: Help a client practice postponing worries and choose which ones need a step.
body_md: Agree on a fixed 15 minute window and a spot to park worries during the day. At the window, your client sorts each worry into one that has a step they can take and one they cannot act on. Check how it went at the next session and adjust the time or length to what is realistic for them. Use your judgment about fit.

fields.label: My worry window time and place
A worry that came up and when
What I told myself to wait until the window
Worries with a step I can take
Worries I cannot act on right now
What I noticed after the window ended

title: Anxiety Passengers on the Bus
summary: A client pictures anxious thoughts as passengers on a bus while they keep driving toward a valued direction.
goal: Help a client act toward a value while anxious thoughts and feelings come along.
body_md: Invite your client to imagine driving a bus toward something that matters to them, with anxious thoughts and sensations as noisy passengers. The task is not to throw them off the bus but to keep driving. Link the metaphor to one small action this week, and let your client adapt the image to something that suits them better.

fields.label: Where my bus is headed and why it matters
Passengers on my bus, the loudest anxious thoughts
What each passenger tells me to do
What happens when I let them shout and keep driving
One small action toward my direction this week

title: Worry Weather Report Craft
summary: A child makes a weather report for their worries, with a parent as the helpful forecaster.
goal: Help a child name the size of a worry and what could help it pass like weather.
body_md: The child draws a weather map for the day, with sunny, cloudy, or stormy spots standing for how big their worries feel, and presents it like a forecaster. The parent listens, asks which weather it is, and shares one calm thing to try. Remind the parent that clouds pass and that the child does not need to be talked out of the feeling. Check in on how the parent responded.

fields.label: Today's weather in my body, drawn as sun, clouds, or storm
The worry that is the biggest cloud
Something that helps a storm pass
What my grown-up said or did that helped
My forecast for tomorrow

title: Worry Detective Card Game
summary: Players draw worry cards and take turns sorting each as a clue, a guess, or a fact.
goal: Help players practice telling facts from guesses when worry sounds sure.
body_md: Write worry statements on cards, or have each player add their own. On each turn the player draws a card, reads it aloud, and decides whether it is a fact, a guess, or a clue worth checking, and the others may add a vote. Players earn a point for each worry they can turn into something to check. Debrief on which worries sounded the surest and what was most surprising.

fields.label: A worry card I drew
Whether I called it a fact, a guess, or a clue and why
What I could check to find out
A worry I would like to test this week
What I noticed about my own worry voice

title: Calm Body Check-In Sheet
summary: A client tracks where anxiety shows up in the body and which small steps ease it.
goal: Help a client notice early body signals and match them with a helpful next step.
body_md: Use this over a week so your client can see patterns in when and where their body signals show up. They log the situation, the sensation, and one small step they tried, without needing to judge it. Review the page together and pick one step to keep. It is a record for conversation, and you decide what it means.

fields.label: The situation I was in
Where I felt it in my body
How strong it felt from 1 to 10
A small step I tried
What happened to the feeling afterward
What I would try next time

title: Thought Balance Sheet for Low Mood
summary: A client writes a heavy thought, then lists what supports it, what does not, and a more balanced version.
goal: Help a client look at low mood thoughts from more than one side.
body_md: Choose one heavy thought from this week, and let your client write it as they heard it. They look at what supports it and what leaves something out, then write a balanced version they could say to a friend. Go slowly, because the balanced version should feel believable. If thoughts of self-harm come up, complete 988 (call or text) with them in session.

fields.label: The heavy thought as I heard it
What makes this thought feel true
What this thought leaves out
What I would say to a friend with this thought
A more balanced version I find believable
If I ever feel unsafe, I will call or text 988 and tell

title: Values Compass for Heavy Days
summary: A client names what matters, then picks one tiny action that fits that value on a low-energy day.
goal: Help a client choose small, value-led actions even when motivation is low.
body_md: Ask your client to name two or three values, then scale each to something doable on their lowest-energy day, such as a text, a short walk, or watering a plant. The point is action before mood changes, not waiting to feel ready. Review which actions felt meaningful, not just which were finished.

fields.label: A value that matters to me
What it looks like on a good day
What a tiny version looks like on a heavy day
What my mind says when I try it
What I did and how it felt
The next small action I will choose

title: Reaching Out Without Pressure Sheet
summary: Both partners name how low mood shows up and what small, low-pressure connection can look like.
goal: Help partners find small ways to stay connected during low mood without added pressure.
body_md: Partner A describes what low mood feels like and what small contact helps, while Partner B names what they notice and what they need to keep going themselves. Together they choose two low-pressure ways to connect this week, such as sitting together or a short walk. Keep it about the two of them, and slow down if either partner feels blamed.

fields.label: Partner A: how low mood shows up for me
Partner A: a small kind of contact that helps
Partner B: what I notice and how I feel about it
Partner B: what I need so I can keep supporting
Two low-pressure ways we will connect this week
A signal we use when one of us needs space

title: Self-Care Pairs Skill Sheet
summary: A client pairs a skill for the body with a skill for the mind to plan around low mood days.
goal: Help a client build a go-to plan using body-based and mind-based skills.
body_md: Use the idea of taking care of the body first, such as sleep, movement, and eating regularly, and then add a skill for the mind. Your client builds pairs they can pick up when mood is low, and tries one between sessions. Adapt each pair to what is realistic for them. If hopeless thoughts come up, complete 988 (call or text) with them in session.

fields.label: A body-based step that helps me, like rest or movement
A mind-based skill that helps me
One pair I will try this week
What gets in the way of the pair
What I will do about that
If I feel unsafe, I will call or text 988

title: Weekly Energy Budget Sheet
summary: A client lists tasks and rates how much energy each takes, then plans a week that fits.
goal: Help a client plan a week around real energy levels, without guilt.
body_md: Work with your client to list weekly tasks and rate each one low, medium, or high effort, then place them across days so heavy ones are spread out and rests are included. The page is a planning aid that you review together at the next session. Ask what felt doable and what needs adjusting rather than what was missed.

fields.label: Tasks I have this week
Low effort tasks
Medium effort tasks
High effort tasks
How I will spread them across the days
What rest looks like for me this week

title: Interruption Recovery Card
summary: A card where a client plans how to find their way back to a task after a phone buzz, a question or a wandering thought.
goal: Help a client build a short, repeatable way back to the task after being pulled away.
duration: 20 minutes, then a week of use
body_md: Have the client name the interruptions that happen most, then write one sentence to leave behind before stepping away so the task is easy to restart. Notice whether the client blames themselves for drifting; the card is about the return, not about never drifting. Review it a week later and keep only the steps they actually used.

fields.label: The interruptions that pull me away most often
What I will write down before I step away from a task
The first small step I will take when I come back
A cue I can put where I will see it
What I did when I got pulled away this week
What I will change on the card

title: Values and Distraction Choice Point
summary: An ACT choice point drawn for moments of distraction, naming what pulls away and what the client wants to move toward.
goal: Help a client notice a distracted moment as a choice and steer toward what matters to them.
body_md: Draw the choice point with the client: the situation at the center, hooks and urges to drift on one side, valued actions on the other. Keep the tone curious and avoid framing drifting as failure. Pick one ordinary moment, such as starting homework or a work email, and rehearse a single move toward what matters.

fields.label: A moment this week when my attention got pulled away
The thoughts, feelings and urges that showed up
What pulled me away from what I care about
What I care about in that situation
One small move toward that I can try next time
How I will notice the choice point

title: Shared Calendar Check-In Routine
summary: A weekly sit-down where both partners look at the shared calendar and name their own parts in keeping it running.
goal: Help partners share planning without one becoming the reminder keeper.
body_md: Both partners name their own part: the partner with attention difficulties picks which reminders they want and how, and the other partner agrees to say the reminder once, kindly, rather than repeat it. Watch for the parent-child dynamic and name it gently. Each partner writes their own answers, then they compare.

fields.label: Partner A: the reminders I want and how I want them
Partner B: how I will remind once, kindly
Partner A: a task I will own this week
Partner B: a task I will own this week
What helped us stay on the same page
What we will change next week

title: Morning Mission Map
summary: A child draws a map of morning stops, such as clothes, breakfast and backpack, and the parent walks it with them.
goal: Help a child learn a morning sequence through a picture instead of repeated reminders.
duration: 30 minutes to draw, then one week of use
body_md: The child draws a map of the morning with a picture at each stop; the parent walks it with them for a few days, pointing to the next stop rather than giving orders, and praises each stop reached. If a child discloses something worrying while drawing, remember your reporting duties. Let the child add stops and decorate it.

fields.label: The stops on my morning map
The stop that is hardest for me
What my parent can do to help at that stop
A fun thing at the end of the map
Which stops I reached this week

title: Support Call Script Card
summary: A short script card a client can read aloud when an urge is strong and they want to reach a supportive person.
goal: Make reaching out during an urge easier by planning the words ahead of time.
body_md: Have the client choose one or two people and write the exact words they would say, including a plain request such as stay on the phone with me. People often skip this step because asking feels exposing, so rehearse it in session. This is an adjunct to the client's own support network and your clinical judgment.

fields.label: The people I could call or text when an urge hits
What I want to say in the first sentence
What I want that person to do
What gets in the way of reaching out
A backup if no one answers

title: Substance Use Cost and Benefit Ledger
summary: A two-column ledger of what substance use gives and costs a client, kept in the client's own words.
goal: Help a client see the pull of substance use and its costs side by side without pressure.
body_md: Invite the client to fill in what substance use does for them as honestly as what it costs; the benefit column is not a trap, and clients tend to engage more when it is respected. Revisit it over several sessions and note shifts. Let the client decide what to do with what they see.

fields.label: What substance use gives me
What it costs me
What I would miss if I stopped
What I would gain if I changed
Which column surprised me
What I want to do with this

title: Choosing Over Craving Compass
summary: An ACT compass pairing common urges with a value-guided action the client can pick instead.
goal: Help a client act on a value while an urge is present instead of waiting for it to leave.
body_md: Ask the client to name a value that matters to them, then link it with one action they can take in an urge moment. The point is willingness to carry the urge while doing something that matters, not suppressing it. Keep the actions small and concrete so they can be done in a hard moment.

fields.label: A value that matters to me
The urge and how it shows up in my body
Thoughts that come with the urge
One action I can take that fits my value
Who or what could remind me of this
How it went when I tried it

title: Wave Skills Pocket Plan
summary: A pocket plan that sorts distress tolerance skills by how long an urge usually lasts and where the client is.
goal: Give a client ready skills matched to the length and place of an urge.
body_md: Work through the skills the client already knows, such as paced breathing, cold water or a brief walk, and place each by setting: home, work, public. Test one in session so it is real, then write the shortest version on a card. Update the plan after it has been used, and keep it flexible.

fields.label: Places where urges show up for me
A skill I can use at home
A skill I can use at work or in public
How long the urge usually lasts
A skill I tried and how it went
What I will add to my card

title: Roll and Reflect Recovery Game
summary: A dice game where each roll prompts a question about urges, support, routines and what a client is working toward.
goal: Open conversation about substance use and change in a low-pressure way in a group.
body_md: Players take turns rolling a die and answering the matching prompt from a list you prepare, with the right to pass on any turn. Set ground rules for respect and privacy at the start and keep sharing at the level people choose. Debrief by asking what each person heard that they might use this week.

fields.label: Prompt one: a moment this week when I handled an urge
Prompt two: a person who supports me
Prompt three: a routine that helps me
Prompt four: a hard time of day and my plan
Prompt five: something I look forward to
Prompt six: something I want to try this week

title: Anger Trigger Timeline
summary: A timeline of the hours before an angry moment to show where stress, tiredness and hurt built up.
goal: Help a client see what built up before anger flared so they can step in earlier.
body_md: Walk back with the client from one recent angry moment, hour by hour, noting hunger, sleep, stress, pain and small irritations. Many clients are surprised how much sits before the visible trigger. Keep it a map of patterns, not of blame, and choose one early point to try something different.

fields.label: The angry moment I want to look at
What was happening an hour before
What was happening earlier that day
How my body felt
What hurt or worry sat underneath
The earliest point I could have done something different

title: Anger Pause Skills Card
summary: A card pairing a signal in the body with a DBT distress tolerance skill the client can use before reacting.
goal: Give a client a body signal and a matching skill to use before an angry reaction.
body_md: Have the client name their early body signals, such as heat, clenched jaw or fast breath, and match each to a skill such as paced breathing, cold water, or stepping out for a short walk. Practice one in session while mildly irritated. If safety toward anyone is a concern, use your own judgment and safety planning in session.

fields.label: The first signals in my body that anger is rising
A skill I can use right then
A place I can go to cool down
What I will say to let people know I am pausing
How I will return to the conversation
What worked when I tried it

title: Anger Cycle Repair Conversation
summary: A guided conversation where each partner names their own anger cycle and one repair move after a heated moment.
goal: Help partners each own their part of a heated pattern and plan a repair together.
body_md: Each partner completes their own half: what they do when anger rises, what they need from the other, and what repair they can offer. Ensure it is safe for both to do this together; if either partner feels afraid of the other, use your clinical judgment before continuing. Have them swap and listen without rebuttal first.

fields.label: Partner A: what I do when I get angry
Partner B: what I do when I get angry
Partner A: what I need in that moment
Partner B: what I need in that moment
One repair move I can offer
What we agree to try next time

title: Feelings Behind the Fire Drawing
summary: A child draws a fire and the softer feelings, such as hurt or worry, that sit underneath it.
goal: Help a child notice feelings under anger and share them with a parent.
body_md: The child draws a fire and then colors the feelings underneath: sad, worried, left out, tired. The parent listens and reflects what they see without correcting or fixing anything, then picks one thing to try next time. If a child discloses something worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: The fire I drew and when it showed up
A feeling hiding underneath the fire
A color I used for that feeling
What I want grown-ups to know
What my parent will do when they see my fire

title: Anger Reset Station Game
summary: A turn-taking game where players pick station cards, such as breathe, stretch and count, and practice resets together.
goal: Let a group practice calming moves while playing so the skills feel familiar.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a station card and acting it out for thirty seconds, while others copy or guess. Add a twist card that sets a mildly annoying scenario to reset from. Debrief by asking which reset felt easiest and which they might use at school or home. Keep it playful and let anyone pass.

fields.label: The reset I tried today
What I noticed in my body after
Which reset I liked best
Where I could use it this week
What I will tell a friend about it

title: Urge Surfing Notes for Compulsions
summary: A client tracks one urge to do a ritual as it rises, peaks and fades without acting on it.
goal: Help a client notice that an urge to ritualize changes on its own over time.
body_md: Use this when a client is ready to stay with one urge for a few minutes and watch what it does. Complete the first prompts together in session so the client knows what to write, then let them fill in the rest during or right after a practice at home. Pace it to what the client chooses, and keep your own judgment about which urge to start with.

fields.label: The urge I noticed and where I was when it showed up
How strong the urge felt at the start, from 0 to 10
What my body felt like as the urge rose
What I did instead of the ritual while I waited
How strong the urge felt at the end, from 0 to 10
What I noticed about how the urge moved

title: Doubt Versus Evidence Columns
summary: A two-column thought record that separates the what-if voice from what the client actually knows.
goal: Help a client sort intrusive doubts from the facts in front of them.
body_md: A familiar thought-record layout adapted for intrusive doubts. The client writes the doubt, then what they know for sure, then what remains uncertain. The aim is not to argue the doubt away or win certainty, but to see the two lists side by side. Notice if the exercise itself turns into a reassurance ritual and adjust as you see fit.

fields.label: The doubt that showed up
How much I felt I had to act on it, from 0 to 10
What I actually know right now
What I cannot know for sure
What I could do that fits with living with that uncertainty
How I feel after seeing both lists

title: Values Over Rituals Compass
summary: A client names what matters most to them and compares it with where rituals pull their time.
goal: Help a client connect one small step to a value rather than to relief from a ritual.
body_md: This ACT-style values exercise lets a client name what they want their days to be about and look honestly at where rituals take time from it. Keep it curious and free of blame. Invite one small, chosen step toward a value, and be ready to revisit it next session, because the step belongs to the client and may need resizing.

fields.label: Three things that matter most to me
A recent day when a ritual took time from one of them
What I wish I had spent that time on
One small step toward that value I could take this week
What might show up inside me when I take that step
What I would say to myself with kindness while I do it

title: Partner Role in Rituals Agreement
summary: Both partners name how the partner joins in rituals and agree on kinder responses together.
goal: Help partners agree on supportive responses that do not feed the ritual cycle.
body_md: Each partner has a part here. The partner with the urges says what support actually helps, and the other partner says what they feel pulled to do when rituals start. Together they pick one response to try, such as a warm acknowledgment without reassurance. Slow, repeated rehearsal in session usually helps more than a long list, and the client sets the pace.

fields.label: Partner with urges: a ritual where I ask my partner to help
Partner with urges: what support feels truly helpful to me
Other partner: what I usually do when this happens
Other partner: how it feels to do it
One warm response we agree to try this week
How we will check in with each other afterward

title: Boss of the Worry Brain Drawing
summary: A child draws the worry brain as a character and practices talking back to it with a parent beside them.
goal: Help a child separate themselves from the loud what-if voice that asks for rituals.
body_md: The child draws their worry brain as a character, gives it a name, and decides what it says. The parent sits close, says calmly that worry brain is not the boss, and does not answer its demands for reassurance. Let the child steer the drawing and the voice. If your child client discloses harm or abuse at any point, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw my worry brain and give it a name
What my worry brain says to me
What my worry brain wants me to do
What I can say back to it
Who is the boss of me
What my parent will do to help me when worry brain gets loud

title: Rescue Plan Card Maker for Panic
summary: A client builds a small card of distress tolerance steps to read while panic is rising.
goal: Help a client carry a short, personal list of steps for the first minutes of panic.
body_md: A distress tolerance card the client writes in their own words and keeps in a wallet or phone. Choose steps they can actually do while their heart pounds, such as paced breathing out longer than in, cold water on the face, or naming five things they see. Rehearse reading the card aloud in session. Complete any prompt that touches on safety with the client yourself.

fields.label: What panic feels like in my body at the very start
A step with cold or temperature that I will try
A breathing step in my own words
Five things I can see or touch right now
A kind sentence I will tell myself
Who I could text, and 988 if I ever feel unsafe, by call or text

title: Panic Mountain Drawing
summary: A child draws a mountain that panic climbs and slides down, with a parent helping name each part.
goal: Help a child see that panic rises, peaks and comes back down.
body_md: The child draws a mountain, marks where panic starts, where it feels biggest and where it slides down again. The parent sits with them and uses a calm, slow voice, naming sensations as they go without rushing the child. Practice breathing in and out like blowing on soup. Keep the pictures the child's own. If your child client discloses harm or abuse at any point, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw a mountain and put a flag where my panic starts
What my body feels like on the way up
What the very top feels like
What helps me slide back down
What my parent does to help me stay brave
A color I will use to show when I feel calm again

title: Name the Sensation Card Game
summary: Players draw sensation cards and decide whether each one is panic, exercise or excitement.
goal: Help clients see that many body sensations have more than one explanation.
body_md: Make cards for sensations such as racing heart, dizziness, tight chest and sweaty hands. Players take turns drawing a card and naming three times a body might feel that way, only one of which is panic. The client scores a point for each reasonable idea. Close with a debrief, asking what it was like to see the same sensation in many settings.

fields.label: The sensation I drew
Three times a body might feel this way
One time it might be panic
One time it might be exercise or excitement
What I noticed during the game
What I want to remember next time my heart races

title: Panic Aftermath Reflection Sheet
summary: A short sheet for the hour after a panic wave, noting what happened and what helped.
goal: Help a client learn from a panic episode without replaying it or judging themselves.
body_md: Have the client fill this in once the wave has passed rather than during it. It is meant to collect what actually helped, not to dissect every thought. If the client starts to ruminate, shorten the sheet and shift to what they can do next. Use it as a conversation starter in session, and decide with the client which ideas are worth repeating.

fields.label: Where I was and what I was doing before it started
What I felt in my body first
What I did to get through it
How long it took to feel steadier, in my own words
What I would like to try next time
One kind thing I can say to myself now

title: Safe Companion Plan for Panic
summary: Partners agree on what the supporter says and does, and what to leave out, when panic arrives.
goal: Help partners respond to panic with calm presence instead of fixing or alarm.
body_md: Both partners fill in their own prompts. The partner who feels panic names what helps and what does not, and the supporter names what they tend to do under stress. They agree on a short script and a signal, then rehearse it in session. Revisit the plan after a real episode and change whatever did not fit. Complete any safety prompt together in session.

fields.label: Partner with panic: words that help me when it starts
Partner with panic: things that make it worse
Supporter: what I usually do when I get scared too
Supporter: a calm sentence I can say
Our signal that means panic is starting
Who we call, including 988 by call or text, if we are worried about safety

title: Pause and Return Parent Skills Card
summary: A parent practices stopping, steadying and coming back to a hard moment with their child.
goal: Help a parent use distress tolerance skills before they respond to a child's behavior.
body_md: A DBT-style card for parents who feel their reactions speed up in a hard moment. The parent writes what a pause looks like for them, such as stepping back, slow breaths or cold water, and how they will return to their child. Rehearse it in session using a recent real moment. The focus is on steadying themselves, and you decide how much to explore beyond that.

fields.label: A moment this week when I felt my reaction speed up
What I noticed in my body first
A skill I can use in ten seconds
What I will say to my child when I step away
How I will come back and reconnect
What I want to remember about being a parent when it is hard

title: Parent Values Letter
summary: A parent writes a brief letter to their child about the kind of parent they want to be.
goal: Help a parent act on their values in the small daily moments of parenting.
body_md: The parent writes to their child, in their own words, about what they hope to stand for. It need not be shared. Use it to look at where daily stress pulls them away from those hopes, and to pick one small action that fits their values. Hold the exercise lightly and with kindness, since many parents arrive already harsh with themselves.

fields.label: What I most want my child to know about me
What kind of parent I want to be
A recent moment when I acted like that parent
A moment when stress pulled me away from it
One small thing I can do this week to act on my values
What I would say to myself when I fall short

title: Bedtime Without a Battle Game
summary: A parent and child take turns drawing steps cards to build a calm routine together.
goal: Help a family build a predictable bedtime that the child helped design.
body_md: Players take turns drawing cards for bedtime steps, such as bath, pajamas, story and lights out, and place them in order on a path. The child may add or reorder one step, and the parent plays along rather than directing. Debrief at the end about which steps felt fun and which felt hard. Adapt the rules to the child's age, and try the routine for a week before changing it.

fields.label: The step I drew and where it goes on the path
A step I would like to add
A step that feels hard for me
What my parent will do to help with that step
How I want bedtime to feel
What we will try tonight

title: Parent Thought Check for Hard Moments
summary: A parent writes the thought that shows up when their child pushes back and tests whether it fits.
goal: Help a parent notice the story behind their reaction and try a balanced alternative.
body_md: A thought record shaped around a parenting moment. The parent notes the situation, the first thought, the feeling and what they did, then looks for a more balanced thought and tries it next time. Be careful that it does not become a way to blame themselves. Work from one recent, ordinary moment, and offer your own judgment on where to go further.

fields.label: The moment with my child
The first thought that went through my mind
The feeling and how strong it was, from 0 to 10
What I did next
A more balanced way to see it
What I could try next time

title: Feelings Weather Chart with Parent
summary: A child and parent draw a weather chart of feelings and use it to talk at the end of the day.
goal: Help a child name feelings and help a parent respond with calm curiosity.
body_md: The child draws a weather picture for each feeling, such as stormy for angry or sunny for happy. The parent then asks which weather it was today, listens, and reflects back what they heard without fixing. Do it together in session first so the parent can see the pace. Parents can repeat it at bedtime. If your child client discloses harm or abuse at any point, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw sunny weather for a happy feeling
Draw stormy weather for a hard feeling
Today my feeling weather was
What made the weather change
What my parent did that helped
What I want my parent to know about my weather

title: Good Enough Parent Standards Check
summary: Tests the rules a new parent holds about doing it right against what actually helps the baby.
goal: Loosen rigid standards that feed guilt and exhaustion in the early months.
body_md: Ask the client to list the shoulds they carry, then sort each one by what the baby needs versus what an imagined judge expects. Watch for standards borrowed from social media or family. Revisit one rule at a time and keep the new wording the client's own.

fields.label: A should I hold about being a parent (for example, I should never need help)
Where I learned that rule
What the baby actually needs in this situation
What I would tell a friend holding the same rule
A good enough version of the rule in my own words
One small thing I will do differently this week

title: Room for Mixed Feelings Practice
summary: Makes space for love, grief, relief and dread to sit side by side in the first months of parenting.
goal: Help a new parent stop fighting mixed feelings and keep caring for the baby and themselves.
body_md: Many new parents believe a difficult feeling means they are doing this wrong. Invite the client to name each feeling as present, without ranking them, and to notice which ones they push away. Keep the focus on the next caring action rather than on resolving the feelings.

fields.label: Feelings I have had since the baby came, including the ones I am ashamed of
Which of them I try hardest to push away
What pushing it away costs me
How it feels in my body when I let it be there for a minute
What I care about that is still true while I feel this
One caring action I can take for the baby or me while the feeling stays

title: Closeness After Birth Pace Talk
summary: Gives both partners a structure for talking about physical and emotional closeness at a pace each can name.
goal: Replace unspoken pressure and avoidance with an honest, paced conversation about closeness.
body_md: Each partner completes their own side first, then shares in turn while the other reflects back without defending or negotiating. The partner who gave birth sets the pace on anything physical, and the other partner's feelings of distance are named without blame. Stop before a decision is forced.

fields.label: Partner A: what closeness means to me right now
Partner A: what feels okay, and what I am not ready for
Partner A: what I miss and how I would like to say so
Partner B: what closeness means to me right now
Partner B: what I worry about when we do not talk about it
Partner B: how I can show care without pressure
Together: one small kind of closeness we both want this week

title: Welcome Home Big Sibling Craft
summary: An older child decorates a welcome card and a helper badge to prepare for life with a new baby.
goal: Give a child a concrete, positive role in the family during a big change.
body_md: The child draws the family including the baby and decorates a helper badge for jobs they choose. The parent sits alongside, names that big feelings about the baby are okay, and plans one short stretch of one-on-one time each day. Offer extra attention if jokes about sending the baby back appear. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw our family with the new baby in it
Draw or write three jobs I can do as a helper
Draw my face when I feel jealous or left out
One thing I would like to do just with a parent
What a parent says when I have a big feeling

title: Sleep-Deprived Skills Card
summary: Pairs a short list of body-first and mind-first skills a parent can reach for in the worst sleep-deprived minutes.
goal: Give an exhausted parent a few skills small enough to use mid-feed or mid-cry.
body_md: Choose skills the client can do one-handed with a baby in their arms, such as cold water on the wrists, paced breathing, or a self-validating phrase. Rehearse them in session and have the client rate how intense things feel before and after. Keep the card small enough to photograph and keep on a phone.

fields.label: The moments I feel closest to my limit
What my body does when I reach that point
Body skill I can use with a baby in my arms
A kind thing I can say to myself in that moment
Who I can text or call for a minute of relief
How strong the feeling was before (0 to 10) and after I tried a skill

title: Worth Prediction Experiment
summary: Turns a belief about being not enough into a prediction the client can test in daily life.
goal: Check a self-critical prediction against what actually happens.
duration: 20 minutes, then one week of testing
body_md: Pick one concrete situation where the client expects to be judged as lacking, such as speaking up in a meeting. Write the prediction and a rating of belief first, run the experiment, then compare. Expect the client to discount good outcomes, so ask what they would count as evidence beforehand.

fields.label: The belief about myself I want to test
The situation where I can test it
What I predict will happen
How strongly I believe the prediction (0 to 100)
What actually happened
What I would conclude if a friend had had this outcome
How strongly I believe the original belief now (0 to 100)

title: Two Truths and a Strength Game
summary: A turn-taking game where players share two true facts and one strength they own, then take a challenge.
goal: Practice naming a strength out loud and receiving a reaction without deflecting.
body_md: Players take turns sharing two ordinary facts and one real strength, and the group guesses nothing; the speaker simply says it and the others respond with a thank you or a question. Set the rule that no one can cancel their own strength with a joke. Debrief on how it felt to say it and to hear it.

fields.label: My two facts and my strength for this round
What I noticed in my body when I said the strength out loud
The moment I wanted to deflect, and what I did instead
A strength someone else named that I agreed with
One place I can name a strength this week

title: Imperfect and Still Worthy Card
summary: Applies radical acceptance to a flaw or mistake so a client can stop treating it as a verdict on their worth.
goal: Hold a mistake with acceptance while still choosing what to repair or change.
body_md: Choose one specific mistake or trait the client is fighting. Walk through accepting that it happened and that it has causes, without approving it, then pair it with a validation statement. Clients often hear acceptance as giving up, so keep naming the next effective step.

fields.label: The mistake or flaw I keep fighting
What I tell myself it says about my worth
What I can accept is simply true (it happened, it had causes)
What I can still change or repair
A validating sentence I can say to myself
How I will notice when I slide back into fighting it

title: Criticism Softening Swap
summary: Partners turn a harsh remark into a feeling and a request, so criticism stops landing on each other's sense of worth.
goal: Help partners speak needs without attacking character, and hear them without collapsing.
body_md: Each partner picks a recent critical remark made or received and rewrites it as a feeling plus one request. The listening partner practices hearing it without proving they are good or bad. Notice who tends to shrink and who tends to sharpen. Slow things down and credit each attempt.

fields.label: Partner A: a critical thing I said or heard recently
Partner A: the feeling and need underneath it
Partner A: my rewrite as a feeling plus a request
Partner B: a critical thing I said or heard recently
Partner B: the feeling and need underneath it
Partner B: my rewrite as a feeling plus a request
Together: what helps us hear a request without taking it as a verdict

title: Words That Help Me Poster
summary: A child draws a poster of kind helper words to swap in when the mean voice in their head shows up.
goal: Give a child a ready set of kinder things to say to themselves.
body_md: The child draws the mean voice as a silly character and then a helper voice with kind words in speech bubbles. The parent hangs the poster somewhere visible and says one helper phrase aloud when they hear the child put themselves down. Ask the parent to model self-talk on their own hard days. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw the mean voice as a silly character
Write or draw what it says to me
Draw the helper voice
Write three kind helper words I can say back
Where we will hang the poster
What my parent will say when they hear the mean voice

title: Awkward Moment Recovery Game
summary: Players draw awkward-moment cards and take turns playing out a calm recovery line in a mock social scene.
goal: Practice recovering from a stumble in conversation so a slip feels survivable.
body_md: Write awkward moments on cards, such as forgetting a name or saying something that lands oddly. Each player draws one, plays it with a partner, and tries a recovery line. The leader plays at the same level and is allowed to fumble. Debrief on how bad it really was and what the audience likely thought.

fields.label: The awkward moment I drew
How bad I predicted it would feel (0 to 10)
The recovery line I used
How bad it actually felt (0 to 10)
What the other person likely noticed
A real moment I could recover from the same way

title: Opposite Action for Social Withdrawal
summary: Walks a client through spotting the urge to withdraw from people and trying the opposite action in small steps.
goal: Act opposite to the urge to avoid when avoiding does not fit the facts.
body_md: Check first that the fear fits the facts of the situation; where it does not, plan an opposite action done fully, with posture, tone and eye contact matching. Start with the smallest version. Debrief the emotion after, not just the outcome, and note the urge fading.

fields.label: The social situation I feel like skipping
The emotion and the urge it gives me
Does the fear fit the facts here? What are the facts?
The opposite action, in a small version
How I will do it fully (posture, voice, eye contact)
How the urge and the feeling changed afterward

title: Brave Hello Practice Cards
summary: A child decorates cards with small friendly actions and tries one at a time with a parent cheering nearby.
goal: Build a child's comfort with greetings and small social steps through play.
body_md: The child decorates cards such as saying hello, asking a name, or sharing a toy, and picks one to try each day. The parent practices the card at home first, then stays close without speaking for the child. Praise the try, not the result. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw my favorite brave hello card
Draw my face before I try it
Draw my face after I try it
Which card I will try first, and when
How a parent helps without doing it for me

title: Supporting a Partner Before Social Events
summary: Partners agree how one can help the other face an event without rescuing or pushing.
goal: Help partners plan social events together so support does not become avoidance or pressure.
body_md: The anxious partner says what helps and what quietly keeps the fear going, such as answering for them or leaving early. The supporting partner shares what they worry about and what they can offer. Agree on a small plan and a signal, and note that staying for the whole event may be a stretch worth trying.

fields.label: Partner A: the event, and what I fear will happen
Partner A: what helps me and what makes it harder in the long run
Partner A: the step I am willing to try
Partner B: what I worry about before these events
Partner B: how I can help without rescuing or pushing
Together: our signal and our plan for staying or leaving
Together: how we will talk about it afterward

title: Firsts Without Them Planner
summary: A client maps upcoming first holidays, birthdays and anniversaries after a loss and plans support for each.
goal: Help a grieving client prepare for hard dates with choices, company and a gentle exit plan.
body_md: Use this with a client facing a first season without someone who died. Go date by date and let the client decide what to keep, change or skip, since there is no right way to spend a hard day. Keep the plan flexible, and revisit it after the date to see what helped and what to adjust next time.

fields.label: A date coming up that I am dreading
What I would like that day to look like
One tradition I want to keep, change or let rest
Who I would like near me, and who I will let know
A gentle way out if the day gets too heavy
One small thing I can do afterward to care for myself

title: Should-Have Thoughts Challenge Sheet
summary: A client writes a should-have thought about a loss and weighs it against what was known at the time.
goal: Soften self-blame after a loss by separating hindsight from what the client knew then.
body_md: Many grieving clients replay what they should have done differently. This sheet uses a familiar thought-record structure to compare hindsight with the information and options the client actually had. Go slowly, and notice whether guilt is carrying love or pain that needs room. It is not meant to argue the client out of sorrow.

fields.label: The should-have thought that keeps returning
How strongly I believe it right now, 0 to 10
What I knew at the time
What I did not know then and know now
What I would say to a friend who had this thought
A kinder, more balanced way to say it
How strongly I believe the original thought now, 0 to 10

title: Waves of Grief Skills Card
summary: A client builds a card pairing the strongest grief waves with one distress tolerance skill each.
goal: Give a grieving client a few named skills for riding out waves of emotion without avoiding the loss.
body_md: Grief tends to arrive in waves, and clients often feel they must either push it away or be swept under. Offer familiar distress tolerance skills such as paced breathing, temperature change or self-soothing with the senses, and let the client choose what fits. Rehearse one skill in session so it is familiar before a wave comes.

fields.label: What a wave of grief feels like in my body
What usually sets a wave off
A skill I could try in the first minute of a wave
A way to soothe myself with my senses
Something that helps me ride it out and let it pass
Who I could reach out to afterward

title: Remembering Together Shoebox Craft
summary: A child decorates a shoebox and fills it with drawings and objects that remind them of someone who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a hands-on way to keep memories and talk about the person.
body_md: The parent helps the child decorate a box and choose or draw things that remind them of the person, then listens as the child explains each one. Let the child lead and do not push for tears or words. The parent's job is to stay close, answer questions simply and honestly, and say that all feelings are welcome. If a child discloses abuse or harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: A picture I drew of the person
Something we did together that I remember
Something that makes me think of them
A feeling I have today, and what color it is
Something I would like to ask or tell them
Who I can show my box to

title: Grief Weather Charades Game
summary: Players act out and guess feelings that come with loss, then share one of their own in a safe, low-pressure round.
goal: Help a family or group name the many feelings grief brings and show that others share them.
body_md: Write feelings that often come with loss, such as sad, angry, numb, relieved, guilty or lonely, on cards. Players take turns acting one out while others guess, and anyone may pass at any time. In the debrief, invite each person to share one feeling they have had lately and notice the ones that overlap. Keep the tone gentle and let people laugh and cry both.

fields.label: A feeling I acted out or guessed
A feeling I did not expect to see on a card
One that I have felt this week
Something I learned about how other people grieve
One thing I would like someone to know about how I am doing

title: Support in the Hard Moments Map
summary: A client in a close relationship lists the moments that feel hardest and who or what can help in each one.
goal: Help a client see where support is already available and where a gap needs attention.
body_md: Use this when a client is struggling in a close relationship and feels alone with it. Have them name the recurring moments that are hardest, then list the people, activities and boundaries that help. The map can show where outside support is missing. Follow the client's lead on whether to share parts of it with the partner.

fields.label: The moment in this relationship that is hardest for me
What I usually do in that moment
What I wish I could do instead
Someone outside the relationship who could support me
One thing I will protect for myself this week
What I would like to bring to my next session

title: Repair After a Fight Plan
summary: Partners agree on how each will cool down, return to talk and repair after an argument.
goal: Help both partners agree on a shared plan for repairing within a day of a fight.
body_md: Walk both partners through what usually happens after a fight and what each wishes would happen. Each names how they cool down, what a good return to the conversation sounds like, and one gesture that signals care. Write the shared plan together and set a time to review it. Name each person's part so the plan does not become one partner's job.

fields.label: Partner A: what I usually do after a fight
Partner A: what I need before I can talk again
Partner B: what I usually do after a fight
Partner B: what I need before I can talk again
How we will let each other know we are ready to return
One thing each of us will say or do to repair
When we will check in on how this plan is working

title: Values in My Closest Relationships Compass
summary: A client names the kind of partner, friend or family member they want to be and small actions that fit.
goal: Link a client's actions in a relationship to the values they choose rather than to old reactions.
body_md: This is a values clarification exercise for a client whose reactions in a relationship pull them away from who they want to be. Have them name two or three values, notice where urges to withdraw, attack or please pull them away, and choose one small committed action. Review next session what happened and what got in the way.

fields.label: The relationship I want to focus on
What matters most to me in it
What I tend to do when I feel hurt or threatened
How that reaction moves me away from what matters
One small action I could take this week that fits my values
A thought or feeling I will make room for while I do it

title: Listening Turns Card Game
summary: Two or more players take turns answering prompt cards while others listen and reflect before replying.
goal: Practice listening and reflecting in a low-stakes way before using it on harder topics.
body_md: Prepare cards with light to medium prompts, such as a favorite memory together or something that made me feel understood this week. One player answers, and the listener reflects back what they heard before adding anything. Swap roles after each card. Debrief on what made it easier or harder to listen, and note anything the players want to try with real issues.

fields.label: A prompt I answered and what I noticed
A time I felt really heard during the game
A time I wanted to jump in or fix
What helped me stay in the listening role
One way I want to listen differently this week

title: Stabilizing Pace Dial Sheet
summary: A client sets how much of any session topic feels workable and names signs to slow down or pause.
goal: Give a survivor of sexual abuse control over pacing, with clear signals and agreed ways to pause.
body_md: Use this at the start of work with a client who has experienced sexual abuse, and return to it often. The client sets their own pace and chooses signals for when to slow down or stop, and you agree on what you will do each time. Do not ask for any details of what happened. The aim is control and safety, and the client can change any answer at any time.

fields.label: A sign in my body that tells me I need to slow down
A word or signal I can use to pause the session
What I would like my therapist to do when I use it
Something that helps me feel more present in the room
A topic I would like to leave alone for now
How I want to feel when I leave a session

title: Self-Blame Compassion Reframe Sheet
summary: A client notes a self-blaming thought and builds a kinder, more balanced response, without describing events.
goal: Help a survivor of sexual abuse notice self-blame thoughts and respond with compassion and perspective.
body_md: Self-blame and shame are common after abuse. This sheet works only with the thoughts that show up now, not with any account of what happened, so keep the client away from retelling. Notice the thought, rate how strongly it is believed, and build a response the client would offer a friend. Slow down if the client becomes overwhelmed and use a grounding step.

fields.label: A self-blaming thought that shows up now
How strongly I believe it, 0 to 10
What I would say to a friend who thought this
A kinder and more balanced thought
How strongly I believe the original thought now, 0 to 10
Something I can do right now to be gentle with myself

title: Safe Place and Present Anchors Practice
summary: A client builds a safe place image and a set of five-senses anchors to use for grounding.
goal: Give a survivor of sexual abuse reliable grounding skills to return to the present.
body_md: Walk the client through choosing a calm place, real or imagined, and a short list of sensory anchors in the room. Practice in session until it works smoothly. Keep the focus on the present and do not ask for memories. If the client feels worse, shift to simply naming objects in the room and orienting to the day and time. If the client mentions thoughts of self-harm, go over 988 (call or text) together.

fields.label: A place where I feel calm or safe
Something I can see right now that is gray, blue or green
A sound I can hear in this room
Something I can touch or feel under my hands
What I will tell myself to remember where and when I am
If I ever feel unsafe, I can call or text 988 or tell this person

title: Reclaiming Choices Values Sheet
summary: A client names areas of life where they want more choice and one small chosen action in each.
goal: Help a survivor of sexual abuse notice their own values and make small chosen steps toward them.
body_md: This exercise focuses on the present and on what the client chooses. Invite them to pick a life area, such as friendships, rest, work or creativity, and name what matters there. Then choose one small action entirely their own and note any thoughts or feelings that arrive. Do not ask for details of the past. Let the client set the pace and change the plan whenever they like.

fields.label: A life area where I want more choice
What matters to me there
One small step I choose for this week
A thought or feeling that might show up as I try it
How I can make room for it and still take the step
Who I could tell about my step, if anyone

title: My Body Is My Own Safety Book
summary: A child draws safe people, safe places and the words to use if something feels wrong or confusing.
goal: Help a child learn that their body is their own and name trusted adults they can tell.
body_md: The parent sits beside the child, and together they draw safe adults, safe places and a plan for what to say if something feels off. Keep language simple and calm and do not question the child about any past events. The parent's role is to listen, believe and stay calm. If a child discloses anything, follow your mandatory reporting duties and tell the parent what happens next.

fields.label: A grown-up I trust and can draw here
A place where I feel safe
A rule I know about my body being my own
The words I can say if something feels wrong
The grown-up I will tell, and how

title: Skill Pairing Before the Storm Sheet
summary: A sheet where a client pairs a calming skill with an early warning sign before distress peaks.
goal: Help a client match the right skill to the earliest sign of rising distress.
body_md: Walk through one recent hard moment and have your client find the first small sign, such as a clenched jaw or racing thoughts, then pick a skill sized for that stage. Clients often reach for big skills too late, so notice whether the match feels realistic. Keep it as a draft you revise together over a few weeks.

fields.label: The first small sign I notice when things start to build
Where that sign shows up in my body or thoughts
A quick skill I could use right at that sign
A bigger skill for when distress is higher
What might get in the way of using them
One place I will keep a reminder of this pairing

title: Opposite Action Coping Check-In
summary: A DBT opposite action check-in for urges that come with a coping choice the client later questions.
goal: Practice noticing an emotion's urge and choosing an opposite action when it does not fit the facts.
body_md: Opposite action works best when the client first names the emotion and checks whether it fits the situation. Use a recent example where the urge was to withdraw or shut down, then plan one small opposite step. Review how it felt in the next session rather than expecting it to feel natural at first.

fields.label: The emotion I felt and what set it off
The urge that came with it
Does the emotion fit the facts? What do I notice?
The opposite action I could try, all the way
One small step I will take this week
How it went, and what I noticed afterward

title: Coping Plan for Two
summary: Partners agree how each wants support during a hard moment and what each will do to help.
goal: Help partners agree on how to support each other's coping without taking it over.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own side first, then you invite them to share and compare. Partner A names what helps and what does not when stressed; Partner B does the same, and then both name one thing they will offer. Watch for fixing or advice-giving and gently steer toward asking what the other wants.

fields.label: Partner A: when I am stressed, what helps me most
Partner A: what does not help, even when meant kindly
Partner B: when I am stressed, what helps me most
Partner B: what does not help, even when meant kindly
What I will offer my partner when they are struggling
How we will ask each other what is needed
When we will check in on this plan

title: Calm Corner Builder
summary: A child designs and stocks a calm corner at home while a parent helps gather items.
goal: Give a child a place and a few chosen tools to use when feelings run big.
body_md: The child draws the calm corner and picks what goes in it, such as a pillow, a drawing pad or a favorite stuffed animal. The parent helps gather the items and agrees to let the child go there without it being a punishment. Practice using it when the child is calm first. If a child discloses anything worrying while drawing, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw my calm corner and what goes in it
Three things I like in my calm corner
What my body feels like when I need to go there
How I want a grown-up to help me
What I will do first when I get there

title: Coping Skill Charades
summary: A group game of acting out coping skills while others guess, followed by a debrief.
goal: Make coping skills memorable and low pressure through play and shared discussion.
body_md: Write skills on slips, such as stretching, counting breaths or calling a friend. Players take turns acting one out silently while the group guesses; the actor scores a point for each correct guess and the guesser gets one too. Close with the debrief prompts, and let people pass on any skill they do not want to act out.

fields.label: The skill I acted out or guessed
A skill from the game I already use
A skill I want to try this week
When I might use it
What I liked about seeing others act them out

title: Feared Thing Fact and Feeling Sheet
summary: A sheet separating what a client knows about a feared thing from what the fear says will happen.
goal: Help a client sort facts from fear-driven predictions before planning practice.
body_md: Have your client name the feared thing and fill in both columns of facts and fears, then look at where they differ. Avoid arguing the fear away; the point is for the client to see the two voices side by side. Revisit after practice to see what changed, and adjust pacing to what your client can tolerate.

fields.label: The thing or situation I fear
What I know about it for sure
What my fear tells me will happen
How strongly I believe the fear, 0 to 10
What I have avoided because of it
What I would like to be able to do instead

title: Safety Behavior Spotting Log
summary: A log for catching small safety behaviors that quietly keep a fear going during exposure practice.
goal: Help a client notice and gradually drop safety behaviors during practice.
body_md: Safety behaviors such as always carrying a phone or standing near the door can feel harmless but may keep the fear alive. Ask your client to log them in ordinary situations and in practice, then choose one to drop at a time. Go slowly and use your judgment on which are reasonable to keep.

fields.label: The situation I was in
The safety behavior I used
What I thought would happen without it
What actually happened
How anxious I felt, 0 to 10
One safety behavior I could try dropping next time

title: Willing to Feel It Phobia Practice
summary: An ACT practice of making room for fear while taking one small step toward something that matters.
goal: Help a client carry fear along while moving toward a valued action.
body_md: Link a feared situation to something the client values, such as traveling to see family or going to a medical visit. Invite them to notice the fear as a visitor and pick a step they would take with it present. Watch for the step being used to push the fear away, and keep returning to the value.

fields.label: Something that matters to me that my fear gets in the way of
The feared situation involved
The thoughts and feelings that show up
A way I can make room for them without fighting
One small step I am willing to take
What I will tell myself as I take it

title: Fear Monster Costume Party
summary: A child draws their fear as a silly monster and gives it a costume while a parent helps.
goal: Help a child see a fear as something smaller and less powerful through drawing.
body_md: The child draws what scares them as a monster, then adds funny clothes or a silly name. The parent listens, does not tease, and asks what the monster says and what the child would like to say back. Use it as a warm-up before any gradual practice. If a child discloses something worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw my fear as a monster
The silly costume I gave it
What the monster says to me
What I want to say back to it
One brave thing I could do this week
Who I want to cheer me on

title: Phobia Practice Dice Game
summary: A table game where players roll for gentle practice cards and talk about what they notice.
goal: Make brave practice feel playful and shared, with each person choosing their own pace.
body_md: Make cards of small brave steps ranging from easy to harder, each tied to a number on a die. Players take turns rolling, may swap for an easier card, and either do the step or say how they would plan it. Everyone sets their own pace, and the debrief asks what surprised them. Do not push anyone toward a card they decline.

fields.label: The card I drew and how I felt about it
What I did or how I would plan it
What happened to my fear while I did it
What surprised me
A step I want to try on my own

title: Appearance Thought Reframe Card
summary: A thought record for appearance-related thoughts, with a balanced response and a next step.
goal: Help a client notice appearance thoughts and test them against what is actually happening.
body_md: Use a recent moment when a client felt bad about how they looked. Walk through the thought, the feeling, the evidence on both sides and a more balanced thought. Many people find it easier to name the thinking trap than to argue with the thought. Keep practicing with ordinary examples before moving to harder ones.

fields.label: The situation and what I felt
The thought about my appearance
A thinking trap it might be, such as mind reading
Evidence that fits and evidence that does not
A more balanced thought
What I will do next

title: Valued Day Without the Mirror Voice
summary: An ACT exercise of choosing a valued action and carrying critical body thoughts along while doing it.
goal: Help a client act on a value while appearance thoughts are present.
body_md: Pick one activity your client has been holding back from, such as swimming, dancing or a social event, and connect it to a value. Invite them to name the critical voice and thank it for trying to help, then go anyway. Defusion phrases like 'I am having the thought that' can help. Keep it voluntary and paced.

fields.label: An activity I have been holding back from
The value behind it
The critical thoughts that show up
How I can name them without arguing
The step I will take with them along
What I noticed afterward

title: Self-Soothing After a Hard Body Day
summary: A DBT card pairing self-soothe and radical acceptance skills for days when body thoughts run loud.
goal: Give a client a short plan of kind, grounded actions for hard body image moments.
body_md: Build the card with the client by choosing one soothing action for each sense, plus a radical acceptance statement that fits them. Practice the plan when they are calm so it is ready on a hard day. Ask what else helps and keep checking whether any item turns into a way of avoiding feelings. If thoughts of self-harm arise, complete a safety conversation in session and share that 988 can be called or texted.

fields.label: Something calming to see
Something calming to hear
Something calming to touch
A smell or taste that soothes me
An acceptance statement I can say to myself
Who I can reach out to, and 988 if I feel unsafe

title: Partner Compliments That Land
summary: Partners share what kind of appreciation lands well and what feels uncomfortable about their bodies.
goal: Help partners offer appreciation in ways that support rather than pressure body image.
body_md: Each partner completes their own side privately, then you help them share. Partner A says which compliments feel good and which feel awkward; Partner B does the same, and each names one thing they will try. Watch for either partner taking a comment as criticism, and slow the pace to keep both feeling heard.

fields.label: Partner A: a kind of appreciation that feels good to me
Partner A: a comment that feels uncomfortable
Partner B: a kind of appreciation that feels good to me
Partner B: a comment that feels uncomfortable
What I will try offering my partner
How we will tell each other when something misses

title: Superhero Body Power Poster
summary: A child draws a poster of what their body can do, with a parent adding a power of their own.
goal: Help a child build pride in what their body does and the people who love it.
body_md: The child draws themselves as a superhero and labels the body powers, such as strong legs for running or quick hands for building.
