The parent adds one power of their own and says what they appreciate in the child's body doing. Keep comments on what bodies do. If a child shares something worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: My superhero name
Powers my body has
A power I want to practice
What my parent noticed my body can do
A power my parent has
Where we will hang our poster

title: Stress Signature Body Map
summary: A client marks where stress shows up in the body, thoughts and actions, and what each signal is asking for.
goal: Help a client notice their own early stress signals before they build.
body_md: Hand the client a simple body outline and invite them to mark where stress tends to show up, then add thoughts and behaviors beside it. Most clients name two or three signals quickly and need a prompt for the quieter ones. Treat their map as their own language for stress, and revisit it after a week of noticing.

fields.label: Where in my body I notice stress first
Thoughts that show up when stress is building
Things I do when stress is high
What my body seems to be asking for
One early signal I will watch for this week

title: Support Circles Map
summary: Concentric circles help a client place the people and places that offer support at different levels of closeness.
goal: Show a client where their support is strong and where it is thin.
body_md: Draw three circles and have the client place names, groups, pets and places in each, from daily support to occasional. Gaps are information, not failure; ask what each circle gives them and what they wish it gave. Finish by choosing one person to reach toward this week and a small first move.

fields.label: People closest to me, and what they give me
People and groups in my middle circle
Places or routines that support me
A circle where I wish I had more support
One small step to reach toward someone this week

title: Weekly Reset Review Sheet
summary: A short end-of-week review of what worked, what drained energy and what to carry into the next week.
goal: Give a client a repeatable way to learn from their own week.
body_md: Use this at the end of a session or as a weekly habit the client keeps on their own. Keep entries short and concrete, one line each, so the review stays light. If a client only lists what went wrong, ask for one thing that went even slightly better and build from there.

fields.label: Something that went better than I expected
Something that drained my energy
A moment I handled in a way I am glad about
What I want to do differently next week
One thing I will protect on my calendar

title: Firm and Kind Boundary Script Builder
summary: Clients draft short, kind and firm sentences for the boundaries they want to set with specific people.
goal: Help a client put a needed boundary into words they can really say.
body_md: Pick one real situation and build the sentence together: what is happening, what the client needs, and what they will do. Rehearse it aloud in session, since written scripts often sound stiffer than the client expects. Talk through the likely pushback and decide in advance how they will respond.

fields.label: The situation where I need a boundary
What I need, in one clear sentence
How I could say it kindly and firmly
What the other person might say back
What I will do if the boundary is not respected

title: Evening Wind-Down Planner
summary: A planner for building a repeatable, screen-light routine for the hour before sleep.
goal: Help a client design a wind-down routine that fits their actual evenings.
body_md: Start from what the client already does at night rather than an ideal routine. Have them pick two or three steps they are willing to try, set a start time, and plan for the evening when it falls apart. Review it a week later and adjust without turning it into a test of willpower.

fields.label: What my evenings look like right now
Two or three calming steps I am willing to try
The time I will start winding down
What usually gets in the way
My plan for a night when the routine falls apart

title: Thought Record Split Screen
summary: A two-column thought record that keeps the situation, the thought and a balanced reply side by side.
goal: Teach a client the core thought-record steps in a form they can finish in minutes.
body_md: Walk through one recent situation together before the client tries it alone. Keep the left side for the situation, feeling and automatic thought, and the right side for evidence on both sides and a balanced reply. Clients often skip the feeling rating, so ask for it first and again at the end.

fields.label: The situation, in one or two sentences
The feeling and how strong it was, 0 to 100
The thought that went through my mind
Evidence that fits the thought and evidence that does not
A balanced reply, and how strong the feeling is now

title: Behavioral Experiment Planner
summary: A planning sheet for testing a prediction in real life: what to try, what to expect and what happened.
goal: Help a client test a belief through action instead of argument.
body_md: Choose a prediction the client holds strongly and design a small, specific test that could go either way. Be clear about what they expect and how they will know. Afterward, spend more time on what they learned than on whether the prediction was right, and plan the next experiment from it.

fields.label: The prediction I want to test
How strongly I believe it, 0 to 100
The experiment I will try, and when
What I expect will happen
What actually happened and what I learned

title: Shared Responsibility Slices Chart
summary: Clients divide up a circle to show all the factors that contributed to an outcome they blame themselves for.
goal: Loosen all-or-nothing blame by making every contributing factor visible.
body_md: Ask the client to list every factor first, including their own part, and rank them before drawing slices. Place their own slice last so the picture is not decided in advance. The point is accuracy, not letting them off the hook, so keep room for a share that really is theirs.

fields.label: The outcome I blame myself for
Everything that played a part, including other people and chance
How I would divide the circle, with my part last
What I notice when I look at the full picture
What I would say to a friend in my place

title: Friend Versus Self Standard Sheet
summary: A sheet that compares the words a client uses with themselves to the words they would offer a friend.
goal: Help a client notice a harsher standard for themselves than for others.
body_md: Ask the client to write what they tell themselves about a recent mistake, then what they would say to a close friend in the same spot. Do not rush to the conclusion; let them read the two side by side and say what they see. Close by asking which version they want to practice this week.

fields.label: A recent mistake or setback
What I say to myself about it
What I would say to a close friend in the same situation
What I notice when I compare the two
A sentence I want to practice using with myself

title: Downward Arrow Belief Ladder
summary: A stepwise worksheet that follows a thought down to the belief underneath by asking what it would mean.
goal: Help a client reach the core belief behind an everyday automatic thought.
body_md: Start with one automatic thought and keep asking, gently, what it would mean about them or their life if it were true. Stop when the answers repeat or the client reaches a short, personal statement. Go slowly and check how they are doing at each step, since this can be tender ground.

fields.label: The first thought, as I noticed it
If that were true, what would it mean?
And if that were true, what would it mean?
The belief that sits at the bottom
How much I believe it, 0 to 100, and where I may have learned it

title: Leaves Floating Downstream Practice
summary: A guided image of placing thoughts on leaves floating down a stream, with a log of what showed up.
goal: Give a client a way to watch thoughts pass without following them.
body_md: Read the image slowly, then ask the client what showed up and what pulled them off the stream. Getting pulled away is the practice, not a mistake, so celebrate every time they noticed and came back. Tell them thoughts do not have to be pushed away or analyzed in this exercise.

fields.label: What thoughts floated by
What pulled me off the stream
How I noticed I had drifted and came back
What it was like to watch instead of follow
Where I could use this in my week

title: Pushing Away Hands Demonstration
summary: A two-step demonstration of how hard it is to hold difficult feelings away, and what changes when they are carried.
goal: Let a client feel, not just hear, the cost of struggling with an inner experience.
body_md: Hand the client a pillow or folder as a stand-in for a hard feeling and have them push it away with their arms straight, then hold it in their lap. Ask what each posture costs them and what they can do with free hands. Keep it playful and let them reach their own conclusion.

fields.label: A feeling I often try to push away
What pushing it away costs me
What it was like to hold it in my lap
What my hands could do while I carry it
One situation where I could carry it instead of pushing

title: Committed Action Small Steps Planner
summary: A sheet that breaks a value into one tiny action, a time and a plan for obstacles.
goal: Turn a valued direction into steps small enough to take this week.
body_md: Begin with a value the client has named and shrink the action until it feels almost too small. Ask when and where it will happen, and which thoughts or feelings will show up and what they will do with them. Review it next session and celebrate any attempt, since the learning is in the doing.

fields.label: A value I care about
A small action that fits it
When and where I will do it
Thoughts or feelings that may come along
What I will do with them and how I will mark it done

title: Values Card Sort Reflection
summary: A reflection sheet that follows a card sort of values, naming the top few and how they show up in daily life.
goal: Help a client name what matters most in their own words.
body_md: Have the client sort value cards into three piles: very important, somewhat important and not for me, and then narrow to five. For each, ask how it shows up now. Gaps between a value and daily life are a conversation, not a grade, and the client decides which gap matters.

fields.label: My top five values, in my own words
How one of them shows up in my life now
One place a value is missing in my days
Whose voice I hear when I think about each value
One value I want to give more room this month

title: Choice Point Diagram Worksheet
summary: A diagram that maps a hard moment into the thoughts and urges that pull away from values and the moves that move toward them.
goal: Help a client spot the fork between away moves and toward moves.
body_md: Draw a fork and ask the client to pick one hard recent moment. On one side list what pulls them away (thoughts, feelings, urges, actions) and on the other what a toward move would look like. Neither side is bad; the question is which one fits who they want to be in that moment.

fields.label: A hard moment I want to look at
Thoughts, feelings and urges that showed up
What I did that moved me away from what matters
What a toward move could have been
What would help me notice the fork next time

title: PLEASE Skills Weekly Tracker
summary: A weekly tracker for the self-care basics of the PLEASE skills: body care, sleep, movement and substances.
goal: Help a client see how basics shape their emotional ups and downs.
body_md: Have the client fill the tracker daily for a week and bring it to session to look for links between basics and emotional intensity. Stay curious about patterns rather than correcting them. Pick one area to adjust and keep the goal small enough that they are likely to succeed.

fields.label: How I looked after my body this week
How my sleep went most nights
How much I moved my body and how it felt
What I noticed about my moods on easier days
One basic I will adjust next week

title: Wise Mind Check-In Card
summary: A pocket card that walks a client from emotion mind and reasonable mind to wise mind in a few questions.
goal: Give a client a quick routine for pausing and finding a balanced response.
body_md: Introduce the card in session with a real decision the client is facing, and have them sit quietly before answering. Ask what emotion mind says, what reasonable mind says and what wise mind adds. Many clients need practice to tell the three apart, so use easy situations first.

title: Coping Ahead for Radical Acceptance Plan
summary: A plan to rehearse accepting a situation that cannot be changed, with the thoughts and actions that will help.
goal: Help a client prepare to meet a hard, unchangeable moment with acceptance.
body_md: Choose a situation the client expects to face and cannot change. Have them name what they cannot control, the urges that will show up and the acceptance moves they will use, such as half smile or willing hands. Rehearse it in imagination, then check in after the event.

title: GIVE Skills Conversation Rehearsal
summary: A rehearsal sheet for a conversation in which a client wants to keep the relationship while asking for something.
goal: Help a client practice staying gentle and interested while making a request.
body_md: Use a real, upcoming conversation and rehearse it in a role-play. Walk through being gentle, acting interested, validating and keeping an easy manner. Switch roles so the client feels the other side. Debrief on what felt natural and what needs more practice.

summary: A planning sheet for building a small kit that soothes through sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
goal: Help a client prepare soothing items before distress arrives.
body_md: Ask the client to pick one or two items for each sense and decide where each lives so it is easy to reach. Test the items in session when possible. Remind them that what soothes is personal, and swap out anything that does not help after a week of trying.

summary: A short, structured weekly talk for partners to share appreciation, concerns and one request.
goal: Give partners a calm, predictable space for small issues before they grow.
body_md: Set a time, a place and a limit of thirty minutes. Each partner shares one appreciation, one concern in soft words and one request, while the other listens and reflects back before replying. Coach them to keep concerns to the week, not the whole history, and end with something warm.

title: Turning Toward Bids Log
summary: A log where partners notice small bids for attention and how each one was answered.
goal: Help partners spot and answer everyday bids for connection.
body_md: Explain that a bid is any small reach for attention, from a comment to a sigh. For a week, each partner jots down bids they made and bids they noticed, and how each was met. Review the log together in session and celebrate the turns toward, even tiny ones, rather than counting misses.

summary: A guided conversation for partners to share hopes, and the stories behind them, without trying to solve anything.
goal: Help partners understand what the other is hoping for.
body_md: Have each partner pick a dream, from small to large, and share the story behind it while the other asks open questions. The aim is to understand, not to plan or negotiate. If a dream clashes with the other partner, note it kindly and bring it back for another day.

summary: A sheet for turning a harsh opener into a gentle one that names a feeling and a request.
goal: Help partners start hard conversations in a way that keeps them talking.
body_md: Have each partner write a harsh opener they have used, then rewrite it as an I-feel statement about a specific situation with a clear request. Role-play both versions and let the listener report how each landed. Expect it to feel awkward at first and encourage practice on small topics.

goal: Make the mental load visible so partners can share it fairly.
body_md: Ask each partner to list tasks, then mark the ones that also take noticing, planning and remembering. Compare maps without blame; the surprise is often that one partner never saw the load. Choose two items to hand over completely, including the thinking, and revisit in a week.

The parent joins in by asking the puppet gentle questions and does not correct anything. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

goal: Give a child something to watch and do that helps them settle.
body_md: Fill a sealed jar with warm water, clear glue and glitter, then shake it and watch the glitter settle together. Pair it with slow breathing and the idea that busy feelings settle with time. The parent makes one too and practices with the child at home when upset feelings show up.

body_md: Cut strips of colored paper and set a spot for the chain at home. Each time the child does, sees or receives something kind, they write or draw it on a link. The parent adds links too, and the family reads the chain together. Keep it about noticing, never a contest or a reward chart.

goal: Help a child name the people they can go to for help.
body_md: Trace the child hand and have them write or draw one helper per finger, such as family, teachers and friends. Ask what each helper does and when the child could go to them. The parent sees the drawing and thanks the helpers. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

goal: Help a child see a scary goal as a path of small brave steps.

summary: Players read short scenes and use clues to guess the feeling behind them.
goal: Build emotion-reading skills through play in a group or family.
body_md: Prepare short scene cards with clues such as a body posture, a tone or a situation. Players take turns reading a card and the others guess the feeling and the clue that led them there. Debrief on how the same clue can mean different things and how we check by asking.

title: Skill Spinner Game
summary: Players spin for a coping skill, then describe when they would use it and try it out.
goal: Help a group practice a range of coping skills in a low-pressure way.
body_md: Divide a paper plate into eight skills and use a paper-clip spinner. On a turn, the player describes a time the skill might help and the group tries it for one minute. Passing is always allowed. Debrief on which skills felt useful and which felt strange.

summary: Players share two true things and one value, and the group guesses which one is the value.
goal: Help a group get comfortable talking about what matters to them.
body_md: Each player writes two true facts about themselves and one value, the way they would say it, and reads them aloud in random order. Others guess which is the value and ask one question about it. Debrief on how it felt to name what matters and to hear others do the same.

title: Cooperative Calm-Down Race
summary: A team game where players pass objects while using calming breaths, with the aim of beating their own time.
goal: Pair calm breathing with teamwork and light competition against oneself.
body_md: Form a circle and pass a soft object while taking one slow breath at each pass. The group tries to better its own time without rushing. Pause to ask how bodies felt at the start and end. Keep the tone cooperative and light, with no losers.

title: Other Side of the Story Role Cards
summary: Players draw a short scene and speak as another person in it, then compare notes.
goal: Help a group practice seeing a situation through another view.
body_md: Prepare scene cards with two people in a small disagreement. Players pair up, draw a card, speak as one person, and then swap. Afterward, each says what they noticed about the other view. Keep scenes everyday and avoid anything close to the real conflicts of group members.

title: Safe Place Detail Builder

goal: Give a client a steady inner anchor they can reach in session and at home.
body_md: Invite the client to choose a place that feels calm, real or imagined, and describe it through each sense. Choose somewhere with no painful associations, and drop it if any appear. Practice returning to it in session first, and keep the focus on the present, not on any memory.

summary: A short log of beliefs that keep feeling true about safety, trust or self, with a gentler alternative to try on.
goal: Help a client notice beliefs that tighten after hard experiences and loosen them one at a time.
body_md: Ask the client to name a belief about safety, trust, power or self-blame that comes up today, without describing past events. Look at what evidence supports it in the present and what a more balanced version might be. Pace the work to their comfort and stop if they get overwhelmed.

summary: A short ACT practice of noticing that memories can be present while the client stays here in this room.
goal: Help a client let hard inner experiences be there without being pulled out of the present.
body_md: Never ask the client to retell what happened. Instead, have them notice sensations and thoughts that arise in the present and name them: here is a memory, here is a feeling. Return to the room by describing what they see and hear. Keep sessions short and check their pace often.

goal: Help a client spot patterns in their state across a day and match a skill to each.
body_md: Give the client a day split into blocks and have them mark where they felt activated, numb or steady. Then choose one skill to try for each state, such as pacing breath for high and movement for low. Look at patterns together and avoid turning the map into a performance score.

goal: Give a child a picture of what keeps them safe and a plan their parent can help with.
body_md: Invite the child to draw themselves in a bubble with the people, pets and objects that help them feel safe, and talk about the picture without asking about past events. The parent learns what helps and adds it to a calm-down plan. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

goal: Help a client see the trade-off in avoidance without pressure to stop it.
body_md: Have the client list situations they avoid, rate the relief and the cost to their life, and pick one to look at. This is a map, not a demand. Many clients are surprised how much avoidance has quietly narrowed their days, so leave room for that reaction and let them choose the next step.

title: Anxiety Prediction Check

goal: Let a client check worry predictions against real outcomes over time.
body_md: The client records each worry as a specific prediction and how likely it feels, then returns to note what happened. After a week, look for patterns, such as how often things went better than feared or how well they coped. Keep it a curiosity exercise rather than a push to stop worrying.

goal: Help a client act on what matters while worry is still present.
body_md: Have the client pick a task or value-led action, notice worry thoughts, label them as worry, and keep going. The point is not to quiet worry but to keep the steering wheel. Ask what the worry said and what they did anyway, and note any small step.

goal: Help partners shape support that comforts without feeding the worry loop.
body_md: Ask the anxious partner what reassurance they seek and how long relief lasts, and the other partner how it feels to give. Agree on a warm alternative, such as listening or a shared calm activity, and trial it for a week. Keep it a team effort against worry, not against the person.

body_md: Prepare cards with everyday worry statements. Players take turns drawing a card and sorting it into one of three piles, explaining why. Debrief on which pile worries land in most often and what one action pile card they could do today.

goal: Give a client data on which small activities tend to help.
body_md: Have the client log three activities a day with energy and mood ratings. In session, look for ones that nudge things up even a little and plan to add more. Expect low-energy days and treat them as information. If the client mentions thoughts of harming themselves, address it in session, and the log includes the 988 line.

Look for evidence on both sides, including past times things shifted, and craft a balanced statement. Check in about safety; the sheet names 988, and any risk talk belongs in session, not homework.

body_md: Together, pick three to five basics that count as a good enough day: eating something, taking medication as already directed by their prescriber, getting outside, reaching one person. Keep the list short and forgiving, and revisit it as the client gets stronger.

body_md: Prepare cards with small, safe challenges, such as saying hello to a stranger. Players choose a challenge level, try one before the next session and report. Always allow trading cards and passing. Debrief on what it was like to try.
