How I felt before
What I did
What happened
What I want to try next

title: Body Talk Trigger Log
summary: A log of moments when body-related comments or media shape mood, and what helped.
goal: Help a client notice what stirs body-related thoughts and what soothes them.
body_md: Ask the client to log moments when comments, images or places stirred body-related thoughts, and what they did. Look for patterns and for what helped. Keep the focus on thoughts, feelings and choices, never on measuring or changing the body.

fields.label: A moment that stirred body thoughts
What was happening around me
What I felt and thought
What helped
A change I could make to my surroundings

title: Body Thought Evidence Sheet
summary: A sheet for looking at a harsh body-related thought and finding a fairer view.
goal: Help a client loosen harsh body-related thoughts.
body_md: Ask for the thought, where it came from and what it makes them do. Look at how they would speak to a friend and at what the body does for them. Never discuss size, weight or food. Build a fairer thought and practice using it.

fields.label: A harsh thought I have about my body
Where I may have learned it
What it makes me do
How I would speak to a friend
A fairer thought

title: Appreciating What My Body Does Practice
summary: A practice of noticing and thanking the body for what it does through the day.
goal: Shift attention from how the body looks to what it does.
body_md: Invite the client to notice moments in a day when the body helps them, such as walking, hugging or laughing. Hold the thoughts about looks lightly and ask what matters to them. Review what stood out and what values showed up.

fields.label: A moment my body helped me today
What it let me do
A thought about looks that showed up
What I did with that thought
What matters to me that my body supports

title: Kind Words About Each Other Exchange
summary: Partners practice noticing and sharing appreciation that is not about appearance.
goal: Help partners build affection and connection beyond looks.
body_md: Have each partner share things they appreciate about the other that are not about looks, such as humor or care. Then each shares what kind of words feel good to hear. Agree to avoid comments on each other bodies and revisit in a week.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciate about you
Partner B: something I appreciate about you
Words that feel good to hear
Comments we will leave out
How we will remind each other

title: Superhero Body Powers Drawing
summary: A child draws themselves as a superhero with powers based on what their body can do.
goal: Help a child value what the body does rather than how it looks.
body_md: Invite the child to design a superhero version of themselves with powers like fast legs or strong hugs, and talk about what real body helps them do. The parent joins in and comments only on what the child does, not looks. Follow reporting duties if harm is disclosed.

fields.label: My superhero name
My body powers
A real thing my body helped me do
What my parent noticed
How I want to use my powers

title: Sunday Reset Review Planner
summary: A one-page look back at the week that sorts what worked, what drained, and one change to try next.
goal: Help a client turn a whole week into one small, doable adjustment.
body_md: Use this at the start or end of a session when a client describes the week as a blur. The three-part sort keeps the review balanced, so wins are named alongside the hard parts. Watch for clients who list only problems; ask for one small thing that went a little better. Keep the next-week change to a single step.

fields.label: The moments this week that went better than I expected
The moments that drained me most
What I needed more of this week
What I needed less of this week
One small change I will try next week
Who or what could help me keep that change going

title: Conversation Rehearsal Planner
summary: A planner for a hard conversation: the goal, the opening line, likely replies, and a plan for staying steady.
goal: Prepare a client to say something difficult in their own words.
body_md: Run this before a conversation the client has been avoiding. Role-play the opening line in session, then trade places so they hear the other person's likely replies. It works best when the goal is about being clear, not about controlling how the other person responds. Check that the plan includes an exit if the talk heats up.

fields.label: The conversation I want to have, and with whom
What I most want the other person to understand
My opening sentence, in my own words
What they might say back
How I will stay steady if it gets tense
How I will end the conversation if I need a break
How I will take care of myself afterward

title: Big Change Transition Plan
summary: A plan for a life change that names what ends, what continues, and what support to line up.
goal: Give a client a steady structure during a move, job change, or other shift.
body_md: Big changes often bring a mix of loss and hope in the same week. Let the client fill in the left side, what is ending, before the right side, what is starting, so the loss is not skipped. Pay attention to the Continues column; clients are often surprised by how much stays the same. Revisit the support list over the next few sessions.

fields.label: The change I am going through
What is ending or being left behind
What is staying the same
What is beginning
What feels hardest about the first month
The people I can lean on
One small routine I want to keep through the change

title: Rest Types Menu
summary: A menu of different kinds of rest (physical, mental, social, sensory, creative) for choosing what actually refills a client.
goal: Help a client match the kind of rest to the kind of tiredness.
body_md: Many clients assume rest means sleep or screens and stay tired. Walk through the rest types together and have them rate which they get least. Ask about the difference between rest that refills and rest that only numbs. Keep choices small and specific, and ask them to try one this week and report back.

fields.label: The kind of tired I feel most often
The kind of rest I get the least of
A way I could get physical rest this week
A way I could rest my mind
A way I could rest my senses, like quiet or dim light
A kind of rest that looks like rest but leaves me still tired
The one rest I will try this week

title: Thank-You and Recognition Log
summary: A weekly log of thanks given, thanks received, and quiet efforts a client noticed in others and in themselves.
goal: Build the habit of noticing effort and kindness in daily life.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Use this with clients whose attention drifts to what is missing. The log has three directions: thanks they gave, thanks they received, and effort they noticed but did not mention. Keep entries concrete and brief. If a client dismisses their own entries, invite them to record what a friend would have noticed.

fields.label: Someone I thanked or could thank this week
Something kind someone did for me
An effort I noticed in someone else
An effort I made that I almost overlooked
How it felt to notice these
Someone I could tell this week how much it mattered

title: Mind Reading Reality Check Card
summary: A sheet that separates what a client knows about another person's thoughts from what they are guessing.
goal: Help a client test a guess about others' thoughts against what is actually known.
body_md: Mind reading shows up in social worries, conflicts, and low mood alike. Have the client write the guess, then list what they actually observed, then at least two other explanations. It is not about proving the guess wrong; it is about loosening certainty. Offer a small way to check in with the person when that is safe.

fields.label: What I think the other person is thinking
What I actually saw or heard
How sure I am, from 0 to 100
Two other explanations that could fit
What I could ask or check, if it is safe to
How sure I am now, from 0 to 100

title: Should-to-Could Rewrite Sheet
summary: A sheet that turns rigid shoulds and musts into flexible preferences a client can live with.
goal: Loosen rigid rules a client holds about themselves and others.
body_md: Notice the words should, must, and have to in a client's speech and bring a few to the page. Ask what the rule is protecting, then draft a softer version such as I would prefer or it would help if. The aim is flexibility, not lowering standards. Ask what the rule costs the client in daily life and in relationships.

fields.label: A should or must I say to myself often
Where I learned that rule
What the rule is trying to protect
What it costs me day to day
My rewrite, using prefer, want, or would help
How I might act differently with the new wording

title: Emotional Reasoning Reality Check
summary: A sheet for the moment a feeling is treated as a fact, with space to separate what is felt from what is known.
goal: Help a client notice when a strong feeling is standing in for evidence.
body_md: Emotional reasoning sounds like I feel like a failure, so I am one. Use a recent example and ask the client to write the feeling and the conclusion separately. The point is not to argue with the feeling, which is real, but to see that the conclusion needs its own look. Pair it with a record of what actually happened.

fields.label: The feeling I had, and how strong it was
The conclusion my feeling pushed me toward
The facts I can point to for that conclusion
Facts that do not fit the conclusion
What I would say to a friend who felt this way
What I can say that honors the feeling without treating it as proof

title: All-or-Nothing Gray Scale
summary: A sliding scale that replaces all-or-nothing judgments with a range from 0 to 100.
goal: Help a client find the middle ground in black-and-white thinking.
body_md: Pick a judgment the client makes in extremes, such as total failure or completely ruined. Draw a line from 0 to 100, fill in what 0, 50, and 100 would actually look like, and then place the situation. Clients are often surprised by where it lands. Revisit the scale when the same all-or-nothing wording returns.

fields.label: The all-or-nothing judgment I made
What a 0 would truly look like
What a 100 would truly look like
What a 50 would look like
Where this situation really falls
What would move it up a few points

title: Problem-Solving Ladder Planner
summary: A six-step page that moves from a stuck problem to a chosen option, a trial, and a review.
goal: Give a client a repeatable way to work through a solvable problem.
body_md: Use this for problems that can actually be acted on, not for worries about things out of anyone's hands. Spend the most time on brainstorming, where clients censor themselves early; encourage silly options too. Ask the client to pick one option and set a small trial, then review it next session rather than judging it on the spot.

fields.label: The problem, stated in one specific sentence
The outcome I would like
Every option I can think of, even silly ones
The good and hard parts of my top three
The option I will try
When and how I will try it
What I learned from the trial

title: Hands as Thoughts Practice
summary: A hands-on defusion exercise where thoughts held close to the face block the view and held at a distance do not.
goal: Let a client feel the difference between being fused with a thought and holding it.
body_md: Ask the client to cup their hands over their face and describe how easy it is to see the room and the person across from them. Then lower the hands to the lap and notice what changes. The thought is still there but they can see around it. Debrief with a real thought the client carries and ask what they could do from the lap position.

fields.label: A thought that often takes over my attention
What it was like with my hands over my face
What it was like with my hands in my lap
What I could see or do differently with the thought at a distance
One thing I care about that I can do with the thought in my lap
A reminder I can use in daily life

title: Radio Doom and Gloom Defusion
summary: A playful practice of treating a client's gloomy mental commentary as a background radio station.
goal: Help a client notice a familiar negative storyline without being run by it.
body_md: Introduce the idea that the mind has a station that plays worst-case predictions, often at the worst moments. Have the client name the station, list its regular headlines, and practice carrying on with a task while it plays. Keep the tone light; the aim is not to turn it off but to stop turning up the volume.

fields.label: The name I would give my gloomy radio station
Its most frequent headlines
When the volume goes up the most
What I tend to do when it is loud
One thing I can do while the radio plays
What I would be doing today if I didn't wait for it to go quiet

title: Values and Goals Card Sort
summary: A sort that separates ongoing values from finishable goals so a client can tell what to aim for and what to live by.
goal: Help a client see that goals can be reached while values stay a direction.
body_md: Many clients fold values and goals together, then feel empty when a goal is met or missed. Have them list things they want, mark which can be checked off, and name the value behind each. Then pick a value to act on today, no matter how any goal turns out. Ask how the sort changes how they speak about their week.

fields.label: Five things I want in my life right now
Which of them can be finished or checked off
The value behind each one
A value I can live out today even if a goal is stuck
One small action that expresses that value
How this changes how I judge my week

title: Five-Minute Noticing Practice
summary: A short present-moment practice built around five things noticed on purpose, with a log for what pulled attention away.
goal: Build a daily habit of returning attention to the present.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Show the practice in session first. The client notices five things they can see, four they can feel, three they can hear, and returns to the list when attention drifts. Slipping away is part of the practice, not a failure, so ask about the return as much as the noticing. Review the log together.

fields.label: Where and when I practiced
Five things I noticed
What pulled my attention away
How I came back
How I felt afterward
When I could do this again this week

title: Hexaflex Reflection Sheet
summary: A sheet that walks a client through the six flexibility processes with one plain question each.
goal: Give a client and clinician a shared picture of where flexibility is strongest and thinnest.
body_md: Use this as a conversation guide, not a score. Each prompt maps to one of the six processes: present moment, acceptance, defusion, self as context, values, and committed action. Let the client star the areas that feel strong and circle the ones that feel stuck. Choose one circled area for the coming weeks, based on their preference and your judgment.

fields.label: How easy it is for me to stay in the present moment, and an example
What I do with uncomfortable feelings
How tightly I hold my thoughts
How I see myself beyond my thoughts and roles
What matters most to me right now
What I am doing, or could do, that fits what matters
The area I most want to work on next

title: IMPROVE the Moment Menu
summary: A menu that turns the IMPROVE skills into a menu of choices for a hard moment.
goal: Give a client a short list of ways to get through a painful moment without making it worse.
body_md: Fill this out in session when the client is calm, so the choices are ready when they are not. Not every letter will fit every client; leave blanks for the ones that do not, and replace prayer with a meaning or comfort practice that suits their beliefs. Rehearse one choice aloud. Remind the client these skills help them get through a moment, not solve the problem.

fields.label: An image that calms me or gives me strength
A meaning I can find in this hard time
A comfort or spiritual practice that fits me
A relaxation I can do in two minutes
One thing I can focus on fully right now
A small vacation I can take in my mind or schedule
An encouraging sentence I can say to myself
The choice I will try first

title: Single-Task Mindfulness Log
summary: A log for doing a single everyday activity with full attention and noting each time the mind wandered.
goal: Build the mindfulness skill of one thing at a time.
body_md: Ask the client to choose one routine task, such as washing dishes or brushing teeth, and give it full attention once a day. Emphasize that wandering and returning is the exercise. In review, ask what they noticed about doing one thing at a time and where multitasking shows up in the rest of their day.

fields.label: The activity I chose
What I noticed with my senses
When my mind wandered, and where it went
How I brought it back
How I felt when I finished
Where I try to do many things at once
One place I could do just one thing this week

title: Effectiveness Not Rightness Card
summary: A pocket card for the moment a client is stuck on being right, with questions that point back to the goal.
goal: Help a client choose the effective move over the satisfying one.
body_md: The Effectively skill asks what will work for the goal in front of the client. Use a recent conflict where being right felt important. Let the client fill the card in session so they can carry it. Be ready for pushback; being effective does not mean giving up values or boundaries, and it is worth saying that out loud.

fields.label: The situation where I wanted to be right
My goal in that situation
What I did that fit the goal
What I did that got in the way
What would be most effective next time
What I need to remember in the heat of the moment

title: Observe and Describe Practice
summary: A paired practice of observing an experience quietly and then describing it in plain facts without judgment words.
goal: Teach the what-skills of observing and describing in daily life.
duration: Ten minutes, three times in one week
body_md: Run one round in session with an object or a sound before sending it home. The client observes silently, then describes using only facts, avoiding words like good, bad, awful, or ugly. Many clients find the judgments sneak in; treat each one as something to notice, not a mistake. Compare how an emotion feels when only described.

fields.label: What I observed, and which sense I used
My description using only facts
Judgment words that crept in
How I would say it without the judgments
A feeling I noticed and described the same way
What I learned from describing

title: Skills Reminder Wallet Cards
summary: A set of small cards a client fills with their own top skills, to carry where they will be needed.
goal: Make favorite coping skills easy to find in the moment.
body_md: Have the client choose three to five skills they have already tried and write each in their own words on a card, with the steps in short form. Laminate or photograph the cards if possible. Revisit after a week and swap out any that were not used. The client picks the skills; you check that the set covers a range of intensities.

fields.label: The skill I want on card one
Its steps in my own words
The skill for card two and its steps
The skill for card three and its steps
Where I will keep the cards
The situation I most want them for
A time I will review the cards

title: Reunion Ritual Plan
summary: A plan for the first twenty minutes after partners reunite each day, with each partner naming what helps them land.
goal: Help partners reconnect in the daily handoff from work to home.
body_md: Partners are often tired and talk past each other in the first minutes at home. Each partner describes what helps them land, such as a hug, quiet, a snack, or a few minutes alone. Then they write one shared ritual. Check that both preferences are heard, not only the louder one. Revisit in a week and adjust.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me land after the day
Partner B: what helps me land after the day
What we each tend to do in the first twenty minutes now
What we each wish the other would do or not do
Our shared reunion ritual, step by step
What we will do on days one of us needs more space
When we will check how it is going

title: Unspoken Rules Inventory
summary: A list where each partner writes the rules they assumed the relationship runs on, then compares and negotiates them.
goal: Bring hidden expectations into the open so partners can choose them together.
body_md: Partners complete the first half separately, then share. Common unspoken rules involve money, time, who initiates, and what counts as respect. Treat differences as information about each person's history, not as faults. Each partner owns their rules by saying I assumed rather than you should. Help them keep, change, or drop each rule together.

fields.label: Partner A: rules I assumed we followed
Partner B: rules I assumed we followed
Rules we both assumed
Rules only one of us assumed
Where each of our rules came from
Rules we choose to keep
Rules we want to change, and a first step

title: Our Story Timeline
summary: A shared timeline of key moments, from first meeting to now, with what each partner remembers and values about them.
goal: Rebuild shared meaning by revisiting the story of the relationship together.
body_md: Have partners draw a line and mark five to eight moments, then each write what they remember in their own words. Differences in memory can be interesting rather than a problem. Steer toward moments of choosing each other and getting through something. If a painful moment comes up, name it briefly and decide together whether it belongs here.

fields.label: Partner A: our first meeting as I remember it
Partner B: our first meeting as I remember it
A time we got through something hard together
A moment I felt proud of us
A moment I felt closest to you
What I admire about us as a pair
A chapter we want to write next

title: Affection Preferences Menu
summary: A menu where each partner lists the kinds of affection they like, how often, and when, to compare side by side.
goal: Help partners talk about affection preferences without blame.
body_md: Each partner marks which forms of affection they enjoy, such as touch, words, notes, time, or small acts, and when they like them. Differences are common and are not a measure of love. Encourage each partner to describe what they enjoy rather than criticize what is missing. Keep the focus on non-sexual affection unless the couple wants to widen it.

fields.label: Partner A: kinds of affection I enjoy most
Partner B: kinds of affection I enjoy most
Times of day or moments I like affection
Times I would rather have space
One kind of affection I would like to try more
One kind I would like us to ask about first
How we will tell each other yes, no, or not now

title: Shared Calendar Conversation Sheet
summary: A weekly sheet where partners place work, chores, time together, and time apart on one page before the week starts.
goal: Reduce hidden scheduling friction by planning the week as a team.
body_md: Partners sit with both calendars and walk through the week. Each names must-do items first, then what they hope for. Look at whether one partner carries more of the planning, and invite them to share it. Always put at least one block of time together and one of time alone on the page.

fields.label: Partner A: my must-do items this week
Partner B: my must-do items this week
Chores and errands we need to split
Time together we are protecting
Time apart each of us wants
A pressure point in the week and a plan for it
What we will review next week

title: Glitter Jar Calm Craft
summary: A child makes a glitter jar and watches the swirl settle while practicing slow breathing.
goal: Give a child a hands-on picture of big feelings settling.
body_md: The child and parent fill a jar with water, clear glue, and glitter, then shake it. While it settles, the child breathes slowly and names how their body feels. The parent joins in and later uses the jar in calm moments, offered as a choice, never as a punishment. Keep the jar sealed and supervised. Remind the parent of reporting duties if the child discloses harm.

fields.label: What I put in my jar and what it looked like
What the swirl made me think of
How my body felt while the glitter settled
A feeling that sometimes swirls inside me
What helps my feelings settle
Where we will keep the jar at home

title: My Calm Corner Design
summary: A child draws and plans a cozy corner at home, and the parent helps set it up and agrees when it is used.
goal: Create a child-chosen place for calming down that is never used as a punishment.
body_md: Have the child draw their ideal calm spot, then choose items such as a pillow, a book, or a stuffed animal. The parent builds it with them at home and practices going there together first. The corner is an invitation, not a consequence. Remind parents about their reporting duties if a child says anything that concerns you about safety.

fields.label: Draw or describe my calm corner
Soft things I want in it
Things to do there when I feel upset
How I will know I want to go there
Who can sit with me if I ask
What my parent will say when I go there

title: Pocket Comfort Stone
summary: A child paints or chooses a smooth stone to carry as a reminder of a calming skill.
goal: Give a child a small, portable reminder of something that helps them feel safe.
body_md: The child chooses a stone, decorates it, and picks a calming skill it stands for, such as slow breathing or squeezing it. The parent practices the skill with the child and agrees on a short phrase to say. Keep it light; the stone is a cue and a comfort. Parents should know the stone is for comfort, and you are available to talk if the child discloses something that worries them.

fields.label: What I drew or painted on my stone
The calm skill my stone reminds me of
A time I might hold it
What I can say to myself when I hold it
Who I can tell when I need help
Where I will keep it

title: Feelings Pizza Drawing
summary: A child draws a pizza and divides it into slices for each feeling they had that day, making bigger slices for bigger feelings.
goal: Help a child see that many feelings can sit together in one day.
body_md: The child draws a circle and cuts it into slices, one for each feeling of the day, sizing slices to match how much they felt it. The parent takes a turn with their own pizza so the child sees feelings are normal for adults too. Listen without fixing. If the child mentions harm or fear at home or elsewhere, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The feelings in my pizza today
Which slice is the biggest
What happened to make that feeling
A small slice that is still important
What my body felt like with the big slice
What I want a grown-up to know about my day

title: Kind Words Postcard
summary: A child writes and decorates a postcard to a future self with kind words, then the parent mails or posts it.
goal: Help a child practice speaking kindly to themselves.
body_md: The child makes a postcard to themselves with a kind message and a picture of something they like about themselves. The parent adds a note of their own, and later reads it with them. The aim is practicing a kind inner voice, not praise for performing. If a child's drawings or words raise safety concerns, use your reporting duties.

fields.label: What I drew on my postcard
Something I like about myself
Something I did that was brave
Kind words I want to hear when I feel down
What a good friend would say to me
When I will read my postcard

title: Feelings Pictionary Relay
summary: A team drawing game where players sketch feelings and situations for teammates to guess.
goal: Build feelings vocabulary through quick drawing and guessing.
body_md: Split into two teams. Each round, one player draws a feeling from a card while teammates guess within a minute, and no letters or words are allowed. After each round, ask what clues told the team the feeling. End with a debrief about which feelings were easy and hard to draw and how people show them. Keep it silly and give every player a turn.

fields.label: The feeling I drew or guessed
The clues that helped
A feeling that was hard to draw
A time I felt it
How my body showed it
What I learned about showing feelings to others

title: Skill Tic-Tac-Toe
summary: A tic-tac-toe board where each square holds a coping skill that the player must describe before claiming it.
goal: Make rehearsing skills a playful, turn-taking activity.
body_md: Draw a three-by-three board and write a coping skill in each square. On their turn, a player describes when and how they would use the skill to claim the square. Opponents may ask one question. The debrief covers which skills players claim often and which they avoid. Clinician judgment guides how deep each answer goes.

fields.label: The skill in the square I claimed
When I would use it
What would make it hard to use
A skill I avoided and why
A skill someone else described that I want to try
The skill I will practice this week

title: Strengths Hot Potato
summary: Players pass an object around the circle and name a strength about another player when the music stops.
goal: Help players hear and give specific strengths in a group.
body_md: Pass a soft object while music plays. When it stops, the holder names one specific strength of the person to their left, with an example. If the group is new, offer sentence starters. Pause for anyone who struggles to accept a compliment. Debrief what it was like to give and to receive. Make sure everyone receives at least one strength.

fields.label: A strength someone named in me
How it felt to hear it
A strength I named in someone else
What made it easy or hard to say
A strength I rarely give myself credit for
Who in my life I could tell about a strength I see in them

title: Story Chain Coping
summary: A group builds a story one sentence at a time about a character facing a problem, adding a coping skill at each turn.
goal: Practice generating coping ideas through shared storytelling.
body_md: Start the story with a character facing a small problem. Each player adds one sentence, and every second turn must include a coping skill the character tries. The story can wander. In the debrief, ask which skills the character used, which the group would try, and how the character felt at the end. Keep the problem mild and let the group steer.

fields.label: The problem our character faced
The skills the character tried
Which one worked best for the character
A skill I would try myself
How the story ended
What I want to remember from the story

title: Mindful Sound Bingo
summary: A bingo card of everyday sounds that players mark as they listen quietly for a few minutes.
goal: Practice mindful listening with a playful goal.
body_md: Hand out cards with sounds such as a door closing, a bird, footsteps, or a hum. Everyone sits quietly and marks a square when they hear that sound. The first to complete a line wins, but everyone gets a turn to share. Debrief what they noticed once they were listening on purpose, and how attention wandered and returned.

fields.label: Sounds I marked on my card
A sound I heard that was not on the card
What my mind did while I listened
How I felt in my body when it was quiet
A place I could listen mindfully this week
What I noticed about my attention

title: Steady in the Storm Anchor Script
summary: A short ACT exercise for steadying the body and attention in the middle of strong feelings, with a client-built script.
goal: Give a client a brief way to feel their feet, name what is here, and re-engage with the room.
body_md: Walk the client through the three steps in session first: notice thoughts and feelings, connect with the body by pushing feet into the floor, then notice the room. The aim is steadiness, not making feelings leave. Keep eyes open if closing them feels unsafe, and never ask for any account of past events. Let the client edit the wording until it sounds like them.

fields.label: The feelings and thoughts I notice are...
One way I can feel my body in the chair or on the floor is...
Five things I can see around me right now are...
A sound I can hear that tells me where I am today is...
The one thing I want to do next, once I feel steadier, is...

title: Nighttime Settling Plan
summary: A client's written plan for the hour before bed that builds in safety cues, comfort, and a way back if they wake.
goal: Help a client create a predictable, safe-feeling evening routine and a plan for waking at night.
duration: 20 minutes, then one week of use
body_md: Evenings can be a hard stretch when the day goes quiet. Build the plan together in session and keep it simple and stabilizing: lights, locks, comfort items, a calming activity, and a short grounding step to use on waking. Adjust to what the client reports and review it the following week. Nothing here asks the client to recall or write about past events.

fields.label: Things that help my space feel safe at night are...
Three calming things I could do in the last hour before bed are...
A comfort item or sensation I want close by is...
If I wake up unsettled, the first thing I will do is...
A person I could reach out to the next day is...
What I noticed after trying the plan was...

title: Safe People Hand Map
summary: A child traces their hand and writes one trusted person on each finger, so they know who to go to.
goal: Help a child name the trusted people they can turn to when they feel scared or upset.
body_md: The child traces a hand, then names a trusted person for each finger and what that person does to help. The parent joins in and listens without quizzing, and keeps the tone warm and unhurried. If the child discloses anything, follow your reporting duties and your clinical judgment. Display the map where the child can see it at home.

fields.label: The person on my thumb is...
The person on my pointer finger is...
The person on my middle finger is...
The person on my ring finger is...
The person on my pinky is...
When I feel scared, the first person I will go to is...

title: Grounding Scavenger Round
summary: A turn-taking game in which players find items in the room by sense, color, or texture to practice settling attention.
goal: Let a client or group practice grounding in a playful, low-pressure way before they need it.
body_md: Rules: players take turns drawing a prompt card such as find something blue, soft, or round, and everyone has 60 seconds to find one. Players name the item aloud and what they notice about it. Debrief by asking which prompts felt steadying and which felt like too much. Keep it optional, let anyone pass, and avoid any discussion of past events.

fields.label: The prompts that helped me feel here and now were...
A sense I find easiest to use for grounding is...
A prompt I would change or skip is...
One place outside this room I could use this game is...
What I noticed in my body during the game was...

title: Hard Day Pacing Agreement
summary: Partners write what each will do and avoid on a hard day, so support stays steady and unpressured.
goal: Help partners agree on how one partner signals a hard day and how the other responds.
body_md: Partner A, the one having the hard day, names early signs, what helps, and what to hold off on. Partner B writes how they will offer support and how they will care for themselves. Keep the conversation on pacing and safety, not on details of the past, and let each partner set limits. Revisit the agreement after a few weeks.

fields.label: Partner A: signs that today is a hard day are...
Partner A: things that help me on a hard day are...
Partner A: things I would like you to hold off on are...
Partner B: how I will check in without pressing is...
Partner B: how I will take care of myself on those days is...
Together: the words or sign we will use to start this plan are...

title: Cope Ahead Rehearsal Plan
summary: A DBT-style plan that has the client picture a worrying situation and rehearse the skills they will use there.
goal: Help a client get ready for a difficult upcoming event by rehearsing specific skills in advance.
body_md: Pick one upcoming situation that brings anxiety and walk through it with the client step by step, naming the skills they will use at each point. The client imagines themselves coping, not perfect. Rehearse out loud in session if you can. Keep the plan short enough to read on a phone, and adjust it after the event together.

fields.label: The situation I am getting ready for is...
The moment I expect to feel the most anxious is...
Skills I could use at that moment are...
What I will say to myself while it is happening is...
The first small step I will take afterward is...

title: Partner Reassurance Reset Plan
summary: Partners agree how to respond when one asks for repeated reassurance, with a kind script for both sides.
goal: Help partners replace repeated reassurance loops with a response both of them can live with.
body_md: The anxious partner names what they tend to ask and what it gives them for a moment. The other partner names how those moments feel on their side. Together they write one warm response and one thing the asking partner can try first. Frame it as a team plan, avoid blame, and note that some reassurance is normal and fine.

fields.label: Partner A: the question I find myself asking again is...
Partner A: what I feel in my body just before I ask is...
Partner B: how I feel when I am asked again is...
Partner B: a kind, short thing I can say is...
Partner A: something I can try before asking is...
Together: how we will check how the plan is going is...

title: Anxiety Myth or Fact Showdown
summary: A two-team quiz game about common beliefs on anxiety, with cards the group sorts into myth, fact, and it depends.
goal: Open up a group conversation about what people believe about anxiety and how those beliefs shape coping.
body_md: Rules: split the group into two teams, read a statement card, and let each team vote myth, fact, or it depends, then explain why. Award a point for a reasoned answer, not just a right one. Debrief on which beliefs people hold personally and which they would like to test. Keep it light and let anyone pass.

fields.label: A belief about anxiety I heard growing up was...
A card that surprised me was...
A belief I would like to test in my own life is...
Something I would tell a friend who believed a myth is...
What I want to remember from the game is...

title: Calm Corner Menu
summary: A client designs a menu of calming options for sight, sound, touch, and movement that they can use at home or school.
goal: Help a client build a personal menu of calming choices they can reach for before anxiety peaks.
body_md: Work through each sense and movement option and let the client pick what actually appeals, not what they think they should choose. Have them try two or three in session and rate how each felt. For younger clients, a parent can help set up a physical corner. Revisit the menu and swap out what no longer helps.

fields.label: Something calming to look at is...
A sound or music that settles me is...
A texture or object that feels good to hold is...
A way of moving that releases tension is...
A place at home or school I could use as a calm spot is...
The option I will try first this week is...

title: Cloud Weather Feelings Mobile
summary: A child makes a hanging mobile of feelings as weather and talks about how storms pass and the sky changes.
goal: Help a child see anxious feelings as changing weather that comes and goes.
body_md: The child cuts or draws clouds, sun, rain, and wind, writes a feeling on each, and hangs them from a hanger. The parent helps tie the pieces and asks what the weather is today, accepting whatever the child says. Hang the mobile in their room and let them move pieces when feelings change. Keep the conversation curious and unhurried.

fields.label: Today my feeling weather is...
The weather that feels biggest to me is...
A cloud that shows how my worries look is...
What helps a storm feel smaller is...
A sunny spot in my day is...

title: Making Room for Heavy Feelings Practice
summary: An ACT practice in which a client notices where heaviness sits in the body and makes room for it while choosing a small action.
goal: Help a client carry low mood while still taking one small step that matters to them.
body_md: Guide the client to notice where the heaviness sits, give it a shape or color, and breathe around it rather than away from it. The point is room, not removal. Then choose one small action tied to a value. Go slowly, and respect a client who finds the body focus hard. If hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm come up, talk about it in session.

fields.label: Where I feel heaviness in my body is...
If it had a shape, color, or weight, it would be...
What it is like to make a little room around it is...
Something that matters to me, even on a heavy day, is...
One small step I can take with the heaviness along is...
If things feel unsafe, I can call or text 988 or tell a trusted person. The first person I would tell is...

title: Accumulating Positive Emotions Planner
summary: A DBT-style weekly plan that adds short-term pleasant events and one long-term value-based step.
goal: Help a client build more small pleasant moments into the week, and one step toward something bigger.
body_md: This is the accumulate positive emotions skill in planner form. Have the client pick a few pleasant events they can do this week, mindful of what feels doable at their current energy. Add one longer-term step. Review it next session, and be curious about what got in the way rather than what was missed.

fields.label: Pleasant things I could do in the next few days are...
The ones that feel doable at my energy level are...
I will do them at these times...
One longer-term thing I care about is...
One small step toward it this week is...
What I noticed after trying them was...

title: Connection Without Pressure Plan
summary: Partners plan small, low-demand ways to stay connected when one partner has low mood and little energy.
goal: Help partners find ways to be close that do not depend on the low-mood partner's energy.
body_md: The partner with low mood names what feels manageable and what feels like too much. The other partner names what connection they miss and what they can offer without asking for much back. Together they choose two or three tiny rituals. Keep it free of blame, and check in on what is working after a week.

fields.label: Partner A: connection that feels manageable right now is...
Partner A: what feels like too much is...
Partner B: what I miss and would like more of is...
Partner B: something I can offer with nothing needed back is...
Together: two small rituals we will try are...
Together: when we will check in about it is...

title: Mood Weather Chart Craft
summary: A child builds a weekly weather-style mood chart with stickers and chooses one kind thing to do on gray days.
goal: Help a child notice and name mood changes and have a plan for lower days.
body_md: The child decorates a weekly chart and picks weather stickers to show how each day felt. The parent fills in alongside, models naming their own mood, and does not judge any day. Together choose one kind thing to do on gray days. Look at the chart weekly and share patterns with the clinician.

fields.label: The weather of my day today is...
On my best day this week I felt...
On my grayest day I felt...
One kind thing I can do on a gray day is...
A grown-up I can tell when I have a gray day is...

title: Self-Critical Voice Rewrite
summary: A CBT sheet where a client catches a harsh inner statement, tests it, and rewrites it in a fairer voice.
goal: Help a client notice self-critical thoughts and practice a more balanced response.
body_md: Ask the client to pick one recent harsh thought, rate how much they believe it, and look at evidence on both sides. Then draft a fairer sentence they could say to a friend. The goal is balance, not forced positivity. Re-rate the belief at the end and watch for the client dismissing the new statement as untrue.

fields.label: The harsh thing my mind said was...
How much I believed it, 0 to 100, was...
Things that fit with that thought are...
Things that do not fit are...
What I would say to a friend who thought this is...
How much I believe the first thought now is...

title: Task Switch Card Game
summary: A card game in which players practice stopping one activity and starting another, with a reset step in between.
goal: Give a client playful practice at the pause, reset, and start steps of switching between tasks.
body_md: Rules: players take turns drawing a task card, work on it for one minute, then draw a switch card with the next task. Between rounds, they say aloud the three reset steps: pause, name what is next, take the first step. Debrief on which switches felt hardest and what helped. Keep the pace friendly and not competitive.

fields.label: The switches that felt easiest were...
The switches that felt hardest were...
The reset step that helped me most was...
A real-life switch I would like to practice is...
Something I will try this week is...

title: Next Action Cue Cards
summary: A set of client-made cards that name the very next physical action for tasks that tend to stall.
goal: Help a client turn vague tasks into one visible, concrete next action they can start.
body_md: Choose three tasks that keep stalling and write each on a card, with the very next physical action on the back, small enough to start in two minutes. Have the client test one in session. Notice what makes a card too vague, and refine it together. Keep the cards where the task happens.

fields.label: A task I keep putting off is...
The very next physical action on it is...
How long that action would take me is...
What might get in the way is...
What I will do if I get stuck is...
How it went when I tried the card was...

title: Boredom Willingness Practice
summary: An ACT practice in which a client notices the pull away from a dull task and practices staying with it for a short stretch.
goal: Help a client notice restlessness and choose to stay with a task that matters to them.
body_md: Pick a task that matters but is dull. The client sets a short timer, notices the urge to switch, names it, and keeps going, then writes what the urge did. The goal is willingness, not force or perfect focus. Pair it with a value so the stay has a reason, and make the stretch short enough to succeed.

fields.label: A task that matters to me but feels dull is...
The pull away from it feels like...
Why it matters to me is...
The length of time I will stay with it is...
What the urge did while I kept going was...
What I would like to try next time is...

title: Weekly Reset Checklist Builder
summary: A client builds a short weekly reset checklist covering space, calendar, and tasks, and picks a regular time to do it.
goal: Help a client set up a brief weekly routine that keeps small things from piling up.
body_md: Build the checklist with the client from what actually slips: papers, calendar, messages, laundry. Keep it to five or six items they can finish in about twenty minutes, and fix a regular day and time with a cue. Expect to revise it after a week or two, and treat a missed reset as information to adjust the plan.

fields.label: Things that pile up for me are...
The items I will put on my reset list are...
The day and time I will do the reset is...
A cue that will remind me is...
Something that makes it more enjoyable is...
What I want to change after a week is...

title: Morning Routine Race Track
summary: A child draws a race track with a stop for each morning step and a parent who cheers at the finish.
goal: Help a child follow a morning routine through a visual path they build themselves.
body_md: The child draws a race track with a pit stop for each morning step, such as clothes, teeth, shoes, and bag. They decorate each stop and put the track at eye level. The parent walks the track with the child for the first days, offers a cheer at the finish, and keeps prompts brief and kind. Adjust the stops together weekly.

fields.label: The first pit stop on my track is...
The next pit stop is...
The stop I forget the most is...
What I will do to remember it is...
How I want my parent to cheer for me is...

title: Trust Rebuilding Check-In Plan
summary: Partners agree on a short regular check-in about substance use, urges and honesty, with a part for each.
goal: Give a couple a predictable, low-heat way to talk about recovery and rebuild trust.
body_md: Run this in session so both partners hear the agreement as it is made. The partner in recovery names what they will share and when; the other partner names what they will ask and how they will respond to hard news. Watch for the check-in turning into questioning, and help them keep it brief, scheduled and kind.

fields.label: Partner in recovery: what I will share at each check-in (urges, hard moments, slips)
Partner in recovery: one thing I will do when I notice I want to hide something
Supporting partner: the questions I will ask, and the ones I will leave alone
Supporting partner: how I will respond when I hear something hard
When and where we will check in, and how long it will last
What we will do if a check-in gets heated
One thing each of us appreciates about the other's effort this week

title: Saying No Practice Role-Play Cards
summary: A card game where players practice saying no to offers of substances in realistic, low-stakes scenes.
goal: Build confidence and ready phrases for turning down substance offers.
body_md: Write scenario cards together beforehand: a friend at a party, a coworker after work, a family gathering. Players draw a card, take the offerer or the refuser role, then swap. Debrief on which phrases felt natural and which felt forced. Keep it playful at first and raise realism gradually, following the client's pace.

fields.label: A situation where someone might offer me a substance
The first thing I would say, word for word
What I would do with my body (move, hold a drink, leave)
What the offerer might say to push back
My second reply if they push
The phrase from the game I want to keep
Who I can text afterward to say I handled it

title: Choice Point for Urges
summary: An ACT choice point map for a moment of substance use urge, sorting moves toward values and moves away.
goal: Help a client notice a hooked moment and pick the next step on purpose.
body_md: Draw the choice point with the client: the situation at the top, a fork below. Moves away from what matters are often quick relief; moves toward are usually harder in the moment. Use a recent real urge and avoid shaming the away moves, since they usually make sense. Revisit the same sheet after practice.

fields.label: A recent moment when I felt an urge to use
Thoughts and feelings that showed up in that moment
What I did, or might have done, that moves me away from what matters
What I did, or could do, that moves me toward what matters
What the away move gives me, and what it costs later
Who or what matters most that I want to move toward
A small toward move I will try next time

title: Free Time Rebuild Planner
summary: A weekly planner for filling the hours that used to belong to substance use with chosen activities.
goal: Replace empty or risky stretches of the week with planned, valued activity.
body_md: Start by listing the times of day that used to involve substance use, because those are usually the open gaps. Help the client choose activities that are realistic and personally meaningful, not just distracting. Review next session what happened, and adjust without judgment if plans fell through.

fields.label: The times of day or week that used to involve substance use
What I miss about those times, and what I do not miss
Activities I used to enjoy before substance use took over
New things I would like to try
My plan for the riskiest time block this week
Who could join me or check in
What I will do if the plan falls apart

title: Evening Self-Soothing Kit
summary: A DBT self-soothe through the five senses menu built for the hours when substance use urges tend to rise.
goal: Give a client a ready set of soothing options for urge-heavy evenings.
body_md: Work through the five senses with the client and have them name specific items they can actually get hold of on an evening: a tea, a playlist, a blanket. Stress that this does not remove urges but gives them something to do while the urge passes. Suggest keeping a physical kit and checking how it worked afterward.

fields.label: Something I can see that calms me
Something I can hear that calms me
Something I can smell that calms me
Something I can taste that calms me
Something I can touch or wear that calms me
The time of evening when urges are strongest
Which two items I will set out before that time

title: Calm Down Corner Builder
summary: A child and parent build a cozy calm corner at home and decide together what goes in it.
goal: Give a child a place and a set of tools for cooling off that they chose themselves.
body_md: The parent and child gather pillows, drawing paper and sensory items and set up the corner together, with the child making the choices. The parent explains the corner is a place to get calm, not a punishment, and practices using it once when everyone is calm. If a child discloses harm at home, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The name I gave my calm corner
Three things I picked to put in it
What my body feels like when I need to go there
What I do first when I get there
What my parent does when I am in my corner
How I know I am ready to come back out
What I want to tell my parent after I cool off

title: Cool Down Relay Game
summary: A team relay where players race to complete calming skills cards instead of racing at full speed.
goal: Make practicing cooling skills active, fun and memorable in a group.
body_md: Set up stations with calming skills such as paced breathing, a cold drink, stretching and counting. Teams take turns, and players must finish each skill slowly to score. The twist of slowing down on purpose usually lands well with teens. Debrief on which skills worked best and when in real life each would be useful.

fields.label: The skill that was easiest to do slowly
The skill that was hardest to do slowly
What changed in my body during the relay
A moment this week when I could use that skill
What I would say to a teammate who is about to blow up
The skill I will keep in my toolkit

title: Checking the Facts on Anger
summary: A DBT check the facts sheet separating what happened from the story attached to it before acting on anger.
goal: Slow down the jump from an event to an angry reaction.
body_md: Choose a recent angry moment. Have the client describe only what a camera would have recorded, then list the interpretations and assumptions. Ask whether the emotion and its intensity fit the facts, and what action would fit. Be careful not to suggest anger is wrong; the aim is a choice about the response.

fields.label: What happened, as a camera would have recorded it
What I told myself it meant
Other possible explanations
What I was feeling and how strong it was (0 to 10)
Does the strength fit the facts, as far as I can tell?
What I wanted to do
What I could do that fits what matters to me

title: Hot Thought Rewind Sheet
summary: A CBT thought record tuned for angry thoughts, such as demands, blame and mind reading.
goal: Help a client catch and test the hot thoughts that fuel anger.
body_md: Anger thoughts often sound like 'should', 'always' and 'on purpose'. Help the client pick out the hottest thought from a recent incident, then look at the facts for and against it. Avoid arguing them out of their feelings; the goal is a more balanced thought they still believe, and a response they can choose.

fields.label: The situation that set off my anger
The hottest thought I had
Words in it like always, never, should or on purpose
Facts that fit this thought
Facts that do not fit it
A more balanced way to say it
How angry I feel now (0 to 10)

title: Anger and What I Value Compass
summary: An ACT values exercise asking what an angry moment shows about what matters and how to act on it well.
goal: Connect anger to the value underneath it and pick a response in line with it.
body_md: Many clients find anger has a value under it, such as fairness, respect or protecting someone. Help them name that value and then compare what anger-driven actions cost against what value-driven actions would look like. Avoid framing anger as a problem to remove; the point is room to choose a response.

fields.label: A recent time I was angry
What I was trying to protect or stand up for
The value underneath it, in a word or two
What I did when angry, and what it cost
What acting on that value could look like instead
What I would have to feel or tolerate to do that
One small way to do it this week

title: Mental Ritual Spotter
summary: A worksheet to help a client notice hidden mental rituals such as checking, reviewing and counting in the head.
goal: Help a client see the covert rituals that keep an intrusive thought cycle going.
body_md: Many people only count visible actions as rituals and miss what happens in the head. Go through the list with curiosity and not criticism, and let the client sort what actually feels like a ritual from ordinary thinking. This is a noticing tool for you to work from, and it does not replace your own judgment.

fields.label: An intrusive thought that shows up for me
What I do in my head right after it (review, repeat, check, argue)
How long I spend doing that
What I hope it will do for me
What happens to the thought afterward
Mental moves I only noticed while filling this out
One I would like to watch for this week

title: Doubt Dial Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment where a client rates a feared outcome, tries a doubtful situation, and compares.
goal: Let a client test what happens when they tolerate doubt without checking.
body_md: Choose a small, specific feared prediction with the client and agree on the exact experiment. They rate their belief in the prediction before and after, noting what they did instead of the ritual. Keep it modest at first, and discuss results without pushing certainty, since the lesson is about living with some doubt.

fields.label: The doubt or fear I am testing
What I predict will happen
How much I believe that (0 to 100)
What I will do, and what I will not do (my usual ritual)
What actually happened
How much I believe the prediction now (0 to 100)
What I learned about doubt

title: Values Before Rituals Direction Sheet
summary: An ACT compass comparing time given to rituals with time given to what matters in the client's life.
goal: Help a client see what rituals take from valued living and where to redirect.
body_md: Ask the client to name their values in several areas of life, then estimate how much time rituals take from each. This can bring up grief or frustration, so give it room. Choose one small, values-based action to do in the place of a ritual-heavy stretch, and keep the language kind and free of blame.

fields.label: Three things that matter most to me
How rituals take time from each of those
A time of day when rituals take the most
What I would like to do with that time
What I fear might happen if I did it
A small values step I will try this week
What I will say to myself if the urge to ritualize gets loud

title: Supportive Not Reassuring Phrase Card
summary: Partners write supportive replies that care for the person without answering the doubt.
goal: Help a partner support their loved one without feeding the reassurance cycle.
body_md: Work with the partner who is asked for reassurance to draft warm replies that recognize feelings and leave the question unanswered, and with the partner who experiences OCD to say what kind of reply would help them. Role-play a few. Expect the supporting partner to feel guilty about holding back, and name that.

fields.label: Partner with intrusive thoughts: how I ask for reassurance
Partner with intrusive thoughts: what kind of reply helps me later
Supporting partner: how it feels to be asked
Supporting partner: three warm replies that do not answer the doubt
How we will signal to each other that the question is a ritual
What we will do together afterward instead
What we will tell each other if it gets tense

title: Thought Bubble Pass Game
summary: A group game where intrusive-style thoughts on cards are passed along and acknowledged without reacting.
goal: Practice letting a thought be there without acting on it, through play.
body_md: Write neutral, silly or mildly uncomfortable thoughts on cards, avoiding anything graphic or truly distressing. Players pass the card clockwise and say, 'I notice a thought that...' then hand it on. Choose content to fit the group so no one is flooded. Debrief on how it felt to notice without arguing or fixing.

fields.label: A thought that was easy to pass along
A thought that felt harder to pass
What I noticed in my body
What I wanted to do when the thought arrived
What it was like to just say 'I notice a thought'
A moment this week I could try it
What I would tell a friend who gets stuck on a thought

title: Calm Breathing Pinwheel Craft
summary: A child makes a pinwheel and uses it to practice slow, steady breaths with a parent.
goal: Give a child a hands-on way to practice slowing their breathing.
body_md: The child decorates and builds a paper pinwheel, then practices blowing it gently and slowly with the parent. Explain that fast breathing is part of how a body gets ready to be brave, and practice when calm so it is familiar. The parent models along with the child. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: The colors I picked for my pinwheel
What my body feels like when it gets really scared
What happens to my pinwheel when I breathe fast
What happens when I breathe slow
Who I practiced with
Where I will keep my pinwheel
How I felt after the slow breaths

title: Sensation Surprise Card Game
summary: A card game where players safely bring on harmless body sensations and rate how strong and how safe they feel.
goal: Practice noticing body sensations without alarm in a playful, structured way.
body_md: Cards name safe activities such as spinning slowly, breathing through a straw or jogging in place. Players take a turn, rate the sensation, and say what they noticed. Choose cards to fit the client's health, and use your judgment on pacing. Debrief on what the sensations felt like and what thoughts came with them.

fields.label: The card I drew
The sensations I noticed
How strong they felt (0 to 10)
The thought that came with them
What happened to the sensation after a minute
A sensation that surprised me
What I want to practice at home

title: Safety Behavior Inventory
summary: A worksheet listing the things a client does to feel safe around panic, and what each costs them.
goal: Help a client see which safety habits keep life small.
body_md: Safety behaviors such as carrying water, sitting near exits or checking a pulse can feel necessary. List them without criticism and note what each one gives and costs. Choose with the client which to test dropping first, if any, and in what order. This is a conversation starter for your own clinical judgment.

fields.label: Things I carry or keep close in case of panic
Places or seats I choose to feel safe
Things I check in my body
What each one gives me
What each one costs me
Which one I might try without first, and when
What I expect to happen if I do

title: Panic Prediction Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment where a client records what they predict during panic and what actually happened.
goal: Compare feared predictions about panic sensations with real outcomes.
body_md: Ask the client to write their prediction when a panic wave begins, such as 'I will faint', and then note what happened. Review a few entries together and look for patterns, such as predictions that did not come true. Keep it curious and not argumentative, and leave medical questions to the client's doctor.

fields.label: Where I was when the panic wave started
What I felt in my body
What I predicted would happen
How sure I was (0 to 100)
What actually happened
How long the strongest part lasted
What I notice across my entries

title: Making Room for Alarm Practice
summary: An ACT practice for letting panic sensations be present while moving toward something that matters.
goal: Practice making room for alarm sensations while doing what the client values.
body_md: Guide the client to notice panic sensations, name them, breathe around them and keep doing a small valued activity anyway. This is not about getting rid of panic. Use a mild sensation first and pace to the client's comfort. Ask afterward what it was like to carry the feeling along instead of fighting it.

fields.label: A valued activity I want to do even with panic around
Sensations I notice when alarm shows up
How I usually fight or escape them
What it would look like to make room for them
What I noticed when I tried
What I did anyway
What I will practice this week

title: Tantrum Storm Shelter Plan
summary: A parent and child build a cozy calm-down shelter and decide together how it gets used.
goal: Give a child and parent a shared, practiced place and script for big feelings.
body_md: Have the parent and child build a small shelter from pillows and a blanket, then decorate it with calming items the child picks. The point is rehearsal while everyone is calm, so the shelter is a place the child chooses rather than a punishment. Coach the parent to stay nearby and quiet. If a child discloses anything worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: The name my child gave our shelter
Three things we put inside it to help us feel calm
The words the parent will say when a storm starts
What my child wants the parent to do while they are inside
How we will know the storm has passed

title: Sibling Squabble Referee Game
summary: A turn-taking card game where siblings and parents practice fair solutions to common arguments.
goal: Let siblings rehearse fair, calm solutions to everyday arguments through play.
body_md: Write common squabbles on cards, such as who sits where or whose turn it is. Players draw a card, act as the referee, and propose a fair fix, with the parent playing too and sometimes giving a deliberately unfair answer for the children to catch. In the debrief, ask which fixes felt fair to everyone. Keep it silly so the children stay open to it.

fields.label: A squabble card we drew
The fix I suggested as referee
Whether everyone felt it was fair, and why
A squabble from home we could try a fix on
A fair fix we want to remember
What the parent will do next time a squabble starts

title: Good Enough Parent Thought Swap
summary: A thought-swap sheet that pairs harsh parenting thoughts with balanced, realistic alternatives.
goal: Help a parent notice perfectionistic parenting thoughts and test more balanced ones.
body_md: Walk the parent through one recent moment when they judged themselves harshly, then separate the situation, the thought and the feeling. Ask them to write a balanced alternative they could believe at least partly. Parents often write what sounds nice but feels untrue, so ask for a rating of belief before and after. Use it alongside your own formulation of the parent's patterns.

fields.label: The parenting moment I judged myself about
The thought that showed up, in my own words
How strongly I believed it, from 0 to 100
What I would say to a friend in the same spot
A more balanced thought I can partly believe
How strongly I believe the balanced thought now

title: Hooked Parent Defusion Cards
summary: Cards that help a parent notice sticky parenting thoughts and hold them lightly while acting on values.
goal: Help a parent unhook from rigid parenting stories and act on what matters to them.
body_md: Ask the parent to name the stories that grab them in hard moments, such as I am failing or my child should not act like this, and write each as a card beginning with I am having the thought that. Practice saying the cards aloud, then choose one small values-based parenting action to take with the thought still present. Keep the tone playful rather than corrective.

fields.label: A sticky story I tell myself as a parent
The same story starting with I am having the thought that
What the thought pushes me to do
What I want my parenting to stand for
One small action I can take with the thought still there

title: Parenting Partners Weekly Check-In
summary: Two parents each name what is working, what feels heavy and what support they want from each other.
goal: Give two parents a short, structured way to align and support each other each week.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own part, then they take turns reading aloud while the other listens without fixing. Partner A speaks first one week and Partner B the next. Watch for the check-in turning into a list of complaints; steer back to one request each. Use it as a bridge between sessions and adapt it to the family's rhythm.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciated about how we parented this week
Partner B: something I appreciated about how we parented this week
Partner A: what felt heaviest for me this week
Partner B: what felt heaviest for me this week
Partner A: one specific thing I would like help with
Partner B: one specific thing I would like help with

title: Nighttime Worry Parking Lot
summary: A bedside worksheet where a new parent parks worries on paper and plans a time to revisit them.
goal: Help a new parent set down nighttime worries and sort which ones need action.
body_md: Introduce this as a bedside page for the worries that show up during night feeds or waking. The parent jots each worry, then marks whether it has an action for tomorrow or is a what-if to let sit. Review together how it went; many parents find the act of writing helps but need permission to keep it brief. Adapt it to what the parent is carrying.

fields.label: The worry on my mind right now
Whether it needs an action tomorrow or is a what-if
If it needs action, the one small step I can take
A kind thing I can tell myself while I wait

title: Wise Mind Moments for New Parents
summary: A brief wise-mind practice a new parent can use between feeds, matching feeling and reasoning.
goal: Give a new parent a quick way to find a steady, balanced response in tiring moments.
body_md: Teach wise mind as the place where feeling and reasoning overlap, and practice it with one recent moment of overwhelm. Ask the parent to name what the emotional mind said, what the reasonable mind said, and what wise mind suggests. Keep the practice short enough to fit between feeds. Check in on how realistic each step is given how little sleep they are getting.

fields.label: A recent moment I felt overwhelmed
What my emotional mind said
What my reasonable mind said
What my wise mind says, in one sentence
One breath or pause I can use before the next feed
A cue in my day that will remind me to try this

title: Visitor Boundaries Script Sheet
summary: A script sheet for setting kind limits on visitors, advice and help in the weeks after a baby arrives.
goal: Help a new parent plan clear, warm limits around visitors and unsolicited advice.
body_md: Many new parents feel guilty saying no to well-meaning family. Use the sheet to name which visits and offers they want, and to draft short sentences they can say or text. Rehearse one or two aloud in session so the words are familiar. The goal is the parent's comfort, not a rulebook; let them decide what to include and revisit it as needs change.

fields.label: Who I want to see in the next few weeks
How long and how often feels manageable
What kind of help I would like most
A kind sentence I can use to say not yet
A sentence I can use when advice is not welcome
Who will help me say these things if I freeze

title: Newborn Care Card Swap
summary: Partners sort caregiving and household tasks onto cards and trade them to find a sustainable shape.
goal: Help two new parents see all the care work and renegotiate who does what.
body_md: Write every task, from night feeds to laundry to remembering appointments, on cards, including the invisible mental load. Each partner sorts the cards into who does it now, then they swap two or three cards and name the part they will each take. Name both partners' parts in the summary. Expect tiredness to color the conversation, so keep each turn short and kind.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I carry right now
Partner B: tasks I carry right now
Partner A: one card I would like to swap and why
Partner B: one card I would like to swap and why
Partner A: what I will take on this week
Partner B: what I will take on this week

title: Mixed Feelings Welcome Practice
summary: An acceptance practice for making room for joy, grief and ambivalence all at once after a baby arrives.
goal: Help a new parent allow mixed feelings about parenthood without judging them.
body_md: Invite the parent to name all the feelings present, including ones they think they should not have, and to notice they can coexist with caring for the baby. Use a simple willingness exercise where each feeling gets a place at the table. Be alert for shame; normalize that mixed feelings are common and leave it to your judgment whether other support is needed.

fields.label: A feeling about this new chapter that is easy to say
A feeling I find harder to admit
Where I notice each feeling in my body
What I tell myself about having these feelings
What I would say to a friend who felt the same
One small thing I care about that I can do with the feelings still here

title: Inner Critic Comic Strip
summary: A child draws their inner critic and a kind helper as comic characters and scripts their conversation.
goal: Help a child separate from a harsh inner voice and practice a kinder reply.
body_md: Have the child draw a three-panel comic: the critic says something mean, the helper responds, and the child decides what to do. Let them design the characters however they like. Invite the parent to listen to the finished comic and to say one thing they appreciate about the child. If a child shares anything worrying, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What my inner critic looks like
What the critic says that bothers me
What my kind helper looks like
What the helper says back
What I decide to do next
Who I could show this comic to

title: Compliment Receiving Rehearsal
summary: A skills sheet for taking in praise with a simple thank-you and noticing the urge to deflect.
goal: Help a client practice accepting a compliment without discounting it.
body_md: Role-play receiving a compliment, noticing the urge to deflect or return one at once. Link it to describing and mindful attention: notice the words, the feeling and the urge, then say thank you and stop. Many clients find this much harder than it sounds, so start with small compliments and let them choose how much to practice outside session.

fields.label: A compliment I got recently
What I said back
What I felt in my body when I heard it
The urge I noticed to push the compliment away
A simple thank-you I can say instead
A time this week I will practice just saying thanks

title: Good Enough Standards Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment that tests what happens when a task is done to a good enough standard.
goal: Help a client test whether lowering a perfectionist standard changes the feared outcome.
body_md: Pick one small task where the client holds a very high standard, and plan to do it at a good enough level on purpose. Record the prediction, the outcome and what they noticed. Keep the experiment small and agree on it beforehand. Review the result with curiosity and let your clinical judgment guide whether to raise the stakes in the next one.

fields.label: The task and the standard I usually hold
What I think will happen if I do it at good enough
How strongly I believe that, from 0 to 100
What I actually did
What actually happened
What I take from this about my standards

title: Worth Is Not Earned Phrase Cards
summary: Defusion phrase cards for the stories that tie a person's worth to performance or approval.
goal: Help a client hold worth-based stories lightly and choose actions by values.
body_md: Ask the client to write the I am only worth it if stories on cards, then practice noticing them as thoughts with silly voices or by saying them slowly. Follow with one action chosen from a value, taken with the story still present. Keep the aim on flexibility rather than winning an argument with the thought.

fields.label: A story about my worth that shows up often
How it sounds when I say it slowly
What it pushes me to do or avoid
A value I want to act on instead
One action from that value that I can take this week
What I will say to myself when the story shows up

title: Strengths Charades Game
summary: A group guessing game where players act out strengths seen in themselves and each other.
goal: Give a group a playful way to name strengths and receive recognition from others.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a strength card, such as patient or brave, and acting out a time they used it while others guess. After each round, someone else adds a time they saw that strength in the player. Debrief by asking what it was like to hear it. Expect some embarrassment and let players pass on a turn.

fields.label: The strength I picked
The story I acted out
What the group saw in me
How it felt to be seen this way
A strength someone else named that I had overlooked
How I can use a strength this week

title: Small Talk Role-Play Deck
summary: A card deck for practicing openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits in low-stakes role-plays.
goal: Let a client practice small talk skills in a playful, low-pressure setting.
body_md: Make cards with settings like a line at a coffee shop and prompts like ask a follow-up question. Players draw, role-play for a minute and the clinician or group gives one thing that went well. Keep the stakes low and let clients choose their level of challenge. In the debrief ask what they predicted versus what happened.

fields.label: The setting I drew
What I predicted would be hard
What I said to open the conversation
One thing that went well
How anxious I felt, from 0 to 10
