title: Blushing and Shaking Acceptance Practice
summary: A practice for letting visible anxiety signs be present while staying engaged in a conversation.
goal: Help a client stay engaged in social moments with visible anxiety present.
body_md: Explore which visible signs, such as blushing, shaky hands or a trembling voice, the client fears others will notice. Practice letting them be there during a short role-play while the client keeps attention on the other person and their value of connection. Avoid framing the goal as getting rid of the signs. Let your judgment shape the pace.

fields.label: The sign of anxiety I most worry people will see
What I fear people will think
What I do to hide it
What I would like to be doing in the conversation instead
A small way I can let it be there this week
What I notice when I do

title: Social Event Teammate Plan
summary: A pre-event plan where partners agree on signals, breaks and how to debrief afterward.
goal: Help partners support each other through a social event without pressure or rescue.
body_md: The partner who feels social anxiety names what would help, and the other partner names what they can offer without taking over. Agree on a break signal, how long to stay and a kind debrief afterward. Name both partners' parts. Watch for the supporting partner answering for the other; coach them to let the person take their own turns.

fields.label: Partner A: what worries me most about this event
Partner B: what I can offer during the event
Partner A: a signal I can use if I need a break
Partner B: how I will respond to the signal
Partner A: one thing I want to try at the event
Partner B: how we will talk about it afterward

title: Hello Challenge Passport
summary: A child collects stamps for small, brave social steps like saying hello, with the parent coaching from the side.
goal: Help a child take small social steps with a parent cheering from nearby.
body_md: Draw a passport together and list small social steps, such as waving at a neighbor or asking a friend a question. The child chooses one at a time and the parent coaches and cheers without doing it for them. Praise the trying, not the outcome. If a child discloses anything worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: A small social step I want to try
How worried I feel about it, from 0 to 10
What my parent will do to help
What happened when I tried it
How I felt afterward
The next stamp I want to earn

title: Social Avoidance Cost Ledger
summary: A ledger that lists what avoiding social situations has protected and what it has cost.
goal: Help a client weigh the short-term relief of avoidance against its costs.
body_md: Ask the client to list situations they avoid, what the avoidance gives them in the moment and what it has taken from their life. Work toward the client's own words about what they want back. Avoid arguing them out of the relief; the relief is real. Use the ledger to choose a first small step together.

fields.label: A social situation I tend to avoid
What avoiding it gives me right away
What it has cost me over time
What I would like to have back
A small step toward it that feels possible
What I will do if it feels too much

title: Anniversary Ritual Designer
summary: A planning sheet for shaping a meaningful ritual around a birthday, anniversary or holiday after a loss.
goal: Help a client plan a chosen way to mark a hard date with support.
body_md: Use this before a hard date, such as a birthday, to help the client choose how they would like to mark it, who to invite and what to do if feelings rise. Rituals can be tiny. Respect that some clients want nothing, which is also a plan. Check how realistic their plan is and what support they have.

fields.label: The date I want to plan for
What I would like the day to hold
Who I would like to share it with
Something that reminds me of the person or what I lost
What I will do if the feelings are heavy
A person I can reach out to afterward

title: Grief Five Senses Comfort Kit
summary: A self-soothing kit built from the five senses to use during waves of grief.
goal: Help a client build a ready kit of comforts for waves of grief.
body_md: Walk through each sense and have the client pick one thing that soothes without avoiding the grief, such as a scent, a song or a soft blanket. Prepare the kit in session so it is ready before a wave arrives. Reinforce that comfort is not forgetting. If a client mentions thoughts of harming themselves, move to your own safety steps in session.

fields.label: Something I can see that comforts me
Something I can hear that comforts me
Something I can smell that comforts me
Something I can taste that comforts me
Something I can touch that comforts me
Where I will keep my kit so it is easy to find

title: Grief Feelings Color Map
summary: A child colors a body outline with the feelings of grief and talks with a parent about each color.
goal: Help a child name grief feelings through color and share them with a parent.
body_md: Give the child a body outline and invite them to choose colors for feelings like sad, mad, worried and missing. They fill in where they feel each one. The parent listens and says what they notice without fixing. Let the child lead and stop whenever they wish. If a child discloses anything worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: The feelings I have about our loss
The color I picked for each one
Where I feel each one in my body
What I do when the feeling is big
Who I can tell when I feel this way
What my parent will do to help

title: Pain of Love Valuing Practice
summary: A practice linking the pain of loss to what the client valued in the person and in their life.
goal: Help a client hold grief and love together and choose values-based actions.
body_md: Invite the client to notice that grief is bound up with what mattered, then name the values the relationship embodied. Choose one small action that carries a value forward, such as kindness or humor, while the pain is present. Avoid rushing toward meaning. Let them lead and use your own judgment about pace.

fields.label: What I miss most about the person or what I lost
The value that relationship stood for
How the pain and love feel together
One small way I could carry that value forward
What gets in the way
Who could join me in this

title: Hard Day Prediction Check
summary: A sheet comparing predictions about a hard day with what actually happened afterward.
goal: Help a client test predictions about difficult dates and notice what helped.
body_md: Before a hard day, the client writes predictions about how it will go and what they will not be able to handle. Afterward, they record what happened and what helped. Reflect on the gap with curiosity, but never push the idea that grief should feel better. Use it as a conversation starter in your own formulation.

fields.label: The hard day I am preparing for
What I predict will happen
How strongly I believe it, from 0 to 100
What helped me get through it
What actually happened
What I want to remember for next time

title: Weekly State of Us Check-In
summary: A short weekly sheet for one partner to name what felt close, what felt strained, and one small request.
goal: Give a client a steady, low-stakes way to bring relationship concerns into session.
body_md: Have the client fill this in once a week, ideally on the same day, and bring it to session. It gives you a quick read on what the client notices about the relationship over time without turning each week into a verdict. Watch for requests that are really complaints, and help the client reshape them into something specific and doable.

fields.label: One moment this week when I felt close to my partner
One moment when I felt distant or tense
What I was feeling and needing in that tense moment
One small, doable request I could make this week
One thing I will do on my side

title: GIVE Skill Rehearsal Card
summary: A rehearsal card for the GIVE interpersonal skill, gentle, interested, validate, easy manner, in one real conversation.
goal: Help a client practice keeping the relationship intact while raising a hard topic.
body_md: Walk the client through each letter of GIVE, then rehearse the opening minute of a real upcoming conversation in session. Clients often hear gentle as giving in, so name the difference. Have them pick just one or two letters to focus on first, and debrief on how the practice felt in the body as well as in the words.

fields.label: The conversation I want to have, and with whom
How I can be gentle in my first sentence
A question showing I am interested in their side
Something I can validate, even if I disagree
What an easy manner would look like for me

title: Partner Assumption Check-Out Sheet
summary: A thought sheet that separates what a partner did from the story the client adds about why.
goal: Help a client notice assumptions about a partner's motives and test them gently.
body_md: Use this after a recent moment of hurt or irritation. The client separates the observable event from the meaning they assigned, then rates how sure they feel and lists other possible explanations. The aim is a wider view, not proof that the partner meant well. Pair it with a plan to ask the partner directly when it feels safe to do so.

fields.label: What my partner said or did, as a camera would record it
The story I told myself about why
How sure I felt in that story, 0 to 100

title: Soft Startup Rewrite Game
summary: A turn-taking card game where players rewrite harsh complaint openers into gentler, specific ones.
goal: Build fluency with raising a concern without blame, using humor and low stakes.
body_md: Write a dozen harsh openers on cards, such as 'You never help.' Players take turns drawing one and rewriting it as a soft startup: feeling, situation, small request. The group votes on the version that would land best. In the debrief, ask what made the rewrites easier or harder, and let couples try one on a real topic only if they choose to.

fields.label: The harshest opener I drew
My rewrite using a feeling, a situation, and a request
What the group liked about the best rewrite
What was hard about softening it
A real concern I could raise with a soft start this week

title: Family Meeting Speaking Token Craft
summary: A child decorates a talking stick that is passed around at family meetings so everyone gets a turn.
goal: Give a family a concrete cue for taking turns when something needs to be discussed.
body_md: The child decorates a stick or cardboard tube with drawings of what makes a good listener. The parent then explains the rule: only the holder talks, and everyone else listens. Try it in session with a light topic like a weekend plan. Parents should model waiting and reflecting back what they heard, and keep early meetings short and positive.

fields.label: Draw or write what a good listener does
Draw or write what I want my family to know about me
One thing that would make our home feel calmer
One fun topic for our first family meeting
What the parent will do to keep the stick rule fair

title: Pacing Dial for Hard Days
summary: A simple dial sheet that helps a client decide how much to take on today and what to set aside.
goal: Support a client in pacing daily demands and choosing gentler options on hard days.
body_md: Introduce this as a way to keep the client in charge of pace, not a measure of progress. The client rates how today feels, then sorts tasks into do now, do small, and wait. It stays entirely in the present and asks for no account of the past. Revisit it in session so the client can notice that slowing down is a choice and a skill.

What I need to get done today no matter what

title: Window of Tolerance Check-In
summary: A card for noticing whether the body is too revved up, too shut down, or steady, and picking a skill to match.
goal: Help a client name their present-moment state and choose a stabilizing skill.
body_md: Teach the idea of a steady zone with revved-up and shut-down edges, then have the client mark where they are right now. Match each state with a skill the client already knows, such as cold water for revved-up or movement for shut-down. Keep it about the present moment only. Practice in session so the client trusts the card before they use it alone.

title: Anchors in the Present Practice
summary: A dropping-anchor style exercise to feel feet, notice surroundings, and return to the room when old reminders surface.
goal: Give a client a short way to come back to the present without having to push anything away.
body_md: Guide the client through noticing their feet, their breath, and five things in the room, while letting any thoughts or feelings be present without engaging them. Offer eyes open as the default and let the client choose. Do not ask what the reminder was about. Practice in session first, then suggest short rehearsals at calm moments rather than only during hard ones.

fields.label: What I noticed when I pressed my feet into the floor

title: Circle of Trusted Adults Hand Map
summary: A child traces a hand and writes or draws a trusted adult on each finger to name who they could tell.
goal: Help a child identify trusted adults and practice who they would go to if something felt wrong.
body_md: The child traces a hand and draws or names five trusted adults, one per finger, with the parent. Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact, focused on who helps rather than on what might happen. If a child discloses anything, stay calm, believe them, and follow your reporting duties. Parents should keep the map somewhere visible at home.

fields.label: Draw or write one grown-up I trust at home
Draw or write one grown-up I trust at school
Draw or write one grown-up in my family I could tell

What my parent will do when I tell them something

title: Safe Person Evidence Sheet
summary: A sheet for gathering present-day evidence about who in a client's life has shown steady, respectful behavior.
goal: Help a client notice trustworthy behavior in the present when trust feels hard to calibrate.
body_md: Many clients find trust swings between all and nothing. This sheet lists specific behaviors a person has shown over time, such as keeping their word or respecting a no, rather than rating the person as safe or unsafe. Go at the client's pace and never ask for details of past events. Use it to plan small, chosen steps of closeness.

fields.label: A person in my life I am considering
Times they respected a boundary or a no
Times they kept their word
Times I felt uneasy, and what exactly happened
What this suggests about how much to share for now

title: Coping Skill Weather Forecast
summary: A planning sheet that matches coping skills to emotional weather: sunny, cloudy, stormy, and foggy days.
goal: Help a client build a ready plan so the right skill is easy to find in each emotional state.
body_md: Have the client name what each kind of day feels like in the body and mind, then choose one or two skills for each. The metaphor makes the plan easy to remember and lets the client notice that different days call for different tools. Revisit it after a week and swap out anything that did not help, without treating that as failure.

fields.label: What a sunny day feels like for me, and a skill to keep it going
What a cloudy day feels like, and a skill that helps
What a stormy day feels like, and a skill for it
What a foggy day feels like, and a skill for it

title: Thought-Then-Skill Pairing Card
summary: A card pairing common unhelpful thoughts with a coping skill and a more balanced thought to say next.
goal: Link a client's recurring thoughts to a skill so the response is ready before the moment hits.
body_md: Ask the client for two or three thoughts that come up often when stress rises, then pair each with a skill and a balanced alternative. Rehearse reading the card aloud in session. The card works best when the balanced thought sounds like the client, not like a slogan, so edit the wording together until it fits.

fields.label: A thought that shows up when I am stressed

title: Dropping Anchor for Hard Moments
summary: A brief exercise to feel the body, notice surroundings, and choose a next step while a hard feeling is present.
goal: Teach a client a portable way to steady themselves without needing the feeling to go away.
body_md: Lead the client through acknowledging what is showing up, connecting with the body by pushing feet down or stretching, and then noticing the room and engaging in the next task. Stress that the feeling does not have to leave. Have the client practice it twice in session and rate how it felt, then pick two moments in the week to try it.

fields.label: What I notice showing up inside right now
What I did to connect with my body
What I noticed around me in the room
What I want to do next that matters to me

title: TIPP Skill Practice Card
summary: A practice card for the TIPP skills, temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation.
goal: Let a client try each fast-acting body skill in a calm moment so they can reach for it under stress.
body_md: Go through each TIPP skill and let the client try a short version in session when they are calm, with their own consent and comfort. Check for any health concerns with the client before cold water or exercise. Clients often skip practice until they are in distress, so schedule rehearsals and have them note which skill suited them best.

fields.label: How I felt in my body before trying a skill
What happened when I tried cold water or a cold pack
What happened when I tried brisk movement
What happened when I tried slow breathing with a longer exhale
What happened when I tried tensing then relaxing my muscles

title: Coping Skill Mime Game
summary: Players act out a coping skill without words while others guess it, then share when they have used it.
goal: Make coping skills memorable and normal to talk about through movement and laughter.
body_md: Write skills on cards, such as walking, calling a friend, or slow breathing. Players take turns acting one out silently while others guess. After each correct guess, the actor says when a similar skill helped them. Debrief by asking which skills people want to try and keep the mood light so nobody feels singled out.

fields.label: The skill I acted out
A time I used this skill or something like it
A skill someone else acted that I want to try
What got in the way when I tried skills before
One skill I will try this week and when

title: Avoidance Cost Ledger for Feared Situations
summary: A two-column ledger listing what avoiding a feared situation protects and what it costs the client's life.
goal: Help a client see the full picture of what avoidance has given and taken before choosing steps.
body_md: Have the client list what avoidance gives them, usually relief, and what it takes, such as trips, jobs, or time with people. The ledger does not argue against the fear. It opens a conversation about what the client wants. Let them lead, and use it to decide if and when to build a gradual set of steps together.

fields.label: The situation or thing I tend to avoid
What avoiding it gives me in the moment
Places, people, or plans avoiding it has cost me
What I would do if the fear were smaller
How much this cost matters to me, 0 to 10
One small step I might consider

title: Fear-Driven Safety Habits Inventory
summary: A list for noticing small things a client does to feel safe around a feared situation and what each one teaches the mind.
goal: Help a client spot subtle protective habits that keep the fear feeling necessary.
body_md: Safety behaviors can be quiet, like carrying a phone, sitting by the exit, or staying with someone. Ask the client to list theirs and mark which are used most. Explore, without pressure, how each one may keep the fear going. Choose one small behavior to drop in a planned step, and check how the client feels before and after.

fields.label: A situation that makes me afraid
Things I do to feel safer in that situation
Which of these I use almost every time
What I fear would happen if I did not do them
One I might try dropping in a small planned step
What I noticed when I tried it

title: Willing Steps Toward a Feared Situation
summary: A sheet connecting a client's values to one small step toward a feared situation, with room for fear to come along.
goal: Help a client choose a step they are willing to take with fear present, tied to what matters.
body_md: Begin with what the client would want to be doing if fear took up less space, then name one small step toward it. Make willingness the focus: the fear may come along. Let the client set the size of the step and a plan for what they will do with thoughts and sensations that show up. Review without judgment, whether or not the step happened.

fields.label: What matters to me that this fear gets in the way of
A small step toward it that I am willing to take
Thoughts and feelings I expect to come along
What I will do when those show up
When and where I will take the step
What I noticed and learned afterward

title: Fear Thermometer Craft
summary: A child builds a paper thermometer to show how big a fear feels and move the marker as they practice.
goal: Give a child a visual, playful way to show how big a fear feels and to notice it changing.
body_md: The child builds a paper thermometer with a sliding marker and colors each level, with the parent helping. During practice, the child moves the marker to show how big the fear feels, and the parent responds with calm curiosity rather than reassurance. Choose small steps together, and praise brave tries over results. If a child discloses unsafe situations, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw or write what I am afraid of
Where the marker is when I think about it
What my body feels like at that level
A tiny brave step I could try with my grown-up
What my grown-up will do while I try
Where the marker was after I tried

title: Brave Dice Challenge
summary: A dice game where each roll picks a small brave step from a list the client built, with a debrief after each turn.
goal: Make gradual practice feel playful and shared, with the client in charge of the steps.
body_md: Before play, the client and clinician list six steps from easier to harder and number them. On each turn the client rolls and tries the matching step, or passes or swaps it for one of equal size. Take turns doing a small brave act of your own to share the risk. In the debrief, ask what they noticed, not whether it was done right.

fields.label: The six steps on my dice list, easiest to hardest
The step I rolled and how I felt before it
What happened when I tried it
What I learned about the fear
A step I want to add or change
What I want to practice before our next session

title: Compliment Redirect Sheet
summary: A sheet for noticing appearance compliments and comments and practicing replies that move toward other topics.
goal: Help a client respond to appearance talk in ways that fit their values.
body_md: Ask the client to collect times they hear appearance comments or give them. Together, brainstorm replies that are simple and true, such as a thank-you and a topic change. Rehearse a few aloud in session. This does not tell the client what to feel about their body. It gives them more choices about the conversations they join.

fields.label: A recent time someone commented on appearance
How I felt in that moment
How I responded
A reply I would like to have ready next time
A topic I would rather talk about
Who I could practice this reply with

title: Comparison Trigger Thought Record
summary: A thought record for moments of comparing appearance to others, separating the trigger, the thought, and a wider view.
goal: Help a client slow down automatic comparisons and respond with a more balanced thought.
body_md: Use this when the client reports comparing themselves to others online or in person. They record the trigger, the automatic thought, and the emotion, then look at what the comparison leaves out and what they would say to a friend. Do not push for positive thoughts. A believable, balanced one is enough, and the client can rate how much they believe it.

fields.label: Where I was and what set off the comparison
The thought that popped up
How I felt, and how strongly, 0 to 100
What this comparison leaves out
What I would say to a friend who had this thought
How I feel now, 0 to 100

title: Values Beyond Appearance Collage
summary: A collage activity connecting the person a client wants to be to actions that do not depend on how they look.
goal: Help a client put their energy toward values-led living, with appearance as one part of the picture.
body_md: The client gathers images, words, or drawings for what they care about, such as friendship, creativity, or curiosity, and then links each to an action for the coming week. Thoughts about appearance may show up while they work, so practice noticing them and returning to the task. Keep the focus on direction, not on convincing the client to like how they look.

fields.label: Three things that matter most to me
An image or word for each of them
Thoughts about my looks that showed up while I worked
What I did when those thoughts showed up
An action this week that fits one of my values
What I would do if appearance thoughts came along

title: Opposite Action for Hiding Practice
summary: A card walking a client through using opposite action when shame about appearance urges hiding or avoiding.
goal: Help a client act against urges to hide or avoid, in small and chosen ways.
body_md: Teach opposite action: when an emotion urges a behavior that does not fit the situation, act in the opposite way. Have the client list hiding urges, such as skipping events or covering up, and pick one small opposite step. First check whether the emotion fits the facts. Debrief after the step on what shifted, with no pressure for a particular result.

fields.label: The emotion I felt and what set it off
The urge to hide or avoid that came with it
Whether the emotion fits the facts of the situation
A small opposite action I could take
When and where I will do it
What I noticed afterward

title: Superpower Body Badge Craft
summary: A child designs a badge showing something their body can do that they are proud of, such as running, hugging, or laughing.
goal: Help a child build pride in what their body does, in a way that is playful and not about looks.
body_md: The child decorates a badge naming a body superpower, such as strong legs for jumping or hands for building. The parent joins by making a badge too, using a function and not appearance. Talk about how bodies are different and that each one is useful in its own ways. Parents should model this kind of talk at home and avoid commenting on looks, their own included.

fields.label: My body superpower
A time my body helped me do something fun
Draw a picture of my badge
A superpower someone in my family has
How I can thank my body today

title: Month-End Pattern Spotting Sheet
summary: A page for scanning the past month to spot what repeated, what helped and what to change.
goal: Use it to help a client see patterns across weeks instead of single days.
body_md: Give it near the end of a month and ask the client to look through a calendar or phone for patterns. Notice which days were best and what they had in common. Keep answers short. The client picks one pattern to keep and one to change, and the choice is theirs.

fields.label: Days this month that went well and what they had in common
Days that were hard and what they had in common
A pattern I noticed that surprised me
One thing I want to keep doing
One thing I want to change next month

title: Energy Giver and Drainer Sort
summary: A two-column sort of everyday activities and people into those that add energy and those that take it.
goal: Use it to give a client a clearer picture of where their energy goes.
body_md: Have the client list a typical week's activities, then sort them together in session. Some items land in both columns, and that is useful to talk about rather than resolve. Look for one drainer that can be shrunk and one giver that can be protected. Frame it as a map the client builds, not a verdict.

fields.label: Activities that usually leave me with more energy
Activities that usually leave me with less energy
Something that is both a giver and a drainer, and why
One drainer I could shrink or schedule differently
One giver I want to protect this week

title: Conversation Prep Planner
summary: A planning page for a hard conversation: what to say, when to say it and what to do afterward.
goal: Use it to help a client enter a difficult conversation with a plan and a landing spot.
body_md: Use it before a conversation the client is dreading, such as with a boss, relative or friend. Rehearse the opening line aloud in session, since writing it and saying it feel very different. Make sure the client plans for what they will do after, whatever the response. The plan is a draft they can set aside if the moment shifts.

fields.label: Who I need to talk to and what I hope will change
The one thing I most want them to understand
My opening sentence, written the way I would actually say it
A reaction I am bracing for, and what I will do if it happens
How I will take care of myself afterward

title: Two-Minute Start Planner
summary: A planner for shrinking a hard-to-start task into a two-minute first step and choosing when to do it.
goal: Use it to help a client get moving on something they keep putting off.
body_md: Have the client name a task they avoid and shrink it until the first step takes about two minutes. Pick a cue in the day for starting. Clients often resist making it small enough, so keep shrinking. Review how the start felt, not how much got done, and let the client choose whether to keep going once begun.

fields.label: A task I keep putting off
The two-minute version of the first step
The moment in my day when I will start
What my mind might say to stop me
What I will do if I get stuck

title: Gratitude Letter Planner
summary: A planning sheet for writing a letter of thanks to someone who made a difference.
goal: Use it to help a client put real appreciation into words and decide whether to share it.
body_md: Invite the client to choose someone safe and uncomplicated to thank. Spend the session on the specific details, since specifics are what make a letter land. Sending it is optional, and some clients will want to write it and keep it. Notice any complicated feelings that surface and make room for them.

fields.label: Someone who helped me, and what they did
What changed for me because of it
A specific moment I still remember
What I want them to know now
Whether I want to send, read aloud or keep this letter

title: Friend Versus Self Voice Comparison
summary: A two-column page comparing the voice a client uses on themselves with the voice they use on a friend.
goal: Use it to help a client hear the gap between self-talk and the kindness they give others.
body_md: Pick a recent hard moment and have the client write what they said to themselves, then what they would say to a close friend in the same spot. Let the client notice the gap. Ask what it would take to try the friend voice for a week and which sentence feels most believable.

fields.label: A moment I was hard on myself
What I said to myself
What I would say to a friend
What is different between the two
One friend-voice sentence I will try

title: Thought Challenge Role Play Script
summary: A script for a role play where the therapist voices the client's thought and the client argues back.
goal: Use it to help a client practice answering a thought out loud before doing it alone.
body_md: Take the voice of the client's thought, using their own words, and let the client respond. Start gently and raise the intensity only as the client stays steady. Swap roles for a round so the client hears you answer the thought. Afterward ask which responses felt true rather than merely clever.

fields.label: The thought I want to practice answering
The words I would use if this thought said it out loud
My best answer, in my own words
What felt weak or unconvincing in my answer
A stronger answer I could use next time

title: Cognitive Rehearsal Imagery Plan
summary: A plan for picturing a coming situation step by step, including coping well with the hard moments.
goal: Use it to help a client mentally rehearse a challenge before facing it.
body_md: Walk the client through a calm, slow rehearsal of an upcoming event, pausing at each hard point to add a coping step. Keep the image realistic rather than perfect. If imagery stirs up more distress than it helps, stop and ground, then try a written version instead. Practice twice in session before suggesting home use.

fields.label: The situation I want to rehearse
The first few things I will see and hear
The hardest moment, and what I will do in it
Something I will say to myself at that point
How I will wrap up and take care of myself after

title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Worrying Sheet
summary: A two-sided sheet for listing what worrying seems to do for a client and what it costs them.
goal: Use it to open up the beliefs that keep worry going.
body_md: Ask the client to be honest about the ways worry feels useful, such as being prepared or showing care, before listing costs. Taking the advantages seriously matters, since clients often defend worry when it is dismissed. Then ask whether each advantage could be had another way. The client decides what, if anything, to try differently.

fields.label: What worrying seems to do for me
What worrying costs me in time, energy or relationships
A time worry really did help me
A time worry did not help at all
Another way I could get the same benefit

title: Behavioral Prediction Rating Sheet
summary: A before-and-after rating page for comparing what a client expects with what actually happens.
goal: Use it to turn a client's predictions into something they can check.
duration: Five minutes before and after a task
body_md: Have the client rate how likely and how bad they expect something to be before an activity, then rate what happened after. Keep the task small and specific so the comparison is clear. If the prediction was right, that is useful information too. Review the gap together and let the client draw their own conclusions.

fields.label: The activity I am about to try
What I expect will happen
How likely I think it is, from 0 to 100
What actually happened
What I make of the difference between the two

title: Thought Bubble Distance Drawing
summary: A drawing exercise placing a hard thought in bubbles at different distances from the client.
goal: Use it to give a client a visual sense of space between themselves and a thought.
body_md: Have the client draw themselves in the middle of a page and write a hard thought in a bubble pressed against them, then redraw it farther away and smaller. Talk about what changes and what stays. The aim is flexibility, not making the thought go away. Offer it as an experiment.

fields.label: The thought I drew in a bubble
What it was like with the bubble right up against me
What changed when I drew it farther away
What I could do with the thought at that distance
A moment this week I could try this

title: Goal Behind the Goal Ladder
summary: A ladder that climbs from a stated goal to the value underneath it and back to a step available today.
goal: Use it to help a client find a doable value-based step beneath a stalled goal.
body_md: Start with a goal the client has stalled on and ask why it matters, then why that matters, until a value appears. Then climb back down to a small step available today. Take your time. Their own wording is the best guide, and some goals may turn out to be less important than they seemed.

fields.label: A goal I have stalled on
Why it matters to me
Why that matters, one step further
The value underneath it all
A step I can take today toward that value

title: Noticing the Story Sheet
summary: A sheet for naming a familiar life story and noticing how it shapes what a client does.
goal: Use it to help a client see a story as a story while still taking it seriously.
body_md: Invite the client to give a recurring story a short title, like The Story of Not Good Enough, and write what it says. Treat the story with respect since it came from real experience. Then ask what the story asks them to do and not do. The aim is flexibility, not proving the story false.

fields.label: The title I would give this story
What the story tells me about myself
What the story pushes me to do or avoid
What it costs me when I follow it every time
What I could do that fits my values while the story is present

title: Compassionate Observer Walk
summary: A guided walk where a client practices noticing thoughts and feelings from a steady, kind vantage point.
goal: Use it to build a perspective that can hold hard experience without being swept away.
body_md: Walk outside with the client, or move around the room, and invite them to narrate what they notice in the surroundings, then in the body, then in thoughts. Keep your own voice slow and warm. Afterward ask what it was like to be the one noticing. Offer it as an experiment and let the client decide how useful it feels.

fields.label: Something I noticed around me on the walk
Something I noticed in my body
A thought I noticed passing through
What it felt like to watch rather than to be pulled along
A place this week I could practice noticing

title: Workable or Not Daily Check
summary: A daily sticky check of whether what a client did moved them toward or away from what matters.
goal: Use it to build a habit of asking whether an action is working for the person they want to be.
body_md: Give the client one or two actions to watch each day rather than the whole day. Frame answers as information and not as grades. Look together for patterns across the week, especially the moves that feel good short term but lead somewhere they do not want to go. Choose one thing to try differently.

fields.label: Something I did today
Whether it moved me toward or away from what matters
What I was trying to feel or avoid when I did it
What else I could have done that fits what matters
What I want to try tomorrow

title: Radical Acceptance Coping Statements
summary: A page for writing statements a client can say to themselves when fighting what cannot be changed.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare words for moments when they are stuck in the fight with reality.
body_md: Ask the client to name something they cannot change right now and write a few statements in their own voice, such as "It is what it is right now." Practice saying them aloud together. Acceptance is not approval, so make that distinction clear. Revise statements that sound hollow.

fields.label: Something I cannot change right now
How I have been fighting it
A statement that feels true and usable
A body cue that tells me I am fighting reality
What I want to do with my energy instead

title: Name It to Tame It Log
summary: A log for putting precise words on an emotion in the moment and noting what happens to its intensity.
goal: Use it to build the habit of labeling emotions as a way to steady them.
body_md: Show the client how to go beyond mad, sad or fine by using a wider feelings list. Ask them to rate intensity before and after naming it. Not every feeling shifts, and that is fine to report. Review the log and look at which situations bring up which emotions.

fields.label: What was happening
The word that best fits what I felt
How strong it was before naming it, 0 to 10
How strong it was after naming it
What I needed in that moment

title: Self-Validation Journal Page
summary: A journal page for finding what makes sense about a client's own reaction without judging it.
goal: Use it to practice treating one's own feelings as understandable.
body_md: Teach the client to look for why a reaction makes sense given the situation and their history, without agreeing it was the best choice. Model the language aloud. Clients who are used to judging themselves may find this awkward at first, so keep the bar low and the examples small.

fields.label: What happened and how I reacted
How I judged myself for it
Why my reaction makes sense given what I know
What I would say to someone I care about in my place
What I need now

title: Describe Skill Practice Sheet
summary: A practice sheet for describing a situation using only facts, without opinions or guesses.
goal: Use it to separate what happened from what a client made of it.
body_md: Ask the client to describe a recent event as a camera would see it, and then list their interpretations separately. Gently flag opinion words that slip into the facts. The exercise often lowers intensity just by slowing things down. Practice on a neutral event first.

fields.label: The event, described only with facts
The interpretations and opinions I added
How I felt when I read the facts alone
How I felt when I read my interpretations
What I will do with this difference next time

title: One-Mindfully Single-Task Log
summary: A daily log for doing one ordinary activity with full attention and noting what pulls attention away.
goal: Use it to build the skill of doing one thing at a time.
body_md: Pick one routine activity, such as washing dishes or walking, and ask the client to give it complete attention for a few minutes. Normalize a wandering mind, and treat each return as the practice. Ask what pulled their attention and what it was like to come back.

fields.label: The one activity I chose today
What I noticed with my senses
What pulled my attention away
How I brought it back
How I felt afterward

title: Weekly Gratitude Turn-Toward Log
summary: A shared log where each partner notes the small ways the other turned toward them this week.
goal: Use it to help a couple notice and name the connection already happening.
body_md: Both partners keep their own list during the week and read them aloud in session or at home. Look for specific, small moments rather than grand gestures. Watch for a partner who dismisses their own list, and invite them to try again. Each partner owns their own part.

fields.label: Partner A: something my partner did that helped me feel close
Partner B: something my partner did that helped me feel close
Partner A: a small moment I almost missed
Partner B: a small moment I almost missed
Together: one thing we want to do more of next week

title: Shared Calendar Planning Guide
summary: A guide for a couple to plan the coming week together so the load, time and downtime feel fair.
goal: Use it to help partners coordinate time without it becoming an argument.
body_md: Have partners fill in their own commitments first, then talk through the overlaps. Look for how each partner wants to protect time with each other and alone time. Try this in session once before sending it home. Both partners should leave with something they asked for and something they agreed to.

fields.label: Partner A: the commitments I have this week
Partner B: the commitments I have this week
Where our time overlaps or collides
Partner A: time I want protected for myself
Partner B: time I want protected for myself
Time we will set aside for just the two of us

title: Conflict Cool-Down Signal Cards
summary: Two cards each partner can raise to ask for a pause, with an agreed plan for how to return to the topic.
goal: Use it to give a couple a simple, agreed way to pause a heated moment.
body_md: Have the couple agree on the signal, the length of the pause and who restarts the conversation, before they need it. Practice once on a mild topic. Remind them that the pause is for settling the body, not for rehearsing arguments. Each partner commits to coming back.

fields.label: Partner A: the signal I will use and what it means
Partner B: the signal I will use and what it means
How long we will pause before we try again
Partner A: what helps me settle during a pause
Partner B: what helps me settle during a pause
Who will start the conversation again, and how

title: Couple Strengths Mapping Sheet
summary: A joint sheet where partners list what each of them does well and what they do well as a team.
goal: Use it to build on what is already working in a relationship.
body_md: Ask each partner to list the strengths they see in the other before their own. Notice who finds it hard to receive praise. End by naming one team strength they can draw on in a current difficulty. Keep the tone concrete and specific.

fields.label: Partner A: three strengths I see in my partner
Partner B: three strengths I see in my partner
Something we do well together
A time we handled something hard well
How we can use that strength on what we are facing now

title: Date Night Rebuilding Planner
summary: A planner for choosing, scheduling and debriefing a low-pressure time together.
goal: Use it to help partners restart shared time that has slipped away.
body_md: Keep it small and doable. Each partner suggests options, and the couple picks one that both agree to. Debrief together afterward on what was enjoyable and what to change. Avoid using the date to solve problems; the goal is time together.

fields.label: Partner A: three things I would enjoy doing together
Partner B: three things I would enjoy doing together
The one we picked and when it will happen
What we will do about phones and distractions
After: what we liked and what we would change

title: Kindness Tree Craft
summary: A child makes a paper tree and adds a leaf each time they notice or do something kind.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and enjoy kindness over days and weeks.
body_md: The child draws or builds a tree and decorates leaves to stick on over the week. The parent helps by pointing out kind moments, noticing out loud and writing a few words on each leaf for younger children. The tree stays somewhere visible at home. Keep it about noticing, not about winning.

fields.label: A kind thing I did
A kind thing someone did for me
How it felt
Who I want to be kind to next
What I will draw on my next leaf

title: Calm Glitter Jar Activity
summary: A child shakes a jar of glitter and watches it settle as a picture of a mind calming down.
goal: Use it to give a child a visual they can use when feelings are swirling.
body_md: Build the jar together with water, glue and glitter, then shake it and watch it settle while breathing slowly. The parent practices alongside the child and offers it later as an invitation, never as a punishment. Explain that the glitter is like thoughts and feelings that settle when given time.

fields.label: What my glitter looked like when I shook it
What it looked like after it settled
A time I feel shaken up like the glitter
What I can do while I wait to settle
Where we will keep the jar

title: Feelings Faces Paper Plate Craft
summary: A child decorates paper plates as faces showing different feelings and talks about when each one shows up.
goal: Use it to help a child connect feeling words with faces and real situations.
body_md: Make several plates with different feelings, using yarn, markers and stickers. The parent joins in and shares a time they felt one of the feelings. Use the finished plates for guessing games at home. Ask open questions, and let the child decide which feelings to make.

fields.label: The feeling I made first
What the face looks like
A time I felt this feeling
What my body feels like when I feel it
What helps me when I have this feeling

title: Courage Badge Design
summary: A child designs a badge for a brave thing they did and a plan for the next one.
goal: Use it to help a child recognize and celebrate small acts of courage.
body_md: The child draws the badge, names the brave thing and decides where to wear or display it. The parent adds a line about what they saw. Keep the focus on effort and trying, rather than results. A repeat badge for each new brave step works well.

fields.label: The brave thing I did
What the badge looks like
Who saw me do it
How I felt before and after
The next brave thing I might try

title: Gratitude Paper Chain
summary: A child writes or draws something they are thankful for on each link of a paper chain that grows across a week.
goal: Use it to give a child a daily habit of noticing good things.
body_md: Cut strips of colorful paper and add a link each day. The parent adds links of their own and reads the chain aloud at the end of the week. Younger children draw rather than write. Hang the chain where the family can see it grow.

fields.label: Something I am thankful for today
Someone who made me smile
Something I like about my home
Something I did that I liked
What I will add to the chain tomorrow

title: Silent Line-Up Feelings Game
summary: A silent group game where players line up by the strength of a feeling and then compare notes.
goal: Use it to help a group see that people experience the same situation at different intensities.
body_md: Name a situation, like getting a surprise, and have players line up without speaking from least to most intense. Players take turns saying where they stood and why. There are no wrong places. In the debrief ask what surprised them and what they learned about each other.

fields.label: The situation we lined up for
Where I stood and why
Where someone else stood that surprised me
What I learned about how people react differently
A feeling I would like to line up for next time

title: Coping Skill Pictionary
summary: A drawing game where players sketch a coping skill and teammates guess it, followed by talking about when they use it.
goal: Use it to make coping skills memorable and fun to review.
body_md: Divide into two teams and give each a stack of skill cards. A player draws the skill without words or letters while teammates guess. After a correct guess, the drawer shares one time the skill might help. Keep score lightly and end on the debrief.

fields.label: The skill I drew or guessed
A time I could use it
A skill I forgot I had
A skill I would like to try this week
What I will tell someone about today

title: Value Stories Dice Game
summary: Players roll dice to pick a value and tell a short true story about living by it.
goal: Use it to help players connect everyday moments to what matters to them.
body_md: Make a value card for each number on the die. Players roll, read the value and tell a short true story. Others can ask one question. Passing is allowed, and some players will prefer a one-sentence answer. In the debrief ask what values showed up most.

fields.label: The value I rolled
A short story of living it
A time I found it hard to live it
Someone who showed me this value
One small way I will use it this week

title: Perspective Swap Cards
summary: Players draw cards with everyday scenarios and describe them as another person in it might see them.
goal: Use it to practice seeing the same event from more than one angle.
body_md: Write scenarios on cards, like a late text reply or a canceled plan. A player draws one and tells it first from their own view and then from another's. The group adds a third view. Keep the scenarios low stakes, and avoid real conflicts among members.

fields.label: The scenario I drew
How I saw it
How someone else might have seen it
A third view the group added
What I will remember about this

title: Strength Spotting Charades
summary: A charades game where players act out a strength and the group guesses and names a time it showed up.
goal: Use it to help a group name strengths out loud in a light, active way.
body_md: Place strength words on cards, such as patient, curious, brave. A player acts one out, and the group guesses. Then each person names a time they used it. Offer a pass for anyone who is shy. Close by asking what the group noticed.

fields.label: The strength I acted out or guessed
A time I used it
A strength I saw in someone else today
A strength I want to use more
One way I will do that this week

title: Safe Now Orientation Sheet
summary: A page for noticing where the client is, what year it is and what is safe in the room right now.
goal: Use it to give a client a quick, steadying way to orient to the present.
body_md: Practice it in session when the client is calm so it is familiar before it is needed. Keep prompts to the present moment only and never ask for details of past events. If the client becomes more activated, slow down, return to the room together and shorten the exercise.

fields.label: Where I am right now
What today's date is
Three things I can see that tell me I am here
One thing in this room that is safe or comforting
How my body feels right now

title: Helpful Thought Practice for Reminders
summary: A card for pairing a common reminder reaction with a steadier thought that fits the present.
goal: Use it to help a client practice present-focused thoughts when something reminds them of the past.
body_md: Work from the present only: ask what the reminder is and what is true now, without exploring the original event. Write the steadier thought together, in the client's words. Some clients prefer it spoken rather than written. Go at their pace and stop if it increases distress.

fields.label: A reminder that has been catching me off guard
What my mind tells me when it happens
What is true about right now
A steadier thought I can use
Who I can reach out to if it gets hard

title: Trauma-Aware Values Check-In
summary: A gentle values check-in that focuses on what a client wants more of in life now.
goal: Use it to keep the future in view alongside the work of feeling safer.
body_md: Keep the questions about the present and the future, and never about the past. Let the client choose the pace and the domains. Small values-based steps, like a short walk with a friend, count. Check in on how the client is feeling after the exercise.

fields.label: Something that matters to me now
A small way I can show up for it this week
What makes that harder right now
Who can support me with it
How I will know I did it

title: Sleep Settling Skills Plan
summary: A plan of skills a client can use at bedtime and during night waking to settle and feel safer.
goal: Use it to give a client a ready set of steps for hard nights.
body_md: Build the plan in session when the client is rested if possible. Include grounding, paced breathing, a safe-room check and a self-soothe menu. Keep it short enough to remember in the dark. Review what worked after a week and adjust. Nothing on the sheet asks the client to revisit any events.

fields.label: What makes bedtime hard for me
Things in my room I can do to feel safer
A grounding step I can use when I wake up
A self-soothing step I like
Who I can contact in the morning if the night is rough

title: Grounding Category Game
summary: A group game of naming items in a category, such as blue things in the room, to practice shifting attention to the present.
goal: Use it to practice grounding in a light, low-pressure way.
body_md: Pick a simple category and go around the circle, each person naming something in the room. Move to harder categories as comfort grows. Keep the tone playful and let people pass. In the debrief ask what the shift felt like. This is a skill practice and not an exploration of anyone's history.

fields.label: The category we used
Something I named
What I noticed in my body as I played
A place I could use this outside the group
Another category I would like to try

title: Worry Time Sorting Sheet
summary: A sheet for sorting worries into those with a next step and those that can only be noticed.
goal: Use it to help a client decide what to act on and what to let be.
body_md: Ask the client to list a day's worries, then sort them together. Some will have a clear next step, and others are what-ifs that cannot be solved today. Do not talk the client out of any worry. The point is choosing where to put attention.

fields.label: Worries on my mind today
Ones I can do something about
The next small step for one of them
Ones I cannot solve today
What I will do with attention for the rest of the day

title: Avoidance Cost and Benefit Chart
summary: A chart for weighing what avoiding something gives a client in the short run against what it costs in the long run.
goal: Use it to bring both sides of avoidance into view.
body_md: Take the short-term relief seriously, since that is what keeps avoidance going. Then list what it takes from the client's life over time. The chart tends to motivate better when the client writes their own costs. Choose one small step from it together.

fields.label: Something I have been avoiding
What I get from avoiding it
What it costs me over time
What I would be doing if it were not in the way
One small step I could take toward it

title: Anxiety Passenger Seat Practice
summary: A metaphor practice where anxiety rides along while the client drives toward something that matters.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values with anxiety present.
body_md: Ask the client to picture driving to a place that matters with anxiety in the passenger seat. It may comment loudly but does not take the wheel. Draw out what the client would do. Check in afterward on how the image felt and adapt if the metaphor does not fit.

fields.label: Where I want to be heading
What my anxiety says from the passenger seat
What I do when it grabs the wheel
What it looks like to keep driving anyway
One small trip I will take this week

title: Anxiety Surge Skills Card
summary: A wallet card listing a few skills a client can use during a surge of anxiety.
goal: Use it to give a client a short, personal list for hard moments.
body_md: Make the card with the client in session, choosing three to five skills they have already tried and liked. Rehearse reading and using it. Keep wording concrete and short, such as cold water or counting breaths. Review after a week and swap out what did not help.

fields.label: The first skill I will try
The second skill I will try
A skill using my body or senses
A kind thing I will say to myself
Who I can reach out to

title: Partner Anxiety Support Plan
summary: A plan where partners agree on how to help when one is anxious, and what not to do.
goal: Use it to help partners support each other without feeding avoidance.
body_md: Each partner describes what helps and what makes it worse. Watch for reassurance cycles and name them kindly. Agree on how the helping partner can offer support without taking over. The anxious partner has the final say on what they want to try.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me most when I feel anxious
Partner B: what I do now when my partner is anxious
Something that does not help, said kindly
What we will try instead
How we will check in after

title: Pleasant Activity Menu Planner
summary: A menu of small, doable activities sorted by effort level for days with low energy.
goal: Use it to make starting easier by having options ready.
body_md: Build the menu in session with the client, from effortless to bigger. Make sure there are options for the worst days. Ask the client to choose one before leaving. A menu that is too ambitious will be set aside, so keep checking effort ratings.

fields.label: Activities that take almost no effort
Activities that take a little effort
Activities that take a lot of effort
One I will try in the next day
What might get in the way and what I will do

title: Hopeless Thought Check Sheet
summary: A thought record adapted for hopeless thoughts, with a space to look at what is still unknown.
goal: Use it to help a client examine hopeless predictions without dismissing them.
body_md: Take hopeless thoughts seriously and ask about what the client knows and does not know. If the client expresses thoughts of ending their life, stop the worksheet and follow your risk procedures, and remind them they can call or text 988 at any time. Complete this in session rather than as homework.

fields.label: The hopeless thought
What makes it feel true
What I do not know for sure

title: Values in Small Steps Practice
summary: A practice for finding a very small action tied to a value, even when motivation is low.
goal: Use it to help a client take values-based steps without waiting to feel like it.
body_md: Choose a value and ask what the smallest version of acting on it looks like. Make the step so small that failing is unlikely. Motivation often follows action, so frame it as an experiment. Debrief gently if it did not happen and shrink it further.

fields.label: A value I care about
The smallest action I can imagine on it
When and where I will do it
What my mind might say to talk me out of it
What I will say back

title: Mood Weather Drawing Journal
summary: A child draws the weather that matches their mood each day, with a few words about what happened.
goal: Use it to give a child a simple way to show how they feel.
body_md: The child draws sun, clouds or rain each evening, and the parent sits with them and listens without fixing. Bring the journal to session so the clinician can see the pattern. If you see persistent withdrawal or talk of hurting themselves, follow your clinical judgment and let the parent know to call or text 988 in an emergency.

fields.label: The weather of my day today
What happened that matches it
Something that made it a little brighter
Something that made it cloudier
What I would like to happen tomorrow

title: Low-Battery Day Card Game
summary: A card game where players draw low-energy days and offer one doable step for each.
goal: Use it to practice small steps for hard days.
body_md: Write low-energy situations on cards, such as not wanting to leave bed. Players draw one and suggest one small step, and the group adds ideas. Keep ideas realistic and kind. Debrief by asking which steps felt doable and which felt too large.

fields.label: The card I drew
The small step I suggested
A step someone else suggested that I liked
A step that felt too big and how to shrink it
One I will try this week

title: Priority Triage Sheet
summary: A sheet for sorting a pile of tasks into do now, do soon, delegate and drop.
goal: Use it to cut an overwhelming list down to a few next moves.
body_md: Have the client write every task without sorting first. Then sort together, asking what happens if each one waits. Aim for no more than three things in the do-now column. Clients often put everything in the top bucket, so use questions rather than telling them.

fields.label: Everything on my mind to do
What must be done today
What can wait a few days
What someone else could do
What I could drop or let go

title: Distraction Parking Lot Log
summary: A log for jotting down distracting thoughts and urges so a client can return to the task.
goal: Use it to help a client capture distractions without acting on them.
body_md: Teach the client to keep a notepad nearby and write each distracting idea in a word or two, then go back. Review what kinds of ideas show up and when. Many clients are surprised by how often the same ones appear. The idea is capture, not suppression.

fields.label: The task I was working on
The distraction that popped up
What I wrote down
What I did to get back
What I noticed about when distractions come

title: Interest and Values Bridge
summary: A sheet for linking a boring but important task to a value so it gets a little more meaning.
goal: Use it to help a client find purpose in tasks that do not hold attention.
body_md: Choose a task the client keeps putting off and trace it to something they care about. Pair it with something enjoyable such as music. This does not make the task fun, but it can make starting less of a fight. Check in on what worked.

fields.label: A task I keep putting off
Why it matters even though it is dull
What I care about that it connects to
Something that could make it a bit easier
When I will start and for how long

title: Interrupting Urge Delay Card
summary: A card with a short delay routine for the urge to cut in, blurt or jump ahead in conversation.
goal: Use it to build a short gap before a client speaks or acts on a sudden urge.
body_md: Name a typical moment, such as cutting in during a meeting, and make a delay routine with the client: hold the thought, jot a key word, wait for a breath. Rehearse in a role play with a low-stakes topic. Expect it to take practice. Celebrate every use, even when the moment still went sideways, and adjust the wording to fit how the client talks.

fields.label: A moment when I blurt or cut in
What I feel in my body just before
The key word I will jot down instead
How long I will wait before speaking
What I will say when it is my turn

title: Household Management Split Sheet
summary: A sheet for dividing household tasks between partners in a way that fits each person's strengths.
goal: Use it to help a couple share the load without resentment.
body_md: Have each partner list tasks they do and tasks they find hard. Divide by strengths and not by fairness alone. Include a system for reminders that does not depend on one partner nagging. Review in a few weeks and adjust. Keep a tone of problem solving.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I do well
Partner B: tasks I do well
Tasks that are hard for each of us

title: Morning Routine Picture Chart
summary: A child and parent make a picture chart of morning steps the child can follow and check off.
goal: Use it to help a child follow a routine without constant reminders.
body_md: The child draws or picks pictures for each step, and the parent places the chart where the child will see it. The parent practices cheering on progress and avoids nagging. Keep the chart short, and change it when the child masters a step.

fields.label: Steps in my morning
Which step is hardest for me
A picture I picked for each step
What I do when I get stuck
How my parent can help without nagging

title: Urge Wave Tracker
summary: A daily tracker of when urges for substance use rise, how strong they get and how long they last.
goal: Use it to help a client see urges as events that rise and pass.
body_md: Show the client how to rate intensity at a few points across an urge. Many clients are surprised that urges peak and fall. Use patterns to plan ahead for the riskiest times. Record, do not judge, and treat every entry as useful information.

fields.label: When the urge started
What was going on
How strong it got, 0 to 10
What I did

title: Substance Use Triggers Chain
summary: A chain from a trigger through thoughts, feelings and actions, with places to break the chain.
goal: Use it to help a client find points where a different choice is possible.
body_md: Walk through a recent event step by step, without shaming. Note the links where an alternative could have fit. Ask which link feels easiest to change first. Keep the focus on the pattern and what the client wants to do next time.

fields.label: The trigger
The thought that followed
The feeling in my body
What I did

title: Values and Substance Use Honest Check
summary: A conversation sheet for looking at how substance use fits with what matters to the client.
goal: Use it to support a client's own reflection on what they want.
body_md: Ask the client to name what matters and how substance use has affected it, without pushing a direction. The client is the expert on their life. Ambivalence is normal, so make room for both sides. Follow up on whichever step the client decides to try.

fields.label: What matters most to me

How it has gotten in the way
What I want more of

title: Support Without Control Sheet
summary: A sheet where partners talk about how to support someone changing substance use without policing them.
goal: Use it to help partners find a helpful role.
body_md: Each partner shares what they need. The partner using substances says what support feels like and what feels controlling. The supporting partner names their own worries and limits. Agree on one thing each will try. Encourage the supporting partner to have their own support too.

fields.label: Partner A: what support looks like to me
Partner B: what I worry about
What feels controlling or unhelpful
What I need for myself
One thing we will each try this week

title: Say No Scenario Cards
summary: Scenario cards for practicing out loud how to say no when offered substance use.
goal: Use it to build a group's comfort with declining an offer in real time.
body_md: Players draw a scenario, such as an offer at a party, and practice a reply with a partner. Share which phrasing felt natural. Keep scenes light, and let anyone opt out of a scene. In the debrief ask which reply they would actually use and who they could call afterward.

fields.label: The scenario I drew
What I said
What felt natural or awkward
A reply I could use next time
Who I could call afterward

title: Anger Ladder Rating Sheet
summary: A ladder for rating anger from mild to intense and noting what happens at each rung.
goal: Use it to help a client spot anger earlier.
body_md: Have the client label steps on the ladder from annoyed to furious and note body cues and urges at each. Spend time on the lower rungs, where choices are easiest. Ask what they can do at each level. Use it to plan which rung to act on.

What angry looks like

title: Hot Thoughts in Anger Sheet
summary: A thought record for the thoughts that fuel anger, with space for other ways to read the situation.
goal: Use it to help a client find options between trigger and reaction.
body_md: Look at the thought that came right before the anger. Check for mind reading, shoulds and blaming. Offer the question what else could be going on. The client decides which reading fits. This is not about talking them out of anger.

fields.label: What happened

title: Anger and What It Protects Practice
summary: A practice for noticing what a client cares about underneath their anger.
goal: Use it to link anger to values and choose actions that fit.
body_md: Ask what the anger is protecting, such as respect or fairness, and what action would serve that. Make room for the feeling without needing it to disappear. Choose one action that fits what the client wants to stand for.

fields.label: A recent time I felt angry

title: Anger Cool-Down TIPP Plan
summary: A plan that adapts TIPP skills for the moments anger spikes.
goal: Use it to give a client body-based ways to bring intensity down.
body_md: Check with the client that cold water, paced breathing and movement are safe for them before including them. Practice in session when calm. Write a plan in order of steps. Encourage them to use it early on the ladder and not at the top.

fields.label: My early warning sign

The second skill

title: Anger Stop Sign Craft
summary: A child makes a stop sign with steps for what to do when anger shows up.
goal: Use it to give a child a visual reminder to pause.
body_md: The child decorates a stop sign and writes or draws three steps, such as stop, breathe and choose. The parent practices at home by modeling the steps when they feel upset themselves. Praise when the child uses a step, however small.

fields.label: What my body feels like when I am angry

title: Intrusive Thought Normalizing Sheet
summary: A sheet that helps a client see that unwanted thoughts are common and do not define them.
goal: Use it to open the conversation about thoughts that feel shameful or scary.
body_md: Go slowly and let the client share only what they are comfortable with. Normalizing helps when it is done respectfully and in the client's own words. Avoid giving reassurance on the content. Focus on how the client responds to the thought.

fields.label: A type of thought that bothers me

title: Compulsion Substitution Plan
summary: A plan for the steps a client will take as they gradually reduce a compulsion.
goal: Use it to build a graded plan for reducing rituals at the client's pace.
body_md: Plan collaboratively and let the client set the pace. List the ritual, a small change, and what to do when the urge to complete it arrives. Prepare for the surge of anxiety and talk about how it rises and falls. Review after each practice.

fields.label: The ritual I want to change

What I expect to feel

title: Uncertainty Is Part of Life Practice
summary: A practice for acting on values while leaving questions about certainty open.
goal: Use it to help a client make room for not knowing.
body_md: Give examples of everyday uncertainty the client already lives with. Practice saying maybe, maybe not, and acting anyway. Never provide certainty about what the client fears. Link steps to something the client wants in life.

fields.label: A question I keep seeking certainty about

title: Partner Response Plan for Rituals
summary: A plan for how a partner responds when the client asks for reassurance or help with a ritual.
goal: Use it to reduce accommodation while keeping warmth.
body_md: Agree on kind, short responses together, such as I care about you and I think you can handle this. Practice them aloud. The partner learns to say it without anger. The client can say what support feels like. Adjust together as it goes.

fields.label: Partner A: how I usually respond to requests
Partner B: how I would like my partner to respond

title: Worry Wizard Story Craft
summary: A child draws and names a worry character and decides how to talk back to it.
goal: Use it to help a child separate from worries that boss them around.
body_md: The child draws the worry wizard and writes what it says. The parent practices not answering its requests and cheers on the child's responses. Avoid giving reassurance, and use a warm, steady tone instead. Review in session how it went.

title: Doubt Dodgeball Debrief Game

goal: Use it to practice responding to doubts without chasing certainty.
body_md: Players toss a soft ball, say a mild doubt and the catcher responds with maybe and keeps going. Keep doubts low stakes. Afterward discuss how it felt to leave a doubt unanswered. Participants may pass at any time.

title: Panic Wave Rating Sheet
summary: A sheet for rating a panic wave as it rises, peaks and falls.
goal: Use it to show a client that the intensity moves and passes.
body_md: Have the client rate intensity every minute during a wave, either in the moment or from memory. Plot it together on a graph. Many clients are surprised by how short the peak is. Respect that panic feels very real, and avoid dismissing it.

title: Safe-Place Exposure Plan
summary: A plan for gradually returning to places or activities a client has avoided since panic.
goal: Use it to build gradual, client-led steps back into avoided places.
body_md: List places in order from easiest to hardest and choose a first step the client is confident about. Plan what to do if panic arrives, which is to stay and let it pass. Discuss how success is staying, not feeling calm. Review after each step.

title: Making Room for Racing Hearts Practice
summary: A practice for allowing fast heartbeat and other sensations while continuing something that matters.
goal: Use it to help a client carry sensations with them.
body_md: Ask the client to notice sensations with curiosity, give them a name and breathe around them. Try during a brief task. Check with the client about any medical concerns first. Review what changed in their relationship with the sensation.

goal: Use it to give a client choices to try when panic comes.
body_md: Have the client choose options for each sense, such as a cold drink or a calming scent. Test a couple in session. Keep the menu where it can be reached fast. After a week review what helped and what to swap.

title: Panic Pals Feelings Craft
summary: A child makes a small pal toy that helps them breathe slowly when their body feels very scared.
goal: Use it to give a child a friend to breathe with during big body feelings.
body_md: The child decorates a small stuffed animal or paper figure and practices breathing with it on their belly. The parent practices alongside and watches for medical concerns that need a doctor. Keep sessions playful, not tense.

title: Family Rules and Routines Map

goal: Use it to give caregivers a shared picture of how the household works.
body_md: Have the caregiver list the few routines that matter most and the expected steps. Keep it short, since long lists are hard to follow. Use positive wording, such as walk in the house. Review after a few weeks to see what is working.

title: Parent Mind-Reading Check
summary: A sheet for catching guesses about why a child acted a certain way and checking other explanations.
goal: Use it to help a parent slow down and consider other reasons for a child's behavior.
body_md: Ask the parent to recall a tough moment and write what they assumed the child meant. Then brainstorm other explanations, such as tiredness, hunger or a skill not yet learned. Keep it compassionate toward the parent, who is usually tired. The parent decides which explanation fits, and which response to try next time.

title: Parenting by Values Reflection
summary: A reflection on the kind of parent a client wants to be and small actions that fit.
goal: Use it to move from guilt toward chosen action.
body_md: Ask what the parent wants their child to remember about them. Link small, doable actions to that. Allow for imperfect days. Notice self-judgment and ask what it asks of them.

title: Parent Validation Practice

goal: Use it to help a parent connect before correcting.
body_md: Teach a short sequence: name the feeling, show you get it, then hold the limit. Role play with hard examples. Clarify that validating is not agreeing. Practice with a child at low stakes first. Review what changed.

title: Calm Parent Corner Craft

goal: Use it to create a shared, no-punishment space for settling.
body_md: The child picks items such as pillows, drawing supplies and a glitter jar. The parent explains it is a place to calm down and not a punishment, and joins in at times. Practice using it when everyone is calm before it is needed.

title: Sleep Protection Plan for New Parents

goal: Use it to help a new parent protect rest within real limits.
body_md: Map the baby's waking pattern and the sleep stretches available. Look at help from partners or family. Be realistic and kind, since rest may still be broken. Check whether the parent has asked for the help they need.

goal: Use it to ease perfect-parent standards during the first months.
body_md: Look at the should thoughts that weigh on the parent. Ask where each came from and what a friend would say. goal: Use it to help a parent make room for mixed feelings.

goal: Use it to normalize asking for and receiving help.

title: Self-Worth Strengths Inventory

goal: Use it to help a client collect concrete evidence of what they do well.
body_md: Ask for examples and not general statements. If the client lists none, ask what close friends would say. Keep a running copy to add to. Notice the effort of receiving praise and give it room.

title: Inner Critic Courtroom

goal: Use it to help a client weigh a harsh voice.

title: Grief Memory Collection Sheet

goal: Use it to help a client keep the person close in a gentle way.

goal: Use it to look at guilt and what-if thoughts after a death.
body_md: Notice the what-ifs and ask what the client knew then. Hindsight changes the picture. Not every thought should be challenged; some express love. Go gently. The client decides which thoughts to look at.

goal: Use it to hold grief and love together.
body_md: Ask what the person cared about and how the client could honor it. Allow sadness to be present. Avoid hurrying the grief. Pick a small act the client can do this week.
