title: Caffeine and Light Cutoff Log
summary: A one-week log of the last caffeine, the last bright screen and the time sleep actually came.
goal: Use it to show a client which evening inputs are moving their sleep onset.
body_md: Most clients have already heard that coffee and phones hurt sleep and have stopped listening, so do not lecture. Have them record three times a night for a week, last caffeine, last bright screen, and roughly when they fell asleep, plus a one-word note on how the night went. Review the week together and let the pattern make the argument. Energy drinks, pre-workout powders and decaf after dinner are the usual hidden caffeine. If nothing in the log moves sleep onset, that is useful too and points you elsewhere.

fields.label: The time of my last caffeine today, and what it was
The time I put down the last bright screen
Roughly when I fell asleep
How the night went, in a word or two
After a week: what the log shows me about my evenings
One cutoff I am willing to move earlier next week

title: Commute Decompression Routine
summary: A planner for the ride or walk home that marks where the workday ends and the evening begins.
goal: Use it to stop a client carrying the workday through the front door.
body_md: Useful for clients whose partner or kids get the leftover irritation from work, and for remote workers whose commute is a hallway. Help them pick a threshold, a train stop, a parking spot, closing the laptop lid, and attach three small acts to it: one that closes work, one that shifts the body, one that opens the evening. Keep the whole thing under ten minutes or it will not survive a bad day. The usual failure is checking email during the decompression; name that in advance and decide what the phone does.

fields.label: My threshold: the moment the workday is over
One thing I do to close work (a note for tomorrow, a last look at the list)
One thing I do with my body between work and home
One thing that opens the evening for me
What my phone does during this time
After a week: what my family or I noticed at the door

title: Notification Triage Sheet
summary: A sort of every app that is allowed to interrupt a client into keep, batch or silence.
goal: Use it to cut the pulls on a client's attention down to the ones they chose.
body_md: Have the client open their phone's notification settings in session and go app by app; abstract conversations about screen time do nothing, this does. Each app lands in one of three columns: keep as it is, batch to a set check-in time, or silence entirely. Expect resistance around messaging apps and a fear of missing something; ask who actually needs to reach them within the hour and route only those through. Set a date two weeks out to review what was missed, which is almost always nothing.

fields.label: Apps that can interrupt me right now (list them all)
Keep: the ones that truly need to reach me within the hour, and who is behind them
Batch: the ones I will check at set times, and when those times are
Silence: the ones that get nothing
What I am afraid I will miss
Two weeks later: what I actually missed, and what I got back

title: Weak Ties Inventory
summary: An inventory of the familiar faces a lonely client already sees each week, and one small step with each.
goal: Help a client build connection from the acquaintances they already have.
body_md: For the client who says they have no one, the close friend they want feels miles away and the gap is paralyzing. This sheet points at the middle ground: the neighbor, the regular at the gym, the coworker from another team, the parent at pickup. List everyone they recognize on sight, then pick two and plan a step one size bigger than now, a name learned, a question asked, a short exchange extended. Keep the goal pleasant contact, not friendship, and review how the exchanges felt rather than how they went.

fields.label: People I see most weeks and would recognize anywhere
The ones I already say hello to
Two I will take one step further this week
The step, one size bigger than what I do now
How each exchange felt, in the moment and after
What I notice about my week when I count these people in

title: Caregiver Respite Menu
summary: A menu of breaks in three sizes a caregiver can take without the person they care for coming to harm.
goal: Use it to give a caregiver real, pre-arranged breaks instead of a vague instruction to rest.
body_md: Caregivers hear self-care advice as one more task, and the obstacle is rarely motivation; it is that no break has been arranged. Build the menu in three sizes: ten-minute breaks that need no cover, half-day breaks that need someone to step in, and overnight or longer breaks that need real planning. For the two larger sizes, name the specific person or service and what they would need to know. Watch for guilt stated as logistics. Agree on one item from each row to take before you meet again.

fields.label: Ten-minute breaks I can take with no cover at all
Half-day breaks, and who could cover for me
A longer break, and what it would take to arrange it
What the person covering needs to know, written down once
The thought that shows up when I imagine taking the break
The one break from each row I will take before next session

title: Survey Method Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment in which the client asks several people what they would think in a feared situation.
goal: Use it to test a belief about how others judge against what others actually say.
body_md: Pick a belief about other people's reactions, for instance that anyone would think less of someone who cried at work. Write the exact survey question with the client so it is neutral and not leading, and agree on four to six people of varied closeness to ask, in person or by text. Predict the answers before the survey goes out and write them down; the gap between prediction and result is the work. Clients sometimes ask only the people who will agree with them, so build the list together. Debrief on what the answers mean for the belief, not just whether they were nice.

fields.label: The belief I am testing
The exact question I will ask (neutral, not leading)
Who I will ask, and how
My prediction of what each person will say
What each person actually said
How much I believe the original belief now, 0 to 100, and why

title: Five-Part Model Map
summary: A map of one recent situation into thoughts, emotions, body sensations and behavior, with arrows between them.
goal: Use it to show a client how the parts of a hard moment feed each other.
body_md: The classic first-session map, sometimes drawn as a hot cross bun. Take one specific recent moment, not a general problem, and fill the four parts with the client's own words, then draw the arrows: the thought that tightened the chest, the tightness that confirmed the thought, the leaving early that kept the belief alive. Clients tend to put thoughts in the emotion box, so slow down and separate them. The map should end with the client seeing at least one arrow they could interrupt, which sets up every later tool.

fields.label: The situation, in one or two sentences
What went through my mind
What I felt (emotions, one word each)
What I noticed in my body
What I did or stopped doing
The arrows: which part set off which
The one link I could try to change first

title: Hindsight Bias Check
summary: A worksheet that separates what a client knew at the time of a decision from what they know now.
goal: Use it to loosen the I-should-have-known thoughts that fuel self-blame after a bad outcome.
body_md: For regret and self-blame after a decision that turned out badly: the missed warning sign in a relationship, the investment, the medical choice for a parent. Draw a line down the page and on the left list only what the client actually knew and could reasonably have known at the time; on the right, what they learned afterward. Clients smuggle hindsight onto the left side, so challenge each item with when exactly they learned it. Then ask what a careful person with only the left column would have decided. Keep this out of trauma material, which needs pacing first.

fields.label: The decision I keep judging myself for
What I actually knew at the time
What I only learned afterward
What a careful person with only the first list would have done
The I-should-have-known thought, and a fairer version
What I would want to do differently with what I know now

title: Historical Test of a Core Belief
summary: A decade-by-decade review of the evidence for and against a core belief across the client's life.
goal: Use it to show a client that a lifelong belief has always had evidence against it too.
body_md: Best after a downward arrow has surfaced a belief such as I am unlovable or I am a failure. Split the client's life into stretches, early childhood, school years, teens, twenties and so on, and for each ask for evidence that seemed to support the belief and evidence that did not fit it. The against column fills slowly at first; prompt for small, ordinary things, a teacher who liked them, a friend who stayed. Finish by rewriting the belief in light of the whole record. Expect emotion in the early stretches and give it room.

fields.label: The belief I am testing, in my own words
Childhood: what seemed to support it, and what did not fit
School years: what seemed to support it, and what did not fit
Teens and early twenties: what seemed to support it, and what did not fit
The years since: what seemed to support it, and what did not fit
Reading the whole record, a fairer version of the belief
How much I believe the old version now, 0 to 100

title: Overgeneralization Exception Finder
summary: A sheet that catches always-and-never thoughts and hunts for the exceptions that disprove them.
goal: Use it to shrink one bad event back to one bad event.
body_md: Teach the client to listen for always, never, everyone, nothing and every time, then pull one such thought from the week. Ask for a count: how many times, out of how many chances. Then hunt for exceptions, even one, from the last month and the last year. The thought usually survives as a milder, true version, I have been late twice this month, rather than vanishing. Teens take to this quickly when the exceptions are concrete. Pair it with a thought record once the client can spot the words on their own.

fields.label: The always or never thought, exactly as it sounded
What actually happened this time
The count: how often has this really happened, out of how many chances?
Exceptions I can find from the last month
Exceptions I can find from the last year
The milder, true version of the thought

title: Two Scales Metaphor Sheet
summary: A worksheet on the two scales: the anxiety dial the client cannot control and the willingness dial they can.
goal: Use it to move a client from trying to turn down anxiety to turning up willingness.
body_md: Draw two dials from 0 to 10. The first is how much anxiety or discomfort is present; the client has spent years trying to turn it down and it has not worked. The second is willingness, how open they are to having the discomfort while doing what matters, and that dial is in their hands. Walk through a recent situation and rate both. The insight lands when the client sees that with willingness at zero, anxiety is stuck at the top. Watch for the client treating willingness as a trick to lower anxiety; if the point is still to get rid of it, the dial is at zero.

fields.label: A recent moment I tried hard to turn the anxiety down
Where the anxiety dial was, 0 to 10
Where my willingness dial was, 0 to 10, and what that looked like
What I was trying to do or protect in that moment
What turning willingness up one notch would look like next time
What I notice about the anxiety dial when I stop fighting it

title: Pliance Versus Tracking Sort
summary: A sort of the client's rules into the ones kept for approval and the ones kept because they work.
goal: Use it to show a client which of their rules are about pleasing others rather than living well.
body_md: Explain the two kinds of rule-following in plain words: pliance is doing a thing because someone would approve or disapprove, tracking is doing it because of what actually happens when you do. List the rules the client lives by, then sort each by asking what would happen if nobody ever found out. Rules kept purely for approval are the ones that tend to run a life off course. This is not about dropping every rule; some pliance keeps a job. The aim is to notice, then choose on workability. Teens with heavy parental expectations get a lot from it.

fields.label: Rules I follow most days, written as always or never
For each one: if no one would ever know, would I still do it?
The rules I keep mainly for someone's approval
The rules I keep because of what actually happens when I follow them
One approval rule that is costing me, and what it costs
What I would do with that rule if I chose on workability alone

title: Carry the Keys Practice
summary: A pocket practice in which a set of keys stands for the thoughts a client carries while still going where they want.
goal: Use it to show a client they can take a hard thought with them rather than wait for it to leave.
body_md: Hand the client their own keys and ask them to let each key be one thought or feeling they wish would go away before they act. Then ask them to put the keys in a pocket and walk to the door, open it, come back. The keys came too, and the walking still happened. Assign it for the week: before a valued action they have been postponing, touch the keys, name what is on the ring, and go anyway. It is small and physical, which is why it sticks. Avoid turning it into a trick to make the thoughts lighter; the keys weigh what they weigh.

fields.label: The thoughts and feelings on my key ring, one per key
The thing I keep waiting to do until they go away
What happened when I carried the keys to the door
This week: the action I took with the keys in my pocket
What the keys felt like during it, and after
What I would do tomorrow if I never had to wait for the ring to be empty

title: Swamp Crossing Metaphor
summary: A worksheet on the swamp between a client and the mountain they chose, and why wading in is not a detour.
goal: Use it to reframe the discomfort of a valued step as part of the path, not a sign to turn back.
body_md: Tell it simply: the client set out for a mountain that matters to them and found a swamp in the way. They did not choose the swamp, but they can choose to wade through it because of where it leads. Then make it concrete: name the mountain, the swamp, the mud they are already standing in and how far the other bank is. The client who has been trying to go around the swamp for years tends to recognize the detour as the thing that has kept them stuck. Return to the image whenever a valued step gets uncomfortable mid-week.

fields.label: My mountain: what I am heading for, and why it matters
My swamp: the discomfort that sits between me and it
Ways I have tried to go around the swamp, and how long that has taken
What it costs me to keep looking for a dry route
The first step into the swamp I am willing to take this week
A reminder to myself for when the mud is deep

title: Thoughts as Pop-Up Ads Practice
summary: A defusion practice that treats intrusive, repetitive thoughts like ads a client can notice and scroll past.
goal: Use it to give a client a light way to notice a sticky thought without closing the browser.
body_md: Ask the client what their mind's most frequent pop-up says, and have them write it as an ad, with a headline and a call to action: You will embarrass yourself. Click here to cancel. Naming the sales pitch is the defusion. Practice in session with a few recent thoughts, then assign noticing for the week: when the ad appears, read the headline silently, label it an ad, and continue what they were doing. Do not let it tip into mocking the thought, which is just another fight. Teens who live online get this instantly.

fields.label: The pop-up my mind shows most often, written as an ad with a headline
What the ad wants me to do (its call to action)
What usually happens when I click
This week: times I noticed the ad and kept doing what I was doing
What I noticed about the ad when I did not click
Other ads my mind runs, so I recognize them next time

title: Recovering From Invalidation Sheet
summary: A skills sheet for the hours after someone dismissed a client's feelings, with check the facts and self-validation.
goal: Use it to help a client steady themselves after being invalidated without retaliating or collapsing.
body_md: For clients whose worst moments follow being told they are overreacting. Walk through a recent instance: what was said, what they felt, what the feeling made them want to do. Then run the skills in order. Check the facts on what was actually said and meant; self-validate the parts of their reaction that make sense; decide whether the relationship needs a DEAR MAN later or simply a note to self; and pick a distress tolerance skill for the next hour. The common trap is using self-validation to prove the other person wrong, so keep the two separate.

fields.label: What was said or done that felt dismissing
What I felt, and how strongly, 0 to 100
Check the facts: what was actually said, and what else it could have meant
The parts of my reaction that make sense given my history and the situation
What I will do for the next hour to get through it
Whether this needs a conversation later, and the one line I would open with

title: Missing Links Analysis
summary: A short analysis of why a planned behavior, like practicing a skill or doing homework, did not happen.
goal: Use it to find exactly where a plan fell through instead of starting a new one.
body_md: Run it in session the moment a client says they did not do the thing, and keep it curious. Four questions in order: did they know what was expected and when, were they willing to do it, did the thought to do it ever come at the time, and if it did, what got in the way. Stop at the first no and solve that link only; most missed homework fails at the third question, the thought never showed up, which calls for a reminder, not a motivation talk. Clients expect to be scolded, so the matter-of-fact tone is the intervention.

fields.label: What I planned to do, and when
Did I know what was expected? If not, what was unclear?
Was I willing to do it? If not, what got in the way of willingness?
Did the thought to do it come to mind at the time? If not, what would have reminded me?
If the thought came, what stopped me then?
The one link I will fix, and how

title: Loving Kindness Practice Sheet
summary: A mindfulness practice that sends the same few kind wishes to an easy person, oneself, and a hard person.
goal: Use it to build a client's capacity for warmth toward themselves and others, one short practice at a time.
body_md: Choose three or four phrases with the client in their own words: may you be safe, may you be at ease, whatever rings true. The order matters: start with someone easy to wish well, a pet counts, then the client themselves, then a neutral person, and only after some days a person they struggle with. Clients who are harsh on themselves often cannot say the phrases to themselves at first; let them say them to the easy person and notice the difference, and treat that gap as information rather than failure. Keep sessions short and the log honest.

fields.label: My phrases, in my own words
The easy person I begin with
What it was like to say the phrases to them
What it was like to say them to myself
The neutral and the hard person I will add, and when
What I noticed over two weeks, in the practice and outside it

title: Self-Reinforcement Schedule
summary: A plan for rewarding a new behavior right after it happens, so it is more likely to happen again.
goal: Use it to help a client make a wanted behavior stick with immediate, honest reinforcement.
duration: 20 minutes to plan, then one week
body_md: DBT behavior change skills applied to the client's own habit. Pick one behavior they want more of, small enough to happen daily, then choose a reinforcer that is immediate, available and actually pleasant to them, not a reward they think they should like. The timing is the lesson: within minutes, not at the end of the week. Many clients will only list punishments for failing; redirect to what follows success. Check that the reinforcer is not the very thing they are trying to cut back on. Review the week's log for whether the behavior rose.

fields.label: The behavior I want to see more of, small enough to do daily
What usually follows it right now (often nothing)
Something I genuinely enjoy that I can give myself within minutes of doing it
A larger reinforcer for a full week of it
This week's log: each time I did it, and what followed
Did the behavior happen more often? What would I adjust?

title: Asking Intensity Dime Check
summary: A sheet that weighs ten factors to decide how firmly to ask for something or how firmly to say no.
goal: Use it to help a client match the strength of an ask or a refusal to the situation.
body_md: The dime game from interpersonal effectiveness. Before the client asks or refuses, walk the ten factors: their capability and the other person's, timing, whether they have done their homework, authority, the relationship, the long-term goal, give and take, and self-respect. Each factor nudges the intensity up or down. Add them up to land somewhere between hinting and insisting, or between a soft maybe and a firm no. Clients who always ask at a whisper or always at a shout find the middle settings here. Pair it with DEAR MAN once the intensity is chosen.

fields.label: What I want to ask for, or what I want to say no to
Can they give it, and can I handle it? Is this the right time?
Have I done my homework, and do I have the standing to ask?
What does this relationship, and my long-term goal with this person, say about how hard to push?
Have I been giving as well as taking? What does my self-respect say?
My intensity, 1 to 10, and the words I will use at that level

title: Accepting Influence Practice
summary: Each partner finds one recent decision where the other's view was brushed aside and practices letting it move them.
goal: Use it to help a couple notice when one partner's input is not landing and practice yielding.
body_md: From the Gottman work on accepting influence, which is about letting a partner's opinion change what you do, not winning or losing. Ask each partner for a recent small decision, a purchase, a weekend plan, where the other's view got waved off. The partner who waved it off restates the other's view until the other says yes, that is it, then names one way they could let it change the outcome. Keep the examples small; big gridlocked topics belong elsewhere. Watch for the partner who yields on everything, which is a different problem, and name it.

fields.label: Partner A: a recent decision where my view did not seem to count
Partner B: that view in my own words, until Partner A agrees I have it
Partner B: one way I could let it change what we do
Partner B: a recent decision where my view did not seem to count
Partner A: that view in my own words, until Partner B agrees I have it
Partner A: one way I could let it change what we do
Both: how it felt to be taken into account, and what we will watch for this week

title: Holiday Hosting Plan
summary: A planner for a couple hosting family, covering who comes, who does what, and the signal for stepping away.
goal: Use it to get a couple through a hosted holiday as a team rather than a pair of exhausted referees.
body_md: Run it several weeks ahead. Partners first write separately what they want from the day and what they dread, then compare; the dread list is where the useful planning lives. Settle the guest list and the length of stay together, divide the visible and invisible jobs, and agree on a private signal either can use that means I need ten minutes. Decide in advance how each partner will handle their own family's hardest member, so the other is not left to do it. The repeat argument is one partner volunteering the other, so flag it before it happens.

fields.label: Partner A: what I want from the holiday, and what I dread
Partner B: what I want from the holiday, and what I dread
Both: who is coming, and for how long
Both: the jobs, visible and invisible, and who owns each
Partner A: how I will handle the hardest person on my side
Partner B: how I will handle the hardest person on my side
Both: our private signal for needing a break, and what happens when it is given

title: Vacation Expectations Alignment Sheet
summary: Partners write what a good trip looks like to each of them before booking, then design one that fits both.
goal: Use it to head off the vacation fight before the suitcase is open.
body_md: Couples rarely say out loud that one of them wants a packed itinerary and the other wants a chair and a book, and they discover it on day two. Have each partner describe their ideal day of the trip separately, including pace, spending, alone time, and how much phone and work is allowed, then compare. Build the trip from the overlap, and give each partner one protected day or half-day that is theirs. Agree on how money decisions get made on the road. Review after the trip; the debrief is where the next trip gets better.

fields.label: Partner A: my ideal day on this trip, from waking to sleeping
Partner B: my ideal day on this trip, from waking to sleeping
Both: where our ideal days overlap
Both: the one protected day or half-day each of us gets
Both: how we will handle spending, phones and work while away
After the trip: what worked, and what we will change next time

title: Alone Time and Together Time Ledger
summary: A one-week ledger of each partner's solitude and shared time, followed by a negotiation of what each needs.
goal: Use it to turn the you-are-never-around fight into numbers both partners can work with.
body_md: For the couple where one feels smothered and the other feels abandoned. Each partner keeps a rough tally for a week of hours alone, hours together but on separate screens, and hours actually together. Clients are regularly surprised by the parallel screen hours, which both partners had been counting as togetherness or as alone time depending on which one they wanted more of. Then each names the amount of each kind they need, and the couple negotiates a week that comes closer for both. Schedule the alone time too, so it stops being stolen.

fields.label: Partner A: this week's hours alone, side by side on screens, and truly together
Partner B: this week's hours alone, side by side on screens, and truly together
Partner A: how much of each I need in a normal week
Partner B: how much of each I need in a normal week
Both: what the ledger showed us that we did not expect
Both: next week's plan for alone time and together time, written on the calendar

title: Overfunctioning and Underfunctioning Map
summary: Partners map the areas where one does too much and the other has gone quiet, and plan one swap.
goal: Use it to interrupt the pattern where one partner's competence and the other's retreat keep each other going.
body_md: Lay out the life areas, money, kids, housework, social plans, health, extended family, and have each partner mark where they overfunction, where they underfunction, and where it is shared. The overfunctioning partner is usually exhausted and resentful, the underfunctioning one usually feels incompetent and criticized, and each blames the other for the pattern. Keep the frame circular: his stepping back invites her stepping in, which invites his stepping back. Pick one area to swap this month, and coach the overfunctioner on tolerating it being done differently.

fields.label: Partner A: the areas where I do most of it, and where I have gone quiet
Partner B: the areas where I do most of it, and where I have gone quiet
Partner A: what it is like to be on my side of the pattern
Partner B: what it is like to be on my side of the pattern
Both: how each of us keeps the other in place
Both: the one area we will swap this month, and what done differently is allowed to look like

title: Brave Voice Megaphone Craft
summary: A child decorates a paper megaphone and practices saying what they need in a big, clear voice while the parent listens and answers.
goal: Use it to give a quiet child a playful way to ask for help and be heard.
body_md: Roll and tape a sheet of paper into a cone and let the child decorate it. Then run three rounds: the child says a small need through it (a drink, a turn, help with a zipper), then a feeling, then something harder they have been holding back. The parent's job is to stop, turn and answer in words, never to tease about the volume. Children who whisper usually need the parent to kneel and wait rather than prompt. If a child uses the megaphone to disclose harm, follow your reporting duties and tell the child they did the right thing by saying it.

fields.label: What I need help with at home
A feeling I want my grown-up to know about
Something that is hard to say in a quiet voice
What my grown-up did when I said it through the megaphone
Where I will keep my megaphone

title: Two Homes Suitcase Craft
summary: A child whose parents live in two homes decorates a paper suitcase with what travels between them, including feelings.
goal: Help a child name what moves between two homes and what stays steady in both.
body_md: Fold a sheet of card into a suitcase with a handle and let the child draw or glue in three kinds of things: objects that go back and forth, feelings that come along, and things that are the same in both homes (a bedtime story, a pet's photo, a rule). Run it with one parent at a time and brief that parent first: they describe their own home only and never ask what happens at the other one. Watch for a child packing worries about a parent being alone; that is material for the parents, not the child. If a child discloses harm in either home, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Things that travel with me between my homes
A feeling that comes along in the suitcase
Things that are the same in both my homes
Something that is hard about changeover day
Something that would make changeover day easier

title: Doctor Visit Comic Strip
summary: A child draws a four-panel comic of an upcoming medical visit, from the waiting room to the snack afterward, with the parent in it.
goal: Use it to make a shot or checkup predictable for a child who dreads it.
body_md: Fold a page into four panels: arriving, waiting, the part the child dreads, and the walk out. The child draws each one with the parent in it doing a specific job (holding a hand, counting, reading aloud). Ask what the child wants the parent to say during the hard panel and write it in a speech bubble; parents tend to promise it will not hurt, which costs them trust, so coach honest words like a pinch that ends. Reread the comic the night before and bring it along. If the dread is about a particular adult rather than the procedure, ask more and follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Panel one: how we get there and who comes with me
Panel two: what I do in the waiting room
Panel three: the hard part, and what my grown-up says and does
Panel four: what happens right after
A question I want to ask the doctor or nurse

title: Screen-Off Countdown Rocket Craft
summary: A child builds a paper rocket with a five-minute countdown that ends screen time, and the parent flies it instead of announcing.
goal: Use it to end screen time without a fight by making the countdown visible and the child the pilot.
body_md: Make a rocket from a paper tube with five numbered windows the child covers one at a time as the minutes pass, and a launch door the device goes behind. The parent starts the countdown at window one, calls the numbers at the same pace every night and keeps a neutral face at launch; the first nights bring a protest at window two, and the rocket wins only if the parent neither argues nor adds minutes. Praise the landing, not the obedience, and draw what the child flies toward on the landing pad. If what a child says about what they watch raises concern, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What I am watching or playing when the rocket starts
What I do at each window as the countdown goes
Where the screen lands at launch
What I fly toward after the screen is off
How launch went tonight, and what my grown-up said

title: Feelings Orchestra Instrument Craft
summary: A child makes a shaker and a drum from kitchen things and plays each feeling loud or soft while the parent matches the volume.
goal: Use it to give a child a way to show how big a feeling is without words.
body_md: Dry rice in a sealed jar makes a shaker and an upturned pot makes a drum. Ask the child to play a happy sound, a worried sound and a mad sound, then to play the same feeling small and then big. The parent copies the child's volume exactly before offering a softer version, which teaches matching before settling; parents who go straight to shushing find the child plays louder. Use the instruments later in the week when the child cannot find words, the parent asking which instrument and how loud. If what the child plays or says points to harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The instruments I made and what each one is for
How I play happy, worried and mad
What a small worry sounds like and what a big one sounds like
What my grown-up did when I played loud
A time this week I could use my instruments instead of words

title: Beat the Clock Task Sprint
summary: A group or family game that races a five-minute timer on a task everyone has been putting off, then compares the dread with what happened.
goal: Use it to show that starting is the hard part and that most dreaded tasks take less than the dread predicts.
body_md: Rules: each player names one small task they have been avoiding (a drawer, an email), predicts how many minutes it needs and how bad it will feel, then everyone starts on the same whistle with a five-minute timer. Turns: at the buzzer each player reports done, partly done or not started, and anyone unfinished gets another five next round. Nobody scores for finishing; points go to the biggest gap between predicted dread and what happened. Debrief on the first thirty seconds and what each player will set a timer for at home. Keep the tasks small or the game proves the opposite.

fields.label: The task I have been putting off
My prediction: how many minutes it will take and how bad it will feel
What actually happened by the buzzer
What the first thirty seconds were like
A task I will set a five-minute timer for this week

title: Headline Rewrite Game
summary: Teams get a catastrophic headline about an ordinary mishap and race to write the fair version, then read both aloud.
goal: Use it to practice catching exaggeration in a group that enjoys competition more than thought records.
body_md: Rules: the leader reads a headline the anxious or angry mind might write (Teen Forgets Homework, Future Ruined; Friend Takes an Hour to Reply, Friendship Over). Turns: each team has ninety seconds to write the fair headline a careful reporter would run, same facts and no spin, then both are read aloud and the room votes on which is closer to the truth. A point per fair headline and a bonus for the funniest exaggerated one, because naming the trick is the skill. After six rounds, players rewrite a headline their own mind ran this week. Debrief on the trick words that showed up most.

fields.label: The exaggerated headline we were given
Our fair rewrite, same facts, no spin
The trick words that made the first one dramatic
A headline my own mind ran this week
My fair rewrite of it

title: Body Language Guess Game
summary: Players show a feeling using only posture and hands, with faces covered, while the group guesses and then checks.
goal: Use it to sharpen reading of body cues and to show how often a guess about someone is wrong.
body_md: Rules: the player draws a feeling card, holds a sheet of paper in front of their face, and shows the feeling with shoulders, hands and stance alone for ten seconds. Turns: the group writes a guess, then the player reveals the card and says how they showed it. A point for every correct guess, and a point to the player if nobody got it. Debrief on which cues were read well, which feelings looked alike from the neck down (bored and sad), and what that means for reading a friend's mood across a room. For clients sure they can tell what others think; the misses do the arguing.

fields.label: The feeling I showed and how I used my body to show it
A feeling I guessed wrong, and what fooled me
Two feelings that looked alike from the neck down
A time I assumed what someone felt from their body and may have been wrong
What I will check before I trust a guess about someone

title: Role Reversal Argument Replay
summary: Pairs replay a small recent disagreement with roles swapped, while the group watches for the line that could have turned it.
goal: Use it to build perspective-taking by having each person argue the other side out loud.
body_md: Rules: a pair picks a low-stakes disagreement one of them had this week with someone not in the room (whose turn for the dishes, a canceled plan) and tells it in two sentences. Turns: they replay it for one minute with roles swapped, each playing the other person as fairly as they can, no caricatures. The audience raises a hand at any line that could have turned the argument, the pair freezes, and they try that line. Then new pairs. Debrief on what it felt like to speak the other side's case and the line each person wishes they had said. Keep live conflicts between members out of the game.

fields.label: The disagreement we replayed, in two sentences
What it was like to argue the other person's side
The line the audience froze on
What I understand now about the other person's position
A line I will try the next time this comes up

title: Broken Record Request Game
summary: A player makes a clear request and calmly repeats it while the others push back, derail and bargain for one minute.
goal: Use it to practice holding a request steady under pressure without escalating or caving.
body_md: Rules: the player writes a one-sentence request (I need the car back by six) and says it. The others take turns with a tactic each: guilt, a joke, a counteroffer, a sulk. The player may acknowledge the tactic in a few words but must return to the same sentence in the same tone within ten seconds, for one minute. Turns rotate so everyone plays both roles. A point to the player for every return and a point to the group each time the player argues or gives in. Debrief on the hardest tactic and how the request sounded by the end. Watch for rising volume; the skill is the same tone.

fields.label: My one-sentence request
The tactic that was hardest to stay steady against
What I said to acknowledge the pushback before returning to my request
How my voice changed over the minute, if it did
A real request I will hold steady this week

title: Startle Recovery Log
summary: A log of startle moments through the week, how long each took to settle and what helped the body come back down.
goal: Use it to show a client their recovery time is shrinking and which settling moves work for their body.
body_md: Startle is often the thing a client is most ashamed of, so frame the log as tracking recovery rather than jumpiness. Each entry records the trigger (a door, a touch from behind), the first body sign, the settling move used and the minutes until they felt ordinary again. Review it for which moves shorten the recovery and which triggers repeat often enough to plan for. Do not ask what the startle reminded them of; the log stays with the body and the present. If recovery times are stretching, or a startle is followed by hours on edge, slow the pace of other work and return to grounding.

fields.label: What set off the startle (a sound, a touch, a movement)
The first thing I noticed in my body
What I did to settle
About how many minutes until I felt ordinary again
What I noticed over the week about which settling moves work

title: Self-Trust Evidence Diary
summary: A daily evidence diary for the belief that one's judgment can no longer be trusted, recording small decisions that went well enough.
goal: Use it to loosen the belief that the client cannot read people or situations since the trauma.
body_md: Many clients after trauma hold a belief like I missed the signs, so I cannot trust my own judgment, and it stops them acting on their own read of anything. Write the belief in their words and rate it. Each day they record two or three ordinary judgments that turned out fine: crossing a street, reading a friend's tone, choosing which line to join. The diary collects the evidence the belief filters out; it never revisits the original event or argues the client should have known. Re-rate the belief weekly. If entries dry up, walk through one day in detail and show how many judgments it contained.

fields.label: The belief about my judgment, in my words, and how much I believe it from 0 to 100
A judgment I made today that turned out fine
Another one, however small
What the belief would have said about this day before I wrote it down
My rating of the belief after a week of entries

title: Reminder Pop-Up Ads Practice
summary: A defusion practice that handles trauma reminders like pop-up ads: notice, name the ad, decline to click and return to the page.
goal: Use it to give a client a light, repeatable way to let a reminder pass without following it.
body_md: Teach it on a mild reminder in session: when the image, phrase or body cue shows up, the client says there is the pop-up, gives it a short ad title (Danger Sale, Not Your Fault Clearance), and names the page they were on, meaning what they were doing a moment before, then puts attention back there. The humor is optional and some clients find it disrespectful to their history, so offer the plain version too. It never asks what the pop-up contains; the title is enough. If a reminder brings a full flashback rather than a pop-up, this is the wrong tool for that moment and grounding comes first.

fields.label: A mild reminder I could practice on
The ad title I give it
The page I was on: what I was doing when it appeared
What happened when I declined to click and went back to the page
A reminder that is too big for this practice and needs grounding instead

title: DEAR MAN for Safety Requests
summary: A DEAR MAN script for asking the people around a client for the practical things that help them feel safe, like a seat facing the door.
goal: Use it to turn unspoken safety needs into clear, calm requests the client can make.
body_md: Clients often arrange their safety silently (arriving early for the right seat, flinching from a hug) and feel ashamed when it fails. Pick one need and build the script: Describe the situation, Express how it affects them without the history, Assert the request, Reinforce what it gives the other person, stay Mindful of the ask, Appear confident, Negotiate a version that works for both. Rehearse aloud with you as the other person. The request names what helps now, never why; the client decides what to share about the past, and the script works without it. Start with someone likely to say yes.

fields.label: The practical thing that helps me feel safe (a warning before touch, a seat facing the door, a lit path)
Describe: the situation where I need it
Express and Assert: how it affects me and what I am asking for
Reinforce: what saying yes gives the other person
Negotiate: a version I could accept if the full request does not work
Who I will ask first

title: Startle and Approach Agreement
summary: Partners agree on how to enter a room, approach from behind, wake each other and touch unexpectedly so neither is caught off guard.
goal: Use it to stop everyday startles from becoming a nightly source of hurt between partners.
body_md: Partner A names the approaches that startle them (a hand on the shoulder from behind, being woken by touch, someone in a dark doorway) and what would work instead (a word from the door). Partner B says what it is like to be flinched away from and what they need in return, usually to hear it is not personal. Write the agreement as specific moves, not promises to be careful, and add how they will repair when one slips, since both will. Keep it on present-day logistics; Partner A decides what, if anything, to share about why. Revisit in a month and drop any rule no longer needed.

fields.label: Partner A: the approaches that startle me and what would work instead
Partner A: what I need from my partner right after I startle
Partner B: what it is like for me when my partner flinches, and what helps me not take it personally
Partner B: the new moves I will make when entering, waking or touching
Both: how we will repair when one of us slips
Both: the date we will review this agreement

title: Overpreparation Cutback Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment that cuts preparation for a task by a set amount and compares the predicted outcome with what happened.
goal: Use it to test whether hours of rehearsing, rereading or checking are protecting the client or feeding the worry.
body_md: Pick one task the client overprepares for (a meeting, a text) and measure the current preparation in minutes or rereads. Set a cutback the client rates as uncomfortable but doable, often a third less, and write the prediction in detail: what will go wrong and how they will know. Run it, then compare. The trap is a quiet substitute, such as rehearsing in the shower instead of the written notes, so ask about it directly. Most find the outcome the same and the relief earlier; when it goes worse, check whether the task needed the preparation or anxiety read a normal hiccup as the disaster.

fields.label: The task and how much I currently prepare for it (minutes, rereads, checks)
The cutback I will try
My prediction: what will go wrong and how I will know
What I did instead of preparing, and any sneaky substitutes
What actually happened and how it compares with my prediction
What I will try cutting back next

title: Anxious Mind Sportscaster Practice
summary: A defusion practice that casts the anxious mind as a sportscaster calling every possible fumble while the client keeps playing.
goal: Use it to help a client hear the running commentary as commentary and stay in the game.
body_md: Introduce the image in session: the mind in the booth narrating the play before it happens (and here comes the stumble, folks). Have the client do a small task while you call it in that voice, then swap so they do the calling, then both notice the game went on regardless. For homework they catch the commentary in the moment, say there goes the booth, and finish the play. It fails when it becomes a way to argue with the commentator, so check that the client lets the line run rather than correcting it. Pair it with a valued action the commentary usually talks them out of.

fields.label: A situation where my mind starts commentating
Three lines the sportscaster typically calls
What I say to myself when I notice the booth has started
The play I kept making while the commentary ran
Something I would do more of if I let the booth talk without listening

title: Avoidance Chain Analysis Sheet
summary: A chain analysis of one avoided task, from vulnerability and prompting event through thoughts, body and urges to the moment of ducking out.
goal: Use it to find the link in the chain where a skill could have kept the client in the situation.
body_md: Choose one recent avoidance the client regrets (canceling a plan, leaving a store) and walk the chain in order: vulnerability factors that morning, the prompting event, each thought, body sensation and urge, the action, and the short and long consequences. Do not accept I just panicked as a link; there are usually five or six between the cue and the exit. Then mark two places a skill could have gone in (paced breathing at the body link, opposite action at the urge link) and write any repair owed. Clients skip the consequences column where the relief shows, so fill it in together.

fields.label: What made me more vulnerable that day (sleep, caffeine, an earlier stress)
The prompting event: what happened right before
The links: each thought, body feeling and urge in the order they came
What I did and the relief it gave me
What it cost me afterward, including with other people
Two links where a skill could have gone in, and which skill
Any repair I owe

title: Anxiety-Led Decisions Review for Two
summary: Partners list the decisions the household has made around one partner's anxiety, from trips not taken to routes always driven.
goal: Use it to help a couple see how much of their shared life anxiety has quietly been deciding.
body_md: Each partner separately lists decisions anxiety has shaped: the vacation not booked, the restaurant always chosen, the party left early. Compare the lists; the anxious partner usually sees fewer items and the other holds some unsaid resentment. Partner A says what each decision protected them from and what it cost; Partner B says what they went along with and what they miss. Then choose one small decision to make differently next month, with a plan for the anxious moments in it. Keep blame out: anxiety decided, and both let it. Watch for Partner B pushing for the biggest item.

fields.label: Partner A: decisions I can see anxiety has made for us
Partner B: decisions I have gone along with because of my partner's anxiety
Partner A: what those decisions protected me from, and what they cost me
Partner B: what I miss, and what I have not said
Both: the one decision we will make differently this month
Both: our plan for the anxious moments in it

title: Butterfly Belly Drawing and Settle Plan
summary: A child draws the butterflies in their tummy, gives them a size and a color, then draws what helps them land, with the parent as helper.
goal: Use it to help a young child link the anxious feeling in their body to a settling move they can ask for.
body_md: Draw a body outline and ask the child where the fluttery feeling lives and to draw the butterflies there, with how many and what color when the feeling is small and when it is big. Then draw the things that help them land: a slow breath, a hand on the tummy, a hug, a quiet corner. The parent's part is to ask which one the child wants when they say the butterflies are flying, and to do it rather than talk them out of the feeling. If the butterflies belong to a particular person or place and what the child says raises concern, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Where the butterflies live in my body
How many there are and what color when the feeling is small, and when it is big
Things that help my butterflies land
The one I will ask my grown-up for first
What my grown-up will do when I say the butterflies are flying

title: Stuck Record Hopeless Thought Practice
summary: A defusion practice that names a repeating hopeless thought as a stuck record and lets it play while the client does the next small thing.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of thoughts like nothing will change without arguing with them.
body_md: Complete it in session rather than as homework, because naming the hopeless thought can bring the mood with it. Ask for the line that plays most (nothing will ever change), have the client say it aloud a few times and notice the sameness, then label it: there is the stuck record again. The move is not to lift the needle but to let it play while they do one small valued thing in the room, such as opening the blinds. Ask directly whether the record ever says they would be better off dead; if so, stay with that first and plan together. Keep to the record's title, never its lyrics.

fields.label: The line my stuck record plays most
What I notice about it after saying it aloud a few times (how old it is, how samey)
The small thing I did in the room while it played
What the record did while I moved: louder, quieter, the same
If the record ever says I would be better off gone, who I will tell, and that I can call or text 988 any time

title: Reconnecting After Going Quiet GIVE Plan
summary: A GIVE skills plan for the first message or call to someone the client went quiet on during a low stretch.
goal: Use it to make the first reach-out after withdrawal short, warm and survivable.
body_md: Clients who withdrew for weeks often think the friend is angry and that any message must open with a long apology. Pick one person and draft it using GIVE: be Gentle (no self-attack in the message), act Interested (a question about them), Validate (acknowledge the gap without a speech) and use an Easy manner (light, one line of warmth). Keep it under four sentences; write the feared reply beside the one they would send a friend in the same spot. Rehearse sending it in session if the client is willing, since a second draft at home rarely gets sent. Agree what they will do while waiting.

fields.label: The person I went quiet on and roughly how long it has been
Gentle: the message with every self-attack taken out
Interested: the question I will ask about them
Validate: how I will acknowledge the gap in one line
Easy manner: the final message, under four sentences
The reply I fear, and the reply I would send a friend who went quiet on me
What I will do with the first hour of waiting

title: Early Signs Watchlist for Two
summary: Partners write the early signs that a low stretch is starting, what each partner will do when they see them and when to call for help.
goal: Use it to catch a dip early and give the supporting partner a job other than worrying.
body_md: Complete it in session, not as homework, because the last prompts reach into crisis. Partner A, who has the low stretches, lists their own early signs (sleeping through the morning, a stopped group chat). Partner B adds the signs they notice first, which are often different and earlier. Agree the move for each stage: a question that is not how are you, a shared walk, a call to the clinician, and the signs that mean call or text 988 together. Write who says what, since partners who notice often say nothing for fear of making it worse. Keep the list short and revisit it after a stretch passes.

fields.label: Partner A: the early signs I notice in myself when a low stretch is starting
Partner B: the signs I notice first, and roughly how many days before my partner names it
Both: what Partner B will do and say at the first signs, and what Partner A wants them not to say
Both: the signs that mean we contact the clinician
Both: the signs that mean we call or text 988 together, and who makes the call
Both: how Partner A will tell Partner B when the watchlist is wrong

title: Flashlight in the Cave Drawing
summary: A child draws a gray-day cave, then flashlight beams that light up small good things, with the parent holding the flashlight at bedtime.
goal: Use it to give a child with low mood a daily way to find one or two good things without being told to cheer up.
body_md: The child draws a cave with themselves inside on a gray day and colors it how the day feels. Then they draw a flashlight and three beams, and in each beam something small the day had: a warm sandwich, a dog they passed. At bedtime the parent holds a real flashlight, shines it on the drawing and asks what goes in the beams tonight, accepting anything offered and never arguing with an empty beam; an empty beam is information, not failure. If what a child says in the cave points to harm, or to wishing they were not here, ask more, follow your reporting duties and tell the parent that day.

fields.label: My cave on a gray day, and what it looks like inside
Beam one: a small good thing today
Beam two: a person or animal who was good to be near
Beam three: something I did, even tiny
What my grown-up did with the flashlight tonight

title: Dominoes of Doing Game
summary: Players lay dominoes in a line, each one a tiny action that follows naturally from the last, then tip the first and watch momentum work.
goal: Use it to show a group how one small action makes the next one easier on a low-energy day.
body_md: Rules: each player gets six paper dominoes and a start card naming a low-energy state (on the couch at two, still in bed at ten). Turns: each player lays one domino with a tiny action that could follow the last one for their start card (sit up, feet on floor, open the blinds); the group may challenge any step that is too big and send it back to be split. When every line has six, each player reads theirs aloud and tips the first domino. Debrief on which first domino felt possible on a real bad day and what each player's own first domino will be this week. A line that reaches the shower wins.

fields.label: My start card: where I am and what the energy is like
My six dominoes, in order, each one tiny
The step the group sent back to be split, and how I split it
The first domino that feels possible on a real bad day
My own first domino for this week, and when

title: DEAR MAN for Workplace Accommodations
summary: A DEAR MAN script for asking a manager or instructor for a concrete adjustment such as written instructions or a quieter desk.
goal: Help a client ask for one specific adjustment at work or school without apologizing or over-explaining.
body_md: Pick one adjustment that would change the week, not a list. Clients with attention and working memory struggles tend to either never ask or ask in a rush of justification, so keep the Describe and Express lines to a sentence each and put the energy into a precise Assert: what, by when, in what form. Rehearse the Reinforce line until it sounds like a benefit to the other person, since that is usually what lands. Watch for the client disclosing more about their attention than they intended; they can name the need without naming a reason.

fields.label: Describe: the situation in one factual sentence
Express: how it affects my work, in one sentence
Assert: the exact adjustment I am asking for
Reinforce: what this makes easier for them or the team
Mindful: the line I will repeat if the conversation drifts
Appear confident: how I will sit, look and sound
Negotiate: a smaller version I could accept
Who I will ask, where and when

title: Hyperfocus and Feeling Unseen Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for a couple where one partner drops into hours of hyperfocus and the other is left feeling forgotten.
goal: Use it to separate the pull of hyperfocus from the message the other partner reads into it.
body_md: Start with the partner who hyperfocuses describing what the state is like from inside, including how little of the room registers, before the other partner says how the silence lands. The usual trap is the unseen partner hearing hyperfocus as a choice and the focused partner hearing hurt as an attack on the one thing they are good at. Have them agree on a signal that is not a tap on the shoulder, a fixed surfacing time with an alarm the focused partner sets themselves, and one short reconnecting gesture afterward. Keep the plan small enough to survive a bad week.

fields.label: Partner A: what hyperfocus is like from inside, and what I do not notice
Partner A: what I am afraid my partner thinks it means
Partner B: what I tell myself when the hours go by
Partner B: what I actually need when my partner surfaces
Our agreed signal that means come up for air
The alarm or surfacing time Partner A will set
The reconnecting gesture we will use afterward
How we will know the plan is working

title: Homes for My Things Map Craft
summary: A child draws a map of their home and gives each often-lost item a labeled home, then does a nightly round-up with a parent.
goal: Use it to turn lost shoes and backpacks into a drawn system the child built and can follow.
body_md: The child draws the rooms, then picks the five things that go missing most and draws a home for each, with a picture label the parent helps tape to the real spot. The parent's job is the two-minute bedtime round-up, walking the map with the child and praising every item already home rather than hunting for the missing one. Do not let the parent redesign the homes; a child will use a system they chose and ignore a tidier one. If the child mentions being punished harshly for lost things or discloses anything that worries you, follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw your house with the rooms you use most
The five things that get lost the most
Draw a home for each thing and give it a name
What my parent and I say at round-up time
How many things were home tonight

title: Pass the Instruction Game
summary: A group game where each player repeats a multi-step instruction, adds one step, and carries it out, stretching working memory.
goal: Use it to practice holding and acting on several steps while laughing at the drops.
body_md: The first player gives a two-step instruction such as touch the door then clap twice, the next player repeats it, does it, and adds a step, and so on round the circle. Rules: no writing, a player may ask for one repeat, and when the chain breaks the group cheers the length it reached and starts fresh. Play three rounds, then a round where players may use any trick they like, such as chunking, saying it aloud or acting it as they hear it, and notice what changes. Debrief on which tricks helped and where the same trick fits in homework or morning routines.

fields.label: The longest chain our group reached
Where my memory tends to drop a step
A trick that helped me hold more steps
A real situation where I lose steps
The trick I will try there this week

title: Impulse Spending Pause Sheet
summary: A pause sheet filled in before any unplanned purchase, naming the pull, the cost in work hours and what the buy is for.
goal: Use it to put a gap between the urge to buy and the click.
duration: Ten minutes per purchase for two weeks
body_md: Ask the client to fill the sheet before buying anything they did not plan that morning, then wait a set time they choose, usually a day, before deciding. Converting the price into hours of their own work and naming what the purchase is really for, whether novelty, relief from boredom or a reward after a hard day, does most of the work. Clients with impulse struggles often skip the sheet when the pull is strongest, so keep the first version to three lines on their phone and expand later. Review the list in session for patterns in time of day and mood rather than scolding the misses.

fields.label: What I want to buy and what it costs
How many hours of my work that is
What was happening just before the pull
What this purchase is really for
How long I will wait before deciding
What I decided, and how I felt the next day

title: If a Lapse Happens Agreement
summary: Partners agree in advance how a lapse in substance use will be told, heard and handled in the first day.
goal: Use it to replace a feared conversation with a rehearsed one both partners already signed.
body_md: Write this while things are steady, never in the week after a lapse. The partner in recovery names how they will tell their partner and what they will do in the first hour, such as calling a sponsor or a support line. The other partner names what they will say, what they will not do, such as searching bags or going silent for days, and what they need for themselves. Watch for the recovering partner promising it will never happen, which makes the agreement feel like an accusation; frame it as the plan every pilot files. Keep the agreement to one page and review it monthly.

fields.label: Partner A: how I will tell you, and by when
Partner A: what I will do in the first hour
Partner A: what I need from you that day
Partner B: what I will say when I hear it
Partner B: what I will not do
Partner B: who I will lean on for myself
What we will do together the next day
When we will review this agreement

title: Grown-Up Jobs and Kid Jobs Sort
summary: A child draws job cards and sorts them into a grown-up jar and a kid jar, finding that fixing a parent's substance use is not theirs.
goal: Use it to lift the sense of responsibility a child carries for a parent's substance use.
body_md: The child draws or dictates jobs on cards, such as making dinner, keeping everyone safe, helping a grown-up stop using, playing and telling a safe adult how I feel, then sorts them into two decorated jars. The sober caregiver sits beside the child and takes the grown-up cards into their own jar aloud. Talk about the behavior, someone's substance use, never a label for the person. Children often slip a grown-up card into their own jar; ask about it gently rather than correcting. If the child describes being unsupervised or otherwise unsafe, follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw or write jobs that happen in my family
The jobs that belong in the grown-up jar
The jobs that belong in the kid jar
A job I was carrying that is not mine
A grown-up who will take that job now
A kid job I want to do more of

title: HALT Charades
summary: A group game where players act out being hungry, angry, lonely or tired and the others guess the state and name a fix.
goal: Use it to make the HALT check automatic before an urge gets a vote.
body_md: Deal cards marked H, A, L or T, with a few scene cards such as after a long shift or alone on a Friday. On each turn a player acts the state without words while the group guesses; the guesser then names one thing that would meet that need within ten minutes, and the actor says whether it would work for them. Rules: no acting out substance use itself, pass any card you like, and the group claps for the guess and the fix equally. Debrief on which of the four states each person spots last in themselves and what their earliest sign of it is.

fields.label: The HALT state I acted and how it felt to show it
The state I find hardest to spot in myself
My earliest sign of that state
A ten-minute fix the group named that I would really use
When I will run a HALT check this week

title: Holiday and Celebration Plan
summary: A planning sheet for a wedding, holiday or party where substance use is expected, covering arrival, drink in hand, exit and backup.
goal: Use it to walk into a celebration with a plan instead of a hope.
body_md: Fill it in at least a week before the event. Get specific on logistics: how the client arrives and leaves without depending on someone who may stay late, what will be in their hand all evening, the one-line reply to offers, and who they will text at a set time. The urge usually peaks at a predictable moment, such as the toast or the point where the sober guests go home, so have them name that moment and a planned move for it. Watch for clients planning to leave the second it gets hard, which can feel like failure; a planned early exit is a win if it is written here.

fields.label: The event, the date and who will be there
How I will get there and how I will get home
What will be in my hand all evening
What I will say when someone offers
The moment the urge is likely to peak and my move for it
Who I will text, and at what time
My planned exit, and the line I will use
How I will mark getting through it

title: After a Slip Thought Record
summary: A thought record for the hours after a slip, catching the all-or-nothing thoughts that turn one use into a run.
goal: Use it to stop the thought I have blown it from deciding what happens next.
body_md: The dangerous moment is not the slip but the thought right after it: I have blown it, the streak is gone, might as well keep going. Have the client record that thought while the slip is recent, rate how much they believed it, and look for the evidence on both sides, then write a reply that is accurate rather than cheerful, such as one use is one use and the next hour is still open. Rehearse it in session with a past slip first so the card exists before it is needed. Watch for shame turning the record into a confession; keep it on the thought, not the character.

fields.label: What happened, in one factual line
The thought that came right after
How much I believed it, 0 to 100
What that thought wanted me to do next
Evidence the thought is true
Evidence it is not the whole story
A more accurate thought, and how much I believe it
What I will do in the next hour

title: Turtle Shell Calm Craft
summary: A child builds a paper-plate turtle and learns its four steps: stop, go into the shell, breathe three times, come out with a plan.
goal: Use it to give a young child a body routine for the moment anger hits.
body_md: Decorate the plate shell together and write or draw the four steps inside it. Practice the shell pose, arms wrapped and head down, with pretend scenarios before anyone is actually angry, since a child will not learn a new move mid-meltdown. The parent's job is to practice the same pose and say the same four words at home, and to praise going into the shell even when the child comes out still cross. Watch for a parent using the turtle as a punishment corner; it is a pause the child chooses. If the child's play or drawings suggest they are being hurt, follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Decorate your turtle and give it a name
The four turtle steps, in my words
Something that makes my turtle want to hide
What I will think about inside my shell
A plan my turtle could come out with
When my parent and I practiced the turtle

title: Shield Up Teasing Practice Game
summary: A group game where one player holds a drawn shield and practices a cool reply to mild scripted teasing from cards.
goal: Use it to rehearse staying level under provocation in a setting the player controls.
body_md: Write the teasing lines on cards before the game, all mild and generic, such as nice shoes or you always lose, and let the group veto any card. The shield player picks a cool-down move in advance, such as a slow breath, a flat so what, or walking to the agreed exit spot, and holds the shield while two players read cards; the player can say stop at any point and the round ends with applause. Rules: only card lines, never personal material, and every player gets a turn at the shield. Debrief on what the body did first and which move was easiest to use while being watched.

fields.label: The cool-down move I chose before my turn
What my body did first when the teasing started
What was easiest about staying level
What was hardest
A real situation where my shield would help
The move I will use there

title: Driving Anger Log
summary: A log kept after drives, recording the trigger, the thought about the other driver, what the client did and what it risked.
goal: Use it to make road anger visible before it costs a license or worse.
duration: Five minutes after each drive for two weeks
body_md: Driving is where a lot of anger shows up unobserved, so this log is often the first honest record a client has of it. Ask them to fill it right after parking, not while driving, and to include the thought about the other driver, which is nearly always a mind-read about intent. Have them rate what they did on a scale from muttering to tailgating and note any passengers, since children in the back seat change the stakes. Review for the patterns that matter: time pressure, specific routes, hunger, or a particular kind of driver. Keep the honesty safe by never shaming the entries.

fields.label: The drive, the time and who was in the car
What the other driver did
What I told myself about them
What I did, from muttering to something riskier
What it could have cost
What I was already carrying before I got in the car
One thing I will do differently on that route

title: Quiet Voice Behavioral Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment testing the belief that nobody listens unless the client raises their voice.
goal: Use it to test what actually happens when a point is made at normal volume.
body_md: Most clients who shout hold a belief that volume is the only thing that gets results, and arguing with that belief rarely moves it. Instead, write the prediction in their words, such as if I say it quietly they will ignore me, pick two low-stakes situations this week, and have them make the same point at a normal volume while keeping the content firm. Record what the other person did within the next minute, since clients tend to count only immediate compliance. Debrief what the data says, including the cases where the quiet version did not work, and what shouting usually costs afterward.

fields.label: The belief I hold about volume, in my words
My prediction for what happens if I say it quietly
How sure I am, 0 to 100
Situation one: what I said, how I said it, what they did
Situation two: what I said, how I said it, what they did
What the results say about my prediction
What shouting usually costs me afterward
My updated belief, and how sure I am now

title: Grievance Story Defusion Practice
summary: A defusion practice for the replayed story of who wronged the client, holding it as a story the mind tells rather than a verdict.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of a grievance the client keeps retelling.
body_md: Have the client write the grievance exactly as the mind tells it, then give the story a title like a film and notice how often the mind replays it and what it does to their body and their day. The point is not to decide whether the story is true; many grievances are accurate and still cost the client their evenings. Practice prefixing the replay with here comes the story again, and ask what they would be doing with the next hour if the story were on in the background rather than center stage. Watch for the client hearing this as being told to forgive; defusion asks nothing of the other person.

fields.label: The story my mind tells about what they did
The title I would give that story
How many times a day my mind replays it
What the replay does to my body and my evening
The line I will say when it starts: here comes the story again
What I would do with the next hour if the story were only background
Something I want to do this week that the story usually crowds out

title: Deliberate Mistakes Drawing Game
summary: A group drawing game where every player must leave a deliberate error in their picture and sit with the not-just-right feeling.
goal: Use it to practice tolerating imperfection in a playful setting with others doing the same.
body_md: Each round the leader names a simple subject, such as a house or a cat, and a required mistake, such as one window crooked or the name misspelled, and players draw for two minutes. Rules: the mistake stays, no fixing, no starting over, and everyone rates their itch to correct it from 0 to 10 before the drawings go on the wall for the rest of the session. Players who feel no itch can up the stakes by signing the drawing. Debrief on what happened to the itch over twenty minutes and which mistakes were hardest to leave. The drawings can go home as reminders.

fields.label: The mistake I had to leave in my drawing
My itch to fix it right after, 0 to 10
My itch twenty minutes later
The mistake that was hardest to leave
What I noticed other players doing with their itch
A small deliberate mistake I could make at home this week

title: Confession Urge Log
summary: A log of urges to confess intrusive thoughts to others, tracking who, what relief came and how soon the doubt returned.
goal: Use it to show how confessing works as a ritual and shorten the reach of the urge.
duration: Five minutes per urge for two weeks
body_md: The urge to tell a partner or parent about an intrusive thought often hides in plain sight as honesty, so introduce the log by explaining that you are tracking relief-seeking, not the content. Each entry records the thought in a word or two, the person the client wanted to tell, whether they did, the relief it brought and how long before the doubt was back. Within a week the entries usually show a relief curve that shortens each time. Pair it with a delay the client picks, and prepare the family member for hearing less, since they often experience the confessions as closeness.

fields.label: The intrusive thought, in a word or two
Who I wanted to tell, and why them
Did I tell them, and how long did I wait first
How much relief it brought, 0 to 10
How long before the doubt came back
What I did instead when I did not confess
What I am noticing about the pattern

title: Theory A and Theory B Sheet
summary: A two-column sheet weighing the client's danger theory against the alternative that the problem is worry, and what each predicts.
goal: Use it to set up the question the client's next weeks will test.
body_md: Write Theory A in the client's own words, such as I am a danger to my family and must check, and Theory B as its alternative: the problem is that I am worried I am a danger and the checking keeps the worry alive. Then work through what each theory predicts about the evidence so far, what living by each has cost, and what each would ask the client to do tomorrow. Do not argue for Theory B; the sheet only has to make it a fair question. Watch for the client treating the sheet itself as reassurance by re-reading it; it is a map for the experiments, not a verdict.

fields.label: Theory A: what I believe the problem is, in my words
Theory B: the problem is that I worry about this, and what I do about the worry
What Theory A says about the evidence I have so far
What Theory B says about the same evidence
What living by Theory A has cost me
What Theory B would have me do tomorrow
A small thing I could do this week that only makes sense under Theory B

title: Rope Drop for Doubt Arguments
summary: A practice for noticing when the client has picked up the rope against a doubt, reviewing and arguing, and dropping it mid-pull.
goal: Use it to end the mental tug-of-war with doubt without needing to win it.
body_md: Mental reviewing and arguing with a doubt is the rope, and most clients do not notice they have picked it up until an hour has gone. Map the client's own signs of pulling, then practice in session with a live doubt: notice the pull, say rope, open the hands and turn attention to the next thing in the room. The doubt stays on the other end; the client stops pulling. Expect the first drops to feel like negligence, and say so beforehand. Keep the practice short and frequent, and review which doubts the client could drop and which still pull them in.

fields.label: The doubts my mind most often argues with
My signs that I have picked up the rope
What a pull costs me in time and attention
The word I will use when I notice: rope
What I will turn toward in the room when I drop it
What dropping felt like the first few times
