title: Cope Ahead Plan for a Ritual-Free Outing
summary: A DBT cope ahead plan rehearsed in imagery for one outing the client will do without checking, washing or seeking reassurance.
goal: Use it to rehearse an outing without rituals until the plan is familiar before the day.
body_md: Choose one specific outing, such as leaving the house for a movie without going back to check the stove, and walk through it in detail: the moment the urge will hit, the skill the client will use, and what they will do if the urge spikes rather than fades. Rehearse the scene in imagery twice in session, with the client describing the urge rising and the skill working, and once more the night before. The usual slip is a plan that quietly includes a ritual, such as one final look; read it back for those. Afterward review the gap between the predicted and the actual urge.

fields.label: The outing I will do without rituals, and when
The moment I expect the urge to hit

What I will do if the urge spikes instead of fading
The scene as I rehearsed it, including the urge passing

What actually happened compared with the rehearsal

title: Panic at Work Plan Sheet
summary: A plan for a panic attack at work: where to go, what to say, how long to stay and how to return to the desk.
goal: Use it to make a workplace panic attack survivable without a sick day or a story.
body_md: Most clients plan for panic at home and are blindsided by it in a meeting. Map the workplace: the nearest private spot, a plausible one-line exit, the longest they will allow themselves away before returning, and what they will do in those minutes. Returning is the part that matters, since leaving for the day teaches the body that the office is the danger. Decide in advance whether anyone at work knows and what the client wants them to do, which is usually less than the colleague would offer. Rehearse the exit line aloud and keep the sheet in the phone rather than a drawer.

title: Looking Panicked Observer Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment testing the belief that everyone can see a panic attack by asking an observer what they actually noticed.
goal: Use it to test how visible panic really is from the outside.
body_md: Write the prediction precisely: what the client believes shows, such as shaking hands or a red face, and how many people in a room would notice. Then run it two ways. In session, have the client bring on sensations through fast breathing or stair climbing while you note what you can actually see and compare with their inner rating. In the week, a trusted person sits with them through a moderate episode and writes what they saw before the client says anything. The gap between felt and seen is usually wide, and the client needs to hear it from a real observer, not from you.

How many people out of ten I think would notice

What the gap between felt and seen tells me

title: The One Who Notices Panic Practice
summary: A self-as-context practice for finding the part of the client that notices the pounding heart, which the panic does not touch.
goal: Use it to give the client a place to stand inside a panic attack that is not the panic.
body_md: Run it first in session when calm: the client notices a sensation, then notices that they are noticing it, then asks who is doing the noticing. Keep the language plain and avoid anything mystical, since clients in panic want a foothold rather than a philosophy. Once the move is familiar, practice it with mild sensations brought on in session, then add it to the first minute of a real episode as a single question: who is noticing this. Watch for the practice becoming a way to push panic away, which turns it into another control strategy; the noticer watches the panic, it does not switch it off.

fields.label: A sensation I noticed, and the part of me that noticed it
What is true about the noticer that is not true about the sensation

What happened when I tried it during a real wave
What the noticer can see that the panic cannot

title: Half-Smile and Willing Hands for Panic
summary: A DBT skill card pairing a half-smile and open, willing hands with the first signs of a panic surge.
goal: Use it to change the body's posture toward panic from bracing to allowing.
body_md: Teach the two body moves when the client is calm: a slight softening at the corners of the mouth, and hands turned open on the lap or at the sides, shoulders down. Both are small enough to do in a checkout line without being seen. The point is that a clenched jaw and fists tell the body the alarm is correct, and the open posture sends a different message without requiring the client to believe anything. Practice while bringing on mild sensations in session, then use at the first sign of a surge. Clients often feel foolish; name it as a posture for the body, not an expression for others.

fields.label: Where I brace first when panic starts: jaw, fists, shoulders
What the half-smile feels like in my face, in my words
What willing hands look like for me in public
The first sign of a surge where I will use them
What changed in the wave when I tried it
What stayed the same

title: When Panic Cancels Plans Conversation
summary: A conversation for a couple whose outings keep ending in a canceled plan, covering what each feels and a fair way to decide next time.
goal: Use it to stop canceled plans from becoming a quiet resentment in the relationship.
body_md: The partner who panics usually carries guilt and the other carries disappointment they feel they are not allowed to voice, and both go unsaid. Let each speak in turn without the other fixing it. Then build a rule for next time that is neither always go nor always cancel: a graded option such as the partner going alone, going for a shorter time, or a planned early exit, and who makes the call. Watch for the non-panicking partner volunteering to cancel everything, which protects the relationship tonight and shrinks it over months. Agree on one plan this month that will go ahead in some form.

Partner A: what I feel after we cancel
Partner B: what I feel when a plan is canceled, including the parts I usually keep to myself

title: Stop Nagging Behavioral Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment testing a parent's prediction of what happens when the reminders stop for one week.
goal: Use it to test the belief that a child only acts when a parent keeps pushing.
body_md: Pick one task the parent reminds about more than three times a day, usually homework, teeth or getting out the door. Write the exact prediction before the week starts, with a number if possible, and agree on a single calm instruction and a natural consequence in its place. Parents tend to count the misses and not the days it went fine, so have them log every day, not just bad ones. If the child is young or the task is a safety one, choose a different task. Review the prediction against the log and ask what the nagging was really doing for the parent.

title: Loosening the Reins Values Sheet
summary: A values worksheet for the parent of a teen who is pulling for independence the parent is not ready to give.
goal: Use it to separate what the parent values from what fear is steering.
body_md: Ask what the parent wants their teen to be able to do at 25, then work backward to what the teen would need to practice now. Fear usually shows up as a rule, no sleepovers, phone checked nightly, and the sheet asks whether that rule serves the value or the fear. Watch for the parent who answers with the teen's flaws instead of their own values; bring it back to what kind of parent they want to be in this stage. End with one small freedom the parent is willing to give while feeling uneasy, and name the unease as the price of the value.

title: Giving In Pros and Cons Grid
summary: A four-box DBT pros and cons grid a parent fills in before the next meltdown about giving in versus holding a limit.
goal: Use it to help a parent decide in a calm moment how they will act in a hot one.
body_md: Fill the grid in session for one specific limit, like screens off at eight. Pros of giving in are real and parents are often ashamed to write them, so name the quiet house and the ended tantrum yourself. The long-term column is where the work is: ask what the child learns each time the limit moves. Then have the parent pick the boxes they want to read when the urge to give in peaks and copy them onto a card for the fridge. Review after a week which box they read and whether it held.

title: Overruled in Front of the Kids Repair
summary: A repair script for the moment one parent contradicts the other's decision in front of the children.
goal: Use it to give a couple a way to fix an undermining moment without a fight.
body_md: Have each partner describe a recent overruling from their seat only: the one who was contradicted and the one who stepped in. The stepping-in partner usually had a reason, often that the first decision felt harsh, and the sheet gives that reason a private channel so it stops leaking out in front of the kids. Agree on a holding phrase for the moment, something like we will talk about it later, and a time within the day to do so. Role-play once in session; the hard part is the overruled partner accepting a later conversation instead of a public win.

Partner B: a time I stepped in, and what I was worried about

title: Hand on My Arm Waiting Signal Craft
summary: A child decorates a wristband and practices the signal for waiting while a parent finishes a call or a sentence.
goal: Use it to replace interrupting with a signal both parent and child can keep.
body_md: The child decorates a paper wristband the parent wears at home as a reminder. The rule is simple: the child puts a hand on the parent's arm, the parent covers it to say I know you are there, and the parent turns to the child within a minute. Practice it in session with you on a pretend call. The parent's part is the one that fails, they forget to cover the hand or make the child wait too long, so rehearse the parent's side more than the child's. Praise the waiting, not the quiet. If a child discloses harm while you work, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw or decorate the wristband and write our signal on it

title: Unsolicited Advice Defusion Sheet
summary: A defusion worksheet for new parents drowning in conflicting advice from family, forums and strangers.
goal: Use it to help a new parent hold advice lightly and act from their own values.
body_md: Collect the advice the parent has received in the last week, verbatim, including from their own mind, and notice that much of it contradicts the rest. Practice labeling each as a thought the mind is offering, so the parent can hear advice without obeying or arguing with it. The trap is turning this into a debate about which advice is right; keep it on workability, whether following it moves the parent toward the parent they want to be. Finish with one piece of advice they will thank and set down, and one they will keep because it fits their values.

title: Check the Facts on What the Crying Means
summary: A DBT check the facts sheet for the story a new parent tells when the baby will not settle.
goal: Use it to separate a baby's crying from the verdict a parent attaches to it.
body_md: Most new parents have a sentence that plays when the baby cries, usually some version of they do not want me or I am failing. Write it down exactly, then check it: what does the crying prove, what else explains it, does the emotion fit the facts and is it the right size. Expect shame to arrive in the room when the sentence is spoken, and slow down there. If the facts fit, the sheet moves to problem solving, like a feeding or sleep plan with the pediatrician; if they do not, agree on an opposite action for the next cry. Keep it short; this is a sheet for the fourth trimester, not an essay.

title: Baby Safety Thermostat Conversation
summary: A couples conversation for partners whose sense of how careful to be with the baby is set at different levels.
goal: Use it to turn a safety standoff into one shared plan for the things that matter.
body_md: One partner checks the breathing hourly and the other says relax, and each thinks the other is the problem. Have each rate their thermostat and name what set it, often a past loss or a story they read. The exercise sorts worries into three piles: what the pediatrician says is safety, what is preference, and what is the anxious partner's mind asking for reassurance. The relaxed partner's job is to take pile one seriously without eye-rolling; the anxious partner's job is to let pile three be met with support rather than a check. Agree on who does what for the top three items.

Partner B: where mine sits, 1 to 10, and what set it there
Partner A: the three things I most want us to do the same way

Both: which of these are safety, which are preference, which are reassurance
Both: our shared plan for the top three, and who does what

title: Feeding Time Busy Box Craft
summary: An older sibling decorates and fills a box of things to do alone while a parent feeds the new baby.
goal: Use it to give a displaced older child a plan for the moments that sting most.
body_md: Feeding is when the older child most often acts up, because the parent is pinned in a chair. The child decorates a shoebox and picks five quiet things for it; the box only comes out at feeding time so it stays special. The parent's part is to sit the child nearby, narrate what they see them doing, and offer a story or a song during the feed so the child is included rather than sent away. Rotate the contents weekly. For the child who insists on helping with the baby every time, add one real helper job to the box. If a child discloses harm while you work, follow your reporting duties.

title: Me Too Card Draw for New Parents
summary: A group game where new parents draw cards of thoughts other parents have had and say me too, pass, or not me.
goal: Use it to break the silence around the thoughts new parents are ashamed of.
body_md: Prepare thirty cards with thoughts such as I felt nothing when I first held them, I miss my old life, I wished I could hand the baby back. Rules: sit in a circle; each turn one player draws and reads a card aloud, then everyone answers me too, pass, or not me on a count of three. No one explains unless they want to; the reader picks the next. Include a few cards on hopelessness and not wanting to be here, read those yourself, and run the game in session, never as homework, so you can follow up individually. Debrief on what hearing me too was like, and send everyone off with the 988 line.

title: Ask for What You Deserve DEAR MAN
summary: A DEAR MAN script for the ask a client with low self-worth keeps not making, like a raise or a fair share of the work.
goal: Use it to let a client practice asking as if their needs count.
body_md: Start by listing the asks the client has swallowed in the last month; the list itself is data about how they rate their own needs. Pick one with a real chance of a yes and build the DEAR MAN line by line, keeping Describe free of apology and Assert in the form I want, not would it be okay if. Clients with low self-worth tend to flood the Express step with justification; cut it to one sentence. Role-play with you as a mildly unhelpful other and rehearse the Negotiate step, since a partial yes is the usual outcome. Debrief on what asking did to their sense of worth, whatever the answer.

title: Reassurance Loop Exit Plan
summary: A couples plan for the loop where one partner keeps asking if they are good enough and the other keeps answering.
goal: Use it to replace a reassurance habit with support that actually lands.
body_md: Map the loop together: the question, the answer, the relief, and how long the relief lasts, usually minutes. The asking partner names what they are really hoping to hear and notices the answer never quite does it; the answering partner names the fatigue they have not said out loud. Agree on a replacement: the asker says the fear out loud as a fear, and the partner responds with one warm line and physical closeness rather than a case for the asker's worth. Expect the loop to get louder in the first week before it quiets. Watch for the answering partner turning this into a reason to withdraw.

title: Teach a Grown-Up Lesson Plan Craft
summary: A child plans and delivers a short lesson on something they know, with the parent as the student.
goal: Use it to let a child feel capable from the inside, not from praise.
duration: 30 minutes, then one lesson at home
body_md: The child picks something they know and the parent does not, a game, a drawing trick, a dinosaur fact, and draws a three-step lesson plan with pictures. The parent's part is to be a real student: ask questions, try it, get it slightly wrong and let the child correct them. Children with low confidence pick something they think is too small; small and real beats big and vague. Debrief on what it felt like to be the one who knew. Skip the praise afterward; ask what the parent learned instead. If a child discloses harm while you work, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Something I know how to do that my grown-up does not
Draw my lesson in three steps
A question my student might ask
How the lesson went

title: Critic Versus Coach Improv Game
summary: A group improv game where one player voices a situation's inner critic and another answers as a fair coach.
goal: Use it to give a group practice hearing and answering a harsh inner voice out loud.
body_md: Rules: a volunteer describes a small real situation, like sending a text with a typo. The player on their left plays the critic for thirty seconds, the player on their right plays a coach who is fair, specific and not sugary. The volunteer then says which lines they would keep. Then the turn passes left so everyone plays all three parts. The critic role is the fun one and groups get loud, so cap it at thirty seconds and stop any critic that drifts from the situation to the person. Debrief on how familiar the critic sounded, which coach lines were believable, and what made the sugary ones fail.

What made a coach line believable, and what made one fall flat
What it was like to play the critic for someone else

title: Over-Apologizing Log
summary: A week-long log of every sorry a client says, sorted into the ones that were owed and the ones that were reflex.
goal: Use it to show a client how often they apologize for existing and to try a replacement.
body_md: Have the client tally every sorry for a week, with a word on what it was for. Most are for taking up space: asking a question, being passed in a corridor, needing a minute. Sort them into owed, reflex and asking permission, and look at the ratio together. Then pick a replacement that fits, usually thank you for waiting or excuse me, and run week two with the swap. The sorting conversation often surfaces the belief underneath, that their needs are an imposition; note it for later work rather than arguing with it now.

title: Hosting at Home Role Split
summary: A couples plan for having guests over that gives the socially anxious partner real roles instead of hiding in the kitchen.
goal: Use it to make hosting a shared job and a graded step rather than an ordeal.
body_md: Hosting is often the social situation a couple avoids longest, and the anxious partner usually ends up washing dishes all night. Plan one small gathering: the anxious partner chooses two roles that put them in the room, like greeting at the door or running the music, and one escape job they can use once, not all evening. The other partner names what they will do when they see their partner retreating, which is to draw them into a conversation, not to announce it. Agree on the signal for a five-minute break and the review question for afterward. Scale up the guest count over several events.

title: Join the Game Recess Map
summary: A child draws the playground and the steps for joining a game already in progress, then practices with a parent.
goal: Use it to give a shy child a concrete way into play instead of watching from the edge.
body_md: The child draws their playground with where the games happen and where they usually stand. Together, mark a route: watch for a minute, stand close, say one line like can I play or whose team needs one, and if the answer is no, try the next game. The parent's part is to rehearse the line at home as a game, playing both a yes and a kind no so the child has done the no before it happens. Keep the line short; shy children add too many words. Review after a week which spot on the map they tried. If a child discloses harm while you work, follow your reporting duties.

title: Follow-Up Question Ping Pong
summary: A pairs game where players keep a conversation going using only follow-up questions, scoring rallies.
goal: Use it to teach that curiosity, not cleverness, keeps a conversation alive.
body_md: Rules: pairs sit facing each other. One player makes a plain statement about their week. The other must respond with a follow-up question that uses something in the statement; the first answers, and the question goes back. A rally ends when someone changes the subject, asks a closed question, or goes silent for five seconds. Count the rally, then swap partners and take turns starting; play three rounds. Clients who fear they have nothing to say find they only need to listen for the next hook. Debrief on which questions opened things up and whether anxiety faded once a rally got going.

fields.label: My longest rally and who it was with
A follow-up question that opened something up

title: Silence Tolerance Log
summary: A log of pauses in conversation, how long they really lasted, and what the client did to fill them.
goal: Use it to loosen the rule that every silence is the client's fault to fix.
body_md: Clients with social anxiety take a two-second pause as an emergency and rush to fill it, often with the apology or the joke they later replay. Have them log pauses for a week, estimating length before and after, and noting who ended the pause and how. Most find the other person ends half of them and that nothing bad followed. In week two, set a target: let three pauses a day run until the other person fills them. Pair it with dropping the filler safety behavior. Review the log for any pause that actually went badly and what was different about it.

title: Felt Image Versus Seen Image Sheet
summary: A CBT sheet comparing the picture a client has of how they look when anxious with what an observer actually sees.
goal: Use it to loosen the felt image that drives self-focus in social situations.
body_md: Ask the client to describe, as a picture, how they believe they looked in a recent anxious moment: the red face, the shaking hands, the stupid expression. Then build the observer's image from outside evidence: what a friend said, a mirror check done calmly, a recording, or your own observation in session. Clients find the felt image comes from how the anxiety feels inside, not from anything seen, and that the two do not match. Finish with a phrase for the moment that points attention outward. Do not argue the felt image away; let the evidence do it over several uses.

title: Still Here People Map
summary: A child draws the people and pets who are still here to look after them after someone has died.
goal: Use it to steady a child's fear that everyone else will leave too.
body_md: After a death, many children quietly fear the next person will go. The child draws themselves in the middle and the people and pets still here around them, with what each one does for them. The parent's part is to sit beside, add names the child forgets, and answer the question that usually comes, will you die too, honestly and simply: everyone dies one day, I plan to be here a very long time, and here is who looks after you if I ever cannot. Rehearse that answer with the parent first. Hang the map by the child's bed. If a child discloses harm while you work, follow your reporting duties.

title: Unhelpful Condolence Rewrite Game
summary: A group game where players draw the clumsy things people say to the grieving and rewrite them into something that helps.
goal: Use it to let a grief group laugh at the lines that sting and name what they wish people had said.
body_md: Prepare cards with lines such as everything happens for a reason and you are so strong. Rules: on each turn a player draws, reads the line in the voice it was said in, and the group votes with a thumb on how much it stung. The player has thirty seconds to rewrite it into something that would have helped; the group may offer one edit each. Add blank cards for lines members have heard. Keep it light; the laughter is the point, and it tips into tears once or twice, so leave room. Debrief on what the helpful rewrites had in common and what each member can tell their own people they need.

A line someone actually said to me

title: Their Belongings Decision Planner
summary: A planner for deciding what to do with a loved one's belongings in stages, without a deadline from anyone else.
goal: Use it to break an overwhelming task into keeps, gives, waits and asks.
body_md: The closet is often the thing a client cannot face months in, or the thing a relative cleared in a weekend. Sort belongings on paper first into keep, give to someone named, let go, and not yet, and make not yet a legitimate pile with a review date rather than a failure. Ask who is pressuring the timeline and what the client wants to say to them. Plan the first physical session at one drawer, with a person present and a stopping time, since clients tend to start at the hardest item. Watch for the keep pile containing everything; that is fine for now and worth noticing out loud.

fields.label: The belongings I am most dreading dealing with
Who is pressuring me about the timeline, and what I want to say to them
Keep: things I want near me
Give: things that belong with a particular person
Let go: things I can release, and how
Not yet: things I will look at again on this date
My first session: which drawer, who is with me, when I stop

title: Feeling Better Is Betrayal Thought Record
summary: A thought record for the moment a grieving client laughs or enjoys something and the guilt lands.
goal: Use it to examine the belief that moving through grief means leaving the person behind.
body_md: Ask for the last time the client caught themselves enjoying something, and what their mind said next: if I am happy I have forgotten them, grief is how I stay loyal. Run it as a standard record with the usual evidence columns, and add one question of your own: what would they have wanted for you today. Clients often answer that one quickly and then argue with their own answer, which is the work. The balanced thought tends to land somewhere near I can carry them and still have a good afternoon. Set a small enjoyment for the week as the behavioral test.

fields.label: The moment I noticed I was enjoying something
The thought that came next
How much I believed it, and what I felt
Evidence that enjoying things means I have left them behind
Evidence that it does not
What they would have wanted for me that afternoon
A balanced thought, and one enjoyment I will allow this week

title: Avoided Places Willingness Walk
summary: An ACT committed action plan for returning to the places a client has avoided since the loss.
goal: Use it to reclaim the restaurant, the route or the room that grief closed off.
duration: 40 minutes, then one visit a week
body_md: List the places the client has steered around since the death: the diner, the park, their room, the grocery aisle. Ask what each place held and what avoiding it is costing, since these are usually the places the relationship lived. Choose the mildest and plan a visit with willingness: how long they will stay, who comes, and what they will make room for, naming the wave before it arrives. The aim is not to feel fine there but to be there with the grief and the memory both. Debrief each visit on what showed up and what they got back. Leave the hardest place until the client asks for it.

fields.label: Places I have avoided since the loss
What each place held, and what avoiding it costs me
The place I will go first, with whom, and for how long
What I expect to show up there, and what I will make room for
What I got back by going
The next place, when I am ready

title: Accepting Influence Card Game
summary: A card game where one player proposes a plan and the other must take one piece of it on board before raising any objection.
goal: Use it to practice accepting a partner's influence before arguing a point.
body_md: Write ten everyday proposals on cards (where to spend a Saturday, how to handle a late bill, which relative to visit). Partner A draws and proposes. Partner B must name one specific part they will accept and say why before saying anything else; only then may they add a concern. Swap after each card. A partner who answers with a but before the yes loses the turn. Score a point for every accept the proposer feels was genuine. Debrief on which cards made accepting hardest and what it felt like to be received first. In a group, pairs rotate so the game is about the skill, not the couple.

fields.label: Partner A: the proposal I drew and how I put it
Partner B: the part I accepted and why
Partner B: the concern I added afterward
The card where accepting was hardest and what got in the way
What it was like to hear my partner take my idea on board
One place this week I will look for something to accept first

title: Resentment Ledger Clearing Sheet
summary: A ledger of the old grievances a client keeps on account against a partner, with a column for what each one is really owed.
goal: Help a client see which resentments need a conversation, which need a request and which they are ready to close.
body_md: Most clients carry a running tally they never say out loud and then spend it all at once in a fight. Have them list each entry plainly, date it roughly, and write what they wanted at the time. Then sort: entries that still need to be heard, entries that are really a standing request, and entries they are willing to write off now that they have seen them on paper. Watch for a client who writes off everything to seem gracious; the ledger only clears when the live ones get an airing. Pick one entry to raise with the partner and plan the wording.

fields.label: The grievances I still keep on account, each in one line
Roughly when each one started
What I wanted from my partner at the time
Entries that still need to be heard
Entries that are really a request I have never made
Entries I am willing to close now
The one I will raise first and how I will put it

title: Raising a Concern Behavioral Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment that tests a client's prediction of how a partner will react when a concern is raised gently and early.
goal: Use it to test the belief that speaking up will only make things worse.
body_md: Clients who swallow concerns usually hold a confident prediction: he will shut down, she will explode, it will cost me the weekend. Pin the prediction down with a percentage of confidence and the exact behavior they expect. Then design a small, low-stakes concern to raise within the week, with a soft opening the client rehearses in session. Afterward compare what happened with what was predicted. The common wobble is choosing a concern too big for a first test; keep it small. If the partner's reaction was in fact harsh, that is real data, and the next step is a different conversation with you.

fields.label: The concern I usually swallow
What I predict will happen if I raise it, and how sure I am
The small concern I will raise this week and the words I will open with
What actually happened
How my prediction held up
What I will try next time

title: Toward and Away Moves in Conflict Sheet
summary: A sheet for sorting what a client does mid-argument into moves toward the partner they want to be and moves away from it.
goal: Use it to help a client pick a toward move for the next argument instead of a reflexive away move.
body_md: Take a recent argument and list every move the client made, including the silences, the eye roll and the closing line. Sort each into toward (in line with how they want to treat this person) or away (driven by the hook of the moment). Away moves are not wrong, they are just costly, and naming them without blame is the work. Then ask what the hook was each time: a thought, a feeling, an old story. Finish by choosing one toward move small enough to do while still angry. Review next session whether the move happened and what the mind said about it.

fields.label: The argument, in a sentence
The moves I made, in order
Which were toward moves and which were away moves
What hooked me before each away move
The person I want to be in a fight, in a few words
One toward move I can make next time even while angry

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Myths Challenge
summary: A DBT sheet for catching the myths that stop a client from asking or saying no in a relationship and writing the challenge to each.
goal: Use it to loosen the beliefs that block a client from using DEAR MAN with a partner.
body_md: Before teaching a script, find out why the client has not asked already. Offer the usual myths (if I ask, I am needy; saying no means I do not love them; a good partner would just know) and have them rate how true each feels from 0 to 100. Then write a challenge to each in their own words, not yours. Clients often agree a myth is false in the abstract and still live by it, so pair every challenge with one request they will make this week while the myth is still loud. Bring the rating back next session to see whether action moved it.

fields.label: The myths about asking or saying no that I half believe
How true each one feels right now, from 0 to 100
Where each myth came from
My challenge to each myth, in my own words
The request I will make this week even while the myth is loud
How true the myth felt after I made the request

title: Medical Appointment Comfort Plan
summary: A plan a survivor builds for an upcoming medical or dental appointment: what to tell the provider, who comes along, how to pace it.
goal: Use it to make routine health care manageable without anyone needing to know the client's history.
body_md: Appointments that involve touch, being undressed or lying back are a common reason survivors skip care, and the plan works best when it is practical. The client decides how much to say, often just that they need things explained first and to be told before each step. Rehearse the one line they will use and a stop word. Plan who waits outside or sits in, what grounding they will use in the chair, and what they will do for themselves afterward. Keep the focus on the appointment ahead, never on history. If the client wants, write the line on a card they can hand over instead of saying it.

fields.label: The appointment and what part of it I expect to be hard
What I will tell the provider, in one or two lines
The word or signal I will use if I need a pause
Who I will bring and what I want them to do
What I will do with my hands, breath and eyes during the hard part
How I will look after myself afterward
Something I can say to myself if it goes less smoothly than planned

title: Healing Pace Thought Record
summary: A thought record for the self-critical thoughts a survivor has about how far along they should be by now.
goal: Use it to examine thoughts like I should be over this, without going anywhere near what happened.
body_md: The target is the thought about recovery, not the memory, so keep the record on the present: a hard week, a bad night, a reaction that surprised them. Capture the thought (I should be past this, everyone else would be fine by now, I am going backward) and the feeling it brings. Then gather evidence for and against, including what progress has actually looked like and what pace anyone could reasonably expect. The balanced thought should be one they can say out loud. If the record drifts into details of the abuse, bring it back to the thought and end with grounding. Do the first one in session.

fields.label: The moment this week when I judged my own progress
The thought about how far along I should be
The feeling that came with it, and how strong
Evidence the thought is accurate
Evidence it is not the whole picture, including progress I tend to discount
A fairer thought about my pace that I can say out loud
How I feel now

title: Willing to Receive Support Practice
summary: An ACT practice for noticing the mind's objections to accepting help from safe people and making a small willing move anyway.
goal: Use it to help a survivor let support in from the people already offering it.
body_md: Many survivors have a safe person or two and still cannot take what is offered: a ride, a text, a hand on the shoulder. Have the client name the offers they turn down and the thoughts that arrive with each (they will think I am weak, I will owe them, it will not help). Treat those thoughts as passengers, not instructions. Then choose one offer small enough to accept this week with the thoughts still present, and decide what willing looks like in the body. Review how the support landed, not whether the thoughts went away. Keep the exercise in the present tense and on present relationships.

fields.label: Support that safe people offer me and I usually decline
The thoughts that show up when someone offers
What declining costs me over a month
The one offer I am willing to accept this week
What willing will look like in my body and my words when I accept
How it actually landed

title: Willing Hands After a Startle Card
summary: A DBT card for using willing hands and a half-smile to settle the body after being startled or touched without warning.
goal: Use it to give a survivor a thirty-second skill for the moments after a jump.
body_md: Being startled is ordinary and survivors often follow it with a second wave of shame about reacting. The card separates the two. Teach willing hands (palms open, fingers unclenched, shoulders dropped) and a half-smile, then practice both in session after a mild, agreed cue such as a knock. The client writes the physical steps in their own order and one factual sentence for afterward (that was a startle, it is over). Pair it with naming three things in the room if they need more. Keep it brief and bodily; this is not the place to explore what the startle connected to.

fields.label: What a startle feels like in my body in the first seconds
The steps of willing hands, in the order that works for me
What my face does for a half-smile
The factual sentence I will say to myself afterward
Three things in the room I can name if I need more
Where I will keep this card

title: Where the Partner's Feelings Go Sheet
summary: A sheet that gives a survivor's partner a place for their own anger and helplessness so the survivor is not left managing both.
goal: Use it to keep the partner's reactions from landing on the survivor.
body_md: Partners of survivors often feel rage at the person responsible, helplessness, or guilt about their own needs, and without a plan those feelings get expressed at the survivor or hidden in a way the survivor can read anyway. Partner B names each feeling and chooses where it goes: a friend, their own counseling, a journal, a walk. Partner A says what they can hear and what they cannot. Agree on the signal Partner B uses when they are flooded so they can step away without it reading as rejection. Nobody discusses what happened; the sheet is about the two of them now.

fields.label: Partner B: the feelings I have about what my partner went through
Partner B: where each one can go that is not my partner
Partner A: what I can hear from my partner, and what I cannot right now
Partner B: the signal I will use when I need to step away for a while
Partner A: what I would like that signal to mean, and what it does not mean
Both: how we will check in on this in a month

title: Skill or Luck Attribution Check
summary: A sheet for reviewing a hard moment that passed and testing whether the client credits the skill they used or writes it off as luck.
goal: Use it to build the belief that coping skills work by crediting them when they do.
body_md: Clients will use a skill, feel better, and then explain the relief by luck, timing or someone else showing up. That leaves the skill unlearned. After any moment that passed, walk through what they did, what changed and when, and have them write the explanation they reached for first. Then ask what evidence points to the skill itself. Rate how much credit they give the skill before and after. Be honest when time or luck did help; the aim is accurate credit, not cheerleading. Over a few weeks the sheet becomes a record of what has actually worked.

fields.label: The hard moment that passed
The skill or skills I used, and when
What changed and roughly when
The explanation I reached for first
Evidence the skill itself made a difference
How much credit I gave the skill before this sheet, and how much now
What this tells me about using it next time

title: Creative Hopelessness Coping Review
summary: An ACT review of every strategy a client has used to get rid of a feeling, with what each cost and whether the feeling left.
goal: Use it to open the question of whether the client's coping is aimed at a fight that cannot be won.
body_md: Run this before building a new skills menu, not after. List everything the client has tried to make the feeling go away, from distraction to planning to avoidance to substances, without judging any of it. For each, note what it cost and whether the feeling is gone for good. The point lands when the client sees the pattern themselves, so resist summarizing it for them. Stay with the discomfort of the list rather than rushing to willingness. Close by asking what they would be doing with the time and energy if the fight were not the job, and let that sit until next session.

fields.label: Everything I have tried to make this feeling go away
What each one cost me in time, money, energy or relationships
Which ones made the feeling leave for good
What I notice looking at the whole list
What I would be doing with the energy if getting rid of the feeling were not the job
What I am willing to try differently

title: Wise Mind Skill Pick Card
summary: A DBT card for choosing a skill in a hard moment by hearing what emotion mind, reasonable mind and wise mind each pick.
goal: Use it to stop a client reaching for the same skill every time regardless of the moment.
body_md: The card has three columns and the client fills all three before acting. Emotion mind wants the fastest relief, reasonable mind wants the sensible option they will not do, and wise mind usually picks something in between. Practice with a recent moment so the client sees how different the three picks are. Clients who always use the same skill tend to be running on one mind only, which the card makes visible. Keep the skills on the card to ones they have already practiced; this is for choosing, not learning. Review which pick they followed and how it went.

fields.label: The hard moment I am in or just had
What emotion mind wants to do right now
What reasonable mind says I should do
What wise mind picks, and how I know it is wise mind
The skill I actually used
How it went, and what I would pick next time

title: Both Tapped Out Coping Plan
summary: A plan for the evenings when both partners are depleted at once and neither can be the steady one.
goal: Use it to keep a shared low point from turning into a fight over who gets to fall apart.
body_md: Most couples have an unspoken rule that one of them holds it together, and the plan is for the nights when that rule fails. Each partner names what they need in the first twenty minutes, what they can offer when they have nothing left, and what they will not say. Agree on a phrase that means we are both done, a parallel reset (same room or separate, agreed in advance), and a time to reconnect. Watch for a partner who scores the night afterward or who always volunteers to be the steady one. Keep the plan short enough to remember when tired.

fields.label: Partner A: how I can tell I am tapped out, and what I need in the first twenty minutes
Partner B: how I can tell I am tapped out, and what I need in the first twenty minutes
Partner A: the small thing I can still offer when I have nothing left
Partner B: the small thing I can still offer when I have nothing left
The phrase that means we are both done tonight
What each of us does for the next hour, and whether we are in the same room
When and how we reconnect

title: Coping Skills Hopscotch Course
summary: A chalk hopscotch course where every square holds a coping skill the child does before hopping on.
goal: Use it to get skills into a child's body through play.
body_md: The child draws the course with chalk outside or tape indoors and picks a skill for each square: a belly breath, a shoulder squeeze, naming a color, a silly face. The parent plays too, doing each skill the whole way and being bad at hopping on purpose so the child gets to coach. Keep the squares to skills the child already knows; the course is for rehearsal. Suggest the parent run it on a calm day so it is familiar before a hard one. If a child discloses harm during play, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The skills I put in my squares
My favorite square and why
The square that is hardest to do
What my grown-up was like at hopscotch
When I could use one of my squares without the course
Who I would teach my course to

title: Naming the Fear Story Practice
summary: An ACT defusion practice where the client gives their phobia's story a title and greets it by name when it starts.
goal: Use it to put a little distance between the client and the story their mind tells about the feared thing.
body_md: Ask the client to write out the story their mind tells when the feared thing appears, start to finish, as if it were a short film. Then give it a title (Here comes the Dog Will Bite story) and practice saying the title out loud in a neutral voice. Rehearse in session with a photo or a mention, then on an easy step from their hierarchy. The story may stay exactly as loud; what changes is whether the client steps into it. Clients sometimes pick a mocking title and use it to argue with the fear, which is just a new fight. A plain title works better.

fields.label: The story my mind tells when the feared thing shows up, start to finish
The title I am giving it
How I will greet it when it starts
What I noticed when I practiced the greeting in session
An easy step where I will try it this week
What the story did and what I did

title: Self-Soothe After an Approach Step Card
summary: A DBT self-soothe card for the hour after an exposure step, so the client comes down without undoing the work.
goal: Use it to plan aftercare that settles the body without turning into avoidance or reassurance.
body_md: Clients often undo a good step by rushing to a phone, a drink or someone to check they are okay. The card plans the hour afterward with the five senses before the step is taken, so settling does not become escape. Keep the soothing plain and short: a warm drink, a familiar song, a shower, a walk. Rule out anything that works as reassurance about the feared thing. Include a line for what they will tell themselves about the step, written in advance so it does not come from the fear. Review whether the aftercare helped them come back for the next step.

fields.label: The step I am taking
Something for each sense that will settle me afterward
Things I will not do in the first hour because they would undo the step
What I will say to myself about the step, written now
Who I will tell, and what I want from them
How ready I felt for the next step

title: Calm Modeling Plan for Partners
summary: A plan where the partner without the fear demonstrates a calm approach while narrating it, and the fearful partner watches first.
goal: Use it to add modeling to a couple's exposure work before the fearful partner takes a step themselves.
body_md: Watching someone handle the feared thing calmly, with a running commentary, is a step many clients can take before any direct contact. Partner B plans what they will do (open the window near the wasp, hold the needle kit, stand on the balcony) and the plain narration they will use: what they see, what their body is doing, that nothing is happening. No teasing, no surprises, no pulling the partner closer. Partner A sets the distance and the stop word and decides afterward whether they want a smaller version to try. Keep each demonstration under five minutes and repeat it rather than extend it.

fields.label: Partner A: the feared thing and the distance I can watch from
Partner A: my stop word and what I need my partner to do when I say it
Partner B: exactly what I will do, step by step
Partner B: the plain narration I will use while I do it
Partner B: what I will not do
Partner A: what I noticed watching, and whether I want a smaller version to try
Both: when we will repeat it

title: Stuffed Stand-In Practice Play
summary: A child practices approach steps on a toy or stuffed version of the feared thing before meeting the real one.
goal: Use it to start graded steps with a stand-in a child can hold and boss around.
body_md: Pick or make a stand-in: a plush dog, a plastic spider, a toy doctor kit for needles. The child decides where it sits in the room, then over several plays moves it closer, touches it, and finally takes charge of it, feeding the dog or giving the doll a shot. The parent follows the child's pace, names feelings out loud and never springs the stand-in on them. Rate the fear with a finger count before and after each play. When the child can boss the stand-in around with ease, plan the first real-world step together. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: My stand-in and what I named it
Where it sits today
My fear fingers before and after I played with it
What I made my stand-in do
What my grown-up said while we played
What I want to try next time
The real thing I might meet when I am ready

title: Spot the Safety Behavior Game
summary: A group game where one player acts out an approach to a feared thing with hidden safety behaviors and the others try to spot them.
goal: Use it to teach a group to recognize the small habits that keep a fear going.
body_md: Prepare cards naming a feared thing and two safety behaviors (gripping a phone, keeping the door in view, holding the breath, looking away, bringing a person). The actor draws a card and mimes a short approach while working the behaviors in. The rest watch and call them out; one point per correct spot, one to the actor for any behavior missed. Rotate so everyone acts once. Debrief with each player naming a safety behavior of their own and what dropping it might feel like. Keep the mimes light; nobody is asked to do real exposure in the game.

fields.label: The card I acted and the behaviors I hid
The behaviors I spotted in other players
Which ones were hardest to see, and why
A safety behavior I use with my own fear
What dropping it might feel like
One I am willing to leave out on my next step

title: DEAR MAN for Unwanted Appearance Comments
summary: A DEAR MAN script for asking a family member or friend to stop commenting on the client's appearance.
goal: Use it to script the ask that most clients have been rehearsing silently for years.
body_md: Pick one person and one recurring comment, not the whole family. Build the script in order: describe the comment plainly, express how it lands, assert the specific ask, reinforce what it would do for the relationship. Then plan staying mindful if the person argues, appearing confident, and what the client is willing to negotiate (a gentler reminder, a code word at the table). The usual trip is a describe step that includes a judgment; keep it to the words the person says. Rehearse with you playing the relative at their worst, and agree how the client will handle it if the comments continue.

fields.label: The person and the comment they keep making
Describe: the comment, in their words, without my opinion of it
Express: how it lands for me
Assert: exactly what I am asking them to do instead
Reinforce: what it would do for us
What I will say if they argue or make it about them
What I am willing to negotiate, and what I am not

title: Avoided Activities Reclaim Plan for Two
summary: A plan for the things a couple has quietly stopped doing because one partner feels exposed, such as swimming, dancing or being in photos.
goal: Use it to bring back shared activities one small, agreed step at a time.
body_md: Couples rarely name the activities they have dropped; they just stop suggesting them. Each partner lists what they miss doing together, and Partner A says which ones feel exposing. Choose one and plan the smallest version: a quiet pool at an off hour, dancing in the kitchen, one photo that stays on a phone. Partner B's job is to go along without commenting on how Partner A looks, before, during or after. Agree on the words that help and a signal for leaving early without a post-mortem. Keep every conversation on what they did together, never on the body.

fields.label: Partner A: things we used to do together that I now avoid
Partner B: what I miss doing with my partner
Both: the one activity we will bring back first, in its smallest version
Partner B: what I will say and what I will not say about appearance before, during and after
Partner A: the signal I will use if I need to leave early
Both: what we will do right after, with no debrief about looks
Both: how it went, and the next version

title: Who I Am Trading Card Craft
summary: A child designs a trading card of themselves with stats for kindness, courage and skills and no line for looks.
goal: Use it to give a child a picture of themselves that is about what they do and who they are.
body_md: Give the child a blank card template with a space for a drawing and five stat lines they choose: fast runner, good at jokes, brave with spiders, kind to the cat. Explain the one rule: nothing about how anyone looks. The parent makes their own card beside the child, following the same rule, and the two trade and read each other's stats aloud. Watch for a parent who sneaks in a looks comment as praise; redirect gently to a doing stat. The cards go on the fridge. If a child discloses harm during the craft, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: My card name and the picture I drew
My five stats
The stat I am proudest of
A stat my grown-up gave me that surprised me
The stats on my grown-up's card
A stat I want to grow next

title: Appearance Talk Buzzer Game
summary: A group game where players improvise an everyday conversation and anyone can buzz an appearance comment and redo the line.
goal: Use it to help a group hear how much everyday talk is about looks and practice saying something else.
body_md: Give two players a scene (meeting at a party, a family dinner, a reunion) and let them improvise for two minutes. Anyone watching can buzz when a line is about someone's appearance, including compliments. The speaker then redoes the line about something else: what the person did, said or is like. One point per fair buzz, one to the speaker for a good redo. Rotate until everyone has played a scene. Debrief on which comments were hardest to replace, which felt like a loss, and what a conversation sounds like when looks are off the table. Keep buzzing playful.

fields.label: The scene I played
The lines I got buzzed on
How I redid them
The appearance comment that was hardest to replace
What I noticed about conversations with looks off the table
One thing I will say instead this week

title: Closet Comfort Inventory
summary: An inventory of a client's clothes sorted by how they feel to wear and move in rather than how they look.
goal: Use it to move getting dressed from a daily judgment to a question of comfort and use.
body_md: Over a week the client notes what they wore and rates only comfort, ease of movement and whether the day's plans were possible in it. No rating for how it looked. Many clients discover a handful of items they wear because they feel right and a larger set kept for a day they expect to look different. The second set is the conversation: what it costs to keep it in view, and whether storing it elsewhere is a kindness. Keep the sheet away from any talk of the body itself; the subject is the clothes. Review which items make a hard morning easier.

fields.label: What I wore each day this week
How each felt to wear and move in
Whether I could do what the day needed in it
Clothes I keep for a day I expect to be different
What keeping those in view costs me each morning
Items that make a hard morning easier
What I will do with the rest

title: Energy Ledger for the Coming Week
summary: A one-page sheet where a client lists what gives and takes energy and plans a realistic week around it.
goal: Use it to plan activity around the client's own energy instead of an ideal week.
body_md: Have the client fill the two columns in session from last week, then sketch the coming week together. Watch for a plan that spends every hour; leave deliberate gaps. Revisit next session and ask what the budget got wrong rather than whether they stuck to it.

fields.label: Three things that gave me energy this week
Three things that drained me this week
What I must do next week, and how much energy each takes
What I can shrink, share, or skip
Where I will leave a gap on purpose

title: Decision Grid With Values Column
summary: A pros and cons grid with an extra column that asks which of the client's values each option serves.
goal: Use it to help a client look at a stuck decision through what matters to them.
body_md: Run it on one real decision the client has been circling. The values column is where the conversation usually changes, so spend time there. You are not steering toward an answer; if the grid is lopsided but the client still hesitates, ask what the grid left out.

fields.label: The decision I am facing
Option A, with pros and cons
Option B, with pros and cons
Which values each option serves
What I would do if I were not afraid of being wrong
One small step I could take this week

title: Good Day, Hard Day Comparison
summary: A two-column log that sets one better day beside one harder day to spot what differed.
goal: Use it to help the client notice ordinary conditions that shift their days.
body_md: Ask for one of each from the last two weeks and fill it in session from memory first. Look together for small differences such as sleep, contact with people, movement and plans. Keep it descriptive; the client is a curious observer, not a judge of their own days.

fields.label: A better day: what happened from morning to night
A harder day: what happened from morning to night
What was different between them
