title: Opposite Action for Anxious Avoidance

goal: Use it to help a client check whether avoidance fits the facts and try the opposite when it does not.
body_md: Work through checking the facts first, because opposite action fits only when the emotion does not match the situation. Pick a small approach step and plan how to do it with full commitment. Review how it went at the next session.

title: Partner Plan for Anxious Evenings

goal: Use it to help partners support each other without taking over or avoiding.
body_md: The partner who is anxious says what helps and what does not. The other says what they can offer. Watch for accommodation, such as always giving reassurance, and explore kinder alternatives. Review the plan after a week and adjust it together.

Partner A: what does not help

title: Tiny Steps Low Mood Planner

body_md: Ask the client to pick actions so small they feel almost silly, such as opening the curtains. Let them choose the order. Review how the steps felt rather than how many were done. If thoughts of self-harm come up, talk it through in session and share 988 (call or text).

goal: Use it to help a client practice finding a gentler thought they can believe.

goal: Use it to help a client stay connected to what matters even when energy is low.

title: Build Mastery Small Wins Log

goal: Use it to help a client spot common distractions and plan a response.

goal: Use it to help a child match what their body feels with what helps.

title: Intrusive Thought Naming Page
summary: A page for labeling an intrusive thought as a thought and noting what the client did in response.
goal: Use it to help a client step back from an unwanted thought and see the pattern that follows.
body_md: Have the client write the thought in a neutral phrase and label it 'I am having the thought that.' Then note what they did next, such as checking or reassurance seeking. Do not argue about content. Look at the cycle and where a small change might fit.

fields.label: The intrusive thought, in neutral words
How anxious or uneasy it made me, zero to ten
What I did in response
What happened to the unease afterward
One small thing I could try differently

title: Exposure Step Planner With Response Delay
summary: A planner that sets an exposure step, a plan not to act on the urge and a tracker for how long they waited.
goal: Use it to help a client practice facing a trigger while delaying a ritual.
body_md: Choose a step the client rates as moderate and agree on how long to delay the ritual. Plan together what they will do while waiting. Record the urge rating at the start and end. Increase gradually and at the client's pace.

fields.label: The situation I will face
The urge I expect
How long I will delay
What I will do while I wait
How the urge changed

title: Doubt Passenger Practice
summary: A practice of letting doubt ride along while continuing with something that matters.
goal: Use it to help a client carry doubt without letting it drive.
body_md: Use the image of doubt as a passenger who gives loud directions. Have the client pick a task that matters and do it with doubt along. Ask what happened to their relationship with the doubt. Do not seek to remove the doubt.

fields.label: What my doubt says
The task I chose
What I did while doubt was along
What mattered to me about doing it

title: Wise Mind About Checking Card
summary: A card for pausing before a check and asking what wise mind says.
goal: Use it to help a client pause and consider a response before doing a ritual.
body_md: Practice the pause in session with a trigger of mild strength. The client writes down what emotion mind says and what wise mind says. Support them in choosing whether to act. Review how the urge changed.

fields.label: What I felt like checking
What emotion mind told me
What wise mind said
What I chose to do

title: Worry Bully Talk-Back Poster
summary: A poster activity where a child names the worry bully and writes brave talk-back lines.
goal: Use it to help a child separate from the worry bully and answer it.
body_md: The child draws the worry bully and gives it a silly name. Together they write short talk-back lines. The parent learns not to give repeated reassurance and to say, 'That sounds like the bully.' Practice the lines with a parent.

fields.label: The name of my worry bully
What it says to me
What I can say back
What I can do instead of what it asks

title: Panic Sensation Prediction Chart
summary: A chart comparing what the client fears will happen in a panic wave with what happened.
goal: Use it to help a client look at the gap between predictions and outcomes.
body_md: Use a recent wave of panic and list the sensations. For each, note the feared meaning and what actually happened. Ask the client to review the chart after a few more waves. Encourage curiosity rather than argument.

fields.label: The sensations I felt
What I feared they meant
What actually happened
How long it took to settle

title: Interoceptive Practice Log
summary: A log for brief, planned exercises that bring on harmless body sensations and the client's response.
goal: Use it to help a client get used to body sensations they fear, in small steps.
body_md: Check the client's health history first and consider a medical check. Try one exercise in session, such as breathing quickly for a short time, and rate the sensations. Assign only exercises practiced together. Increase slowly.

fields.label: The exercise I did
Sensations I noticed
How much I feared them, zero to ten
What happened as I stayed with it

title: Carrying Panic Through the Day Practice
summary: A practice of taking panic along when doing something that matters instead of waiting for it to go.
goal: Use it to help a client do what matters even with the possibility of panic.
body_md: Ask what the client has stopped doing because of panic. Pick one small version and plan it with the panic allowed along. Rate what they learned afterward. Do not make the goal 'no panic.'

fields.label: Something I stopped doing
The small version I will try
What I will say to my mind
What I noticed afterward

title: Paced Breathing and Temperature Reset
summary: A reset using slow exhale-focused breathing and cool water to settle body arousal.
goal: Use it to help a client settle the body in a wave of panic.
body_md: Try both skills in session and ask which one the client prefers. Advise on health considerations for cold water. Practice at calm times first so the skill is familiar. Review how it felt.

fields.label: The skill I tried first
What changed in my body
Which one I prefer
When I will use it

title: Panic Plan Partners Can Follow
summary: A short plan for partners about what to say and do when panic arrives.
goal: Use it to help partners support a panic wave in a calm, steady way.
body_md: The person who has panic says what helps and what does not. The partner practices short, calm statements. Rehearse in session. Agree on a signal and a plan for afterward, including a check-in rather than a postmortem.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps in a wave
Partner A: what does not help
Partner B: what I will say and do
The signal we will use
What we will do afterward

title: Calm Reset Plan for Parents
summary: A plan for what a parent will do in the first minute of a hard moment with their child.
goal: Use it to help a parent plan a pause before they respond.
body_md: Name a real moment that happens often. The parent writes a pause, a phrase and a first action. Rehearse with a role play. Keep it short and realistic, and note repair is always possible later.

fields.label: The moment that is hardest for me
What I notice in my body
The pause I will take
The words I will say
How I will repair if I need to

title: Parent Thought Reframe Sheet
summary: A sheet that turns harsh parent thoughts into balanced ones that support better responses.
goal: Use it to help a parent notice thoughts that fuel reactive parenting.
body_md: Collect thoughts like 'they are doing it on purpose.' Explore other explanations such as tiredness or need. Be careful not to imply blame. Ask what response fits the balanced thought.

fields.label: A thought I had about my child
How it made me feel
Another way to see it
What I could do with that view

title: Parent Best Self Compass
summary: A compass for choosing a parenting action based on who the parent wants to be.
goal: Use it to help a parent act on values when emotions run high.
body_md: Ask the parent to name three qualities they want their child to remember. Connect each to a small action. Name the hooks that pull them away. Review how it felt to act on a value.

fields.label: Qualities I want my child to remember
A small action for each
What pulls me away
What I will do when I notice it

title: Validating My Child Practice Page
summary: A page for practicing validating a child's feeling before problem solving.
goal: Use it to help a parent show understanding of a child's feelings first.
body_md: Review levels of validation with simple examples. Practice with a role play where the clinician plays the child. Watch for 'but' after validation. Assign one validating moment a day.

fields.label: A feeling my child had
A validating sentence I could say
What I did instead
What I will try next time

title: Family Feelings Pointer Wheel
summary: A craft where the family builds a wheel to point at how each person feels at the day's start.
goal: Use it to help families notice and share feelings in a simple way.
body_md: The child decorates the wheel and chooses the feeling choices with the parent. Use it daily for two weeks. The parent models by pointing first and responding with curiosity. Keep the wheel on the fridge or door.

fields.label: The feelings I chose for the wheel
How I like others to respond
Where we will keep it
When we will use it

title: Rest and Help Request Planner
summary: A planner for deciding when to rest and what help to ask from whom in the first weeks with a baby.
goal: Use it to help a new parent plan rest and ask for specific help.
body_md: Ask for concrete help, like a two-hour nap block. List possible helpers and a request for each. Role-play asking. Include in the note a reminder for clients to tell their care team if they feel unsafe. Share 988 (call or text).

fields.label: When I most need rest
Who could help and with what
The words I will use to ask
If I feel unsafe or overwhelmed, who I will call, including 988 (call or text)

title: New Parent Harsh Thought Record
summary: A thought record for harsh thoughts about being a new parent.
goal: Use it to help a new parent notice and soften harsh thoughts about themselves.
body_md: Collect thoughts like 'I should know what to do.' Look for the evidence and a gentler view. Note sleep loss. Keep the tone warm and avoid labeling anything as a condition.

fields.label: The thought I had
What I felt
What I would say to a friend
A kinder thought

title: Values in the Early Weeks Page
summary: A page for choosing small actions that fit what matters in the early weeks of parenting.
goal: Use it to help a new parent act on values within a limited day.
body_md: Name two values the parent wants to keep. Then choose very small actions, such as a minute of eye contact. Accept the day as it is. Ask what noticing these moments does.

fields.label: Two things that matter to me
A tiny action for each
What gets in the way
What I will do when it does

title: Self-Soothe for Night Feeds Kit
summary: A kit list of gentle sensory comforts for night feeds and long nights.
goal: Use it to help a new parent prepare calming steps for hard nights.
body_md: Build a small kit of safe, simple items together. Think of dim light, a warm drink or a soft song. Practice using it once in the room. Remind the client to make a plan with their partner for rest.

fields.label: What I can see or hear
What I can smell or taste
What I can feel in my hands
Who can take over so I can rest

title: Night Shift Teamwork Agreement
summary: An agreement on how partners share nights, chores and check-ins in the first months.
goal: Use it to help partners share the load and stay connected.
body_md: Each partner lists what they are carrying. Then they draft shifts and a weekly check-in. Look for fairness, not equality of hours. Revisit the plan every week since needs change.

fields.label: Partner A: what I am carrying
Partner B: what I am carrying
Our shifts for the week
How we will check in

title: Qualities I Like in Me Inventory
summary: An inventory of qualities the client sees in themselves and moments that show them.
goal: Use it to help a client build a grounded list of strengths with examples.
body_md: Ask for a quality and a recent moment that shows it. If the client struggles, invite what a friend would say. Keep notes in the client's words. Revisit the list weekly and add to it.

fields.label: A quality I like in myself
A moment that shows it
What a friend would say about me
One I want to grow

title: Self-Criticism Evidence Review
summary: A review of a harsh self-judgment with evidence for and against it.
goal: Use it to help a client look at the facts behind a harsh self-judgment.
body_md: Choose a recurring self-criticism. Fill in evidence on both sides and ask for a fairer summary. Notice how the client talks to themselves, and practice a different voice. Do not push an overly positive claim.

fields.label: The criticism I say to myself
Evidence that supports it
Evidence that does not
A fairer sentence

title: Self as Context Observer Notes
summary: Notes from watching the self that notices, rather than the self described by thoughts.
goal: Use it to help a client see themselves as more than a set of stories.
body_md: Guide a short exercise of noticing thoughts, body and feelings from an observer view. Then ask the client what stays the same. Keep it practical. Ask how the observer view changes their relationship to a harsh story.

fields.label: A story I tell about myself
What I notice when I watch it
What stays the same in me
What I choose to do next

title: Validate Myself Daily Cards
summary: Cards with self-validating sentences the client can say about feelings and effort.
goal: Use it to help a client acknowledge their own feelings without judgment.
body_md: Write a few validating sentences with the client, such as 'It makes sense I feel this way.' Practice aloud. Ask how it feels. Assign one daily use.

fields.label: A feeling I had today
A sentence that validates it
How it felt to say it
When I will use these cards

title: Compliment Circle With a Twist
summary: A group game of giving and receiving specific, non-appearance compliments.
goal: Use it to help players practice giving and receiving specific recognition.
body_md: Players take turns giving a specific compliment about a quality or action. The receiver says thank you and nothing more. Rule out comments on appearance. In the debrief, ask what was hard about receiving.

fields.label: A compliment I gave
One I received
What was hard to accept
What I want to remember

title: Social Spotlight Reality Check
summary: A page comparing how much the client thinks others noticed with what they actually saw.
goal: Use it to help a client check the spotlight effect on their own events.
body_md: Pick a recent event. Compare the client's beliefs with what a friend might have noticed. If possible, have them ask a trusted person. Be gentle about conclusions.

fields.label: The event
What I think they noticed
What a friend says they noticed
What I take from this

title: Attention Shift Conversation Test
summary: An experiment comparing a conversation with attention on self against attention on the other person.
goal: Use it to help a client test what happens when attention moves outward.
body_md: Plan two short conversations. In one, focus on self-monitoring. In the other, focus on listening. Compare anxiety and experience. Discuss what the contrast suggests.

fields.label: How I felt with attention on myself
How I felt with attention on them
What I noticed about the conversation
What I will try again

title: Social Moments Values Page
summary: A page connecting a social situation with a value and a willing step.
goal: Use it to help a client go toward people while anxious.
body_md: Pick a value, such as friendliness or curiosity. Plan a social action that fits and a way to carry the anxiety along. Keep the steps small. Ask what mattered about the action.

fields.label: The value I want to act on
A social step that fits
What my mind will say
What I will do with that

title: GIVE Skill Rehearsal Cards
summary: Cards to rehearse the GIVE skills in a short conversation.
goal: Use it to help a client practice warm, relationship-minded conversation.
body_md: Walk through gentle, interested, validate and easy manner. Practice each with a clinician role play. Use a low-stakes topic. Give feedback on what went well first.

fields.label: The conversation I practiced
The part of GIVE that came easiest
The part that was harder
What I will try this week

title: Small Talk Spin Game
summary: A group game using spinner topics to practice starting and ending short conversations.
goal: Use it to help players practice small talk in a safe setting.
body_md: Make a spinner of casual topics. Players pair up and talk for one minute and then swap. Keep it light and let anyone pass. In the debrief, name what was easier than expected.

fields.label: Topic I spun
What I said
What was easier than expected
What I want to try outside

title: Grief Anniversary Plan
summary: A plan for a hard date: what the client wants to do, who they want near and how they will care for themselves.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare for a date that carries extra weight.
body_md: Plan ahead for birthdays, holidays or anniversaries. Let the client choose between marking the day, keeping it quiet or a mix. Name one person to contact. Check in after the date to see what helped.

fields.label: The date and what it means
How I want to spend it
Who I want near me
How I will care for myself afterward

title: Grief Thought Check for Self-Blame
summary: A check of self-blame thoughts about the loss, with kinder and fairer views.
goal: Use it to help a client look at guilt-heavy thoughts with more balance.
body_md: Collect thoughts like 'I should have known.' Explore what the client knew at the time and what hindsight adds. Do not argue away their sorrow. Offer a view that includes both love and limits.

fields.label: The thought I keep having
What I knew at the time
What I know now that I could not know then
A fairer sentence

title: Honoring Their Memory Through Action
summary: A practice of keeping a bond with someone lost by choosing actions that honor them.
goal: Use it to help a client let grief and love sit side by side.
body_md: Ask what the client loved about the person and what they valued together. Then plan one small act that carries it. Let pain be present. Return to how the act felt next time.

fields.label: What I loved about them
What we valued together
A small act that carries it forward
How it felt

title: Getting Through a Grief Wave Card
summary: A card with skills for getting through a wave of grief without making it worse.
goal: Use it to help a client get through a hard wave of grief.
body_md: Build a card with a few skills from the distress tolerance set that suit grief. Include one comfort and one connection. Try it in session. Mention that waves are expected.

fields.label: Skills that help during a wave
One comfort I can reach
One person I can reach
How I will know the wave is passing

title: Memory Garden Drawing Book
summary: A drawing book where a child draws memories of someone they miss as flowers.
goal: Use it to give a child a gentle way to remember and talk about a loss.
body_md: The child draws a flower for each memory and tells a bit about it. Let them lead and stop when they want. The parent learns to listen without fixing and to expect feelings to come and go in waves. Answer questions about death honestly and simply.

fields.label: A memory I drew
How I feel about it
What I miss most
Who I can talk to about it

title: Needs and Requests Translator
summary: A sheet that turns a complaint into a need and a clear request.
goal: Use it to help a client turn criticism into a request their partner can act on.
body_md: Start with a real complaint and ask what need sits under it. Then write a request that is specific and doable. Role-play saying it. Avoid blame words.

fields.label: The complaint I have
The need underneath
My request in one sentence
How I will say it kindly

title: Relationship Mind Reading Check
summary: A check of assumptions about a partner's thoughts, with ways to test them.
goal: Use it to help a client check assumptions before reacting.
body_md: List assumptions that show up in conflict and mark how sure the client feels. Think of other explanations and a way to ask. Practice the asking line aloud.

fields.label: The assumption I made
How sure I felt
Other explanations
A question I could ask

title: Partner I Want to Be Compass
summary: A compass for choosing actions that match the kind of partner the client wants to be.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values in a tense moment.
body_md: Ask about the partner they want to be on their best day. Then choose small actions. Identify the hooks that tempt them to defend or withdraw. Practice a response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be
A small action that fits
What hooks me
What I do when I notice it

title: DEAR MAN for Hard Requests Rehearsal
summary: A script sheet for rehearsing a request with DEAR MAN.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare a clear and respectful request.
body_md: Go through each letter and write the client's own words. Role-play with the clinician. Coach on staying with the point and on a calm tone. Review after use.

fields.label: The situation I describe
How I express my feelings
What I ask for
What I offer in return

title: Weekly Relationship Check-In Guide
summary: A guide for a weekly talk that covers appreciation, concerns and plans.
goal: Use it to help partners keep up with each other before small things build up.
body_md: Set a regular time and keep it to about forty-five minutes. Start with appreciation, then take turns on concerns, then plan. The listener summarizes before responding. Stop if either partner is flooded.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciate
Partner B: something I appreciate
A concern from each of us
Our plan for the week

title: Safety and Support Circle Map
summary: A map of the people, places and routines that help a client feel safe now.
goal: Use it to help a client identify present-day sources of safety and support.
body_md: This tool is about the present. Do not ask for details of what happened. Have the client name people, places and routines that feel safe, and mark where more support is needed. Remind them about 988 (call or text) and other supports for hard moments.

fields.label: People who help me feel safe
Places that feel safe
Routines that steady me
Who I can contact if I feel unsafe, including 988 (call or text)

title: Self-Blame Thought Pacing Sheet
summary: A sheet for looking at self-blame thoughts at a pace the client controls, without retelling events.
goal: Use it to help a client notice self-blame and consider a fairer view in the present.
body_md: Keep to thoughts, not events. The client names a thought and a fairer thought that places responsibility where it belongs. Pause if they feel flooded and ground. Stay in session with this one rather than homework.

fields.label: A thought I have about myself
How strongly I believe it, zero to ten
A fairer thought
What helps me feel grounded now

title: Present Moment Anchors and Values Page
summary: A page that pairs anchors for the present with values the client wants to move toward.
goal: Use it to help a client feel anchored in the present and take small steps toward what matters.
body_md: Start with anchors such as feet on the floor and sounds in the room. Then name a value and a small action. Keep the pace slow and the client in charge. Include a way to stop.

fields.label: Anchors that help me feel here
A value I care about
A small step toward it
How I will pause if I need to

title: Boundaries and Safe Choices Practice
summary: A practice of stating a boundary and choosing safe, supportive options in current relationships.
goal: Use it to help a client practice boundaries in relationships today.
body_md: Work on current boundaries and choices, not past events. Practice a short sentence and a plan if it is not respected. Role-play with clinician. Make sure the client knows they decide the pace.

fields.label: A boundary I want in a current relationship
My sentence
What I will do if it is not respected
Who supports me

title: My Body Is My Own Rules Poster
summary: A poster activity about body safety rules, safe adults and telling someone.
goal: Use it to help a child learn body safety rules and who to tell.
body_md: The child decorates a poster with simple rules and draws safe adults on a hand. Use plain, age-appropriate words and no details of harm. The parent learns to respond calmly if their child tells them something. If a child discloses abuse, follow your mandated reporting duties and local rules.

fields.label: A rule about my body that I know
Safe adults I can tell
What I can say if something feels wrong
Where I will hang my poster

title: Coping Menu by Time and Place
summary: A menu sorting coping skills by where the client is and how much time they have.
goal: Use it to help a client pick a skill that fits the moment.
body_md: Make a grid of places (home, work, public) and times (one minute, ten minutes, an hour). Fill in skills for each cell. Test one in session. Keep a copy on a phone.

fields.label: Skills for one minute
Skills for ten minutes
Skills that work in public
Skills I want to learn

title: Coping Ahead Rehearsal Sheet
summary: A sheet that prepares for a hard event with thoughts, steps and coping plans.
goal: Use it to help a client rehearse coping before a hard event.
body_md: Choose an upcoming event. Walk through what could go wrong and what the client could do. Rehearse in imagination or role play. Review after the event.

fields.label: The event
What could be hard
What I can do
What I will tell myself

title: Does My Coping Move Me Toward What Matters
summary: A check of whether each coping habit helps in the short term and the long term.
goal: Use it to help a client sort habits by whether they move them toward what matters.
body_md: List coping habits and ask whether each works toward a valued life. No habit is shamed. Mark which to keep, adjust or add to. Return to the list after a week.

fields.label: A coping habit I use
What it gives me now
What it costs me later
Keep, change or add to it

title: TIPP and Self-Soothe Mix Card
summary: A pocket card combining a body-based skill and a soothing skill.
goal: Use it to help a client have quick skills ready for hard moments.
body_md: Choose one TIPP element and one soothing sense. Write both on a card. Try them in session. Remind about health considerations for cold or exercise.

fields.label: The body skill I chose
The soothing skill I chose
When I will use them
How I felt after trying them

title: Coping Skills Acting Relay
summary: A relay where teams act out coping skills for others to guess and then discuss.
goal: Use it to help players recall and share coping skills in a fun way.
body_md: Make cards with skills. Teams act them out for guesses. After each round, ask when the skill might help. Close by asking each player to choose one to try.

fields.label: A skill I acted out or guessed
When it could help
One I want to try
Who can remind me

title: Fear Ladder With Support Notes
summary: A ladder of feared situations from easiest to hardest, with notes on support for each rung.
goal: Use it to help a client plan graded steps toward a feared situation.
body_md: Build the ladder with the client and rate each rung. Add support such as a person or a skill. Start with a rung they rate as moderate. Revisit and reorder as needed.

fields.label: The feared situation
Steps from easiest to hardest
Difficulty of each, zero to ten

title: Fear Prediction and Outcome Table
summary: A table to record what the client predicts and what happened in a feared situation.
goal: Use it to help a client compare predictions with what happened.
body_md: Fill the first two columns before each exposure and the last two afterward. Compare and look for differences. Do not rush to a conclusion. Plan the next step.

fields.label: What I predict will happen
How afraid I expect to be

title: Fear Along for the Ride Practice
summary: A practice of taking a step toward a feared situation with fear present and a value in mind.
goal: Use it to help a client do a valued thing while afraid.
body_md: Name what the fear stops them from doing and why that matters. Pick a step and rate willingness. Practice with the fear along. Ask what they noticed.

fields.label: What my fear stops me from doing
Why that matters to me
The step I will take
What I noticed

title: Opposite Action Approach Plan
summary: A plan for approaching a feared situation when the fear is not matching the facts.
goal: Use it to help a client approach rather than avoid when facts support it.
body_md: Check the facts first. If the situation is safe, plan an approach step with full commitment in posture and words. Practice in session. Review how it went.

fields.label: The fear and the facts
My approach step
How I will do it fully
What happened

title: Brave Steps Sticker Board
summary: A board with steps toward a feared thing, with a sticker for each step tried.
goal: Use it to help a child approach a fear in small steps with a parent cheering.
body_md: The child draws the feared thing small and then picks steps on a board. A sticker goes on for each try, whatever the outcome. The parent practices encouraging without pushing and avoids rescuing at the first sign of worry.

fields.label: My fear in a small drawing
My first brave step
My second brave step
Who will cheer me on

title: Body Appreciation Function List
summary: A list of things the client's body lets them do, feel and share.
goal: Use it to help a client notice what their body does for them.
body_md: Ask for functions and experiences, such as hugging a friend or walking in the park. Add sensory moments. Avoid any appearance talk. Review the list and add items weekly.

fields.label: Things my body lets me do
Moments I enjoyed with my body
Something I am grateful for

title: Appearance Thought Pause Log
summary: A log of thoughts about appearance, what triggered them and a kinder way to respond.
goal: Use it to help a client notice appearance thoughts and respond with flexibility.
body_md: Collect triggers such as mirrors or social media. Ask for the thought and its effect on the day. Explore other things to attend to. Keep the focus on thoughts and actions.

fields.label: What set off the thought
The thought
What I did next
A kinder response

title: Values Beyond Appearance Page
summary: A page for choosing actions guided by values instead of by looks.
goal: Use it to help a client move toward what matters, whatever thoughts about appearance say.
body_md: Ask what the client would do more of if appearance thoughts were quieter. Choose a small action. Name the hooks. Revisit after practice.

fields.label: What I would do if the thoughts were quieter
A small step toward it
What my mind says
What I do with that

title: Self-Validation and Kindness Cards
summary: Cards with validating and kind statements for hard moments about how one looks.
goal: Use it to help a client respond to a hard moment with validation.
body_md: Write statements together, such as 'It is hard to feel this way and I can be kind to myself.' Practice aloud. Choose one for the mirror or phone. Revisit and refine.

fields.label: A hard moment
A validating sentence
A kind action I can take
Where I will keep these cards

title: Kind Words Mirror Frame Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a frame and writes kind words about who they are.
goal: Use it to help a child build a kind voice about themselves.
body_md: The child decorates a frame with words about who they are, such as brave or funny. Avoid words about looks. The parent writes words they see in their child too. Hang it where the child will see it.

fields.label: Words about who I am
Words my family sees in me
My favorite thing to do

title: Energy Budget Weekly Planner
summary: A one-page planner where a client spreads limited energy across the week by listing what gives and drains it.
goal: Use it to help a client plan a week around real energy rather than good intentions.
body_md: Walk through one ordinary week with the client and let them place their own activities on the page. Notice whether the drains outnumber the refuels and whether anything on the list is there out of obligation alone. Invite the client to move one item rather than overhaul the week, and look at the plan together the next time you meet.

fields.label: Things that drain my energy

title: Decision Pros and Cons With Values Column
summary: A decision grid with a fifth column that asks which values each option serves.
goal: Use it to help a client weigh a choice by what matters to them, not only by pros and cons.
body_md: Pick a real decision the client is facing and fill the grid in session. The values column often shifts the conversation, because a long list of pros can matter less than one value that keeps showing up. Let the client do the writing and resist steering toward an answer; the page is there to slow the decision down, not to settle it.

fields.label: The decision I am facing
Option A: what it gives me and costs me
Option B: what it gives me and costs me
The values each option serves
What I notice when I read it all back
My next small step on this decision

title: One-Line Boundary Sentence Builder
summary: A fill-in page for drafting a short, kind, firm sentence to use when saying no.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare the words for a boundary before the moment arrives.
body_md: Pick one situation the client has been avoiding and build the sentence together, then say it aloud in session. Clients often draft something long and apologetic; invite them to cut it down to one clear line. Practice out loud matters more than the written version, and the page can go in a pocket or a phone note afterward.

fields.label: The situation where I need a boundary
What I want to happen instead
My one-sentence boundary
What I might be tempted to add or apologize for
What I will do if the other person pushes back
How I will take care of myself afterward

title: Sleep Wind-Down Routine Designer
summary: A page for a client to design an evening routine step by step, from last screen to lights out.
goal: Use it to help a client shape an evening routine they can actually keep.
body_md: Ask what the client already does in the hour before bed and build from there instead of handing over a standard list. Aim for three or four steps they believe they could do on a tired night. Check in the next session about which steps survived the week and which were quietly dropped, and treat dropped steps as information.

fields.label: What my last hour before bed looks like now
Things that help me wind down
Things that wind me up that I could move earlier
My three or four step routine
What I will do if I cannot fall asleep
What might get in the way and what I will do about it

title: Support Network Map With Roles
summary: A page for mapping who helps with what: practical help, listening, fun and honest feedback.
goal: Use it to help a client see which kinds of support they have and which are thin.
body_md: Have the client write names in circles by role, since one person rarely covers everything. Gaps are worth noticing without judgment; a client may have plenty of fun people and no one to call on a bad night. Choose one gap to work on together, such as one small ask of one person this week, and revisit it next session.

fields.label: People I can turn to for practical help
People who listen well
People I have fun with
People who tell me the truth kindly
A role that feels thin right now
One small ask I could make this week

title: Three Column Thought Record Starter
summary: A beginner thought record with three columns: situation, thought and feeling, plus a first balanced thought.
goal: Use it to introduce thought records with fewer columns before the full version.
body_md: Do the first one together in session using a recent, mildly upsetting moment rather than the worst week. Keep the focus on separating what happened from what the mind said about it. Many clients stall on the balanced thought; accept a modest one such as "maybe, but not certain" and build from there across later weeks.

fields.label: The situation in a sentence
The thought that went through my mind
The feeling and how strong it was from 0 to 10
What else could be true
A more balanced thought I could try on
How strong the feeling is now from 0 to 10

title: Downward Arrow Meaning Chain
summary: A page that follows a thought down through "and what would that mean?" questions to a deeper belief.
goal: Use it to help a client trace a surface thought to the belief underneath it.
body_md: Start with one automatic thought and keep asking what it would mean about the client until a core statement appears, then stop and check in on how the client is doing. This can stir feelings, so pace it and leave time to step back. The belief that surfaces becomes material for later work, not a conclusion about the client.

fields.label: The thought I started with
If that were true, what would it mean?
And if that were true, what would it mean?
The belief at the bottom, in my own words
How strongly I believe it from 0 to 100
What I notice in my body as I write this
Something that is also true about me

title: Fortune Telling Prediction Tracker
summary: A tracker for writing down a prediction before an event and what really happened afterward.
goal: Use it to help a client test their forecasts against real outcomes over several days.
body_md: Ask the client to write each prediction before the event and rate how sure they are, then return to it afterward. The value comes from the pattern across several entries, not any one result. Look together for predictions that were close, ones that were far off, and the ones the client never got to test because they avoided the event.

fields.label: What I predict will happen
How sure I am from 0 to 100
What I will watch for
What really happened
How close my prediction was
What I will take from this for the next prediction

title: Responsibility Pie Chart Worksheet
summary: A pie chart exercise for dividing responsibility for an outcome among all the factors involved.
goal: Use it to help a client see all the contributors to an outcome, not only themselves.
body_md: Have the client list every factor that played a part before drawing any slices, and save themselves for last. Clients who over-own outcomes usually run out of pie quickly. Notice how the client reacts to a smaller slice; relief, doubt and guilt are all common, and each is worth a conversation rather than a correction.

fields.label: The outcome I feel responsible for
Everyone and everything else that played a part
My slice, drawn last, and why
How I feel looking at the whole pie
What is still mine to learn from or repair
What I would say to a friend in this spot

title: Worry Time and Action Sorting Page
summary: A page for sorting worries into ones with a next step and ones to set down, tied to a daily worry slot.
goal: Use it to help a client separate worries they can act on from ones they cannot.
duration: Ten minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Introduce a fixed daily slot and have the client jot worries as they come, then sort them during the slot. Actionable worries get one small step with a date; the rest get a note and a deliberate set-down. Expect the sorting to feel odd at first and review the page together to see which pile fills faster.

fields.label: Worries I jotted down today
Worries I can do something about
One small step and when I will do it
Worries I cannot act on today
How I will set those down
How I felt when the slot was over

title: Leaves on a Stream Defusion Practice
summary: A guided practice where thoughts are placed on leaves floating down a stream, with space to log the experience.
goal: Use it to help a client practice watching thoughts pass without grabbing them.
body_md: Lead the image slowly in session, then ask what it was like rather than whether it worked. Many clients find their mind keeps wandering off the stream, which is the practice itself. Offer it as one way of relating to thoughts and invite the client to try short rounds at home on a day that is not already hard.

fields.label: What my mind put on the leaves
When I got pulled into the thought
How I noticed and came back
What the thoughts felt like when they were on leaves
Where I could try this in my week

title: Values Versus Goals Sorting Page
summary: A page that separates directions to keep walking from finish lines to cross.
goal: Use it to help a client tell a value from a goal and link one to the other.
body_md: Ask the client for a goal they care about, then ask what it is in service of, until a direction appears. A value cannot be finished; a goal can be ticked off. Clients sometimes list what others want for them, so gently ask whose voice each item carries and keep the final list in their own words.

fields.label: A goal I am working toward
The value underneath that goal
A value that has no finish line
A way I could live that value today in a small way
Something I do that does not match this value
What I want to move toward this week

title: Passengers on the Bus Rehearsal Page
summary: A page built on the passengers on the bus metaphor, with space to name the passengers and the direction.
goal: Use it to help a client keep driving toward a value with difficult passengers aboard.
body_md: Let the client name the passengers, such as doubt or fear, and the place the bus is headed. Passengers shout and the driver still chooses the route. Ask what the client has tried to get passengers off the bus and what it cost. Keep the tone light, and ask about a concrete turn they could take this week.

fields.label: Where my bus is headed
The passengers who shout the loudest
What they say
What I have done to try to throw them off
What it cost me
The next turn I will take with them on board

title: Self-Compassion Break Practice Card
summary: A short pause card with three steps: notice the pain, remember others feel it, and offer a kind phrase.
goal: Use it to give a client a brief pause to use in a hard moment.
body_md: Practice the three steps once in session using a mild, current difficulty. Let the client choose a phrase that sounds like them rather than a script, since borrowed phrases often ring false. Ask how a hand on the chest or a deep breath lands, and treat any discomfort with kindness toward oneself as worth talking about.

fields.label: What is hard for me right now
How others also meet something like this
A kind phrase in my own words
What I noticed in my body as I said it
Where I could use this card this week

title: Willingness Dial Check-In
summary: A dial from 0 to 10 that asks how willing a client is to feel something in order to do something that matters.
goal: Use it to help a client gauge willingness before choosing a next step.
body_md: Ask the client to pick a valued step and rate willingness to feel what comes with it. A middle number is useful: ask what would move it up or down by one. Smaller steps often raise the number. Treat a low rating as information about the size of the step, not as resistance, and plan the step the client rates highest.

fields.label: A step that matters to me
The feelings that come with it
My willingness from 0 to 10
What would raise it by one point
A smaller version of the step
When I will try it

title: PLEASE Basics Seven-Day Tracker
summary: A tracker for the PLEASE skills: physical illness, eating, avoiding mood-altering substances, sleep and exercise.
goal: Use it to help a client watch the basics that make emotions harder or easier to manage.
body_md: Review the five areas together and let the client pick one to work on instead of all five. Notice where an area is steady and name it as a strength. For the line on substances, keep the tone curious and nonjudgmental. Go over the tracker the following session and look for links between the basics and hard days.

fields.label: My sleep this week
My eating pattern this week
Movement I got this week
Substance use this week, in my own words
Anything about my physical health that needs attention
The one area I will work on

title: Radical Acceptance Coping Statements Page
summary: A page for drafting short statements that help a client accept a painful fact that cannot be changed.
goal: Use it to help a client practice accepting a reality without approving of it.
body_md: Choose a situation that cannot change and keep the page about acceptance, not approval. Write statements together and see which ones the client can say without arguing with them. Acceptance is practiced in small rounds and often comes with sadness; leave time for that. Revisit the statements across several sessions.

fields.label: The fact I am struggling to accept
What I wish were different
What accepting it does not mean
A statement I can say to myself about it
What I notice in my body when I say it
One thing I can still choose

title: FAST Skill Self-Respect Rehearsal
summary: A rehearsal page for the FAST skills: fair, apologies only when warranted, stick to values, truthful.
goal: Use it to help a client keep self-respect while asking for something or saying no.
body_md: Pick a real interaction and rehearse it aloud, noting where the client slides into over-apologizing or bending the truth. Pair it with the DEAR MAN page if the client has it. Most clients benefit from naming which letter is hardest and rehearsing that line a few times before the conversation happens.

fields.label: The conversation I need to have
What is fair to myself and the other person
Where I tend to apologize too much
The value I want to stick to
The honest line I will use
How I will feel if it goes badly

title: Pros and Cons of Acting on Urges Grid
summary: A four-box grid for weighing short-term and long-term pros and cons of acting on an urge versus resisting it.
goal: Use it to help a client slow down before acting on a strong urge.
body_md: Fill all four boxes honestly, since the pros of acting on the urge are real and skipping them rings false. Clients often find the long-term column does the work. Keep a copy somewhere handy for the next time an urge hits, and ask what could make the long-term boxes feel closer in the moment.

fields.label: The urge I want to look at
Pros of acting on it
Cons of acting on it
Pros of resisting it
Cons of resisting it
What I choose to do next time
What will help me remember this grid

title: Wise Mind ACCEPTS Distraction Menu
summary: A menu of distraction ideas arranged by the ACCEPTS letters, with space for personal picks.
goal: Use it to help a client build a list of distractions that suit them.
body_md: Go through each letter and ask the client what has worked for them before, then fill in the menu together. Distraction is a short-term tool for getting through a wave, not a way to avoid the feeling for good. Ask the client to try two items before the next session and bring back what helped and what did not.

fields.label: Activities I could do (A)
Ways to help someone else (C)
Comparisons that put things in perspective (C)
Emotions I could bring in on purpose (E)
Pushing away for a short while (P)
Thoughts and sensations to occupy me (T and S)
My top three picks

title: Appreciation Exchange Sheet
summary: Both partners write specific appreciations and read them aloud to each other.
goal: Use it to help partners practice noticing and voicing what they value in each other.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own side first, then reads to the other while the listener only says thank you. Specifics matter: "you made coffee while I was rushing" lands better than "you are great." Watch for one partner struggling to find items and slow down rather than push; the quiet moments are part of the work.

fields.label: Partner A: something specific my partner did this week
Partner A: what it meant to me
Partner B: something specific my partner did this week
Partner B: what it meant to me
What it was like to hear it from my partner
One appreciation each of us will say out loud this week

title: Gentle Start-Up Rewrite Page
summary: Partners rewrite a harsh opening line into a gentle one with a feeling, a situation and a request.
goal: Use it to help partners begin hard topics in a way that keeps the other person listening.
body_md: Each partner brings a recent complaint as it was first said, then rewrites it using "I feel, about what, and I need." Practice saying the new version aloud in session. Expect some stiffness at first; the point is the shape of the sentence. Listeners reflect back what they heard before responding.

fields.label: Partner A: how I said it the first time
Partner A: my rewrite with a feeling and a request
Partner B: how I said it the first time
Partner B: my rewrite with a feeling and a request

A topic we will start gently this week

title: Shared Calendar and Chore Fairness Talk
summary: A guided talk for partners to list household tasks, who does what and what feels fair.
goal: Use it to help partners talk through the division of everyday tasks without blame.
body_md: Have both partners list tasks, including the invisible ones such as planning and remembering, then compare lists. Differences in what each sees are often the first surprise. Keep the conversation about the shared load, not who is at fault, and end with one change each partner agrees to try for a week.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I carry, including the invisible ones
Partner B: tasks I carry, including the invisible ones
Tasks we both forget or avoid
What feels unfair to each of us
What each of us appreciates about the other's load
One change we will each try this week

title: Trust Rebuilding Small Promises Log
summary: Partners track small promises made and kept to rebuild reliability one step at a time.
goal: Use it to help partners rebuild trust through small, visible follow-through.
body_md: Both partners choose modest promises they can actually keep, such as texting when running late. The log records promise made, kept or missed and what happened. Missed promises are discussed without punishment. Go slowly and watch whether the partner who was hurt sets the pace; trust rebuilds on their timing, not the clock.

fields.label: Partner A: a small promise I will keep
Partner B: a small promise I will keep
What I did and whether I kept it
What my partner noticed
What was hard to follow through on
What we will promise for next week

title: Small Daily Rituals Partner Planner
summary: A planner where partners choose small daily and weekly rituals for staying connected.
goal: Use it to help partners pick small, regular moments that keep them close.
body_md: Ask each partner about small moments they miss, such as a morning goodbye or a Friday walk, then pick a few both can keep. Small and repeated beats big and rare. Check next time which rituals stuck, and let go of ones that felt like chores rather than adding more.

fields.label: Partner A: small moments I miss
Partner B: small moments I miss
Rituals we already have
A daily ritual we will try
A weekly ritual we will try
What will help us keep them going

title: Feelings Weather Report Craft
summary: A child makes a paper weather report to show how they feel today with sun, cloud, rain or storm cards.
goal: Use it to give a child a simple, playful way to share how they feel.
body_md: The child cuts or draws weather symbols and presents a pretend forecast about their day. Let them pick any symbol and any story; there are no wrong answers. The parent watches the report and asks one curious question, and can repeat it at breakfast or bedtime at home. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Today's weather inside me
What made it that kind of weather
What the weather needs to change
A forecast for tomorrow
What my parent can do when it storms

title: Calm Down Jar Making Activity
summary: A child fills a jar with glitter and water to watch swirls settle while practicing slow breathing.
goal: Use it to give a child something to watch and hold while a big feeling settles.
body_md: Make the jar together and shake it while the child names a feeling. Watch the glitter settle for a few slow breaths. The parent joins in so the jar is something shared and not a consequence, and keeps it in a spot where the child can reach it. Seal the lid well and supervise younger children.

fields.label: A feeling that shakes me up
What my body feels like when shaken
How I breathe while the glitter settles
What I notice when it is calm
Where my jar lives at home

title: Superhero Strengths Cape Craft
summary: A child decorates a cape or cuff with their strengths and the powers they use to cope.
goal: Use it to help a child name what they are good at and what helps them through hard things.
body_md: The child designs a hero and lists strengths and coping powers, such as asking for help or taking big breaths. Include effort and kindness along with talents. The parent adds powers they see in their child and ties the cape to a daily moment, such as wearing it before a hard task.

fields.label: My hero name
My strengths and powers
The power I use when I feel scared
The power I use when I feel mad
A power my family sees in me

title: Worry Monster Feeding Box Play
summary: A child feeds written or drawn worries to a decorated box monster that keeps them for the parent to check.
goal: Use it to give a child a safe, playful place to put worries outside their head.
body_md: Decorate a box together and cut a mouth. The child feeds it drawings or words about worries, and a parent opens it at a set time to talk through any the child wants to share. This gives worries a home without forcing a talk. Remind parents not to argue with the worry; listen and help find one next step.

fields.label: What my worry monster looks like
A worry I will feed it today
How my body feels after I put it in
Who opens the box with me
When we will open the box

title: Brave Body Breathing Buddy Game
summary: A child lies down with a stuffed animal on their belly and watches it rise and fall during slow breathing play.
goal: Use it to help a child feel their breath as a calming tool through play.
body_md: Lie the child down with a favorite stuffed animal on their belly and have them rock it gently with breath. Count in slow turns and make it silly to keep it fun. The parent does it too and offers it at bedtime or after a hard moment. Keep it short and stop if the child loses interest.

fields.label: My buddy's name
What it felt like to rock my buddy
When my breath felt slow
A time I could use this at home
What my parent and I will do together

title: Feelings Charades Group Game
summary: Group members act out feelings without words while others guess, then talk about the clues.
goal: Use it to help a group notice how feelings show up in faces, voices and bodies.
body_md: Prepare cards with feelings of varied intensity. Players take turns acting while others guess, then the actor says what the feeling is like for them. Debrief with questions about which feelings were hard to guess and what the body does. Set a rule that no one is pushed to act a feeling they would rather skip.

fields.label: A feeling I found easy to act out
A feeling that was hard to guess
What my body does with a strong feeling
A feeling I notice in others
What I learned from the debrief

title: Pick-a-Skill Story Bingo
summary: Bingo cards filled with coping skills that players mark as they share when they used them.
goal: Use it to help a group remember and trade coping skills they already have.
body_md: Hand out cards with coping skills on each square. Players mark a square by telling a short story about using it. First to a line shares one skill someone else mentioned. Debrief on which skills were new, which surprised people and which they could try this week. Keep stories brief so everyone gets a turn.

fields.label: A skill I have used
A skill I heard that I want to try
A skill I would add to the card
When I could use one this week
What I noticed about how others cope

title: Perspective Taking Story Dice
summary: Players roll dice to build a short scenario and tell it from two different points of view.
goal: Use it to help a group practice seeing a situation through another person's eyes.
body_md: Roll dice that pick a person, a place and a problem, and have two players tell the same event from each side. Rotate roles so everyone tries each view. Debrief by asking what changed when the story was told from the other side and when the group sees this in daily life. Keep scenarios fictional.

fields.label: The story we rolled
What the first person felt and wanted
What the second person felt and wanted
What changed when I took the other view
Where I could use this in real life

title: Gratitude Treasure Hunt Relay
summary: Teams hunt around the room for items that prompt a gratitude share, passing a token along each round.
goal: Use it to give a group a lively way to practice noticing what is good.
body_md: Hide or place objects around the room and send pairs to find them, then each finder shares something they are thankful for linked to the object. The token passes so everyone shares. Debrief on how noticing felt and which shares stuck with them. Keep the pace light and let people pass without comment.

fields.label: Something I am grateful for today
Something small I almost missed
Something someone did for me
How it felt to share
How I could notice good things this week

title: Calm Down Statues Freeze Game
summary: A freeze-dance variation where players hold a calm pose and breathe whenever the music stops.
goal: Use it to help children and groups practice stopping and settling the body.
body_md: Play music and have players move, then stop it so they freeze in a pose and take three slow breaths. Vary the rounds with slow motion or a feeling to move to. A parent or aide can join in. Debrief by asking what they noticed in their bodies when the music stopped and where else they could freeze and breathe.

fields.label: What my body felt like when moving fast
What it felt like when I froze
How my breathing changed
A time I could freeze and breathe
Who I could play this with at home

title: Safe Place Inventory Page
summary: A page where a client lists real places, objects and people that feel safe or steady right now.
goal: Use it to help a client build a list of present-day anchors for steadiness.
body_md: Keep everything on the page in the present: where the client feels safest today, what they can see, hear or touch there, and who is nearby. Do not ask for details of past events. If the client drifts toward memories, gently return to the room and the five senses. The finished page is a reference for hard moments.

fields.label: A place where I feel safest right now
What I can see there
What I can hear or touch there
A person or pet who helps me feel steady
An object I can keep close
Where I will keep this page

title: Then Versus Now Orientation Cards
summary: Cards that pair a reminder with a present-day fact check: date, place, what is around me.
goal: Use it to help a client tell a reminder from present danger by checking the here and now.
body_md: Have the client write a common reminder on one side and present-day facts on the other, such as today's date and who is in the room. Do not review past events. The cards are a pacing tool and a way to orient. Practice using them in session first with a mild reminder, then agree on when the client might carry them.

fields.label: A reminder that stirs things up
What my body tells me it means
Today's date and where I am
What is actually around me right now

title: Choosing a Direction After Hard Times Page
summary: A page for naming values and one small step that moves a client toward what matters, at their own pace.
goal: Use it to help a client reconnect with what matters while keeping the pace gentle.
body_md: Keep this in the present and the future: what the client cares about, and one small step that fits their energy today. Do not ask for a story of what happened. If strong feelings arise, pause and use a grounding step before continuing. Let the client decide when to stop.

fields.label: Something I care about

title: Wave Surfing With Skills Card
summary: A pocket card that lists skills for getting through a rush of reminders: temperature, paced breathing, orienting.
goal: Use it to give a client a short list of skills to use when reminders hit.
body_md: Build the card together from skills the client has already tried and liked. Include one temperature step, one breathing step and one orienting step. Practice each briefly in session while calm. If the client feels unsafe or thinks about harming themselves, they can call or text 988 at any time; make sure this is on the card.

fields.label: A skill that cools my body down

A way I can orient to the room

title: Five Senses Orientation Scavenger Game
summary: A group game where players find items in the room for each sense and share one steadying thing they noticed.
goal: Use it to give a group a playful way to practice orienting to the present.
body_md: Call out a sense and give each player a minute to find something in the room that matches, then each shares one thing. Keep the room calm and the pace slow, and let players pass. No one is asked about the past. Debrief by asking what helped them feel more here and when they could use it outside the group.

fields.label: Something I saw
Something I heard
Something I touched
Something that helped me feel more here
When I could try this outside the group

title: Worry Versus Problem Sorting Sheet
summary: A two-column page for separating worries that have a next step from worries that are open questions.
goal: Use it to help a client sort what they can act on from what they cannot settle today.
body_md: Have the client list current worries and sort each into one column or the other. The solvable column gets one next step and a day; the open column gets a way of carrying uncertainty for now. Notice how many worries sit in the open column. Revisit the page next session and see which ones moved.

fields.label: Worries on my mind

title: What Is the Likelihood and What Could I Handle Page
summary: A page that asks how likely a feared event is and, if it happened, what the client could do.
goal: Use it to help a client weigh both the odds and their own coping.
body_md: Ask for the feared event, an honest rating of how likely it is, and then spend most of the time on what the client could do if it did happen. Many clients overestimate the odds and underestimate their coping. Do not argue the likelihood; let the questions do the work and note what the client says about their own resources.

title: Anxiety Along for the Walk Practice
summary: A walking practice where a client carries anxiety as a companion and keeps moving toward something that matters.
goal: Use it to help a client move with anxiety present instead of waiting for it to leave.
body_md: Take a short walk in session or describe one. The client names the anxious thoughts and sensations as walking companions and notices their steps anyway. Ask what the client would do if anxiety came along. The aim is movement toward a valued place, not making the feeling go away.

fields.label: Where I am walking toward and why it matters

title: Check the Facts for Anxious Feelings Page
summary: A page that walks through the DBT steps for checking whether an emotion fits the facts.
goal: Use it to help a client check whether the size of anxiety fits the situation.
body_md: Walk through the steps: name the emotion, the event, the interpretation, the threat and the outcome. If the facts do not fit, the client practices acting opposite to the urge; if they do, they problem solve. Be careful to validate the feeling first, since checking facts can sound like disbelief if rushed.

title: Partner Plan for Anxious Evenings Talk
summary: A guide for partners to agree on how they will respond when anxiety is high in the evening.
goal: Use it to help a couple agree on supportive responses to anxiety without taking over.
body_md: Each partner describes what helps and what does not. The anxious partner names what they want, such as company or space; the other says what they can offer. Watch for reassurance that keeps the cycle going and talk about gentler alternatives. Write a short plan both can keep and review it in a week.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps when my anxiety is high
Partner A: what does not help
Partner B: what I can offer

title: Small Pleasures and Meaning Log
summary: A daily log for one pleasant moment and one meaningful moment, however small.
goal: Use it to help a client notice small moments of enjoyment and meaning during low mood.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Ask the client to jot one moment of each kind per day, with a mood rating. On low days the entries may be tiny, and that counts. Review the log for links between activities and mood and let the client draw the conclusions. If thoughts of harm arise, complete a safety conversation in session and remind them that 988 can be called or texted.

summary: A page for turning "the whole day was a failure" into a more precise account of what happened.
goal: Use it to help a client replace sweeping day-level judgments with specifics.
body_md: Ask the client to write the sweeping thought about a recent day, then list what actually happened in order, including small things that went fine. Look at the difference between the first sentence and the list. Keep it gentle; a client who feels flat may only manage a few lines, and that is enough to start.

Ask what each action says about the value and what gets in the way, and revisit the ladder to add rungs as energy shifts.

body_md: Name the urge to withdraw and ask whether it fits the facts. If staying in does not serve the client's goals, plan one small opposite action, such as texting one person. Validate how heavy it feels before suggesting action. Pick an action the client rates as doable and check on it next session.
