body_md: Have the client name things their body does for them, such as walking, hugging or breathing, and a kind or neutral word for it. Pair with mindful attention to a sensation without judgment. Skip any focus on looks. Ask for a daily practice of one sentence.

fields.label: Something my body does for me today
A neutral or kind word for my body
A sensation I noticed without judging
What a wise mind says about my body
When I will practice this

title: Partner Words About Bodies Agreement
summary: An agreement on how partners speak about their own and each other's bodies.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on kind and respectful talk about bodies.
body_md: Each partner shares which comments feel supportive or hurtful, including jokes. They agree on words to avoid, on what to say instead and on a way to flag a comment that stings. Emphasize that appreciation can focus on character and shared moments. Review after a week.

fields.label: Partner A: comments that hurt
Partner B: comments that hurt
Words and jokes we agree to leave out
What we can say instead
How we will flag a comment that stings

title: Body Thank-You Notes Craft
summary: A craft where a child writes thank-you notes to parts of their body for what they do.
goal: Use it to help a child feel thankful for their body and what it does.
body_md: The child writes or draws notes such as thank you legs for running. The parent joins in and avoids comments about looks. Display the notes. Talk about how the body helps them play and learn.

fields.label: A thank-you note to my legs
A thank-you note to my hands
A thank-you note to another body part
What I like doing most
Who I will show my notes to

title: Weekly Energy Ledger Page
summary: A one-week page where a client logs what gives and what drains their energy.
goal: Use it to help a client see where their energy goes across an ordinary week.
body_md: Ask the client to fill in one line a day, even when the day was dull. Review it together next session and look for patterns of timing, people and places rather than for faults. Let the client decide which one drain they would like to change first.

fields.label: Something that gave me energy today
Something that drained my energy today
What time of day I felt most like myself
One small change I could try next week

title: Needs and Wants Two-Column Sort
summary: A sorting page that separates what a client needs from what they merely want right now.
goal: Use it to help a client tell a real need from a pressure to give in or please someone.
body_md: Have the client brain-dump everything on their mind, then sort each item into needs or wants. Expect some items to move columns as you talk. The aim is clarity, not a verdict; the client names which columns feel right.

fields.label: Everything pulling at me right now
The items that are needs
The items that are wants
One need I have been putting off

title: Evening Wind-Down Reflection Page
summary: A short nightly page for closing out the day with a few honest lines.
goal: Use it to give a client a steady end-of-day routine that is more reflection than review.
body_md: Keep the page short so it survives tired evenings. Invite the client to write what happened without grading it. If a client uses it to criticize themselves, bring that to session and rewrite the prompts together.

fields.label: One thing that went okay today
One thing I am letting go of tonight
One thing I am grateful for
What would make tomorrow a bit easier

title: Support Circle Map Page
summary: A set of concentric circles where a client places the people they can lean on.
goal: Use it to help a client see who is in their support network and where it is thin.
body_md: Draw three rings and have the client place names by how close and how reliable each person feels. Gaps are useful information, not failures. Pick one person to reach toward this week and plan the first small message together.

fields.label: People in my closest circle
People in my middle circle
People I would like to move closer
One message I could send this week

title: Small Wins Rolling Log
summary: A running page for writing down small wins, however modest they seem.
goal: Use it to help a client notice progress that gets lost when they only watch for problems.
body_md: Ask for at least one line a day and accept anything, including getting out of bed or answering a text. Read the log aloud at the start of session. If the client dismisses their wins, ask what a friend would say about the same line.

fields.label: Today I managed to
What it took to do that
Who or what helped
A win from this week I almost forgot

title: Thought Courtroom Cross-Examination Page
summary: A courtroom-style page for questioning a hot thought with evidence on both sides.
goal: Use it to help a client weigh the evidence for and against a distressing thought.
body_md: Pick one thought the client believes strongly and let them act as both lawyer and judge. Push gently for facts rather than feelings on each side. The verdict is theirs, and a partial verdict is a perfectly good result.

fields.label: The thought on trial
Evidence that supports it
Evidence that does not support it
The verdict I can live with
How strongly I believe it now, 0 to 100

title: Prediction Versus Outcome Tracker
summary: A table for writing what a client expects to happen and then what really happened.
goal: Use it to help a client test their predictions against what actually unfolds.
body_md: Choose three or four predictions the client is willing to check. They fill in the first columns before the event and the last after it. Look for gaps between expectation and outcome, and ask what they make of the gap.

fields.label: What I expect will happen
How sure I am, 0 to 100
What actually happened
What I notice about the difference

title: Double-Standard Technique Page
summary: A page for comparing how a client talks to themselves with how they would talk to a friend.
goal: Use it to help a client notice a harsher standard for themselves than for others.
body_md: Start with a situation where the client is hard on themselves. They write what they say to themselves, then what they would say to a friend in the same spot. Compare the two without pushing; many clients see it unprompted.

fields.label: The situation
What I say to myself
What I would say to a friend in the same spot
What I can take from the friend version

title: Mind Reading Fact-Check Sheet
summary: A sheet for separating what another person said from what the client assumed they meant.
goal: Use it to help a client tell observed facts apart from guesses about what others think.
body_md: Use a recent moment where the client was sure someone thought badly of them. Split the page into what was seen or heard and what was assumed. Brainstorm two or three other explanations, then decide whether a small check-in with the person makes sense.

fields.label: What I saw or heard
What I assumed the person thought
Other things it could have meant
A way to check it out if I choose to

title: Rule Flexibility Rewrite Page
summary: A page for turning a rigid personal rule into a more flexible preference.
goal: Use it to help a client loosen a must or should rule that keeps them stuck.
body_md: Find a rule the client lives by, often phrased as must, should or always. Explore where it came from and what it costs. Then draft a softer version together and have the client test it in one situation this week.

fields.label: The rule I live by
Where I learned it
What it costs me
A more flexible version
A small place to try the new version

title: Noisy Passengers Bus Route Rehearsal Page
summary: A page built on the passengers-on-the-bus metaphor for staying on course with noisy thoughts.
goal: Use it to help a client keep driving toward what matters while difficult thoughts ride along.
body_md: Walk through the metaphor aloud first, then let the client name their loudest passengers and where the bus is headed. Ask what the passengers say and what the client does anyway. Keep the tone light; humor often helps.

fields.label: The direction I want to drive in
My loudest passengers
What they tell me to do
What I can do while they keep talking

title: Hands as Thoughts Pushing-Away Experiment
summary: An in-session experiment using the hands to show what struggling against a thought feels like.
goal: Use it to help a client feel the difference between fighting a thought and holding it loosely.
body_md: Have the client press their palms hard against their face, then rest them in their lap. Debrief what each felt like and what life is like when everything is spent on pushing. Link it to one thought they have been fighting.

fields.label: A thought I have been pushing away
What pushing it away costs me
What happened when I held it loosely
One thing I would do with my hands free

title: Values Compass Weekly Check-In
summary: A weekly page that points a client back to their values and the actions that served them.
goal: Use it to help a client see how close the week stayed to what matters to them.
body_md: Pick two or three domains the client cares about, such as family, work or health. Each week they note one action that moved toward each value. Celebrate the small ones and look at what got in the way without judging it.

fields.label: A value I want to follow this week
One action that fit it this week
What got in the way
One action for next week

title: Willingness Dial Page
summary: A dial from zero to ten for rating how willing a client is to feel something in order to act on a value.
goal: Use it to help a client choose how much discomfort they are willing to carry for something meaningful.
body_md: Name one valued action and the feeling that comes with it. The client turns the dial to their honest number today. If it is low, shrink the action rather than the number. Willingness is a choice made fresh each time.

fields.label: The valued action I am considering
The uncomfortable feeling that comes with it
My willingness today, 0 to 10
A smaller version that moves my number up

title: Thoughts Floating Downstream Practice Log
summary: A log for practicing the leaves-on-a-stream exercise and noting what showed up.
goal: Use it to help a client practice watching thoughts drift by without following them.
body_md: Lead the exercise once in session so the client has felt it. At home they place each thought on a leaf and let it float. Normalize drifting off; noticing and returning is the practice. Review the log for what hooks them most.

fields.label: When I practiced
A thought that landed on a leaf
A thought that was hard to let float by
How it felt when I came back to the stream

title: TIPP Skills Quick Card
summary: A pocket card that lists the TIPP skills for bringing a surge of emotion down fast.
goal: Use it to give a client a short list of body-based skills for the peak of an emotional surge.
body_md: Teach each of the four parts in session and have the client try the safe ones with you. Ask them to note which they would actually use in the moment. Remind them to skip any part that does not suit their body or health.

fields.label: The situations when I feel a surge
The TIPP skill I will try first
What I noticed in my body after it
Where I will keep this card

title: Does the Feeling Fit the Facts Worksheet
summary: A step-by-step page for checking whether an emotion fits the facts of a situation.
goal: Use it to help a client see whether the size of a feeling matches what actually happened.
body_md: Walk through the steps with a recent event: the emotion, what happened, the interpretations, and whether the feeling fits the facts. Validate the feeling first. The point is not to talk anyone out of an emotion but to see the situation clearly.

fields.label: The emotion I felt
What happened, only the facts
The story I told myself about it
Whether my feeling fits the facts

title: PLEASE Self-Care Basics Weekly Grid
summary: A weekly grid for tracking sleep, eating, movement, and rest habits that shape vulnerability to strong emotion.
goal: Use it to help a client notice how basic self-care shapes how easily emotions swell.
body_md: The client ticks off the self-care basics each day, with a line on how they felt. Look for links between a rough stretch and a stretch of poor sleep or skipped care. Choose one habit to strengthen and keep it small.

fields.label: The self-care habit I want to strengthen
How I slept this week
A day I felt more vulnerable and why
One step to try next week

title: GIVE Skills Conversation Planner
summary: A planner for using the GIVE skills to keep a relationship steady during a hard talk.
goal: Use it to help a client stay gentle, interested, validating and easy in a difficult conversation.
body_md: Choose a conversation the client expects to be tense. They plan one phrase for each GIVE part. Role-play the opening in session. Clients often find validation the hardest part, so give it extra time and practice.

fields.label: The conversation I need to have
A gentle opening line
A way to show I am interested
A validating thing I can say
How I will stay easy about it

title: Radical Acceptance Coping Ahead Page
summary: A page that pairs radical acceptance with coping ahead for something the client cannot change.
goal: Use it to help a client plan to meet an unavoidable hard situation with acceptance and a plan.
body_md: Choose an upcoming event the client cannot avoid. They name what they are fighting and write the accepting statements they can offer themselves, then rehearse the plan in imagination. Acceptance does not mean approval, so say that plainly.

fields.label: The situation I cannot change
What I keep fighting about it
An accepting thing I can tell myself
My plan for coping ahead

title: Weekly State of the Union Planner
summary: A planner for a calm weekly conversation about what is working in a couple.
goal: Use it to give partners a regular, low-stakes time to talk about the relationship.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own side before the talk. Agree on a time and place that is not mealtime or bedtime. Start with appreciations, move to one topic each, and end with a plan. Partner A speaks first one week, Partner B the next.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciated this week
Partner B: something I appreciated this week
Partner A: one thing I would like us to talk about
Partner B: one thing I would like us to talk about
One thing we agree to try together this week

title: Specific Appreciation Trading Cards
summary: A set of cards where partners write specific appreciations and trade them.
goal: Use it to help partners notice and name what they value in each other.
body_md: Each partner writes three specific appreciations, naming an action and what it meant, not general praise. They swap and read aloud. Notice who finds it harder to receive; that is worth a gentle conversation.

fields.label: Partner A: a specific thing my partner did that I valued
Partner B: a specific thing my partner did that I valued
Partner A: how it felt to hear mine read aloud
Partner B: how it felt to hear mine read aloud

title: Bid and Response Tally Sheet
summary: A tally sheet for counting the small bids for attention partners make and how they are met.
goal: Use it to help partners notice the small moments of reaching out and turning toward.
body_md: Explain bids with an everyday example, like pointing out a bird or sighing. Each partner marks bids noticed and whether they were turned toward, away from or against. Review without blame; the goal is awareness, then one small change.

fields.label: Partner A: a bid I made this week and what happened
Partner B: a bid I made this week and what happened
A bid I missed and what I would do now
One way we can notice bids more

title: Shared Calendar Fairness Talk Page
summary: A page for talking through who carries which tasks and how the load feels to each partner.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about household and family load with specifics instead of blame.
body_md: Have each partner list the tasks they carry, including invisible planning work. Compare lists side by side before any problem-solving. Partners decide together what shifts, and one change is enough for the first week.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I carry, including planning
Partner B: tasks I carry, including planning
What surprised each of us about the lists
One task we will move or share

title: Dream Within Conflict Conversation Guide
summary: A guide for hearing the hope or story beneath a stuck disagreement.
goal: Use it to help partners understand what a recurring disagreement means to each of them.
body_md: Choose a disagreement that keeps returning. Each partner takes a turn as speaker while the other only asks curious questions. Look for the meaning, history or dream underneath. The task is understanding, not agreeing, and you can set a timer.

fields.label: Partner A: what this issue means to me
Partner B: what this issue means to me
Partner A: a hope I have connected to it
Partner B: a hope I have connected to it
One small step we can both support

title: Feelings Weather Station Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds a little weather station to show how they feel today.
goal: Use it to help a child name feelings by matching them to weather.
body_md: The child makes a dial with sun, clouds, rain and storm and moves the pointer to match how they feel. The parent checks in at set times and reflects what they see without fixing it. Weather changes, which is a helpful message in itself.

fields.label: The weather inside me today
What made the weather change
What helps when it is stormy
Who I can tell about my weather

title: Calm-Down Jar Building Guide
summary: A guide for building a glitter jar a child can watch settle when they feel upset.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on way to slow down and watch big feelings settle.
body_md: Build the jar together with a clear bottle, warm water, glitter glue and glitter. The parent practices with the child and uses it as an invitation, never as a punishment or a time-out. Keep it somewhere easy to reach.

fields.label: The colors I picked for my jar
What my feelings look like when they are shaken up
What I do while the glitter settles
When I want to use my jar

title: My Brave Badge Design Page
summary: A drawing page where a child designs a badge for a brave thing they did.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and celebrate their own acts of courage.
body_md: The child draws a badge and decorates it, naming a time they felt nervous and did it anyway. The parent adds a sticker or a sentence of specific praise about the effort. Brave means doing it while scared, not not being scared.

fields.label: A brave thing I did
How my body felt before I did it
What I said to myself
The name of my badge

title: Worry Eater Puppet Craft
summary: A craft where a child makes a puppet that eats written-down worries.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful way to name worries and hand them off.
body_md: Make a puppet from a paper bag or sock with a big mouth. The child writes or draws a worry and feeds it in. The parent listens and does not argue with the worry. Check the puppet together at a set time each day.

fields.label: The name of my worry eater
A worry I fed to it today
What the worry eater says back
What I can do after I feed it

title: Helping Hands Tracing Page
summary: A page where a child traces their hands and fills the fingers with ways they help.
goal: Use it to help a child see the many ways they are helpful and capable.
body_md: The child traces both hands and writes or draws one way they help on each finger. The parent adds a finger about something they noticed. Display it where the child sees it daily and update it when they learn something new.

fields.label: A way I help at home
A way I help at school or with friends
A way I help myself
A new way I want to help

title: Emotion Charades Round
summary: A charades game where players act out feelings and the group guesses.
goal: Use it to help a group practice reading and naming emotions through body and face.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a feeling card and acting it without words while others guess. Rule: no pointing at real people. Debrief with how they knew, which feelings were hardest to read, and what each one feels like in the body.

fields.label: The feeling I acted out
The clue that gave it away
A feeling that was hard to guess
What I learned about reading others

title: Coping Skill Bingo Card Game
summary: A bingo game where players mark off coping skills they have tried this week.
goal: Use it to encourage a group to try and talk about many different coping skills.
body_md: Each card has coping ideas such as walking, music or breathing. Players mark squares for what they tried and a line wins a small prize. A turn includes saying how it went. Debrief on which skill surprised them and which to carry forward.

fields.label: The skill I marked off first
What happened when I tried it
A skill I want to try next
A skill I would add to the card

title: Thought Detective Card Game
summary: A card game where players hunt for the clue that a thought might be a trap.
goal: Use it to help players practice spotting thinking traps in everyday examples.
body_md: Deal situation cards with a thought written on them. On a turn the detective names the trap and offers a fairer thought; the group votes with a thumbs up. Rotate the detective role. Debrief on which traps they recognize in their own thinking.

fields.label: The trap I spotted
A fairer thought I offered
A trap I notice in my own thinking
What I will watch for this week

title: Values Bidding Auction Round
summary: A play-money auction where players bid on values and talk about what they chose.
goal: Use it to help players see which values matter most when they have to choose.
body_md: Each player gets the same play money and bids on value cards like honesty, family or adventure. Run three rounds with one rule: you cannot buy everything. In the debrief, ask what they gave up and what the bids say about how they spend their lives.

fields.label: The value I bid the most on
A value I wanted but could not afford
What surprised me about my bids
One way I can act on my top value this week

title: Pass the Compliment Circle Game
summary: A circle game where players pass a ball and share a specific kind word.
goal: Use it to help a group practice giving and receiving kind words.
body_md: Players pass a ball around the circle; the holder gives a specific compliment to the next person about something they did, and the receiver says thank you without deflecting. Skip appearance. Debrief on how it felt to give and to receive.

fields.label: A compliment I gave
A compliment I received
What was hard about saying thank you
Someone I will give a kind word to this week

title: Window of Tolerance Daily Check Page
summary: A daily page where a client notes whether they felt too revved up, too shut down, or steady.
goal: Use it to help a client notice their own zones of arousal and what moves them between them.
body_md: Introduce the three zones in plain words and let the client mark where each part of the day landed. Do not ask for any detail about past events. Look together for what helps them return to steady and keep to the stabilizing side of the work.

fields.label: Where I was today: revved up, steady or shut down
What was happening around me
What helped me come back toward steady
One thing to try tomorrow

title: Stuck Point Today-Only Page
summary: A page for noticing present-day beliefs like "I cannot trust anyone" without describing past events.
goal: Use it to help a client examine a current belief and its effect now, with no event details written down.
body_md: Keep the focus on the belief as it shows up this week, never on the story behind it. The client names the belief, what it makes them do and a fairer, more balanced version. Complete it in session, and pace it so the client stays steady.

fields.label: A belief that gets in my way today
How it shows up this week
What it makes me do or avoid
A more balanced way to say it

title: Values After Hard Times Compass
summary: A compass page for choosing what matters now and one small step toward it.
goal: Use it to help a client reconnect with what they care about alongside difficult memories.
body_md: Frame values as a direction chosen in the present, not a requirement to revisit the past. The client picks one area and a step that feels safe and doable. Keep the pace in their hands and stop whenever they ask.

fields.label: Something that matters to me now
A small step that feels safe
What might get in the way
Who could be beside me for this step

title: Crisis Survival Kit Packing List Card
summary: A card for listing what goes in a physical kit for hard moments.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare a set of grounding items and contacts ahead of time.
body_md: Pack a real box or bag together: a scented item, something cold, a soothing playlist, a note from someone kind. Include supports and 988, call or text, on the card. Complete the card in session and revisit what is in the kit often.

fields.label: Things that help me feel grounded
Things that help my body calm down
People I can contact, and 988 (call or text) if I am in crisis
Where my kit will live

title: Partner Pause Signal Agreement
summary: An agreement where partners pick a signal for needing a break when something feels triggering.
goal: Use it to help partners pause kindly and return to each other when one feels overwhelmed.
body_md: Each partner chooses a word or gesture that means a pause is needed, and the other agrees to honor it without asking why. Set a time to reconnect. Neither partner is asked to explain past events. Practice the signal once in session.

fields.label: Partner A: our pause signal and what it means to me
Partner B: how I will respond when I see it
What helps each of us come back
When we will reconnect after a pause

title: Worry Dragon Cave Drawing
summary: A drawing activity where a child sketches a worry as a dragon and gives it a cave.
goal: Use it to help a child see a worry as something separate they can draw and set boundaries around.
body_md: The child draws the dragon, names it and draws a cave where it stays when not needed. The parent asks curious questions and does not try to talk the dragon out of existence. Revisit the drawing and add what the child does when the dragon shows up.

fields.label: What my worry dragon looks like
What it says to me
What I can say back
Where the dragon stays in its cave

title: Calm Breath Relay Game
summary: A team relay where each leg ends with a slow breath before the next player starts.
goal: Use it to help a group link slow breathing with the feeling of getting ready for something.
body_md: Teams complete a simple task, then each player takes three slow breaths before passing the baton. Make it playful rather than competitive. In the debrief ask when a breath like this could help in daily life and what they noticed in their bodies.

fields.label: How my body felt before the breaths
How my body felt after
A time this could help me
What I would tell a friend who feels nervous

title: Anxiety Body Signals Sketch Map
summary: A body outline where a client marks where they notice anxious sensations and what each feels like.
goal: Use it to help a client recognize early body signals of anxiety so they can respond sooner.
body_md: Give the client an outline and colored pencils. They mark where tightness, heat, flutter or tingling appears and write a word for each. Compare it with their situations over the week. Early recognition gives them more time to use a skill.

fields.label: Where I feel anxiety in my body
What each sensation feels like
The earliest signal I notice
What I could do when I notice it

title: Likelihood Versus Cost Worry Page
summary: A page that separates how likely a feared outcome is from how bad it would be and how the client would cope.
goal: Use it to help a client look at a worry in two parts: the odds and the coping plan.
body_md: Choose one worry. The client rates likelihood honestly, writes the worst case in plain words and then describes how they and their supports would handle it. Many clients overlook the coping step; slow down there and let them build it.

fields.label: The worry
How likely it really feels, 0 to 100
If it happened, how I would handle it
Who could help me

title: Anxiety as Weather Report Page
summary: A page for describing anxiety like a weather report and choosing actions in any weather.
goal: Use it to help a client act on their values even when anxious weather is passing through.
body_md: Invite the client to give a short weather report for the day, such as foggy with a chance of dread. Then ask what they want to do today whatever the forecast. Humor helps. The point is making room for the weather while still moving.

fields.label: Today's anxiety weather report
What I want to do today anyway
What the weather tells me to do
One step I will take in this weather

title: Build Mastery Small Steps Card
summary: A card for choosing one small task each day that brings a sense of mastery.
goal: Use it to help a client build a sense of accomplishment through tiny, doable tasks.
body_md: Pick tasks that are very small and clearly finishable, such as washing five dishes or answering one message. The client records the task and how it felt to complete it. If tasks keep getting missed, make them smaller rather than pushing harder.

fields.label: The small task I picked today
Whether I did it
How it felt to finish
A slightly bigger task for tomorrow

title: Gentle Check-In Script for Low Days
summary: A short script partners can use when one of them is having a low stretch.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about low days kindly and agree what support looks like.
body_md: Partners write what helps and what does not on low days, then agree on a few check-in words. Include crisis planning: complete the safety line in session, not as homework. Make sure each partner knows to call or text 988 or the clinician if safety is a concern.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me on a low day
Partner B: how I can show I care without fixing
Our check-in words
If either of us talks about not wanting to live, we call or text 988 or call the clinician

title: Sunshine Jar Good Things Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a jar and drops in a note for each good moment of the day.
goal: Use it to help a child notice small good moments, even on gloomy days.
body_md: The child decorates a jar and each evening writes or draws one good moment on a note. The parent adds one too and reads the notes together on the weekend. Do not push; on a hard day a drawing or a single word counts.

fields.label: A good moment today
Who was part of it
How my body felt in that moment
A good thing I want to do this weekend

title: Tiny Task Quest Board Game
summary: A board game where players move along a path by completing tiny real-life tasks.
goal: Use it to make small activity steps playful for a group and talk about what helps them begin.
body_md: Players roll a die and land on spaces with tiny tasks such as stretch, text a friend or step outside. They do it in the room or plan it for later. Debrief on which task felt easiest and what helps them start when energy is low.

fields.label: The tiny task I did or planned
How I felt after it
What helps me start when I have low energy
A tiny task I will try this week

title: Energy and Mood Daily Pairing Log
summary: A log that pairs activities with energy and mood ratings across the day.
goal: Use it to help a client see which activities lift or sink their day.
body_md: The client records the main activity of each part of the day with an energy and a mood number. Review it together for activities that nudge the numbers up, even slightly. Pick one to do more of; avoid reading the pattern as a verdict.

fields.label: Morning: what I did, energy 0 to 10, mood 0 to 10
Afternoon: what I did, energy 0 to 10, mood 0 to 10
Evening: what I did, energy 0 to 10, mood 0 to 10
What I notice about the pattern

title: Task Start Friction Finder Page
summary: A page for finding what makes a task hard to start and shrinking the first step.
goal: Use it to help a client find the specific friction that stops them beginning a task.
body_md: Choose one task the client keeps putting off. They list what makes it hard to start, such as unclear steps or boredom, then design a two-minute first step. Frame it as a design problem, not a character problem.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off
What makes it hard to start
A two-minute first step
What I can set up in advance to make it easier

title: Values Over Distraction Pull Page
summary: A page for noticing the pull of distraction and choosing a valued action instead.
goal: Use it to help a client notice what pulls their attention and choose where it goes.

summary: A short practice using an open palm to rehearse making room for an uncomfortable feeling.
goal: Use it to help a client physically rehearse the stance of willingness.
body_md: Lead it in session first so the client knows how it feels. Contrast a clenched fist, which is pushing away, with an open palm, which is making room. Invite them to notice what changes in their shoulders and breath. Not everyone enjoys body-based practice; offer a seated or eyes-open version.

fields.label: A feeling I tend to clench against
What the clenched version feels like
What the open-palm version feels like
Where I could use the open palm this week
What I will do while I make room for it

title: Valued Living Compass Check-In
summary: A check-in across a few life areas comparing how important each is with how much the client has lived it lately.
goal: Use it to help a client find the area where a small valued step would matter most.
body_md: Choose four or five areas with the client rather than using a fixed list. Rate importance and recent action separately. The gap is where the conversation lives, but do not treat it as a score to fix everywhere at once. Pick one area and one step that is small enough to happen this week.

fields.label: The life areas I want to look at
How much each matters to me, 1 to 10
How much I have lived it lately, 1 to 10
The area with the biggest gap
One small step I will take there

title: Leaves on a Stream Thought Parade Log
summary: A log used after the leaves-on-a-stream exercise to record what drifted by and how it felt to watch.
goal: Use it to help a client practice watching thoughts without hooking into them.
body_md: Guide the exercise live, then use the log. Many clients get frustrated when thoughts do not stay put on a leaf; normalize that and invite them to simply come back. The log tracks what showed up, not whether they did it right. Offer short versions to use at home.

fields.label: A few thoughts that floated by
What I noticed when I labeled them as thoughts
When I got pulled into a thought
How I came back to watching
Where I could use this during the week

title: TIPP Body Reset Rehearsal Card
summary: A card for rehearsing the temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing and paired relaxation skills before they are needed.
goal: Use it to help a client practice the TIPP steps while calm so they are ready when upset.
body_md: Rehearse each step in session, choosing the ones that are realistic for the client's body and setting. Cold water is not right for everyone, so talk through any health concerns first. Have the client rank the four by how doable they are. A practiced card in a pocket beats a perfect plan they have never tried.

fields.label: The step I find easiest to do
The step I find hardest
Where I could do each one in my day
What I notice in my body after paced breathing
When I will rehearse this again

title: Radical Acceptance Turning-the-Mind Log
summary: A log for the many times a client has to turn the mind back to acceptance on one painful fact.
goal: Use it to help a client see acceptance as something they return to again and again.
body_md: Explain that accepting a hard reality is rarely a single decision; the mind drifts back to fighting it. The client marks each time they notice and turn back. Include the fact being accepted, written plainly. Be clear that acceptance is not approval. Review the log for what made turning easier.

fields.label: The reality I am working on accepting
Times I noticed myself fighting it
What I said or did to turn my mind back
What made turning easier
What I can do next with this reality as it is

title: Opposite Action Experiment Planner
summary: A planner for choosing one emotion-driven urge and trying the opposite action in a small, safe way.
goal: Use it to help a client test what happens when they act opposite to an urge that is not serving them.
body_md: Start by checking whether the emotion fits the facts; opposite action is for when it does not, or when acting on it will not help. Pick a low-stakes situation first. The client predicts what will happen, tries it, and records the result. Practice the full opposite action, including posture and tone.

fields.label: The emotion and the urge it brings
Whether the emotion fits the facts
The opposite action I will try
What I predict will happen
What actually happened
What I learned about the urge

title: Pros and Cons of Skills Use Versus Old Habit Sheet
summary: A two-by-two sheet comparing using a skill with falling back on an old habit, in the short and the long run.
goal: Use it to help a client weigh a hard moment honestly and choose with their eyes open.
body_md: Fill in the old habit side first so the client feels heard about what it gives them. Then fill in the skill side. Resist arguing; the sheet does the persuading. Keep a copy handy for the next time the old habit pulls. Clients often discover that the short-term pro of the old habit is real and still not worth the long-term con.

fields.label: The old habit and the moment it shows up
What it gives me now
What it costs me later
The skill I could use instead
What it gives me and costs me
My choice this time

title: Wise Mind Walking Reflection Page
summary: A page used after a mindful walk to notice where emotion and reason meet.
goal: Use it to help a client find wise mind through attention to the body and surroundings.
body_md: Take a short walk with the client or assign one, asking them to pay attention to feet, breath and what they see. Afterward they note what felt calm and what felt busy. Wise mind is hard to describe, so use their own words. A question to carry: what does my wise mind say about the thing I am facing?

fields.label: Where I walked
What my feet and breath felt like
What my emotional mind said
What my reasonable mind said
What wise mind says about my situation

title: Repair Attempt Preference Menu for Partners
summary: Each partner lists the repair moves that work for them and shares them as a menu.
goal: Use it to help a couple recognize and accept each other's attempts to repair mid-conflict.
body_md: Each partner works alone first, then they swap. Partner A lists repairs that would help them and Partner B does the same. Ask each to name one repair the other already does that they have missed. Model receiving a repair attempt in session. Many couples find they were offering repairs in a language the other did not hear.

fields.label: Partner A: repairs that help me when we are tense
Partner B: repairs that help me when we are tense
A repair my partner already offers that I missed
A repair I would like to try offering
How we will signal we are making a repair attempt

title: Weekly Appreciation Handoff Cards
summary: Partners write one specific appreciation a day and hand the card over.
goal: Use it to help a couple build a daily habit of noticing what is going right between them.
body_md: Each partner writes one card a day about something specific the other did. Keep them short and about actions, not traits. Do not make it a scoreboard. In session, ask each how it felt to write and how it felt to receive. If one partner struggles to find anything, explore that gently rather than pressing.

fields.label: Partner A: what I appreciated today
Partner B: what I appreciated today
How it felt to receive a card
Something I want more of
What we will keep doing next week

title: Stress Tag Team Agreement
summary: A short agreement for how each partner wants help on a heavy day and what to avoid saying.
goal: Use it to help a couple name what support looks like before the next stressful day arrives.
body_md: Each partner answers separately about what helps and what does not on a heavy day, then they compare. Look for mismatches such as one wanting solutions and the other wanting company. Write the agreement in plain words they can both live with. Review it after a real stressful day to see what held.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me on a heavy day
Partner B: what helps me on a heavy day
What each of us wants to avoid hearing
How we will ask for what we need
When we will check this agreement again

title: Unspoken Rules We Inherited Interview
summary: Partners compare the unspoken rules each grew up with about money, anger, affection and chores.
goal: Use it to help a couple see that some clashes come from different family habits, not from one partner being wrong.
body_md: Ask each partner to answer for their own family first, then listen without correcting. Common themes are who handles money, how anger is shown and who cleans up. Invite curiosity rather than blame. End by choosing one rule they want to keep, one to retire and one to rewrite together.

fields.label: A rule in my family about money or chores
A rule about how anger or upset was shown
A rule about affection
A rule we want to keep
A rule we want to retire or rewrite

title: Two-Lane Conversation Practice Sheet
summary: A structure with a speaker lane and a listener lane for a conversation about one topic.
goal: Use it to help partners stay in their lane long enough to feel heard.
body_md: One partner speaks for a short fixed time while the other only listens and then reflects back what they heard, without defending. Swap. Choose a mild topic first, not the biggest fight. Coach the listener to reflect, not rebut. Check afterward what it felt like to be in each lane.

fields.label: The topic we chose
Speaker: what I want my partner to understand
Listener: what I heard
What the speaker would add or correct
What it felt like to listen without defending

title: My Feelings Weather Window Craft
summary: A paper window frame where a child draws the weather that matches the feeling inside.
goal: Use it to help a child show a feeling through a picture when words are hard to find.
body_md: Let the child decorate the frame and draw today's weather through it. Ask what kind of day it is inside. Parents can later use the window as a quick check-in at home by asking what weather it is. Follow the child's lead on the drawing and avoid interpreting it for them.

fields.label: The weather I drew today
What feeling that weather matches
What would make the weather change
Who I can show my window to

title: Calm Down Jar With Sparkles Build
summary: The child builds a sparkle jar and uses it to watch their upset settle.
goal: Use it to help a child watch a big feeling settle like glitter in water.
body_md: Build the jar together with water, glue and glitter, sealed well. Show how shaking it looks like a big feeling and how watching it settle is something the child can do. Parent role: keep the jar somewhere the child can reach and sit with them rather than send them away with it. It is a tool for company, not a punishment.

fields.label: What my sparkles look like when I am upset
How long it takes them to settle
What I feel in my body while I watch
Where our jar lives at home

title: Bravery Badge Maker
summary: A child designs badges for brave things they did and earns new ones across the week.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and name the brave things they do, big or small.
body_md: Have the child decorate blank paper badges and name the brave act on each. Ask a parent to notice and name small acts at home, like trying something new. Keep the badges about effort and not outcome. Check in on which ones the child is most proud of and what kind of bravery they want to try next.

fields.label: A brave thing I did this week
What my badge looks like
What helped me be brave
A brave thing I want to try next
Who I will tell about it

title: Feelings Zoo Animal Matching Play
summary: The child matches animals to feelings and acts them out.
goal: Use it to help a child connect feelings with bodies and faces through play.
body_md: Lay out animal cards and let the child pick one for each feeling, then act it out. A parent joins, matches too and says what their animal feels. Take turns guessing. Do not correct the child's choices; a sleepy lion for worry is theirs. The goal is a shared vocabulary for use at home.

fields.label: The animal for my happiest feeling
The animal for my angry feeling
The animal for my worried feeling
Which animal is like me today
How my parent and I can use our animals at home

title: Goodnight Worry Mailbox Craft
summary: A decorated box where a child posts worries before bed for a parent to read together.
goal: Use it to help a child hand off bedtime worries so they do not have to carry them alone.
body_md: Build the mailbox from a small box and slot. The child draws or dictates a worry, posts it, and the parent promises a short time in the morning to read it together. Parent role: stay calm, listen, and avoid long reassurance at bedtime. Reporting duties apply if a child discloses anything about being unsafe.

fields.label: What my mailbox looks like
A worry I posted tonight
Who reads the mail with me
What we do with the worry in the morning

title: Skill of the Day Spinner Game
summary: Players spin for a coping skill, then act out or describe when they would use it.
goal: Use it to help a group rehearse skills in a quick, low-pressure round.
body_md: Make a spinner with a skill on each wedge. Rules: spin, describe a time you would use the skill, and the group adds one tip. Turns rotate around the circle and anyone can pass. Debrief by asking which skills people want to take home and which were new. Keep the energy light so the learning sticks.

fields.label: The skill I landed on
A moment I would use it
A tip from the group I liked
The skill I will try this week

title: Two Facts and a Strength Guessing Game
summary: Players share two true things and one strength, and the group guesses which is the strength.
goal: Use it to help a group practice naming strengths out loud without awkwardness.
body_md: Rules: each player states three things, two ordinary facts and one real strength, and others guess the strength. Turns go clockwise. For debrief, ask what it was like to say a strength and what was easier, the facts or the strength. Support players who feel stuck by letting the group offer ideas.

fields.label: Two true things about me
A strength I named
What it felt like to say it
A strength I heard in someone else

title: Emotion Charades Pass the Card
summary: Players act out a feeling card in silence while the group guesses and shares a time they felt it.
goal: Use it to help a group recognize feelings in bodies and talk about when they show up.
body_md: Rules: draw a card, act out the feeling without words, group guesses. The guesser then shares a brief time they felt it, or passes. Turns rotate. Debrief on how feelings looked different on different people. For children, a parent or helper can act too. Keep it playful and let anyone sit out a round.

fields.label: The feeling I acted out
How the group knew
A time I felt something like that
A feeling that was hard to act out

title: Problem-Solving Relay Game
summary: Teams pass a problem card down the line, each adding one possible solution.
goal: Use it to help a group brainstorm many solutions before choosing one.
body_md: Rules: each team gets a problem card and a timer. Players take turns adding one solution each, no judging, and the last player circles the one the team would try. Debrief by asking how it felt to hear so many options and what changed when nobody shot ideas down. Link it to a real problem someone is facing.

fields.label: The problem on our card
Solutions our team came up with
The one we would try and why
A real problem I could use this on

title: Mindful Moment Bingo Challenge
summary: Players mark squares for small mindful moments across the week and bring the card back.
goal: Use it to help a client notice the present moment in everyday life through a simple challenge.
body_md: Make a card with squares like noticing the taste of the first bite or the feel of warm water. Rules: mark a square when you do it, and bring the card back. Turns are not needed; it is a solo challenge shared in session. Debrief on the easiest and hardest squares and what the client noticed.

fields.label: The squares I marked
The easiest moment to notice
The hardest one
Something I noticed that surprised me

title: Present-Day Anchors Inventory
summary: An inventory of people, places and objects that tell the client's body it is here and now.
goal: Use it to help a client gather present-day anchors they can reach for when reminders arise.
body_md: Keep this entirely in the present: what is in the room, who is reliable, what is safe today. Do not ask for details about past events. Have the client carry a short list on a phone or card. Revisit it as anchors change, and add new ones when the old ones stop working.

fields.label: People who help me feel steady
Places where my body relaxes a little
Objects I can hold or look at
Sounds or smells that remind me I am here now
The anchor I will keep with me this week

title: Reminder Versus Danger Sorting Sheet
summary: A sheet for sorting what is a reminder of the past from what is a present-day risk.
goal: Use it to help a client pause and check what is happening now when a reminder hits.
body_md: Work only with present-day situations the client names, not with the memory itself. The sheet asks what is here now, what is a reminder, and what actually puts them at risk today. Move slowly and let the client set the pace. If the sheet stirs up too much, stop and ground first.

fields.label: A moment when my body reacted strongly
What was actually happening around me
What it reminded me of, in a few words only
What is different about today
What I can do to help my body settle

title: Making Room While Staying Grounded Pacing Sheet
summary: A pacing sheet that pairs willingness with grounding so a client approaches hard feelings in small amounts.
goal: Use it to help a client make room for feelings in measured steps while staying anchored.
body_md: Pacing is the point: small amounts, then back to the anchors. Teach the client that they decide when to pause. Avoid inviting detail about what happened. Check how the practice felt in the body and adjust the length down if it was too much. Some clients prefer to start with only noticing a sensation.

fields.label: A feeling I could make a little room for today
How long I will stay with it before I ground
My grounding anchor for coming back
What I noticed in my body
How I decided to pause or continue

title: Window Pacing Dial for Hard Days
summary: A dial from calm to overloaded with a skill matched to each setting.
goal: Use it to help a client notice where they are on the dial and match a skill to it.
body_md: Draw the dial together and agree on what each zone feels like for this client. At the high end, grounding and paced breathing come first; at the low end, gentle movement or contact. This is a personal tool, not a measurement. Review which skills fit which zone and update the dial after hard weeks.

fields.label: What a calm day feels like in my body
What starting to overload feels like
A skill for when I am starting to overload
A skill for when I feel shut down
Who I can contact if the dial goes too high

title: Here and Now Orientation Card Game
summary: A card game where players name what they can see, hear and touch in the room right now.
goal: Use it to help a group practice noticing the present moment in a light, predictable way.
body_md: Rules: each card asks for one thing in the room, like something blue or something soft. Players take turns drawing and answering, and anyone can pass. Keep it playful and predictable. Debrief on how it felt to look around and which cards were easiest. It is practice in orienting, not a discussion of the past.

fields.label: The card I drew
What I noticed in the room
What my body felt like afterward
A way I can do this on my own

title: Worry Postponement Window Calendar
summary: A weekly calendar that places a short worry window and tracks what is left over at the end.
goal: Use it to help a client set worries aside until a set time and see how many are still there.
body_md: Choose a window that is not near bedtime. The client jots worries as they come and revisits the list in the window. Many find that fewer need attention by then. Expect it to feel unnatural at first; keep the window short and consistent. Ask what was left on the list and what they did with it.

fields.label: When my worry window is each day
Worries I wrote down to save for later
Which ones still mattered when the window came
What I did about the ones that mattered
What I noticed about my day outside the window

title: Uncertainty Tolerance Experiment Log
summary: A log for deliberately leaving small things uncertain and recording what happens.
goal: Use it to help a client test how it feels to not know and not fix.
body_md: Pick small, safe uncertainties, such as not rechecking a message. The client predicts the distress, tries it, and records the actual result. Increase gradually. Be clear that the aim is not to prove anything bad cannot happen but to build comfort with not knowing. Review the pattern in what they predicted versus what they felt.

fields.label: The small uncertainty I chose
How much distress I predict, 0 to 100
What I did instead of fixing it
How much distress I felt
What I learned about not knowing

title: Anxious Mind as a Chatty Neighbor Defusion Sheet
summary: A sheet that casts the anxious mind as a chatty neighbor whose talk can be noted without obeying.
goal: Use it to help a client notice worry as talk rather than instructions.
body_md: Invite the client to name their mind's recurring lines as if a neighbor said them over the fence. Humor often helps. The client chooses what to do while the neighbor keeps talking. Be careful not to dismiss worry as silly; the point is choice, not suppression. Practice during the week and bring back the best lines.

fields.label: What my neighbor said this week
What it wanted me to do
What I chose to do instead
What mattered more to me than listening

title: Anxiety Body Check and Soothe Plan
summary: A body scan paired with a menu of soothing skills for each sensation.
goal: Use it to help a client link body sensations with a skill that eases them.
body_md: Walk through the body from head to feet, naming where anxiety shows up. For each spot, choose a skill, such as paced breathing for the chest or a warm drink for the hands. The plan should be small enough to use at a desk. Review which pairings the client actually used.

fields.label: Where anxiety shows up in my body
A skill that fits each place
Which skill I will try first
What happened when I used it
What I will add to my plan

title: Worry Monster Name and Tame Drawing
summary: A child draws their worry as a monster, gives it a silly name and decides what it needs.
goal: Use it to help a child make a worry less scary by drawing and naming it.
body_md: Let the child draw their worry as a creature and give it a name and a silly voice. Ask what it is afraid of and what it needs to calm down. A parent watches and learns the language the child uses, then uses it at home. Do not rush to talk the child out of the worry; simply make room for it.

fields.label: What my worry monster looks like
Its silly name
What it is afraid of
What it needs to calm down
What a parent can say when it shows up

title: Low-Mood Day Menu of Minimums
summary: A menu of the smallest versions of daily tasks for days when everything feels heavy.
goal: Use it to help a client keep a floor under their day when energy is very low.
body_md: Build the menu on a better day so it is ready on a hard one. Each item is the minimum: a glass of water, one text, five minutes outside. Avoid making it a to-do list that becomes another source of guilt. Review which minimums were used and which felt too big, and shrink those.

fields.label: The smallest way I can take care of my body
The smallest way I can connect with someone
The smallest thing I can do outside
A minimum for something I usually care about
Where I will keep this menu

title: Mood and Activity Pairing Chart
summary: A chart that pairs daily activities with mood ratings to find what lifts and what drains.
goal: Use it to help a client find which activities are worth doing more or less.
body_md: Ask for entries at set times of day with two ratings, pleasure and sense of accomplishment. At review, look for the surprises, such as a short walk that scores higher than expected. Pick one activity to schedule more of. Keep the tone curious; the chart is not a verdict on the client's week.

fields.label: What I did in this time block
Pleasure, 0 to 10
Sense of accomplishment, 0 to 10
What stood out when I looked across the week
One activity I will schedule more of

title: Small Valued Steps for Heavy Days Planner
summary: A planner that connects a value to the smallest step that can be taken even when mood is low.
goal: Use it to help a client act on a value without waiting to feel better first.
body_md: Choose one value and the tiniest action that fits it, such as texting a friend as an act of connection. Explain that action can come before the feeling. Check the plan against the client's actual energy and shrink it if it looks heavy. Celebrate the doing, not the mood afterward.

fields.label: A value that matters to me
The smallest step that fits it
When and where I will do it
What my mind may say about it
How I will do it anyway

title: Reasons to Stay and Support Card
summary: A pocket card with the client's reasons, supports and a place for 988.
goal: Use it to help a client keep their reasons and their supports within reach.
body_md: Complete it with the client in session, not as homework. Use their words for the reasons. Include people to contact and the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) if thoughts of ending their life come up. Check whether the card feels usable and update it together, and follow your own risk procedures.

fields.label: Reasons that matter to me
People I can contact and how
Things I can do to get through a hard hour
The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988
Where I will keep this card

title: Partner Support Plan for Low Mood Weeks
summary: A plan for how a partner can help in low-mood weeks without taking over.
goal: Use it to help a couple agree on supportive actions and boundaries during heavy stretches.
body_md: Each partner says what helps and what they can offer. Keep requests concrete, like cooking together or a short walk. The supporting partner also names what they need so they do not burn out. Treat the plan as a draft and review it after a hard week.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps when my mood is low
Partner B: what I can offer
What I need so I do not burn out
A signal we will use when it is a heavy day
When we will review this plan

title: Doorway Launch Pad Setup Sheet
summary: A sheet for setting up a spot by the door with everything needed for leaving.
goal: Use it to help a client cut down the scramble before leaving the house.
body_md: Walk through the client's usual exits and list what gets forgotten. Set up one visible spot for keys, wallet and bag. Keep it simple and visual. Ask what usually breaks the system and plan for that. Check back in a week and move things around until it fits the client's habits.

fields.label: What I usually forget when I leave
What I need at the launch pad
Where the launch pad will go
What usually breaks my system
How I will remember to use it

title: Task Starting Barriers Log
summary: A log of what gets in the way of starting a task and the smallest first move.
goal: Use it to help a client see the barrier to starting and shrink the first step.
body_md: Have the client log tasks they put off and what felt hard about the start. Look for patterns like unclear first steps or boredom. Pair each barrier with a tiny first move of two minutes or less. Avoid framing delay as a character flaw. Review which first moves actually got things going.

fields.label: The task I put off
What made it hard to start
The first two-minute move
What happened when I tried it
What I will try next time

title: Values Behind the Pile Sorting Sheet
summary: A sheet that links neglected tasks to the values behind them to build motivation.
goal: Use it to help a client reconnect with why a task matters before they start it.
body_md: Pick a task that has been sitting, then ask what value it serves, such as care for family or financial peace. Writing the reason can lift the dread. Keep it short. Pair it with a small action step and a time. Do not use values as a stick; the aim is meaning.

fields.label: A task that has been waiting
The value behind it
What my mind says about starting
The tiny step I will take today
When I will do it

title: Household Rhythm Agreement for Two
summary: A weekly agreement on who does what and when, with reminders chosen by the person doing it.
goal: Use it to help a couple share household tasks without nagging or resentment.
body_md: Each partner lists tasks they can own and how they want to be reminded. The reminder should come from the doer's system, not the partner's voice. Check fairness of effort together. Revisit after two weeks and renegotiate. Name strengths of each partner too so it does not become a list of faults.

fields.label: Tasks Partner A will own
Tasks Partner B will own
How each of us wants to be reminded
What we do when a task slips
When we will review this agreement

title: Focus Mission Control Board Craft
summary: A craft board where a child sets out a mission with steps and a timer.
goal: Use it to help a child break a task into steps they can see and tick off.
body_md: Build the board with pictures for each step and a sand timer or kitchen timer. The child picks a mission, like getting ready for school, and moves a marker along. Parent role: set the board up, cheer progress, and keep reminders to a single prompt. Adjust the steps if the child gets stuck at one.

fields.label: My mission
The steps on my board
How long my timer runs
What helps me keep going
What my parent does to help

title: Urge Wave Surfing Log
summary: A log of an urge from rise to peak to fade, with what the client did while it passed.
goal: Use it to help a client see that urges rise and fall and that they can ride one out.
body_md: Ask the client to record the time, the urge strength and what they did to ride it out. Use their own words for urges and substance use. Review the log for what made the wave shorter or easier. Do not frame a lapse as failure; look at what the log shows about triggers and supports.

fields.label: What set off the urge
Strength at the start, 0 to 10
What I did while it passed
Strength after, 0 to 10
What helped most

title: Substance Use Chain Analysis Sheet
summary: A step-by-step sheet tracing the links before and after a moment of substance use.
goal: Use it to help a client find where in the chain a different choice was possible.
body_md: Walk through one recent moment from the earliest trigger forward, without shame. Mark the links where something else could have happened. The aim is a clearer map, not blame. Pick one link to practice changing. Use plain words like substance use and urges.

fields.label: The earliest trigger I can see
The thoughts and urges that followed
What I did next
What happened afterward
A link where I could try something else

title: Urge Surfing With Values Anchor Practice
summary: A practice that pairs noticing an urge with a reminder of what the client cares about.
goal: Use it to help a client stay with an urge while keeping a value in view.
body_md: Describe the urge as a wave with a rising, peak and fade. The client names a value they want to protect, such as trust or health, and holds it in mind during the practice. Rehearse in session with a mild urge. Keep language about substance use matter-of-fact.

fields.label: The urge I am noticing
Where I feel it in my body
The value I want to keep in view
What I do while it passes
What I notice when it fades

title: Urge Skills Menu by Length of Wave
summary: A menu of distress tolerance skills grouped by how long the urge may last.
goal: Use it to help a client pick a skill that fits how intense and how long an urge is.
body_md: Sort skills into quick (cold water, paced breathing), medium (a walk, calling someone) and longer (an activity or meeting). The client rates which they would really use. Add a contact for support. Review which items worked and replace the ones that did not.

fields.label: Quick skills I could use in a minute
Medium skills for twenty minutes
Longer skills for a rough evening
A person I can contact
The skill I will try first

title: Trigger Cards and Coping Moves Game

title: Questions Without Answers After Loss Page
summary: The client lists unanswerable questions after a loss and practices holding them without needing an answer.
goal: Use it to help a client carry the questions that have no answers.
body_md: Invite the client to write the questions they keep asking, such as why or what if. Notice how the mind searches for a reason. Practice a kind line to say to oneself when the questions return.

What happens when I search for an answer
A kind thing I can say to myself
Someone I can share the questions with

title: Making Room for Missing Them Practice
summary: The client allows missing someone to be present while choosing a small way to honor the relationship.
goal: Use it to help a client carry love and loss together.
body_md: Let the client describe what missing feels like in the body. Then pick a small act that honors the relationship. Go at their pace and expect tears. Offer silence when needed.

fields.label: What missing them feels like
Something I loved about them
A small way to honor them this week
Who can be with me

title: Grieving Differently Together Talk Guide
summary: Partners share how each grieves and agree on how to support one another.
goal: Use it to help partners respect different ways of grieving.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B describe how they grieve and what support they want, without asking the other to grieve the same way. Agree on signals for needing space or company and plan a check-in.

Partner B: how I grieve

title: Memory Rock Garden Craft
summary: The child paints rocks with memories of someone they miss and arranges them in a small garden.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on way to remember someone.
body_md: Provide smooth rocks and paint and let the child decide what to put on each one. Arrange them in a small garden at home. Parents are invited to share their own memories. Follow the child's lead and keep the mood open.

What I painted on the rocks
A favorite memory
Where we will keep the garden

title: Needs and Wants Sort for Two
summary: Each partner sorts what they need from the relationship from what they would like, then they compare.
goal: Use it to help partners tell core needs from preferences before a hard talk.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B each sort items into needs, wants and flexible, then share one need they have not said plainly. The listening partner reflects before responding. Keep it to one need each and plan a next step together.

fields.label: Partner A: my needs and my wants
Partner A: a need I have not said aloud

Partner B: a need I have not said aloud

title: Interpretation Check in Conflict Page
summary: The client lists the story they told in a conflict and other stories that could also fit.
goal: Use it to help a client slow down the stories that heat up conflict.
body_md: Take a recent conflict and write the facts, the interpretation and the feeling. Brainstorm other possible reasons for the other person's behavior. Ask what the client could check out rather than assume.

The story I told myself
Other stories that could fit
What I could ask to check

title: Who I Want to Be in Conflict Page
summary: The client names the qualities they want to show in conflict and a small action for each.
goal: Use it to help a client act from values when a conversation gets heated.
body_md: Ask what kind of partner, friend or family member they want to be when things get hard. List qualities and translate each into a concrete behavior. Practice one in session and plan for a recent flashpoint.

fields.label: Qualities I want to show in conflict
What each looks like in action

title: Repair After a Fight Skills Plan
summary: The client plans a repair after a fight using validation, an apology where fitting and a request.
goal: Use it to help a client reach out after conflict in a way that invites repair.
body_md: Work through what the client wants after the fight, then draft a short message or script with validation, a fitting apology and a clear request. Role-play it. Check if the timing feels right before they send it.

fields.label: What happened in the fight
What I want from the repair
What I might say, step by step

title: Weekly State of the Union Meeting Guide
summary: Partners hold a brief weekly meeting with appreciation, what went well and one issue to work on.
goal: Use it to give partners a regular, calm space to talk about the relationship.
body_md: Set a time, a place and a start with appreciations. Then each partner names what went well and one issue. Keep to one issue and use soft startups. End with a plan and a hug if both want one. Review in session.

Partner B: what I appreciated this week

title: Choice and Control Daily Menu
summary: The client lists small choices available to them each day and picks a few to practice.
goal: Use it to help a client rebuild a sense of choice and control in small daily ways.
body_md: Work from the present only. The client lists everyday choices, from what to wear to who to see, and marks the ones they want to practice. Praise any choice, however small. No details of past events are asked for.

fields.label: Small choices I can make today

How it felt to choose

title: Where Responsibility Belongs Reminder Cards
summary: The client writes reminder cards that place responsibility where it belongs, with no need to recount events.
goal: Use it to help a client hold steady against self-blame in the present.
body_md: Work in the present: the client writes brief statements to counter self-blame without describing events. Practice reading them aloud. Check if any statement feels untrue and adjust. Offer to pause at any time.

fields.label: A self-blame thought that shows up
A statement that feels true and kind
Who in my life says kind things like this
Where I will keep the cards

title: Small Steps in My Own Time Values Page
summary: The client picks values and one tiny action, at a pace that they set and can change at any time.
goal: Use it to help a client move toward what matters without being rushed.
body_md: Emphasize that pacing is in the client's hands. They name values and choose one tiny action to try, with permission to stop. Offer breaks and grounding as needed. No narrative is needed.

fields.label: Something that matters to me
One tiny action I could take
What pace feels right
What I will do if it feels like too much

title: Soothing Skills for Body Reminders Menu
summary: The client builds a menu of soothing and grounding skills for moments the body feels on alert.
goal: Use it to give a client ready steps when the body feels on edge.
body_md: List skills by sense: temperature, textures, scents, sounds, movement. Practice two in session. Let the client decide what is comfortable, and drop anything that does not feel safe. Plan who to contact if needed.

fields.label: Skills for my hands and skin
Skills for sound or scent
Movement that helps
People I can reach out to

title: Support Network and Pacing Plan
summary: The client maps people and places that feel safe and plans how fast to share and what to share.
goal: Use it to help a client plan support and pacing on their own terms.
body_md: Map supports as circles from closest to more distant and note what the client wants from each. They decide how much to share and when. Call or text 988 appears in the plan for hard nights. Mandatory reporting duties apply if a minor is involved.

fields.label: People and places that feel safe
What I want from each
What I will share and what I will keep private

title: Coping Skill Trial Tracker
summary: The client tries one skill at a time, rates how it worked and keeps the ones that fit.
goal: Use it to help a client find the skills that really work for them.
body_md: Pick a skill and a situation and ask the client to rate distress before and after. Keep a running page of skills and notes. Retire what does not help without judgment and add what does to a short toolbox.

Situation

title: If-Then Coping Plan Cards
summary: The client writes if-then cards that link a specific trigger to a chosen coping step.
goal: Use it to help a client decide in advance what they will do when stress hits.
body_md: Pick two or three recurring triggers and write if-then plans for each in specific terms. Practice aloud. Keep cards where they can be found quickly and review after a week to see which plans were used.

fields.label: Trigger one
If it happens, then I will
Trigger two
If it happens, then I will

title: Choosing a Skill That Serves Values Page
summary: The client tests whether a coping move moves them toward what they care about or just brings relief.
goal: Use it to help a client choose skills with their values in mind.
body_md: Ask the client to list moves they use under stress and sort them by whether they bring relief only or also serve what they value. Neither is wrong, but notice costs. Pick one skill to add.

fields.label: Moves I use when stressed
What each gives me in the short run
What each costs or gives in the long run
A skill I will add

title: ACCEPTS Distraction Pick Card
summary: The client chooses distraction skills from the ACCEPTS list and rates each after trying it.
goal: Use it to give a client ready distraction ideas for hard moments they cannot change.
body_md: Go through the ACCEPTS list and mark the ones that sound doable. Try one in session. Distraction is for riding out a moment, not for avoiding issues forever, so plan a return to the problem later.

title: Coping Skills Memory Match Game
summary: Players match skill cards with situation cards and explain why the skill fits.
goal: Use it to help players link coping skills to real situations.
body_md: Make paired cards, one with a situation and one with a skill. Rules: turn over two cards, make a match, and explain why the skill fits. Scoring is for explanations, not just speed. Debrief on skills players want to try.

fields.label: A pair I matched
Why the skill fits

A situation I will use it in

title: Fear Rating Step Log
summary: The client rates fear on a thermometer across practice steps and notes how it changes.
goal: Use it to help a client track how fear changes as they stay with a step.
body_md: Agree on a rating scale and a practice step. The client records fear before, at peak and after, with notes on what they did. Look at the shape of change together and plan the next step at their pace.

fields.label: The practice step
Fear before and at the peak
Fear after
