title: Imagined Versus Actual Outcome Comparison
summary: The client writes what they expect to happen, tests it and compares it with what did happen.
goal: Use it to help a client check fearful predictions against real results.
body_md: Before a practice step the client writes the feared outcome and how likely it feels. Afterward they record what happened. Compare the two and discuss what to try next. Gently note outcomes that were better than feared.

fields.label: What I expect will happen
How likely it feels
What actually happened
What I learned

title: Bringing Fear Along on the Climb Page
summary: The client takes a step toward something they value with fear coming along instead of waiting for it to leave.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values while carrying fear.
body_md: Link a feared situation to something the client wants, such as travel or health care. They name the fear, thank it and decide the step. Practice breathing and noticing. Keep the pace in the client's hands.

fields.label: What I want that fear gets in the way of
The fear I will bring along
The step I will take
How I carried the fear

title: Approach Plan for Avoided Places
summary: The client uses opposite action to plan a gradual approach to a place or object they avoid.
goal: Use it to help a client plan small approaches instead of avoidance.
body_md: Confirm that the fear is out of step with the actual risk, then plan steps that approach the avoided place or object. Use relaxed breathing and a half smile. Record each step and how the urge to avoid changed.

fields.label: The place or thing I avoid
The urge to avoid and what it says
Steps of my approach plan
How the urge changed

title: Brave Steps Sticker Chart Craft
summary: The child decorates a path chart and earns a sticker for each brave step toward something they fear.
goal: Use it to help a child and parent track small brave steps.
body_md: Draw a winding path with steps and let the child decorate it. Choose very small first steps with the child and parent. Parents give a sticker and warm words for trying, whether or not it went well, and avoid pushing.

fields.label: The thing I want to get closer to
My first brave step
What my grown-up will say
How it felt to place the sticker

title: Social Media Feed Body Talk Audit
summary: The client reviews what their feeds say about bodies and chooses what to keep, mute or add.
goal: Use it to help a client shape feeds that feel kinder to how they see themselves.
body_md: Ask the client to scroll their feeds with you and note how each account makes them feel. Choose a few to mute and a few to add. Focus on the feeling, not comparison of bodies. Review how it went after a week.

fields.label: Accounts that leave me feeling worse
Accounts that leave me feeling better
What I will mute, keep or add
How my feed feels after a week

title: Body Talk Habits Reframe Page
summary: The client notices unkind talk about their body and writes a fairer or neutral reply.
goal: Use it to help a client turn down the volume on harsh body talk.
body_md: Collect a few harsh lines the client says about their body and where they happen. Write neutral or kind replies in their voice. Aim for believable rather than glowing. Practice aloud and review which ones stuck.

fields.label: A harsh line I say about my body
When it shows up
A neutral or kind reply
Which reply felt most believable

title: Body as Home Not Project Page
summary: The client explores what changes when they treat the body as a home to live in rather than a project to fix.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values instead of waiting to feel good about their body.
body_md: Ask the client what they put off until they feel better about their body. Link each to a value and pick one to do now with the thoughts along for the ride. Keep the talk on living, not looks.

fields.label: Things I put off because of how I feel about my body
Values behind them
One I will do now
Thoughts that will come along

title: Kind Action Against Body Avoidance Card
summary: The client uses opposite action to approach activities they avoid because of body shame.
goal: Use it to help a client step toward avoided activities with kindness.
body_md: Name the emotion, such as shame, and its urge to hide. Choose an avoided activity and plan a small step. Add a kind self-statement. Review afterward how the urge to hide shifted and what to try next.

fields.label: What I avoid out of shame
The urge it brings
The small step I will take
A kind thing I will say to myself

title: Compliments Beyond Appearance Game
summary: Players trade compliments about character, skills and actions, never appearance.
goal: Use it to help a group practice noticing and naming what they value in each other beyond looks.
body_md: Rules: draw a prompt card such as a skill, a kind action or a quality, and give a compliment that fits it to another player. Appearance is off limits. Debrief on how it felt to give and receive such compliments.

A compliment I received

A quality I want to notice more

title: Energy Budget for the Week Ahead
summary: The client lists the week's demands and sorts them by how much energy each takes and gives back.
goal: Use it to help a client plan a week that leaves room for rest and for what matters to them.
body_md: Have the client list the coming week's commitments, then mark each as draining, neutral or refilling. Look together at the balance and choose one swap or one protected rest slot. Keep it practical; the client decides what is realistic.

title: Two-Column Decision Map
summary: A grid where the client weighs a decision against what they value, not just pros and cons.
goal: Use it to help a client slow down a stuck decision and see it through their values.
body_md: Ask the client to name the decision and two options, then fill both columns. The extra row, what this says about what I care about, often shifts the conversation from fear to direction. Resist advising; let the grid do the work.

title: Small Wins Evening Ledger
summary: A running page for recording small things done, with a note on what each took.
goal: Use it to help a client notice effort that a harsh inner judge tends to skip.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Ask for two or three entries a day, kept deliberately small. Review in session by reading entries back aloud rather than summarizing them. Notice whether the client discounts entries and gently ask what they would say if a friend wrote them.

fields.label: Something I did today

title: Hard Talk Rehearsal Planner
summary: The client scripts a hard conversation: the goal, the opening line and a plan if it goes sideways.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare for a difficult talk so they can stay steady in it.
body_md: Pick one real conversation coming up. Work through the opening line out loud, not only on paper, and agree on a pause phrase the client can use. Afterward the client notes how it went, which is more useful than whether it went well.

title: Evening Handoff to Tomorrow
summary: A short end-of-day page that moves open tasks and worries onto paper before bed.
goal: Use it to help a client set down the day's loose ends so the evening can wind down.
duration: Ten minutes daily for one week
body_md: Suggest doing it away from the bed at a set time. The point is to park, not solve: each worry gets one next action or a note that nothing can be done tonight. Review in session what got easier and what stuck.

goal: Use it to help a client move from a hot thought to a reply that fits more of the facts.
body_md: Walk through one recent upset moment, moving from situation to feeling to automatic thought to evidence both ways. Spend the most time on the final line, a balanced reply in the client's own words, and have them rate belief before and after.

Facts that do not fit it

goal: Use it to help a client check a prediction against what actually happens.
body_md: Have the client state the prediction as specifically as they can, with a rating, and design a small test they would actually do. Agree on what result would count before running it. At review, compare outcome and prediction without grading the client.

goal: Use it to help a client see which parts of the day lift or lower their mood.
body_md: Introduce it as data collection, not homework to get right; partial entries are fine. At review, look for patterns in time of day, company and activity, then choose one slot to adjust. Keep the client's curiosity ahead of judgment.

summary: A sheet that follows a thought down to the belief underneath it, then looks for another view.
goal: Use it to help a client name a deeper belief and begin to hold it more loosely.

goal: Use it to help a client link daily choices to what matters most to them.

title: Passengers on the Bus: Who Is Along for the Ride

goal: Use it to help a client keep driving toward a value while hard passengers come along.

title: Fork in the Road Choice Map

goal: Use it to help a client spot the moment of choice when a hard feeling shows up.

goal: Use it to help a client put small good experiences into the week on purpose.

goal: Use it to help partners build a regular, low-stakes space for warmth and small asks.

goal: Use it to help partners agree on repair moves ahead of time so they are easier to use mid-conflict.

title: Feelings Weather Window Craft
summary: The child decorates a paper window and draws today's inside weather for feelings.
goal: Use it to help a child name a feeling through a picture before they have to find the words.
body_md: Give the child a paper window frame to draw and color the weather inside: sunny, stormy, foggy, or mixed. Ask them to tell you about the picture. A parent can help by taking the window home and checking in once a day, using the weather instead of questions.

fields.label: The weather inside me today
Where I feel it in my body
What makes the weather change
What helps when it is stormy
Who I can show my window to

title: Calm Down Jar Building Session
summary: The child builds a glitter jar and uses it as a way to watch their body settle.
goal: Use it to give a child a tool to practice slowing down alongside a caring adult.
body_md: Build the jar together with water, glue and glitter. Shake it and breathe together while the glitter settles. Tell the parent that the jar is a shared tool, never a punishment or a forced time-out, and practice with it when things are calm.

fields.label: What my jar looks like
What I thought about while watching it settle
What my body felt like
When I might use my jar
Who I can use it with

title: Brave Steps Ladder Poster
summary: The child draws a ladder of small brave steps and colors each rung when they try it.
goal: Use it to help a child take small steps toward something that feels hard, at their own pace.
body_md: The child draws the ladder with the goal at the top and tiny steps on the rungs. A parent's role is to cheer effort, not outcomes, and never push a step the child is not ready for. Agree on one rung to try this week.

fields.label: The big thing I want to do
My first tiny step
My next steps up the ladder
Who cheers me on
How I will celebrate a step

title: Kindness Chain Paper Links
summary: The child makes a paper chain with one link for each kind act they notice or do.
goal: Use it to help a child notice kindness around them and in themselves.
body_md: Give the child strips of paper to color and write on. Each link records something kind they did or saw. A parent adds links too, which makes it a shared project. Look at the chain together and talk about how it grew.

fields.label: A kind thing I did
A kind thing someone did for me
How it felt
A kind thing I want to do tomorrow

title: Safe People Fingers Drawing
summary: The child traces a hand and writes or draws a trusted person on each finger.
goal: Use it to help a child name the people they can go to when something is hard or worrying.
body_md: Trace the child's hand and have them put a trusted person on each finger. Ask what each person does that helps. Let the parent see it at the end. If a child discloses anything about safety or harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The people on my fingers
What each one does that helps
How I can tell them I need help
A time someone helped me
A grown-up I would tell if I felt unsafe

title: Feeling Charades Remix
summary: Players act out feelings without words while others guess, then share a time they felt it.
goal: Use it to help a group build a shared language for feelings through play.
body_md: Rules: each turn, a player draws a feeling card and acts it out silently; others guess. The actor then says when they last felt it, if they choose. Pass is always allowed. Debrief on which feelings were hardest to show and to name.

fields.label: A feeling that was easy to act out
A feeling that was hard
A time I felt one of these
What I noticed about others' faces and bodies

title: Coping Ideas Bingo Night
summary: A bingo card of coping skills that players cross off by trying or sharing them.
goal: Use it to help a group see how many ways there are to cope and try new ones.
body_md: Rules: each card holds coping skills in the squares. Take turns sharing a time you used one to cross it off, or try a quick one in the room. First to a line calls bingo, but everyone shares at the end. Debrief on which skill they want to try.

fields.label: Skills I already use
One I want to try
One I saw a peer use
When I will use it

title: Worry Monster Tag
summary: A movement game where a worry monster chases players until they use a calming skill to become safe.
goal: Use it to help children and teens practice a calming skill under light pressure.
body_md: Rules: one player is the worry monster. Tagged players freeze until a peer helps them with a calming skill, such as a breath or a grounding count. Rotate the monster. Debrief on what skills helped and how the frozen player felt.

fields.label: What the worry monster felt like to me
Which skill helped most
How it felt to be helped
A skill I want to remember

title: Strengths Spotlight Circle
summary: Players take turns naming a strength they see in another player, and the spotlight player responds.
goal: Use it to help a group practice noticing and receiving positive feedback.
body_md: Rules: one player sits in the spotlight while others each name a strength they have seen, with an example. The spotlight player says thank you and one thing they heard. Anyone may pass. Debrief on how receiving felt compared with giving.

fields.label: A strength someone named in me
A strength I named in someone else
What was hard about receiving
A strength I want to use this week

title: Perspective Dice Roll
summary: Players roll a die to see a situation from different points of view, including their own future self.
goal: Use it to help a group practice flexible thinking about a tough situation.
body_md: Rules: describe a situation; each roll assigns a viewpoint such as a friend, a coach or yourself next year, and the player says what they would notice or say. Players may pass. Debrief on what shifted when the viewpoint did.

fields.label: The situation I brought
A viewpoint that helped
What I noticed from it
What I will keep from this

title: Safe Place Inventory Card
summary: The client lists the places, objects and sensory details that feel steady right now.
goal: Use it to help a client build a set of present-moment anchors to return to when things feel unsteady.
body_md: Keep the focus on the here and now: places, people and objects that feel safe today, with sensory details. Do not ask about what happened. Let the client rate how steady each feels, and invite them to carry the card or photograph it.

fields.label: A place that feels steady to me
What I see, hear and feel there
A person who helps me feel safe
An object I can hold or look at
How steady each feels (0 to 10)

title: Orienting to Now: Five Corners of the Room
summary: A grounding routine of naming what is in each corner of the room, with a log of when it helped.
goal: Use it to give a client a quick way to anchor in the present when reminders pull them back.
body_md: Practice it together while calm: look at each corner, name colors, shapes and one sound, and say today's date aloud. Agree on when to use it. Ask the client to keep a short log of use, and remind them that it is a skill, not a test.

fields.label: When I might need to anchor
What I noticed in each corner
Today's date and where I am
What changed in my body after
Where I will practice it again

title: Making Room for Reminders: A Pacing Page
summary: The client sets a pace for approaching hard material by choosing what to leave for now.
goal: Use it to help a client practice choosing their pace and acting on values when reminders show up.
body_md: Work only with what the client chooses to bring, and agree that anything can be set aside. Link a value to one small action, and list what to do if a reminder arrives. The emphasis is on pacing and choice, not on retelling anything.

fields.label: A value I want to live by
A small action toward it
What reminders may show up
What I can do if they come
What I want to set aside for now

title: Cozy Corner Home Plan
summary: The child draws and plans a cozy corner at home with a parent.
goal: Use it to help a child have a predictable, comforting space and a way to ask for it.
body_md: The child draws the corner and chooses soft items, a light and a favorite object. A parent builds it at home and agrees on how the child asks to use it, without it being a punishment. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties and keep the child's safety first.

fields.label: My cozy corner and what is in it
What makes it feel safe
How I ask to go there
Who can come with me
What I do there

title: Present Moment Scavenger Hunt
summary: Players search the room for items by color, texture and sound to practice anchoring in the present.
goal: Use it to help a group practice a grounding skill through light, low-pressure play.
body_md: Rules: call a category such as something soft, something blue or something that makes a sound, and players find and show an item. No one is required to explain anything. Debrief on how attention felt and when they could use this.

fields.label: What I found
How my body felt while searching
Where I could use this skill
A category I would add

title: What-If Chain Cutter
summary: The client writes a what-if chain, then steps back with questions about likelihood and coping.
goal: Use it to help a client see how a worry grows and respond to it with a question instead of a spiral.
body_md: Have the client write the first what-if and each one that follows, then circle the point where the chain left the facts. Add two questions: how likely is it, and how would I cope if it happened. Keep the tone curious.

fields.label: The first what-if
The next what-ifs in the chain
Where the chain left what I know
How likely, honestly
If it did happen, how I would cope

title: Body Signals Map for Worry
summary: The client marks where worry shows up in the body and what each signal is asking for.
goal: Use it to help a client notice early body signals so they can respond sooner.
body_md: On an outline, the client marks where they feel worry and writes a short description. Then they pair each signal with one response such as a slower breath or a stretch. Patterns often show up across weeks, so repeat it.

fields.label: Where I feel worry in my body
What the signals feel like
What each signal seems to be saying
A response I can try for each
How I will remember to notice

title: Anxiety as a Pushy Passenger
summary: The client gives worry a voice and character, then practices acting on a value with the passenger along.
goal: Use it to help a client change how they relate to worry rather than argue with it.
body_md: Invite the client to name and describe the worry character and what it demands. Then choose a value-based action and practice doing it while the character talks. Ask what it was like to act with worry riding along.

fields.label: What my worry character says and sounds like
What it wants me to do
What I care about instead
A small action I will take with it along
What I notice when I do

title: Worry Dragon Drawing and Tamer Kit
summary: The child draws a worry dragon and builds a kit of calming tools to tame it.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful way to talk about worry and to try calming tools.
body_md: Have the child draw the dragon and describe what it says. Then fill a small kit with tools such as a breathing card, a stress ball or a drawing. A parent learns the tools too and offers them calmly, without pushing the child to talk.

fields.label: What my dragon looks like
What it whispers
Tools in my tamer kit
Who helps me tame it
When I will use a tool

title: Uncertainty Dice
summary: Players roll for small uncertain situations and practice acting without all the answers first.
goal: Use it to help a group practice tolerating uncertainty in small, playful steps.
body_md: Rules: roll a die and carry out the small uncertain task listed, such as choosing a snack without reading the label first or picking a seat at random. Share what you predicted and what happened. Debrief on how uncertainty felt and how it passed.

fields.label: My prediction before I tried
What actually happened
How uncertainty felt in my body
A small uncertainty I want to try this week

title: Low Mood Day Plan: The Smallest Version
summary: A planner for a hard day that sets out the smallest versions of key activities.
goal: Use it to help a client keep a thread of activity going when energy and motivation are low.
body_md: Together, break each usual activity into a minimal version, such as a five-minute walk or one dish. The client picks two for the day and notes their mood before and after. Be careful to praise effort, not size. Mention 988 (call or text) if thoughts of ending life appear.

fields.label: An activity I usually want to do
Its smallest version
Two I will do today
My mood before and after
If thoughts of ending my life come up, I can call or text 988

title: Pleasure and Mastery Log
summary: The client logs activities and rates both how pleasant and how accomplishing each felt.
goal: Use it to help a client notice which activities bring enjoyment and which bring a sense of achievement.
body_md: Introduce the two ratings separately, since many clients find the second rises even when the first stays flat. At review, pick the highest-rated activities and plan more of them. Keep entries brief.

fields.label: Activity
Pleasure (0 to 10)
Mastery (0 to 10)
What I noticed
Activities I want to repeat

title: Values Over Mood: Doing It Anyway Cards
summary: The client writes value-based actions on cards to do whether or not their mood agrees.
goal: Use it to help a client act on what matters when feelings say to stay put.
body_md: The client lists values and writes one small action per card. They draw a card each day and do it with mood as it is. At review, ask what the mood did, not whether the action worked. Be curious, not pushy.

fields.label: A value that still matters
A small action for it
What my mood says about doing it
What I did
What I noticed

title: Opposite Action for Withdrawal
summary: The client plans small steps to reach out or go out when low mood pulls toward withdrawing.
goal: Use it to help a client try opposite action when withdrawing is not serving them.
body_md: Name the urge to withdraw and check whether it fits the facts today. Plan one small act of reaching out or going out, all the way. Debrief afterward on mood and on what made it easier.

fields.label: The urge I notice
What it tells me to do
A small step the other way
How I will do it all the way
What happened

title: Partner Check-In for Low Mood Days
summary: Partners agree ahead of time what helps and what does not on a hard day.
goal: Use it to help partners support each other on low mood days without pressure.
body_md: Each partner says what helps, what does not, and how to ask. Agree on a signal for a hard day and on two small ways to connect. Include a safety line: if thoughts of ending life come up, call or text 988 together.

fields.label: What helps me on a hard day
What does not help
How I will tell my partner
Two small ways we can connect
If thoughts of ending life come up, we can call or text 988

title: Launch Pad for Starting Tasks
summary: A short pre-start list that lowers friction for the first two minutes of a task.
goal: Use it to help a client get a task started by shrinking the first step.
body_md: Pick one task the client avoids starting. Work out the smallest visible first step, what to set out ahead, and a cue to begin. Practice the first two minutes in session. Treat it as a design problem, not a character flaw.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off
The first two-minute step
What I can set out ahead of time
My cue to start
What gets in my way

title: Time Estimate Check: Guess, Time, Compare
summary: The client guesses how long tasks take, times them, and compares to adjust planning.
goal: Use it to help a client plan with more realistic time estimates.
body_md: Pick three recurring tasks. The client writes a guess, times the task, and compares. After a week, look for patterns, such as tasks that run long, and add buffer. Keep it light and curiosity-driven.

fields.label: Task
My guess
How long it took
What I notice
How much buffer I will add

title: Body Double Challenge Chart
summary: The child and a parent pick a task and work side by side, with a drawn chart of check-in stars.
goal: Use it to help a child begin and stay with a task with a calm adult nearby.
body_md: The child and parent sit near each other, each working on something, and check in at set times. The child colors a star at each check. The parent keeps encouragement warm and avoids hovering or correcting.

fields.label: The task I will do
How long I will work
Who sits with me
My check-in times
How I reward myself after

title: Beat the Timer Sprint Game
summary: Players race a visible timer on short real tasks and plan a brief reward after each round.
goal: Use it to help a group practice starting and finishing in short bursts.
body_md: Rules: choose a small task, set a timer for a short sprint, and work until it rings. A break follows. Tally rounds but never rank people. Debrief on what helped focus and what pulled attention away.

fields.label: What I worked on
What helped me stay with it
What pulled me away
A sprint length that works for me

title: Household Reminder System Design
summary: Partners design a shared system for reminders and handoffs that does not rely on nagging.
goal: Use it to help partners swap reminders for a system both can live with.
body_md: Partners name the tasks that get dropped and design a visible system together, such as shared calendars or a hand-off spot. Agree the person with the task owns the reminder. Discuss how each feels when a reminder comes.

fields.label: Tasks that get dropped
How reminders feel to me
A system we will try
Who owns each reminder

title: Urge Trigger and Response Log
summary: The client logs the situation, thought, urge and what they did, noting what helped.
goal: Use it to help a client see patterns in urges to use substances and plan responses.
body_md: Introduce it as a way to understand urges, not to confess. Look for patterns in time, place and feeling at review, then pick one trigger to plan for. Do not shame slips; ask what the log can teach.

fields.label: Where and when the urge showed up
What I was feeling
What I thought
What I did

title: Urge Surfing with Values Anchor
summary: The client rides an urge like a wave while naming the value they want to act on.
goal: Use it to help a client notice an urge rise and fall without acting on it.
body_md: Guide the client to notice where the urge sits in the body and watch it change. Pair it with a value they are protecting. Practice in session, then have them try it once and report. The urge can stay; the client picks the action.

fields.label: Where I feel the urge in my body
How strong it is at the start (0 to 10)

title: Distract, Soothe and Delay Menu for Urges
summary: The client builds a menu of ways to delay acting on an urge for substance use.
goal: Use it to help a client choose ways to wait out an urge using distress tolerance skills.
body_md: Have the client build a menu of distracting, soothing and delaying options and pick three for the week. Ask them to set a delay of ten minutes and note what happened. Frame a delay as a skill, not a test.

Things that soothe me

title: Support Network Map for Recovery
summary: A map of people and places that support the client's goals around substance use.
goal: Use it to help a client see who and what supports them and where to add more.
body_md: Draw circles for close, helpful and occasional supports, and add places and activities. Then mark where support is missing and plan one person or group to reach out to. Keep the tone respectful and led by the client's goals.

fields.label: People who support my goals
Places and activities that support me

title: Partner Plan for Hard Moments with Urges
summary: Partners agree on what each will do and say when urges show up.
goal: Use it to help partners work out supportive responses to urges that avoid blame.
body_md: Each partner says what they want from the other when an urge appears and what they will not do. Agree a signal and a short script. Review after a week and adjust together.

fields.label: What helps when I notice an urge
What does not help

title: Cool Down Ladder for Rising Anger
summary: The client maps the steps of anger from first signal to peak and picks a skill for each rung.
goal: Use it to help a client catch anger earlier and match a skill to how high it has climbed.
body_md: Draw a ladder from calm to peak. The client writes body signals at each rung and picks a skill: a pause low down, a cold-water or paced-breathing skill higher up. Rehearse one in session. The aim is choice, not suppression.

title: Anger Hot Thoughts Sheet
summary: The client finds the thoughts that fuel anger and looks for fairer, more flexible alternatives.
goal: Use it to help a client see the meaning they add to a trigger and test other readings.
body_md: Take one recent flare-up. Separate the trigger from the thought about it, then look for other possible readings. Keep validation of the feeling first; the feeling makes sense, and the question is which reading helps.

title: Volcano Pressure Gauge Craft
summary: The child builds a paper volcano or gauge and marks what to do at each level of pressure.
goal: Use it to help a child notice rising anger and choose a calming step before it erupts.
body_md: The child decorates a gauge with green, yellow and red zones and writes or draws what helps in each. A parent learns the signals too and coaches calmly, praising the pause rather than correcting the outburst.

title: Pause Button Role-Play Cards
summary: Players act out short frustrating scenes and practice hitting a pause before responding.
goal: Use it to help a group rehearse pausing and choosing a response in safe, short scenes.
body_md: Rules: draw a scene card, act it out, and a teammate calls pause so the actor can choose a skill before responding. Rotate roles. Debrief on how the pause changed the scene and what was hard.

title: Time-Out Agreement for Heated Moments
summary: Partners agree on how to call a break, how long, and how to come back to the talk.
goal: Use it to help partners step away from a heated moment and return without blame.
body_md: Partners agree on a word or signal, a length of break, what each will do to settle, and who reopens the talk. Practice the signal once calmly. The break is not an escape; the return is part of the plan.

goal: Use it to help a client plan graded practice that builds tolerance for uncertainty.
body_md: Build the ladder together with ratings. Choose a rung the client is willing to try, define what delaying or dropping the ritual looks like, and agree on how long to stay. Debrief on what they predicted and what happened.

goal: Use it to help a client change their relationship to intrusive thoughts and keep living by their values.
body_md: Describe thoughts as weather that arrives without invitation. Ask what happens when the client fights them and what happens when they let them pass while doing something that matters. Practice with one example in session.

title: Ritual Time Log
summary: The client tracks when rituals happen, how long they take and what they cost in the day.
goal: Use it to help a client see how much time and energy rituals take, and where to start.

title: Parent Values Heading Check
summary: The parent names the kind of parent they want to be and one small action toward it this week.

summary: A ladder of 'and if that were true, what would it mean?' questions that traces a thought to the belief beneath it.
goal: Use it to help a client find the core belief that keeps a surface thought going.
body_md: Start from a thought that carries strong feeling. Repeat the question calmly and stop when the client's answers begin to repeat. Clients may feel raw at the bottom of the ladder, so leave time to steady and ask what they would like to say back to that belief.

fields.label: The thought I start with
If that were true, what would it mean about me?
And if that were true, what would it mean?
The belief at the bottom of the ladder
Where I learned it, and what I would say back to it

title: Bus Driver Direction Rehearsal
summary: A guided metaphor exercise where difficult thoughts ride as passengers while the client keeps driving toward a value.
goal: Use it to help a client keep moving toward what matters while unwelcome thoughts come along.
body_md: Walk through the metaphor, then ask the client to name their loudest passengers and the direction they want to drive. Clients often try to throw passengers off, so notice that and ask what it costs. Close by choosing one small trip this week.

fields.label: The direction I want to drive my life
My loudest passengers, in their own words
What happens when I stop to argue with them
What driving on with them aboard would look like
One small trip I will take this week

title: Hands as Thoughts Metaphor Practice
summary: A hands-on practice: hold hands tight over the face, then at arm's length, to feel the difference distance makes.
goal: Use it to give a client a felt sense of stepping back from a thought.
body_md: Have the client press hands over their face and describe what they can do, then hold them out and describe the difference. The point is that thoughts stay and become workable at a distance. Adapt the language for younger clients and keep it light.

fields.label: What I could do with my hands tight over my face
What changed when I held them at arm's length
A thought I want to hold at arm's length this week
What I could do with that thought still there
Where I might catch myself holding thoughts too close

title: Workability Check Sheet
summary: A sheet that asks what a client has been doing about a problem and whether it is moving them toward the life they want.
goal: Use it to help a client look at what their strategies cost and what they give.
body_md: Ask the client to list what they have tried, then to rate each strategy on short-term relief and long-term cost. Avoid calling any strategy bad; the question is whether it works for the life they want. Expect some grief about effort that did not pay off and make room for it.

fields.label: The problem I keep trying to solve
Things I have done to deal with it
What each one gave me in the short term
What each one cost me over time
What I want to try that moves me toward my values

title: Observer Self Notes
summary: A notes page for practicing the view of oneself as the one who notices thoughts, feelings and sensations.
goal: Use it to help a client practice noticing experience from a steady, observing place.
body_md: Try a short exercise first, such as noticing the body for a minute, then use the page for recording what the observer saw. Some clients find the idea abstract; use 'the part of you that noticed' as a bridge. Practice on mild moments before hard ones.

fields.label: Something I noticed in my body
Something I noticed in my mind
What was aware of both of those
A time this week I could notice from that place
What I noticed about noticing

title: Values Versus Goals Sorting Sheet
summary: A sorting sheet that separates values, which are ongoing directions, from goals, which can be finished.
goal: Use it to help a client tell a direction they care about from a target they can check off.
body_md: Give examples of each, then ask the client to sort their own list. Many clients have goals but no stated values, or the reverse. Choose one value and turn it into one small goal for the week. The client owns the words, not you.

fields.label: Things I want to achieve
Ways I want to live, whatever I achieve
Which of those are directions and which are finish lines
A value I want to act on this week
One small goal that expresses it

title: Fast Body Reset Practice Card
summary: A practice card for the four body-based skills of temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing and paired relaxation.
goal: Use it to help a client rehearse a fast body-first skill before they need it.
body_md: Practice each skill when the client is calm, then again at a moderate level of distress in session if appropriate. Check that the client is able to do physical activity and use cold safely, and adjust if not. Ask which skill they would reach for first and why.

fields.label: How distressed I am, 0 to 10, before I try a skill
The skill I tried and how long I did it
How distressed I am afterward
Which skill felt easiest to remember
Where I will keep a reminder of it

title: Wise Mind Doorway Practice
summary: A visualization and note page for finding the place where emotion and reason meet before acting.
goal: Use it to help a client pause and look for the wise-mind answer to a hard choice.
body_md: Lead a short image of walking down steps to a quiet center, then ask the question the client is facing. Some clients hear nothing at first; that is fine, and practice on small questions helps. Notice whether the answer comes from fear, anger or calm.

fields.label: The question I want to ask my wise mind
What my emotional mind says
What my reasoning mind says
What I notice when I get quiet
What I might do next

title: Opposite Action Experiment Sheet
summary: A sheet for naming an emotion, its urge, and an opposite action to try when the feeling does not fit the facts.
goal: Use it to help a client test whether acting against an emotion's urge changes how it feels.
body_md: Check first that the emotion does not fit the facts, since the skill is not for emotions that do. Pick a low-stakes try. Ask the client to act all the way, including posture and tone. Review what shifted, even slightly.

fields.label: The emotion and how strong it is, 0 to 10
What the emotion urges me to do
The opposite action I will try
What I did, all the way
How strong the emotion is afterward

title: Assertive Ask Script Builder
summary: A script page that builds a request or a no one step at a time using the DEAR MAN steps.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare and rehearse an assertive ask before the real conversation.
body_md: Choose a real request. Have the client fill each line, then role-play it twice, once with you pushing back. Watch for apologizing language that sneaks in. Ask them to adjust the plan and report back after they try it.

fields.label: What I want to ask for or say no to
The facts, in one or two sentences
How I feel and why it matters to me
The clear ask, in one sentence
What I will say if the person pushes back

title: Coping Ahead Rehearsal Plan
summary: A plan for picturing a hard event ahead of time and rehearsing the skills to use in it.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare for a situation they expect to be difficult.
body_md: Select an event with a date, such as a family dinner. Walk through the likely hard moments and attach a specific skill to each. Rehearse in imagination with the client, including a moment when the plan wobbles, and what they will do then.

fields.label: The event and when it is
The hardest moments I expect
The skill I will use in each moment
What I will say to myself if it gets rough
How I will take care of myself afterward

title: Weekly State of the Relationship Agenda
summary: An agenda partners use once a week to share appreciation, raise one issue and plan a shared item.
goal: Use it to give a couple a steady, brief rhythm for talking about the relationship.
body_md: Teach it in session with a low-stakes topic first. Each partner fills the sheet alone, then they take turns, with the listener only reflecting back. Set a timer and end on appreciation. Check next session whether they used it and what got in the way.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciated this week
Partner B: something I appreciated this week
Partner A: one thing I would like to talk about, kindly
Partner B: one thing I would like to talk about, kindly
Together: one thing we will plan or do this week

title: Gentle Opening Rewrite Practice
summary: A practice sheet where each partner rewrites a harsh opening complaint as a gentle one.
goal: Use it to help partners practice raising a concern without blame.
body_md: Ask each partner to write a real complaint as it first comes out, then rewrite it as 'I feel, about what, I need.' Have them read the rewrite to each other. Notice if one partner's rewrite still carries blame and coach lightly. Keep it about one issue.

fields.label: Partner A: how my complaint first comes out
Partner A: my soft start-up version
Partner B: how my complaint first comes out
Partner B: my soft start-up version
What we each noticed when we heard the rewrite

title: Argument Easing Menu for Two
summary: A menu of small phrases and gestures partners agree on to ease tension during an argument.
goal: Use it to help a couple build their own set of repair moves before they need them.
body_md: Have each partner write what helps them in the middle of a heated moment, then trade lists and pick a few shared ones. Rehearse using one during a mild disagreement in session. Agree on a signal that is not an accusation.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me soften during a fight
Partner B: what helps me soften during a fight
Repair moves we both like
Our signal for a pause
How we will come back to the topic afterward

title: Specific Thanks Exchange Cards
summary: Small cards each partner fills with something specific they valued about the other and exchanges.
goal: Use it to help partners notice and name what is going right between them.
body_md: Ask for specific actions rather than general praise, such as 'you made the coffee before I woke.' Some couples find it awkward at first, so model one yourself. Each partner reads the card aloud and the other says only thank you.

fields.label: Partner A: something specific my partner did that I valued
Partner B: something specific my partner did that I valued
How it felt to hear it
What I would like more of
A small thing I will do for my partner this week

title: Household Load Fairness Talk
summary: A sheet for listing the visible and invisible work of a shared home and talking about how it is divided.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about who carries what, without scoring each other.
body_md: List tasks, including planning and remembering, which often go unseen. Each partner marks who does it now and who they would like to do it. Watch for score-keeping and redirect to what each needs. End with one change to try for two weeks.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I carry that the other may not see
Partner B: tasks I carry that the other may not see
Tasks I would like to hand off or share
What each of us needs to feel it is fair
One change we will try for two weeks

title: Inside Weather Pointer Station
summary: A child builds a paper weather station and moves a pointer to show how they feel today.
goal: Use it to give a child a simple way to name feelings and show them without words.
body_md: Have the child draw sun, cloud, rain and storm and decorate the pointer. Ask them to set it for today and tell you what the weather is like inside. Parents can check the station at home, asking 'what is the weather?' without trying to fix it.

fields.label: Today's weather inside me, drawn or described
What made the weather change
What I do when it is stormy
Who I can tell when it is stormy
How my grown-up can help

title: Worry Monster Home Design
summary: A child draws a worry monster and designs a cozy home for it, putting worries to rest for the night.
goal: Use it to help a child give worries a place to go outside their head.
body_md: Have the child draw the monster, name it and design a home with a door. Worries get written on slips and posted into it. The parent's job is to take the slip without arguing with it. Keep the monster silly rather than scary.

fields.label: My worry monster's name and what it looks like
One worry I will feed to the monster tonight
What the monster's home has to keep it cozy
What I can do while the monster rests
What my grown-up does when I post a worry

title: Calm Jar Build and Use
summary: A child makes a glitter jar and watches it settle while practicing slow breathing.
goal: Use it to give a child a visual, hands-on way to slow down when upset.
body_md: Fill a clear jar with water, glitter and a drop of soap; shake and breathe while the glitter settles. Tell the child it is a tool for a break, not a punishment. The parent keeps the jar where it can be reached and practices alongside without directing.

fields.label: What I named my calm jar
What the glitter reminds me of
What I felt in my body as it settled
A time I might use it
How my grown-up can invite me to use it

title: Brave Badge Collection
summary: A child designs badges for brave things they do, one at a time, and collects them in a pouch.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and celebrate small acts of bravery.
body_md: Draw badge shapes together and let the child decide what counts as brave, including telling the truth or trying a new food. Parents give badges only for effort, not outcome, and avoid pushing exposure to earn one. Review the collection each session.

fields.label: The brave thing I did
What my badge looks like
What I told myself to do it
Who saw it or helped
A brave thing I want to try next

title: Five Trusted Helpers Hand Map
summary: A child traces a hand and writes a trusted person on each finger, a map of who they can turn to.
goal: Use it to help a child name the people they can go to when something feels wrong.
body_md: Trace the child's hand and have them name one helper per finger and what each is good for. If a child names a worry about safety or discloses harm, follow your reporting duties and your agency's procedure. Parents get a copy to keep up at home.

fields.label: The five people I can go to
What each helper is good at
What I might say to start a hard talk
A time a helper helped me
Who I would tell if I felt unsafe

title: Skill Toss Beanbag Game
summary: Players toss a beanbag onto a floor grid of coping skills and then tell when they would use the skill.
goal: Use it to help a group practice recalling coping skills through movement and play.
body_md: Rules: tape a grid of skills on the floor. Each player tosses, names the skill their bag lands on, and gives a real example of using it. Teammates add a second example. Debrief on which skills felt most useful.

fields.label: The skill I landed on
When I could use it
A skill I want to try this week
What another player said that helped
What I learned from the game

title: Emotion Charades Relay
summary: Players act out feelings in teams while the others guess, then share when they have felt it.
goal: Use it to help a group recognize feelings in faces and bodies.
body_md: Rules: split into two teams. A player draws an emotion card and acts it out without words, and the team guesses in 30 seconds. The actor then says one time they felt it. Take turns. Debrief on which feelings were hardest to show or guess.

fields.label: The emotion I acted out
What my body does when I feel it
A time I felt it
The feeling that was hardest to guess
What I learned about others' feelings

title: Values Auction
summary: Players bid play money on values to learn what matters most when they cannot have everything.
goal: Use it to help a group discover which values they will pay the most to protect.
body_md: Rules: each player gets 100 play dollars and a list of values, such as honesty, adventure and family. Bid in rounds, and a value goes to the top bidder. Debrief on surprises: what they bought, what they let go and what it says about their priorities.

fields.label: The value I bid the most on
A value I let go and how it felt
What I would do to live that value this week
What surprised me about my bids
What I heard from other players

title: Coping Card Go Fish
summary: A card game where players collect matching pairs of coping skills and describe how they use them.
goal: Use it to give a group repeated, playful exposure to a menu of coping skills.
body_md: Rules: make a deck with pairs of skill cards. Players take turns asking for a match, and every pair made is described aloud with an example. The winner has the most pairs, but everyone shares a favorite in the debrief.

fields.label: A skill pair I made
How I use that skill
A skill I had never tried
One I will practice this week
What I noticed about the other players' skills

title: Two Truths and a Strategy
summary: Players share two true stories of a hard moment and one made-up one, and the group guesses the invented one and names a skill.
goal: Use it to help a group trade real experiences and practice naming the skills they used.
body_md: Rules: each player tells three short stories about stress, two true and one invented. The group guesses the false one and suggests a skill that fit the true ones. Keep disclosure light and let anyone pass. Debrief on what was easy to share.

fields.label: The true story I shared
The strategy that fit it
What the group suggested
A strategy I want to try
What it was like to share

title: Safe Place Anchor Card
summary: A card where a client describes a real or imagined calm place with its sights, sounds and textures to return to when stirred up.
goal: Use it to give a client a steady, portable anchor for moments of overwhelm.
body_md: Build the place from the senses and keep it free of any memory of what happened. If the place turns upsetting, switch to another or to a current-room anchor. Practice it in session when the client is calm so it is ready later. Pace is the client's.

fields.label: The place I picture, real or imagined
What I see there
What I hear and smell there
What my body feels like there
How I will remind myself to go there

title: Window of Tolerance Check-In Strip
summary: A strip a client uses to mark whether they feel too revved, steady or shut down at points in the day.
goal: Use it to help a client notice their activation level and choose a skill that fits.
body_md: Teach the three zones in plain words and have the client mark the strip a few times a day. Pair each zone with one skill, such as grounding for revved and movement for shut down. Do not ask for details of what triggered it; the marks and the skill are enough.

fields.label: Where I was on the strip this morning
Where I was this afternoon
Where I was this evening
What helped me move toward steady
The skill I want to practice more

title: Reminder or Danger Sorting Sheet
summary: A sorting sheet that helps a client separate things that remind them of the past from things that signal danger now.
goal: Use it to help a client check the present moment against a reminder that feels like danger.
body_md: Keep it in the here and now: list a recent trigger, what the body did, and what is true in the room today. Do not ask for the original event. If the client floods, pause and ground. Pacing matters more than finishing the sheet.

fields.label: Something that stirred me up recently
What my body did
What is actually true around me right now
Whether this is a reminder, a danger, or both
What helps me feel here and now

title: Five-Sense Soothing Kit Planner
summary: A planner for gathering objects for each sense into a kit a client can reach for on hard days.
goal: Use it to help a client assemble comforting sensory options they can use right away.
body_md: Let the client choose each item, such as a smooth stone, a scent or a playlist. Test one in session. Some scents or sounds can themselves be reminders, so drop anything that stirs things up. Put the kit where it can be found easily.

fields.label: Something I can look at that calms me
Something I can hear that calms me
A scent I like
Something comforting to touch or taste
Where I will keep my kit

title: Grounding Scavenger Walk
summary: Players hunt for items in the room by sense, color or texture and share one they find, a movement-based grounding game.
goal: Use it to help a group practice grounding by attending to the present environment.
body_md: Rules: call a prompt such as 'find something blue' or 'something rough.' Players move, find it and say what they notice. Take turns calling prompts. Debrief on what they noticed in their bodies. It stays in the present, and anyone may sit out.

fields.label: Something I found and what I noticed
How my body felt after moving
A prompt I would add
A time I could use this outside the group
What I learned about my attention

title: Uncertainty Experiment Plan
summary: A plan for deliberately tolerating one small uncertainty and recording what happens.
goal: Use it to help a client test how they cope when they do not get certainty.
body_md: Pick a small, safe uncertainty, such as not rechecking a message. Have the client predict how bad it will be, then record what happened. Clients often hunt for reassurance, so name it kindly and agree on what to do instead.

fields.label: The small uncertainty I will try to leave open
What I predict will happen
What I did instead of seeking certainty
What actually happened
What I learned about coping with not knowing

title: Worry Weather Report
summary: A page for noticing worry as passing weather and writing a short report of it without arguing with it.
goal: Use it to help a client watch worry come and go without engaging every thought.
body_md: Ask the client to write a forecast, such as 'worry front moving in, expect gusts of what-ifs.' The playful tone creates distance. Practice with one worry in session, then have them write a daily report. Note what they do on days the weather is stormy.

fields.label: Today's worry forecast
The what-ifs in the storm
What I did while the weather passed
What I cared about doing anyway
Tomorrow's plan, whatever the weather

title: Worry Bubble Pop Poster
summary: A child draws worry bubbles, then pops each with a silly or brave thought and breath.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful way to name worries and answer them.
body_md: Draw bubbles, write a worry in each, and have the child pop it with a finger, saying a brave answer. Parents join by asking 'what would your brave self say?' rather than reassuring each worry. Display the poster at home.

fields.label: A worry bubble I drew
What I said to pop it
How my body felt after I popped it
A brave answer I want to remember
How my grown-up can help me pop bubbles

title: Shared Worry Plan for Partners
summary: A plan for an anxious partner and a supportive partner to agree how to respond when worry spikes.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on support that does not feed reassurance seeking.
body_md: Have each partner say what helps and what backfires. The supporter often reassures repeatedly; agree on one validating phrase and one check-in instead. Rehearse once and revisit the plan after two weeks.

fields.label: Partner A: what I need when I feel worried
Partner B: what I do now when my partner is worried
What helps and what backfires, in our words
The phrase we will use
When we will check how the plan is working

title: Body Tension Scan Log
summary: A daily log for rating tension in the jaw, shoulders, stomach and hands and noting what helped it ease.
goal: Use it to help a client link physical tension to anxious moments and try a response.
duration: Five minutes daily for a week
body_md: Introduce a brief scan in session and ask for rating once or twice a day. Many clients are surprised by how much they hold. Review the log for patterns and pick one release skill, such as slow exhale or stretching.

fields.label: Tension in my jaw and shoulders, 0 to 10
Tension in my stomach and hands, 0 to 10
What was happening just before
What I did to ease it
What I noticed afterward

title: Hopeless Day Safety Note
summary: A short sheet for planning how to stay safe and connected on days when hopelessness feels heavy.
goal: Use it to help a client name early signs, supports and steps for their hardest days.
body_md: Complete this with the client in session, not as homework. Ask directly about thoughts of self-harm and respond to what you hear using your own clinical judgment and procedures. The sheet lists supports and includes 988, which the client can call or text at any hour.

fields.label: Signs that a day is getting heavier
People I can reach out to
Things I can do to stay safe and calm
Places or people that help me feel less alone
If I am in danger, I can call or text 988 or go to the nearest emergency room

title: Activity and Mood Match-Up Chart
summary: A chart that pairs daily activities with mood ratings to show which ones lift or lower mood.
goal: Use it to help a client see which activities connect with a better day for them.
body_md: Ask for a small list of activities and a rating for each. Avoid urging activities the client dreads; start from what has some pull. Review for the surprises, such as a short walk that moved things, and choose one to add.

fields.label: An activity I did today
My mood before, 0 to 10
My mood after, 0 to 10
One that lifted my mood a little
One I want to do again this week

title: Heavy Thoughts as Passing Clouds
summary: A page for writing the heavy thoughts of a low day as clouds and noticing the sky behind them.
goal: Use it to help a client make room for low-mood thoughts while still taking one valued step.
body_md: Draw the sky with the client and write thoughts on clouds. Then ask what they would still like to do that day, however small. The step stays small and chosen by them. Do not push brightness.

fields.label: A heavy thought I wrote on a cloud
What the sky behind it looks like
What matters to me even on low days
One small step I can take today
What I will say to myself if the clouds stay

title: Self-Care Floor Plan for Low Days
summary: A plan listing the smallest set of care steps a client will do even on the worst day.
goal: Use it to help a client protect a minimum of basic care when energy is very low.
body_md: Ask the client to name a floor, such as water, a shower and one message to someone. Make it so small it can always be done. Check later how it held up and adjust without judgment.

fields.label: My smallest care steps for a low day
What gets in the way of them
Who could remind me
How I will know I met my floor
A kind thing to say to myself afterward

title: Joy Hunt Group Game
summary: Players share small things that gave them a flicker of interest and score points for specific details.
goal: Use it to help a group notice and name small moments of pleasure or interest.
body_md: Rules: each round, players share a small moment from the week, and the group awards points for details such as sights or sounds. Keep it low pressure; passing is fine. Debrief on what they could do again.

fields.label: A small moment of interest I shared
What I noticed about it
What others shared that I liked
One I could try again
What I learned from the game

title: Task Time Guess and Check Log
summary: A log where a client guesses how long tasks will take, records actual time and notes the gap.
goal: Use it to help a client calibrate how long tasks really take.
body_md: Pick three routine tasks, such as showering or an email. The client guesses first, then times it. Most find consistent gaps, which can inform buffers in their schedule. Keep the tone as data, not a verdict on them.

fields.label: The task
My guess of how long it will take
How long it actually took
What I added or forgot
The buffer I will give it from now on

title: Body Doubling Setup Card
summary: A card where a child or teen plans who sits nearby while they start a task and what the job is.
goal: Use it to help a young person start tasks with a steady presence beside them.
body_md: Explain that a helper working quietly nearby can make starting easier. The parent's role is to be present without directing or correcting. Decorate the card, choose a start signal and a short work timer with a break.

fields.label: The task I will start
Who will sit near me
What we will say to start
How long I will work before a break
What I will do on my break

title: Partner Reminder Agreement
summary: A worksheet where partners agree on reminders and shared systems without nagging or parent-child dynamics.
goal: Use it to help partners set up a reminder system that both can live with.
body_md: The partner with attention struggles chooses reminder methods; the other states what they will and will not do. Watch for a drift into monitoring. Agree on a trial period and a check-in.

fields.label: Partner A: what reminders help me and how I want them
Partner B: what I am willing to do and not do
Tasks we will put in a shared system
How we will check in
What we will do when a reminder is missed

title: Next Right Step Break-Down Sheet
summary: A sheet that breaks a big task into tiny physical steps, with the first one small enough to start now.
goal: Use it to help a client get past overwhelm by naming the very next step.
body_md: Choose a task the client keeps avoiding and ask for steps so small they take two minutes. The first step is often just opening a file. Praise starting, not finishing. Have them text you or a friend when step one is done.

fields.label: The task that feels too big
The very first tiny step
The second tiny step
What might distract me and what I will do
How I will reward starting

title: Focus Sprint Relay Game
summary: Players do short timed focus sprints on a task, pass a baton and cheer each other through a break.
goal: Use it to help a group experience short sprints with built-in movement breaks.
body_md: Rules: set a timer for five minutes. Players work on a small task, then pass the baton and take a one-minute movement break. Debrief on what made it easier or harder to stay on the task.

fields.label: The task I worked on
What helped me stay with it
What got in the way
What I did on my break
A sprint I could use at home

title: Urge Wave Minute-by-Minute Log
summary: A log for riding out an urge to use a substance by noting its peak and how it changes with time.
goal: Use it to help a client watch an urge rise and fall without acting on it.
body_md: Teach the wave image and ask the client to log the urge's strength every few minutes. Many are surprised it passes. Do not shame a log entry where they used; ask what they learned. Keep language about substance use and urges.

fields.label: The urge and what set it off
Its strength at the start, 0 to 10
Its strength after ten minutes
What I did while it passed
What I learned about urges

title: Substance Use Pros and Cons Balance
summary: A four-box balance of the good and hard parts of continuing and of changing substance use.
goal: Use it to help a client voice both sides of their relationship with substance use.
body_md: Let the client fill all four boxes and avoid arguing with the pros. Ambivalence is normal. Ask what each side says about what matters to them. Revisit the sheet over time because it will change.

fields.label: What I get from using substances
What it costs me
What I would gain from change
What I would miss or worry about
What this tells me about what I care about

title: Values Over Urges Compass
summary: A compass page for naming values and choosing a step in their direction when an urge is present.
goal: Use it to help a client make room for urges while acting on what matters.
body_md: Have the client name two or three values and one action for each. Then discuss what they will do when an urge shows up, with the urge allowed to be there. Keep the action concrete and doable the same day.

fields.label: A value I want to live by
An action that fits it
What my urges say to me
What I will do with the urge present
Who I will tell about my step

title: Hardest Minutes Skill Menu for Urges
summary: A menu of skills for getting through the hardest minutes of an urge without using substances.
goal: Use it to help a client choose their own set of skills for moments of high urge.
body_md: Ask for skills that use the body, attention, other people and time. Test two in session. Plan for the hardest times of day. Pair with an agreed contact for support.

fields.label: My hardest times of day for urges
Body skills I can use
Attention skills I can use
People I can call

goal: Use it to help a group see how styles of handling conflict land.

goal: Use it to help partners build clear communication about comfort, pacing and consent.

goal: Use it to help a client cope in ways that fit what matters to them.

goal: Use it to help a client notice and soften critical thoughts about how they look.

goal: Use it to help a client connect with what matters beyond appearance.

goal: Use it to help a client practice describing instead of judging.

goal: Use it to help partners build appreciation that does not rest on appearance.

goal: Use it to help a client build a calm, repeatable evening routine.
