title: Calm-Down Jar Building Activity
summary: A hands-on activity where a child builds a glitter jar and uses it for a calm pause.
goal: Use it to give a child a physical tool for slowing down.
body_md: Build the jar together with a clear bottle, warm water, glue and glitter. The child shakes it and watches it settle while breathing slowly. The parent practices with them and keeps the jar somewhere easy to reach. Present it as a pause, never as a punishment.

fields.label: Draw my calm-down jar
What do I notice when the glitter falls?
When could I use my jar?
Who will practice with me?

title: Brave Staircase Picture Plan
summary: A drawing of a staircase where each step is a small brave thing a child wants to try.
goal: Use it to help a child plan small brave steps one at a time.
body_md: The child draws a staircase and names the top step as the big goal. Together you fill in smaller steps below it. The parent says one step they will cheer for. Choose a first step the child is willing to try this week and celebrate it, however small.

fields.label: Draw my staircase
The big brave thing at the top
The first small step at the bottom
Who will cheer for me?

title: Kindness Garden Planting Game
summary: A pretend garden where each kind act a child does grows a paper flower.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and enjoy kind acts.
body_md: Draw a big garden bed. Each time the child does or notices a kind act that week, they add a paper flower. The parent helps spot acts and adds some of their own. At the next visit, count the flowers and talk about the one the child liked most.

fields.label: Draw my garden
A kind thing I did
A kind thing someone did for me
How it felt to give or get a flower

title: Worry Monster Snack Box Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a box for a friendly monster that holds their written or drawn worries.
goal: Use it to give a child a safe, playful place to put worries.
body_md: Decorate a small box with eyes and a mouth slot. The child draws or tells a worry and feeds it to the monster, then picks a time to open the box with a parent. Never force a worry; let them choose. The parent listens and thanks the monster.

fields.label: Draw my worry monster
A worry I am feeding it today
What the monster says back
What I can do when I feel it

title: Skills Bingo Card Game
summary: A bingo game where each square is a coping skill and players mark squares as they describe using one.
goal: Use it to help a group recall and talk about the skills they use.
body_md: Make cards with skills in the squares. Players take turns telling when they used a skill or when they could, and mark a square. First to complete a line shares a favorite skill. Debrief by asking which squares were easiest and hardest to fill.

fields.label: Skills I marked off
One I used this week
One I want to try
What I learned from others

title: Two Truths and a Strength Round
summary: A round of two true statements and one strength a player has, with the group guessing which is the strength.
goal: Use it to help group members name strengths in a light, playful way.
body_md: Each player writes two ordinary truths about themselves and one strength, then reads them aloud in any order while the group guesses the strength. Keep guesses kind. Debrief by asking how it felt to say a strength out loud and what surprised them.

fields.label: My two truths
My strength
What I learned about someone else
How it felt to name a strength

title: Emotion Charades Challenge
summary: A charades game where players act out feelings and others guess, then talk about when they feel them.
goal: Use it to help children and teens name feelings with their bodies and voices.
body_md: Write feelings on cards. Players act one without words while others guess, then share a time someone might feel that way. Rotate turns and keep it playful. Debrief by asking which feeling was hardest to act or to guess.

fields.label: A feeling I acted
How my body showed it
A time I felt it
A feeling that was hard to guess

title: Many Ideas Relay Game
summary: A team relay where each player adds one idea to solve a pretend problem before passing the baton.
goal: Use it to help a group practice generating several solutions to a problem.
body_md: Give each team a problem card. Players pass a baton, and each adds one idea, silly or sensible, before passing. After time, teams pick their favorite and explain why. Debrief by asking how coming up with many ideas changed how stuck they felt.

fields.label: The problem my team got
An idea I added
The idea we chose and why
How I can use this on a real problem

title: Calm Dice Challenge
summary: A dice game where each number matches a calming activity players try for one minute.
goal: Use it to help players try different calming activities in a fun way.
body_md: Make a list of six calming activities, such as breathing, stretching, naming five sounds. A player rolls, does the matching activity for a minute and rates how they feel. Take turns. Debrief by asking which activities were helpful to try again.

fields.label: The activity I rolled
How I felt before and after
My favorite activity
Where I could use it

title: Safe Place Senses Builder
summary: A page for building a calm, safe place in the imagination with sights, sounds and textures.
goal: Use it to give a client a steady inner place to return to.
body_md: Build the place in session at the client's pace, and let them stop at any moment. Choose a place that is neutral or pleasant, not tied to a person who may be complicated. Keep to the present and the senses; no memories of events are needed. Practice returning to it briefly each session.

fields.label: Where my safe place is
What I see there
What I hear
What I feel against my skin
What I smell or taste
A word that brings me back to it

title: Window of Tolerance Zone Map
summary: A map where a client marks signs of being too revved up, too shut down or steady, and what helps in each zone.
goal: Use it to help a client notice which zone they are in and what helps.
body_md: Draw three bands and have the client place their own signs in each: body, thoughts, behavior. Then list what helps them move back toward steady. Stay with signs and skills only; there is no need to describe past events. Check in about the map each week.

fields.label: Signs that I am too revved up
Signs that I am shut down
Signs that I am steady
What helps when I am revved up
What helps when I am shut down
One person I can contact

title: Reminder Cards for Present-Moment Orientation
summary: Pocket cards that help a client remind themselves of the date, place and what is safe right now.
goal: Use it to help a client orient to the present when reminders pull them away.
body_md: Write cards with the client: today's date, where I am, what I can see that is different from before. Role-play pulling one out. Keep cards short and kind. Pair them with a skill such as paced breathing and invite the client to adjust wording until it feels true.

fields.label: Today's date and where I am
Three things I can see that are here and now
What is safe about right now
A skill I will use next
A kind sentence to say to myself

title: Values Compass for Rebuilding
summary: A compass that points a client toward what matters to them now, at their own pace and without retelling events.
goal: Use it to help a client reconnect with values and small actions.
body_md: Invite the client to name a few values and one small action for each this week. Do not ask for the story of what happened. Notice if the discussion pulls them into distress and pause for grounding. Keep the action small, safe and chosen by them.

fields.label: Something that matters to me
A tiny action that fits it
What might get in the way
What I need to feel safe doing it
Who can support me

title: Here-and-Now Scavenger Hunt
summary: A game of finding things in the room by color, texture or sound to bring attention to the present.
goal: Use it to give a client or group a playful way to practice grounding.
body_md: Call out clues such as something blue, something soft, something that makes a sound. Players find and describe items, then rate how steady they feel. Keep it voluntary and let anyone pass. Debrief by asking which clue helped most and when they could use it.

fields.label: What I found
Which clue helped me most
How steady I feel, 0 to 10
Where I could use this at home

title: Worry Time Boundary Planner
summary: A planner for setting a short daily worry window and parking worries outside it.
goal: Use it to help a client contain worry to a set time.
body_md: Choose a 15-minute slot that is not near bedtime. During the day the client jots a worry on a parking list and returns to it in the window, then notes which still matter. Clients often find many have faded. Do not demand that they stop worrying; just move it.

fields.label: My worry window time and place
Worries I parked today
Which still matter in the window
One I can act on
One I can let go for now

title: Anxious Thoughts as Weather ACT Page
summary: A page using weather as an image for anxious thoughts that come and go.
goal: Use it to help a client treat anxious thoughts as passing weather.
body_md: Ask the client to describe the forecast in their head today, then name what they can do whatever the weather. Weather metaphors can seem simple; invite them to adjust the image so it fits. Close with one action toward a value they will take even if clouds remain.

fields.label: Today's forecast in my mind
What the clouds say
What I want to do anyway
A value I am heading toward
One step I can take in any weather

title: Worry Tummy Helper Drawing
summary: A drawing where a child shows where worry lives in the body and draws a helper to calm it.
goal: Use it to help a child connect body feelings with worry and calming helpers.
body_md: Have the child draw an outline of a body and color where worry shows up. Then draw a helper, such as a deep breath or a hug. The parent learns the child's signals and practices the helper with them. Keep it playful and accept the child's picture as it is.

fields.label: Color where worry lives in my body
Draw my helper
What my helper does
Who can help me use it

title: Anxiety Early Signals Tracker
summary: A tracker for the body, thought and behavior signs that show up early, before anxiety builds.
goal: Use it to help a client catch anxiety signals sooner.
body_md: The client notes each time they notice rising anxiety, what the first signal was and what they did. Look for patterns in timing and place. This is about noticing, not rating or judging. Share what stands out and pick one early signal to respond to differently next week.

fields.label: Date and time I noticed it
The first signal I noticed
What was going on around me
What I did
What I might try earlier next time

title: Anxiety Uncertainty Dice Game
summary: A game where each roll names a small uncertain situation and players practice saying a coping statement.
goal: Use it to help players practice tolerating small uncertainties with humor.
body_md: Make six cards of ordinary uncertain situations, such as not knowing what is for dinner. Players roll, read the card and say how they would handle it. The group offers kind statements. Debrief by asking where in life they notice the same pull to know for sure.

fields.label: The uncertain thing I rolled
My coping statement
One real uncertainty this week
How I can handle it

title: Small Joys Spotting Log
summary: A log where a client records one small pleasant moment each day and the thought that went with it.
goal: Use it to help a client notice pleasant moments that low mood can hide.
body_md: Start by saying that the goal is to notice, not to feel great. The client logs one small moment a day, such as warm tea or a text from a friend. Review which moments mattered and plan to add one on purpose. Be ready for days with nothing; that is information.

fields.label: Today's small moment
What was happening
What I felt in my body
What I thought
One I could add on purpose tomorrow

title: Low Energy Day Menu
summary: A menu of tiny actions a client can pick from on days when energy is very low.
goal: Use it to give a client a short list of doable actions for hard days.
body_md: Write the menu together with actions that take five minutes or less: a glass of water, step outside, one text. The client chooses one, not all. If the client mentions thoughts of ending their life, follow your usual steps and remind them 988 (call or text) is available any time.

fields.label: Things that take under five minutes
One for my body
One for connection
One for my space
Which I will pick on my next hard day
Who I could tell: 988 (call or text) is there any time

title: Self-Kindness Letter Planner
summary: A planner for writing a short letter from a caring friend's point of view to the client themselves.
goal: Use it to help a client practice a kinder voice toward themselves.
body_md: Ask the client to imagine a friend who knows their struggles and cares. They write what that friend would say. Some find this hard; offer sentence starters. Do not insist on a certain tone. Read it aloud if they are willing and ask how it lands.

fields.label: Someone who cares about me
What they would notice I am going through
What they would say about my effort
What they would encourage me to do
How I feel after reading it

title: Mood and Activity Link Chart
summary: A chart linking activities to mood so a client can pick actions that build a sense of mastery or pleasure.
goal: Use it to help a client see which activities lift mood and plan more.
body_md: The client records activities and tags each as pleasure or mastery, with a mood rating. Review what stands out and plan two more of the best ones. Resist saying they should feel better; let the pattern speak. Adjust choices if energy is low.

fields.label: Activity and time
Pleasure or mastery
Mood before and after
What stands out
Two I will plan for next week

title: Partner Support for Low Mood Plan
summary: A plan for partners to agree on how one can support the other on low days without pressure.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on helpful support for low mood.
body_md: The partner with low mood says what helps and what does not. The other says what they can offer and what they need for themselves. Agree on one daily check-in. Keep blame out of it. If either mentions thoughts of ending their life, say 988 (call or text) is there any time and follow your usual steps.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps on low days
Partner A: what does not help
Partner B: what I can offer
Partner B: what I need for myself
A check-in we both can keep
If it feels like too much: 988 (call or text)

title: Task Start Ramp Worksheet
summary: A worksheet that breaks the first five minutes of a task into a ramp of tiny steps.
goal: Use it to help a client get started on a task they keep putting off.
body_md: Pick one task. Write the first physical action, such as opening the document or putting on shoes, then a two-minute version and a five-minute version. Add a cue and a reward. Clients often plan the whole project; keep them to the first ramp.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off
The first physical action
A two-minute version
A cue that will remind me
A small reward after
Who can check in with me

title: Dragon Chase Time Game for Kids
summary: A play activity where a child races a timer dragon to finish one small task and earns a sticker.
goal: Use it to help a child practice finishing short tasks with a playful timer.
body_md: Draw a dragon on a card and set a visual timer. The child works on one small job, like putting toys in a bin, before the dragon arrives. The parent cheers and notes what worked. Keep the task short and the tone fun, never a race against shame.

fields.label: Draw my dragon
The small job I did
How much time I used
What helped me keep going

title: Body Doubling Check-In Game
summary: A game where players work alongside a partner on separate tasks and check in with a score.
goal: Use it to help players try body doubling and see if company helps focus.
body_md: Pair players. Each names a task, works for ten minutes in the same room, and then checks in for a minute. Switch roles. Debrief by asking what changed with another person nearby and whether they could arrange it at home.

fields.label: My task
How focused I was, 0 to 10
What my partner did that helped
Where I could use a work buddy

title: Working Memory Cue Plan
summary: A plan for putting reminders where the client will see them at the moment they need them.
goal: Use it to help a client set up visible cues for things they forget.
body_md: List things that get forgotten and for each decide the point of use: the door, the phone, the bed. Reminders hidden in notes do not help; place them where the action happens. Test one cue for a week and adjust. Avoid framing forgetting as a flaw.

fields.label: Things I often forget
Where I need to remember them
A cue I can put there
What might block the cue
How I will check if it works

title: Shared Household Task Board for Partners
summary: A board where partners list household tasks, who does them and a visible way to track them.
goal: Use it to help partners share tasks without nagging.
body_md: Partners list household tasks and mark who does which, aiming for fairness as they define it. Use a visible board so memory does not carry the load. Agree on how reminders will be given, with a request instead of a complaint. Review in two weeks.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I do now
Partner B: tasks I do now
Tasks that fall through
How we will make them visible
How we will remind each other kindly

title: Urge Surfing Notes Sheet
summary: A sheet for noting the rise and fall of an urge and what the client did while it passed.
goal: Use it to help a client ride out urges for substance use.
body_md: The client notes each urge's start, peak and ending, plus what they did. Emphasize that urges rise, peak and fall. Don't judge a use; look at what was different when they waited. If someone feels unsafe, follow your usual steps and name 988 (call or text).

fields.label: When the urge started
What triggered it
How strong, 0 to 10, at its peak
What I did while it passed
How it changed
If I feel unsafe: 988 (call or text)

title: Reasons and Values for Change Page
summary: A page connecting a client's reasons for change around substance use to what they value.
goal: Use it to help a client reconnect with why change matters to them.
body_md: Ask the client what they want their life to stand for, then link it to choices about substance use. Avoid labels for people; speak about the substance use and urges. Ambivalence is welcome; ask what the part that wants to keep using is protecting.

fields.label: What matters most to me
How substance use fits or clashes with that
Reasons I want change
What a part of me worries about
One step toward what matters

title: Trigger Chain Analysis Sheet
summary: A sheet that traces a day when substance use happened, link by link, to find a point where a different choice was possible.
goal: Use it to help a client find places to intervene in a chain of events.
body_md: Go step by step through what came before: events, feelings, thoughts, urges. Keep a kind, curious tone; shame shuts the conversation down. Choose one link where a different move could be tried, and plan it. Do not require full disclosure.

fields.label: The situation that began it
Feelings and thoughts that came next
The urge
What I did
A link where I could do something different
What I need to try it

title: Recovery Day Structure Planner
summary: A planner for laying out a day with hour blocks for routine, support and activities that do not involve substance use.
goal: Use it to help a client fill risky hours with planned activity.
body_md: Mark the hours in which urges have been strongest and plan something specific for each. Include meals, movement, contact with support and rest. Avoid overfilling. Review next session, noting what held and what did not without judgment.

fields.label: Hours when urges are strongest
What I will do in those hours
Who I can contact
Healthy routines I will keep
What I will change if the plan slips

title: Rebuilding Trust Conversation Guide
summary: A guide for partners to talk about trust after substance use has strained the relationship.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about trust without blame.
body_md: Set ground rules first: one speaks, one listens, either can pause. The partner who used substances says what they are doing to rebuild trust; the other says what they need to see. Avoid demands for details. Plan one trust-building action each week.

fields.label: Partner A: what I am doing to rebuild trust
Partner B: what I need to see
Partner A: what I need from you
Partner B: what I can offer
One action we agree on this week

title: Anger Early Warning Body Map
summary: A body map where a client marks where anger shows up first and what they can do at the first sign.
goal: Use it to help a client catch anger early.
body_md: Draw an outline and mark the body signs of anger from first to last. Then pair each early sign with a small skill: a pause, a drink of water, leaving the room. Practice noticing in session. Anger often hides other feelings; ask what is under it.

fields.label: Where I feel anger first
What it feels like
What I think when it starts
A skill I will use at the first sign
What I might be feeling underneath

title: Cool-Down Volcano Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds a paper volcano and lists calm-down moves for each level.
goal: Use it to give a child a picture for anger and ways to cool down.
body_md: Draw a volcano with three levels: simmering, bubbling, erupting. The child writes or draws cool-down moves at each level. The parent practices one move with the child. Anger is normal; the work is about what we do with it.

fields.label: Draw my volcano
What makes me simmer
What my body does when I bubble
Cool-down moves I will try
Who can help me cool down

title: Anger Reset Relay Game
summary: A relay where players take a calming step at each station before passing the baton.
goal: Use it to help players practice calm-down steps in a lively way.
body_md: Set up stations: breathe, stretch, count backward, say a kind sentence. A player does each in turn, rating their calm at the end. Take turns and cheer for effort. Debrief by asking which station helped and where they could use it at home.

fields.label: The station I liked best
How calm I felt, 0 to 10
When I could use it
What got in the way

title: After the Anger Look-Back Sheet
summary: A sheet for looking back at an angry moment, what it cost and how to repair.
goal: Use it to help a client reflect on and repair after an angry moment.
body_md: Review a recent moment without lecturing. The client names the trigger, thoughts and actions, then the cost to them and others. End with a repair step, such as an apology or a plan. Safety first: if anyone was hurt, follow your usual duties.

fields.label: What happened
What I was thinking
What I did
What it cost me and others
A repair I can make
What I will try next time

title: Cooling Off Timeout Plan
summary: A plan for stepping away from heated moments with a return time and what to do during the break.
goal: Use it to help a client use a break skillfully.
body_md: Write the plan with a phrase for leaving, a place to cool down, an activity for the break, and a time to come back. Make clear a break is not avoidance. If a partner is involved, they agree to the plan ahead. Practice the phrase aloud.

fields.label: The phrase I will say to call a break
Where I will go
What I will do to cool down
How long I will take
How I will return to the conversation

title: Compulsion Delay Log
summary: A log for noting an urge to do a compulsion, how long the client delayed it and what happened.
goal: Use it to help a client practice delaying compulsions by small steps.
body_md: Pick one compulsion and agree on a delay the client can manage, such as two minutes. They log the urge, the delay and what the anxiety did. Stay with what happens rather than getting rid of discomfort. Build up gradually with the client leading.

fields.label: The urge
How long I delayed
What my anxiety did
What I noticed
The delay I will try next

title: Intrusive Thoughts Defusion Cards
summary: Cards for stepping back from intrusive thoughts by naming them as thoughts rather than facts.
goal: Use it to help a client change their relationship with intrusive thoughts.
body_md: Write the most common thought, then a few defusion phrases such as I am having the thought that. Practice saying them in session. Normalize that many people have odd thoughts. Avoid asking for reassurance-like answers about what a thought means.

fields.label: An intrusive thought
I am having the thought that
What my mind tells me to do
What I want to do instead
A value I can act on

title: Exposure Ladder Builder
summary: A ladder of situations ranked from mildly to very distressing, built together as a plan for gradual practice.
goal: Use it to help a client build a graded exposure plan.
body_md: List feared situations, rate each, and order them. Begin with a rung the client is willing to try. Plan response prevention in advance: what they will not do afterward. Review each week and move at their pace, never faster.

fields.label: Situations that bother me
Rating of each, 0 to 100
Where I will start
What I will not do afterward
What I will notice
Who knows my plan

title: Bug Zapper Helper Drawing
summary: A drawing where a child gives the OCD bug a silly name and draws how they will boss it back.
goal: Use it to help a child externalize intrusive worries in a playful way.
body_md: Have the child name and draw the pest that bugs them, then draw themselves bossing it back. The parent learns not to join in reassurance or rituals and practices a kind reply instead. Keep it light; the child leads.

fields.label: Draw the bug
Its silly name
What it tells me to do
How I will boss it back
What my parent can say

title: Not Sure Dare Game
summary: A game of small dares to tolerate not being sure, with a debrief on what happened.
goal: Use it to help players practice sitting with uncertainty.
body_md: Make cards of safe dares such as leaving a note slightly crooked or saying maybe. Players pick a card, do it and rate their discomfort at the start and end. Keep dares comfortable and voluntary. Debrief on what happened versus predictions.

fields.label: The dare I chose
Discomfort before and after
What I thought would happen
What did happen

title: Panic Wave Rating Log
summary: A log that tracks how a panic wave rises, peaks and falls, and what the client did while it passed.
goal: Use it to help a client see panic as a wave that passes.
body_md: Have the client log each wave: trigger, body sensations, thoughts, peak rating and how long it lasted. Review for the shape of the wave rather than the cause. Ask what they predicted would happen and what did. Rule out medical concerns through the proper channel.

fields.label: Date, time and place
Body sensations I noticed
What I feared would happen
Peak rating, 0 to 10
How long it lasted
What I did while it passed

title: Slow Exhale Rehearsal Card
summary: A card for practicing slow paced breathing when calm so it is ready during a surge.
goal: Use it to help a client rehearse a slower breath before they need it.
body_md: Teach a longer exhale than inhale, such as four in and six out, and practice together. Check for any medical reason a client should not hold breath. Practice daily when calm and rate how they feel before and after. Do not promise it will stop panic.

fields.label: My breathing count
When I will practice each day
How I felt before and after
What got in the way
Where I will keep this card

title: Body Sensation Experiment Sheet
summary: A sheet for planning safe exercises that bring on harmless body sensations to learn what they do.
goal: Use it to help a client learn that sensations pass without harm.
body_md: Choose one exercise such as spinning in a chair or breathing through a straw, after any medical clearance. The client predicts, tries it with you, then compares. Go at their pace and let them stop. Plan one for practice at home.

fields.label: The sensation I fear
My prediction
The exercise I tried
What actually happened
What I learned
The next one I will try

title: Panic Helper Cape Drawing
summary: A drawing where a child makes a hero cape with the calm moves they use when their body feels alarmed.
goal: Use it to help a child connect big body feelings with calming moves.
body_md: Have the child decorate a cape and write calm moves on it: slow breaths, squeezing a pillow, saying it will pass. The parent practices one with them and learns to stay near and calm. Praise effort and keep it playful.

fields.label: Draw my hero cape
My calm moves
What my body feels when alarmed
What my parent does to help

title: Moving Through Panic Values Page
summary: A page for a client to choose a value-led action even when panic sensations show up.
goal: Use it to help a client move toward what matters with sensations present.
body_md: Ask what panic has made the client stop doing, then choose a small step toward it with panic invited along. The aim is not to avoid sensations but to keep moving. Plan an easy first step and review how it went.

fields.label: Something panic keeps me from
Why it matters to me
A small step I will take
Sensations I may notice

title: Calm Before Correcting Parent Plan
summary: A plan for a parent to pause, breathe and respond calmly before correcting a child.
goal: Use it to help a parent respond rather than react.
body_md: Ask the parent to name the moments they react fastest, then choose a pause phrase and a calm action. Role-play one scenario. Normalize that parents get stressed. Do not frame this as blame; invite curiosity about what tends to precede reactions.

fields.label: Moments when I react fastest
What I feel in my body
My pause phrase
What I will do before I respond
What I will say to my child

title: Praise That Sticks Practice Page
summary: A page where a parent and child practice specific praise and a child records what they did well.
goal: Use it to help parents give specific, warm praise.
body_md: Model specific praise such as I liked how you waited for your turn. The parent writes three they can give this week; the child draws or says one thing they are proud of. Praise effort, not outcome. Keep it playful, not corrective.

fields.label: Three things I can praise this week
Exactly what I will say
Draw something I am proud of
How it felt to hear praise

title: Co-Parenting Agreement Conversation
summary: A conversation guide for two caregivers to agree on a few shared routines and responses.
goal: Use it to help caregivers align on a few shared expectations.
body_md: Pick two or three issues, such as screens or bedtime. Each caregiver says what they want and why. Aim for a small agreement and a plan to review. Avoid trying to settle everything at once. Respect that parents may have different styles.

fields.label: Caregiver A: what I want and why
Caregiver B: what I want and why
What we agree on

title: Family Rule Charades Game
summary: A charades game where family members act out house rules and kind ways to follow them.
goal: Use it to help families talk about expectations in a playful way.
body_md: Write family rules on cards. Players act them out while others guess, and then say why the rule matters. Parents join in. Debrief by asking which rule is easiest to follow and which could use a tweak.

fields.label: A rule I acted out
Why it matters
One rule that is hard
What would help me follow it

title: Parent Self-Care Anchor DBT Page
summary: A page where a parent chooses small self-care anchors and a skill for the hardest part of the day.
goal: Use it to help a parent protect small moments for themselves.

title: Leaves on the Stream Daily Practice Log
summary: A log for a defusion practice where thoughts are placed on leaves floating down a stream.
goal: Use it to help a client practice letting thoughts pass without following or fighting them.
duration: Five minutes daily for a week
body_md: Guide the practice once in session so the client knows the image. At home they note when they tried it and what thoughts floated by. Common snags are getting caught in a thought and judging the practice as failing. Noticing that they got caught and returning is the practice.

fields.label: When and where I practiced
Thoughts that floated by
A moment I got caught on a leaf
How I came back
How my body felt afterward

title: Values Compass Quarter Check
summary: A compass-style page for rating how closely the client is living by four chosen values.
goal: Use it to help a client check how their actions line up with the values they named.
body_md: Have the client name four values in their own words, then rate each for how much their recent actions have matched it. Ask about the gap, not the score. Pick one value for a small action in the next week. Avoid shoulds; the client chooses the direction.

fields.label: Four values in my own words
How closely my days match each (0 to 10)
The value with the biggest gap
One small action that fits it
What may show up when I try
How I will make room for that

title: Willingness Dial Worksheet
summary: A dial the client turns to show how willing they are to feel something uncomfortable for a valued step.
goal: Use it to help a client notice and adjust their willingness to carry discomfort toward something they care about.
body_md: Name one valued step and the discomfort that comes with it, then have the client set the dial from 0 to 10. Ask what would move it up a notch, or what a smaller version of the step might be. Do not push the dial higher than the client wants. Willingness is a choice they make again each time.

fields.label: The step I care about taking
The discomfort that comes with it
My willingness today (0 to 10)
What would move it up one notch
A smaller version of the step
What I will do this week

title: Self as Context Observer Page
summary: A page that helps a client practice stepping back and noticing the one who notices their experience.
goal: Use it to help a client get a bit of distance from thoughts and feelings by noticing the observing self.
body_md: Lead a short observer exercise in session, such as noticing thoughts, feelings and sensations as passing contents. Then use the page to capture what the client saw. Some clients find the idea abstract, so offer the image of the sky and the weather. Keep it curious and light.

fields.label: What I noticed in my body
What I noticed in my thoughts
What I noticed in my feelings
Who or what was noticing all of that
What stayed the same while the rest changed

title: Crossroads Choice Point Sketch
summary: A map that marks the moment of a hard feeling and the two directions a client can take from it.
goal: Use it to help a client spot a choice point and name moves toward and away from what matters.
body_md: Draw a crossroads with the hook in the center. The client lists the thoughts and feelings that show up, then moves that take them away and moves that take them toward. Practice on a recent moment, not a hypothetical one. It helps to leave the map with the client for use between sessions.

fields.label: The moment that started it
Thoughts and feelings that showed up
Moves that take me away from what matters
Moves that take me toward what matters
The direction I chose
What I want to try next time

title: Emotion, Reason and Wise Mind Pause Card
summary: A short card for noticing emotion mind, reasonable mind and wise mind in a moment of difficulty.
goal: Use it to help a client practice finding a wise mind response between the two extremes.
body_md: Walk through a recent moment, asking where each mind was speaking. The client then writes what wise mind might say. Some clients struggle to find it at first, so offer a breath or a hand on the belly. It can be used in session as a pause before a hard conversation.

fields.label: The situation
What emotion mind was saying
What reasonable mind was saying
What wise mind might say
How I could act from that

title: IMPROVE Letters Moment Menu
summary: A menu built on the IMPROVE letters, where a client picks ways to get through a hard moment.
goal: Use it to help a client choose a way to get through a hard moment without making it worse.
body_md: Go through imagery, meaning, prayer or peace, relaxation, one thing in the moment, vacation and encouragement. The client circles what appeals and writes a concrete version of each. Practice one in session so it feels real. Keep a copy handy where the client can see it.

fields.label: A hard moment I want a plan for
Imagery I could use
A meaning I can find in it
One thing I can do in the moment
A short break I can take
An encouraging thing I can say to myself

title: FAST Skills Self-Respect Sheet
summary: A worksheet using fair, apologies, stick to values and truthful for a conversation where self-respect is at stake.
goal: Use it to help a client keep their self-respect in a conversation without over-apologizing.
body_md: Take a situation where the client tends to give in or over-explain. Walk through being fair, not apologizing unless it is needed, sticking to values and being truthful. Role-play a line or two. Clients often notice how much they apologize by habit; point it out gently.

fields.label: The conversation I am preparing for
What being fair looks like here
What I do not need to apologize for
The value I want to stick to
The truthful thing I will say
How I will feel afterward if I do it

title: Check the Facts Flowchart
summary: A flowchart that moves from an emotion to the event, the interpretation and whether the facts fit.
goal: Use it to help a client check whether their emotion fits the facts of a situation.
body_md: Start with the emotion, then what happened in plain words, and the story the client told about it. Ask what is fact and what is interpretation. If the facts fit the emotion, problem-solve; if not, practice acting opposite. Keep the tone curious so the client does not feel told their feelings are wrong.

fields.label: The emotion and how strong it is (0 to 10)
What happened, in facts only
The story I told myself about it
Facts that fit or do not fit that story
Does my emotion fit the facts?
What I will do next

title: Act Opposite Week Log
summary: A log for trying the opposite of an emotion urge and noting what happened afterward.
goal: Use it to help a client try acting opposite to an unhelpful urge and see what changes.
body_md: Pick an emotion whose urge is not helping, such as withdrawing when sad. The client names the urge, plans the opposite step and notes both the feeling before and after. Fully committing to the step matters, including body posture and tone. Review the log for patterns rather than perfection.

fields.label: The emotion and the urge
The opposite action I planned
Feeling before (0 to 10)
What I did
Feeling after (0 to 10)
What I noticed

title: Weekly State of the Relationship Chat
summary: A short weekly check-in with parts for each partner and a shared plan.
goal: Use it to give a couple a steady, calm time each week to say what is working and what needs care.
body_md: Each partner fills their own side first, then they take turns reading aloud with no interrupting. Partner A shares one appreciation and one request, then Partner B does the same. End by agreeing on one small thing to do this week. If it gets heated, pause and return to it later.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciated this week
Partner A: one request for next week
Partner B: something I appreciated this week
Partner B: one request for next week
Together: one thing we will do this week

title: Gentle Opening Rewrite Sheet for Partners
summary: A sheet where each partner rewrites a harsh complaint as a gentle opening.
goal: Use it to help partners raise a concern without opening with blame.
body_md: Each partner picks a recent complaint and writes how it came out. Then they rewrite it using "I feel... about... and I need...". Take turns reading the new versions to each other. Coach the listener to just receive it first. Expect some awkwardness; practicing aloud helps.

fields.label: Partner A: how I said it before
Partner A: my soft version
Partner B: how I said it before
Partner B: my soft version
What we noticed when we heard the new versions

title: Shared Meaning Rituals Page
summary: A page where partners list daily and weekly rituals that matter to them and choose one to start.
goal: Use it to help a couple build small shared rituals that bring them closer.
body_md: Each partner lists rituals they remember, enjoy or would like, such as a morning coffee or a walk. Compare lists and look for overlap. Choose one to try for two weeks. Rituals work when they are small and repeatable, not grand.

fields.label: Partner A: rituals I enjoy or miss
Partner B: rituals I enjoy or miss
Where our lists overlap
The one we will try for two weeks
When and where we will do it

title: Partner Repair Phrase Menu
summary: A menu of phrases and gestures each partner prefers for calming a tense moment.
goal: Use it to help partners agree ahead of time on ways to repair during a disagreement.
body_md: Each partner picks the repairs that feel good to them, such as "can we start over" or a hand on the shoulder, and marks any that feel bad. Share lists and agree on a few to use. Practice one in session. Repairs work best when both agree on them before an argument.

fields.label: Partner A: repairs that help me
Partner A: repairs that do not help me
Partner B: repairs that help me
Partner B: repairs that do not help me
The ones we both agree to try

title: Division of Daily Tasks Talk Sheet
summary: A sheet for naming the tasks each partner carries and talking about how fair it feels.
goal: Use it to help a couple talk about who does what in a way that avoids score-keeping.
body_md: Each partner lists the visible and invisible tasks they do, including planning and remembering. Compare lists and ask how each feels about the share. Avoid tallying; the aim is to understand. Choose one task to shift or share. Revisit in a month.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I carry, including the invisible ones
Partner B: tasks I carry, including the invisible ones
How the share feels to each of us
One task we will shift or share
When we will check back in

title: Worry Monster Drawing and Feeding Box
summary: A craft where a child draws a worry monster and feeds it folded worries through a slot in a box.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful way to name worries and set them outside themselves.
body_md: Help the child decorate a small box with a mouth. They draw or write worries on slips and feed them in. Tell the parent they can use the box at home at bedtime and read the slips only if the child invites it. Keep the tone playful, and follow your reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw your worry monster
What does it like to eat?
A worry I fed it today
How my body feels after feeding it
Where we keep the box at home

title: Calm Down Jar Glitter Build
summary: A build-it activity where a child makes a glitter jar and watches it settle as they breathe.
goal: Use it to give a child a visual way to notice that big feelings settle with time and breath.
body_md: Make the jar together with water, clear glue and glitter, sealed tightly. Shake it for the feeling and breathe while it settles. Tell the parent to offer the jar as an invitation, never as a punishment. Practice when calm so it is easy to use when upset.

fields.label: The feeling I shook into my jar
What my glitter looked like
How my breathing felt while it settled
When I might use my jar
What my grown-up can do to help

title: Feelings Weather Sliding Window Craft
summary: A craft with a paper window the child slides to show today's feelings as weather.
goal: Use it to help a child show and name feelings through weather pictures.
body_md: Draw a sunny, cloudy, rainy and stormy scene on strips and slide them behind a cut-out window. The child shows how they feel at check-in. Ask the parent to look at it once a day and say "thanks for showing me". Weather changes, which is a helpful message in itself.

fields.label: Today's weather inside me
Why it is that weather
A time it changed
What helps when it is stormy
Who I can show my window to

title: Brave Steps Sticker Ladder Poster
summary: A poster where a child draws a ladder of small brave steps and adds a sticker for each one tried.
goal: Use it to help a child break a hard thing into small steps they can try one at a time.
body_md: Choose one thing the child wants to get better at and draw a ladder with five rungs, smallest at the bottom. The child decorates it and colors a rung after each try. Tell the parent to cheer for trying, not for how it went. Rungs can be re-ordered if one is too big.

fields.label: The thing I want to get braver about
My smallest step
The next steps up my ladder
What I tell myself when it is hard
How my grown-up can cheer for me

title: Kindness Seeds Garden Craft
summary: A paper garden where a child plants a seed for each kind thing they notice or do.
goal: Use it to help a child notice kindness given and received, including toward themselves.
body_md: Give the child a paper garden and seed stickers. Each kind act, small or large, gets a seed and a few words. Invite one seed for something kind to themselves. Ask the parent to add a seed when they see kindness. Look at the garden together at the next session.

fields.label: A kind thing I did
A kind thing someone did for me
A kind thing I did for myself
How it felt to plant it
What I want my garden to look like

title: Opposite Day Emotion Charades
summary: A group game of acting out an emotion and then the opposite action.
goal: Use it to help a group see what acting opposite to an emotion looks and feels like.
body_md: Write emotions on cards. A player draws one and acts it out, then the group guesses. The player then acts the opposite action, such as approaching instead of hiding. After a few rounds, debrief: which was easier to act, and how did the body feel in each? Rules: no words, and everyone gets a turn.

fields.label: The emotion I acted
The opposite action I acted
Which was easier and why
What my body felt in each
When I could try the opposite in real life

title: Thought Traps Bingo
summary: A bingo game where players mark common thinking traps as the leader reads everyday examples.
goal: Use it to help a group learn to recognize common thinking traps in everyday situations.
body_md: Make bingo cards with traps such as mind reading, catastrophizing and all-or-nothing thinking. Read short examples and let players mark the trap they hear. Turns pass round the circle, and a winner is the first row. Debrief by asking which trap each person notices most in their own thinking.

fields.label: The trap I noticed most in the game
An example from my own life
How I could answer that thought
A trap I want to watch for this week

title: Values Bidding Auction Game
summary: A group game where players use play money to bid on values and see what they are willing to give up.
goal: Use it to help a group see which values matter most when they have to choose.
body_md: Give each player the same amount of play money and a list of values to bid on. Take turns as auctioneer, and bids close when no one raises. Afterward debrief: what did you spend on, what did you let go, and what surprised you? There are no wrong values, only a picture of what matters today.

fields.label: What I spent most of my money on
A value I let go and how that felt
What surprised me
One way I could live a top value this week

title: Skills Toolbox Relay
summary: A relay game where teams race to match coping skills to situations on cards.
goal: Use it to help a group practice matching coping skills to the situations they fit.
body_md: Make situation cards and skill cards. Teams take turns sending a runner to pick a situation and place a skill that fits it. The team agrees on an answer before the next runner goes. The aim is a good match, not speed alone. In debrief, ask which skills they would really use.

fields.label: The skill I would most use
A situation I matched it to
A skill I want to learn more about
How I will remember it

title: Flashlight Strengths Circle
summary: A circle game where each player is the spotlight while others name a real strength they have seen.
goal: Use it to help a group give and receive specific, honest recognition of strengths.
body_md: Pass a flashlight around. The spotlight player sits quietly while each other member names one strength and an example. The receiver says "thank you" only. Rules: be specific, be true, and no "but". Debrief on how it felt to hear it and which strengths surprised them.

fields.label: A strength someone named in me
How it felt to hear it
A strength I named in someone else
A strength I want to use this week

title: Safe and Settled Things List Page
summary: A page where a client lists places, objects and sensations that feel safe and settled to them.
goal: Use it to help a client build a personal list of things that bring a sense of safety.
body_md: Keep the focus on the present: what feels safe now, not on what happened. Ask for sights, sounds, textures and people. If a listed item brings up something hard, set it aside without comment and choose another. Clients can keep the page where they will see it.

fields.label: A place that feels safe or calm to me
Something I can see there
Something I can hear or feel there
Someone or something that helps me feel safe
One way to bring a piece of it into my day

title: Stuck Thought Gentle Reframe Sheet
summary: A sheet for noticing a hard "stuck" thought and writing a kinder, more balanced one beside it.
goal: Use it to help a client notice stuck thoughts about safety or self-blame and practice a balanced alternative.
body_md: Work with a present-day thought, such as "I am never safe", not the details of an event. Ask the client to rate belief, then write what a trusted friend might say. Keep the pace slow and pause to ground if needed. Do not ask for a written account of what happened.

fields.label: A thought that keeps coming back
How strongly I believe it today (0 to 100)
What a trusted friend might say to me
A more balanced thought
How I feel when I read it

title: Making Room for Hard Memories Page
summary: A page for practicing making room for a hard memory's feelings at the edge of attention, with an anchor for the present.
goal: Use it to help a client practice staying present with a hard feeling without being pulled into it.
body_md: Keep this to feelings and sensations in the present moment, not a retelling. Pair each noticing with an anchor, such as feet on the floor. Agree beforehand on a stop signal and use it freely. Short and repeatable beats long.

fields.label: A feeling I noticed in my body
Where in my body I felt it
My anchor in the present
What I did to make a little room for it
What I want to do with my day after this

title: Temperature Change Cooling Card
summary: A card for using cold water or a cool pack to bring down intense body activation.
goal: Use it to give a client a quick body-based option for a surge of intense feeling.
body_md: Teach it in session first: cool water on the face, or a cold pack held for a short time while breathing out slowly. Check with the client about health concerns first, and use their judgment. Have them record what they used and how it went.

fields.label: What was happening when I needed this
What I used to cool down
My feeling level before (0 to 10)
My feeling level after (0 to 10)
Where I will keep what I need

title: Hard Day Support Preferences Plan
summary: A plan where each partner says what helps and what does not on a hard day.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on how to support each other when one is having a rough day.
body_md: Each partner lists what helps and what does not, with no need to explain why. The supportive partner reads it back. Agree on a signal for needing space and one for needing company. Neither partner is asked to share details of anything painful.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps on a hard day
Partner A: what does not help
Partner B: what helps on a hard day
Partner B: what does not help
Our signals for space and company

title: Anxiety Body Map Coloring Page
summary: A body outline the child colors to show where worry feels like it lives.
goal: Use it to help a child notice where worry shows up in the body.
body_md: Hand the child crayons and a body outline and ask where worry feels strong. Let them choose colors and shapes freely. Tell the parent that the page is for noticing, and that they can ask about colors at home. Close with a calming breath, such as smelling a flower.

fields.label: Color where worry lives in my body
The color I picked for worry
What worry feels like there
What helps that spot feel better
Who I can tell when I feel it

title: Worry or Wise Sorting Game
summary: A card game where players sort thoughts into worry voice and wise voice.
goal: Use it to help a group tell worried thoughts from wiser, more balanced ones.
body_md: Write thoughts on cards, such as "everything will go wrong". Players take turns drawing one, placing it in the worry or wise pile, and defending the choice. For worry cards, the player writes a wiser version. Debrief: which worry voice sounds most like yours?

fields.label: A worry card that sounded like me
A wiser version I wrote
How I feel reading the wise version
A worry I want to answer this week

title: Avoidance Costs and Gains Ledger
summary: A ledger where a client lists what they avoid, what it gives them now, and what it costs over time.
goal: Use it to help a client see the short-term gains and long-term costs of avoiding.
body_md: Ask for three things the client avoids, then fill in what avoidance gives and what it takes away. The ledger is not a judgment. Look at the costs together and pick one avoided thing to approach in a small way. Revisit after a week.

fields.label: Something I avoid
What avoiding gives me right away
What avoiding costs me over time
A small step toward it
What I will do this week

title: Not Knowing Small Steps Log
summary: A log for trying a small step in uncertainty and recording how it felt and what happened.
goal: Use it to help a client practice tolerating not knowing in small, planned steps.
body_md: Choose a low-risk step, such as not checking a message for an hour. The client predicts what will happen, tries it and records the result. Review both what happened and how the feeling rose and fell. Increase difficulty only when the client is ready.

fields.label: The uncertain situation I tried
What I predicted would happen
What I felt, and how strongly (0 to 10)
What actually happened
What I noticed about not knowing

title: Worry Passengers on the Bus Worksheet
summary: A worksheet using the passengers-on-the-bus image to practice carrying worry while driving toward a value.
goal: Use it to help a client keep moving toward what matters while worries ride along.
body_md: Describe the bus: the client drives, and worries are noisy passengers who cannot take the wheel. They name a destination tied to a value and a few passengers. The passengers may keep talking; the client keeps driving. Ask what the client wants to do at the next stop.

fields.label: Where I want my bus to go
The loudest passenger and what it says
What I do when it shouts
A small step I can take toward my destination
What I would say to a passenger who will not quiet down

title: Accumulating Positives Weekly Plan
summary: A weekly plan that schedules short-term pleasant events and long-term steps toward what matters.
goal: Use it to help a client add pleasant moments and a longer-term step into a low-energy week.
body_md: Choose small events the client can do in 10 minutes. Add one longer-term step toward a value. Ask them to note being fully present for the event, since attention is part of the skill. If energy is very low, start with one event.

fields.label: A pleasant event I can do this week
When I will do it
A longer-term step toward something I care about
What I noticed while doing it
What got in the way

title: Low Mood Partner Check-In Cards
summary: A set of cards where partners say how they are doing and what they need.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about low mood without pressure to fix it.
body_md: The partner with low mood picks a card, such as "I need quiet" or "I need a walk", and the other partner responds. Practice in session. If either partner mentions thoughts of self-harm, stop and follow your safety steps, and remind them of 988, which they can call or text.

fields.label: Partner A: a card I would use
Partner B: how I will respond to it
Partner B: a card I would use
Partner A: how I will respond to it
If things feel unsafe, we call or text 988 and tell...

title: Feelings Mountain Painting Activity
summary: A painting where a child shows sad and heavy feelings as parts of a mountain scene.
goal: Use it to help a child show heavy feelings through color and a scene.
body_md: Offer paint and paper and ask for a mountain with weather. The child chooses what the clouds, valleys and sunny spots stand for. Tell the parent that the painting is a way to start a talk, and not to ask for explanations. Follow your reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Paint your mountain
What the clouds stand for
What the sunny spot stands for
What I do when the weather is heavy
Who I can sit with when it is cloudy

title: Small Wins Scavenger Hunt
summary: A scavenger hunt where players collect small good moments from their week.
goal: Use it to help a group notice small good moments that are easy to miss when mood is low.
body_md: Each player gets a list of prompts like "something that made me smile" or "a thing I got done". They take turns reading what they found. Rules: small counts, and nobody has to fill every line. Debrief on which prompts were hardest.

fields.label: A small win I found this week
A prompt I could not fill
What I notice about small moments
One I want to look for this week

title: Doing and Feeling Link Chart
summary: A chart where a client rates mood and mastery alongside daily activities to see patterns.
goal: Use it to help a client see how what they do links with how they feel.
body_md: The client records an activity and rates mood and sense of accomplishment for each part of the day. At review, look for activities that lift or drop mood without judging. Choose one that lifted to add more of. Keep entries brief so it is doable.

fields.label: The activity
Mood during it (0 to 10)
Sense of accomplishment (0 to 10)
An activity that lifted my mood
One I want to add this week

title: Tiny First Step Task Ladder
summary: A worksheet that breaks a dreaded task into a ladder of tiny first steps.
goal: Use it to help a client get a task started by shrinking the first step.
body_md: Choose one task the client keeps putting off. Break it down until the first step takes under two minutes, then rank the steps. The client picks a time to try the first rung. Review what made it easier or harder, and adjust the ladder.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off
The tiniest first step
The next three steps
When I will try step one
What might get in the way and what I will do

title: Boring but Valued Tasks Page
summary: A page connecting a dull task to the value behind it and a way to carry the boredom.
goal: Use it to help a client do a tedious task by linking it to something they care about.
body_md: Pick one tedious task and ask what it makes possible. The client names the value and the feeling of boredom, then plans how to make room for it, such as a timer or music. Willingness to be bored is the skill, not liking the task.

fields.label: The task I find boring
What it makes possible for me
The value behind it
How I will make room for the boredom
A reward or pause I will take after

title: Impulse Pause and Choose Card
summary: A card for pausing before acting on an impulse and picking a response.
goal: Use it to help a client slow down between an impulse and what they do next.
body_md: Teach a short pause, such as counting a breath, then asking what the impulse wants and what the client wants. They write the options and pick one. Practice with a low-stakes example. The goal is a gap, not never acting on impulse.

fields.label: The impulse I noticed
What it wants me to do
What I want for later
Two other options
What I chose and how it went

title: Shared Reminder System Planner
summary: A planner where partners agree on reminders and who holds which task, without nagging.
goal: Use it to help partners build a reminder system they both feel okay with.
body_md: Each partner lists tasks that slip and how they would like to be reminded. Agree on tools, such as a shared calendar or a note at the door, and on tone. Decide how a missed reminder is handled. Check back on what works after two weeks.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks that slip and how I would like to be reminded
Partner B: tasks that slip and how I would like to be reminded
The system we choose
What we say when a reminder is missed
When we will adjust it

title: Morning Routine Picture Strip Craft
summary: A craft where a child draws or photographs each morning step on a strip they can follow.
goal: Use it to give a child a picture guide for a morning routine they help to design.
body_md: The child draws or poses for each step, such as getting dressed, and glues the pictures in order on a strip. Tell the parent to point to the strip instead of repeating instructions, and to praise steps done. Adjust the strip with the child after a week.

fields.label: The steps in my morning
Which step is hardest
A way to make it easier
What my grown-up will do to help
How I will feel when I finish

title: Refusal Skills Card Game
summary: A card game where players draw situations and practice saying no to substance use offers.
goal: Use it to help a group rehearse ways to decline substance use in a pressure moment.
body_md: Make cards with situations and with refusal styles, such as a direct no, a change of subject or leaving. Players draw both, role-play for 30 seconds and rate how it felt. Turns rotate, and the group offers tips. Debrief on which style fits each person.

fields.label: A situation I drew and what I said
A refusal style that felt natural
One that felt awkward
A situation I will plan for this week

title: Urge Surfing Wave Tracker
summary: A tracker where a client notes an urge, rides it out and rates how it rose and fell.
goal: Use it to help a client see that urges for substance use rise, peak and pass.
body_md: Teach the wave image in session. The client logs each urge, what set it off, the peak rating and how long until it eased. Look for the pattern of rising and falling. Note what helped, like moving or calling someone, and plan to use it.

fields.label: What set off the urge
How strong it got (0 to 10)
What I did while it was there
How long until it eased
What I would do again

title: Triggers, Thoughts and Choices Chain
summary: A chain from a trigger to a thought, an urge and the choices at each link.
goal: Use it to help a client find the points in a chain where a different choice is possible.
body_md: Take a recent urge for substance use and lay out the chain: trigger, thought, feeling, urge and action. At each link, ask what else the client could have done. Choose a link to practice changing. Keep a nonjudgmental tone throughout.

fields.label: The trigger
The thought that came
The feeling and the urge
What I did
A different choice at one of the links

title: Life Beyond Substance Use Values Page
summary: A page where a client names the values and life areas they want to move toward.
goal: Use it to help a client connect with what they care about beyond substance use.
body_md: Ask about relationships, work, health and play and what the client wants in each. Then ask what their substance use has done to those areas, without blame. Pick one area and one small action. Return to the page when urges are strong.

fields.label: What matters to me in my relationships
What matters to me in work or school

goal: Use it to help a client feel the difference between holding thoughts and being buried by them.

goal: Use it to help a client let worry be present while acting on what matters.
