summary: A sheet for looking at "I should have" thoughts after a loss and weighing them.
goal: Use it to help a client look kindly at guilt in grief.
body_md: Write the "should have" thought, then what the client knew at the time, what they did out of care and what a friend would say. The aim is perspective, not removing the pain. Go at the client's pace.

fields.label: The thought I keep having
What I knew then
What I did out of care
What I would say to a friend
A kinder sentence I can hold

title: Values in Our Relationship Page
summary: A page for naming what the client wants to bring to their relationship and one step.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values rather than on frustration.
body_md: Ask what kind of partner or friend the client wants to be, apart from what the other does. Identify one step this week. Notice when frustration pulls the other way and what a values-led choice might be.

fields.label: What kind of partner I want to be
What I do when I am frustrated
A values-led step this week
What gets in the way
How I will notice and return to it

title: GIVE Skills Practice Page
summary: A page for planning to use gentle, interested, validating and easy manner in a talk.
goal: Use it to help a client keep a relationship in view during a hard talk.
body_md: Choose an upcoming conversation and plan each GIVE step. Role-play it and ask the client how the other person might feel. Aim for practice, not perfection.

fields.label: The conversation I will have
How I will be gentle
How I will show interest
How I will validate
How I will keep an easy manner

title: Complaint to Request Rewrite Sheet
summary: A sheet for turning a complaint into a specific, kind request.
goal: Use it to help partners ask for what they need without blame.
body_md: Each partner writes a recent complaint and rewrites it as "I feel, I need, would you" in one line. Role-play the delivery and the response. Keep the focus on one request at a time.

fields.label: Partner A: my complaint
Partner A: my request
Partner B: my complaint
Partner B: my request
How the request felt to hear

title: Family Feelings House Drawing
summary: A drawing of a house with a room for each family member showing their feelings.
goal: Use it to help a child show how they see their family.
body_md: The child draws a house, adds family members in rooms and chooses faces or colors for each. Ask what is in each room. Tell the parent to listen without fixing. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw the house and rooms
How each person feels
Where I feel safest
What I wish for
Who I tell about big feelings

title: Needs and Wants Sorting Game
summary: A game where players sort cards into needs and wants in relationships and discuss.
goal: Use it to help a group tell needs from wants.
body_md: Cards list things like time alone and gifts. Players sort them into two piles and explain. Others may question once. Debrief on what moved piles and why.

fields.label: A need I sorted
A want I sorted
What I learned from others
A need I want to ask for

title: Safety and Support Map
summary: A map of safe people, safe places and next steps a client can reach for.
goal: Use it to help a client build a present-day circle of safety and support.
body_md: Focus on who and where is safe now. Do not ask for details of what happened. Include a trusted adult, a hotline and a safe place. For a minor, consider your reporting duties. Share 988 (call or text) if the client feels unsafe.

fields.label: People I feel safe with
Places where I feel safe
A trusted adult I can tell
What I can do if I feel unsafe
988 (call or text) and other numbers I will keep

title: Self-Blame Gentle Check Sheet
summary: A sheet for looking at self-blame thoughts without retelling events.
goal: Use it to help a client loosen blame that belongs elsewhere.
body_md: Focus on the thought, not on the event: "What do I tell myself, and what would I tell a friend?" Never ask for details. Acknowledge that blame belongs to the person who caused harm. Stop if the client is overwhelmed.

fields.label: A thought of blame I have
How much I believe it
What I would say to a friend
Who holds responsibility
A kinder sentence I can try

title: Body Anchors and Values Page
summary: A page pairing gentle body anchors with something the client wants to do.
goal: Use it to help a client feel present and move toward what they value.
body_md: Offer anchors the client can choose or decline, such as feeling feet on the floor. Offer no touch or eye contact without consent. Ask about one valued action. Keep it brief and paced.

fields.label: An anchor I choose
What I notice in the room
Something I value
A small action toward it
What I do if it feels like too much

title: Distress Tolerance Safety Card
summary: A card of skills for surges of distress, kept in the client's phone or pocket.
goal: Use it to give a client calming and safe options in the moment.
body_md: List skills the client picks, such as cold water, naming five things they can see and calling a friend. Rehearse. Include a plan if they feel unsafe, with 988 (call or text). Keep the card out of anyone's hands the client does not choose.

fields.label: Skills I will use first
What I see, hear and feel right now
Who I can call
What I do if I feel unsafe, including 988 (call or text)
Where I will keep this card

title: Consent and Pacing Conversation Guide
summary: A guide for partners to talk about pacing, signals and consent in daily closeness.
goal: Use it to help partners set signals and a pace the survivor leads.
body_md: The partner who has experienced abuse sets the pace and chooses signals; the other listens. Do not ask for past details. Plan a stop word and a way to reconnect afterward.

fields.label: Partner A: what pace feels okay
Partner B: how I will respond to a stop
Our signals and stop word
How we reconnect after a pause
What we will talk about next time

title: Calm Corner Design Craft
summary: A craft where a child plans and decorates a calm corner at home.
goal: Use it to help a child pick things that help them settle.
body_md: The child draws or builds a calm corner with items they choose, such as a pillow, a book and a glitter bottle. The parent offers it as a kind choice, not a punishment. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my calm corner
Things I will put in it
What I do there
When I will use it
How my grown-up can help

title: Coping Skill Relay Game
summary: A relay where teams act out a coping skill and the other team guesses it.
goal: Use it to review coping skills in an active way.
body_md: Divide into teams. A member draws a skill card, acts it out without words and the team guesses it. Next member goes. Debrief on skills people want to add to their own lists.

fields.label: A skill I acted out
A skill I did not know
A skill I want to try
When I will use it

title: Coping Skills by Time Available Page
summary: A page sorting skills into one minute, ten minutes and an hour.
goal: Use it to help a client pick a skill that fits the time they have.
body_md: Build the list from skills the client already uses. Mark their favorites. Plan which one they will use at work, at home and at night. Review next time.

fields.label: One-minute skills
Ten-minute skills
One-hour skills
My favorite and why
Where I will keep this list

title: Believable Coping Lines Card Builder
summary: A page for writing short coping statements for hard moments.
goal: Use it to give a client believable lines to say to themselves.
body_md: Brainstorm lines for a hard situation and test which feel believable. Avoid forced positivity. Put the best three on a card or phone note and practice them aloud.

fields.label: A hard situation
What I tend to tell myself
A line that feels believable
Another that might help
Where I will keep the card

title: Making Room for Feelings Practice Page
summary: A practice of allowing a feeling while doing a small valued action.
goal: Use it to help a client use skills to move toward what matters.
body_md: Name the feeling and where it is felt. Invite the client to make space for it with a slow breath and then take a valued action. Ask what changed, if anything, and what happened to the action.

fields.label: The feeling I noticed
Where I feel it
What I did to make room
The valued action I took
What I noticed afterward

title: Cope Ahead for Facing a Fear
summary: A page for planning skills to use before and during a planned fear exposure.
goal: Use it to help a client rehearse skills before facing what they fear.
body_md: Choose a step on the fear ladder. Plan what the client will do before, during and after, and rehearse the skill in imagination. Ask what could make the step feel safer to try.

fields.label: The step I will try
What I expect to feel
Skills I will use before
Skills I will use during
How I will reward myself after

title: Supporter Coach Plan for Partners
summary: A plan where the supporting partner learns how to coach without pushing.
goal: Use it to help a partner cheer the other on in facing a fear.
body_md: The person facing the fear says what helps and what does not. The partner writes short supportive lines and agrees not to push or rescue. Rehearse one step together.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps me and what does not
Partner B: what I can say and do
The step we will try
A signal to pause
How we will celebrate after

title: My Brave Meter Drawing
summary: A drawing of a thermometer the child colors to show how scared they feel at each step.
goal: Use it to help a child rate fear and see it change.
body_md: The child draws a thermometer with levels and picks colors. They rate fear before and after a small step. Tell the parent to cheer effort and avoid forcing. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw your meter
How scared I am before
What I tried
How scared I am after
Who helped me

title: Climb the Fear Steps Board Game
summary: A board game where players move along a ladder of small steps toward a fear.
goal: Use it to make graded steps feel playful and shared.
body_md: Draw a path with steps from easy to hard. Players roll to move and say how big the step feels. Rule: any step can be repeated. Debrief on what steps feel doable.

fields.label: The step I landed on
How big it feels
What I could do next
Who can help me

title: Fear Prediction and Outcome Page
summary: A page for writing what the client expects before facing a fear and what happened.
goal: Use it to help a client compare feared and actual outcomes.
body_md: Write the prediction with a rating of how sure the client is. After the step, record what happened and what they learned. Repeat with the same or a harder step.

fields.label: The fear step
What I think will happen
How sure I am, 0 to 100
What happened
What I learned

title: Body Thought Check Sheet
summary: A sheet for catching harsh thoughts about one's body and writing a fairer view.
goal: Use it to help a client loosen harsh body thoughts.
body_md: Collect a recent harsh thought, what triggered it and what it asked the client to do. Weigh evidence and write a fairer line focused on function and values rather than looks. Do not discuss numbers or measurements.

fields.label: The harsh thought I had
What set it off
What it urged me to do
A fairer view
What I did instead

title: Body as Ally Values Page
summary: A page about what the client wants their body to help them do.
goal: Use it to help a client link their body to values rather than looks.
body_md: Ask what the client wants to do in life that involves their body, such as hugging, dancing or traveling. Note the thoughts that get in the way and plan one small action.

fields.label: Things I want my body to help me do
A value behind each one
Thoughts that get in the way
One small action this week
What I will do with the thoughts

title: Mirror Time Observe and Describe Practice
summary: A practice of describing what one sees and notices without judging.
goal: Use it to help a client practice nonjudgment toward their reflection.
body_md: The client describes neutral facts such as color of eyes or shape of a smile, then notices judgments and lets them be. Offer to start with a hand or another part they choose. Stop if distress rises.

fields.label: What I observed
Where judgments showed up
How I labeled them
What I felt
What I will practice this week

title: Appreciation Without Appearance Exchange
summary: An exchange where partners appreciate each other for actions and character.
goal: Use it to help partners build closeness beyond looks.
body_md: Partners take turns naming things they appreciate that are not about appearance. Receivers say thanks and note how it lands. Discuss comments that help and those that do not.

fields.label: Partner A: what I appreciate
Partner B: what I appreciate
What landed well
Comments that do not help me
What we will say more of

title: Feelings Beyond the Mirror Drawing
summary: A drawing of what makes the child special that cannot be seen in a mirror.
goal: Use it to help a child value their qualities and actions.
body_md: The child draws a mirror and fills it with things like kindness, humor and trying hard. Tell the parent to praise actions and character. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw your mirror
Things in me no one can see
Something I did that I am proud of
What my friends like about me
What my grown-up says

title: Small Wins Evening Notebook Page
summary: A nightly page for jotting down three small things that went acceptably, however ordinary.
goal: Use it to help a client notice ordinary moments that went well.
duration: Five minutes nightly for a week
body_md: Ask the client to write three small, concrete things each night, such as answering a call or making the bed. Read the page together at the next session and ask what they notice about which wins come easily. Keep it modest; if every entry feels forced, shrink the bar rather than the client.

fields.label: Today's date and how the day felt overall
First small thing that went acceptably
Second small thing that went acceptably
Third small thing that went acceptably
What I did to make one of them happen
What I want to carry into tomorrow

title: Values-Based Decision Grid
summary: A two-column grid for weighing a decision by what each choice offers and what it asks of the client.
goal: Use it to help a client slow down a big choice and check it against what matters to them.
body_md: Work through one real decision in session so the client sees how to use the grid alone. Ask the client to name the values behind each column in their own words. The grid sorts information; the decision stays with the client, and you can note when a choice feels pressured by someone else.

fields.label: The decision I am facing
Choice A and what it offers me
Choice A and what it asks of me
Choice B and what it offers me
Choice B and what it asks of me
Which values each choice serves
What I need to find out before I decide

title: Compassionate Letter Outline
summary: A fill-in outline for writing a kind letter to oneself about a hard moment, using a friend's voice.
goal: Use it to give a client structure for speaking to themselves the way they would to a friend.
body_md: Offer the outline when a client is harsh with themselves but warm with others. Model the friend's voice aloud first, since many clients stall on a blank page. Read the finished letter together and ask what it was like to hear. Do not push anyone to keep a letter they find uncomfortable.

fields.label: The hard moment in a sentence or two
What a good friend would notice about how I am feeling
What that friend would want me to know
One kind thing I can do for myself today
A line from this letter I can carry with me

title: Three Rings of Support Placement Map
summary: Concentric circles where the client places the people, groups and places that support them.
goal: Use it to help a client see who is around them and where support is thin.
body_md: Draw three rings with the client at the center: close, helpful and occasional. Let them place names without judging who belongs where. Gaps are information for you both, not failures. End by picking one person or place they might reach toward this week and what the first step looks like.

fields.label: People in my closest ring
People or groups in my middle ring
People or places in my outer ring
Who I wish were closer, and why
One person I could reach toward this week
What I would say or do to reach out

title: Conversation Rehearsal Script Page
summary: A page for drafting and rehearsing the opening lines of a hard but ordinary conversation.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare what they want to say and how they want to say it.
body_md: Choose a conversation the client has been putting off, such as asking a boss for a day off. Draft the first two sentences and rehearse them aloud with you. Ask what they predict the other person will say and plan one reply. Let the client change the words until they sound like themselves.

fields.label: The conversation and who it is with
What I most want the other person to understand
My first two sentences
What I think they might say back
How I will reply
How I will feel if it goes differently than planned

title: Friend Versus Self Advice Comparison Page
summary: A page comparing the advice a client gives a friend with what they tell themselves in the same situation.
goal: Use it to help a client notice when their self-talk is harsher than the advice they would give others.
body_md: Use it when a client's self-criticism sounds nothing like how they treat other people. Fill in the friend's side first, because it is easier. Then ask what stops them from saying the same to themselves. Avoid arguing the point; let the contrast do the work and invite them to try the friend's version this week.

fields.label: The situation and what I tell myself
What I would say to a friend in the same spot
The words and tone I would use with that friend
What gets in the way of using that voice on myself
A fairer thing I can say to myself this week

title: Cost of Worrying Ledger
summary: A two-sided ledger of what a client believes worry does for them and what it takes from them.
goal: Use it to help a client look at worry as a habit with both costs and perceived benefits.
body_md: Take the perceived benefits seriously; many clients believe worry keeps them prepared or safe. Write both columns before comparing them. Then ask what else could do that job at a lower cost. The aim is curiosity about the habit, not convincing the client to stop worrying.

fields.label: A worry that visits me often
What I believe worrying does for me
What worrying costs me in time and energy
What it costs my body and sleep
What it costs my relationships
Another way to get what I want from worrying

title: Many Possible Readings Spoke Wheel
summary: A wheel with spokes for other possible explanations of an event the client read negatively.
goal: Use it to help a client generate more than one reading of an ambiguous event.
body_md: Choose a recent event the client read in the worst light, like an unanswered text. Fill the first spoke with the explanation they landed on, then ask for at least four others, including silly ones. Ask which they could test. Warm up with a neutral example if the client resists.

fields.label: The event and what I first assumed
A second explanation
A third explanation
A fourth explanation, even a silly one
How I could find out which is closest
How I feel now compared with before

title: Rule Rewrite Worksheet
summary: A worksheet for turning rigid personal rules into flexible preferences.
goal: Use it to help a client loosen 'must' and 'should' rules that keep driving distress.
body_md: Collect two or three of the client's 'always' and 'never' rules from the session and bring them here. Ask where each rule came from and who it serves. Rewrite one together, then have the client try living by the flexible version in a small, low-stakes way before the next visit.

fields.label: A rule I live by (I must, I should, I never)
Where I learned this rule
What happens when I break it, or fear I will
What the rule costs me
A flexible version that still keeps what I care about
A small way to try the new version this week

title: Feeling Is Not Proof Separation Cards
summary: A card sequence separating how something feels from what is known about it.
goal: Use it to help a client notice when a strong feeling is being treated as proof.
body_md: Pick a moment where the client said 'I feel like a failure, so I am one' or similar. Have them write the feeling and the conclusion on separate lines. Then list what they know for sure. Keep it light and brief; the skill is noticing the jump, which grows with repetition.

fields.label: The feeling I had, and how strong it was
The conclusion my mind drew from it
What I know for sure about the situation
What I do not yet know
What I would conclude if I set the feeling aside

title: Bus Driver and Loud Passengers Rehearsal Log
summary: A script and log for the bus metaphor, with the client driving toward a value while difficult thoughts ride along.
goal: Use it to help a client practice moving toward a value without waiting for their thoughts to quiet.
body_md: Run the metaphor aloud first and let the client cast their own passengers, naming the thoughts that shout loudest. Then ask where the bus is headed. Practice letting a passenger talk while the client keeps driving. Check afterward that it did not feel like ignoring or fighting the thoughts.

fields.label: Where I want my bus to go (a value)
The passengers who shout at me, in their own words
What each passenger wants me to do
What I do when I let them take the wheel
One turn toward my value I can make this week
How I will thank a passenger and keep driving

title: Hands Over Face Thought Distance Practice
summary: A short practice using the hands to feel the difference between holding a thought tight and holding it loosely.
goal: Use it to give a client a felt sense of unhooking from a thought.
body_md: Guide the client to press their hands over their face as if the thought were right on top of them, then lower them to the lap. Ask what changed in how much they could see. Pair it with one real thought. Skip the face-covering step with any client who may find it unsettling.

fields.label: The thought I want to practice with
What I notice with my hands pressed to my face
What I notice when I lower them to my lap
What I can do with my hands free
When this week I could try this on my own

title: Weekly Values Direction Compass Page
summary: A weekly page asking how closely the client's actions pointed toward their chosen values.
goal: Use it to help a client check direction each week without judging themselves.
body_md: Have the client name three values at the start and keep them at the top. Each week, ask what they did that pointed toward each one, however small, and where they drifted. Treat drift as information. If the client is hard on themselves, ask what a kind coach would say.

fields.label: The three values I am steering by
One thing I did this week that pointed toward each
Where I drifted and what pulled me off course
What I would like next week to look like
One small step I choose for next week

title: Willing Hands Obstacle Log
summary: A log of the obstacles to a chosen action and the client's willingness to carry them along.
goal: Use it to help a client name what shows up when they try something that matters and make room for it.
body_md: Start with one concrete action the client cares about. List what usually shows up: thoughts, feelings, urges, sensations. Ask whether they would be willing to carry those along for the sake of the action, and how much, from 0 to 10. Willingness is a choice, not a feeling, so do not push a high number.

fields.label: The action I care about
The thoughts that show up when I try
The feelings and sensations that show up
How willing I am to carry them, from 0 to 10
What would make it a little easier to say yes
What I will do and when

title: Sky and Weather Journal
summary: A journal built on the metaphor of the self as the sky and experiences as passing weather.
goal: Use it to help a client practice noticing experiences without being defined by them.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Introduce the sky and weather image in session and let the client adapt it. The daily entry asks them to name the weather and then the part of them that notices it. Some clients find this abstract at first, so give a concrete example from their own week and keep entries short.

fields.label: Today's weather inside me (thoughts, feelings, sensations)
The part of me that noticed the weather
What the weather wanted me to do
What I did instead, if anything
What stayed the same about me through the day

title: Camera View Versus Story Walkthrough
summary: A step-by-step page for separating the facts of an event from the story and feelings around it.
goal: Use it to help a client test whether an emotion fits the facts of a situation.
body_md: Walk through one recent upset. Ask for the event described as a camera would, then the interpretations, then the emotion and its intensity. Compare the emotion with the facts and decide together whether it fits. The aim is a closer look, not talking the client out of feeling.

fields.label: What happened, as a camera would record it
The interpretations and assumptions I made
The emotion I felt and how strong it was
Whether the facts fit the size of that emotion
What I can do that suits the facts

title: Urge Versus Opposite Step Planner
summary: A planner for choosing an action opposite to an emotion's urge when the emotion does not fit the facts.
goal: Use it to help a client rehearse opposite action in small, safe steps.
body_md: Choose an emotion where the urge is making things worse, such as withdrawing when sad. First check with the client that the emotion does not fit the facts. Then plan one small opposite step, including the body language and tone that go with it. Practice it in session if you can.

fields.label: The emotion and its urge
Whether the facts fit this emotion
The opposite action I could take
How I will do it all the way, including posture and voice
When I will try it this week
How I felt after

title: Wise Mind Pause Card
summary: A pocket card with a short script for pausing and checking in with wise mind before acting.
goal: Use it to give a client a quick stop between a strong feeling and what they do next.
body_md: Make the card with the client in session so the words are theirs. Practice a pause with a mild upset first. The card works best when rehearsed before it is needed, so assign a few trial runs in calm moments this week.

fields.label: What I feel in my body when I need to pause
The first words I say to myself to stop
Where I breathe from, and for how long
The question I ask my wise mind
What I do next after the pause

title: PLEASE Skills Weekly Log
summary: A seven-day log of sleep, movement, eating and substance habits that influence emotional vulnerability.
goal: Use it to help a client notice how basic care shapes how easily emotions swing.
body_md: Introduce the idea that the body's state makes emotions easier or harder to manage. The log asks about care, not performance. Review it without praise or blame, looking for one small habit the client wants to adjust. Handle the food question gently and keep it about regular care, never rules.

fields.label: Last night's sleep and how rested I feel
Whether I took care of any health needs today
What I ate and whether I ate regularly
Any substances I used
How much I moved my body
My emotional vulnerability today, from 1 to 10

title: Dreaded Event Skills Rehearsal Sheet
summary: A sheet for imagining a hard situation and rehearsing skills before it happens.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare skills for a situation they already dread.
body_md: Pick a real upcoming event. Ask the client to describe it in detail, name the emotions and urges likely to come up, and choose skills for each. Then have them rehearse in imagination, picturing the skill working. Stay with a mildly hard event first so rehearsal builds confidence.

fields.label: The situation coming up and when
The emotions and urges I expect
The skills I plan to use
What I will say and do, step by step
What I will do if the plan does not go as hoped
How I will take care of myself afterward

title: Partner Weekly Appreciation and Plans Meeting Guide
summary: A guide for a weekly check-in where each partner has time to speak and be heard.
goal: Use it to give a couple a short, regular space for appreciation, concerns and plans.
body_md: Set up the meeting in session and rehearse the order: appreciations, what went well, concerns raised softly, and plans for the coming week. Each partner takes a turn writing their part first. Remind them to keep it short and stop if either partner feels flooded, then resume later.

fields.label: Partner A: three things I appreciated about my partner this week
Partner B: three things I appreciated about my partner this week
Partner A: one concern, stated softly
Partner B: one concern, stated softly
What we each heard the other say
One thing we will each do before next week

title: Repair Phrase Menu
summary: A menu of phrases each partner can offer to calm a tense moment and get back on track.
goal: Use it to help a couple pick words they will actually say when an argument heats up.
body_md: Have each partner circle phrases that would help them hear from the other, and cross out any that would sound false. Then they choose a few for themselves to offer. Rehearse one in session during a mild disagreement. The couple should write phrases in their own voices so they sound natural.

fields.label: Partner A: phrases from my partner that would help me calm down
Partner B: phrases from my partner that would help me calm down
Partner A: phrases I can offer in a tense moment
Partner B: phrases I can offer in a tense moment
How we will signal that we want to repair
When we will practice this together

title: Dreams Within Conflict Interview
summary: An interview for uncovering the hopes and meanings underneath a recurring disagreement.
goal: Use it to help partners hear what the other cares about behind a stuck issue.
body_md: Pick one recurring disagreement. One partner speaks as the other listens with curiosity and asks open questions about what the position means to them. Then switch. The goal is understanding, not agreement; stop anyone from problem-solving until both have been heard.

fields.label: The issue we keep returning to
Partner A: what this issue means to me and where it comes from
Partner B: what this issue means to me and where it comes from
Partner A: a hope I have that sits underneath it
Partner B: a hope I have that sits underneath it
One thing we can honor in each other's dream

title: Stress-Reducing Conversation Sheet
summary: A sheet for taking turns to talk about outside stress while the partner listens as an ally.
goal: Use it to help partners support each other about stress that comes from outside the relationship.
body_md: Each partner chooses a stressor from work, family or health. The listener practices staying on the speaker's side and holding back advice unless asked. Coach them to ask what would help most. Debrief about how it felt to be listened to and to listen.

fields.label: Partner A: a stress from outside our relationship
Partner B: what I understood about how that feels
Partner B: a stress from outside our relationship
Partner A: what I understood about how that feels
What each of us needs from the other when stressed
One small way we will support each other this week

title: Bids and Responses Tracker
summary: A tracker where each partner notes the small bids for connection they offered and how they were met.
goal: Use it to help partners notice the everyday moments where connection is offered and answered.
body_md: Explain a bid as a small reach for attention, like a comment or a gesture. Each partner logs bids they made and bids they noticed from the other. Review for patterns without scorekeeping; some couples turn this into blame, so keep the focus on noticing and appreciating.

fields.label: Partner A: a bid I made today and how it was met
Partner B: a bid I made today and how it was met
Partner A: a bid I noticed from my partner
Partner B: a bid I noticed from my partner
A bid I missed or wish I had answered differently
What we want to do more of

title: Paper Plate Feelings Forecast Craft
summary: The child builds a paper weather station and moves the arrow to show how they feel today.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete, playful way to name and share how they feel.
body_md: The child decorates a paper plate with weather pictures like sunny, stormy and foggy and attaches a movable arrow. Ask them to show you today's weather and what made it that way. Send the station home and tell the parent to check it with the child once a day without fixing the feeling. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw the weather station and today's weather
What made today's weather this way
The weather I like best and why
The weather that is hardest and what helps
What my grown-up can do when it storms

title: Worry Monster Shoebox
summary: The child decorates a shoebox monster and feeds it written or drawn worries before bed.
goal: Use it to give a child a safe place to put worries so they can rest.
body_md: Provide a box with a slot and let the child give the monster a silly name and face. Worries go in as words or drawings, and a parent can read a few together the next day. Tell the parent to respond with warmth and a small plan, not reassurance alone. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my worry monster and give it a name
Worries I feed to my monster
What my monster looks like when it is full
What helps me feel calm after I feed it
What my grown-up does when I tell them a worry

title: Calm Jar Build
summary: The child fills a jar with water, glitter and glue, and watches it settle while practicing slow breathing.
goal: Use it to show a child that big feelings settle if given time and calm breaths.
body_md: The child shakes the jar and watches the glitter fall while breathing slowly with you. Link it to feelings: shaken is upset, settled is calm. Tell the parent to keep the jar somewhere the child can reach and to use it with them, not as a punishment. Never use it as a time-out tool.

fields.label: Draw my calm jar
What my feelings look like when the glitter is swirling
What my body feels like when the glitter settles
When I could use my jar
Who I can use it with

title: My Helper Hand
summary: The child traces a hand and writes or draws a trusted helper on each finger.
goal: Use it to help a child name the people they can turn to and what each can help with.
body_md: The child traces their hand and picks five people or places to turn to. Ask what each helper does best. Tell the parent that a child should have at least one adult at home on the hand and to add to it as needed. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm or names an unsafe person.

fields.label: Trace my hand and draw a helper on each finger
The helper I talk to when I am scared
The helper who makes me laugh
What I would tell a helper if I felt sad
One new helper I want to add

title: Coping Cape Design
summary: The child designs a superhero cape covered with their own coping powers.
goal: Use it to help a child see their coping skills as strengths they carry.
body_md: The child decorates a paper cape with symbols for skills like breathing, asking for a hug or drawing. Ask for the cape's name and its hardest challenge. Tell the parent to wear it with the child sometimes and remind them of their powers. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my cape and name my hero
My coping powers
The monster that is hardest to beat
Which power I will use first
How my grown-up can help my powers work

title: Feelings Charades Turn Cards
summary: Players act out feelings from cards while others guess, then share when they felt that way.
goal: Use it to help a group practice reading and naming feelings in a playful setting.
body_md: Each player draws a card and acts out the feeling without words. The group guesses, and the actor shares a time they felt it if they wish. Taking a turn is optional. In the debrief, ask which feelings were hardest to show or guess and what clues helped. Keep it light and stop if someone looks overwhelmed.

fields.label: The feeling I acted out
How the group guessed it
A time I felt this way
The feeling that was hardest to guess
What I learned about showing feelings

title: Coping Skills Bingo Night
summary: A bingo card of coping skills where players mark each one they have tried this week.
goal: Use it to encourage a group to try a wide set of coping skills and trade ideas.
body_md: Make cards in advance with skills such as walking, drawing, a call to a friend or a breathing exercise. Over the week players mark skills they use. At the next session, call out skills and have players tell how it went. The first full line shares a story. Debrief on which skills they will keep.

fields.label: The skills I marked this week
The skill that helped most and why
A skill I want to try next
A skill from someone else I would like to borrow
What I will keep doing

title: Perspective Dice Game
summary: Players roll dice to pick a character and respond to a situation from that character's point of view.
goal: Use it to build flexibility in taking other perspectives.
body_md: Create a list of six characters, such as a friend, a teacher, a younger self, an older self, a pet and a stranger. Each player rolls, reads a short situation and answers as that character. The debrief covers what shifted and what was hard. Keep the situations mild at first.

fields.label: The character I rolled and the situation
What this character would say
How I felt speaking as them
What I noticed about my own view
How I might use this in a real situation

title: Pretend Coins Values Bidding Game
summary: Players bid with pretend coins on values cards to find out what matters most to them.
goal: Use it to help players discover which values they are willing to spend on.
body_md: Give each player the same number of coins and a deck of values like family, honesty, adventure and health. Run an auction where only the highest bids win. After the auction, players explain what they bid on and what they let go. Debrief on whether their real week matches their bids.

fields.label: The values I bid on most
The value I was sorry to lose
What my bids told me about myself
One value I want to spend more time on
One step I can take this week

title: Skill Showdown Card Game
summary: Two teams draw problem cards and race to name coping skills that fit, then explain how they would use them.
goal: Use it to help players build a larger set of skills and fit them to situations.
body_md: Prepare problem cards, like a long wait or an argument with a friend. Teams alternate drawing, offering a skill and explaining it. Points go for creativity and fit, not for the fastest answer. In the debrief, ask which skills seemed most realistic and which ones the group wants to practice.

fields.label: The problem I drew
The skill my team picked
Why it fits
A different skill I would try
What I will practice before next time

title: Revved, Shut Down or Workable Pacing Card
summary: A card for noting when the client feels too revved, too shut down or in a workable zone.
goal: Use it to help a client notice their state and choose a pace that feels workable.
body_md: Draw three zones with the client and let them name their own signs for each, in the body and in thinking. Use the card at the start of sessions to set the pace. It is about noticing and pacing, not about revisiting what happened. Remind the client that 988 (call or text) is available any time they feel unsafe.

fields.label: Signs in my body when I am too revved up
Signs when I am too shut down
Signs that I am in my workable zone
What helps me move toward the workable zone
What I need to slow down or stop in a session
If I ever feel unsafe, I can call or text 988 and tell someone

title: Grounding Menu by Sense
summary: A menu of grounding skills sorted by the five senses that the client chooses from.
goal: Use it to give a client a personal set of grounding skills for hard moments.
body_md: Try several grounding skills in session, such as holding something cold, naming colors or pressing feet to the floor, and have the client rate each. Keep the ones that help and cross off the rest. The client builds the menu from tools they can use anywhere. This stays in the present and does not require details of the past.

fields.label: Sights that help me feel here and now
Sounds that help
Touch or temperature that helps
Smells or tastes that help
Movements that help
The three skills I will carry with me

title: Safe Anchors and Values Page
summary: A page linking what feels steadying now with what the client wants their life to be about.
goal: Use it to help a client connect small safe actions to the life they want.
body_md: Start by listing people, places and routines that feel steady, then ask what the client wants to move toward. Keep the focus on the present and future. Go slowly: it is fine for the client to leave a section blank. Check in about how the page felt before the end of the session.

fields.label: People, places and routines that feel steady
What I want more of in my life
One small thing I can do toward that this week
What might get in the way
What I can say to myself when it is hard
Who I can ask for support

title: Five Senses Landing Game
summary: A turn-taking game where players name things they can notice around the room to arrive in the present.
goal: Use it to help a group practice grounding in a light, low-pressure way.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a sense card and naming something they notice in the room. Passing is always allowed. Debrief on which prompts felt easiest and what they would use outside session. Choose a quiet, predictable room and tell players the game never asks for their stories.

fields.label: The sense I drew and what I noticed
The prompt that felt easiest
The prompt I would use outside session
How my body felt after the game
One place I could play this on my own

title: Safe Place Drawing and Helper List
summary: The child draws a place that feels safe and lists the grown-ups who help keep them safe.
goal: Use it to help a child name what feels safe and who can help.
body_md: Invite the child to draw a real or imaginary safe place and add the helpers around it. Do not ask for details of upsetting events. Tell the parent how to keep routines steady and what to say if the child shares worries. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my safe place
What I see, hear and feel there
Who keeps me safe
What I do when I feel scared
What my grown-up can say to help

title: Small Not-Knowing Prediction Log
summary: A log for testing predictions about how bad uncertainty will feel in a small, planned way.
goal: Use it to help a client try small amounts of uncertainty and compare predictions with what happened.
duration: Two weeks, ten minutes per entry
body_md: Choose a small uncertain choice the client usually avoids, such as not checking a message right away. Record the prediction before and the result after. Look for the gap between the two without promising any outcome. Increase the step only when the client agrees it is time.

fields.label: The uncertain situation I will try
What I predict will happen
How anxious I expect to feel, from 0 to 10
What actually happened
How anxious I actually felt
What I learned for the next try

title: Where Worry Lives in My Body Sketch
summary: An outline of a body where the client marks where anxiety is felt and what each sensation is like.
goal: Use it to help a client link anxiety to body sensations and choose a response.
body_md: Ask the client to color the places where they feel anxiety and describe each sensation in a few words. Notice with them how sensations come and go. Then list one thing that helps for each area. Keep the language descriptive and avoid telling them what the sensations mean.

fields.label: Where in my body I feel anxiety
What those sensations feel like
What the sensations tell me to do
What I do when they show up
What helps each one a little

title: Anxiety as a Passenger Page
summary: A page for describing anxiety as a traveling companion and choosing actions while it rides along.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values while anxiety is present.
body_md: Ask the client to describe their anxiety as a character who travels with them. What does it say, and what does it want? Then identify one valued action to take with the character along. Keep a light, curious tone. Check that this is not being used to avoid feeling anything.

fields.label: How I describe my anxiety as a character
What it says to me most
What it wants me to avoid
A valued action I want to take anyway
How I carry it along while I act
What I did and what happened

title: Worry Time Card Game
summary: A card game where players sort worries into act now, schedule for later or let float by.
goal: Use it to help players practice sorting worries by what they can do about them.
body_md: Players write real or sample worries on cards, then take turns placing them in three piles. Others can ask a question about the placement. The debrief asks what made sorting hard and which pile surprised them. Passing a card is always allowed.

fields.label: A worry I sorted and where it went
What helped me decide
A worry that did not fit a pile
What I can do now about one worry
What I will let float by

title: Worry Dolls Build and Tell
summary: The child makes small worry dolls from craft sticks and tells each one a worry before bed.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful ritual for setting worries aside at night.
body_md: The child decorates three or four dolls and gives each a worry to hold. Tell the parent to keep the dolls near the bed, listen to what the child shares, and not try to talk the worry away. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my worry dolls
The worry each doll holds
What I say to the dolls at night
What helps me feel safe in bed
What my grown-up does when I tell them

title: Doing and Feeling Day Grid
summary: A chart linking daily activities with mood so the client can see which actions lift or lower it.
goal: Use it to help a client find small activities that are connected with a better day.
body_md: Ask the client to log one activity per block and rate mood from 1 to 10. At the next session, look at the high and low points together. Start with tiny activities, like stepping outside. If hopelessness comes up, ask about safety in session and share that 988 (call or text) is open any time.

fields.label: Time of day and what I did
My mood from 1 to 10
Whether the activity felt like pleasure or like achievement
What I notice across the week
One activity to add next week
If I feel unsafe, I can call or text 988

title: Tiny Steps Ladder
summary: A ladder of very small actions for days when energy is low.
goal: Use it to help a client choose a step small enough to take even on a hard day.
body_md: Build the ladder from the bottom with the client, starting with steps that take under two minutes. Let them choose what counts. When a step feels too big, split it. Review by noticing what was done rather than what was missed.

fields.label: The smallest thing I can do on my worst day
A slightly bigger step
A step that needs a little energy
A step that includes another person
The step I will try today
How I will notice and give myself credit

title: Values When Life Feels Flat Page
summary: A page for naming what matters even when interest and energy are low.
goal: Use it to help a client reconnect to values when motivation is missing.
body_md: Ask the client what used to matter and what they might still care about, without requiring the feeling to return first. Pick one tiny value-linked action and plan it. Do not argue with flat feelings; invite action alongside them. Ask about safety and name 988 (call or text).

fields.label: Things that mattered to me before
Things I still care about even a little
One tiny action linked to a value
What my mood tells me about doing it
What I will do anyway and when
If I feel unsafe, I can call or text 988

title: Daily Enjoy and Accomplish Pair Planner
summary: A weekly plan with one thing for pleasure and one for mastery each day.
goal: Use it to help a client balance enjoyable moments with a small sense of accomplishment.
body_md: Define pleasure as enjoyable and mastery as satisfying or capable. Plan one of each for every day, keeping them small. Review what happened with curiosity. If days fall through, ask what got in the way and resize the plan.

fields.label: Pleasant activities I could do
Things that give me a sense of mastery
This week's plan, day by day
What got in the way
What I felt after the ones I did
What to adjust next week

title: Partner Support for Low Mood Conversation
summary: A guide for a partner to ask how to help when the other has low mood, and for both to plan.
goal: Use it to help partners talk about what support is useful and what is not.
body_md: The partner with low mood describes what helps and what does not. The other listens first and asks what they can do. Together they pick one small, shared activity. Remind the partner that their role is support, not fixing, and that they need their own care too.

fields.label: Partner with low mood: what helps me and what does not
Partner listening: what I heard
Partner listening: what I find hard
One small thing we can do together
How each of us will care for ourselves
When we will check in again

title: Launch Pad Spot Setup
summary: A page for choosing one spot at home where everything needed for leaving the house is kept.
goal: Use it to help a client reduce last-minute scrambling with one visible home base.
body_md: Walk through leaving the house and list what is needed each time. Choose a spot near the door and decide how it will be visible and easy. Keep it simple; one system the client likes beats a complex one. Review how it went and adjust.

fields.label: What I need when I leave the house
Where I will keep it all
How I will see it before leaving
What usually gets in the way
What I will do when something is missing
How I will check it this week

title: Body Doubling Craft Hour Plan
summary: A parent and child plan for working side by side on a task, with a timer and a sticker chart.
goal: Use it to help a child start a task with company and short breaks.
body_md: The child and parent decorate a timer card and pick a task. The parent works nearby on something else, and both take short breaks. Tell the parent to stay calm, notice effort and skip lectures. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw our work spot
The task I will start
How long I will work before a break
What I will do on my break
What my grown-up does while I work

title: Time Sense Estimation Game
summary: Players guess how long tasks take, then time them and compare.
goal: Use it to build a feel for how long things take.
body_md: Each player guesses how long a small task will take, then does it with a timer. Compare guesses with real times and talk about patterns without scoring against anyone. In debrief, ask how they will use this when planning a day. Keep tasks simple.

fields.label: The task and my guess
How long it actually took
Was I faster or slower than I guessed
What this tells me about planning
One real task I will time this week

title: Task Start Barrier Log
summary: A log of what gets in the way of starting a task and what small trick helps.
goal: Use it to help a client find the specific barrier at the start of a task.
body_md: Ask the client to log tasks they delayed and what they noticed in the moment before starting. Then try one start trick, like a two-minute timer. Look at the barriers together. Avoid labeling delay as laziness.

fields.label: The task I put off
What I thought or felt before starting
What got in the way
A trick I tried to start
What happened after I started
What I will try next

title: Household Load Reset Meeting Sheet
summary: A sheet for partners to list shared tasks and decide who takes what with reminders that work.
goal: Use it to help partners divide tasks in a way that fits how each of them works.
body_md: List household tasks and each partner's preferences. Agree on reminders that are not nagging, such as a shared calendar. Keep blame out by discussing systems, not character. Review after one week.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I can take and how I remember them
Partner B: tasks I can take and how I remember them
Tasks that need a new system
How we will remind without nagging
How we will thank each other
When we will review

title: Urge Rise and Fade Timeline Log
summary: A log for tracking an urge from start to peak to fade, with notes on what was noticed.
goal: Use it to help a client see that urges rise and pass without acting.
duration: One week, five minutes per urge
body_md: Ask the client to record the time, the cue and the intensity as they ride the urge. Notice together how it changed. Do not promise it will end in a set time. If substance use occurred, treat it as information, not failure.

fields.label: Where I was and what set off the urge
Strength of the urge from 0 to 10 at the start
What I noticed in my body and thoughts
What I did while it rose
Strength at the end
What I learned about urges

title: Values Behind Substance Use Page
summary: A page for exploring what substance use gives the client and what it takes from their values.
goal: Use it to help a client look at substance use in light of what matters to them.
body_md: Approach with curiosity and no judgment. Ask what substance use does for them and how it fits their values. Pick one small action toward a value that does not involve using. Support their choices and keep their goals central.

fields.label: What substance use gives me
What it takes from what I care about
What I value in my life
One action toward a value without using
Who I want to be around
What I will do when an urge comes

title: Urge Surfing and Distraction Plan
summary: A plan combining mindful awareness of urges with distraction and self-soothing options.
goal: Use it to give a client a tool set for moments when urges are strong.
body_md: List high-risk times and choose a mix of skills: mindful noticing, distraction and self-soothing. Rehearse one in session. Include people to contact. If the client is in crisis, name 988 (call or text).

fields.label: High-risk times and places for urges
Mindful steps I can take
Distractions that work for me
Self-soothing that works
People I can contact
If I am in crisis, I can call or text 988

title: Recovery Support Week Planner
summary: A weekly planner placing supports, routines and enjoyable activities in the client's days.
goal: Use it to help a client build a week that supports their goals around substance use.
body_md: Fill the week with supports such as meetings, calls, exercise and fun. Mark the riskiest hours and add support there. Be realistic; a full plan the client keeps is better than a perfect one. Review each week.

fields.label: My goals around substance use
Supports I will use this week
Routines I will keep
Enjoyable things I will schedule
The riskiest times and my plan
Who I will tell about the plan

title: Family Conversations About Substance Use Guide
summary: A guide for a partner or family member and the client to talk about substance use, impact and support.
goal: Use it to help partners speak openly about substance use without blame.
body_md: Set ground rules: speak for yourself, no labels, and pause when heated. Each partner shares what they notice, how it affects them and what they hope for. Close with one agreement. Offer separate support for the partner too.

fields.label: Partner using: what I want my partner to know
Partner using: how I see my goals
Partner listening: what I notice and how it affects me
Partner listening: what I hope for
What each of us needs
One agreement for this week

title: Anger Trigger and Thought Log
summary: A log linking triggers, hot thoughts, body signs and actions during anger.
goal: Use it to help a client spot the thoughts that fuel anger and the point to pause.
duration: One week, ten minutes per entry
body_md: Fill in an entry in session for a recent event. Ask what the client told themselves just before the anger peaked. Then write a calmer version of the thought. Do not label anger as bad; it is information. Keep safety in mind and check on any risk to others.

fields.label: What happened
The thoughts that came up
Where I felt anger in my body
What I did
A calmer thought I could try
What I will do differently next time

title: Cool Down Skills Ladder
summary: A ladder of skills from quick body resets to longer calming steps for anger.
goal: Use it to give a client a set of ways to bring anger down by degrees.
body_md: Build the ladder from fast skills like cold water or paced breathing up to longer ones like a walk. Try two in session and rate their effect. The client picks which belongs at each rung. Add a step for returning to the conversation later.

fields.label: Skills that work in seconds
Skills that need a few minutes
Skills for a longer cool down
What I say to leave a tense moment
How I come back to the conversation
Which skill I will practice first

title: Heat Levels Paper Volcano Build
summary: The child builds a paper volcano and marks the warning signs before it erupts, with cool-down tools.
goal: Use it to help a child notice early anger signals and practice cooling down.
body_md: Build a volcano with levels and ask the child what their body does at each. Add calm-down tools at the lower levels. Tell the parent to praise early cool-downs and talk about repair afterward, not punishment. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my volcano
What happens in my body as it heats up
My warning signs
What cools me down
What my grown-up does to help

title: Anger Thermometer Role Play Game
summary: Players draw scenarios, rate the heat and pick a skill to bring the temperature down.
goal: Use it to help players practice choosing skills at different anger levels.
body_md: Create scenario cards and a thermometer. Players rate the heat, choose a skill and act out the response with a partner. Others suggest alternatives. Debrief on what worked and why. Keep scenarios mild and allow passing.

fields.label: The scenario I drew and my heat rating
The skill I picked
How it went in the role play
What someone else suggested
What I will try in real life

title: Pause Signal and Come-Back Pact
summary: An agreement partners make for taking a break during conflict and when to come back.
goal: Use it to help partners pause heated conversations and return respectfully.
body_md: Partners agree on a signal, how long the break lasts and what each does during it. The one who calls it must also return. Practice calling it in session. Make sure the break is not a way of leaving the other behind. If there is any fear of harm, speak with each partner separately.

fields.label: Our signal for a break
How long we will take
What I will do during the break
How I will return to the conversation
What I need from my partner during a break
When we will practice

title: Intrusive Thought Practice Rungs Planner
summary: A ladder of steps from easier to harder situations with notes on staying without rituals.
goal: Use it to plan gradual practice with situations that set off intrusive thoughts.
body_md: Build the ladder with the client, ranking steps by distress. Agree on which rituals to skip at each step and how to stay with the feeling. Start at a low rung and practice together. Move up only when the client is ready. This is a planning page that supports your own clinical judgment.

fields.label: Situations that set off my intrusive thoughts
Ranking from easiest to hardest
The first step I will try
The ritual I will skip
How I will stay with the feeling

title: Thoughts Are Not Instructions Defusion Page
summary: A page practicing the difference between having an intrusive thought and acting on it.
goal: Use it to help a client notice thoughts as thoughts and choose actions by values.
body_md: Have the client write an intrusive thought as 'I am having the thought that...'. Say it in a silly voice and ask what changes. Then pick a value-based action. Be careful not to use defusion as another ritual; check how it felt.

fields.label: An intrusive thought I notice
I am having the thought that...
What changes when I say it that way
What the thought wants me to do

title: Ritual Time Tracker
summary: A tracker for noticing how much time rituals take and what they cost.
goal: Use it to help a client see the time and energy that rituals use.
body_md: Ask the client to log rituals without judgment: when, how long and what came before. Review for patterns and discuss what they are giving up. Keep it descriptive so shame does not grow.

fields.label: Time and what set off the ritual
What I did and for how long
What I felt before and after
What I missed because of it
What I would rather be doing
One small step I will try

title: Worry Bully Talk-Back Cards
summary: The child draws the worry bully and writes brave talk-back lines on cards.
goal: Use it to help a child separate themselves from a bossy worry voice.
body_md: The child draws the bully and gives it a silly name. Together write talk-back lines like 'I do not have to do what you say.' Tell the parent to avoid giving reassurance on repeat and to cheer on brave choices. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: Draw my worry bully
What the bully tells me to do
My brave talk-back lines
One time I did not listen
How my grown-up can cheer me on

title: Roll and Leave It Unchecked Dice Game
summary: Players roll for small uncertain tasks and try them without checking or fixing.
goal: Use it to help players practice tolerating small uncertainty together.
body_md: Create a die of mild tasks such as leaving a drawer open or writing without rereading. Players take turns and report how they felt. Do not use this with anyone for whom a task feels too hard. Debrief on what was surprising.

fields.label: The task I rolled
What I felt before I did it
What I felt afterward
What I noticed about uncertainty
A task I will try this week

title: Panic Sensation Experiment Plan
summary: A plan to induce a safe harmless sensation in session and notice what happens.
goal: Use it to help a client test fears about body sensations.
body_md: Pick a sensation such as spinning in a chair or breathing quickly. Ask for predictions before and results after. Stay with the client throughout. Check for medical concerns with the client before using any exercise that changes breathing.

fields.label: The sensation I will try
What I predict will happen

title: Minute by Minute Surge Replay Page
summary: A page for describing a panic wave from rise to fall, with what was done.
goal: Use it to help a client see how panic rises and passes.
body_md: Ask the client to describe a recent wave minute by minute. Mark the peak and the fade. Ask what they did and what might help next time. Do not say what the sensations mean beyond describing them.

fields.label: Where I was when it began

title: Slow Exhale and Cold Pack Pocket Card
summary: A card with paced breathing and cold-water steps for sudden surges of arousal.
goal: Use it to give a client quick skills for the body in a panic wave.
body_md: Practice a paced exhale and holding a cold pack in session. Ask the client which works best. Write steps on a card. Check for medical issues before using temperature skills.

title: Making Room for the Wave Page
summary: A page for dropping the fight with panic sensations and choosing a values action.
goal: Use it to help a client let the wave pass while doing what matters.
body_md: Explain that struggling can make the wave feel stronger. Ask the client to name the sensations and let them be there. Then pick a value-led action in the next hour. Check how they felt about it.

title: Panic Balloon Breathing Craft

title: Fear Ladder With Safety Behavior Notes
summary: A ladder of feared situations with notes on safety behaviors to drop at each step.
goal: Use it to help a client plan gradual steps and notice what they lean on.
body_md: Build the ladder with the client and list what they lean on at each step. Start with a manageable rung. The clinician and client set the pace.

title: Feared Outcome Probability Review Page
summary: A page for looking at what a client fears will happen and what has happened before.
goal: Use it to help a client compare predictions with past experience.
body_md: Ask the feared outcome and how often it has actually happened. Do not push reassurance. Plan a small test.

title: Fear Beside Values Crossroads Page
summary: A page for placing a fear beside the valued life it blocks.
goal: Use it to help a client choose steps toward what matters with fear present.
body_md: Name what the fear costs in the client's life, then link one step to a value. Keep the step small and let the client decide how big it is. Review what happened next time without judging the result.

title: Fear Fighter Badge Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a badge for each brave step toward a fear.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and celebrate small brave steps.
body_md: The child designs badges. The parent awards one for each step tried, not for results. Follow your reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

summary: A board game where players move forward by doing small brave challenges.
goal: Use it to help a group practice small steps toward fears.
body_md: Players pick challenge cards matched to their level. Rules: choose your own level, cheer for others. Debrief on what was hard.

title: Body Appreciation Letter Page
summary: A letter page for thanking the body for what it lets a client do.
goal: Use it to help a client shift attention to what the body does for them.
body_md: Focus on function, such as hugging or walking. Avoid anything about appearance changes or measuring. Let the client write in their own voice.

title: Looks Comparison Thought Check Page
summary: A page for catching comparing thoughts and answering them.
goal: Use it to help a client notice comparison and answer it kindly.
body_md: Ask where the comparing happened, such as social media. Examine the thought and plan changes to what they see. Never mention measuring the body.

summary: A page for naming what matters in life apart from appearance.
goal: Use it to help a client act on values rather than on appearance worries.
body_md: Ask what the client would do if appearance thoughts did not run the day. Choose one small action. Let them lead.

title: Mirror Kindness Sticker Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a mirror card with kind sticker messages.
goal: Use it to help a child practice kind words about themselves.
body_md: The child decorates a card with kind words about who they are. The parent reads it with them. Keep focus on character and abilities, never appearance. Follow your reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

goal: Use it to help a group practice noticing qualities beyond looks.
